questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with tingling in the lateral three fingers and loss of sensation at the base of the thumb on the dorsal hand. Which nerve is involved?
questions.explanation: Radial nerve The patient’s symptoms of tingling in the lateral digits and loss of sensation at the dorsal base of the thumb point to the superficial branch of the radial nerve. This nerve provides cutaneous sensation to the dorsum of the hand, particularly the first web space and the dorsal aspect of the lateral three-and-a-half fingers, excluding the nail beds. The ulnar nerve (Option B) supplies the medial one-and-a-half digits and is not involved here. While the median nerve (Option C) supplies the lateral three-and-a-half digits, its distribution is primarily palmar and includes only the distal dorsal phalanges (fingertips); it does not supply the dorsal root of the thumb. The Anterior Interosseous Nerve (Option D) is a purely motor branch of the median nerve and has no cutaneous sensory distribution. Therefore, the specific loss of sensation on the dorsal aspect of the thumb base confirms radial nerve involvement.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the afferent limb of the corneal reflex?
questions.explanation: Trigeminal nerve The corneal reflex is an important protective reflex of the eye that involves both a sensory (afferent) and a motor (efferent) component. The afferent limb is carried by the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), specifically its ophthalmic division (V₁). This division supplies sensory innervation to the cornea and detects tactile or noxious stimuli applied to it, transmitting the impulse to the brainstem. The efferent limb of the corneal reflex is mediated by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), which innervates the orbicularis oculi muscle, producing bilateral blinking in response to corneal stimulation.The optic nerve (Option A) is involved in visual pathways and serves as the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex, not the corneal reflex. The trochlear nerve (Option D) innervates the superior oblique muscle and has no role in corneal sensation or blinking.Therefore, the trigeminal nerve is the correct answer, as it provides the sensory input necessary to initiate the corneal reflex.

questions.stem: What is the type of cartilage present in the histology section given below?
questions.explanation: Hyaline cartilage The histology section shows a homogeneous, glassy (translucent) basophilic matrix with chondrocytes housed in lacunae, often arranged in small isogenous groups. This appearance is characteristic of hyaline cartilage, the most common cartilage type in the body, found in costal cartilages and tracheal rings. Elastic cartilage (Option B) would show a dense network of dark-staining elastic fibers within the matrix, providing flexibility to structures like the auricle. Fibrocartilage (Option D) contains heavy bundles of Type I collagen and fewer chondrocytes, often arranged in rows, and lacks a perichondrium; it is found in intervertebral discs. While articular cartilage (Option C) is a form of hyaline cartilage, it is a specific anatomical designation for cartilage covering joint surfaces; the general tissue type shown is hyaline. Therefore, based on the classic "glassy" matrix and cellular arrangement, hyaline cartilage is the correct histological diagnosis.

questions.stem: A renal biopsy section is provided in the image. Identify the type of cells indicated by the marked area in this histological specimen.
questions.explanation: Lacis cells The marked cells in the renal biopsy are Lacis cells, also known as extraglomerular mesangial cells or Goormaghtigh cells. These cells are a critical component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) and are located in the triangular space between the afferent and efferent arterioles and the macula densa. Their primary role is to facilitate signal transmission between the macula densa and the JG cells, thereby regulating renin secretion and blood pressure. Macula densa cells (Option A) are specialized tubular cells in the distal tubule that sense sodium concentration. Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells (Option B) are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole that produce renin. Podocytes (Option D) are epithelial cells covering the glomerular capillaries, forming the filtration barrier. Given the specific anatomical location between the arterioles, the marked cells are Lacis cells.

questions.stem: Identify the lymphatic structure from the histology section given below?
questions.explanation: Thymus The histology section displays a distinct lobulated architecture, which is characteristic of the thymus. Each lobule is divided into a darker, peripheral outer cortex (rich in immature T-cells) and a lighter, central inner medulla. A pathognomonic feature found in the thymic medulla is Hassall’s corpuscles, which are concentric whorls of keratinized epithelial cells. In contrast, a tonsil (Option A) would show lymphoid follicles with germinal centers and an overlying stratified squamous epithelium with crypts. A lymph node (Option B) also contains follicles but is distinguished by its subcapsular sinus and distinct paracortical region. The spleen (Option C) is characterized by red and white pulp and does not have this lobular cortex-medulla arrangement. Therefore, the lobulated appearance and medullary characteristics confirm that the structure is the thymus. 6. questions.stem: Identify the level of lymph nodes indicated in the marked region of the neck in the given anatomical image.
questions.explanation: Level II The marked lymph nodes are located along the upper part of the internal jugular vein, extending from the skull base to the hyoid bone, which corresponds to Level II (Upper Jugular Nodes). This level includes the clinically significant jugulodigastric node, which is frequently involved in malignancies of the oropharynx and nasopharynx. Regarding the distractors, Level Ia (Option B) refers to submental nodes in the midline under the chin, and Level Ib (Option C) refers to submandibular nodes lateral to them. Level IV (Option D) consists of lower jugular nodes located between the cricoid cartilage and the clavicle. The vertical position of the nodes along the superior third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle as shown in the image confirms they belong to Level II. Identifying these levels is crucial for staging and planning neck dissections in head and neck cancer patients.

questions.stem: What is the most common defect in a ventricular septal defect?

options.text: Non-development of the perimembranous part of the septum

questions.explanation: Membranous defect The most common type of ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the membranous (or perimembranous) defect, accounting for approximately 80% of all cases. These defects occur in the membranous part of the interventricular septum, located below the crista supraventricularis. Muscular (trabecular) defects (Option A) are also common, particularly in infants, and may present as multiple defects known as "Swiss cheese" VSDs; they have a high rate of spontaneous closure. Inlet defects (Option C) represent about 8% of all VSDs and are frequently associated with Trisomy 21. Outlet or infundibular defects (Option D) are located below the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) within the outlet septum of the right ventricle. VSDs generally result from the incomplete development or fusion of various septal components during embryonic cardiac formation. While muscular defects are prevalent, the membranous type remains the most frequently encountered in clinical practice and carries a high potential for spontaneous closure.

questions.stem: The afferent limb of the corneal (wisp) reflex is carried by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), specifically via the nasociliary nerve.
questions.explanation: Trigeminal Nerve The corneal reflex (blink reflex) is a protective mechanism that triggers bilateral eyelid closure when the cornea is stimulated. The Trigeminal nerve (CN V), specifically the ophthalmic division (V1), is responsible for the afferent limb of this reflex. Sensory fibers from the cornea travel via the nasociliary branch of V1 to the trigeminal sensory nucleus in the brainstem. The Facial nerve (CN VII) (Option A) mediates the efferent limb, sending motor signals to the orbicularis oculi muscle to contract and close the eye. The Oculomotor nerve (CN III) (Option C) controls eyelid elevation and most extraocular muscles but is not part of this reflex pathway. The Abducens nerve (CN VI) (Option D) is responsible for lateral eye movement and is unrelated to the blink response. Clinically, testing this reflex is essential for assessing brainstem integrity and the function of cranial nerves V and VII.

questions.stem: Identify the structure marked in the image given below (arrow pointing to a layer between the tonsil and superior constrictor muscle).
questions.explanation: Pharyngobasilar fascia The structure marked in the image, located between the superior constrictor muscle and the tonsil, is the pharyngobasilar fascia. This fascia is a tough, fibrous layer that lines the inner surface of the pharyngeal muscles and attaches the pharynx to the base of the skull. The buccopharyngeal fascia (Option A) is located on the outer surface of the superior constrictor muscle. The capsule (Option B) refers to the specialized fibrous layer that immediately surrounds the palatine tonsil. The superior constrictor muscle (Option C) forms the main muscular portion of the tonsillar bed but is located deep to the pharyngobasilar fascia in this cross-section. Other important structures in the tonsillar bed include the facial artery (tonsillar branch) and the paratonsillar vein, which are significant during surgery. Understanding these anatomical layers is critical for safe surgical dissection during tonsillectomy.

questions.stem: Identify the marked area in the image given (arrow pointing to the space between the uterus and rectum).
questions.explanation: Pouch of Douglas The marked area in the pelvic image is the Pouch of Douglas, also known as the rectouterine pouch. It is the lowest and most dependent point of the peritoneal cavity in a standing female, located between the posterior wall of the uterus and the anterior wall of the rectum. Morrison’s pouch (Option A) is the hepatorenal space in the upper abdomen, which is the most dependent part when lying supine. The vesicouterine pouch (Option B) is located anteriorly between the uterus and the bladder, situated higher in the pelvic cavity. The ischioanal fossa (Option D) is a fat-filled space located on either side of the anal canal, below the pelvic diaphragm. The Pouch of Douglas is a clinically significant site for the accumulation of fluids like blood, pus, or ascites. 12. A histological section is shown, with an arrow indicating a large, flask-shaped cell located in the middle layer. Identify the cell marked by the arrow. NODIA

questions.stem: What stage of embryonic development is shown in the following image?
questions.explanation: Blastocyst The image illustrates a blastocyst, which typically forms around Day 5 of embryonic development. It is identifiable by its unique structure: an outer layer of cells called the trophoblast (which forms the placenta), a cluster of cells inside called the inner cell mass (which becomes the embryo), and a central fluid-filled cavity known as the blastocoel. A morula (Option A) is an earlier stage (Day 4) consisting of a solid ball of 16–32 cells without a cavity. An ovum (Option B) is the single-cell unfertilized egg. A gastrula (Option D) is a later stage (Day 14+) where the embryo differentiates into three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm). Implantation into the endometrial wall begins as the blastocyst stage is reached. Understanding these distinct morphological stages is fundamental for studying embryogenesis.

questions.stem: An image is shown with a structure marked “X,” representing a layer on the outer surface of the pharynx. Identify the structure indicated
questions.explanation: Buccopharyngeal fascia The marked structure is the buccopharyngeal fascia, a thin layer of the deep cervical fascia that covers the external surface of the pharyngeal constrictor muscles. It extends from the skull base to the esophagus and forms the anterior boundary of the retropharyngeal space. Prevertebral fascia (Option B) covers the vertebral column and prevertebral muscles, forming the posterior boundary of the same space. Pharyngobasilar fascia (Option C) is located on the inner surface of the pharyngeal muscles, attaching the pharynx to the skull. Alar fascia (Option D) is a separate component located between the buccopharyngeal and prevertebral layers. Understanding these facial planes is clinically vital for localizing deep neck infections and abscesses.

questions.stem: Identify the type of cartilage?
questions.explanation: Hyaline cartilage The histological image shows hyaline cartilage, identifiable by its glassy, homogeneous extracellular matrix (ECM) rich in Type II collagen. Chondrocytes are seen residing within spaces called lacunae. Hyaline cartilage is the most common type and is found in articular surfaces, the respiratory tract, and the fetal skeleton. Elastic cartilage (Option B) contains dense networks of elastic fibers, making it more flexible, and is found in the outer ear and epiglottis. Fibrocartilage (Option C) contains thick bundles of Type I collagen, providing high tensile strength for intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis. Calcified cartilage (Option D) is hyaline cartilage that has accumulated calcium salts, often seen during bone development or aging. The lack of visible fibers in the matrix confirms this as hyaline.

questions.stem: Identify the tarsal bone marked by the arrow in the given X-ray of the right foot.
questions.explanation: Navicular The arrow points to the navicular bone, a wedge-shaped tarsal bone situated on the medial aspect of the midfoot. It is anatomically located between the talus (proximally) and the three cuneiform bones (distally). On a dorsoplantar or oblique X-ray, its position on the medial side is highly distinctive. The cuboid bone (Option B) is located on the lateral aspect of the foot. The intermediate cuneiform (Option C) and lateral cuneiform (Option D) are located distal to the navicular and articulate with the metatarsals. Accurate identification of midfoot tarsal bones is essential for diagnosing fractures and dislocations in trauma cases. Based on the medial position between the talar head and the cuneiforms, the bone indicated is the navicular. 17. What is the embryological cause of this anomaly? questions.stem: A 46-year-old man is diagnosed with a tumor involving the left lobe of the liver, and a left-sided hemihepatectomy is planned. Which lobes of the liver are removed during this surgical procedure?
questions.explanation: 2, 3 and 4 Functional liver anatomy is based on Couinaud’s segments, which are determined by vascular supply and biliary drainage. A left hemihepatectomy involves the surgical resection of the entire functional left lobe, which consists of segments II, III, and IV . Segment I (the caudate lobe) is functionally distinct and is typically not resected in a standard hemihepatectomy unless specifically indicated (Option B). Segments V , VI, VII, and VIII (Option C) comprise the functional right lobe of the liver. Option D is incorrect because Segment V is part of the right lobe. Therefore, segments 2, 3, and 4 are the correct anatomical targets for a left hemihepatectomy.

questions.stem: Which of the following veins are involved in the formation of esophageal varices?
questions.explanation: Left gastric vein Esophageal varices result from portal hypertension, usually due to liver cirrhosis. When portal blood flow is obstructed, portosystemic anastomoses form at specific sites. At the lower end of the esophagus, the portal circulation (represented by the left gastric vein) meets the systemic circulation (represented by the esophageal veins draining into the azygos system). Increased pressure in the left gastric vein causes the submucosal esophageal veins to become dilated and tortuous, forming varices. The right gastric vein (Option B) drains the lesser curvature but is not the primary contributor to lower esophageal varices. The left gastroepiploic vein (Option C) and right gastroepiploic vein (Option D) drain the greater curvature into the splenic and superior mesenteric veins, respectively, and are not part of the esophageal portosystemic shunt. Therefore, the left gastric vein is the key portal vessel involved.

questions.stem: Injury to which part causes difficulty in dorsiflexion of the foot?
questions.explanation: B In the provided image, point B identifies the common peroneal nerve as it courses superficially around the neck of the fibula. This nerve is highly susceptible to injury at this site. It branches into the deep and superficial peroneal nerves, with the deep peroneal nerve responsible for innervating the tibialis anterior muscle. This muscle is the primary driver of dorsiflexion (lifting the foot upward). An injury at point B results in "foot drop," where the patient cannot dorsiflex the foot. The sciatic nerve (Point A) would cause much more extensive leg weakness. The tibial nerve (Point C) innervates the posterior compartment, and its injury would cause difficulty in plantarflexion (pointing the foot down). While the deep peroneal nerve (Point D) also causes foot drop, the injury at the fibular head (B) is the more classic clinical site.

questions.stem: Which structure is formed by the structure indicated by the arrow?
questions.explanation: Nucleus pulposus The arrow identifies the notochord, an embryonic midline structure derived from mesoderm that serves as the primitive axial skeleton. While it mostly disappears during development, its remnant persists as the nucleus pulposus, the gelatinous core of the adult intervertebral disc. The annulus fibrosus (Option A) is the tough outer ring of the intervertebral disc, but it originates from the sclerotome portion of the mesoderm rather than the notochord itself. The neural tube (Option C) is formed from ectoderm; although its formation is induced by signals from the notochord, it is not a direct derivative. The septum transversum (Option D) is another mesoderm-derived structure that contributes to the formation of the diaphragm and is unrelated to the notochordal pathway. Therefore, the notochord's specific adult anatomical legacy is the creation of the nucleus pulposus, which functions to absorb spinal compression.

questions.stem: A diabetic worker sustains a stab injury to the central part of his palm. Three days later, he develops swelling, severe pain, and inability to extend the middle and ring fingers. Pus collection in a palmar space is suspected. Which palmar space is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: B A central palm stab injury followed by swelling, pain, and restricted movement of the middle and ring fingers indicates an infection of the midpalmar space (labeled B). This deep anatomical compartment is bounded anteriorly by the palmar aponeurosis and posteriorly by the metacarpals. The hypothenar space (Option A) is located on the ulnar side and primarily involves the little finger. The thenar space (Option C) is situated on the radial side, typically associated with infections of the thumb and index finger. The dorsal subaponeurotic space (Option D) is located on the back of the hand rather than the palm. Because the injury was central and the symptoms affect the third and fourth digits, the midpalmar space is the specific site of pus accumulation. Hand infections in diabetic patients are particularly serious due to impaired healing and increased susceptibility to deep-space abscesses.

questions.stem: Which is the narrowest part of the adult laryngeal airway?
questions.explanation: Glottis In the adult larynx, the glottis—specifically the rima glottidis, which is the narrow opening between the true vocal cords—represents the narrowest part of the airway. This site is critical for voice production and regulating airflow. The supraglottic region (Option A), which contains the epiglottis and false cords, is wider than the glottic opening. The subglottic region (Option C) is located below the vocal cords; while it is the narrowest part of the larynx in infants and children, it is wider than the glottis in adults. The trachea (Option D) is a significantly larger tubular structure and is much wider than any part of the laryngeal apparatus. Understanding these anatomical differences is vital for intubation and airway management, as the glottis is the primary point of resistance in adults, whereas the subglottis is the limiting factor in pediatric patients. 24. The upper part of the uncinate process commonly attaches to? (A) Middle turbinate

questions.stem: The artery that is palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon is?
questions.explanation: Posterior tibial artery The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus within the tarsal tunnel. It is standardly palpated at this location—midway between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon—to assess the distal circulation of the lower limb. A useful mnemonic for the structures passing under the flexor retinaculum is "Tom Dick ANd Harry": Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery, tibial Nerve, and flexor Hallucis longus. The anterior tibial artery (Option A) runs in the anterior compartment and becomes the dorsalis pedis. The dorsalis pedis (Option C) is palpated on the top of the foot between the first and second metatarsals. The popliteal artery (Option D) is located behind the knee joint in the popliteal fossa. Thus, the posterior tibial is the only artery located in the medial ankle region specified.

questions.stem: A patient is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident with a head injury. He is conscious, but when questioned about the incident, his responses are irrelevant despite fluent speech. Which area of the brain is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: Superior temporal gyrus The patient's presentation of fluent but irrelevant speech characterizes Wernicke's aphasia, also known as receptive aphasia. This condition results from a lesion in Wernicke's area, located in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. These patients can produce speech with normal rate and rhythm, but they lack comprehension of language, leading to "word salad" answers. A lesion in the pre-central gyrus (Option A) would cause motor weakness or paralysis on the contralateral side rather than a language disorder. Damage to the inferior frontal gyrus (Option B) causes Broca's aphasia, where speech is non-fluent and effortful, though comprehension is relatively preserved. Brain stem injuries (Option D) would typically involve severe motor/sensory deficits or altered consciousness rather than an isolated fluent aphasia. Thus, the disconnect between speech production and meaningful content localizes the injury to the superior temporal gyrus.

questions.stem: Which anatomical structure is indicated at the site marked within the anatomical snuff box?.
questions.explanation: Extensor pollicis brevis The anatomical snuff box is a triangular depression on the lateral aspect of the wrist. Its lateral (anterior) boundary is formed by the tendons of the Abductor pollicis longus and the Extensor pollicis brevis. The medial (posterior) boundary is formed by the tendon of the Extensor pollicis longus. The image points to the lateral boundary, making Extensor pollicis brevis the correct identification. Adductor pollicis (Option A) is a deep muscle of the hand and not a boundary of this space. Flexor pollicis longus (Option C) is located on the volar aspect of the wrist. While the Cephalic vein (Option D) and the superficial branch of the radial nerve cross over the snuff box, they are not the tendon structure highlighted. The floor of the snuff box contains the radial artery and the scaphoid bone, making it a critical site for palpating the pulse and assessing scaphoid fractures.

questions.stem: Common carotid artery pulse is taken at the level of?
questions.explanation: Cricoid cartilage. The common carotid artery pulse is typically palpated in the neck, lateral to the larynx. Specifically, it is assessed at the level of the cricoid cartilage, which corresponds to the C6 vertebrae level. At this point, the artery can be compressed against the prominent carotid tubercle (Chassaignac's tubercle) of the C6 transverse process. The bifurcation of the common carotid into internal and external branches usually occurs higher, at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4 level), which corresponds to the laryngeal prominence (Option B). The suprasternal notch (Option C) is too low for a reliable carotid pulse, and the angle of the mandible (Option D) is the site for the facial artery or the termination of the external carotid. Clinically, the carotid pulse is the most reliable peripheral pulse to check during cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Understanding these surface landmarks is essential for rapid clinical assessment and procedures such as carotid endarterectomy or central line placement.

questions.stem: A patient presents with recurrent infections arising from the lesion depicted in the image. Based on the clinical features and appearance of this lesion, which of the following statements regarding it is correct?

options.text: Derived from ectoderm of 1st and 2nd arch
Derived from the pouch of 1st and 2nd arch
Derived from mesoderm of 1st and 2nd arch
Derived from ectoderm of 3rd and 4th arch

questions.explanation: Derived from ectoderm of 1st and 2nd arch. The clinical image depicts a preauricular sinus, a common congenital malformation. Developmentally, the external ear (pinna) is formed by the fusion of six auricular hillocks (of His) derived from the ectoderm of the first (Mandibular) and second (Hyoid) pharyngeal arches. A preauricular sinus results from the incomplete fusion of these hillocks, specifically between the first and second arches. Because it originates from the skin-forming layer, it is an ectodermal derivative lined with squamous epithelium. Pharyngeal pouches (Option B) are endodermal and give rise to structures like the Eustachian tube and tonsils. Mesodermal derivatives (Option C) include the cartilages and muscles of the arches. The third and fourth arches (Option D) contribute to the lower neck and laryngeal structures. These sinuses often remain asymptomatic unless they become infected, requiring antibiotics or surgical excision. They are frequently found anterior to the helix or the tragus.

questions.stem: The structure shown originates from which pharyngeal arch during embryological development?
questions.explanation: 1 The image displays the malleus and incus, which are two of the three middle ear ossicles. Embryologically, the malleus and incus are derived from the cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch, known as Meckel's cartilage. Specifically, the dorsal end of Meckel's cartilage ossifies to form these structures. In contrast, the stapes (except for its footplate) is derived from the cartilage of the second pharyngeal arch, known as Reichert's cartilage (Option B). The third arch (Option C) gives rise to the greater horn of the hyoid and the stylopharyngeus muscle. The fourth arch (Option D) contributes to laryngeal cartilages like the thyroid and epiglottis. Understanding ossicular development is vital for diagnosing congenital hearing loss syndromes, such as Treacher Collins, where first arch derivatives are malformed. The malleus remains attached to the tympanic membrane, while the incus acts as a bridge to the stapes, facilitating sound conduction to the inner ear. 31. Muscle inserted on lesser trochanter? NODIA

questions.stem: Mention the type of joint present at the marked region.
questions.explanation: Saddle The arrow in the X-ray identifies the first carpometacarpal (CMC) joint, which is the articulation between the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal. This joint is functionally classified as a saddle (sellar) joint. Saddle joints feature reciprocal concave-convex surfaces that allow for a wide range of motion, including flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and uniquely, opposition. Ellipsoid joints (Option A), such as the wrist (radiocarpal) joint, allow for biaxial movement but lack the axial rotation seen in saddle joints. Condylar joints (Option B), like the knee, allow primarily for flexion and extension with limited rotation. Plane joints (Option C), found between the other carpal bones, permit only limited gliding movements. The saddle configuration of the first CMC joint is what gives the human thumb its exceptional mobility and ability to grasp objects, making it a common site for osteoarthritis due to the high mechanical loads it bears during daily activities.

questions.stem: In the given image, the tendon marked by the arrow is?
questions.explanation: Flexor carpi radialis The tendon indicated in the image lies on the radial (lateral/thumb) side of the anterior wrist, which corresponds to the flexor carpi radialis (FCR). This tendon becomes prominent when the wrist is flexed, especially during a clenched fist. The flexor carpi radialis originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and inserts into the bases of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals. Functionally, it is responsible for flexion and abduction of the wrist. Due to its position, the FCR tendon is located just lateral to the palmaris longus, which lies more centrally. In the image, the marked tendon is clearly not in the midline, ruling out palmaris longus, and instead is positioned toward the radial side, confirming it as flexor carpi radialis.Why other options are incorrect: 1. Palmaris longus → Midline tendon 2. Flexor carpi ulnaris → Ulnar (medial) side 3. Flexor digitorum superficialis → Deep tendon

questions.stem: The subcostal line corresponds to which vertebrae level?
questions.explanation: L3. The subcostal line (or subcostal plane) is a transverse anatomical plane used to divide the abdomen into nine regions. It is defined as the horizontal line connecting the lowest points of the costal margins, which typically correspond to the 10th costal cartilages. This plane passes through the body of the L3 vertebra. It should not be confused with the transpyloric plane (Option B), which passes through the L1 vertebra and marks the pylorus of the stomach. The T12 level (Option A) corresponds to the origin of the celiac trunk and the esophageal hiatus. The L2 level (Option C) is the site where the spinal cord typically ends (conus medullaris) and the renal arteries originate. The subcostal plane at L3 serves as an important landmark for the third part of the duodenum and the lower borders of the kidneys. Understanding these vertebral levels is essential for accurate physical examination and the interpretation of cross-sectional abdominal imaging in clinical practice.

questions.stem: Which artery runs in close relation to the region of the skull depicted in the image?
questions.explanation: Middle meningeal artery The image identifies the Pterion, a critical anatomical landmark where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and greater wing of the sphenoid bones meet. The anterior (frontal) branch of the middle meningeal artery (MMA) runs directly deep to the Pterion on the internal surface of the skull. This area is clinically significant because the skull is thin at the Pterion, making it vulnerable to fractures from lateral head trauma. A fracture here can rupture the MMA, leading to an epidural (extradural) hematoma, which typically presents with a "lucid interval" followed by rapid neurological deterioration. The anterior cerebral artery (Option A) is located deep in the longitudinal fissure between brain hemispheres. The internal carotid (Option B) enters the skull base far more medially. The deep temporal arteries (Option D) supply the temporalis muscle on the external surface of the skull. Rapid surgical intervention via a burr hole at the Pterion is often required to evacuate an MMA-related hematoma. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: During a modified radical neck dissection, which of the following anatomical structures is not preserved?
questions.explanation: Submandibular gland. Neck dissections are performed to remove lymph nodes involved in head and neck cancers. A modified radical neck dissection (MRND) is defined by the removal of all lymph node levels (I-V) while preserving one or more of the non-lymphatic structures typically removed in a "radical" dissection. These structures include the Sternocleidomastoid muscle (Option A), the Internal jugular vein (Option B), and the Spinal accessory nerve (Option C). However, the submandibular gland (found in Level Ib) is routinely excised during MRND because it is intimately associated with the Level I lymph nodes, and its preservation would compromise the oncological thoroughness of the procedure. Preserving the spinal accessory nerve is particularly crucial to avoid "shoulder syndrome," characterized by pain and limited abduction. MRND aims to achieve a balance between effective cancer control and minimizing functional morbidity. Distinguishing between radical, modified radical, and selective neck dissections is a core requirement for surgical oncology and ENT clinical practice.

questions.stem: Identify the marked structure:
questions.explanation: Internal capsule The image provided is an axial section of the human brain, specifically at the level of the basal ganglia. The arrow points to a V-shaped white matter structure situated between the thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus (globus pallidus and putamen) laterally. This is the internal capsule, a vital pathway containing both ascending and descending tracts that connect the cerebral cortex with the brainstem and spinal cord. It consists of an anterior limb, genu, and posterior limb. The body of the fornix (Option B) is located more superiorly and medially near the midline. The globus pallidus (Option C) is a component of the lentiform nucleus located lateral to the internal capsule. The lateral ventricle (Option D) is the fluid-filled space located medially to the caudate nucleus. Understanding this neuroanatomy is crucial for localizing strokes, as the internal capsule is a frequent site for lacunar infarcts leading to significant motor and sensory deficits.

questions.stem: Identify the marked structure:
questions.explanation: Lienorenal ligament The provided cross-sectional diagram of the abdomen highlights a structure connecting the hilum of the spleen to the front of the left kidney. This is the lienorenal (or splenorenal) ligament. It is a vital anatomical landmark as it contains the splenic artery, splenic vein, and the tail of the pancreas. The gastrosplenic (splenogastric) ligament (Option A) connects the stomach to the spleen and contains the short gastric vessels. The greater omentum (Option C) is a large, apron-like fold of visceral peritoneum that hangs down from the stomach. The lesser omentum (Option D) connects the lesser curvature of the stomach and the duodenum to the liver. During splenectomy, surgeons must be extremely careful when mobilizing the lienorenal ligament to avoid damaging the tail of the pancreas, which lies within its folds. Knowledge of these peritoneal reflections is essential for understanding the spread of intra-abdominal infections and malignancies.

questions.stem: Which ganglion is located in the area indicated in the image?
questions.explanation: Otic ganglia The image indicates the infratemporal fossa, specifically the region just below the foramen ovale. The otic ganglion is a small parasympathetic ganglion located in this area, immediately below the foramen ovale and medial to the mandibular nerve. It serves as a relay station for secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland. The ciliary ganglion (Option B) is located within the orbit, posterior to the eyeball. The pterygopalatine ganglion (Option C) resides in the pterygopalatine fossa, accessible through the sphenopalatine foramen. The submandibular ganglion (Option D) is located on the hyoglossus muscle, suspended from the lingual nerve. The otic ganglion receives preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the lesser petrosal nerve (a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve). Postganglionic fibers then travel via the auriculotemporal nerve to stimulate the parotid gland. Precise knowledge of these cranial nerve ganglia and their locations is fundamental for diagnosing various autonomic dysfunctions in the head and neck region.

questions.stem: Which type of epithelium lines the trachea?
questions.explanation: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar The trachea is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, often referred to as respiratory epithelium. Although it appears layered (stratified) because cell nuclei are at different heights, every cell is actually in contact with the basement membrane, making it a "pseudo" stratified tissue. This epithelium contains goblet cells that secrete mucus to trap inhaled particles and cilia that move the mucus upward toward the pharynx (the mucociliary escalator). Simple squamous epithelium (Option A) lines the alveoli for gas exchange. Transitional epithelium (Option B) is characteristic of the urinary tract, such as the bladder, allowing for distension. Stratified squamous epithelium (Option C) is found in areas prone to abrasion, like the esophagus and skin. In chronic smokers, the tracheal epithelium may undergo metaplasia, changing to stratified squamous epithelium to survive the irritation, which unfortunately destroys the protective ciliary mechanism, leading to a persistent "smoker's cough."

questions.stem: Which muscle movements are related to the Abducens nerve?
questions.explanation: Lateral rectus The Abducens nerve (Cranial Nerve VI) is purely a motor nerve that innervates a single extraocular muscle: the lateral rectus. The primary function of the lateral rectus muscle is to abduct the eye, moving it laterally away from the midline. The medial rectus (Option B), superior rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique (Option D) are all innervated by the Oculomotor nerve (CN III). The superior oblique muscle (Option C) is innervated by the Trochlear nerve (CN IV). A classic mnemonic for eye muscle innervation is , where 6 refers to the abducens and 4 to the trochlear. Clinical paralysis of the abducens nerve results in the inability to abduct the affected eye, leading to convergent strabismus (esotropia) and horizontal diplopia (double vision) that worsens when looking toward the side of the affected muscle. This nerve has a long intracranial course, making it susceptible to damage from increased intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: Which anatomical structure is located approximately 25 cm from the central incisor?
questions.explanation: Cricopharynx According to many clinical/endoscopic sources (as in your key), the cricopharynx (upper esophageal sphincter) is located approximately 25 cm from the central incisors. It marks the junction of the pharynx and esophagus and acts as a functional sphincter preventing air entry during respiration and reflux during swallowing. It is also a key site evaluated in conditions like dysphagia and Zenker’s diverticulum.Why other options are incorrect: (B) Arch of Aorta: This produces a physiological constriction slightly lower, around 30 cm, not at 25 cm in this reference system. (C) Left principal bronchus: It crosses the esophagus at about 35 cm, causing another constriction, but is located further down. (D) Diaphragm: The esophageal hiatus is found at 40–45 cm, representing the lowest constriction near the gastroesophageal junction. 43. questions.stem: Which nerve innervates the muscle responsible for the movement shown below?
questions.explanation: Spinal accessory nerve The image depicts a person shrugging their shoulders, an action primarily performed by the trapezius muscle. The spinal accessory nerve (Cranial Nerve XI) provides motor innervation to the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid muscles. Shrugging tests the upper fibers of the trapezius. The long thoracic nerve (Option B) supplies the serratus anterior muscle; damage to this nerve leads to "winging of the scapula". The axillary nerve (Option C) supplies the deltoid and teres minor muscles. The radial nerve (Option D) innervates the triceps brachii and the extensor muscles of the forearm. Clinically, injury to the spinal accessory nerve—often occurring during neck surgeries like lymph node biopsies—leads to shoulder droop and the inability to shrug the shoulder on the affected side. Patients may also experience difficulty in rotating their head to the opposite side due to involvement of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Precise anatomical knowledge of this nerve is essential for both neurologists and surgeons.

questions.stem: Identify the muscle that is defective in the given image.
questions.explanation: Gluteus medius and Gluteus minimus The image illustrates the Trendelenburg sign, where the pelvis drops toward the unsupported side during the swing phase of gait. This indicates a weakness or paralysis of the hip abductors on the stance leg side, specifically the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus. These muscles are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. Normally, they contract on the weight-bearing side to keep the pelvis level. The gluteus maximus (Option B) is the primary extensor of the hip. The piriformis (Option C) and obturator internus (Option D) are lateral rotators of the hip. A positive Trendelenburg sign can be caused by superior gluteal nerve injury, hip dislocation, or fractures of the greater trochanter. Patients often compensate for this weakness by leaning their trunk toward the affected stance leg, a movement known as a Trendelenburg gait or compensated gluteal lurch. This is a fundamental clinical sign in orthopedics and neurology for assessing hip stability.

questions.stem: What type of joint exists between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone?
questions.explanation: Synchondrosis The joint between the epiphysis and the diaphysis of a growing long bone is the epiphyseal plate (growth plate), which is a type of synchondrosis. This is a primary cartilaginous joint where the bones are joined by hyaline cartilage. These joints are typically temporary and allow for longitudinal bone growth. A symphysis (Option A) is a secondary cartilaginous joint where bones are joined by fibrocartilage, such as the pubic symphysis or intervertebral discs. A synostosis (Option C) occurs when a joint completely ossifies and becomes bone, which is what happens to the epiphyseal plate once growth is complete. A syndesmosis (Option D) is a fibrous joint where bones are joined by an interosseous ligament, like the inferior tibiofibular joint. Understanding the nature of the epiphyseal plate is critical in pediatric orthopedics, particularly when managing Salter-Harris fractures, which involve injuries through this cartilage layer and can potentially lead to stunted or asymmetric limb growth if not treated correctly.

questions.stem: A patient has a cavernous sinus infection affecting the nerve located medially within the sinus. To assess involvement of the abducens nerve, in which direction should you ask the patient to move their eye?
questions.explanation: Lateral The cavernous sinus contains several cranial nerves (III, IV , , , and VI). The abducens nerve (CN VI) is unique because it travels through the center of the sinus, medially placed near the internal carotid artery, while the others are in the lateral wall. As established previously, the abducens nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which is responsible for abducting the eye. Therefore, to test its function and confirm involvement, the clinician must ask the patient to look laterally (away from the midline). Looking superiorly (Option A), inferiorly (Option B), and medially (Option C) primarily tests the muscles innervated by the oculomotor nerve (CN III). In cavernous sinus thrombosis, the abducens nerve is often the first nerve affected due to its central location. Patients will present with an inability to move the eye outward and will experience double vision when trying to do so. This clinical correlation is a classic "must-know" for medical examinations.

questions.stem: During a laryngeal surgical procedure, a patient develops loss of sensation above the vocal cords. Which nerve primarily supplies sensory innervation to this area?
questions.explanation: Superior laryngeal nerve The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is the primary structure providing sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa situated above the level of the vocal folds (vocal cords). This nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane alongside the superior laryngeal artery to supply the vestibule of the larynx. In contrast, the recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option B) is responsible for sensory innervation below the level of the vocal cords and motor supply to all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. The glossopharyngeal nerve (Option C) provides sensory supply to the oropharynx and the posterior third of the tongue, but not the internal larynx. The external laryngeal nerve (Option D) is a purely motor nerve that innervates the cricothyroid muscle. Injury to the internal laryngeal nerve typically results in a loss of the protective cough reflex, significantly increasing the risk of aspiration. Therefore, the specific anatomical boundary mentioned—above the vocal cords—definitively identifies the superior laryngeal nerve as the responsible sensory mediator. 49. questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient presents with gait instability, particularly noticeable when standing on one leg. On examination, standing on the left leg causes the right side of the pelvis to drop. Paralysis of which muscle group is responsible for this finding?

options.text: Right gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Left gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Right gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus

questions.explanation: Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus The physical exam finding described is a positive Trendelenburg sign. In this case, the drooping of the right pelvis when standing on the left leg indicates that the hip abductors of the stance leg (left) are paralyzed or weak. These abductors are the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus, innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. Normally, these muscles contract on the weight-bearing side to prevent the pelvis from tilting toward the unsupported side. Paralysis of the right-sided muscles (Options A and C) would cause the left pelvis to sag. The gluteus maximus (Option B) is primarily an extensor of the hip rather than an abductor, and its weakness leads to a "lurching" gait but not pelvic sagging in the coronal plane. Instability while walking, or a "waddling gait," is common when these muscles are compromised. Therefore, the sag on the right side while weight-bearing on the left side definitively localizes the pathology to the left gluteus medius and minimus.

questions.stem: Describe the structural composition of the outer nose?

options.text: Upper 1/2 is bony, and lower 1/2 is cartilaginous
Upper 2/3rd is bony and the lower 1/3rd is cartilaginous

questions.explanation: Upper 1/3rd bony and lower 2/3rd cartilaginous The structural framework of the external human nose is composed of both rigid bone and flexible cartilage. The upper one-third of the nose is supported by bone, specifically the paired nasal bones and the frontal process of the maxilla. The lower two-thirds of the nose is composed of hyaline cartilage, which includes the major alar cartilages, lateral nasal cartilages, and the cartilaginous part of the nasal septum. This arrangement provides stability at the root while allowing for flexibility and airway regulation at the tip and nostrils. Option A and Option B provide incorrect proportions for these components. Understanding this specific 1:2 ratio of bone to cartilage is essential in plastic and reconstructive surgery (rhinoplasty) and in managing nasal fractures. Fractures typically involve the upper bony bridge, whereas trauma to the lower portion often results in cartilaginous deviation or septal hematoma. Consequently, the correct anatomical description characterizes the upper third as bony and the lower two-thirds as cartilaginous.

questions.stem: Identify the sinus that is labeled in the provided image.
questions.explanation: Maxillary sinus The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities within the skull bones surrounding the nasal cavity. The arrow in the provided image points to the largest paranasal sinus, located within the body of the maxilla, inferior to the orbits. This is the maxillary sinus (Antrum of Highmore). The frontal sinuses (Option A) are located superior to the orbits within the frontal bone. The ethmoid sinuses (Option C) are a complex of small air cells located between the orbits and the upper nasal cavity. The pyriform sinus (Option B) is not a paranasal sinus; it is a recess in the laryngopharynx, making it an anatomical distractor. The maxillary sinus is clinically significant as it is frequently involved in sinusitis, and its close proximity to the roots of the upper molar teeth means that dental infections can sometimes spread to the sinus. Identifying these structures on imaging or diagrams is fundamental for diagnosing common otorhinolaryngological conditions and planning surgical drainage procedures.

questions.stem: If a single zygote divides between 9 and 12 days after fertilization, what type of twins are most likely to result?
questions.explanation: Monochorionic monoamniotic The classification of monozygotic twins depends entirely on the timing of zygote cleavage. When division occurs late, specifically between 9 and 12 days after fertilization, the amnion has already formed. Consequently, the twins will share a single placenta and a single amniotic sac, resulting in monochorionic monoamniotic (MoMo) twins. Cleavage before 3 days results in dichorionic diamniotic twins (Option A). Division between 4 and 8 days leads to monochorionic diamniotic twins (Option C), which is the most common type. If division occurs even later than 13 days, incomplete cleavage results in conjoined twins (Option B). MoMo pregnancies are high-risk due to the potential for umbilical cord entanglement and twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome. Understanding this embryological timeline is vital for obstetricians to provide appropriate prenatal monitoring and risk assessment. Since the amnion forms around day 8, a split occurring on day 9-12 inevitably forces the fetuses into a shared environment within the same amniotic cavity.

questions.stem: Identify the segment marked in red color in the image given below:
questions.explanation: V The image shows the anatomical segmentation of the liver based on Couinaud’s classification. The red-colored area lies in the right lobe, specifically in the anterior-inferior portion. This region corresponds to Segment V , which is situated below the portal plane and anterior to the right hepatic vein. Segment V receives blood supply from the right branch of the portal vein and drains via the right hepatic vein, making it a part of the functional right liver.Why other options are incorrect: 1. Option (B) IVa refers to the superior part of the left medial segment, located above the portal plane and closer to the middle hepatic vein. The red region is not in the left lobe nor in a superior position. 2. Option (C) VII represents the posterior-superior segment of the right lobe, located deep and toward the back. The highlighted region is anterior and inferior, not posterior. 3. Option (D) II is part of the left lateral superior segment, positioned high and to the left of the falciform ligament, which does not match the shown location. 55. questions.stem: Identify the structure marked in the image given below.
questions.explanation: Internal Capsule The provided image is a horizontal (axial) section of the human brain at the level of the basal ganglia. The marked structure is a V-shaped band of white matter situated between the thalamus and caudate nucleus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally. This is the internal capsule, a major highway for motor and sensory fibers connecting the cerebral cortex with the brainstem and spinal cord. The external capsule (Option A) is a thinner band of white matter located lateral to the putamen. The putamen (Option C) is the large, lateral portion of the lentiform nucleus. The caudate nucleus (Option D) is the C-shaped gray matter structure located in the wall of the lateral ventricle, medial to the internal capsule's anterior limb. Strokes involving the posterior limb of the internal capsule are common and result in significant contralateral hemiparesis. Precise identification of these deep brain structures is fundamental for neurologists to localize lesions based on a patient's clinical deficits.

questions.stem: Identify the section of the intestine shown in the barium study below
questions.explanation: Jejunum The barium study image displays a characteristic "feathery" or "plume-like" mucosal pattern, which is diagnostic for the jejunum. This appearance is due to the presence of numerous, prominent circular mucosal folds called plicae circulares (valvulae conniventes). In contrast, the ileum (Option A) has fewer folds, appearing smoother on barium studies. The transverse colon (Option B) and splenic flexure (Option D) would show haustrations (sacculations), which are much larger and more widely spaced than the small intestinal folds. Barium meal follow-through is a valuable radiological tool for evaluating malabsorption syndromes or obstructions. In conditions like Celiac disease, the jejunal folds may become flattened, a process known as "jejunization" of the ileum or loss of the feathery pattern. Consequently, the high density of valvulae conniventes seen in the upper small bowel loops of the provided radiograph definitively identifies the section as the jejunum rather than the distal ileum or large intestine.

questions.stem: Identify the type of pelvis in the given image below
questions.explanation: Gynecoid pelvis The pelvis shown in the image has a rounded, wide pelvic inlet, smooth contours, and a broad subpubic angle, which are characteristic features of a gynecoid pelvis. This is the typical female pelvis and is considered most favorable for childbirth because it provides ample space for the passage of the fetal head. In a gynecoid pelvis, the sacrum is wide and curved, the ischial spines are not prominent, and the pelvic cavity is spacious and well-proportioned. These features are clearly visible in the given image, confirming that it belongs to the gynecoid type. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Android pelvis: Has a heart-shaped inlet and narrow subpubic angle, resembling a male pelvis. (C) Anthropoid pelvis: Has an oval inlet elongated in the anteroposterior direction, not round. (D) Platypelloid pelvis: Has a flat, wide inlet with reduced anteroposterior diameter, unlike the shown shape.

questions.stem: Structure passing through the foramen marked by the arrow
questions.explanation: Thoracic duct The image shows the diaphragm from its inferior aspect, with an arrow pointing to a specific opening. This opening corresponds to the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, which is located at the level of T12 vertebra. The aortic hiatus transmits three main structures: the descending aorta, the thoracic duct, and sometimes the azygos vein. Among the given options, the thoracic duct is the correct structure passing through this foramen. The thoracic duct is the main lymphatic channel of the body. It carries lymph from the lower limbs, abdomen, left side of the thorax, left upper limb, and left side of the head and neck. After passing through the aortic hiatus, it ascends in the posterior mediastinum and ultimately drains into the junction of the left internal jugular vein and left subclavian vein. The oesophagus passes through the oesophageal hiatus (T10), the inferior vena cava passes through the caval opening (T8), and the sympathetic trunk passes behind the diaphragm, not through this foramen. Hence, option C is correct. 60. Based on the image shown, which nerve is most likely to be injured if a fracture occurs at the site indicated by the arrow? Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: What is the medical term used to describe a clavicular fracture that occurs during childbirth?
questions.explanation: Cleidotomy Cleidotomy is the medical term for the intentional surgical division or fracture of one or both fetal clavicles. This rare and extreme procedure is performed during difficult deliveries, specifically in cases of severe shoulder dystocia where other maneuvers have failed, or in destructive operations for a dead fetus. By fracturing the clavicle, the shoulder girdle diameter is reduced, allowing the body to pass through the birth canal. Craniotomy (Option A) involves reducing the size of the fetal head. Symphysiotomy (Option B) is a surgical procedure to widen the maternal pelvis by dividing the pubic symphysis. The Zavanelli maneuver (Option C) involves pushing the fetal head back into the uterus to perform an emergency cesarean section. Cleidotomy is generally considered a procedure of last resort due to the potential for neonatal injury, but it can be life-saving for the mother when vaginal delivery is obstructed. Thus, the specific term for fetal clavicle fracture in this context is cleidotomy.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches the trauma patients brought to the casualty?

options.text: Penetrating injury to eustachian tube- CSF otorrhea
Penetrating injury to eye- Battle sign

questions.explanation: Gaze palsy-Mid brain lesion In clinical neurology and trauma assessment, specific physical signs are linked to localized brain injuries. A lesion in the midbrain (specifically the pretectal area or superior colliculi) characteristically results in vertical gaze palsy, a component of Parinaud's syndrome. Option A is incorrect because an extradural hemorrhage typically causes an ipsilateral dilated pupil (Hutchinson's pupil) due to uncal herniation compressing the oculomotor nerve, not a pinpoint pupil (which suggests pontine injury or opioid overdose). Option B is incorrect because CSF otorrhea results from a fracture of the petrous part of the temporal bone, not an isolated injury to the eustachian tube. Option C is incorrect as the Battle sign (ecchymosis over the mastoid) is a classic indicator of a base of skull fracture in the middle cranial fossa, not a direct eye injury. Therefore, the connection between gaze palsy and midbrain pathology is the only anatomically and clinically correct pairing provided in the list.

questions.stem: Condition below is due to lack of fusion of which prominence?

options.text: Lateral nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Lateral nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Medial nasal prominence and mandibular prominence

questions.explanation: Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence The image depicts a unilateral cleft lip, a common congenital malformation. Embryologically, the upper lip is formed by the fusion of the two medial nasal prominences (which form the philtrum) and the two maxillary prominences (which form the lateral parts of the lip). A cleft lip results from the failure of one of these maxillary prominences to fuse with the medial nasal prominence on that side. Lack of fusion between the lateral nasal and maxillary prominences (Option A) would result in an oblique facial cleft, which is much rarer. The mandibular prominences (Options B and D) fuse in the midline to form the lower lip and jaw, and are not involved in upper lip formation. Understanding these developmental milestones is essential for diagnosing craniofacial anomalies. Surgical repair (cheiloplasty) is typically performed at around 3 months of age to restore normal appearance and function, highlighting the importance of precise embryological knowledge in pediatric surgery.

questions.stem: Identify the histological slide shown below of the structure
questions.explanation: Pancreas The given histological slide shows closely packed acinar cells with dark-stained nuclei and granular cytoplasm, characteristic of the exocrine pancreas. In addition, there are lighter-staining regions scattered within the tissue, one of which is indicated by the arrow. These pale areas represent the Islets of Langerhans, the endocrine component of the pancreas. This combination of dark exocrine acini and light endocrine islets is a hallmark feature of pancreatic tissue. The acini are responsible for secreting digestive enzymes, while the islets produce hormones such as insulin and glucagon. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Lymph node: Shows lymphoid follicles and germinal centers, not acini or islets. (B) Glomerulus: Found in the kidney, characterized by a tuft of capillaries within Bowman’s capsule. (C) Spleen: Shows red pulp and white pulp, not glandular acinar arrangement.

questions.stem: Splenic artery is present in which of the structures as given in the image?
questions.explanation: 4 The splenic artery is a major branch of the coeliac trunk and follows a tortuous (curved) course along the superior border of the pancreas before reaching the spleen. In cross-sectional anatomy (CT/MRI or diagrams), it is typically identified as a wavy vessel running posterior to the stomach and along the pancreas, not just within the spleen itself. In the given image, label (4) corresponds to the region along the pancreas where the splenic artery runs. Hence, the artery is “present” in relation to this structure rather than inside the spleen. This makes option (D) correct. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Lesser omentum: Contains vessels like the hepatic artery, not the splenic artery. (B) Coeliac trunk: This is the origin of the splenic artery, not where it is primarily traced. (C) Spleen: Although supplied by the splenic artery, the vessel is identified before entering the spleen, mainly along the pancreas. 66. questions.stem: A patient with a diagnosed fracture is referred to a higher center. On examination, the forearm pulses are not palpable. Based on the X-ray of the upper arm shown, which artery is most likely to have been injured?
questions.explanation: Brachial artery The X-ray displays a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, which is a common pediatric elbow injury. In this type of fracture, the sharp edge of the proximal bone fragment is frequently displaced anteriorly, where it can easily compress or lacerate the brachial artery. This explains the loss of distal pulses in the forearm. If untreated, this vascular compromise can lead to Volkmann's ischemic contracture. The radial artery (Option A) and ulnar artery (Option B) are branches of the brachial artery that begin distal to the elbow; while they would lose their pulse, the primary site of injury is the parent vessel. The anterior interosseous artery (Option D) is a deeper branch and is not typically the cause of major pulse loss in this context. Management requires urgent orthopedic reduction and potentially vascular repair. Identifying the high risk to the brachial artery in supracondylar fractures is a classic and life-saving requirement in emergency medicine and orthopedics.

questions.stem: At what vertebrae level does the indicated structure correspond?
questions.explanation: T4-T5 intervertebral disc The image indicates the carina, which is the site of the bifurcation of the trachea into the left and right main bronchi. In a living, upright person, this anatomical landmark typically corresponds to the level of the T4-T5 intervertebral disc. This level also coincides with the sternal angle (Angle of Louis) on the anterior chest wall. It is a critical landmark in thoracic anatomy, marking the boundary between the superior and inferior mediastinum. Options A, B, and C refer to different thoracic levels. It is important to note that the level of the carina can shift slightly during deep inspiration (descending to T6). However, the standard anatomical "textbook" level for the tracheal bifurcation is the T4-T5 disc. Identifying this level is essential for correctly positioning endotracheal tubes during intubation and for interpreting chest radiographs. Consequently, the bifurcation is fixed as a primary reference point at the T4-T5 vertebral junction.

questions.stem: Identify the type of pelvis in the given image below
questions.explanation: Android The pelvis in the given image shows a heart-shaped (triangular) pelvic inlet, which is the hallmark feature of an android pelvis. The anterior segment is narrow, and the side walls appear convergent, giving the inlet a more constricted appearance. Additionally, the subpubic angle is relatively narrow, and the sacrum is more prominent and directed forward, all of which are characteristic of the android type. The android pelvis resembles the typical male pelvis and is considered less favorable for childbirth due to its reduced space and narrower outlet. These features match the structure shown in the image, confirming option (C). Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Platypelloid pelvis: Shows a flat, wide inlet (transverse > AP), not heart-shaped. (B) Anthropoid pelvis: Has an elongated oval inlet (AP > transverse), not triangular. (D) Gynecoid pelvis: Has a rounded, spacious inlet, which is not seen here. 70.
