What is the most likely diagnosis?(A) Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking Syndrome (B) Lagophthalmos (C) Myasthenia Gravis (D) 3rd CN palsy Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: When asked about her age, a woman states that she is 39 years old and explains this by saying she is married to an older man and has two children aged 15 and 18 years. Which psychiatric disorder does this presentation suggest?
questions.explanation: Circumstantial speech Circumstantial speech is a thought disorder where the patient provides excessive, unnecessary, and tedious details before eventually reaching the point or answering the original question. In this case, the woman was asked her age but detailed her marriage and children first, although she did ultimately answer "39 years old". Derailment (Option A) involves a loosening of associations where speech shifts randomly between unrelated topics without any logical connection. Flight of ideas (Option C), often seen in mania, is characterized by rapid, pressured shifting between topics, often with only superficial associations. Tangentiality (Option D) is similar to circumstantiality, but the key difference is that the patient never actually returns to answer the original question. Recognizing these patterns is essential for accurate psychiatric diagnosis and mental status examinations. Circumstantiality is frequently seen in individuals with personality disorders or organic brain syndromes.

questions.stem: A patient has a history of ocular injury caused by a flying foreign body and is later diagnosed with hemochromatosis. Which substance is most likely responsible for the abnormal deposition seen in this condition?
questions.explanation: Iron The patient’s history of a "flying foreign body injury" and subsequent diagnosis of hemochromatosis points to iron as the involved substance. Intraocular iron foreign bodies can cause a condition called siderosis, where iron undergoes electrolytic dissociation and deposits in ocular tissues. This leads to toxic degenerative changes, including a pathognomonic rusty ring in the lens capsule (the earliest sign) and pigmentary retinal dystrophy. While systemic hemochromatosis is a metabolic disorder, a metallic intraocular foreign body provides a local source of iron deposition. Aluminum (Option B) typically causes fibrosis but not the widespread toxic changes seen in siderosis. Wood (Option C) and glass (Option D) are non-metallic and often inert, though wood carries a high risk of bacterial infection (endophthalmitis). CT scanning is the investigation of choice to localize metallic foreign bodies. Removal via magnets or forceps is the standard treatment.

questions.stem: A patient with visual disturbances has a past history of cataract surgery. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) findings are shown. Which syndrome is most likely associated with these findings?
questions.explanation: Irvine-Gass Syndrome Irvine-Gass Syndrome is a specific form of cystoid macular edema (CME) that occurs as a complication following cataract surgery. The Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) finding characteristically shows intraretinal cystoid spaces and a loss of the normal foveal depression due to fluid accumulation. Posner-Schlossman Syndrome (Option A) involves recurrent episodes of high intraocular pressure and mild uveitis but is not associated with this pattern of macular edema. Central Serous Retinopathy (Option C) presents with neurosensory retinal detachment, often showing an "ink-blot" pattern on angiography, rather than the intraretinal cysts seen in CME. Elschnig Pearls (Option D) are clusters of epithelial cells on the posterior lens capsule that cause opacification, not retinal edema. Treatment for Irvine-Gass Syndrome often involves topical NSAIDs or steroids to reduce inflammation and promote fluid absorption. Most cases resolve within several months, but some require more aggressive intravitreal therapy.

questions.stem: The cover–uncover test is commonly used to assess ocular alignment disorders. Which of the following conditions cannot be detected using this test?
questions.explanation: Amblyopia Amblyopia, or "lazy eye," is a reduction in vision that occurs because the brain favors one eye over the other during early development. While it can be caused by strabismus, the cover-uncover test itself is used only to detect ocular deviations, not to diagnose amblyopia. Latent squint or heterophoria (Option A) is detected by the uncover test, as the eye moves to refixate only when the cover is removed. Manifest squint or heterotopia (Option B) is identified by the cover test, where the eye under the paddle remains still while the uncovered eye moves to take up fixation. Lateral nystagmus (Option C) refers to involuntary rhythmic eye movements; although the cover-uncover test is not the primary diagnostic tool, it can sometimes exacerbate or reveal these movements. The cover-uncover test is a fundamental part of the pediatric ophthalmic exam for identifying horizontal and vertical strabismus.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with excessive tearing (epiphora). On probing, a soft obstruction is encountered at 7 mm. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: Conjunctival Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) A child with epiphora (excessive tearing) and a "soft block" at 7 mm on probing indicates a canalicular obstruction rather than a nasolacrimal duct (NLD) blockage. For proximal obstructions in the canaliculi, the preferred treatment is Conjunctival DCR, also known as Lester Jones tube placement. This procedure bypasses the blocked canaliculi by placing a permanent drainage tube from the conjunctival sac directly into the nasal cavity. Endonasal DCR (Option A) and External DCR (Option C) are used for distal obstructions in the nasolacrimal duct where a "hard block" is felt against the lacrimal bone. Dacryocystectomy (Option D) involves the complete removal of the lacrimal sac and is usually a last-resort procedure for chronic infection or malignancy, not for restoring functional drainage. Correct diagnosis of the site of obstruction is essential for selecting the appropriate surgical approach.

questions.stem: A patient presents with crusting of the eyelids along with a sensation of fine threads or strands between the cornea and the eyelids. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic Blepharitis Chronic blepharitis is a common inflammation of the eyelid margins characterized by eyelid crusting, redness, and a "thready" or gritty sensation. This is often due to bacterial colonization (most commonly Staphylococci) or dysfunction of the oil glands at the lid margin. Yellow crusts typically form at the root of the eyelashes, and removing them may reveal small ulcers that bleed easily. Dry Eye Syndrome (Option B) causes discomfort and a foreign body sensation but does not typically feature the prominent lid margin crusting seen here. Meibomian Gland Dysfunction (Option C) contributes to dry eye and lid discomfort but refers specifically to the blockage of the oil glands. Conjunctivitis (Option D) primarily involves the conjunctival surface, presenting with significant redness and discharge rather than localized lid margin disease. Treatment focuses on lid hygiene with warm compresses and mild cleansers to remove accumulated secretions.

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 5-year-old child from a migrant worker family is brought to the emergency department with fever and a characteristic skin rash. Ophthalmic examination reveals the presence of Bitot’s spots. What is the most appropriate management in this case?

options.text: Isolate and give nutritional supply with vitamin A supplement
Give measles vaccine and vitamin A supplement
Institutional Isolation, nutritional management with vitamin A supplement

questions.explanation: Isolate and give nutritional supply with vitamin A supplement The combination of fever, a characteristic skin rash, and Bitot's spot in an unvaccinated child suggests measles complicated by Vitamin A deficiency. Isolation is the first priority to prevent the spread of the highly communicable measles virus. Nutritional support and high-dose Vitamin A supplementation are critical, as measles acutely depletes Vitamin A stores, significantly increasing the risk of blindness (xerophthalmia) and mortality. Giving the measles vaccine (Options B and D) is inappropriate because the child already has the active disease. Institutional isolation (Option C) is generally unnecessary for uncomplicated cases without general danger signs like respiratory distress. Standard management for measles includes antipyretics, fluid intake, and humidification. Vitamin A dosage depends on age, with 200,000 IU typically given on days one and two for children over one year.

questions.stem: A patient presents with proptosis that increases when bending down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Orbital Varices Orbital varices are abnormal, dilated veins within the orbit that typically present with intermittent proptosis. A characteristic diagnostic feature is that the bulging of the eye increases during maneuvers that raise venous pressure, such as bending down, coughing, or performing the Valsalva maneuver. These lesions are usually unilateral and slowly progressive. Thyroid Eye Disease (Option B) is the most common cause of proptosis but is typically bilateral and does not fluctuate rapidly with head position. Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (Option C) presents with painful proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, and systemic signs of infection rather than postural changes. Orbital Cellulitis (Option D) is an acute, painful infection of the orbit featuring redness, swelling, and fever. Diagnosis of orbital varices is aided by CT scans showing dense structures that enlarge during a Valsalva maneuver. Treatment is only needed for severe symptoms or optic nerve compression.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the normal conjunctival flora?
questions.explanation: Staph Epidermidis The normal ocular surface is colonized by a variety of microorganisms that form the commensal flora. Staphylococcus epidermidis is widely recognized as the most frequently isolated and abundant species of the normal conjunctival flora in healthy individuals. It is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus that generally maintains a symbiotic relationship with the host. While Staphylococcus aureus (Option A) can be found in a small percentage of healthy eyes, it is more commonly associated with pathogenic states like blepharitis or conjunctivitis. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option C) and Haemophilus influenzae (Option D) are not typically considered part of the normal resident flora; they are more often transient colonizers or primary pathogens responsible for acute bacterial conjunctivitis, particularly in the pediatric population. Understanding the normal flora is clinically essential because these commensals can become opportunistic pathogens following ocular surgery or trauma. Preserving this delicate microbial balance is one reason why the indiscriminate use of topical antibiotics is generally discouraged.

questions.stem: A patient has different refractive powers in each eye, with +5 D in one eye and +1 D in the other. What diagnosis does this suggest?
questions.explanation: Anisometropic amblyopia The presence of a significant difference in refractive power between the two eyes, such as +5D and +1D, is known as anisometropia. This disparity causes the brain to receive two images of different sizes or clarity, which it cannot easily fuse. Over time, the brain may suppress the image from the eye with the higher refractive error to avoid double vision, leading to anisometropic amblyopia (lazy eye). While "refractive errors" (Option A) is a broad category, it does not specifically address the difference between eyes or the resulting visual deficit. Amblyopia (Option B) is the general term for reduced vision in one eye, but "anisometropic amblyopia" is the most specific diagnosis describing the cause in this scenario. Malingering (Option D) refers to the intentional faking of visual symptoms for secondary gain and is not a medical refractive diagnosis. Early screening and correction with glasses or contact lenses, often followed by patching the stronger eye, are critical to restoring normal vision development.

questions.stem: A patient has sudden loss of vision and there is no fundus glow. There is no history of trauma, what could be the likely cause?
questions.explanation: Vitreous hemorrhage A sudden, painless loss of vision accompanied by an absent fundus glow (loss of red reflex) is a hallmark of vitreous hemorrhage. In this condition, blood fills the vitreous cavity, obstructing the path of light and preventing the visualization of the retina. Common non-traumatic causes include proliferative diabetic retinopathy and retinal vein occlusion. Acute anterior uveitis (Option B) typically presents with pain, redness, and a constricted pupil, and the fundus glow is usually preserved unless severe inflammatory debris is present. Optic neuritis (Option C) causes sudden vision loss that is often painful with eye movement, but the fundus glow remains intact as the vitreous remains clear. Acute congestive glaucoma (Option D) is characterized by severe pain, a red eye, and a hazy cornea; while the red reflex may be diminished due to corneal edema, "loss of fundus glow" is more specifically associated with vitreous opacity. B-scan ultrasonography is the investigation of choice to evaluate the posterior segment when the fundus is obscured.

questions.stem: Which disorder is characterized by the presence of a cherry-red spot on the retina?
questions.explanation: Tay-Sachs disease A cherry-red spot on the retina is a classic clinical finding observed in several metabolic storage disorders and vascular conditions. It occurs because the fovea remains transparent and reveals the underlying red choroid, while the surrounding ganglion cells are swollen and opaque due to the accumulation of storage material. Tay-Sachs disease is the most well-known lysosomal storage disorder associated with this sign, caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hexosaminidase A. Fabry's disease (Option B) is more commonly associated with cornea verticillata rather than a cherry-red spot. Gaucher's disease (Option C) typically presents with hepatosplenomegaly and bone pain; while ocular findings exist, they rarely include a classic cherry-red spot. Von Gierke's disease (Option D) is a glycogen storage disease that primarily affects the liver and kidneys, not the retina. Besides storage diseases, a cherry-red spot is also a pathognomonic finding in Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO), which is an ophthalmic emergency requiring immediate intervention to restore blood flow.

questions.stem: Which of the following do not represent the corrected refractive error?
questions.explanation: Presbyopia This question focuses on the nature of common visual impairments. Myopia (Option A), Hyperopia (Option B), and Astigmatism (Option D) are true ametropic refractive errors caused by a mismatch between the eye's axial length and its focusing power. Presbyopia, however, is not a refractive error in the traditional sense; it is an age-related loss of accommodative amplitude. It occurs because the natural lens loses its elasticity and the ciliary muscles weaken, making it difficult to focus on near objects. While it is corrected with glasses (like refractive errors), its underlying mechanism is physiological aging rather than a structural refractive mismatch. Myopia involves light focusing in front of the retina, while hyperopia involves light focusing behind it. Astigmatism occurs when the cornea or lens has an irregular curvature. Therefore, while all four impact vision, presbyopia is distinct as a progressive age-related condition of the lens's dynamic focusing ability rather than a static refractive state of the eye.

questions.stem: A young boy from a low socioeconomic background presents with hyperemia and yellowish nodules at the limbus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Phlyctenular conjunctivitis Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is an allergic hypersensitivity reaction of the conjunctiva and cornea to endogenous microbial proteins, most commonly those from Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is frequently seen in children from poor socioeconomic backgrounds who may have underlying malnutrition or subclinical tuberculosis. The characteristic clinical finding is a small, yellowish-grey nodule at the limbus (the phlycten) surrounded by a localized area of hyperemia. Bitot's spots (Option A) are dry, foamy patches on the conjunctiva associated with Vitamin A deficiency and are not usually hyperemic. Pterygium (Option B) is a wing-shaped fibrovascular growth onto the cornea, typically seen in older adults with chronic sun exposure. Pinguecula (Option C) is a common, non-progressive yellowish thickening of the bulbar conjunctiva that does not involve the limbus in the same inflammatory manner. Management of phlyctenular conjunctivitis involves topical steroids and, crucially, investigating and treating the underlying cause, such as tuberculosis or staphylococcal blepharitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is associated with the Curtain falling sign?
questions.explanation: Retinal detachment The "curtain falling" sign (or curtain-like loss of vision) is a classic symptom of retinal detachment. As the retina peels away from the underlying pigment epithelium, the patient perceives a dark shadow or "curtain" descending over their field of vision. This is often preceded by flashes of light (photopsia) and a sudden onset of "floaters". Macular degeneration (Option B) causes a gradual loss of central vision rather than a sudden peripheral "curtain". Optic atrophy (Option C) involves the death of the optic nerve fibers and typically results in a slow, progressive decline in vision and color perception. Acute anterior uveitis (Option D) presents with a painful, red eye and photophobia, but not the specific curtain-like visual field loss. Sudden painless vision loss described as a curtain that resolves quickly is known as amaurosis fugax, which is often a precursor to a stroke. However, in a persistent state, it remains a hallmark of retinal detachment, which requires urgent surgical repair.(A) Retinal detachment The "curtain falling" sign (or curtain-like loss of vision) is a classic symptom of retinal detachment. As the retina peels away from the underlying pigment epithelium, the patient perceives a dark shadow or "curtain" descending over their field of vision. This is often preceded by flashes of light (photopsia) and a sudden onset of "floaters". Macular degeneration (Option B) causes a gradual loss of central vision rather than a sudden peripheral "curtain". Optic atrophy (Option C) involves the death of the optic nerve fibers and typically results in a slow, progressive decline in vision and color perception. Acute anterior uveitis (Option D) presents with a painful, red eye and photophobia, but not the specific curtain-like visual field loss. Sudden painless vision loss described as a curtain that resolves quickly is known as amaurosis fugax, which is often a precursor to a stroke. However, in a persistent state, it remains a hallmark of retinal detachment, which requires urgent surgical repair.

questions.stem: A young patient presents with recurrent seasonal conjunctivitis marked by intense itching and excessive watering of the eyes. Given that this is an immediate hypersensitivity reaction, which cell type primarily mediates these symptoms?
questions.explanation: Mast cells The clinical presentation of seasonal conjunctivitis, characterized by recurring intense itching and tearing, is a classic Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Mast cells are the primary mediators in this immediate allergic response. When a sensitized individual is exposed to seasonal allergens like pollen, IgE antibodies already bound to the surface of mast cells trigger degranulation. This release of pre-formed inflammatory mediators, most notably histamine, causes the characteristic symptoms of redness, itching, and chemosis. While eosinophils (Option A) are often recruited later in the allergic cascade and contribute to chronic inflammation, they are not the primary cells responsible for the immediate, acute symptoms. Neutrophils (Option C) are typically associated with acute bacterial infections and are not central to the allergic pathway. Lymphocytes (Option D), particularly T-cells, play roles in delayed hypersensitivity but are not the primary drivers of the rapid, IgE-mediated symptoms seen in seasonal allergic conjunctivitis. Therefore, mast cell stabilization and histamine blocking are key therapeutic strategies for these patients. 59. A patient presents with reduced visual acuity after cataract surgery and is found to have posterior capsular opacification on examination. Which type of laser is used for its treatment? (A) Femto laser (B) Nd YAG laser (C) Argon fluoride (D) Argon NODIA

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient presents with difficulty responding to bright light. On examination, the pupillary light reflex is absent, while the near (accommodation) reflex is intact. Where is the lesion most likely located?
questions.explanation: Pretectal area of the midbrain The absence of the light reflex with the preservation of the near reflex is known as light-near dissociation. This phenomenon occurs when a lesion interrupts the pathway from the optic tract to the Edinger–Westphal nucleus but spares the fibers coming from the cortex for accommodation. This lesion is classically located in the pretectal area of the midbrain. Common causes include neurosyphilis (Argyll Robertson pupil) and Parinaud’s syndrome. Optic nerve lesions (Option A) cause an afferent defect, abolishing both light and near reflexes. Oculomotor nerve lesions (Option B) abolish reflexes and cause ptosis. The Edinger–Westphal nucleus (Option C) is the motor output for both reflexes; damage there would abolish both. Thus, the midbrain pretectal area is the only site where these reflexes can be dissociated.

questions.stem: A girl develops eye pain after returning from a picnic and reports poor hygiene while handling her contact lenses. What is the most likely cause of her condition?
questions.explanation: Acanthamoeba Improper contact lens hygiene, particularly combined with exposure to contaminated water (picnic/outdoor setting), is a primary risk factor for Acanthamoeba keratitis. This free-living protozoan can invade the cornea, causing severe pain out of proportion to clinical signs, redness, and photophobia. A classic advanced sign is a ring-shaped stromal infiltrate. Plasmodium (Option B) causes malaria and does not affect the eye in this manner. While Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option C) is a common bacterial cause of contact lens keratitis, the clinical context of outdoor water exposure often points toward protozoal causes in exams. Herpes simplex (Option D) causes dendritic ulcers and is not specifically linked to contact lens hygiene. Therefore, Acanthamoeba is the most likely cause.

questions.stem: The following light reflex is seen in a patient. How much is the deviation?
questions.explanation: 45 PD The image demonstrates the Hirschberg test, used to estimate the degree of ocular deviation. According to this test, each 1 mm of displacement of the corneal light reflex from the center corresponds to approximately 15 prism diopters (PD) of deviation. When the reflex is located at the corneal periphery (limbus), it indicates a deviation of roughly 45 PD. A 30 PD deviation (Option A) would be seen if the reflex was midway between the center and the limbus. 90 PD (Option C) represents a massive deviation where the reflex falls on the sclera. Degree (Option D) is not the standard clinical unit for this test, which uses prism diopters. Thus, the limbal position of the reflex confirms a 45 PD deviation.

questions.stem: A patient presents since birth with ptosis and a right eye positioned in a “down and out” posture. Which cranial nerve palsy is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: 3rd nerve palsy The "down and out" eye position is the classic sign of an oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy. CN III supplies the superior, inferior, and medial recti, as well as the inferior oblique. When these are paralyzed, the lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) act unopposed, pulling the eye outward and downward. The accompanying ptosis results from paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris, also supplied by CN III. 4th nerve palsy (Option A) causes vertical diplopia and an "up and in" eye position. 6th nerve palsy (Option C) results in an "inward" deviation (esotropia) due to medial rectus action. 7th nerve palsy (Option D) affects facial expression and eye closure but not eye position. Thus, the "down and out" triad with ptosis confirms CN III involvement.

questions.stem: A posterior staphyloma was observed on indirect ophthalmoscopy. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: High myopia A posterior staphyloma is an ectasia (outpouching) of the posterior sclera. It is most commonly seen in pathological or high myopia. Progressive elongation of the globe in myopia leads to mechanical stretching and thinning of the posterior pole, resulting in this structural deformity. Hypermetropia (Option B) involves a shorter axial length and is not associated with scleral ectasia. Primary open-angle glaucoma (Option C) causes optic nerve cupping but not global scleral thinning. Retinitis pigmentosa (Option D) is characterized by "bone-spicule" pigmentation and vessel attenuation, not staphylomas. Therefore, posterior staphyloma is a hallmark diagnostic feature of degenerative high axial myopia.

questions.stem: A patient presents to the outpatient department with ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. On evaluation, a diagnosis of superior orbital fissure syndrome is made. Which cranial nerves are compressed in this condition?
questions.explanation: III, IV , V1, VI Superior orbital fissure syndrome involves compression of the structures passing through the cleft between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bone. These include the oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), abducens nerve (CN VI), and the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1). Compression leads to total ophthalmoplegia (inability to move the eye) and ptosis. The maxillary nerve (V2) (Option B) is not affected because it passes through the foramen rotundum. The optic nerve (CN II) (Options C and D) is also spared because it enters the orbit through the separate optic canal. Thus, any syndrome resulting in extraocular muscle paralysis along with sensory loss in the forehead (V1) but sparing vision (CN II) and the mid-face (V2) specifically localizes to the superior orbital fissure. 30. What is the order of insertion of muscles on Annulus of Zinn? 1. Medial rectus 2. Inferior rectus 3. Lateral rectus

questions.stem: Superior rectus
questions.explanation: A, B, C, D The Annulus of Zinn (or common tendinous ring) is a circular fibrous structure at the apex of the orbit that serves as the origin for the four rectus muscles. In standard anatomical descriptions and medical board questions, the order of insertion around the ring is often listed as: 1. Medial Rectus (A) 2. Inferior Rectus (B) 3. Lateral Rectus (C) 4. Superior Rectus (D) This follows a clockwise or counter-clockwise sequence around the optic foramen. This anatomical landmark is critical because it surrounds the optic nerve and the ophthalmic artery. Additionally, several cranial nerves (III, VI, and the nasociliary branch of V) pass through the ring to enter the orbit. Options B, C, and D provide incorrect sequences of these muscles. Understanding the relationships at the orbital apex is essential for diagnosing orbital apex syndrome and planning complex orbital surgeries. The annulus acts as a structural anchor, ensuring the coordinated movement of the eye by the extraocular muscles.

questions.stem: The first line of treatment for glaucoma in adults is?
questions.explanation: PG analogues In modern ophthalmology, Prostaglandin (PG) analogues (such as latanoprost, bimatoprost, or travoprost) are considered the first-line medical treatment for primary open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension in adults. They are highly effective at lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) by increasing the uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor. Their advantages include once-daily dosing and a relatively mild systemic side-effect profile compared to other agents. Atropine (Option B) is a cycloplegic that can actually worsen angle-closure glaucoma. Acetazolamide (Option C) is a potent carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used for acute pressure spikes but is not preferred for long-term first-line therapy due to systemic side effects. Pilocarpine (Option D) is a miotic drug that was once first-line but is now rarely used due to frequent side effects like brow ache and blurred vision. Beta-blockers (like timolol) are often the second-line or alternative first-line choice. Consistently maintaining low IOP is critical to prevent progressive optic nerve damage and permanent vision loss.

questions.stem: Sudden painful loss of vision in one eye is due to the lesion at?
questions.explanation: Optic nerve Sudden, painful loss of vision in one eye is the classic clinical presentation of Optic Neuritis, an inflammatory lesion of the optic nerve. This is most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis. The pain is typically retro-orbital and is significantly worsened by eye movements. Lesions at the Optic chiasma (Option B) typically result in bitemporal hemianopia—a painless, bilateral visual field defect. Lesions of the Optic tract (Option C) or the Visual cortex (Option D) cause homonymous hemianopia affecting the field of vision in both eyes, and these are almost always painless. Other causes of sudden vision loss, like Central Retinal Artery Occlusion or Retinal Detachment, are characteristically painless. Therefore, the combination of sudden onset, lateralization to one eye, and localized pain points specifically to an optic nerve pathology. Immediate ophthalmological and neurological evaluation is required, often involving MRI of the brain and orbits to assess for demyelinating disease. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: What is the gold standard method for intraocular pressure measurement?
questions.explanation: Goldmann applanation tonometer The Goldmann applanation tonometer (GAT) is universally recognized as the gold standard method for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP). It works on the Imbert-Fick principle, measuring the force required to flatten a constant area (3.06 mm) of the cornea. It is highly accurate and is the standard against which all other tonometers are compared. Hertel's exophthalmometer (Option A) measures the degree of eyeball protrusion (proptosis) from the orbit, not pressure. A Gonioscope (Option B) is used to visualize the drainage angle of the eye. The Tonopen (Option D) is a portable handheld device that is useful for patients who cannot sit at a slit lamp, but it is less accurate than GAT. Accurate IOP measurement is fundamental for the diagnosis and management of glaucoma. GAT readings can be influenced by central corneal thickness, which must be accounted for using pachymetry. Regular GAT assessment is the cornerstone of monitoring glaucoma patients to ensure they remain at their target pressure to prevent optic nerve damage.

questions.stem: Which of the following eye signs can be appreciated in the image?
questions.explanation: Tache noire The image shows a dark brown–black horizontal band on the exposed sclera, with surrounding dryness. This is characteristic of tache noire, a postmortem change seen in eyes that remain partially open after death. It occurs due to drying of the sclera, leading to discoloration, typically appearing as two triangular patches or a horizontal band.Key feature: 1. Drying and pigmentation of exposed sclera 2. Seen in postmortem eyes, especially when eyelids are not fully closed Why other options are incorrect: (B) Kevorkian sign: Refers to retinal vessel segmentation (trucking), not visible externally (C) Corneal changes: Include opacity or clouding, not localized dark patches (D) Vitreous humour changes: Internal eye changes, not visible on external inspection The visible dark scleral band clearly indicates tache noire, a classic postmortem ocular sign.

questions.stem: Identify the given instrument:
questions.explanation: Eye speculum The image displays a Barraquer wire eye speculum, a fundamental instrument in ophthalmology. It is used to retract and hold the eyelids open during surgical procedures like cataract extraction or corneal repair. Its lightweight, spring-wire design allows it to maintain lid retraction without placing excessive pressure on the globe itself. A universal retractor (Option A) is a generic term for several hand-held or self-retaining retractors used in general surgery. Doyen's speculum (Option B) is a large, heavy retractor used in abdominal or vaginal surgery. A mouth clamp (Option C) is used in anesthesia or oral surgery to keep the patient's jaws separated. Because the instrument's size and delicate frame are clearly designed for the periorbital area, it is identified as an eye speculum. Familiarity with such specialty instruments is a core requirement for medical licensing exams.

questions.stem: A patient presents with sudden, painful vision loss and a fixed, vertically oval pupil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute congestive glaucoma The combination of sudden severe eye pain, blurred vision, and a mid-dilated, fixed, vertically oval pupil is pathognomonic for Acute Congestive Glaucoma (Angle-closure glaucoma). The eye will often appear red (ciliary congestion) and feel "stony hard" on palpation due to critically high intraocular pressure. Macular degeneration (Option A) results in a slow, painless loss of central vision. Optic neuritis (Option B) causes painful vision loss, but the pupil will exhibit an Afferent Pupillary Defect (Marcus-Gunn pupil) rather than being fixed and oval. Acute anterior uveitis (Option D) also causes a painful red eye, but the pupil is characteristically small and irregular (miotic) due to sphincter spasm and synechiae. Acute glaucoma is a medical emergency that requires immediate pressure-lowering agents followed by laser peripheral iridotomy.

questions.stem: What could be the cause of sudden painless loss of vision?
questions.explanation: Central Serous retinopathy Central Serous Retinopathy (CSR) typically presents as a sudden, painless blurring of vision or the appearance of a dark spot (scotoma) in the center of the visual field. It is caused by the accumulation of subretinal fluid in the macula, often associated with stress. Chemical injuries (Option A) are extremely painful and cause immediate structural damage. Acute congestive glaucoma (Option B) and acute iridocyclitis (Option C) are both characterized by severe eye pain, redness, and photophobia. Other major causes of painless sudden vision loss include Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) and Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO). Since CSR involves a simple fluid shift without acute inflammation or mechanical destruction, it is the only painless option listed. Most cases of CSR resolve spontaneously, although monitoring is necessary to prevent permanent photoreceptor damage.

questions.stem: Which is the type of cataract seen following a blunt trauma?
questions.explanation: Rosette cataract A Rosette-shaped cataract is the classic finding associated with blunt (concussive) trauma to the eye. The mechanical shock causes fluid to infiltrate the lens fibers, typically following the lines of the lens sutures, which creates a characteristic flower-like or star-shaped opacity. Christmas tree cataract (Option B) is a polychromatic opacity seen in myotonic dystrophy. Snowflake cataract (Option C) is the hallmark of uncontrolled, acute juvenile diabetes mellitus. Sunflower cataract (Option D) is caused by copper deposition (chalcosis) and is classically seen in Wilson's disease. While traumatic cataracts can also appear as a "Vossius ring" (pigment deposit on the lens), the rosette pattern is the most frequently tested morphological description for trauma. Surgery is required if the opacity significantly impairs the patient's vision or if there is associated lens instability.

questions.stem: Oil drop cataract is seen in?
questions.explanation: Galactosemia An "oil-drop" cataract is a pathognomonic early sign of Galactosemia, an inborn error of metabolism. Because the body cannot process galactose, dulcitol (galactitol) accumulates in the lens. This creates an osmotic gradient that pulls fluid into the lens fibers, resulting in a central opacity that resembles a drop of oil when viewed through a slit lamp. Wilson's disease (Option B) is associated with a sunflower cataract. Gaucher's disease (Option C) and Tay-Sachs disease (Option D) are lysosomal storage disorders; Gaucher's may show pinguecula-like spots, while Tay-Sachs is famous for the "cherry-red spot" on the retina. Importantly, oil-drop cataracts are often reversible if a galactose-free diet is implemented early in infancy. Detecting this sign is critical, as it can be the first diagnostic clue to a potentially life-threatening systemic metabolic condition.

questions.stem: Which nerve defect causes lagophthalmos?
questions.explanation: 7th nerve Lagophthalmos refers to the inability to close the eyelids completely, which leads to corneal exposure and potential ulceration. This condition is primarily caused by paralysis of the orbicularis oculi muscle, which is the muscle responsible for eyelid closure. The orbicularis oculi is innervated by the 7th cranial nerve (facial nerve). Therefore, facial nerve palsy is the most common cause of lagophthalmos. The 6th nerve (Option B) innervates the lateral rectus muscle, and its palsy results in medial strabismus. The 4th nerve (Option C) supplies the superior oblique muscle, and its defect causes vertical diplopia. The 5th nerve (Option D) provides sensory innervation to the face and motor innervation to the muscles of mastication, but it does not control eyelid closure. Clinical management of lagophthalmos focuses on ocular surface protection using lubricants, moisture chambers, or surgical procedures like tarsorrhaphy to prevent exposure keratopathy and permanent vision loss.

questions.stem: A patient presents with complaints of blurred vision. On ophthalmic examination, aqueous flare and keratic precipitates are noted. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Iridocyclitis The clinical findings of blurred vision, aqueous flares (protein in the anterior chamber), and keratic precipitates (KP - inflammatory cells on the corneal endothelium) are diagnostic for anterior uveitis, specifically iridocyclitis. Flare and cells are the hallmarks of active inflammation in the anterior segment. Intermediate uveitis (Option A) primarily involves the vitreous (vitritis) and pars plana. Posterior uveitis (Option B) involves the retina or choroid. While Toxoplasma (Option D) is a major cause of posterior uveitis (retinochoroiditis), "iridocyclitis" is the most direct anatomical diagnosis for the anterior chamber findings described. Clinically, these patients also present with eye pain, redness (ciliary congestion), and photophobia. If untreated, active iridocyclitis can lead to complications like posterior synechiae, secondary glaucoma, and cataracts. Management typically involves topical corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and cycloplegic agents to relieve pain and prevent synechiae. A thorough systemic workup is often necessary to identify underlying autoimmune or infectious causes.

questions.stem: Shield ulcer is seen in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Spring catarrh A shield ulcer is a specialized, serious complication seen in severe cases of Spring catarrh (also known as Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis or VKC). VKC is a chronic, bilateral, allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva, most common in young boys living in warm, dry climates. The ulcer is typically oval or transverse, located in the upper half of the cornea. It is thought to result from the mechanical rubbing of giant papillae ("cobblestones") on the upper tarsal conjunctiva against the corneal surface, combined with toxic inflammatory mediators. Phlyctenular conjunctivitis (Option B) involves small yellowish nodules at the limbus. Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (Option C) also causes corneal issues but the "shield ulcer" is specifically pathognomonic for VKC. Autoimmune conditions (Option D) can cause various peripheral corneal ulcers (like Mooren's) but not this specific type. Management of a shield ulcer is difficult, requiring intensive topical steroids, lubricants, and occasionally surgical debridement to promote healing and prevent permanent scarring.

questions.stem: Conjunctival xerosis is caused by which vitamin deficiency?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A Conjunctival xerosis (drying of the conjunctiva) is one of the earliest clinical manifestations of Vitamin A deficiency and is a component of the xerophthalmia spectrum. Vitamin A is essential for maintaining the health of the epithelial surfaces and the function of the goblet cells that produce the lubricating mucus layer of the tear film. Without it, the conjunctiva becomes dry, dull, and loses its luster. This can progress to Bitot's spots—foamy white patches on the bulbar conjunctiva. Vitamin C deficiency (Option C) causes scurvy, which results in hemorrhages but not primary xerosis. Deficiencies in Vitamins K and D (Options B and D) do not have direct primary manifestations as ocular surface drying. Severe Vitamin A deficiency eventually leads to corneal xerosis and keratomalacia (total melting of the cornea), resulting in irreversible blindness. This is a major preventable public health problem in many developing nations. Prevention involves dietary diversification and national Vitamin A supplementation programs for young children.

questions.stem: Which of the following cataracts is seen in blunt trauma?
questions.explanation: Rosette cataract A rosette cataract is the characteristic type of lens opacification that develops following blunt trauma to the eyeball. The concussion force causes the lens fibers to separate or opacify along their natural suture lines, creating a flower-shaped or "rosette" appearance, usually at the posterior capsule. This may appear immediately after injury or can be delayed. Blunt trauma can also cause a "Vossius ring" (pigment on the anterior lens). Toxic cataracts (Option B) result from exposure to certain drugs (like steroids or chlorpromazine). Metabolic cataracts (Option C) are associated with systemic diseases like diabetes ("snowflake" cataract) or galactosemia ("oil-drop"). Nuclear cataract (Option D) is a common form of age-related (senile) cataract characterized by hardening and yellowing of the lens nucleus. Recognizing the rosette pattern is critical for establishing a history of ocular trauma. Traumatic cataracts often require surgical intervention if they significantly impair vision or are associated with other injuries like lens subluxation or glaucoma.

questions.stem: Xeropthalmia is considered a public health problem if the prevalence of bitot spot is more than?
questions.explanation: 0.5% According to WHO and national guidelines, xerophthalmia (the ocular manifestations of Vitamin A deficiency) is classified as a significant public health problem in a community based on specific prevalence thresholds. For Bitot's spots (X1B stage), the threshold is a prevalence of more than 0.5% among the preschool-age child population. Other thresholds include night blindness (XN) > 1%, conjunctival xerosis (X1A) > 0.01%, and corneal xerosis/ulceration (X2/X3) > 0.01%. Options A (0.01%), B (0.05%), and D (1%) are incorrect values for the Bitot spot criteria. Reaching or exceeding these thresholds signals the need for urgent community-wide interventions, such as universal Vitamin A supplementation, fortification of food staples, and intensive health education. These prevalence surveys are vital for monitoring the effectiveness of nutrition programs and identifying high-risk geographic areas. Eradicating xerophthalmia is a primary goal in pediatric public health to prevent avoidable childhood blindness and reduce overall childhood mortality.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is brought with a lesion involving the right eye. Histopathological examination shows Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes. Based on this finding, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Retinoblastoma The presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histopathological examination is pathognomonic for Retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood. These rosettes consist of a ring of columnar tumor cells surrounding a central lumen, representing an attempt at retinal differentiation. Clinically, retinoblastoma characteristically presents in a young child (most often before age 5) with leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex or "cat's eye" reflex) and occasionally strabismus. Optic nerve glioma (Option B) is a tumor of the nerve itself, not the retina. Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option C) is the most common primary orbital malignancy in children but does not originate within the eye. Ocular melanoma (Option D) is the most common primary eye cancer in adults, not children. Early diagnosis of retinoblastoma is critical to save both the life and the vision of the child. Treatment modalities include chemotherapy, cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, and enucleation in advanced cases.

questions.stem: Identify the instrument?
questions.explanation: Lims forceps The instrument shown has fine, delicate tips with an angled (bayonet-like) design, which allows better visualization and access without obstructing the surgical field. This configuration is characteristic of Lim’s forceps, commonly used in ophthalmic surgeries, especially for handling delicate ocular tissues.The slender tips and slight angulation help surgeons work precisely under magnification, making it ideal for microsurgical procedures.Why other options are incorrect: (A) McPherson forceps : Typically have very fine, straight tips used for corneal suturing; less prominently angled (C) Artery forceps : Larger, hemostatic instrument with locking mechanism; not delicate or angled like this (D) SR holding forceps : Used to hold sutures; design differs and lacks this fine angled tip

questions.stem: A 72-year-old patient, known to have diabetes mellitus, presents with a gradual decrease in vision one month after undergoing cataract surgery. Fundoscopic examination reveals a characteristic honeycomb or flower-petal pattern in the retina. This finding is suggestive of which condition?
questions.explanation: Cystoid macular edema The "honeycomb appearance" or "flower petal pattern" observed during fluorescein angiography of the retina is the classic finding for Cystoid Macular Edema (CME). This pattern results from the accumulation of fluid in cystic spaces within the Henle's layer of the macula. CME is a common cause of vision decrease following cataract surgery (Irvine-Gass syndrome), and the risk is significantly higher in patients with Diabetes Mellitus (DM). Central serous retinopathy (Option B) involves a localized serous detachment of the neurosensory retina, usually showing a "smoke-stack" leak on angiography. Retinal detachment (Option C) is a separation of the retina from the pigment epithelium. Diabetic retinopathy (Option D) encompasses a range of findings including microaneurysms and hemorrhages, but the specific petaloid appearance refers to the resulting macular edema. Management of post-surgical CME typically involves topical NSAIDs and corticosteroids. In diabetic patients, ensuring stable blood sugar levels is also critical for resolution.

questions.stem: Which criteria is not included in the definition of severe NPDR?
questions.explanation: Looping in all quadrants The international clinical grading for Severe Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR) follows the "4-2-1 rule". A patient is classified as having severe NPDR if they meet any one of the following criteria: 1. More than 20 intraretinal hemorrhages in each of the four quadrants (Option B). 2. Definite venous beading in two or more quadrants (Option D). 3. Prominent Intra-Retinal Microvascular Abnormalities (IRMA) in one or more quadrants. Microaneurysms (Option A) are the earliest sign of NPDR and are present in all stages, but their specific count in all quadrants is not the primary diagnostic threshold for "severe" compared to the 4-2-1 rule. Venous looping (Option C) is a common vascular change in diabetes, but it is not one of the specific criteria used in the 4-2-1 rule to define the "severe" stage. Recognizing severe NPDR is critical because these patients have a very high risk of progressing to Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) within one year. Close monitoring and timely pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) can prevent severe vision loss in these high-risk individuals. 42. A patient develops endophthalmitis following cataract surgery. On examination, visual acuity is limited to hand movements. Based on this level of vision, what is the appropriate treatment? (A) Intravitreal antibiotic injections (B) Pars planar vitrectomy (C) Redo surgery NODIA

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is diagnosed with a diabetic cataract that has developed over the past three months. Which substance is responsible for the formation of this type of cataract?
questions.explanation: Sorbitol + Fructose The pathophysiology of diabetic cataracts is primarily linked to the polyol pathway. In a state of chronic hyperglycemia, the enzyme aldose reductase becomes active in the crystalline lens. This enzyme converts excess intracellular glucose into sorbitol. Because sorbitol is a sugar alcohol that does not easily diffuse out of the lens cells and is only slowly metabolized by sorbitol dehydrogenase into fructose, it accumulates significantly. This accumulation creates a high osmotic gradient, drawing water into the lens fibers, leading to swelling, hydropic degeneration, and eventually permanent lenticular opacification. While glucose (Option A) is the starting substrate and fructose (Option B) is the final product, it is the combination of the osmotic effect of sorbitol and its subsequent conversion to fructose that drives the structural damage. Lactose (Option C) is relevant to galactosemic cataracts but not diabetic ones. Therefore, the accumulation of sorbitol and fructose is the critical metabolic event leading to the rapid development of cataracts in patients with poorly controlled diabetes.

questions.stem: Which muscle serves as the yoke muscle for the right lateral rectus?
questions.explanation: Left medial rectus Yoke muscles, also known as contralateral synergists, are pairs of muscles—one in each eye—that work together to move both eyes simultaneously in the same direction (conjugate gaze). According to Hering's law of equal innervation, when a command for a version movement is sent, both muscles in the yoke pair receive equal nervous stimulation. For rightward horizontal gaze (dextroversion), the right lateral rectus must contract to abduct the right eye, while the left medial rectus must contract to adduct the left eye. Thus, the left medial rectus is the yoke muscle for the right lateral rectus. The right superior oblique (Option A) is involved in depression and intorsion. The left lateral rectus (Option C) is the yoke muscle for the right medial rectus during leftward gaze. The right medial rectus (Option D) is the antagonist to the right lateral rectus in the same eye. Understanding these pairings is essential for diagnosing paralytic strabismus and identifying which cranial nerves or muscles are dysfunctional during clinical motility testing.

questions.stem: In relation to the orbital wall, where are the canaliculi located as they open into the lacrimal sac?
questions.explanation: Medial wall The lacrimal drainage system is strategically located at the medial aspect of the orbit. Tears enter the system through the superior and inferior puncta, travel through the canaliculi, and eventually empty into the lacrimal sac. The lacrimal sac sits within the lacrimal fossa, which is formed by the lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla, both located on the medial orbital wall. The canaliculi typically join to form a common canaliculus before entering the lateral wall of the lacrimal sac, but this entire complex is situated at the medial canthus. The lateral wall (Option A) contains the lacrimal gland, which produces tears, but not the drainage sac. The superior (Option C) and inferior (Option D) walls form the roof and floor of the orbit, respectively, and do not house the primary lacrimal drainage structures. Clinically, knowledge of this medial location is vital during procedures like dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) or when managing medial canthal trauma to avoid permanent damage to the tear drainage pathway.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child is diagnosed with amblyopia affecting the right eye. To promote visual development in the weaker eye, which management option is most appropriate to recommend?

options.text: Spectacles or refraction with a near addition

questions.explanation: Occlusion Therapy Amblyopia, often called "lazy eye," is a developmental disorder where the brain fails to process inputs from one eye, favoring the other. At age three, the visual system is still plastic, making early intervention critical. Occlusion therapy, which involves patching the stronger "good" eye for several hours a day, is the gold-standard treatment. By forcing the brain to use the weaker, amblyopic eye, it stimulates the development of the corresponding visual cortex. Observation (Option A) is inappropriate as amblyopia does not resolve spontaneously and can lead to permanent vision loss. While refractive correction (Option B) is often the first step if an error exists, it is frequently insufficient on its own and must be followed by patching. Radial keratotomy (Option D) is an obsolete refractive surgery for myopia and is never used in pediatric amblyopia management. Therefore, occlusion therapy remains the most effective and widely used method to restore balanced vision in young children before the critical period of visual development ends around age seven to nine.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy shows progressive loss of coordination over six months. Examination reveals a cauliflower-like mass in the left eye, leukocoria, and absence of the red reflex. Histopathology demonstrates Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes. Which gene is implicated in this condition?
questions.explanation: Rb gene The presentation of leukocoria (white pupillary reflex), an absent red reflex, and a cauliflower-like intraocular mass in a young child is highly suggestive of retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood. The microscopic finding of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes—clusters of cuboidal or columnar cells arranged around a central lumen—is a pathognomonic histological feature of this tumor. Retinoblastoma is caused by a mutation in the RB1 tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 13q14. According to Knudson’s "two-hit" hypothesis, both alleles of the RB1 gene must be inactivated for the tumor to develop. The ATP7B gene (Option B) is associated with Wilson's disease, which causes Kayser-Fleischer rings. The rhodopsin gene (Option C) is linked to retinitis pigmentosa. The FBN1 gene (Option D) is mutated in Marfan syndrome, often causing ectopia lentis. Thus, given the classic clinical and histological findings, the RB1 gene mutation is the definitive genetic cause. Early diagnosis is vital to save the patient's life and, if possible, preserve vision and the eye.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old individual with a history of presbyopia suddenly finds they can read fine print, such as a newspaper, without using glasses. What is the most likely diagnosis explaining this change in vision?
questions.explanation: Index myopia The phenomenon where an elderly patient suddenly regains the ability to read without glasses is colloquially known as "second sight." This is most commonly caused by nuclear sclerosis, a type of age-related cataract. As the lens nucleus becomes more dense and dehydrated, its refractive index increases. This "index myopia" shifts the patient's overall refraction toward nearsightedness. For a presbyopic patient who previously required plus-powered reading glasses, this new myopic shift compensates for their loss of accommodation, allowing them to focus on near objects again without assistance. Index hypermetropia (Option B) would worsen the ability to see near objects. "Regression of presbyopia" (Option C) is a misnomer, as the physiological hardening of the lens that causes presbyopia is irreversible; the change is refractive, not accommodative. While the improved near vision is a temporary convenience, it usually signals the progression of a cataract that will eventually blur distant vision significantly. Therefore, index myopia due to nuclear cataract is the correct clinical diagnosis for this specific visual change.

questions.stem: A patient presents with pain and redness in the right eye after sustaining an injury while welding. On examination, the finding shown in the image below is noted. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: Removal by 26G needle The clinical scenario describes a classic corneal foreign body, a common occupational injury among welders and metalworkers. The accompanying image shows a metallic fragment embedded in the superficial corneal layers. The immediate management involves the removal of the foreign body to prevent infection and promote healing. This is typically performed at the slit lamp using a sterile 26-gauge needle or a specialized ophthalmic burr after applying topical anesthesia. If a "rust ring" has formed around the metallic site, as is common with iron-based fragments, it must also be carefully debrided. Steroids (Option A) are generally avoided initially as they can delay epithelial healing and mask infection. Surgical exploration (Option B) is reserved for suspected globe perforations, which are not indicated by this superficial presentation. Keratoplasty (Option C), or corneal transplant, is a radical procedure for end-stage corneal disease and is not an initial treatment for a foreign body. Following removal, a topical antibiotic ointment and sometimes a patch or bandage contact lens are prescribed. 67.
