questions.stem: A skin graft was performed on an immuno compromised patient using tissue obtained from another immuno compromised donor. Several weeks later, the recipient developed contractures along with systemic symptoms. What is the most likely underlying cause of this complication?

options.text: Rejection due to recipient T8 cells

questions.explanation: Graft-versus-host diseaseGraft-versus-host disease (GVHD) occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes recognize the recipient's tissues as foreign and mount an immune attack. This typically occurs when an immunocompromised host is unable to reject the donor cells. In the context of a graft from another immunocompromised individual, donor lymphocytes may still be present. GVHD presents with systemic features such as fever, rash, diarrhea, and liver dysfunction, along with local changes like contractures. Graft failure (Option B) is a local event resulting from poor blood supply leading to early necrosis, not systemic symptoms weeks later. Host-versus-graft rejection (Option C) requires a functioning recipient immune system, which is absent here. Delayed wound healing (Option D) is common in immunocompromised states but does not account for the systemic multi-organ involvement. Therefore, GVHD is the most probable cause.

questions.stem: A woman presents with a breast lump accompanied by skin dimpling and retraction of the nipple. Involvement of which anatomical structure is most likely responsible for the skin dimpling observed in this case?
questions.explanation: Suspensory (Cooper’s) ligamentsSkin dimpling in cases of breast carcinoma is caused by the malignant infiltration and subsequent contraction of the suspensory ligaments of Cooper. These fibrous bands extend from the deep pectoral fascia through the breast tissue to the dermis. When a tumor invades these ligaments, they shorten and pull the overlying skin inward, creating a "dimpled" or "puckered" appearance. Lactiferous ducts (Option A) are primarily responsible for nipple retraction when they are infiltrated and shortened by a central tumor. Infiltration of the pectoral fascia (Option C) results in fixation of the breast to the chest wall, rather than skin dimpling. Malignant invasion of subcutaneous fat (Option D) contributes to the palpable mass but does not create the dimpling effect. Thus, the mechanical pulling on Cooper's ligaments is the direct anatomical cause of this specific clinical finding.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old male infant has a scrotal swelling present since birth, which has now become acutely painful, erythematous, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Strangulated inguinal herniaThe infant has a congenital scrotal mass (likely an inguinal hernia) that has suddenly become painful, erythematous, and irreducible, indicating that the blood supply to the trapped tissue is compromised. This is the definition of a strangulated hernia, a surgical emergency where delayed treatment leads to bowel necrosis. Acute epididymo-orchitis (Option A) is rare in infants and would not involve an irreducible groin mass. Testicular torsion (Option B) presents with acute pain but would not have been present from birth. An incarcerated hernia (Option D) is irreducible but does not yet have vascular compromise; therefore, it lacks the severe redness and systemic tenderness seen in strangulation. Physical examination shows a tense, extremely tender mass with no cough impulse. Immediate resuscitation followed by surgical exploration is mandatory.

questions.stem: A patient undergoes split-thickness skin grafting for a burn injury of the arm. On the sixth postoperative day, he develops stiffness of the arm during physiotherapy. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Passive extension of the joint under direct visualization of the graft
Remove the graft and regraft the area

questions.explanation: Passive extension of the joint under direct visualization of the graftBy post-operative day 6, a split-thickness skin graft is in the early phase of fibrovascular ingrowth. If the patient develops stiffness during movement, the most appropriate management is passive extension under direct visualization. This allows the therapist to gently increase the range of motion while ensuring that the graft is not experiencing shearing forces that could cause displacement or partial loss. Surgical excision of contractures (Option A) is only performed on mature, months-old scars, not on a fresh graft. Continuing physiotherapy blindly (Option C) risks damaging the fragile graft if the stiffness is due to improper adhesion. Removing the graft (Option D) is unnecessary unless there is clear evidence of total graft failure, such as infection or necrosis. Thus, cautious supervised movement is the preferred rehabilitation strategy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a recommended treatment for esophageal varices?
questions.explanation: Endoscopic ligationEndoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) is the first-line treatment for both the management of acute variceal hemorrhage and secondary prophylaxis. It involves placing elastic bands around the varices to cause thrombosis and eventual obliteration. TIPS (Option B) is an effective procedure but is reserved as a salvage therapy when endoscopic and pharmacological treatments fail to control bleeding. Intravenous labetalol (Option C) is not used; instead, non-selective beta-blockers like propranolol are used for primary prophylaxis to reduce portal pressure. While prophylactic antibiotics are standard in variceal bleeding (usually ceftriaxone), oral amoxicillin (Option D) is not the standard choice and has no role in the direct control of bleeding. Thus, EVL is the definitive recommended endoscopic intervention.

questions.stem: Identify the type of ulcer?
questions.explanation: Venous ulcerThe ulcer shown is located in the gaiter area (the medial aspect of the lower leg), which is the classic site for a venous ulcer. These ulcers result from chronic venous insufficiency and are typically shallow with irregular, sloping edges. Arterial ulcers (Option A) are usually found on the toes or heels, are very painful, and have "punched-out" edges. Diabetic and Neuropathic ulcers (Options C and D) typically occur on the weight-bearing pressure points of the foot, such as the metatarsal heads or the heel, and are often painless due to associated neuropathy. The location and appearance of the lesion in the image are pathognomonic for venous disease. 213. Given below what is the correct sequence of Damage control surgery? 1. Patient selection 2. Primary exploration 3. ICU care

questions.stem: Secondary exploration
questions.explanation: 1,2,3,4Damage Control Surgery (DCS) is a specialized surgical strategy for unstable trauma patients. The sequence is: 1. Patient selection: Identifying physiologically "exhausted" patients who cannot tolerate a definitive operation. 2. Primary exploration: An abbreviated surgery to control hemorrhage and contamination. 3. ICU care: Stabilization in the ICU to correct the "lethal triad" of acidosis, hypothermia, and coagulopathy. 4. Secondary exploration: Returning to the OR for definitive repair once the patient is stable. Any other sequence, such as those in Options B, C, or D, would violate the physiological principles of DCS. Therefore, the 1-2-3-4 sequence is the only standard protocol.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate treatment for an 8 cm chylolymphatic mesenteric cyst?

options.text: Resection of the cyst along with the adjacent bowel

questions.explanation: EnucleationChylolymphatic mesenteric cysts are benign, well-encapsulated lymphatic malformations. Because they typically do not infiltrate the intestinal wall and have a blood supply independent of the bowel, complete enucleation is the preferred treatment. This allows for total removal of the cyst while preserving the adjacent intestine. Aspiration (Option A) is inadequate due to extremely high rates of recurrence and risk of infection. Resection of the adjacent bowel (Option C) is only necessary if the cyst is firmly adherent to mesenteric vessels or has an enterogenous origin. Conservative management (Option D) is avoided because these cysts can cause complications like torsion, hemorrhage, or rupture. Therefore, surgical enucleation is the definitive standard of care.

questions.stem: A patient is planned for laparoscopic surgery under general anesthesia as a day care procedure. Which of the following factors would make him unsuitable for day care surgery?

options.text: Home is 45 minutes away from the hospital
The surgical procedure is expected to last slightly over 1 hour
No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperatively
The patient has had general anesthesia in the past without complications

questions.explanation: No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperativelyThe presence of a responsible adult attendant at home for the first 24 hours is a non-negotiable safety requirement for day care (ambulatory) surgery under general anesthesia. Post-anesthesia patients may have impaired judgment and a risk of falls or adverse reactions to pain medication. Living 45 minutes away (Option A) is generally acceptable as it allows for timely return if complications arise. A 1-hour surgery (Option B) is well within the typical limits for day care procedures. A previous history of uncomplicated anesthesia (Option D) is a positive indicator of suitability rather than a contraindication. Without a caregiver to monitor the patient, they cannot be safely discharged on the day of surgery.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a history of penetrating chest trauma. On examination, marked tracheal deviation is noted. What is the immediate step in management?
questions.explanation: Needle decompression Severe tracheal deviation following penetrating chest trauma is a pathognomonic sign of a tension pneumothorax. This occurs when air trapped in the pleural space shifts the mediastinum and compresses the heart and opposite lung, leading to rapid obstructive shock. Immediate needle decompression using a large-bore cannula (typically in the 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line) is mandatory and life-saving. Waiting for a chest X-ray (Option B) or performing an E-FAST ultrasound (Option C) is dangerous because it delays critical intervention in a clinically diagnosed emergency. While 100% oxygen (Option D) is part of general stabilization, it will not relieve the mechanical pressure causing the tracheal shift and circulatory collapse. Once the pressure is relieved by a needle, a definitive intercostal chest drain (ICD) must be placed. Thus, clinical diagnosis and immediate decompression are the priorities.

questions.stem: A patient is found to have a ring-shaped lytic lesion in the bone on imaging. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Brodie's abscessA ring-shaped lytic lesion surrounded by a thick, reactive sclerotic rim is the classic radiographic appearance of a Brodie's abscess. This is a localized, subacute or chronic form of osteomyelitis, most often found in the metaphysis of long bones like the tibia. The central lytic area represents pus, while the sclerotic rim is new bone laid down in response to the infection. A simple bone cyst (Option B) appears as a lucent area but typically lacks the thick sclerotic border. An aneurysmal bone cyst (Option C) is characterized by an expansile "soap bubble" appearance and internal fluid levels, not a simple ring shape. An osteoid osteoma (Option D) involves a very small radiolucent "nidus" within a massive area of cortical sclerosis, differing from the balanced ring lesion seen here. Therefore, Brodie's abscess is the most accurate diagnosis.

questions.stem: Identify the pathology in the child.
questions.explanation: Umbilical HerniaThe image shows a soft swelling protruding directly through the navel, which is characteristic of an umbilical hernia. This condition occurs in children due to the incomplete closure of the umbilical ring through which abdominal contents can bulge. The protrusion typically becomes more apparent when the child cries or strains. Spigelian hernia (Option B) occurs laterally along the semilunar line and is very rare in children. Inguinal hernia (Option C) presents as a swelling in the groin or scrotum due to a patent processus vaginalis. Femoral hernia (Option D) appears below the inguinal ligament and is mostly seen in adult females. Most pediatric umbilical hernias close spontaneously by age 2 to 3 years and require only observation unless they persist or become symptomatic. Therefore, based on the anatomical site, umbilical hernia is the correct identification.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy presents to the outpatient department with right testicular pain following a blow from a cricket ball two hours earlier. Examination reveals severe testicular tenderness and absence of the cremasteric reflex. What should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation: USG Arterial DopplerThe clinical findings of sudden, severe testicular pain following trauma, combined with an absent cremasteric reflex, are highly suggestive of testicular torsion. While trauma is the inciting event, the clinical signs point toward vascular compromise of the spermatic cord. Current guidelines recommend an urgent USG Arterial Doppler as the first diagnostic step to assess blood flow. An absence of arterial flow confirms torsion and necessitates immediate surgery. NSAIDs (Option B) only provide symptomatic relief and would dangerously delay the diagnosis of a surgical emergency. Venous Doppler (Option C) is less reliable for confirming the arterial ischemia that defines torsion. Although surgical exploration (Option D) is the definitive treatment, the trauma history lowers the pre-test probability slightly, making Doppler the preferred initial confirmatory investigation. Timely detorsion within the 6-hour "golden period" is essential to ensure testicular salvage. PEDiatriCS

questions.stem: A child presents with Kawasaki disease with multiple small coronary artery aneurysms. Treatment is?
questions.explanation: Aspirin for 6 weeksIn patients with Kawasaki disease who develop small coronary artery aneurysms, low-dose aspirin therapy is typically continued for a duration of 6 to 8 weeks. This timeframe corresponds to the period of highest thrombotic risk during the vascular remodeling process, as these small aneurysms often regress over time. Lifelong aspirin (Option A) is generally reserved for patients with large or giant aneurysms where the risk of thrombosis remains permanently high. A 4-week course (Option B) is usually too short for cases with known coronary involvement. Dual antiplatelet therapy with clopidogrel (Option D) is reserved for more severe cases with higher risks of occlusion. Additionally, the administration of IVIG during the acute phase is crucial to reducing the overall risk of aneurysm formation. Therefore, a 6-week course of aspirin is the standard management for small aneurysms.

questions.stem: An infant is being evaluated for recurrent seizure episodes, and EEG findings reveal hypsarrhythmia. Which medication is preferred for the management of this condition?
questions.explanation: ACTHThe finding of hypsarrhythmia on an EEG is pathognomonic for infantile spasms, also known as West syndrome. This is a severe epileptic encephalopathy occurring in infants. The first-line pharmacological treatment is adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which is highly effective in stopping the spasms and improving the EEG pattern. Vigabatrin (Option B) is also an effective treatment and is considered the first-line choice specifically for cases associated with tuberous sclerosis, but ACTH remains preferred for idiopathic or other symptomatic cases. Valproate (Option C) is a broad-spectrum anticonvulsant but is less effective for this specific syndrome. Carbamazepine (Option D) is not indicated and may actually worsen the condition in infants with West syndrome. Therefore, ACTH is the gold standard for the initial management of hypsarrhythmia. 230. questions.stem: A 7-year-old child is brought to the clinic with fatigue and difficulty concentrating. The mother reports a history of eating non-food substances such as chalk and soil over the past few months. Peripheral blood smear shows microcytic, hypochromic red blood cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency anemiaThe consumption of non-food items like chalk or soil is a behavior known as pica, which is a classic clinical indicator of iron deficiency. Inadequate iron levels lead to impaired hemoglobin synthesis, which manifests on a peripheral smear as microcytic (small) and hypochromic (pale) red blood cells. This diagnosis is further supported by symptoms of fatigue and poor concentration. Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option A) results in macrocytic (large) RBCs. Thalassemia major (Option C) also causes microcytic anemia but typically presents much earlier in infancy with severe splenomegaly and distinct facial features. Lead poisoning (Option D) causes anemia but is typically characterized by basophilic stippling on the smear rather than pure hypochromia from iron loss. Thus, the pica combined with microcytic cells confirms iron deficiency anemia.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with exertional breathlessness and a history of cyanotic spells. On examination, digital clubbing is present, and a harsh systolic murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border. A chest X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tetralogy of FallotThe combination of cyanotic spells (Tet spells), clubbing, and a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border points toward Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF). The provided chest X-ray shows the pathognomonic boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot), caused by right ventricular hypertrophy and a narrow pulmonary pedicle. TAPVC (Option B) classically shows a "snowman" or "figure-of-eight" heart. Transposition of the Great Arteries (Option C) would show an "egg-on-a-string" heart and usually presents within days of birth rather than at age 5. Atrial Septal Defect (Option D) is typically acyanotic and shows increased pulmonary vascular markings on X-ray. Thus, the specific radiological sign and history of cyanotic spells confirm TOF.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant presents to the emergency department with a respiratory rate of 66 breaths per minute, accompanied by chest indrawing and nasal flaring, with no other significant clinical findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: PneumoniaUnder WHO IMNCI guidelines, for an infant aged 2–12 months, a respiratory rate of ≥50 breaths per minute qualifies as fast breathing (tachypnea). This patient, at 4 months old with a rate of 66, clearly meets the criteria for pneumonia. While chest indrawing and nasal flaring are present, the absence of "general danger signs"—such as inability to feed, lethargy, cyanosis, or convulsions—means the condition does not yet qualify as severe pneumonia (Option B). Severe asthma (Option C) is rarely diagnosed in infants this young and typically involves recurrent wheezing rather than isolated acute tachypnea. A common cold (Option D) would not present with significant respiratory distress or a respiratory rate this high. Standard treatment for non-severe pneumonia involves administering oral dispersible Amoxicillin and home-based care with a 5-day follow-up.

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant presents with jaundice characterized by elevated conjugated (direct) bilirubin, dark urine, and pale (clay-colored) stools. The baby is otherwise feeding well on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Biliary atresiaThe presentation of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, dark urine, and clay-colored (pale) stools in a 2-week-old infant is a classic hallmark of biliary atresia. Clay-colored stools occur because bile pigments cannot reach the intestine due to obstructed or absent bile ducts. Dark urine results from the renal excretion of water-soluble conjugated bilirubin. Gilbert's syndrome (Option B) and Crigler-Najjar syndrome (Option C) both cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and would not present with pale stools or dark urine. Physiological jaundice (Option D) is also unconjugated, typically peaks within the first week, and leaves stool and urine color unaffected. Biliary atresia is a progressive condition; while infants may appear healthy initially and feed well, the jaundice will worsen without surgical intervention (the Kasai procedure).

questions.stem: A child presents with recurrent sinusitis and repeated pulmonary infections, and genetic analysis reveals a mutation in the CFTR gene. Which diagnostic test is considered the gold standard for confirming this condition?
questions.explanation: Sweat chloride testThe gold standard for confirming a diagnosis of Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is the quantitative pilocarpine iontophoresis sweat chloride test. In CF patients, the chloride concentration in sweat is pathologically elevated, with levels ≥60 mMol/L being diagnostic. CF is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, leading to thick secretions that cause recurrent sinusitis and pulmonary infections. A lung biopsy (Option B) is highly invasive and not used for CF diagnosis. A chest X-ray (Option C) may show non-specific findings like hyperinflation or bronchiectasis but cannot confirm the disease. A nasal swab culture (Option D) may detect colonizing bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa but is not diagnostic of the underlying genetic defect. Pancreatic insufficiency is another hallmark present in over 85% of cases.

questions.stem: A teenage individual who was raised as a girl presents with primary amenorrhea and absence of secondary sexual characteristics. On examination, there is tall stature, small testes, and gynecomastia, with normal testosterone levels. Which genotype is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation: 47,XXYThe clinical findings of tall stature, small firm testes, and gynecomastia in a phenotypic male (who may have had ambiguous gender assignment earlier) are classic for Klinefelter syndrome. This condition is characterized by a 47,XXY genotype. Individuals with Klinefelter syndrome often experience primary testicular failure, which may result in testosterone levels ranging from low to low-normal, accompanied by elevated gonadotropins. A 45,X genotype (Option A) corresponds to Turner syndrome, which presents with short stature and a female phenotype. Genotype 46,XX (Option B) represents a normal female karyotype. The 47,XYY genotype (Option D) typically produces tall males with normal fertility who are often asymptomatic. Thus, the specific triad of eunuchoid proportions, gynecomastia, and small testes identifies the 47,XXY genotype.

questions.stem: A child presents with abdominal distension and hepatomegaly, with the liver palpable 8 cm below the costal margin and smooth on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glycogen Storage Disease (GSD)Massive, smooth hepatomegaly in a child often points to metabolic disorders like Glycogen Storage Disease (GSD). In GSD subtypes such as Von Gierke disease, the liver becomes uniformly enlarged due to the excessive accumulation of glycogen within hepatocytes. The lack of nodularity or focal masses on palpation suggests a diffuse, infiltrative process rather than a tumor. Lysosomal Storage Diseases (LSD) like Gaucher or Niemann-Pick also cause hepatomegaly but are typically accompanied by massive splenomegaly and developmental regression, which are not described here. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (Option C) is rare in children and would present as a firm, irregular, nodular liver. Autoimmune hepatitis (Option D) usually causes milder enlargement associated with jaundice and fatigue. Thus, smooth, massive hepatic enlargement in early childhood is highly characteristic of a storage-related metabolic defect like GSD. 246. A 12-year-old child presents with short stature. Assessment shows that the bone age is delayed compared to the chronological age. The child has no dysmorphic features and is otherwise healthy. What is the most likely diagnosis? (A) Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (B) Familial short stature (C) Achondroplasia NODIA

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child weighing 40 kg presents with intellectual disability. On examination, the upper segment–to–lower segment (US:LS) ratio is 1.1 : 1. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: RicketsIn a healthy 10-year-old, the normal US:LS ratio is approximately 0.9:1, reflecting the fact that the lower segment (legs) has grown longer than the upper segment. A ratio of 1.1:1 indicates a disproportionate shortening of the lower segment relative to the upper body. This is commonly seen in childhood rickets, where defective bone mineralization leads to limb deformities and stunted long-bone growth. Cretinism (Option A) and Hypothyroidism (Option D) typically cause proportionate short stature rather than a specific US:LS disparity. Achondroplasia (Option C) results in a much more extreme ratio (often ~1.5:1) present from birth. Thus, the specific finding of moderate limb shortening in a healthy 10-year-old identifies rickets as the most likely underlying cause.

questions.stem: A newborn presents with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, intrahepatic cholestasis, elevated alkaline phosphatase levels, and liver biopsy showing eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules suggestive of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. What is the most common cause of jaundice in this condition?
questions.explanation: Neonatal hepatitisNeonatal hepatitis is a primary cause of liver dysfunction in newborns, presenting with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The specific biopsy finding of eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules is highly suggestive of Alpha-1 Antitrypsin deficiency, which is a significant metabolic cause of neonatal hepatitis. Hypoplasia of the biliary tract (Option A) involves underdeveloped ducts and presents with cholestasis but is not the most common neonatal cause. A choledochal cyst (Option C) involves extrahepatic bile duct dilation and would typically be identified on imaging rather than by PAS-positive granules. Physiological jaundice (Option D) is a temporary condition that presents with unconjugated bilirubinemia, not the conjugated form seen here. Thus, the clinical constellation of cholestatic markers and specific histological inclusions confirms neonatal hepatitis. ortHoPEDiCS

questions.stem: A young adult presents with a fracture of the neck of the femur. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation: Internal fixationIn young adults, the primary goal of managing a femoral neck fracture is to preserve the patient's native hip joint. Unlike elderly patients, young adults have a robust blood supply and better bone healing potential, making anatomical reduction and internal fixation (e.g., using screws or a plate) the treatment of choice. External fixation (Option A) is typically reserved for temporary stabilization in severe polytrauma and is not a definitive treatment for this fracture. Hemiarthroplasty (Option C) replaces only the femoral head and is reserved for elderly, low-demand patients. Total hip replacement (Option D) is the gold standard for arthritic hips or active elderly patients with displaced fractures but is avoided in young adults due to the limited lifespan of prosthetic implants. Therefore, internal fixation is the most appropriate strategy to ensure long-term joint function in a young patient.

questions.stem: A man falls onto his shoulder with his head forced to the opposite side and subsequently develops the shown deformity. Which cervical nerve root values are most likely to be involved in this injury?
questions.explanation: C5 and C6A traumatic separation of the head and shoulder causes a traction injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, specifically affecting the C5 and C6 nerve roots. This results in Erb's Palsy, which presents with a characteristic "waiter's tip" posture where the arm is held limp by the side, internally rotated at the shoulder, and pronated at the forearm. C6 and C7 (Option B) involve the middle trunk and do not produce this specific classic posture. C7 and C8 (Option C) affect lower plexus functions like wrist and finger movement rather than the shoulder. C8 and T1 (Option D) involve the lower trunk, typically injured by upward arm traction, resulting in Klumpke's palsy, which presents with intrinsic hand muscle weakness and sometimes Horner's syndrome. Because the mechanism involves downward shoulder traction and affects the upper limb's proximal segments, C5 and C6 are the damaged roots.

questions.stem: A man sustains trauma to the lateral aspect of his right knee. Two days later, he develops difficulty in walking due to dragging of the toes and reports numbness over the upper lateral part of the leg and the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: Common peroneal nerveTrauma to the lateral knee, particularly around the fibular neck, often damages the common peroneal nerve because it is superficial and highly vulnerable at that site. Damage here results in "foot drop"—where the toes drag during walking—due to paralysis of the dorsiflexors. It also causes sensory loss over the lateral leg and the dorsum of the foot. The tibial nerve (Option A) controls plantarflexion and sensation on the sole; its injury would not cause foot drop or numbness on the foot's top. The deep peroneal nerve (Option C) is a branch that controls dorsiflexion, but injury to it alone would not explain the sensory loss over the lateral leg. The femoral nerve (Option D) innervates the anterior thigh and is unrelated to foot dorsiflexion. Therefore, the combined motor and sensory deficits specifically identify a common peroneal nerve injury.

questions.stem: FBN gene mutation is seen in which of the following genetic disorders?
questions.explanation: Marfan syndromeMarfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant multisystem connective tissue disorder caused by a mutation in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15q21. This gene encodes fibrillin-1, a protein essential for forming microfibrils that provide structural support to tissues. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (Option A) is typically caused by defects in collagen synthesis, such as types III or V . Homocystinuria (Option C) results from a deficiency in cystathionine beta-synthase; while it mimics the Marfanoid appearance, its genetic basis is different . von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (Option D) is caused by the VHL gene on chromosome 3p. Classic Marfan clinical features include a tall, thin build, joint laxity, and ectopia lentis (lens dislocation). Therefore, the FBN1 mutation is the definitive genetic marker for Marfan syndrome. oBS anD G ynE 253. A patient has a history of dilation and curettage (D&C). questions.stem: Oral contraceptive pill prevents all except?
questions.explanation: Cervical cancerOral contraceptive pills (OCPs) offer significant protective benefits against several malignancies but are associated with a slightly increased risk of cervical cancer, particularly with long-term use. This is likely due to hormonal influences on HPV persistence. Conversely, OCPs are well-documented to prevent epithelial ovarian cancer (Option B) by suppressing ovulation and endometrial cancer (Option C) by providing a progestin-dominant environment that counteracts estrogen's proliferative effects. Evidence also suggests a modest protective effect against colon cancer (Option D). Because the use of OCPs does not protect against cervical malignancy and may instead elevate the risk, Option A is the correct "except" choice in this profile. Regular screening remains essential for OCP users to monitor for cervical neoplasia.

questions.stem: What is the importance of the following manoeuvre?

options.text: To protect from tearing of the perineum
To pull the baby out faster
To facilitate controlled extension of the fetal head
To rotate the shoulders during delivery

questions.explanation: To protect from tearing of the perineumThe image depicts the Ritgen manoeuvre (perineal support), where one hand supports the fetal head and the other applies controlled counter-pressure through the perineum. Its primary clinical importance is to protect the perineum from sudden overstretching and tearing by regulating the speed and angle of head extension during crowning. While it does involve controlled extension (Option C), the ultimate goal of that control is the prevention of trauma. This maneuver is not intended to accelerate delivery (Option B); in fact, it is used to slow down an abrupt expulsion. Shoulder rotation (Option D) is managed by distinct techniques after the head has been delivered. Thus, the maneuver is a protective strategy to minimize maternal perineal injury and neonatal scalp trauma during the final moments of the second stage of labor.

questions.stem: Identify the procedure.
questions.explanation: Hegar's signThe image demonstrates a bimanual examination used to elicit Hegar's sign, a probable sign of pregnancy typically detected between 6–8 weeks of gestation. It is characterized by the softening of the lower uterine segment, which allows the cervix and the body of the uterus to feel like separate structures upon palpation. This softening results from hormonal changes increasing vascularity and edema. Chadwick’s sign (Option A) is the bluish discoloration of the cervix. Goodell’s sign (Option B) is the softening of the cervix itself. Piskacek’s sign (Option D) involves asymmetric enlargement of the uterus due to lateral implantation. The specific technique shown—pressing the cervix from below and the fundus from above to feel the thin, soft isthmus—is the definitive method for identifying Hegar's sign.

questions.stem: Fetal anaemia is primarily determined by Doppler assessment of which artery?
questions.explanation: Middle cerebral arteryFetal anemia is best assessed using Doppler to measure the peak systolic velocity (PSV) in the Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA). In anemic fetuses, decreased blood viscosity and increased cardiac output lead to a measurable increase in blood flow speed. An MCA-PSV > 1.5 multiples of the median (MoM) is a strong indicator of moderate-to-severe anemia. The umbilical artery (Option B) primarily assesses placental resistance and is used to monitor IUGR. The ductus venosus (Option C) evaluates fetal cardiac function and late-stage compromise. The uterine artery (Option D) measures maternal blood flow to the placenta to screen for preeclampsia risk. Because the MCA Doppler specifically reflects the fetal hemodynamic compensation for low hemoglobin, it is the primary diagnostic tool for fetal anemia.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida presents with painful vaginal bleeding during the first trimester. Ultrasonography shows a well-formed gestational sac with central embryonic echoes and visible fetal cardiac activity, indicating a viable fetus. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Threatened abortionThe clinical scenario of vaginal bleeding in the first trimester with a confirmed viable fetus (fetal cardiac motion) and an intrauterine gestational sac on ultrasound is diagnostic of a threatened abortion. In this condition, the internal cervical os remains closed, and the pregnancy has a high chance of continuing successfully with conservative management. In an inevitable abortion (Option A), the cervical os is open, and miscarriage is certain. Incomplete abortion (Option C) involves the partial expulsion of products of conception through an open os. A complete abortion (Option D) is characterized by the total expulsion of products followed by os closure. Since the ultrasound confirms a healthy, living embryo despite the bleeding, the diagnosis remains "threatened" rather than inevitable or complete.

questions.stem: A patient with a known marginal placenta presents for follow-up evaluation. Ultrasonography reveals a 4 × 4 cm placental mass extending beyond the uterus and invading the urinary bladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Placenta percretaPlacenta percreta is the most severe grade of the placenta accreta spectrum. It occurs when chorionic villi penetrate through the entire thickness of the myometrium and the uterine serosa, often invading adjacent pelvic organs such as the urinary bladder. Placenta previa (Option A) refers only to the location of the placenta near or over the internal os without invasion. Placenta accreta (Option C) involves adherence to the myometrium without penetration. Placenta increta (Option D) involves invasion deep into the myometrium but not through the serosa. Because the ultrasound explicitly identifies invasion into the bladder, the condition has progressed beyond the myometrium, confirming the diagnosis of percreta. This requires complex surgical management, often including a hysterectomy and partial cystectomy.

questions.stem: A patient develops profuse uterine bleeding following a lower segment cesarean section (LSCS). Despite administration of oxytocin, the bleeding persists. What should be the next immediate step in management?
questions.explanation: Uterine balloon tamponadeIn cases of persistent atonic postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) where first-line uterotonics like oxytocin fail, the next recommended step is mechanical intervention. Uterine balloon tamponade (e.g., using a Bakri balloon) is the preferred first-line mechanical measure. It is a minimally invasive, fertility-preserving procedure that applies hydrostatic pressure to the uterine walls to control bleeding and allow for patient stabilization. Uterine artery embolization (Option B) is an alternative for stable patients but requires interventional radiology. Internal iliac artery ligation (Option C) is a more complex surgical procedure reserved for refractory cases. Hysterectomy (Option D) is the definitive last resort for life-threatening hemorrhage after conservative measures have failed. Thus, balloon tamponade is the appropriate immediate next step.

questions.stem: Patient has variable deceleration. What does that indicate?
questions.explanation: Umbilical cord compressionVariable decelerations are defined as abrupt decreases in the fetal heart rate (FHR) that vary in timing, duration, and shape (often appearing as a "V", "U", or "W" on the tracing). These are the most common type of deceleration and are primarily caused by transient umbilical cord compression. This compression leads to a brief state of fetal hypoxia, which triggers reflex vagal stimulation and a subsequent drop in FHR. In contrast, early decelerations (Option B) are caused by fetal head compression and mirror the uterine contractions. Late decelerations (Option C) indicate uteroplacental insufficiency and start after the peak of a contraction. Maternal hypotension (Option D) typically results in prolonged decelerations or baseline bradycardia due to reduced uterine blood flow. Therefore, the specific "variable" pattern on a cardiotocograph is the clinical signature of cord compression. NODIA

questions.stem: In a case of face presentation during labor, which diameter is seen?
questions.explanation: SubmentobregmaticIn face presentation, the fetal head is in a state of complete extension, making the face the presenting part with the chin (mentum) as the denominator. The engaging diameter in a fully extended head is the submentobregmatic diameter, which measures approximately 9.5 cm. This diameter allows for a favorable vaginal delivery if the mentum is in an anterior position. Mentobregmatic (Option A) refers to a 13.5 cm diameter seen in brow presentation, which is the largest diameter and often leads to obstructed labor. Suboccipitobregmatic (Option B) is the 9.5 cm diameter associated with a well-flexed vertex presentation, which is the most common and favorable for normal delivery. Occipitofrontal (Option C) is a 11.5 cm diameter found in a deflexed vertex presentation. Consequently, the submentobregmatic diameter is the specific anatomical landmark for a face presentation.

questions.stem: During the management of shoulder dystocia during childbirth, which maneuver is typically attempted first as the initial step?
questions.explanation: McRoberts maneuver The McRoberts maneuver is the critical first-line physical intervention for managing shoulder dystocia. It involves hyperflexing the mother's thighs against her abdomen. This action flattens the sacral promontory and rotates the symphysis pubis superiorly, increasing the space available for the anterior shoulder to pass under the pelvic bone. Rotational maneuvers like the Rubin (Option C) and Woods corkscrew (Option B) are performed only if simpler measures like McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail. Delivery of the posterior arm (Option D) is an internal maneuver attempted later in the algorithm. Because of its high success rate and relative simplicity, the McRoberts maneuver is the mandated starting point in emergency shoulder dystocia protocols.

questions.stem: OCPs can be given in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: HIVOral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are safe for use in women with HIV infection. While clinicians must monitor for potential drug-drug interactions with certain antiretroviral therapies, HIV itself is not a contraindication to their use. In contrast, moderate to severe Hypertension (HTN) (Option A) is a contraindication because estrogen increases the risk of stroke and myocardial infarction. Diabetes Mellitus (DM) (Option B) with vascular complications or a duration of >20 years is a contraindication due to heightened cardiovascular risk. Hyperlipidemia (Option D) is also a contraindication as OCPs can further alter lipid profiles and increase the risk of arterial thrombosis. Therefore, among the choices provided, HIV is the only condition where OCP use is generally acceptable.

questions.stem: A woman sustains a perineal tear during childbirth. Examination shows involvement of less than 50% of the external anal sphincter. According to the classification of perineal tears, how should this injury be described?
questions.explanation: Grade 3aPerineal tears are classified by the depth of tissue involvement. A Grade 3a tear involves less than 50% of the thickness of the external anal sphincter (EAS). Grade 2 (Option A) involves only the perineal muscles but spares the anal sphincter entirely. Grade 3b (Option B) involves more than 50% of the EAS thickness. Grade 4 (Option D) is the most severe, involving the entire anal sphincter complex (both external and internal) and the anal epithelium (mucosa). Proper identification is crucial because Grade 3 and 4 tears require specialized surgical repair to prevent future fecal incontinence. Given the specific clinical finding of <50% EAS involvement, Grade 3a is the only correct classification.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. She has been reared as a female, shows no breast development, and ultrasonography reveals absence of the uterus. Karyotype analysis demonstrates a 46,XY chromosomal pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency 17α-hydroxylase deficiency is a rare form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia that prevents the production of sex steroids (androgens and estrogens). In a 46 XY individual, the lack of testosterone results in female external genitalia, but the presence of anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) means the uterus is absent. Furthermore, the lack of estrogen prevents breast development. Swyer syndrome (Option C) would feature an XY karyotype but would have a uterus present because the streak gonads fail to produce AMH. MRKH syndrome (Option B) is 46 XX with normal breasts. Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (Option A) would show normal breast development due to the peripheral conversion of testosterone to estrogen. Thus, 17-hydroxylase deficiency is the only condition matching all findings.

questions.stem: What is the co-test in cervical cancer screening?
questions.explanation: HPV and PAP smearCo-testing for cervical cancer screening involves the simultaneous performance of HPV DNA testing and a Pap smear (cytology). This dual approach is highly effective because HPV testing identifies the presence of the causative virus (high-risk strains 16 and 18), while the Pap smear detects pre-malignant cellular changes. VIA (Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid) (Options B and C) is a low-cost screening method used primarily in resource-limited settings. Colposcopy (Option D) is a diagnostic follow-up tool used to investigate abnormal screening results rather than a primary screening "co-test". In standard guidelines, co-testing with HPV and Pap smear is the gold standard for women aged 30–65.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to subcutaneous contraceptive implant?
questions.explanation: Undiagnosed genital bleedingUndiagnosed genital bleeding is an absolute contraindication (WHO Category 4) for all hormonal contraceptive methods, including subcutaneous implants. The primary concern is that the bleeding might be caused by an underlying malignancy (like cervical or endometrial cancer) that could be masked or its diagnosis delayed by hormonal use. Hypertension (Option A) and Diabetes (Option B) are not contraindications for progestin-only implants unless they are severe or accompanied by major vascular disease. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) (Option C) is a contraindication for intrauterine devices but not for subcutaneous implants, which do not interact with the pelvic organs directly. Therefore, the etiology of bleeding must be clarified before the implant can be safely used.

questions.stem: A woman with a previous cesarean section presents in labor with contractions occurring three times in ten minutes. The membranes are intact, and there are no signs of fetal distress. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Perform artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) and monitor

questions.explanation: Perform artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) and monitorIn a patient with a prior cesarean undergoing a Trial of Labor After Cesarean (TOLAC), the goal is to allow natural progress while minimizing risks. Since the patient is stable with regular contractions and no fetal distress, performing an Artificial Rupture of Membranes (ARM) is an appropriate next step to stimulate endogenous prostaglandins and enhance labor naturally. Oxytocin (Option A) should be used with extreme caution in TOLAC due to the increased risk of uterine rupture. Instrumental delivery (Option C) is only indicated during the second stage of labor, not the first. A repeat cesarean (Option D) is not currently indicated as there is no evidence of labor arrest or fetal compromise. Thus, ARM provides a safe method of labor augmentation.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with lower abdominal discomfort. An intraoperative (surgical) image is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these findings?
questions.explanation: Mature cystic teratomaThe surgical findings of a cystic ovarian tumor containing hair and sebaceous material are diagnostic of a mature cystic teratoma, also known as a dermoid cyst. These are common benign tumors that originate from all three germ layers: ectoderm (skin, hair), mesoderm (muscle, bone), and endoderm. Serous cystadenoma (Option A) is a unilocular epithelial tumor more common in older women and would not contain hair. Immature teratoma (Option B) is a malignant, solid tumor containing primitive neuroepithelium rather than mature skin appendages. Endometrioma (Option D), or a "chocolate cyst," is filled with thick, old blood resulting from endometriosis. Because the image clearly demonstrates mature structures like hair and teeth, the mature cystic teratoma is the correct identification.

questions.stem: In Pap smear cytology, which of the following is the most appropriate fixative used to preserve cellular details immediately after smearing?
questions.explanation: 95% ethanolFor a conventional Pap smear, immediate fixation is critical to stabilize cellular structures and prevent air-drying artifacts. The standard fixative used is 95% ethanol, which works by precipitating proteins and maintaining the life-like appearance of the cells for microscopic examination. Formaldehyde (Options A and D) is a cross-linking fixative most commonly used for whole tissue preservation in histology but is not the primary fixative for cytological smears. 70% ethanol (Option C) is generally used as a disinfectant rather than a cytology fixative. Cells are collected from the cervical transformation zone, smeared onto a slide, and immediately immersed in or sprayed with 95% ethanol. This ensures the precise detail of the nucleus and cytoplasm is preserved for cancer screening. NODIA

questions.stem: A woman presents with multiple small, pink- colored papules on the face, each showing central umbilication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Molluscum contagiosumThe presence of multiple small, pink, umbilicated papules (dome-shaped with a central dimple) is the classic clinical presentation of molluscum contagiosum. This is a viral infection caused by a poxvirus and is highly common in children. Herpes simplex (Option B) presents as grouped vesicles on an erythematous base rather than umbilicated papules. Human Papillomavirus (HPV) (Option C) causes warts, which are typically hyperkeratotic and rough, lacking central umbilication. Acne vulgaris (Option D) is characterized by comedones, inflammatory papules, or pustules, but not umbilicated papules. Therefore, the characteristic "dimple" or central umbilication described in the scenario is pathognomonic for molluscum contagiosum.

questions.stem: Identify the given condition and its treatment.

options.text: Staphylococcal scalded syndrome with Inj cephalexin

questions.explanation: Staphylococcal scalded syndrome with Inj cephalexinThe clinical image demonstrates widespread erythema and superficial desquamation, which is the hallmark of Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS). SSSS is caused by an exfoliative toxin produced by Staphylococcus aureus, which causes the top layer of the epidermis to detach, creating a "scalded" appearance. Treatment requires intravenous (IV) antistaphylococcal antibiotics to target the systemic bacterial cause, alongside supportive care similar to burn management. Epidermolysis bullosa (Option B) is a genetic disorder of skin fragility rather than an infection. Impetigo bullosa (Option C) is a localized form of staphylococcal infection presenting with large blisters but not widespread peeling. Erythema multiforme (Option D) is a hypersensitivity reaction characterized by "target lesions". Therefore, given the extensive peeling and pediatric presentation, SSSS treated with appropriate antibiotics is the correct diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the characteristic lesion of Kaposi sarcoma?

options.text: A white, striated lesion that cannot be scraped off

questions.explanation: A raised, purple-red lesionKaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a malignancy caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals such as those with HIV/AIDS. The characteristic lesions typically begin as flat, reddish-purple macules and progress into raised, palpable plaques and nodules. This violaceous (purple-red) appearance is a pathognomonic sign resulting from the deposition of hemosiderin and extravasated red blood cells within the tumor. A yellow lesion with pus (Option A) indicates a bacterial infection like an abscess. A white, striated lesion (Option B) describes lichen planus or oral hairy leukoplakia. Small red erosions (Option D) are non-specific findings for various inflammatory skin conditions. Therefore, the raised purple-red morphology is the definitive clinical description for Kaposi sarcoma lesions.

questions.stem: A patient diagnosed with borderline tuberculoid leprosy presents with the given clinical findings. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is involved, and which nerve is characteristically enlarged in this condition?
questions.explanation: Type 4 & greater auricular nerveThe patient demonstrates a visibly thickened greater auricular nerve in the neck. In borderline tuberculoid leprosy, acute inflammation of nerves and skin lesions indicates a Type 1 (reversal) reaction. This reaction is a form of delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) caused by a sudden increase in the cell-mediated immune response to Mycobacterium leprae. Type 1 reactions (Option A) are immediate IgE-mediated allergies. Type 2 reactions (Option B) are antibody-mediated. Type 3 reactions (Option C) involve immune complexes, such as Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL), which is the clinical manifestation of a Type 2 leprosy reaction. Because the reversal reaction specifically involves a T-cell mediated response and commonly affects the greater auricular nerve, the pairing in Option D is correct.

questions.stem: A patient presents to the dermatology clinic with recurrent skin lesions similar to those shown in the image. He reports that these lesions consistently appear within a few hours of taking NSAIDs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fixed drug eruptionsThe description of a well-demarcated erythematous patch that recurs at the same site within hours of drug exposure is diagnostic of a Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE). Common triggers include NSAIDs, sulfa drugs, and certain antibiotics. FDEs typically heal leaving behind characteristic post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Erythema multiforme (Option B) presents with "target" or "iris" lesions and usually does not recur consistently on the exact same site upon re-exposure. Drug-induced pigmentation (Option C) involves persistent color changes like blue-grey or brown rather than acute inflammatory red plaques. Herpes (Option D) produces painful, grouped blistering lesions unrelated to specific drug intake. Given the history of recurrence at a specific site immediately following NSAID ingestion, FDE is the only viable clinical diagnosis. 285. questions.stem: In the image shown, identify the function of the marked structure on the endotracheal tube.

options.text: Prevention of air leakage and aspiration
Suctioning of lower respiratory tract secretions

questions.explanation: Prevention of air leakage and aspirationThe marked structure on the endotracheal tube (ET) is the inflatable cuff. Its primary function is to create a physical seal between the tube and the tracheal wall once it is inflated with air. This seal serves two critical purposes: it ensures that positive pressure ventilation is efficient by preventing air leakage around the tube, and it protects the airway from aspiration by blocking secretions or vomit from entering the lower respiratory tract. Monitoring airway pressure (Option B) is done through the ventilator circuit, and suctioning secretions (Option D) requires a separate suction catheter. Visualization of the vocal cords (Option A) is achieved using a laryngoscope during the initial intubation. Proper cuff pressure management (typically 20–30 cm H₂O) is essential to prevent tracheal mucosal ischemia.

questions.stem: During general anesthesia, which peripheral nerve is most commonly stimulated with a nerve stimulator to monitor the depth of neuromuscular blockade?
questions.explanation: Ulnar nerveThe ulnar nerve is the standard site for peripheral nerve stimulation during anesthesia to monitor neuromuscular blockade (NMB). It is preferred because it is superficial at the wrist and provides a clear, measurable motor response in the adductor pollicis muscle. This response accurately reflects the depth of muscle relaxation and helps determine the timing for reversal or extubation. The radial nerve (Option A) is deeper and less reliable for this purpose. The median nerve (Option C) is typically used for somatosensory monitoring rather than NMB. While the tibial nerve (Option D) can be monitored, it is technically more difficult and less standardized than the ulnar approach. Thus, the ulnar nerve remains the gold standard.

questions.stem: A patient under general anesthesia is identified to be in a “cannot intubate, cannot ventilate” (CICV) situation. What is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?
questions.explanation: Perform a cricothyroidotomyA "cannot intubate, cannot ventilate" (CICV) scenario is a critical anesthesia emergency that requires an immediate surgical airway to prevent hypoxic brain injury. An emergency cricothyroidotomy is the fastest and most reliable method because the cricothyroid membrane is superficial and easy to access quickly. Nasopharyngeal airways (Option A) and laryngeal mask airways (Option C) are non-invasive measures that by definition have already failed in a CICV state. A tracheostomy (Option D) is a complex surgical procedure that takes significantly more time to perform than a cricothyroidotomy and is not suitable for a rapid hypoxic emergency. Therefore, cricothyroidotomy is the mandated life-saving intervention. 289. A patient with known hyperthyroidism who is not receiving treatment is scheduled for a total thyroidectomy. Pre-anesthetic evaluation has been inadequately performed. What is the most serious complication that is most likely to occur during surgery? (A) Hyperthermia (B) Hypothermia (C) Arrhythmia (D) Hypothyroidism (C) Arrhythmia In a patient with uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, the body is in a hypermetabolic state with significantly increased sensitivity to catecholamines. Surgical stress or manipulation of the thyroid gland can precipitate a life-threatening "thyroid storm" (thyrotoxic crisis). The most immediate and dangerous intraoperative manifestation of this crisis is severe cardiac arrhythmia, such as atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardia. While hyperthermia (Option A) is a classic sign of thyroid storm, arrhythmias pose a more acute threat to hemodynamic stability during the procedure. Hypothermia (Option B) is generally associated with prolonged surgery in cold environments, not thyrotoxicosis. Hypothyroidism (Option D) is an expected long-term consequence of a total thyroidectomy but would not occur as an acute intraoperative complication. Therefore, managing heart rate and rhythm via preoperative beta-blockade and antithyroid medications is essential to prevent these intraoperative cardiac emergencies. raDioL oG y 290. questions.stem: Identify the investigation shown in the image:
questions.explanation: MammographyThe image presents the two standard views used in breast cancer screening: the Mediolateral Oblique (MLO) view and the Craniocaudal (CC) view. This characterizes mammography, a diagnostic tool that uses low-dose X-rays and breast compression to achieve high-resolution images of breast tissue. The MLO view is critical as it captures the upper outer quadrant and the pectoralis muscle. While mammography is technically a form of X-ray (Option C), "Mammography" is the specific clinical term for this specialized breast imaging study. CT scans (Option B) and MRIs (Option D) use entirely different cross-sectional technologies and do not present the breast in these specific compressed CC/MLO views. Therefore, the architectural detail and standard positioning confirm that the investigation is a mammogram.

questions.stem: A man is brought to the hospital with bizarre behavior and an inability to recall his personal identity or the events surrounding his travel over a distance of 100 km. Collateral history reveals that he experienced a traumatic earthquake a few months earlier. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dissociative amnesiaThe patient’s inability to recall his identity combined with purposeful travel (100 km) and no memory of the journey constitutes dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue. This condition is directly linked to a recent severe traumatic stressor, such as the earthquake mentioned in the history. Dissociative identity disorder (Option B) involves two or more distinct personality states, which is not described here. Schizophrenia (Option C) is a psychotic disorder characterized by hallucinations and disorganized thought rather than isolated identity loss. Global amnesia (Option D) is typically caused by organic conditions like stroke and does not specifically follow trauma. Since the amnesia is localized to personal information following an identifiable psychological trauma, dissociative amnesia is the most specific diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old software professional presents with disturbed sleep, low mood, and stress persisting for the past three months, which he relates to ongoing workplace difficulties. He has no previous psychiatric history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Adjustment disorderThe patient’s presentation fits the criteria for adjustment disorder. This condition involves emotional or behavioral symptoms (low mood, stress) in response to an identifiable stressor (work pressure) beginning within three months of the stressor's onset. The distress is often disproportionate to the stressor and causes functional impairment. Generalized anxiety disorder (Option B) requires a minimum of six months of excessive worry regarding multiple domains. Acute stress disorder (Option C) follows a "traumatic" event (e.g., natural disaster) and lasts less than one month. PTSD (Option D) also requires exposure to a life-threatening trauma and specific symptoms like re-experiencing and hyperarousal, which are absent here. As the symptoms are a direct response to common workplace stress and within the 3-month window, adjustment disorder is the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A woman presents with excessive talkativeness, increased activity levels, markedly reduced need for sleep, and impulsive spending sprees. When questioned about her behavior, she becomes irritable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bipolar I + ManiaThe symptoms described—excessive talkativeness, hyperactivity, decreased need for sleep, and impulsive spending—are diagnostic of a manic episode. These behaviors, combined with irritability when confronted, fulfill the core criteria for Bipolar I Disorder. Bipolar II with hypomania (Option B) is less severe; hypomania does not cause significant functional impairment and lasts at least four days without psychosis. This patient’s reckless spending indicates significant impairment, favoring mania. Obsessive-compulsive disorder (Option C) involves repetitive rituals to neutralize intrusive thoughts, which does not match this case. Schizophrenia (Option D) is characterized by hallucinations and delusions rather than the elevated mood and energy seen here. Therefore, the clear manic presentation confirms Bipolar I.

questions.stem: A person holds a fixed false belief that he owns a large amount of property and that someone he knows is attempting to take it away from him. Which type of delusion best describes this belief?
questions.explanation: Delusion of grandeur and persecutionThis patient is experiencing two distinct delusions. The belief that he owns extensive property is a delusion of grandeur, which is a false and exaggerated belief in one’s own importance or wealth. The belief that someone is trying to take it away from him is a delusion of persecution, characterized by the false belief that one is being targeted, harassed, or conspired against. Delusions of reference (Option B) involve believing that neutral events (like news reports) are directed personally at oneself. Nihilistic delusions (Options C and D) involve the false belief that the self or the world does not exist. Since the patient's beliefs are focused on self-importance and being harmed by others, "grandeur and persecution" is the correct clinical description.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis in a child who has persistently poor mathematical abilities despite having a normal IQ and otherwise age-appropriate learning skills, and who shows no improvement even after one year of specialized mathematics tutoring?
questions.explanation: Specific learning disorderThis child’s persistent difficulty with mathematics despite normal intelligence and adequate educational interventions is diagnostic of a Specific Learning Disorder (SLD). Under DSM-5, this term covers impairments in reading, writing, and mathematics (dyscalculia). ADHD (Option A) causes academic issues through inattention or impulsivity rather than a specific skill deficit. Mathematics Learning Disorder (Option B) is the specific description, but "Specific Learning Disorder" is the broader and clinically preferred diagnostic term in standardized examinations. Asperger’s Syndrome (Option C) involves social communication deficits; children with this condition often excel in mathematics. Given the persistence of the mathematical deficit despite tutoring, SLD is the most accurate over arching diagnosis. 

questions.stem: Voltage gated calcium channel present on T-tubule is?
questions.explanation: Dihydropyridine receptorIn skeletal muscle, the excitation-contraction coupling process relies on the transmission of action potentials down the T-tubules. The specific voltage-gated L-type calcium channel located on the T-tubule membrane is the Dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR). When an action potential reaches the DHPR, it undergoes a conformational change that mechanically triggers the opening of the Ryanodine receptor (RyR) (Option D), which is the calcium-release channel located on the adjacent terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The SERCA pump (Option A) is an ATP-dependent pump responsible for sequestering calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum to initiate relaxation. The troponin-myosin complex (Option B) represents the contractile proteins where calcium eventually binds to initiate cross-bridge cycling. Understanding the DHPR-RyR interaction is essential for comprehending muscle physiology and pathologies such as malignant hyperthermia, where defective RyR channels lead to uncontrolled calcium release and hypermetabolic crises when exposed to certain anesthetic agents. 12. questions.stem: Apoptotic bodies comprise of?
questions.explanation: Include cytoplasm+intranuclear material +organelle. Apoptosis is "programmed cell death," a tidy process designed to remove unwanted cells without triggering inflammation. During apoptosis, the cell shrinks and the DNA fragments. The cell then breaks apart into several membrane-bound fragments called apoptotic bodies. These bodies comprise cytoplasm, tightly packed organelles, and fragments of the nucleus (intranuclear material). Because they are enclosed in an intact plasma membrane, the toxic cellular contents do not leak out. Options B, C, and D are incomplete descriptions of these bodies. These fragments are rapidly recognized by phagocytes (like macrophages) through "eat-me" signals such as the flip of phosphatidylserine to the outer membrane leaflet. This efficient clearance prevents the inflammatory response that typically follows necrosis. Apoptosis is a vital physiological process during embryogenesis, immune system regulation, and the removal of DNA-damaged cells. Its dysregulation can lead to autoimmune diseases or cancer, making it a central theme in cell pathology.

questions.stem: Which mutation is linked to the philadelphia chromosome?
questions.explanation: Reciprocal translocation. The Philadelphia chromosome (Ph) is a specific genetic abnormality associated with Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML). It results from a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, specifically written as t(9;22)(q34;q11). In this process, a part of the ABL1 gene from chromosome 9 breaks off and attaches to the BCR gene on chromosome 22. This fusion creates the BCR-ABL1 hybrid gene, which codes for a continuously active (constitutive) tyrosine kinase protein. This unregulated kinase drives the uncontrolled proliferation of white blood cells. Inversion (Option A) and deletion (Option B) involve different types of structural chromosomal rearrangements. Insertion (Option D) involves a non-reciprocal movement of DNA. The Ph chromosome is present in over 95% of CML patients and is the specific target of tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy like imatinib. Its discovery was a landmark in oncology, proving that a specific chromosomal translocation could directly cause cancer.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a recent history of travel to Africa presents with fever, altered mental status, and focal neurological deficits. Laboratory investigations identify an infecting organism that possesses a unique ability to adhere to vascular endothelium, enabling sequestration within blood vessels and thereby evading splenic clearance. What is this phenomenon known as?
questions.explanation: Cytoadherence.The clinical history of travel to Africa, fever, and neurological deficits (Cerebral Malaria) combined with the blood smear point to Plasmodium falciparum infection. A unique and lethal property of P. falciparum is cytoadherence. This occurs when the parasite expresses proteins (like PfEMP-1) on the surface of infected red blood cells (iRBCs), forming "knobs." These knobs bind to endothelial receptors (like ICAM-1 or CD36) in capillary beds. This sequestration prevents the iRBCs from passing through the spleen, where they would be cleared by macrophages. Rosetting (Option A) is the adherence of iRBCs to uninfected RBCs, which also contributes to microvascular obstruction. Agglutination (Option B) is a general term for cell clumping. Schizogony (Option D) is the asexual reproductive phase within the host. Sequestration in the brain leads to the confusion and coma seen in cerebral malaria. Understanding these mechanical properties of the parasite is critical for managing severe malaria and predicting its multisystem complications.

questions.stem: Which type of appendiceal carcinoma is most frequently associated with the development of pseudomyxoma peritonei?
questions.explanation: Adenocarcinoma Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is characterized by the accumulation of mucinous (jelly-like) material within the peritoneal cavity. It most commonly results from the rupture of a mucin-producing tumor of the appendix. The tumor most frequently responsible is a mucinous adenocarcinoma of the appendix. When this tumor ruptures, it releases mucin-secreting epithelial cells into the peritoneal cavity. These cells continue to produce mucin, leading to progressive accumulation and the characteristic “jelly belly” appearance.Although earlier terminology included mucinous cystadenoma, current understanding classifies most of these lesions under the spectrum of appendiceal mucinous neoplasms, with adenocarcinoma being the clinically significant and commonly tested answer. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Mucinous cystadenoma → Older term; less emphasized in exams (C) Carcinoid tumor → Neuroendocrine, non-mucinous (D) Serous cystadenoma → Typically ovarian, not appendiceal

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a painless, mobile, rubbery mass in her left breast. Histopathological examination of the lesion is shown in the provided image. Based on the clinical features and histological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fibroadenoma. The clinical description of a "mobile, rubbery mass" (often called a "breast mouse") in a young woman is classic for a fibroadenoma. Histologically, it is a biphasic tumor consisting of both proliferating connective tissue (stroma) and glandular epithelium. The glands are often compressed into slit-like spaces by the overgrowing stroma, creating the "intracanalicular" or "pericanalicular" patterns seen in the image. Invasive ductal carcinoma (Option A) would show nests of malignant cells with significant atypia invading the stroma. Phyllodes tumors (Option C) are also biphasic but show much higher stromal cellularity and characteristic "leaf-like" projections. Lobular carcinoma in-situ (Option D) shows small, uniform cells filling the acini without stromal invasion. Fibroadenomas are benign and do not increase the risk of cancer significantly. They are estrogen-sensitive and may enlarge during pregnancy or regress after menopause. Management typically involves reassurance or simple excision if the lesion is growing or causing patient anxiety.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with early satiety, marked splenomegaly extending up to the umbilicus, and clinical features of bleeding such as petechiae. Laboratory evaluation reveals a markedly elevated white blood cell count of 85,000/cu.mm, with the peripheral blood smear showing immature B-cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: ALL. The patient’s presentation of massive splenomegaly (manifesting as early satiety), thrombocytopenia (leading to petechiae and bleeding), and marked leukocytosis is highly suggestive of an acute hematological malignancy. The key diagnostic clue is the presence of immature B cells (lymphoblasts) on the peripheral blood smear, which is characteristic of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL). ALL is the most common leukemia in children, but it can also occur in adolescents and young adults. The malignant lymphoblasts typically express terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) and B-cell markers such as CD10 (CALLA), supporting the diagnosis.Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML, Option A) would show myeloblasts, often with Auer rods. Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML, Option B) is characterized by a full spectrum of granulocytic precursors and is associated with the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL). Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL, Option C) usually affects elderly patients and shows mature small lymphocytes. ALL is a medical emergency requiring prompt initiation of chemotherapy. Splenomegaly occurs due to infiltration of malignant cells into the reticuloendothelial system.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless testicular swelling. Following orchidectomy, histopathological examination of the tumor demonstrates the presence of Reinke crystals within the tumor cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leydig cell tumor. A Leydig cell tumor is a non-germ cell tumor of the testis. The pathognomonic histological finding is the presence of Reinke crystals—rod-shaped, eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic inclusions. These tumors are often hormonally active, secreting androgens or estrogens, which can lead to symptoms like precocious puberty in children or gynecomastia in adults. Sertoli cell tumors (Option A) typically show well-defined tubules but lack Reinke crystals. Seminoma (Option C) is the most common germ cell tumor, characterized by large, uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and a lymphocytic infiltrate. Yolk sac tumors (Option D) are common in infants and show characteristic Schiller-Duval bodies. Most Leydig cell tumors are benign, but approximately 10% are malignant. They typically present as a painless, firm testicular mass. Surgical orchidectomy is the standard treatment. Identifying Reinke crystals is a favorite "trigger" in medical exams for specifically naming the Leydig cell tumor, differentiating it from the more common germ cell malignancies. 41.
