questions.stem: What is the most effective method for locating an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation: Nucleotide scan.Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine-secreting tumors. While 90% are in the adrenal medulla, "extra-adrenal" types (paragangliomas) can occur anywhere along the sympathetic chain. The most effective method for locating these ectopic tumors is a nucleotide scan (Option C), specifically the MIBG (Meta-iodobenzoguanidine) scan. MIBG is a catecholamine precursor that is taken up by chromaffin tissue, allowing the scan to "light up" the tumor anywhere in the body. VMA excretion (Option B) (urinary vanillylmandelic acid) is a biochemical test used to diagnose the presence of a tumor but cannot locate it. X-rays (Option A) are not sensitive enough to detect these soft-tissue masses. Clinical examination (Option D) may detect hypertension or a rare abdominal mass but is not an accurate localization tool . MIBG scans are superior to CT/MRI for extra-adrenal cases because they identify functionally active tumors across a whole-body survey. Therefore, functional imaging via nucleotide scanning is the gold standard for localization. PSy CHiatry

questions.stem: What is the term for a child born when a woman pretends to be pregnant and later uses the child to extort a man?
questions.explanation: Supposititious child.In forensic medicine and legal terms, a supposititious child (Option A) is one who is falsely substituted or presented as the biological offspring of a woman who was never actually pregnant, usually for the purpose of defrauding or extorting an inheritance or a man. Superfecundation (Option B) refers to the fertilization of two ova within the same cycle by two different acts of intercourse, potentially by different fathers. A posthumous child (Option C) is born after the death of the father. Superfetation (Option D) is the fertilization of a second ovum while a woman is already pregnant, resulting in two fetuses of different ages . The term "supposititious" specifically implies a fraudulent claim of parentage involving deception about a pregnancy. This is a rare but legally significant concept in cases of disputed maternity or inheritance fraud. Therefore, the fraudulent presentation of a child defines the supposititious category.

questions.stem: A patient is asked to copy the face of a clock, and the resulting drawing is shown below. What is the correct term used to describe this finding?
questions.explanation: Hemispatial neglect.The image displays a classic result of the "Clock Drawing Test" where the patient has crowded all the numbers onto the right side of the clock face, completely ignoring the left side. This is the hallmark of Hemispatial Neglect (Option B) (also known as unilateral neglect). This condition usually results from a lesion in the right parietal lobe (often after a stroke), causing the patient to lose awareness of the left half of their environment. Confabulation (Option A) is the fabrication of memories seen in Korsakoff syndrome. Kinetic apraxia (Option C) is the loss of ability to perform fine, skilled movements despite normal strength. Asterixis (Option D) is a "flapping tremor" of the hands seen in hepatic or metabolic encephalopathy . Because the patient has completely failed to represent one side of the spatial layout, hemispatial neglect is the only accurate neurological term. This test is a simple and effective bedside screening tool for parietal dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old patient presents with a history of mood disturbance, as illustrated in the accompanying image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rapid cycling disorderThe image shows a mood chart depicting 4 or more distinct mood episodes within 12 months, oscillating between mania and severe depression — the defining feature of Rapid Cycling Disorder.Key Diagnostic Features visible in chart: 1. 4+ episodes within 12 months 2. Swings between full mania and severe depression 3. Episodes separated by periods of normal mood 4. Meets DSM-5 criteria for rapid cycling specifier in Bipolar disorder Why other options are wrong: (A) Bipolar disorder is incorrect because while rapid cycling is a specifier of bipolar disorder, the chart specifically shows 4+ episodes in 12 months making rapid cycling the more precise and specific diagnosis here. (B) Dysthymia is incorrect because dysthymia presents as chronic, persistent mild depression lasting at least 2 years — no manic or hypomanic episodes occur, completely inconsistent with the mood chart shown. (D) Cyclothymia is incorrect because cyclothymia shows hypomanic and mild depressive episodes — never reaching full mania or severe depression thresholds. The chart clearly shows full manic and severe depressive episodes ruling out cyclothymia.

questions.stem: Which type of learning is demonstrated when a medical intern is guided step by step on how to correctly elicit the knee reflex?
questions.explanation: Psychomotor learning.In medical education, learning objectives are categorized into three domains. Psychomotor learning (Option B) involves the acquisition of physical skills and manual dexterity, such as the correct technique for using a reflex hammer to elicit a knee jerk. This type of learning requires the coordination of cognitive understanding with physical performance. Cognitive learning (Option A) focuses on the acquisition of knowledge, facts, and theoretical concepts. Affective learning (Option C) pertains to the development of attitudes, professional values, and empathy. Repeated learning (Option D) is a method of study but not a recognized educational domain. Because the intern is being taught a specific procedural skill that requires physical action and precision, it is the classic example of psychomotor development. Clinical rotations are designed to bridge the gap between classroom cognitive knowledge and hands-on psychomotor proficiency. Therefore, mastering clinical examination techniques is a core psychomotor task.

questions.stem: What is the term used for a disease that is not native to a country and is introduced from another country?
questions.explanation: Exotic.In epidemiology, an exotic disease (Option D) is one that is not normally present in a given country or geographical region but is introduced from an external source (abroad). The 25-year-old male diagnosed at an Indian airport upon arrival represents an imported or exotic case. An endemic disease (Option A) is one that is constantly present in a specific population or region (e.g., malaria in parts of India). An epidemic (Option B) is a sudden, large-scale outbreak of a disease in a specific area. A zoonotic disease (Option C) is one that is transmitted from animals to humans, such as rabies or anthrax . Exotic diseases are a major focus of international health regulations and airport quarantine measures to prevent the domestic spread of "new" pathogens. Therefore, because the condition originated outside the country's borders, "exotic" is the correct epidemiological classification for this imported case.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops auditory hallucinations and is unable to identify the source of the voices approximately seven hours after undergoing an appendectomy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: DeliriumA patient developing auditory hallucinations 7 hours post-surgery is classic presentation of postoperative delirium — an acute confusional state caused by physiological disturbance following surgery including anesthesia effects, hypoxia, electrolyte imbalance, or pain medications.Key features pointing to Delirium: 1. Acute onset after surgery 2. Hallucinations — perceptual disturbances 3. Postoperative setting — classic trigger 4. Unable to identify source — disorientation characteristic of delirium Why other options are wrong: (A) Delirium tremens is incorrect because delirium tremens occurs 48-72 hours after alcohol withdrawal — not 7 hours post-surgery. No history of alcohol dependence or withdrawal is mentioned here. (B) Acute transient psychotic disorder is incorrect because ATPD requires symptoms lasting at least 1 day with sudden onset psychosis — postoperative hallucinations have a clear organic physiological cause making delirium more appropriate diagnosis. (D) Alcoholic hallucinosis is incorrect because alcoholic hallucinosis occurs in chronic alcoholics experiencing withdrawal, typically 12-24 hours after stopping alcohol — no alcoholism history is mentioned and surgical context clearly points to delirium.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of involuntary body jerking without loss of consciousness, tongue biting, or post-episode confusion, and all investigations are normal. Which condition should be considered in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Malingering.The 18-year-old presents with "pseudoseizures" or jerk-like movements. The absence of classic epileptic signs—such as confusion (post-ictal state), tongue biting, or urinary incontinence—along with normal medical tests (EEG, CT), suggests that the behavior is not an organic seizure. If the patient is consciously and intentionally producing these symptoms to achieve a specific external gain (like avoiding school, work, or legal trouble), the correct term is malingering (Option A). Factitious disorder (Option B) also involves intentional symptom production, but the goal is to play the "sick role" rather than for external gain. Somatization syndrome (Option C) involves involuntary symptoms in response to psychological stress. Hypochondriasis (Option D) is an excessive preoccupation with having a serious disease . Malingering is not a psychiatric illness but a behavior. Given the age and the non-epileptic nature of the movements, malingering for secondary gain is a key forensic and clinical consideration.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man reports excessive, uncontrollable worry about everyday activities, financial matters, and his health for the past two years, accompanied by restlessness, fatigue, and disturbed sleep. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Generalized anxiety disorder.The patient meets the DSM-5 criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) (Option D): excessive and uncontrollable worry about a variety of topics (finances, health, daily life) occurring more days than not for at least six months. He also exhibits the required physical symptoms, including restlessness, fatigue, and disturbed sleep. Depression (Option A) primarily involves a low mood and loss of interest rather than pervasive worry. Illness anxiety disorder (Option B) is limited to worries about having a serious illness. Somatoform disorder (Option C) involves multiple unexplained physical complaints. GAD is a chronic condition that significantly impairs daily functioning. It is often treated with a combination of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and medications like SSRIs or SNRIs . Because the man's anxiety is broad, persistent, and accompanied by physiological tension, GAD is the definitive clinical diagnosis for his presentation.

questions.stem: Jet-black discoloration of the tongue accompanied by tactile hallucinations is characteristic of abuse of which substance?
questions.explanation: Cocaine.A classic and pathognomonic presentation for chronic cocaine abuse is the combination of jet-black pigmentation of the tongue and tactile hallucinations (Option D). The tactile hallucinations are famously known as "cocaine bugs" or Magnan’s sign, where the user feels insects crawling under or on their skin (formication). The black tongue discoloration results from the chemical effects of the drug or contaminants when smoked. Heroin (Option A) and Opium (Option B) are opioids that cause miosis and respiratory depression but not these specific features. Alcohol (Option C) withdrawal can cause hallucinations but not the black tongue sign . Cocaine is a powerful stimulant that increases synaptic dopamine. The presence of formication often leads to self-excoriation as the user tries to "pick" the bugs out. Therefore, the visual sign of a black tongue combined with the sensation of crawling insects is the definitive forensic identifier for cocaine toxicity.

questions.stem: Which pair of neurotransmitters is associated with depression?
questions.explanation: Serotonin and norepinephrine.The "monoamine hypothesis" of depression proposes that the condition results from a deficiency of certain neurotransmitters in the brain. The two most critical neurotransmitters involved are Serotonin and Norepinephrine (Option B). Serotonin (5-HT) regulates mood, sleep, and appetite, while norepinephrine (noradrenaline) is involved in energy, focus, and the stress response. Most modern antidepressants work by increasing the synaptic levels of these two chemicals . For example, SSRIs target serotonin, while SNRIs target both. While dopamine (Option C) also plays a role in the brain's reward system and its lack can contribute to anhedonia (loss of pleasure), the most standard pairing taught in medical and psychiatric texts regarding the core pathophysiology of depression is serotonin and norepinephrine. GABA (Option A and D) is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter and is more closely associated with anxiety disorders. Therefore, the "monoamine" pair is the correct answer.

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis in a girl who has normal language development but predominantly focuses on watching her own hands and shows minimal social interaction with others?
questions.explanation: Rett's SyndromeRett's Syndrome is the correct diagnosis. A girl with normal early development who subsequently shows hand-wringing/hand-watching stereotypies and social withdrawal is the classic presentation of Rett's syndrome — an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder occurring exclusively in females.Key Diagnostic Features: 1. Occurs exclusively in females 2. Normal early development followed by regression 3. Characteristic hand stereotypies — wringing, watching, mouthing 4. Social withdrawal and loss of purposeful hand use 5. Language may be preserved initially then regresses Why other options are wrong: (A) ADHD is incorrect because ADHD presents with inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity — not hand stereotypies or social withdrawal. No characteristic hand-focusing behavior occurs in ADHD. (B) Autism is incorrect because while autism shows social withdrawal, it occurs in both sexes, lacks the characteristic hand-watching stereotypies and normal early developmental period followed by regression specific to Rett's. (C) Asperger's Syndrome is incorrect because Asperger's presents with normal intelligence, social difficulties, and restricted interests — no hand stereotypies, regression, or gender specificity as seen in Rett's syndrome.  NODIA

questions.stem: Which muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve?
questions.explanation: All of the above The ulnar nerve is the primary motor nerve of the hand, responsible for fine motor control. It innervates all the intrinsic muscles of the hand except for the three thenar muscles (Abductor Pollicis Brevis, Flexor Pollicis Brevis, Opponens Pollicis) and the lateral two lumbricals (1st and 2nd), which are supplied by the median nerve. Let's analyze the options: (A) The Dorsal interossei (DAB) are responsible for finger abduction and are all supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. (B) The Abductor digiti minimi is a key muscle of the hypothenar eminence, which is entirely supplied by the ulnar nerve. (C) The 4th lumbrical (along with the 3rd) is one of the two medial lumbricals, which are supplied by the ulnar nerve, in contrast to the 1st and 2nd lumbricals (supplied by the median nerve). Since the ulnar nerve supplies all three of these structures, the correct answer is (D) All of the above.

questions.stem: What is the function of the muscle that attaches to the indicated area?
questions.explanation: Depression The image indicates the gluteus medius muscle, which arises from the outer surface of the ilium and inserts into the greater trochanter of the femur. The gluteus medius is one of the principal muscles of the hip and plays a crucial role in maintaining pelvic stability during locomotion.The primary function of the gluteus medius is abduction of the thigh at the hip joint. In addition, it is responsible for stabilizing the pelvis during walking or standing on one leg. When one foot is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius on the opposite side contracts to prevent the pelvis from tilting downward. This action is essential for maintaining balance and proper gait. Weakness of this muscle results in a positive Trendelenburg sign. The muscle does not primarily produce protraction or retraction, which are movements associated with the scapula. It also does not cause elevation in this context. While it contributes to hip abduction and medial rotation, among the given options, the closest related movement affecting pelvic mechanics is depression, referring to stabilization and prevention of pelvic drop. Therefore, the correct answer is : (C) Depression

questions.stem: Which nerve is not related to olfaction?
questions.explanation: Hypoglossal Olfaction (the sense of smell) is a complex sensation. While the olfactory nerve (CN I) is the primary nerve for detecting odorants, other nerves contribute to the overall perception. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) (B) is related because it provides general sensation from the nasal mucosa, detecting chemical irritants or qualities like the "cooling" of menthol or the "burn" of ammonia (chemosensation).The glossopharyngeal (CN IX) (C) and vagus (CN X) (D) nerves are related because they mediate taste from the posterior tongue and pharynx. The perception of "flavor" is a combined sensory experience that intimately links retronasal olfaction with taste.In contrast, the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) (A) is a purely motor nerve. It supplies the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue (except palatoglossus), controlling tongue movement. It has no sensory function related to smell, taste, or flavor perception.

questions.stem: What is the nerve supply to the piriform fossa?
questions.explanation: Internal laryngeal nerve The piriform fossa (or recess) is a depression in the laryngopharynx located on either side of the laryngeal inlet. The sensory innervation of the larynx is divided by the vocal cords. The mucosa above the vocal cords, which includes the piriform fossa, is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve (A). This nerve is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, which arises from the vagus (CN X). This innervation is critical as it provides the sensory (afferent) limb of the cough reflex for this area. (B) The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the mucosa below the vocal cords. (C) The external laryngeal nerve is a motor nerve that supplies the cricothyroid muscle. (D) The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies sensation to the oropharynx (e.g., tonsils, posterior tongue), which is superior to the piriform fossa.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the emergency department complaining that food is stuck in his throat. Examination reveals a bone lodged in the left piriform recess. Which function is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation: Cough reflex This clinical scenario is a direct application of the anatomy from the previous question. The piriform recess is innervated by the internal laryngeal nerve. This nerve provides the sensory afferent limb for the cough reflex (A) for any foreign material at or above the laryngeal inlet. A foreign body, such as a fishbone, lodged in this recess can mechanically or by local inflammation/edema, "anesthetize" the nerve endings. This impairs the protective reflex, which normally detects the foreign body and triggers a cough to expel it. This impairment significantly increases the risk of aspiration. The gag reflex (B) is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) in the oropharynx, a different location. Mastication (C) (CN V) and salivation (D) (CN VII, CN IX) are unrelated to this specific location.

questions.stem: What is the action of the muscle marked in the image?
questions.explanation: Hip abduction The image displays the posterior view of the hip, with arrows pointing to the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles. These muscles originate from the ilium and insert on the greater trochanter of the femur. Their primary and most powerful action is hip abduction (B), which is the movement of the thigh away from the body's midline. These muscles are the main abductors of the hip. They also play a crucial role in pelvic stability. When standing on one leg, the gluteus medius and minimus on the standing side contract isometrically to prevent the pelvis from dropping on the opposite (swinging) side, a function tested by the Trendelenburg test. While the anterior fibers of these muscles can assist in internal rotation (A), their main function is abduction. Knee extension (C) and knee flexion (D) are actions at the knee joint, controlled by the quadriceps and hamstrings, respectively. 7. Referred pain from the dura mater of the marked area involves:

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a boundary of the hepatocystic triangle?
questions.explanation: Cystic artery The hepatocystic triangle, also known as the Triangle of Calot, is a critical anatomical space for surgeons, especially during a cholecystectomy (gallbladder removal). Its boundaries are: 1. Medially: The common hepatic duct (A) 2. Laterally: The cystic duct (B) 3. Superiorly: The inferior (visceral) surface of the liver (C) The cystic artery (D) is a vital structure, but it is a content of the triangle, not a boundary. The triangle is significant because it typically contains the cystic artery, the cystic lymph node (of Lund), and autonomic nerves. The surgeon must carefully identify all three boundaries of the triangle to safely locate and ligate the cystic duct and cystic artery within it, avoiding damage to the common hepatic duct.

questions.stem: Which muscles are supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve?
questions.explanation: Peroneus longus & Brevis The common peroneal (fibular) nerve divides into two main branches: the superficial and deep peroneal nerves. 1. The superficial peroneal nerve (also called the superficial fibular nerve) supplies the muscles of the lateral compartment of the leg. These muscles are the Peroneus longus and Peroneus brevis (A). Their primary function is eversion of the foot, and they also assist in plantarflexion. 2. The deep peroneal nerve (deep fibular nerve) supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg. These muscles are responsible for dorsiflexion of the foot and extension of the toes. They include the tibialis anterior, Extensor hallucis longus (B), extensor digitorum longus, and Peroneus tertius (C). Therefore, only the peroneus longus and brevis are supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve.

questions.stem: A teenager comes to the emergency department with wrist pain after falling off his skateboard and has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Which bone is most likely fractured?
questions.explanation: Scaphoid This is a classic clinical presentation. A fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) is the most common mechanism for a scaphoid fracture (A). The anatomical snuffbox is a triangular depression on the dorsal, radial side of the wrist. Its floor is formed by the scaphoid bone, and tenderness upon palpation in this specific area ("snuff-box tenderness") is the hallmark clinical sign of a scaphoid fracture. The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. It is critical to diagnose and treat properly because it has a tenuous, retrograde blood supply, which puts it at high risk for avascular necrosis and non-union (failure to heal) if the fracture is missed. The trapezium (D) also lies in the snuffbox floor but is fractured far less often. The trapezoid (B) and capitate (C) are not associated with snuffbox tenderness.

questions.stem: What is the diagnosis suggested by the eye movement abnormality shown in the image?
questions.explanation: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia The image depicts a classic Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO) (A), specifically a left INO. The diagram shows that on attempted right gaze: 1. The left eye (which should be adducting) fails to move medially past the midline. 2. The right eye (which is abducting) moves fully and exhibits nystagmus. This specific combination—failure of adduction on the affected side with nystagmus in the abducting contralateral eye—is pathognomonic for an INO. It is caused by a lesion in the Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF) on the same side as the adducting deficit (in this case, the left MLF). The MLF is the pathway that coordinates the 6th nerve nucleus (for abduction) with the contralateral 3rd nerve nucleus (for adduction). A 6th nerve palsy (C) would cause a failure of abduction. A 3rd nerve palsy (B) would involve ptosis and a "down and out" eye.

questions.stem: Primary muscle repair in cleft lip surgery involves reconstruction of which muscle?
questions.explanation: Orbicularis oris A cleft lip is a congenital defect resulting from the failure of fusion of the facial prominences during embryonic development. This defect creates a gap in the upper lip. The key muscle that is disrupted is the Orbicularis oris (A). This is the circular muscle that surrounds the mouth and acts as the oral sphincter, responsible for closing and puckering the lips. In a cleft lip, the muscle fibers do not form a continuous ring; instead, they are interrupted and run abnormally, inserting onto the margins of the cleft. A primary goal of surgical cleft lip repair (cheiloplasty) is to dissect these abnormal muscle fibers, re-orient them into their correct horizontal position, and suture them together. This "primary muscle repair" is essential to restore normal lip function (like suckling), symmetry, and cosmetic appearance. The orbicularis oculi (B) , levator palpebrae superioris (C) , and masseter (D) are muscles of the eye and jaw, respectively, and are not involved. 13. Match the following anatomical structures with their correct image labels: 1. Seminal vesicles 2. Ureter 3. Prostate

questions.stem: Vas deferens
questions.explanation: 1-D, 2-C, 3-A, 4-B In the given male pelvic anatomy diagram, label D represents the seminal vesicles. These are paired, elongated, sac-like glands located posterior to the urinary bladder and superior to the prostate. They appear as folded or coiled structures and contribute fructose-rich fluid to semen. C Label indicates the ureter, a narrow muscular tube that carries urine from the kidneys to the urinary bladder. In the diagram, it is seen descending from above and entering the bladder posteriorly. A Label corresponds to the prostate gland, which is a rounded, walnut-sized structure situated just below the urinary bladder and surrounding the proximal urethra. It secretes prostatic fluid that forms an important component of semen. B Label represents the vas deferens. This thick muscular tube carries sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct. It ascends from the testicular region, curves around the bladder, and joins the duct of the seminal vesicle. Thus, the anatomical positions confirm option (D) as correct. 14. Match the cardiac anatomical features with their corresponding labels: Column 1 Column 2 1. Receives oxygenated blood from pulmo - nary veins A. Ascending aorta 2. Lies anterior to as - cending aorta B. Right ventricle NODIA

questions.stem: Hypertrophy in pul- monary stenosis D. Left atrium
questions.explanation: 1-D, 2-C, 3-A, 4-B Let's match each statement from Column 1 to the correct structure in Column 2. 1. "Receives oxygenated blood from pulmonary veins": This is the functional definition of the Left atrium (D). 2. "Lies anterior to ascending aorta": In the superior mediastinum, the Pulmonary trunk (C) arises from the right ventricle and passes anterior and to the left of the ascending aorta before bifurcating. 3. "Arises from LV": The Ascending aorta (A) is the great vessel that originates from the base of the left ventricle (LV), carrying oxygenated blood to the body. 4. "Hypertrophy in pulmonary stenosis": Pulmonary stenosis is a narrowing of the pulmonary valve, which increases the pressure the Right ventricle (B) must pump against (increased afterload). This chronic pressure overload causes the muscle of the right ventricle to thicken (hypertrophy). The correct matches are: 1-D, 2-C, 3-A, 4-B. This corresponds to option (B).

questions.stem: By what mechanism does the marked structure exert its effects on nearby cells?
questions.explanation: Paracrine The image shows a histology slide of the pancreas. The "marked structure" is the Islet of Langerhans, a pale-staining cluster of endocrine cells, surrounded by the darker-staining exocrine acinar tissue. The Islets contain multiple cell types (e.g., alpha, beta, delta cells) that secrete different hormones (e.g., glucagon, insulin, somatostatin). These cells are in close proximity and regulate each other's function. This form of local, cell-to-cell signaling, where a hormone released from one cell acts on an adjacent cell, is the definition of paracrine signaling (C). For example, insulin secreted by beta cells inhibits glucagon release from neighboring alpha cells, and somatostatin from delta cells inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion. This local paracrine network is essential for fine-tuning the endocrine output of the pancreas. PHYSIOLOGY

questions.stem: Which of the following is seen in high altitude?
questions.explanation: Respiratory alkalosis An high altitude, the atmospheric pressure is lower, leading to a decreased partial pressure of inspired oxygen (PO 2 ). This causes hypoxemia (low oxygen in the blood), which is sensed by the peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies). These chemoreceptors stimulate the respiratory center in the brainstem to increase the rate and depth of breathing (hyperventilation). This is a compensatory mechanism to increase oxygen intake. However, this hyperventilation also causes an excessive "blowing off" of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ). Since CO 2 is a volatile acid in the blood (forming carbonic acid), its excessive loss leads to a decrease in arterial PCO 2 . A primary decrease in PCO 2 raises the blood pH, resulting in respiratory alkalosis (D). This is the primary, acute acid-base disturbance seen at high altitude.

questions.stem: IGF-1 and IGF-2 are structurally most similar to which molecule?
questions.explanation: Insulin Insulin-like growth factors IGF-1 and IGF-2 are structurally most similar to insulin. They are single-chain polypeptides with significant amino acid sequence homology to proinsulin, but in their active circulating form, they closely resemble insulin in overall three-dimensional structure. Both IGFs contain A and B domains analogous to insulin’s A and B chains, along with additional C and D domains. Although they are synthesized as larger precursor molecules, their functional structure shows strong similarity to insulin, including conserved disulfide bonds that stabilize the molecule.Functionally, IGFs also share similarities with insulin. While insulin primarily regulates glucose metabolism, IGF-1 and IGF-2 mainly promote growth, cell proliferation, and differentiation. However, because of their structural resemblance, IGFs can weakly bind to insulin receptors at high concentrations.They are not most similar to preproinsulin, proinsulin, or C-peptide. Preproinsulin and proinsulin are precursor forms in insulin synthesis, and C-peptide is simply a connecting peptide removed during insulin maturation. Therefore, the best answer is Insulin.

questions.stem: During which situation does the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli increase?
questions.explanation: Inspiration The fluid lining the alveoli is coated with pulmonary surfactant, a substance that reduces surface tension. This reduction is not static; it changes with the breathing cycle. During expiration (A), the alveoli decrease in size. This compresses the surfactant molecules on the surface, increasing their concentration and dramatically decreasing surface tension, which prevents the alveoli from collapsing.During inspiration (B), the alveoli expand, and their surface area increases. This spreads the surfactant molecules farther apart, decreasing their concentration at the air-liquid interface. With this "dilution" of surfactant, its tension-reducing effect is lessened, and the surface tension of the fluid lining increases (or, more accurately, returns towards its higher baseline).Posture (C, D) affects ventilation-perfusion matching but not the direct physics of alveolar surface tension in this manner. 19. Which of the following are features of Bezold Jarisch reflex? 1. Hypopnea 2. Tachycardia 3. Bradycardia 4. Hypotension (A) 1,2,3 (B) 1,3,4 (C) 1,3 (D) All of the above As  EXAMINATION PAPER MAY-2025 (B) All of the above The Bezold-Jarisch reflex is a cardio-inhibitory reflex, meaning it slows down and unloads the heart. It is a protective reflex originating from chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors in the ventricular walls, often triggered by noxious stimuli, certain drugs, or situations like an "empty" ventricle in severe hypovolemia. The reflex arc involves vagal afferents and efferents. The classic triad of responses is: 1. Hypotension (4), caused by peripheral vasodilation (inhibition of sympathetic tone). 2. Bradycardia (3), caused by a surge in parasympathetic (vagal) output to the heart. 3. Apnea or Hypopnea (1) (a decrease in respiratory rate or depth). Tachycardia (2) (a fast heart rate) is the opposite of this reflex. Therefore, the correct features are 1, 3, and 4. This corresponds to option (B).

questions.stem: In a normal awake person resting with eyes closed, which EEG waves diminish when the eyes are opened?
questions.explanation: Alpha waves Alpha waves (C) (8-13 Hz) are the dominant EEG rhythm in a normal adult who is awake and at rest with their eyes closed. This state is often called "eyes-closed-relaxed." These waves are most prominent in the occipital (visual) cortex. The most characteristic feature of this alpha rhythm is its immediate attenuation (reduction or blocking) as soon as the person opens their eyes or engages in a mental task. This "alpha block" signifies the brain shifting from a relaxed, idling state to an active, processing state, which is characterized by higher-frequency, lower-amplitude Beta waves (A). Theta waves (B) and Delta waves (D) are associated with drowsiness and deep sleep, respectively.

questions.stem: Given a latent period of 10 ms, a contraction period of 40 ms, and a relaxation period of 40 ms, how would you calculate the tetanizing frequency?
questions.explanation: 25 Hz Tetanizing frequency is the minimum stimulation frequency required to cause individual muscle twitches to fuse into a smooth, sustained contraction (tetanus). This fusion occurs when a new stimulus arrives before the muscle has finished relaxing from the previous one. To achieve complete, fused tetanus, the next stimulus must arrive before the relaxation phase can even begin. This means the time interval (T) between stimuli must be equal to or less than the contraction period.Given Contraction Period (T) = 40 ms To convert milliseconds (ms) to seconds (s): T = 40 / 1000 = 0.04 secondsFrequency (f) is the inverse of the time period (f = 1 / T).f = 1 / 0.04 s = 25 HzTherefore, a stimulation frequency of 25 Hz (or higher) will send a new impulse every 40 ms, initiating a new contraction just as the previous one peaks, leading to fused tetanus. The latent period and relaxation period are not needed for this specific calculation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of feed forward mechanism?

options.text: HR increases from supine to standing
Increase in cardiac output in response to anemia

questions.explanation: HR increases from supine to standing A feed-forward mechanism is an anticipatory control system. It initiates a response before a change (or "error") in the system is actually detected, in anticipation of that change. (A) HR increases from supine to standing: This is the best example. As a person initiates the action of standing, the central nervous system sends signals (central command) that increase heart rate (HR) before the blood pressure has a chance to drop from the effects of gravity. This anticipatory rise helps prevent orthostatic hypotension. (B) Vasoconstriction in response to cooling: This is a classic negative feedback loop. The stimulus (cold) is detected, and the body responds (vasoconstriction) to correct the error (heat loss). (C) Increase in cardiac output in response to anemia: This is a negative feedback compensation. The body detects the error (low oxygen delivery) and responds (increasing cardiac output) to compensate. (D) Temperature regulation: This is a prime example of a system controlled by negative feedback. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: A patient comes to the OPD with fever. Which area is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Pre-optic nucleus Fever is a regulated rise in the body's thermoregulatory set-point, which is controlled by the hypothalamus. The specific "thermostat" of the body is located in the Pre-optic nucleus (also called the pre-optic area) of the anterior hypothalamus (B). During an infection, inflammatory cytokines (pyrogens) stimulate the production of Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in this region. PGE2 then acts on neurons within the pre-optic nucleus to "raise" the set-point. The rest of the body then perceives the normal temperature as being "too cold" relative to this new, higher set-point. This triggers heat-generating mechanisms (e.g., shivering, peripheral vasoconstriction) that cause the body temperature to rise until it matches the new febrile set-point.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a mechanism by which ADH acts?

options.text: Increases water permeability in collecting ducts
Increases absorption of urea in medullary collecting duct
Increases absorption of NaCl in thin ascending limb
Increases absorption of urea in descending limb of loop of Henle

questions.explanation: Increases absorption of NaCl in thin ascending limb Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also called vasopressin, primarily acts on the late distal tubule and collecting duct of the nephron. Its main function is to conserve water and concentrate urine. ADH increases water permeability in the collecting ducts (Option A) by inserting aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane of principal cells via V2 receptor activation and cAMP signaling. This allows more water to be reabsorbed into the bloodstream.ADH also increases urea permeability in the inner medullary collecting duct (Option B). This enhances urea recycling into the medullary interstitium, helping maintain the hyperosmotic medullary gradient necessary for water reabsorption.However, ADH does not increase NaCl absorption in the thin ascending limb (Option C). The thin ascending limb has limited active transport capacity and is relatively impermeable to water; ADH does not significantly act here. Sodium reabsorption in the ascending limb is primarily a function of the thick ascending limb via the NKCC2 cotransporter.Option (D) is incorrect physiologically, but the best answer among the given choices is (C).

questions.stem: Tight junctions are mainly found in which region of the cell?
questions.explanation: Apical Tight junctions (zonula occludens) are located at the apical region of epithelial cells. They form the most apical part of the junctional complex and encircle the cell like a belt. Because they are positioned at the top of the lateral membrane, just beneath the apical surface, they are commonly described in exams as being present in the apical region. Their main function is to seal adjacent epithelial cells together, preventing paracellular movement of substances. This helps maintain selective permeability and preserves cell polarity by separating the apical and basolateral membrane domains.Structurally, tight junctions are composed of proteins such as claudins and occludin, which create a barrier to diffusion between cells. Since they are the uppermost component of the junctional complex, the best exam-oriented answer is Apical. BIOCHEMISTRY

questions.stem: Two specimens from two different patients are received. Which technique can be used to confirm that they come from different individuals (in the context of Mycobacterium tuberculosis)?
questions.explanation: RFLP The question asks for a technique to determine if two Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) isolates are from different individuals, which is the fundamental task of molecular epidemiology—tracking an outbreak. This requires a "fingerprinting" method to compare the strains. Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP) (A) is the classic, gold-standard method for M.tb genotyping. It uses restriction enzymes to cut the bacterial DNA, and the resulting fragments are separated by size. The pattern, often based on the IS6110 insertion sequence, creates a unique "fingerprint." If the RFLP patterns from the two patients are different, it confirms they are infected with different strains and are not part of the same immediate transmission chain. Mutation analysis (B) and Pyrosequencing (C) are techniques used to look for specific, known mutations (e.g., for drug resistance), not to generate a comprehensive genomic fingerprint. RAPD (D) is another, older fingerprinting method, but RFLP is the traditional standard for M.tb.

questions.stem: Match the following blotting techniques with the type of biomolecule they detect: Blotting Technique Detects A. Southern blot 1. RNA B. Northern blot 2. Lipids C. Western blot 3. DNA D. Eastern blot 4. Protein
questions.explanation: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 This is a foundational concept in molecular biology, with the names being a famous mnemonic. A. Southern blot: Named after its inventor, Edwin Southern, this technique is used to detect specific sequences of DNA (3). B. Northern blot: Named by analogy (as a "geographic" opposite), this technique is used to detect specific sequences of RNA (1), and is often used to quantify gene expression. C. Western blot: Following the naming convention, this technique uses antibodies to detect specific Proteins (4). D. Eastern blot: This is a less common term that can refer to the detection of post-translational modifications or, as in this context, other biomolecules like Lipids (2). The correct matches are: A - 3B - 1C - 4D - 2This combination corresponds to option (A). 28. A 90-kg obese man is consuming a carbohydrate-rich diet. Which enzyme or intermediate is likely to be increased in his body? 1. Malonyl CoA 2. Acetyl CoA Carboxylase 3. PDH

questions.stem: Citrate Lyase
questions.explanation: 1,2,3,4 This scenario describes a high-energy, high-carbohydrate state, which strongly promotes de novo lipogenesis (fat synthesis). All four listed components are key players in this pathway. 1. A carbohydrate-rich diet leads to high glucose, high insulin, and high glycolysis, producing pyruvate. Pyruvate enters the mitochondria and is converted to acetyl-CoA by Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (PDH) (3), which is activated (dephosphorylated) by insulin. 2. This acetyl-CoA combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate. When energy needs are met, excess citrate is shuttled from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm. 3. In the cytoplasm, Citrate Lyase (4) cleaves citrate back into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. This is the source of cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis. 4. The rate-limiting, committed step of lipogenesis is catalyzed by Acetyl-CoA Carboxylase (ACC) (2), which carboxylates acetyl-CoA to form Malonyl-CoA (1). ACC is allosterically activated by citrate and also activated by insulin-mediated dephosphorylation. Therefore, in this fed state, the entire pathway is active, and all four enzymes and intermediates will be elevated.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not inhibit cytochrome c oxidase in the electron transport chain?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide (NO) Cytochrome C oxidase (Complex IV) is the final enzyme in the electron transport chain, transferring electrons to molecular oxygen. It contains heme iron and copper centers that are targets for several classic poisons. Cyanide (CN) (C) and Hydrogen Sulfide (H 2 S) (D) are potent inhibitors that bind to the ferric (Fe 3+ ) state of the heme a3 iron, preventing electron transfer and halting aerobic respiration. Carbon Monoxide (CO) (A) also inhibits Complex IV , but it binds to the ferrous (Fe 2+ ) state of the heme iron, competing with oxygen for the same binding site. This is the same mechanism by which it binds to hemoglobin. In contrast, Nitric Oxide (NO) (B) is primarily a physiological regulator of Complex IV , not a classic toxic blocker. While very high, non-physiological concentrations of NO can inhibit the enzyme, its normal role is as a reversible, signaling molecule that modulates respiration rates based on cellular needs. Therefore, in the context of classic ETC "blockers" or poisons, NO is the exception. 30. At what pH does glycine exist predominantly in its zwitterionic form, as indicated on its titration curve?

questions.stem: Which of these tissues is unable to take up glucose in states of insulin resistance, absence of insulin, or diabetes mellitus?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle Glucose uptake into cells is mediated by glucose transporters (GLUTs). The most important distinction is between insulin-dependent and insulin-independent transporters. Skeletal muscle (A) and adipose tissue are the primary users of the GLUT4 transporter. GLUT4 is an insulin-dependent transporter, meaning it is stored in intracellular vesicles and only translocates to the cell membrane to facilitate glucose uptake in response to insulin signaling. Therefore, in a state of insulin absence (like Type 1 Diabetes) or insulin resistance (like Type 2 Diabetes), glucose uptake into skeletal muscle is severely impaired. In contrast, the Brain (C) uses GLUT1 (at the blood-brain barrier) and GLUT3 (on neurons), both of which are insulin-independent to ensure a constant, vital supply of glucose. Red blood cells (B) exclusively use insulin-independent GLUT1. The Kidney (D) uses insulin-independent GLUT1 and GLUT2 (as well as SGLT) for glucose reabsorption from the filtrate. PATHOLOGY

questions.stem: Least common finding in diabetic kidney is
questions.explanation: Armani Ebstein Diabetic nephropathy is characterized by several progressive structural changes. GBM (Glomerular Basement Membrane) thickening (D) is one of the earliest and most consistent findings. Mesangial widening (C), due to the accumulation of extracellular matrix, is also a very early and common feature, which eventually progresses to the classic nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions). Podocyte loss (A) and effacement of their foot processes are now understood to be critical and common events that directly contribute to the development of albuminuria. The Armani-Ebstein lesion (B) refers to the presence of glycogen-filled vacuoles within the epithelial cells of the renal proximal convoluted tubules (pars recta). While this finding is virtually pathognomonic for diabetes mellitus, it is a rare finding in modern practice. It was historically seen in patients with extremely poor glycemic control and massive glycosuria, often in the setting of diabetic ketoacidosis, before effective insulin therapy was widely available. Therefore, among the choices, the Armani-Ebstein lesion is the least common finding in a modern context.

questions.stem: Alleles of gene pool belong to
questions.explanation: Population The term "gene pool" is a core concept in population genetics. It is defined as the complete set of all genes and their different alleles (genetic variations) that are present within a specific population (C). A population is a group of individuals of the same species that live in the same area and are capable of interbreeding. The gene pool represents the entire genetic diversity available to that population, which serves as the raw material for natural selection and evolution. An individual (A) carries only a small subset of the total gene pool (a maximum of two alleles for any given gene). A family (B) represents a closely related subset of the gene pool, but not its entirety. A single cell (D) contains the genetic information of only one individual. Thus, the concept of a "gene pool" is only meaningful at the level of a population.

questions.stem: In which type of thyroid carcinoma are multiple lytic skull lesions typically seen?
questions.explanation: Follicular carcinoma The metastatic patterns of thyroid cancers differ significantly. Follicular carcinoma (B) is classically known for its tendency to spread via hematogenous (bloodstream) dissemination, in contrast to papillary carcinoma, which spreads via lymphatics. Common sites for distant metastases from follicular carcinoma are the bone and lungs. Bone metastases are often osteolytic (bone-destroying) and can present as multiple lytic lesions on imaging. The skull, ribs, and vertebrae are common sites. Therefore, multiple lytic lesions in the skull are a classic presentation of metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma. Papillary carcinoma (A) is the most common type and primarily spreads to cervical lymph nodes. Hurthle cell carcinoma (C), a variant of follicular carcinoma, also has a high propensity for vascular invasion and distant bone metastases, but follicular carcinoma is the classic answer. Thyroid lymphoma (D) is a hematological malignancy and does not typically present with lytic bone lesions as its primary feature.

questions.stem: You would test for BRCA1 (and usually BRCA2) mutations, with BRCA1 being the primary gene associated with a strong family history of both breast and ovarian cancers.
questions.explanation: BRCA1/2 A strong family history of both breast and ovarian cancer is the classic hallmark of Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer (HBOC) syndrome. This syndrome is most commonly caused by an inherited germline mutation in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes (A). Mutations in these genes confer a significantly increased lifetime risk for developing breast cancer (often early-onset, triple-negative, or bilateral) and epithelial ovarian cancer, as well as other cancers like pancreatic and prostate cancer (especially BRCA2). While the other genes are also tumor suppressors, they are associated with different syndromes. P53 (B) mutations cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, which involves a wide array of cancers (sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, adrenocortical carcinoma). PTEN (C) mutations cause Cowden syndrome, linked to breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancers. CDH1 (D) mutations cause hereditary diffuse gastric cancer and lobular breast cancer. For the specific combination of breast and ovarian cancer, BRCA1/2 testing is the most appropriate first step.

questions.stem: BRCA testing is done by
questions.explanation: Whole exome sequencing Testing for hereditary cancer syndromes like those caused by BRCA1/2 mutations involves identifying any of a vast number of possible pathogenic variants (mutations) that can occur anywhere along the entire coding sequence of these large genes. The most comprehensive and standard modern method for this is Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS). Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) (B) is a broad NGS technique that sequences all coding regions (exons) of the genome, which would include the BRCA genes. In clinical practice, a more "targeted" NGS panel that focuses on BRCA1/2 and other relevant cancer-susceptibility genes is often used. RT-PCR (A) and qPCR (C) are methods used to detect and quantify RNA (gene expression), not to identify unknown DNA mutations. Southern blot (D) is an older technique used to detect large-scale DNA rearrangements or deletions. While large deletions can occur in BRCA, they are typically tested for using MLPA (Multiplex Ligation-dependent Probe Amplification), and the primary method for finding the more common point mutations and small insertions/deletions is sequencing.

questions.stem: Identify the incorrect association
questions.explanation: TP53 Mucosal neuroma This question assesses knowledge of hereditary cancer syndromes. The incorrect association is TP53 - Mucosal neuroma. Mucosal neuromas are a pathognomonic feature of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B), which is caused by a germline mutation in the RET proto-oncogene, not TP53. TP53 mutations cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, associated with sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenocortical carcinoma.The other associations are correct: 1. BRCA2 (A) mutations, known for breast/ovarian cancer, also significantly increase the risk of prostate cancer (often aggressive) and pancreatic cancer. 2. PTEN (B) mutations cause Cowden syndrome, which has a high risk of thyroid cancer (follicular type), breast cancer, and endometrial cancer. 3. STK11 (C) mutations cause Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, which, in addition to hamartomatous polyps, increases the risk for several cancers, including breast cancer.

questions.stem: Caspase-1 mediated cell death with inflammation is known as
questions.explanation: Pyroptosis Pyroptosis (A) is a lytic, highly inflammatory form of programmed cell death. It is defined by its dependence on the activation of Caspase-1. Pyroptosis is typically triggered by intracellular pathogens or danger signals, which are sensed by cytosolic inflammasomes (e.g., NLRP3). The inflammasome complex then cleaves pro-Caspase-1 into its active form. Active Caspase-1 has two key functions: 1. It cleaves the pore-forming protein Gasdermin D, which inserts into the cell membrane and causes cell lysis (oncosis) and the release of intracellular contents. 2. It cleaves pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 into their active, mature forms, which are then released from the lysing cell, driving a potent inflammatory response. Necroptosis (B) is also programmed and inflammatory but is caspase-independent (mediated by RIPK1/RIPK3/MLKL). Ferroptosis (C) is iron-dependent cell death via lipid peroxidation. Necrosis (D) is an un-programmed, pathological form of cell death.

questions.stem: Most common inherited bleeding disorder is
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand disease Von Willebrand disease (vWD) (A) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, with an estimated prevalence of up to 1% of the general population, although the number of clinically symptomatic individuals is lower. It is caused by a quantitative or qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor (vWF), a protein crucial for platelet adhesion (primary hemostasis) and for stabilizing Factor VIII in circulation. It typically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (e.g., easy bruising, nosebleeds, menorrhagia).Hemophilia A (C), a deficiency of Factor VIII, is the second most common inherited coagulation disorder, but it is much rarer than vWD, affecting approximately 1 in 5,000-10,000 males. Hemophilia B (D), a Factor IX deficiency, is even less common. Factor V deficiency (B) is an extremely rare bleeding disorder. Therefore, vWD is by far the most prevalent inherited bleeding disorder.

questions.stem: In which condition is erythropoietin considered beneficial for treatment?
questions.explanation: Anemia in chronic kidney disease Erythropoietin (EPO) is a hormone produced primarily by the peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in response to tissue hypoxia. It stimulates the bone marrow to produce red blood cells (erythropoiesis). In Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) (A), the progressive damage to the kidneys leads to a failure of these cells to produce adequate EPO. This results in the classic "anemia of chronic disease" or "anemia of CKD," which is a normocytic, normochromic anemia. This is a state of true EPO deficiency. Therefore, treatment with synthetic EPO (recombinant human erythropoietin or other erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, ESAs) is a cornerstone of management, as it directly replaces the missing hormone. In Nutritional anemia (C), the problem is a lack of substrates (e.g., iron, B12), and EPO levels are appropriately high. In Aplastic anemia (D), the bone marrow stem cells have failed; EPO levels are extremely high, but the marrow cannot respond. In MDS (B), the anemia is complex, and while some patients may respond to EPO, the most direct and classic indication is CKD.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with easy bruising and petechiae, a platelet count of 18,000/mm³, normal hemoglobin and leukocyte counts, and a recent mild upper respiratory infection. Her peripheral smear is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: Oral corticosteroids This patient has isolated thrombocytopenia (platelet count 18,000/mm³) with normal hemoglobin and leukocyte counts, a normal peripheral smear, and a recent viral infection. This presentation is classic for immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), an autoimmune condition in which antibodies (usually IgG) target platelets, leading to their destruction in the spleen. In adults with symptomatic ITP or platelet count below 30,000/mm³, the first-line treatment is corticosteroids (such as oral prednisone or dexamethasone). Steroids reduce antibody production and decrease splenic clearance of platelets.Platelet transfusion is reserved for severe or life-threatening bleeding, as transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed. Bone marrow biopsy is not routinely required when the clinical picture clearly suggests ITP. Splenectomy is considered a second-line therapy for chronic or steroid-refractory cases. Therefore, the most appropriate next step is oral corticosteroids. NODIA

questions.stem: A deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase is associated with which pattern of bilirubin levels?

options.text: Direct bilirubin increased, indirect bilirubin decreased, and urine urobilinogen/urobilin increased
Direct bilirubin normal, indirect bilirubin increased, and urobilinogen normal
Raised direct bilirubin, normal indirect bilirubin, and absent urine bilirubin
Indirect bilirubin increased, direct bilirubin normal, and raised urine urobilinogen

questions.explanation: Indirect bilirubin increased, direct bilirubin normal, and raised urine urobilinogen Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is an inherited enzymatic defect that makes red blood cells highly susceptible to oxidative stress. G6PD normally generates NADPH through the pentose phosphate pathway, which helps maintain glutathione in its reduced form. Reduced glutathione protects red blood cells from oxidative damage. When G6PD is deficient, oxidative stress (from infections, certain drugs, or fava beans) leads to hemolysis. During hemolysis, hemoglobin is released and broken down into heme, which is converted into biliverdin and then into unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin. Because this bilirubin is produced in excess, its level in blood rises. The liver itself is structurally normal and capable of conjugation, so direct (conjugated) bilirubin remains normal. However, increased amounts of unconjugated bilirubin reach the liver and then the intestine after conjugation.In the intestine, bilirubin is converted into urobilinogen. Since more bilirubin is being processed due to hemolysis, more urobilinogen is formed and reabsorbed into the bloodstream, leading to increased urinary urobilinogen levels.Thus, G6PD deficiency produces indirect hyperbilirubinemia with normal direct bilirubin and raised urine urobilinogen, corresponding to option (D).

questions.stem: Neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis is caused by which organism?
questions.explanation: Corynebacterium kroppenstedtii Idiopathic Granulomatous Mastitis (IGM) is a rare, chronic inflammatory breast condition. While often labeled "idiopathic," a specific subgroup known as Cystic Neutrophilic Granulomatous Mastitis has been strongly and specifically associated with infection by the lipophilic, gram-positive rod Corynebacterium kroppenstedtii (A). This organism is fastidious and difficult to culture, which is why the association was only recently established. It is thought to colonize and infect the breast ducts, triggering a robust inflammatory response characterized by granulomas (collections of histiocytes) and a prominent neutrophilic infiltrate, often leading to abscesses and sinus tracts. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (C) causes tuberculous mastitis, which features classic caseating granulomas, but not typically a neutrophilic component. Staphylococcus aureus (D) causes acute suppurative mastitis or abscesses, which are rich in neutrophils but do not form the organized granulomas of IGM. Corynebacterium minutissimum (B) is known for causing the superficial skin infection erythrasma.

questions.stem: Which of the following malignancies is unrelated to obesity?
questions.explanation: Stomach Obesity is a major modifiable risk factor for many cancers, acting through mechanisms like chronic inflammation, insulin resistance, and hormonal (adipokine/estrogen) dysregulation. There are well-established, strong links between obesity and Pancreatic cancer (B), Meningioma (C), and Multiple myeloma (D). The relationship with Stomach cancer (A) is more complex and site-specific. Obesity is a strong risk factor for cancer of the gastric cardia (the upper part of the stomach), which is thought to be mediated by the increased prevalence of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in obese individuals. However, obesity is not strongly associated, and may even be inversely related, to cancers of the non-cardia stomach (the main body and antrum), which are more commonly linked to H. pylori infection. Because the association is not straightforward and is location-dependent (unlike the clear links for B, C, and D), "Stomach" is the most likely correct answer for a malignancy that is not uniformly related to obesity.

questions.stem: Histopathological features of granulosa cell tumor include all except:
questions.explanation: CA-125 positivity Granulosa cell tumor (GCT) is the most common malignant sex cord-stromal tumor of the ovary. It has a set of classic histopathological and immunohistochemical features. 1. Call-Exner bodies (A) are a pathognomonic finding, representing small, rosette-like structures where granulosa cells arrange around a central eosinophilic, PAS-positive space. 2. Coffee bean nuclei (D) is the descriptive term for the tumor cell nuclei, which are ovoid and have a prominent longitudinal groove. 3. Inhibin A (B) is an immunohistochemical stain. As GCTs are derived from granulosa cells, they produce inhibin, and the tumor cells show strong, diffuse positivity for inhibin, making it a key diagnostic marker. CA-125 (C) is a tumor marker, both in serum and on immunohistochemistry, that is characteristic of epithelial ovarian cancers (e.g., serous carcinoma). While serum CA-125 can sometimes be elevated in GCT, it is not a specific or characteristic histopathological feature of the tumor cells themselves and is not used for primary diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which stain is not used to identify organisms in a renal transplant biopsy?
questions.explanation: Congo red In a renal transplant (immunocompromised) patient, a biopsy is often stained to rule out opportunistic infections. Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) (A) is the classic stain for fungi, highlighting fungal walls in black. It is used to identify Pneumocystis, Candida, or Aspergillus.PAS (Periodic Acid-Schiff) (B), while a standard stain for basement membranes, also stains fungal walls (magenta) and can help identify them.Masson Fontana (C) is a stain for melanin. It is used in microbiology to identify the capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans, which contains melanin-like pigments.In contrast, Congo red (D) is a special stain used to identify amyloid deposits. Amyloid stains orange-red with Congo red, and under polarized light, it exhibits a pathognomonic "apple-green" birefringence. This stain is used to diagnose amyloidosis, a protein deposition disease, and is not used to identify infectious organisms.

questions.stem: Why does not every Helicobacter pylori infection lead to ulcers?

options.text: Disease associated with host factors and environmental influences
Increased risk of peptic ulcer disease when H. pylori is present with NSAIDs
H. pylori infects the antrum even in asymptomatic individuals
Majority of H. pylori infections are asymptomatic

questions.explanation: Majority of H. pylori infections are asymptomatic Helicobacter pylori is a spiral-shaped, gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the gastric mucosa, particularly the antrum. Although it is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease and is associated with gastritis, gastric carcinoma, and MALT lymphoma, most infected individuals never develop clinically significant disease. The reason not every infection leads to ulcers is that the majority of infections remain asymptomatic. Many people harbor the organism for years without developing mucosal damage severe enough to produce ulceration. Ulcer formation depends on multiple interacting factors such as bacterial virulence (e.g., CagA, VacA strains), host immune response, gastric acid secretion levels, genetic susceptibility, and environmental influences like smoking or NSAID use.In many individuals, the infection causes only mild chronic gastritis without disrupting the protective mucosal barrier to the extent required for ulcer formation. Therefore, while H. pylori infection is common worldwide, only a small proportion of infected individuals develop peptic ulcers.Hence, most H. pylori infections do not lead to ulcers because they are asymptomatic and non-ulcerative in the majority of cases.

questions.stem: In which of the following situations does transplant rejection not occur?
questions.explanation: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)Transplant rejection is an immune response mediated by the recipient's T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes, which recognize the donor graft as foreign. This requires a functional adaptive immune system. Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) (C) is a group of genetic disorders characterized by a profound failure of both T-cell and B-cell development and function. Patients with "classic" SCID have no adaptive immune system and are therefore incapable of mounting an immune response. They cannot recognize or attack a foreign graft, so transplant rejection does not occur. (Instead, they are at high risk of Graft-versus-Host Disease from any T-cells within the transplant). Bare lymphocyte syndrome (A) is a type of SCID, so it is also correct, but SCID is the broader and more definitive answer. DiGeorge syndrome (D) involves T-cell deficiency but is often partial, so rejection is still possible. Chronic granulomatous disease (B) is a defect in phagocyte (innate) immunity, but T-cell (adaptive) immunity is intact and fully capable of rejection.

questions.stem: Identify the structure labeled in the histology image shown.
questions.explanation: Terminal bronchiole A terminal bronchiole is the last part of the conducting portion of the respiratory system. It is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium (often ciliated) and may contain Clara (club) cells. Importantly, its walls do not contain alveoli, which distinguishes it from respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts. In the given histology image, the labeled structure appears as a small airway with a relatively continuous wall and a well-defined lumen. There are no outpouchings of alveoli opening directly into its wall. This rules out: 1. Respiratory bronchiole – would show alveoli budding from its walls. 2. Alveolar duct – would have almost entirely alveolar walls with very little continuous bronchiolar epithelium. 3. Bronchus – would contain cartilage plates and submucosal glands, which are absent here. Since the structure lacks cartilage, lacks glands, and does not show alveoli arising from its wall, it corresponds to a terminal bronchiole, the final purely conducting airway before the respiratory portion begins. 50.
