questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy was found by his father to have agonal breathing at 5 AM while asleep. He was taken to the emergency department, where an ECG was obtained. Based on the ECG findings, what is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Brugada Syndrome The ECG shows a characteristic pattern of coved-type ST-segment elevation greater than 2 mm in the right precordial leads (V1-V3), followed by a negative T-wave. This is the pathognomonic Type 1 Brugada pattern. Brugada syndrome is an inherited cardiac channelopathy, caused by mutations in the sodium channel gene (SCN5A), that predisposes individuals to ventricular tachyarrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, often during sleep or rest. The clinical history of a young boy experiencing agonal respiration during sleep is a highly alarming presentation consistent with a malignant arrhythmic event, which strongly supports this diagnosis. Early repolarization syndrome has ST elevation but typically with a notched J-point and concordant T-waves. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may show deep T-wave inversions or signs of LVH, and atrial fibrillation would show an irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves, none of which are seen here.

questions.stem: Comment on the diagnosis from the ECG shown below.
questions.explanation: Second-degree infra-nodal heart block On the ECG strip, there are regular P waves occurring at a constant rate, but not every P wave is followed by a QRS complex. Some atrial impulses fail to conduct to the ventricles, resulting in dropped QRS complexes. The PR intervals of the conducted beats appear constant rather than progressively lengthening. This pattern is characteristic of Mobitz type II second-degree A V block, which usually occurs below the A V node, in the His-Purkinje system (infra-nodal level). In contrast, first-degree heart block shows prolonged PR interval but no dropped beats. Complete heart block demonstrates total A V dissociation, where atrial and ventricular rhythms are independent. A V dissociation can occur in various settings and does not necessarily imply complete block.Mobitz type II is clinically significant because it can progress to complete heart block and often requires pacemaker insertion. The presence of sudden non-conducted P waves with constant PR intervals in conducted beats supports the diagnosis of second-degree infra-nodal (Mobitz type II) heart block.

questions.stem: A male patient with a history of COPD is experiencing dyspnea and arrives at the emergency department. His arterial blood gas analysis reveals a pH of 7.28, pCO2 of 60 mmHg, and HCO3 - of /meqL28 . Based on these findings, what is the most accurate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Inadequately compensated respiratory acidosis To interpret the Arterial Blood Gas (ABG), we assess pH, , and . The pH is 7.28, which is below the normal range (7.35-7.45), indicating acidosis. The is 60 mmHg, which is high (normal range 35-45 mmHg), indicating a respiratory cause for the acidosis. The is 28 meq/L, which is slightly elevated (normal range 22-26 meq/L). This elevation in bicarbonate represents a metabolic compensation attempt by the kidneys to counteract the respiratory acidosis by retaining bicarbonate. However, since the pH is still in the acidotic range and has not returned to normal (7.35-7.45), the compensation is inadequate or partial. Therefore, the correct diagnosis is inadequately compensated respiratory acidosis, which is a common finding in an acute exacerbation of COPD.

questions.stem: Which is not a risk factor for Ca Gall Bladder?
questions.explanation: Polyp <10 mm Gallbladder carcinoma has several well-established risk factors. Gallstones (cholelithiasis) are the single most important risk factor, with the risk increasing with the size of the stones; a stone >3 cm significantly elevates the risk. A porcelain gallbladder, characterized by intramural calcification, carries a very high risk of underlying malignancy. Chronic inflammatory conditions of the biliary tree, such as Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis, also increase the risk. Gallbladder polyps are another known risk factor, but the risk is highly dependent on their size. Polyps that are less than 10 mm (1 cm) in diameter are generally considered to have a very low malignant potential and are often managed with ultrasound surveillance. In contrast, polyps greater than 10 mm are associated with a higher risk of malignancy and are a clear indication for cholecystectomy. Therefore, a small polyp (<10 mm) is not considered a significant risk factor.

questions.stem: A young woman presents to the emergency department with pain and vomiting. Examination reveals a swelling located lateral and below the pubic tubercle, and X-ray findings indicate intestinal obstruction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Strangulated Femoral Hernia The anatomical location of the swelling is key to this diagnosis. A femoral hernia occurs when abdominal contents protrude through the femoral canal, emerging through the femoral ring. The neck of a femoral hernia sac is located inferior to the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vein. Therefore, a palpable lump lateral and inferior to the pubic tubercle corresponds precisely to the location of a femoral hernia. These hernias have a narrow neck, making them highly prone to incarceration and strangulation, which would present with symptoms of intestinal obstruction like pain and vomiting. An inguinal hernia (B) would typically present as a swelling superior to the pubic tubercle. Adhesions (A) are a common cause of obstruction but do not produce an external swelling. An appendicular mass (D) is located in the right iliac fossa.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old patient diagnosed with Grade II steatohepatitis, who drinks 2–3 alcoholic beverages daily and has a BMI of 29, seeks guidance. Given their condition and habits, what is the most appropriate advice to provide?

options.text: Lifestyle modification + vitamin E + Ursodeoxycholic acid

questions.explanation: Lifestyle modification + regular exercise The patient has steatohepatitis (inflammation of the liver with fat accumulation), which is likely multifactorial, being contributed to by both alcohol consumption and factors related to metabolic syndrome (BMI of 29 is overweight). The cornerstone of management for both alcoholic and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is lifestyle modification. This includes complete cessation of alcohol, a healthy diet to promote weight loss, and regular exercise. Exercise improves insulin sensitivity and helps mobilize hepatic fat. While Vitamin E and Pioglitazone have been studied for non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), their use is typically reserved for biopsy-proven NASH in non-diabetic and diabetic patients, respectively, and lifestyle changes remain the primary intervention. Ursodeoxycholic acid is not effective for steatohepatitis. Therefore, the most crucial and universally agreed-upon recommendation is a comprehensive lifestyle change focusing on diet, exercise, and alcohol abstinence. 108. questions.stem: Which of the following acts by the mechanism illustrated in the given image?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pyogenes The image illustrates the mechanism of action of a superantigen. Unlike conventional antigens that are processed and presented in the peptide-binding groove of an MHC molecule, a superantigen binds externally to the MHC Class II molecule on an antigen-presenting cell and to the Vβ region of the T-cell receptor on a T-cell. This cross-linking bypasses the need for specific antigen recognition and leads to the massive, non-specific activation of a large fraction (up to 20%) of the T-cell population. This results in a "cytokine storm" and can cause systemic inflammation and shock. Streptococcus pyogenes produces several superantigens, such as the streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (e.g., SpeA, SpeC), which are responsible for the clinical manifestations of scarlet fever and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. Cholera toxin, botulinum toxin, and C. difficile toxins have different mechanisms of action (e.g., ADP-ribosylation, SNARE protein cleavage).

questions.stem: A farmer presents with fever, the clinical findings shown in the image, a creatinine level of 1.4, and a platelet count of 88,000. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Scrub typhus The clinical presentation of fever, thrombocytopenia (platelet count of 88,000), and mild renal impairment (creatinine of 1.4) in a farmer is suggestive of several zoonotic infections. However, the presence of an eschar (the necrotic lesion shown in the image) is a pathognomonic finding for scrub typhus. Scrub typhus is caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi and is transmitted by the bite of a chigger (larval mite). The chigger bite often results in an inoculation lesion that develops into a painless, dark-centered necrotic eschar with a surrounding erythematous halo. This finding, combined with the systemic symptoms and patient's occupation (exposure to mites in vegetation), makes scrub typhus the most likely diagnosis. Brucellosis, leptospirosis, and anthrax present differently and do not typically feature this type of eschar.

questions.stem: In which of the following does the genetic material show adenine not equal to thymine?
questions.explanation: HIV Chargaff's rules state that in double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), the amount of adenine (A) is equal to the amount of thymine (T), and the amount of guanine (G) is equal to the amount of cytosine (C). This rule applies to any organism with a dsDNA genome. Human mitochondrial DNA (A), E. coli bacteria (B), and Herpesviruses (D) all have dsDNA genomes, so in them, A=T and G=C. The Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) (C) is a retrovirus, and its genome consists of two copies of single-stranded RNA (ssRNA). Because its genetic material is single-stranded, there is no complementary strand to enforce the base-pairing rules. Therefore, the amounts of adenine and uracil (the RNA equivalent of thymine) are not necessarily equal, and the same is true for guanine and cytosine. This makes HIV the correct answer.

questions.stem: After 3 days of dengue infection, diagnosis can be made by all except which of the following?
questions.explanation: ELISA for antibody During a primary dengue infection, the virus and viral components are detectable first, followed by the host's immune response. On day 3 of the illness, the patient is typically in the acute viremic phase. During this time, the dengue virus itself can be detected, so methods like viral load measurement or RT-PCR (which detects viral RNA) would be positive. The dengue NS1 antigen is a viral non-structural protein that is secreted into the blood during active infection and is detectable by ELISA from day 1 up to day 9. In contrast, the host's antibody response takes time to develop. IgM antibodies, which are detected by ELISA, usually do not appear until day 4-5 of the illness and then rise to detectable levels. Therefore, on day 3, an antibody ELISA is the least likely test to be positive and is not the recommended diagnostic method for this early stage.

questions.stem: A rural resident has been experiencing CNS symptoms and loss of vision for 12 days. Electron microscopy reveals the organism shown in the image. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Acanthamoeba The image shows an amoeboid organism with irregular shape and characteristic spine-like projections (acanthopodia). These thorn-like pseudopods are a distinguishing feature of Acanthamoeba species.Clinically, Acanthamoeba can cause: 1. Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis (GAE) — a subacute CNS infection seen in immunocompromised individuals 2. Acanthamoeba keratitis — leading to vision loss, especially in contact lens users The patient’s CNS symptoms and vision loss over days to weeks strongly suggest Acanthamoeba infection. In contrast: 3. Naegleria fowleri causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), which is acute and rapidly fatal, and its trophozoites do not show acanthopodia. 4. Balamuthia also causes GAE but lacks the characteristic spine-like projections seen here. The presence of acanthopodia in the image confirms the organism as Acanthamoeba.Thus, the most likely causative organism is Acanthamoeba.

questions.stem: Vibrio cholerae disrupts which extracellular cell adhesion?
questions.explanation: Occludens Vibrio cholerae causes profuse watery diarrhea primarily through the action of cholera toxin, which leads to massive secretion of chloride ions and water into the intestinal lumen. However, recent research has also highlighted the role of other virulence factors in disrupting the intestinal barrier integrity. The cholera toxin's effect is compounded by proteases and other factors that disrupt the tight junctions between intestinal epithelial cells. Tight junctions, also known as zonula occludens, are multiprotein complexes that seal the paracellular pathway. The main transmembrane proteins forming these junctions are occludins and claudins. Disruption of these junctions by V . cholerae increases the permeability of the intestinal barrier, contributing to the massive fluid loss. Cadherins are components of adherens junctions, while integrins mediate cell-matrix adhesion. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: Which diagnostic investigation should be performed first to confirm the suspected diagnosis in a 26-year-old woman presenting with palpitations, weight loss, tremors, sweating, and diarrhea?
questions.explanation: TSH and free T4 The patient's constellation of symptoms—palpitations, weight loss despite a good appetite, tremors, heat intolerance (sweating), and diarrhea—is classic for hyperthyroidism or thyrotoxicosis. The initial and most crucial step in confirming this diagnosis is to perform thyroid function tests. The best initial screening and diagnostic tests are the measurement of serum Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) and free Thyroxine (free T4). In primary hyperthyroidism (the most common cause, e.g., Graves' disease), the thyroid gland overproduces T4 and/or T3, which suppresses the pituitary's production of TSH. Therefore, the characteristic biochemical finding is a low or undetectable TSH level with an elevated free T4 and/or free T3 level. While antibody tests (B) and ultrasound (D) are important for determining the underlying etiology (e.g., Graves' disease vs. toxic nodule), the initial confirmation of the hyperthyroid state relies on TSH and free T4 levels.

questions.stem: What is the recommended medication for treating watery diarrhea that occurs in a patient who developed this symptom while taking ampicillin for a URTI?
questions.explanation: Fidaxomicin A patient who develops watery diarrhea while taking ampicillin most likely has antibiotic-associated diarrhea due to overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile. Broad-spectrum antibiotics like ampicillin disrupt the normal intestinal flora, allowing C. difficile to proliferate and produce toxins (toxin A and toxin B). These toxins cause inflammation of the colon, leading to diarrhea, abdominal pain, and sometimes pseudomembranous colitis. Current guidelines recommend Fidaxomicin as the preferred first-line treatment for an initial episode of C. difficile infection. Fidaxomicin is a narrow-spectrum, bactericidal antibiotic that specifically targets C. difficile with minimal effect on normal gut flora. This selective action results in lower recurrence rates compared to oral vancomycin. It is administered orally and acts locally within the gastrointestinal tract.Metronidazole is no longer first-line except when other agents are unavailable. Ciprofloxacin may worsen the condition. Bezlotoxumab is used only to prevent recurrence, not as primary therapy. Thus, fidaxomicin is recommended.

questions.stem: Which diagnosis is most likely in a 30-year-old patient who presents with a week-long high fever, neck stiffness, a positive Kernig’s sign, and CSF findings of lymphocytic predominance, protein 80 mg/dL, glucose 20 mg/dL, with an RBS of 140 mg/dL?
questions.explanation: Tubercular meningitis The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis provides key clues. The presence of lymphocytosis (an increased number of lymphocytes) points away from typical acute bacterial meningitis, which usually causes a neutrophilic pleocytosis. The CSF glucose level is significantly low ($20~mg/dl$), especially when compared to the serum glucose (CSF/serum glucose ratio is <0.4), which is characteristic of infections where organisms consume glucose, such as bacterial or tuberculous meningitis. Viral meningitis typically has normal glucose levels. The protein level is moderately elevated ($80~mg/dl$). This combination of subacute onset, lymphocytic pleocytosis, very low glucose, and moderately high protein is the classic CSF profile for tubercular meningitis. Viral meningitis would have normal glucose, while bacterial meningitis would typically show a much higher cell count consisting of neutrophils.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man presents with neck stiffness and optic disc swelling. CSF analysis shows a capsulated fungus, confirmed by a positive India ink stain. In this context, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The pressure inside the skull remains unchanged.
Delay antiretroviral therapy by 4-6 weeks after the initiation of antifungal treatment.
Begin treatment with fluconazole taken by mouth.
Brain imaging shows changes $in>80\%$ of patients.

questions.explanation: Delay antiretroviral therapy by 4-6 weeks after the initiation of antifungal treatment. The clinical picture describes cryptococcal meningitis, a common opportunistic infection in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS. A major concern in managing this condition is the risk of Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS) if antiretroviral therapy (ART) is started too soon. IRIS can lead to a paradoxical worsening of symptoms and increased intracranial pressure. Therefore, current guidelines recommend starting antifungal therapy first and delaying the initiation or re-initiation of ART for at least 4-6 weeks. This allows for a reduction in the fungal burden before the immune system is reconstituted by ART. Intracranial pressure is almost always elevated, often severely. Initial treatment (induction phase) for cryptococcal meningitis requires intravenous amphotericin B (often with flucytosine), not oral fluconazole. Brain imaging is often normal in the early stages.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old diabetic man falls and later develops high fever, cough, shortness of breath, and confusion. His chest X-ray shows lobar consolidation, and his lab results reveal elevated BUN and creatinine. What is the most suitable management approach?

options.text: Discharge home on amoxicillin with clavulanic acid.

questions.explanation: Inpatient management with levofloxacin. This patient has community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). To determine the appropriate management, we use a severity score like CURB-65 (Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30, Blood pressure <90/60, Age ≥65). This patient scores at least 3 points (Confusion, elevated BUN, Age ≥65), indicating severe pneumonia that requires inpatient management, likely in an ICU setting. For severe CAP , guidelines recommend combination therapy. Standard inpatient therapy for non-severe CAP often involves a respiratory fluoroquinolone like levofloxacin or a beta-lactam (like ceftriaxone) plus a macrolide (like azithromycin). Given the severity and the options, inpatient management with a respiratory fluoroquinolone is a very appropriate choice. Discharging the patient home would be unsafe. Monotherapy with ceftriaxone might be insufficient as it doesn't cover atypical pathogens.

questions.stem: A known RA (Rheumatoid Arthritis) patient presents to the ER with hypotension. She abruptly stopped her medications. Her vitals and labs show: HR 110= bpm, /BP 80 40= mmHg, blood /,agar mg dl50= Na 130= meq/L, ./ .Km eq L60= What should be the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Hydrocortisone This patient is presenting with an adrenal crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency). Patients with chronic inflammatory diseases like rheumatoid arthritis are often on long-term steroid therapy, which suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. Abrupt cessation of these steroids can lead to an inability to produce endogenous cortisol, resulting in an adrenal crisis, especially under physiological stress. The clinical picture of hypotension, shock, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia is classic for this condition. While IV fluids and vasopressors may be needed for support, the cornerstone and most critical immediate treatment is the administration of stress-dose hydrocortisone. This directly replaces the deficient glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity, reversing the underlying pathophysiology. Sodium bicarbonate might be used for severe acidosis but is not the primary treatment.

questions.stem: Workup of a 25-year-old hotel worker shows the following profile:• HBsAg = Negative • Anti-HBs = Negative • HBeAg Negative • Anti-HBe Negative • Total anti-HBc = Positive What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Window period/Gap period In this serological profile:HBsAg = NegativeAnti-HBs = NegativeHBeAg = NegativeAnti-HBe = NegativeTotal anti-HBc = PositiveThe key finding is isolated anti-HBc positivity. During the natural course of acute hepatitis B infection, there is a phase called the window period. In this period, HBsAg has disappeared, but anti-HBs has not yet appeared. Therefore, both HBsAg and anti-HBs are negative. The only detectable marker during this time is anti-HBc, particularly IgM anti-HBc, which indicates recent infection. Total anti-HBc includes both IgM and IgG antibodies, so its positivity supports exposure to hepatitis B virus.Chronic hepatitis B would show persistent HBsAg positivity. An inactive carrier state also requires HBsAg positivity. Remote past infection would typically show anti-HBs positivity along with anti-HBc.Since HBsAg and anti-HBs are both negative but anti-HBc is positive, the most appropriate diagnosis is the window (gap) period of acute hepatitis B infection.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman diagnosed with ulcerative colitis is having 3–4 episodes of bloody diarrhea per day. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for her condition?
questions.explanation: Sulfasalazine The patient's presentation suggests mild-to-moderate active ulcerative colitis. The first-line treatment for inducing and maintaining remission in such cases is an aminosalicylate (5-ASA) compound. Sulfasalazine is a classic 5-ASA drug that consists of sulfapyridine linked to mesalamine (5-ASA). The mesalamine component has a topical anti-inflammatory effect on the colonic mucosa. Other 5-ASA preparations like mesalamine itself are also used. For patients with mild-to-moderate disease, these agents are effective and generally well-tolerated. Azathioprine is an immunomodulator used for steroid-dependent or refractory disease. Budesonide is a corticosteroid used for induction of remission in Crohn's disease or moderate UC, but 5-ASAs are typically tried first. Bezlotoxumab is a monoclonal antibody for preventing C. difficile recurrence and has no role in UC. NODIA

questions.stem: What is the stain used for cervical smear?
questions.explanation: Papanicolaou stain The stain used for a cervical smear, commonly known as a Pap smear or Pap test, is the Papanicolaou stain. This is a polychromatic staining technique developed by Dr. Georgios Papanikolaou. It uses a combination of stains, including hematoxylin for the nucleus and other cytoplasmic stains like Orange G and Eosin Azure, to provide excellent differentiation of various cell types found in the smear. This allows cytopathologists to detect cellular abnormalities, including precancerous changes (dysplasia) and cervical cancer, with high precision. Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) is the standard stain for histopathology (tissue sections), not cytology smears. Giemsa stain is used for peripheral blood smears and bone marrow. Congo red is a special stain used to identify amyloid deposits.

questions.stem: For a 65-year-old woman with epithelial ovarian cancer presenting with peritoneal metastasis and ascites, what is the typically recommended sequence of treatment?
questions.explanation: Debulking followed by chemotherapy The standard of care for advanced epithelial ovarian cancer (Stage III/IV) is primary debulking surgery (or cytoreductive surgery) followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. The goal of the surgery is to remove all visible tumor ("optimal debulking" to no residual disease, if possible), as the amount of residual disease is a powerful prognostic factor. Following recovery from surgery, the patient typically undergoes multiple cycles of platinum-based chemotherapy (e.g., carboplatin and paclitaxel) to treat any microscopic residual disease. An alternative approach, neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by interval debulking surgery, is reserved for patients who are medically unfit for extensive primary surgery or have disease that is deemed unresectable upfront. Radiotherapy has a very limited role in the primary management of advanced epithelial ovarian cancer. Therefore, the most common and recommended sequence is surgery first, then chemotherapy.

questions.stem: When counseling a 39-year-old G6P3A3 woman with three prior LSCS complicated by placenta accreta spectrum, which point would typically not be included in the counseling discussion?
questions.explanation: Risk of bowel injury A patient with multiple prior cesarean sections who develops a placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) disorder is at extremely high risk for severe maternal morbidity. Counseling must be comprehensive. The main risks include: 1 Massive obstetric hemorrhage (excessive bleeding): This is the most significant and life-threatening risk. 2 Cesarean hysterectomy (chances of hysterectomy): This is often the planned and necessary management to control bleeding. 3 Injury to adjacent organs: Because the placenta often invades through the uterine wall anteriorly into the bladder, the risk of bladder injury is very high and a specific, expected complication. While bowel injury is a potential risk in any complex abdominal surgery, it is less of a direct and specific complication of PAS itself compared to bladder injury. The placenta in PAS is typically located anteriorly over the old C-section scar, directly adjacent to the bladder, whereas the bowel is located more posteriorly. Therefore, while mentioned, it would be less emphasized than the near certainty of bleeding and high risk of bladder injury and hysterectomy.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks presents with painful vaginal bleeding and decreased fetal movements. Examination shows a tense uterus measuring 34 weeks, absent fetal heart rate, BP 160/90, and on vaginal exam the cervix is 6 cm dilated, 70% effaced, with a vertex at –3 and intact membranes. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Initiate antihypertensives and perform artificial rupture of membranes (ARM)
Commence antihypertensive treatment and proceed with emergency LSCS.
Administer tocolytics and prepare for vaginal delivery.

questions.explanation: Initiate antihypertensives and perform artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) This patient's presentation is classic for a severe placental abruption, complicated by severe hypertension and intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD). The management goals are now focused entirely on the mother's safety. Since the fetus is already deceased (FHR absent), there is no fetal indication for an emergency Cesarean section. In fact, a vaginal delivery is generally safer for the mother, especially in the setting of potential coagulopathy (DIC) which can accompany severe abruption. The patient is already in active labor (6 cm dilated). The most appropriate management is to: 1 Initiate antihypertensives to control her dangerously high blood pressure and prevent maternal complications like stroke. 2 Augment labor to achieve a prompt vaginal delivery. Artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) is a key step to accelerate labor and may also help reduce intrauterine pressure. An emergency LSCS would expose the mother to unnecessary surgical risks.

questions.stem: In a woman in labor with a cervix that is 70% effaced, 3 cm dilated, and a palpable “bag of worms,” what is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Rupture membranes to confirm cord prolapse.

questions.explanation: Proceed with emergency LSCS A palpable "bag of worms" on vaginal examination in a laboring patient is the classic description of a funic presentation or an impending umbilical cord prolapse with intact membranes. This is an obstetric emergency because if the membranes rupture, the cord will prolapse into the vagina, where it can be compressed by the fetal presenting part, cutting off blood flow and oxygen to the fetus. The definitive management is immediate delivery. Therefore, the most appropriate action is to prepare for and proceed with an emergency Lower Segment Cesarean Section (LSCS). While waiting for the C-section, measures should be taken to prevent cord compression, such as placing the mother in the knee-chest position and manually elevating the presenting part off the cord. Rupturing the membranes or starting oxytocin would be catastrophic as it would worsen the situation and lead to fetal compromise.

questions.stem: Causes of non-immune hydrops fetalis are all except:
questions.explanation: ABO incompatibility Hydrops fetalis is the excessive accumulation of fluid in fetal extravascular compartments and body cavities. It is broadly divided into immune and non-immune types. Non-immune hydrops accounts for about 90% of cases and has numerous causes, including cardiac abnormalities (structural or arrhythmic), chromosomal anomalies (e.g., Turner syndrome, trisomies), and infections (e.g., Parvovirus B19, CMV). Immune hydrops is caused by maternal red blood cell alloimmunization, where maternal antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red blood cells, leading to severe anemia and heart failure. The classic cause is Rh incompatibility. ABO incompatibility is another cause of immune-mediated hemolysis (hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn), but it very rarely causes hydrops. Since ABO incompatibility is an immune-mediated process, it is the exception in a list of causes for non-immune hydrops.

questions.stem: What serves as a reliable indicator of perinatal asphyxia?
questions.explanation: Cord pH <7.2 Perinatal asphyxia is a condition of impaired gas exchange leading to fetal hypoxemia and hypercapnia. The most objective and reliable evidence of a significant intrapartum hypoxic-ischemic event is the analysis of umbilical cord arterial blood gas. Severe metabolic or mixed acidemia, demonstrated by a low cord blood pH, is a key criterion. According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), a cord arterial pH of <7.0 is a major indicator of an acute hypoxic event. While a pH of <7.2 is less severe, it still represents significant acidemia and is the most reliable objective marker among the choices provided. Low APGAR scores can be caused by factors other than asphyxia (e.g., maternal medication, prematurity). Hypotonia and hypocalcemia are potential consequences of asphyxia but are not primary diagnostic indicators and lack specificity. 179. A PAP smear from a 45-year-old woman with a left ovarian mass is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.stem: What is the likely cause of the patient’s condition based on the CSF findings of elevated lymphocytes, increased protein (63), and reduced glucose (20)?
questions.explanation: Tuberculous meningitis The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis provides key clues to the etiology of meningitis. The presence of a lymphocytic pleocytosis (increased lymphocytes) argues against typical acute bacterial meningitis, which is characterized by a predominance of neutrophils. The significantly decreased glucose level (hypoglycorrhachia), often less than 40% of the serum glucose level, is a hallmark of infections where organisms actively consume glucose, such as bacterial, fungal, or tuberculous meningitis. Viral meningitis typically presents with normal CSF glucose. The moderately increased protein level is also consistent with an infectious or inflammatory process. This specific combination—a subacute clinical course with lymphocytic pleocytosis, very low glucose, and elevated protein—is the classic CSF profile for Tuberculous Meningitis. 132. Match the following: 1. Trisomy 13 a. GLU-V AL re - placement 2. Trisomy 18 b. Edwards syn-drome 3. Trisomy 21 c. Down syndrome

questions.stem: Sickle cell anemia d. Patau syndrome
questions.explanation: 1-d, 2-b, 3-c, 4-a This question requires matching genetic conditions with their common names or molecular basis. Trisomy 13 is the chromosomal abnormality that causes Patau syndrome. Trisomy 18 is the cause of Edwards syndrome. Trisomy 21 is the most common autosomal trisomy and is the genetic basis for Down syndrome. Sickle cell anemia is a molecular disease caused by a specific point mutation in the beta-globin gene, which leads to the replacement of glutamic acid (GLU) with valine (V AL) at the sixth position of the beta-globin protein chain. Therefore, the correct matches are 1-d, 2-b, 3-c, and 4-a. The other options present incorrect associations between these well-known genetic disorders and their definitions.

questions.stem: A patient in the ICU being treated for sepsis had an initial arterial blood gas (ABG) showing: .pH 69= ; pO2 = 80 mm Hg; pCO5 52 = mm Hg; /HCOm eq L103 = . A repeat ABG 2 hours later showed: pH = 6.7; pO2 100= mm Hg; pCO2 20= mm Hg; /HCOm eq L53 = . What factor is most likely responsible for the observed changes in the ABG results?

options.text: Excessive air and less heparin in ABG sample
Excess air and more heparin in ABG sample
Less air and more heparin in ABG sample
Less air and less heparin in ABG sample

questions.explanation: Excess air and more heparin in ABG sample This question describes common pre-analytical errors in ABG sampling. The changes from the first to the second sample are a significant drop in pCO 2 (from 55 to 20), a rise in pO 2 (from 80 to 100), and a worsening acidosis (pH drop, HCO 3 drop). Contamination of the blood sample with excess air (an air bubble) will cause the pO 2 of the blood to move towards the pO 2 of room air (~150 mmHg) and the pCO 2 to move towards the pCO 2 of room air (~0 mmHg), explaining the rise in pO 2 and the drastic fall in pCO 2 . The use of excess liquid heparin as an anticoagulant can cause a dilution error, lowering the measured HCO 3 and pCO 2 . The heparin itself is also acidic and can contribute to a lower pH. Therefore, the combination of excess air and excess heparin best explains the specific changes observed between the two ABG samples.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with blood in her stool and has firm, enlarged inguinal lymph nodes. A contrast-enhanced CT scan reveals a suspicious malignant mass in the lower gastrointestinal tract. Where is this mass most likely situated?

options.text: Anal canal inferior to the pectinate line

questions.explanation: Anal canal inferior to the pectinate line The lymphatic drainage of the rectum and anal canal is divided by the pectinate (dentate) line. The area superior to the pectinate line, including the proximal rectum and sigmoid colon, drains primarily to the internal iliac and inferior mesenteric lymph nodes. The area inferior to the pectinate line, which is derived from the embryonic proctodeum (ectoderm), has lymphatic drainage similar to the perianal skin. This drainage goes to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. Therefore, the presence of enlarged inguinal lymph nodes in a patient with a lower gastrointestinal malignancy strongly suggests that the primary tumor is located in the anal canal, inferior to the pectinate line. Tumors in the distal or proximal rectum or sigmoid colon would typically metastasize to internal pelvic or abdominal lymph nodes, not the inguinal nodes.

questions.stem: What are the characteristics of sweat chloride and pancreatic chloride levels in individuals with cystic fibrosis?

options.text: Chlorine concentration increase in pancreatic secretion
Chlorine concentration normal in pancreatic secretion

questions.explanation: Chlorine transport decrease in sweat Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene, which codes for a chloride ion channel. The function of this channel differs depending on the tissue. In the duct of the sweat gland, the CFTR channel is responsible for reabsorbing chloride from the primary sweat into the body. When the channel is defective, this reabsorption fails, leading to a high concentration of chloride in the sweat, which is the basis for the diagnostic sweat test. So, chloride transport out of the sweat duct is decreased. In contrast, in secretory epithelia like the pancreas and respiratory tract, the CFTR channel's primary role is to secrete chloride into the lumen, which drives the movement of water and creates thin, watery secretions. In cystic fibrosis, this chloride secretion is defective, leading to thick, viscous mucus that obstructs the ducts. SURGERY

questions.stem: Which of the following tumor markers are positive for seminoma?1 PLAP 2 OCT3/4 3 NANOG 4 HCG
questions.explanation: 1,2,3,4 Seminoma is the most common type of testicular germ cell tumor. Its diagnosis is aided by a panel of immunohistochemical markers. Placental-like alkaline phosphatase (PLAP) is a classic membrane marker that is positive in the majority of seminomas. OCT3/4 and NANOG are nuclear transcription factors that are markers of pluripotency and are considered highly sensitive and specific for seminoma and embryonal carcinoma. They are consistently expressed in virtually all seminomas. Human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) can also be focally positive in seminomas due to the presence of scattered syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells. While elevated serum hCG is found in only about 10-15% of cases, the tumor cells themselves can show positivity on IHC. Therefore, all four listed markers can be positive in a seminoma.

questions.stem: Which is the most important prognostic factor of breast cancer patients?
questions.explanation: Pathological staging Pathological staging is considered the most important prognostic factor in breast cancer because it incorporates multiple critical determinants of outcome into a single comprehensive system. It is based on the TNM classification, which includes tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N), and presence or absence of distant metastasis (M). After surgical removal of the tumor, pathological staging provides accurate information about the true extent of disease. Although lymph node status is a very strong individual prognostic factor, it is actually a component of pathological staging. Similarly, tumor size and hormone receptor status (ER/PR) are important, but they represent only parts of the overall disease profile.Pathological stage correlates closely with survival rates, recurrence risk, and treatment decisions. Higher stages indicate greater tumor burden and worse prognosis. It guides decisions regarding chemotherapy, radiotherapy, hormonal therapy, and targeted therapy.Therefore, because it integrates tumor size, nodal status, and metastasis into one standardized assessment, pathological staging is the single most important prognostic factor in breast cancer patients.

questions.stem: Body Surface Area (BSA)
questions.explanation: 45% This question likely refers to estimating the total body surface area (TBSA) affected by a burn in an adult using the "Rule of Nines." The Rule of Nines is a standardized method used to quickly assess the percentage of the body affected by burns. In an adult, the body is divided into regions that represent approximately 9% or multiples of 9% of the TBSA. The allocations are: Head and Neck (9%), each Upper Limb (9% each), Anterior Trunk (18%), Posterior Trunk (18%), each Lower Limb (18% each), and the Perineum (1%). The question is incomplete, but if it describes burns to the entire anterior trunk (18%), the entire posterior trunk (18%), and one entire arm (9%), the total would be 18 + 18 + 9 = 45%. Other combinations are possible, but 45% is a plausible total derived from major burn areas. NODIA

questions.stem: What is the appropriate initial management for a 9-month-old infant who has a respiratory rate of 48 breaths per minute but shows no chest retractions or other symptoms?

options.text: Send back home after starting oral antibiotics

questions.explanation: No treatment needed According to the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI), the diagnosis of pneumonia in infants aged 2 to 12 months is based on the presence of fast breathing or chest in drawing. For this age group, fast breathing is defined as a respiratory rate of 50 breaths per minute or more. This infant's respiratory rate is 48 breaths per minute, which is within the normal range. Furthermore, the infant shows no danger signs like chest retractions, grunting, lethargy, or inability to feed. In the absence of both fast breathing (tachypnea) and any danger signs, the child does not meet the criteria for pneumonia. The condition is likely a simple cough or cold that does not require antibiotic treatment. Therefore, the most appropriate management is to reassure the parents and advise on supportive care at home, with no specific medical treatment needed.

questions.stem: An 18-day-old infant presents with fever, cough, and vesicles on the trunk and upper limbs. The mother reports a history of genital ulcers one year ago that have since healed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex This clinical scenario is highly suggestive of neonatal herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. Key features pointing to this diagnosis include the patient's age (neonate, 18 days old), the presence of a vesicular rash, systemic symptoms (fever, cough), and a maternal history of genital ulcers. Neonatal HSV is most commonly acquired during delivery (perinatally) from a mother with an active genital HSV infection, although the infection can be asymptomatic in the mother. The presentation can be localized to the skin, eyes, and mouth (SEM disease), involve the central nervous system (CNS disease), or be disseminated. Varicella (chickenpox) in a neonate is possible but less likely, especially with the specific maternal history. Molluscum contagiosum presents as umbilicated papules, not vesicles. HPV causes warts and is not associated with this acute presentation. The combination of neonatal age, vesicles, and maternal history makes HSV the most probable diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the least teratogenicity?
questions.explanation: HSV-2 (Herpes Simplex Virus-2) Teratogenicity refers to the ability of an agent to cause congenital malformations during fetal development. Rubella, CMV , and Varicella are well-established teratogens. Congenital Rubella Syndrome can cause deafness, cataracts, and cardiac defects. Congenital CMV is a leading cause of sensorineural hearing loss and neurodevelopmental disabilities. Congenital Varicella Syndrome, though rare, can cause limb hypoplasia, skin scarring, and eye defects. In contrast, Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) is not considered a classic teratogen. The primary risk from maternal HSV is neonatal herpes, which is an infection acquired by the infant during or shortly after birth (perinatally), rather than a congenital malformation syndrome caused by in-utero infection during organogenesis. While intrauterine HSV infection can rarely occur and cause severe damage, the overwhelming majority of HSV-related disease in newborns is perinatal. Therefore, compared to the other viruses listed, HSV-2 has the least teratogenic potential.

questions.stem: A 4-day-old infant is brought to the pediatric clinic with suspected pulmonary hypertension. Which of the listed inhalational agents is approved for treating this condition?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide Inhaled Nitric Oxide (iNO) is a selective pulmonary vasodilator and is the standard, FDA-approved treatment for Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN). PPHN is a condition where the infant's circulation fails to transition from fetal to newborn patterns, leading to high pressure in the pulmonary arteries, right-to-left shunting of blood, and severe hypoxemia. When inhaled, nitric oxide diffuses into the pulmonary vascular smooth muscle, activating guanylate cyclase and increasing cGMP levels, which causes smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation specifically in ventilated areas of the lung. This improves ventilation-perfusion matching and reduces pulmonary artery pressure without causing systemic hypotension. The other agents listed—methoxyflurane, sevoflurane, and halothane—are volatile anesthetic agents used for general anesthesia and are not used for the primary treatment of PPHN.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl has had fever and a retro-orbital headache for 2 days. She tests positive on both the tourniquet test and the NS1 antigen test. Which of the following is a criterion for severe disease?
questions.explanation: AST and ALT >1000 The patient has confirmed dengue fever. The WHO classifies dengue into "dengue without warning signs," "dengue with warning signs," and "severe dengue." Severe dengue is defined by the presence of severe plasma leakage (leading to shock or fluid accumulation with respiratory distress), severe bleeding, or severe organ involvement. A marked elevation in liver transaminases, specifically AST or ALT levels ≥ 1000 IU/L, is a criterion for severe organ involvement (severe hepatitis). Continuous vomiting and liver enlargement >2 cm are considered warning signs that predict progression to severe disease, but they are not criteria for severe dengue itself. Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia are common laboratory findings in all forms of dengue fever and do not define severe disease. Therefore, the significantly elevated liver enzymes (AST and ALT > 1000) is the only option listed that is a direct criterion for classifying the illness as severe dengue. ORTHOPEDICS

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with bilateral, symmetrical tenderness in the joints of her hands and ankles, along with marked early-morning stiffness but no redness on examination. Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis This presentation is highly characteristic of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). The key features are: an insidious onset of symmetrical polyarthritis affecting small joints (hands, ankles), and significant morning stiffness lasting for a prolonged period (typically >1 hour). The absence of erythema does not rule out RA, as synovitis can present primarily with swelling, warmth, and tenderness without prominent redness. Osteoarthritis typically involves larger, weight-bearing joints asymmetrically, and morning stiffness is usually brief (<30 minutes). Gout typically presents as an acute, intensely painful, and erythematous monoarthritis, most commonly in the great toe. Psoriatic arthritis can be symmetrical but is often asymmetrical ("sausage digits" or dactylitis) and is associated with psoriasis. Given the symmetry, joint distribution, and prolonged morning stiffness in a middle-aged female, RA is the most likely diagnosis.

questions.stem: For which type of fractures does the Hawkins classification apply?
questions.explanation: Talus The Hawkins classification is a system used specifically to categorize fractures of the neck of the talus. The talus is a crucial bone in the ankle joint that has a tenuous blood supply, making it highly susceptible to avascular necrosis (A VN) after a fracture. The Hawkins classification is prognostically important as it correlates the degree of fracture displacement with the risk of developing A VN. 1. Type I: Undisplaced vertical neck fracture. 2. Type II: Displaced fracture with subtalar joint subluxation/dislocation. 3. Type III: Displaced fracture with both subtalar and tibiotalar joint dislocation. 4. Type IV: (Added later) Type III with additional talonavicular joint dislocation. The risk of A VN increases significantly from Type I to Type IV . This classification does not apply to fractures of the tibia, humerus, or calcaneus, which have their own respective classification systems. 162. questions.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect related to the given image?

options.text: Result from the aberrant migration of primordial germ cells

questions.explanation: Prechordal plate anomaly The image shows a large sacrococcygeal teratoma (SCT), the most common congenital tumor in newborns. SCTs arise from pluripotent primordial germ cells from Hensen's node that fail to migrate correctly during embryonic development (C). They are true teratomas, meaning they contain tissues derived from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm), so it is common to find differentiated structures like teeth and hair within them (B). The majority of SCTs diagnosed at birth are histologically benign (mature teratomas) (A), although there is a risk of malignant transformation, which increases with the age at diagnosis. A prechordal plate anomaly (D) is related to developmental defects in the anterior midline of the embryo, leading to conditions like holoprosencephaly, and is not associated with the pathogenesis of sacrococcygeal teratomas, which originate at the caudal end of the embryo.

questions.stem: A child is brought to the ER in an unconscious state after severe vomiting and abdominal pain episodes. /m inHR 100= and /BP 100 60= mm Hg. Work-up shows .,pH 72= blood glucose 300 mg/dL, and ketones 3+. What should be the best management?

options.text: Infusion of 0.05-0.1 U/kg dose insulin after 1 hour of IVF
0.1 Unit/kg insulin stat followed by infusion of 0.5 U-0.1 U/kg dose insulin and IVF
./Uk g01 insulin subcutaneous stat followed by IVF
IVF followed by subcutaneous 0.1 U/kg insulin

questions.explanation: Infusion of 0.05-0.1 U/kg dose insulin after 1 hour of IVF The child presents with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a life-threatening complication characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. The cornerstone of management is correcting dehydration, hyperglycemia, electrolyte imbalances, and acidosis. The first priority is fluid resuscitation with intravenous fluids (IVF), typically an isotonic solution like 0.9% saline. Insulin therapy should not be started until after the initial fluid bolus and after at least one hour of fluid replacement. This is crucial because giving insulin immediately can cause a rapid shift of water into brain cells, potentially leading to cerebral edema. An insulin bolus is no longer recommended in pediatric DKA for the same reason. The standard protocol is to start a continuous intravenous infusion of regular insulin at a rate of 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour after the initial hour of fluid therapy.

questions.stem: A child arrives with acute respiratory distress, and examination shows a scaphoid abdomen. Which of the following interventions should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation: Bag and mask ventilation The clinical picture of a newborn in respiratory distress with a scaphoid (sunken) abdomen is highly suggestive of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). In CDH, abdominal organs herniate into the chest cavity, compressing the developing lung and causing pulmonary hypoplasia. In this situation, bag and mask ventilation is contraindicated. This is because it forces air not only into the lungs but also into the stomach and intestines. The air insufflated into the herniated abdominal viscera will cause them to distend further, increasing the compression on the already hypoplastic lung, worsening the respiratory distress, and compromising cardiovascular function. The immediate management requires endotracheal intubation to secure the airway and provide controlled positive pressure ventilation directly to the lungs, bypassing the gastrointestinal tract. Oxygen therapy is also essential.

questions.stem: A child is receiving oxygen through a nasal cannula at 3 L/min. What is the delivered FiO 2 (fraction of inspired oxygen)?
questions.explanation: 30% In oxygen therapy using a nasal cannula, the delivered FiO₂ increases approximately 4% for every 1 L/min increase in oxygen flow, starting from room air.Room air contains about 21% oxygen. The approximate formula used clinically is:FiO₂ ≥ 21% + (4 × flow rate in L/min)For a flow rate of 3 L/min:FiO₂ ≥ 21% + (4 × 3)FiO₂ ≥ 21% + 12%FiO₂ ≥ 33%However, because nasal cannula provides variable FiO₂ (depending on the patient’s tidal volume, respiratory rate, and inspiratory flow), the delivered oxygen concentration is usually approximated.Clinically accepted values are: 1 L/min → 24% 2 L/min → 28% 3 L/min → 30% 4 L/min → 36% 5 L/min → 40% Thus, at 3 L/min, the commonly accepted delivered FiO₂ is approximately 30%, making option (B) correct.

questions.stem: What feature is not typically associated with Down syndrome?
questions.explanation: Caudal regression Caudal regression syndrome is a rare congenital disorder characterized by abnormal development of the lower (caudal) end of the spine. It is most strongly associated with uncontrolled maternal diabetes mellitus, not Down syndrome (Trisomy 21). The other features listed are commonly associated with Down syndrome. Short stature is a nearly universal finding. Hypothyroidism, most often congenital, occurs with increased frequency in individuals with Down syndrome, necessitating newborn screening. Hearing loss is also very common, affecting up to 75% of individuals, and can be conductive, sensorineural, or mixed. Other common features of Down syndrome include characteristic facial features (upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, flat nasal bridge), intellectual disability, congenital heart defects (especially atrioventricular septal defects), and an increased risk of duodenal atresia and leukemia. Because caudal regression is not a recognized feature of Trisomy 21, it is the correct answer.

questions.stem: A child developed a fever following the DPT vaccine at 6 weeks. Now at 10 weeks, the child is due for the next dose. What is the recommended approach?
questions.explanation: Give DPT Vaccination A mild to moderate fever is a common, expected, and self-limited side effect following the DPT (Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus) vaccination. It is not considered an adverse event or a contraindication to future doses. The fever is typically due to the inflammatory response to the vaccine components, particularly the whole-cell pertussis component in older formulations. According to immunization guidelines, common, anticipated reactions like fever, local soreness, or irritability do not preclude subsequent vaccination. True contraindications to the pertussis component of the DPT vaccine are rare and include severe events like an immediate anaphylactic reaction or the development of encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose. Since a simple fever is not a contraindication, the child should continue with their immunization schedule as planned to ensure they are protected. Therefore, the correct course of action is to administer the DPT vaccination at 10 weeks.

questions.stem: A child has had fever for 6 days along with a strawberry tongue, conjunctival congestion, and skin peeling. What is the appropriate management for this presentation?
questions.explanation: IVIg The clinical presentation—prolonged fever (>5 days), strawberry tongue, bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, and skin peeling (desquamation) of the extremities—is classic for Kawasaki disease. This is an acute, febrile, systemic vasculitis of medium-sized arteries, primarily affecting young children. The most serious complication is the development of coronary artery aneurysms, which can lead to myocardial infarction and sudden death. The cornerstone of treatment is the administration of Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIg), typically a single high dose of 2 g/kg. IVIg significantly reduces the incidence of coronary artery aneurysms from approximately 25% to less than 5%. High-dose aspirin is also a standard part of the initial therapy for its anti-inflammatory effects, which is then reduced to a low dose for its anti-platelet effects. While both A and B are part of the management, IVIg is the most critical intervention for preventing long-term cardiac complications. 154. questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has had recurrent blisters and oral ulcers for 3 years, and the histology shown is provided. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris The combination of clinical history and histological findings is pathognomonic for Pemphigus Vulgaris. Clinically, this autoimmune blistering disease is characterized by painful, flaccid bullae and erosions on the skin and mucous membranes, with oral involvement being very common and often the first manifestation. The provided histology confirms the diagnosis by showing a suprabasal, intraepidermal split. This occurs due to acantholysis—the loss of adhesion between keratinocytes—caused by autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 and 1. The basal layer of keratinocytes remains attached to the basement membrane, creating a characteristic "row of tombstones" appearance. In contrast, Bullous Pemphigoid, Dermatitis Herpetiformis, and Linear IgA disease are all subepidermal blistering diseases, meaning the split occurs below the entire epidermis, which would appear different histologically.

questions.stem: Mark the correct statement/statements regarding Inner and Outer hair cells?I. Inner hair cells are in a single row and transmit auditory impulses. II. Outer hair cells are in 3-4 rows and modulate function of inner hair cells. III. Outer hair cells are more responsible for movement of Tectorial membrane. IV . Outer and inner hair cells present in the ratio of 3:1.

options.text: I, II and IV are correct
I, II and III are correct

questions.explanation: I, II and IV are correct 1. Statement I is correct. Inner hair cells (IHCs) are arranged in a single row along the cochlea and are the primary sensory receptors of hearing. They convert mechanical sound vibrations into electrical impulses and transmit auditory signals through the cochlear nerve to the brain. 2. Statement II is also correct. Outer hair cells (OHCs) are arranged in three to four rows and function mainly as modulators. They possess electromotility due to the motor protein prestin, allowing them to contract and elongate. This action amplifies basilar membrane vibrations and enhances the sensitivity and frequency selectivity of inner hair cells. 3. Statement III is incorrect. The primary movement of the tectorial membrane results from sound-induced vibration of the basilar membrane. Outer hair cells mainly amplify and fine-tune this motion rather than being directly responsible for moving the tectorial membrane. 4. Statement IV is correct. Outer hair cells outnumber inner hair cells in approximately a 3:1 ratio. Therefore, statements I, II, and IV are correct. ANAESTHESIA

questions.stem: What is the correct sequence of steps for intubation? a. Flexion of lower cervical spine and extension of Atlanto-occipital joint b. Inflate cuff of endotracheal tube c. Introduce a laryngoscope from the right side of mouth d. Confirm the position of tube
questions.explanation: a, c, b, d The correct sequence for a standard orotracheal intubation is as follows: 1 Position the Patient (a): First, the patient's head and neck must be positioned correctly to align the oral, pharyngeal, and tracheal axes. This is achieved by placing the patient in the "sniffing position," which involves flexion of the lower cervical spine and extension at the atlanto-occipital joint. 2 Perform Laryngoscopy (c): The laryngoscope blade is introduced into the right side of the patient's mouth, sweeping the tongue to the left to expose the glottic opening. 3 Insert and Secure the Tube (b): Once the vocal cords are visualized, the endotracheal tube is passed through them into the trachea. Immediately after insertion, the cuff is inflated to create a seal in the trachea. 4 Confirm Placement (d): Finally, the position of the tube must be confirmed to ensure it is in the trachea and not the esophagus. This is done by observing chest rise, auscultating for bilateral breath sounds, and, most reliably, by detecting end-tidal CO2 with capnography. Therefore, the correct sequence is a, c, b, d. RADIOLOGY

questions.stem: Two doctors were asked to interpret 100 X-rays, and the resulting Kappa value is 0.71. How should this be interpreted?
questions.explanation: Good The Cohen's Kappa coefficient (κ) is a statistical measure of inter-rater reliability or agreement for categorical items. It accounts for the possibility of agreement occurring by chance. The interpretation of the Kappa value can vary slightly, but the Landis and Koch scale is widely accepted: 1. κ ≥ 0: Poor agreement 2. κ = 0.01–0.20: Slight agreement 3. κ = 0.21–0.40: Fair agreement 4. κ = 0.41–0.60: Moderate agreement 5. κ = 0.61–0.80: Substantial agreement 6. κ = 0.81–1.00: Almost perfect agreement A Kappa value of 1.0 indicates perfect agreement, while a value of -1.0 indicates perfect disagreement. A value of 0.71 falls squarely within the "Substantial agreement" range, which is often colloquially referred to as "Good" agreement. It indicates that the two doctors have a high level of consistency in their X-ray interpretations, well beyond what would be expected by chance.

questions.stem: The banana sign is seen in:
questions.explanation: Spina bifida The "banana sign" is a classic prenatal ultrasonographic finding that is strongly associated with an open spina bifida. Spina bifida is a neural tube defect where the spinal column fails to close properly. In most cases, this is associated with an Arnold-Chiari II malformation, where the posterior fossa structures (cerebellum and brainstem) are pulled downwards into the foramen magnum. This downward displacement causes the cerebellum to lose its normal dumbbell shape and become flattened and curved anteriorly, resembling a banana. The banana sign is often seen in conjunction with the "lemon sign," which is a scalloping or indentation of the frontal bones of the fetal skull. The presence of these signs on a second-trimester ultrasound is highly suggestive of an open neural tube defect. 191. A child presents with breathlessness. On chest x-ray, the following object is seen. Identify? NODIA

questions.stem: A patient is found to have a tear in the antero-inferior portion of the glenoid capsule and labrum. What is this lesion called?
questions.explanation: Bankart's lesion The lesion described is a Bankart's lesion. This is the essential pathology in traumatic anterior shoulder instability and consists of a detachment of the anteroinferior portion of the glenoid labrum from the glenoid rim. This injury occurs during an anterior shoulder dislocation when the humeral head is forced out of the glenoid socket, tearing the labrum, capsule, and inferior glenohumeral ligament complex. If a piece of the glenoid bone is fractured along with the labrum, it is termed a "bony Bankart." In contrast, a Hill-Sachs lesion is a compression fracture or impaction deformity on the posterosuperior aspect of the humeral head. It occurs concurrently with a Bankart lesion when the soft humeral head impacts against the hard anterior glenoid rim during the dislocation event. The description in the question specifically refers to the labral tear, which is the Bankart's lesion.

questions.stem: In which of the following fractures is the three bony point relationship maintained?
questions.explanation: Supracondylar fracture The "three bony point relationship" of the elbow refers to the alignment of the medial epicondyle, the lateral epicondyle, and the tip of the olecranon. In a normally extended elbow, these three points form a straight line. When the elbow is flexed to 90 degrees, they form an isosceles triangle. This relationship is disrupted in an elbow dislocation, as the olecranon (part of the ulna) moves out of its normal articulation with the humerus. However, in a supracondylar fracture, the fracture line is located on the distal humerus above the epicondyles. Therefore, the relationship between the two epicondyles and the olecranon remains intact because the distal fragment (containing the epicondyles) moves along with the ulna and radius. Fractures of the epicondyles themselves (options A and B) can cause local swelling that obscures the landmarks, but the fundamental geometric relationship of the three points is preserved relative to the olecranon. Supracondylar fracture is the classic example where this relationship is maintained despite significant deformity.

questions.stem: A woman in the outpatient department has arthritis affecting multiple joints symmetrically, including the wrists, hands, and feet. She reports morning stiffness lasting more than an hour, along with swollen and tender joints. Which type of arthritis is most likely suggested by these findings?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis This clinical picture is a classic presentation of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). The key diagnostic clues are: 1 Symmetric polyarthritis: Involvement of the same joints on both sides of the body is a hallmark of RA. 2 Joint Distribution: The predilection for small joints of the hands (wrists, MCP , PIP joints) and feet is characteristic. 3 Inflammatory Nature: The presence of swollen and tender joints indicates synovitis. 4 Prolonged Morning Stiffness: Stiffness lasting more than one hour is highly suggestive of an inflammatory arthritis like RA, as opposed to the brief stiffness seen in osteoarthritis. Osteoarthritis is typically asymmetrical and causes stiffness for less than 30 minutes. Gout usually presents as an acute, severe monoarthritis. Psoriatic arthritis can be symmetrical but is often asymmetrical and may be accompanied by skin or nail changes. The combination of all these features makes RA the most probable diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures is not typically implicated in a positive Trendelenburg gait?
questions.explanation: Sciatic nerve A positive Trendelenburg sign or gait is caused by weakness of the hip abductor muscles, primarily the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus. These muscles are responsible for stabilizing the pelvis during the single-leg stance phase of gait. When they are weak, the pelvis drops on the opposite (unsupported) side. The innervation for both the gluteus medius and minimus muscles comes from the superior gluteal nerve. Therefore, damage to this nerve or weakness in these muscles will lead to a Trendelenburg gait. The sciatic nerve innervates the posterior thigh muscles (hamstrings) and all the muscles of the lower leg and foot. While a very high lesion could potentially affect nerves branching off near the hip, it is not the primary nerve responsible for hip abduction, and its injury is not the typical cause of a Trendelenburg gait. Therefore, the sciatic nerve is the structure not typically implicated. OBS & GYNE

questions.stem: A girl using DMPA for contraception has menstrual bleeding on her expected date and then again on day 15 of the same cycle. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Perform a urinary pregnancy test (UPT) before administering DMPA
Administer DMPA along with 7 days of barrier contraception

questions.explanation: Perform a urinary pregnancy test (UPT) before administering DMPA Irregular menstrual bleeding and spotting are the most common side effects of DMPA, a progestin-only injectable contraceptive. While this bleeding pattern is often an expected side effect, it can also be a sign of other conditions, including pregnancy or an ectopic pregnancy. The most critical step before administering the next dose of any contraceptive, especially in the context of abnormal bleeding, is to rule out pregnancy. A urinary pregnancy test (UPT) is a quick, inexpensive, and reliable method to do this. Administering DMPA to a pregnant woman is contraindicated. Therefore, the safest and most appropriate next step in management is to perform a UPT. If the test is negative and other causes are ruled out, the DMPA can be administered, and the patient can be counseled about the common side effect of irregular bleeding.

questions.stem: Among the following tumors, which is a virilizing tumor of the ovary?
questions.explanation: Arrhenoblastoma Virilizing tumors are those that secrete androgens, leading to the development of male secondary sexual characteristics in a female, such as hirsutism, clitoromegaly, voice deepening, and temporal balding. The classic example of a virilizing ovarian tumor is the Arrhenoblastoma, also known as a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor. These are rare sex cord-stromal tumors that contain testicular structures (Sertoli and Leydig cells) which produce androgens. In contrast, Theca cell tumors are typically estrogen-producing, causing symptoms like abnormal uterine bleeding. Brenner tumors are usually benign and hormonally inactive. Carcinoid tumors of the ovary can be hormonally active but typically produce serotonin, leading to carcinoid syndrome, not virilization. Therefore, arrhenoblastoma is the correct answer.

questions.stem: How do sweat chloride levels and pancreatic chloride levels typically appear in individuals with cystic fibrosis?

options.text: Chlorine concentration increase in pancreatic secretion
Chlorine concentration normal in pancreatic secretion

questions.explanation: Chlorine transport decrease in sweat Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene, which codes for a chloride ion channel. The function of this channel differs by organ. In the ducts of sweat glands, the CFTR channel's primary role is to reabsorb chloride ions from the sweat back into the body. In CF, this channel is defective, leading to decreased reabsorption (transport) of chloride. This failure to reabsorb chloride results in a high concentration of chloride in the sweat, which is the basis of the sweat chloride test for diagnosing CF. Therefore, statement B is correct. In contrast, in the pancreas, the CFTR channel normally secretes chloride into the pancreatic ducts, which helps draw water into the secretions. In CF, defective chloride secretion leads to thick, dehydrated pancreatic secretions, which obstruct the ducts. This means chloride concentration in pancreatic secretions is decreased, not increased or normal.

questions.stem: In a patient with uterine inversion in whom the placenta is still attached, what is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Excise the placenta before repositioning the uterus
Reposition the uterus inside without removing the placenta
Transfer the patient to the operating theater for surgical repositioning of the uterus under general anesthesia

questions.explanation: Reposition the uterus inside without removing the placenta Acute uterine inversion is a rare but life-threatening obstetric emergency. The cardinal rule in managing an inversion with the placenta still attached is to reposition the uterus immediately without first attempting to remove the placenta. Attempting to separate the placenta before the uterus is repositioned can trigger massive, uncontrollable hemorrhage from the exposed, atonic placental implantation site. The attached placenta can also act as a handle to help guide the repositioning (Johnson's maneuver). Once the uterine fundus is returned to its normal anatomical position, uterine tone is restored, which constricts the blood vessels. After repositioning and administration of uterotonics, the placenta can then be safely removed. Transferring to the operating theater may be necessary if manual repositioning fails, but the first attempt should be made immediately upon diagnosis. 171. questions.stem: Determine the diagnosis indicated by the provided image.
questions.explanation: Acromegaly The image shows an individual with characteristic facial features of acromegaly. These features include a prominent brow (frontal bossing), an enlarged nose, thickened lips, and prognathism (protrusion of the jaw). Acromegaly is a hormonal disorder that results from excessive production of growth hormone (GH) by a pituitary adenoma in adulthood. Since the epiphyseal plates of the long bones have already closed, excessive GH cannot cause an increase in height. Instead, it leads to the enlargement of acral parts (hands, feet) and the characteristic coarsening of facial features, as well as soft tissue swelling and various metabolic complications. Gigantism (A) is caused by excess GH before the fusion of the epiphyseal plates, leading to excessive linear growth. Down's syndrome and dwarfism have entirely different clinical appearances and etiologies.

questions.stem: Which of the following criteria corresponds to ASA grade III?

options.text: Patient is moribund, can't survive without surgery
Severe illness which is a constant threat to life

questions.explanation: Severe illness The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status classification system is used to assess the preoperative health of a patient. ASA Grade III is defined as a patient with a severe systemic disease that is not incapacitating but does cause some functional limitation. Examples include poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension, stable angina, or a history of myocardial infarction more than three months ago. This is distinct from ASA II (A), which is a patient with mild systemic disease. It is also different from ASA IV (C), which is a patient with a severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life. ASA V (B) describes a moribund patient not expected to survive without the operation. Therefore, "Severe illness" is the best description for ASA III among the choices.

questions.stem: A patient reports genital pain, and on examination, there are painful vesicles along with tender lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Herpes Simplex Virus Type 2 (HSV-2) The clinical presentation of multiple, grouped painful vesicles on an erythematous base in the genital region, accompanied by tender, painful regional lymphadenopathy, is the classic picture of a primary genital herpes infection. While both HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause genital herpes, HSV-2 is historically and still more commonly associated with genital tract infections. A primary infection is often accompanied by systemic symptoms like fever and malaise. In contrast, HPV (B) typically causes painless warts (condyloma acuminata). Herpes Zoster (shingles) (C) is a reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus and presents as a dermatomal, usually unilateral, vesicular rash. While HSV-1 (D) can cause genital lesions, it is more traditionally associated with orofacial infections ("cold sores"), and HSV-2 remains the most frequent cause of genital herpes.

questions.stem: A patient arrives at the emergency department displaying symptoms of hypotension (blood pressure at 90/60 mmHg), following the abrupt cessation of a medication previously prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis. Laboratory tests reveal hyperkalemia (potassium level at 6.5 mEq/L), normonatremia (sodium level at 139 mEq/L), alongside signs of dehydration, pronounced hypotension (/90 40 mmHg), and hypoglycemia (blood glucose at /)mg dL40 . Considering these clinical signs, which medication is imperative for the immediate management of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Hydrocortisone This patient is presenting with an adrenal crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency). Patients with chronic inflammatory diseases like rheumatoid arthritis are often on long-term steroid therapy, which suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. Abrupt cessation of these steroids can lead to an inability to produce endogenous cortisol, resulting in an adrenal crisis, especially under physiological stress. The clinical picture of hypotension, shock, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia (though masked here), and hyperkalemia is classic for this condition. While IV fluids and vasopressors may be needed for support, the cornerstone and most critical immediate treatment is the administration of stress-dose hydrocortisone. This directly replaces the deficient glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity, reversing the underlying pathophysiology. Sodium bicarbonate might be used for severe acidosis but is not the primary treatment.

questions.stem: A patient with fever and eschar. What will be the treatment?
questions.explanation: Doxycycline The combination of fever and a cutaneous eschar is a classic presentation for a rickettsial infection, most notably scrub typhus (caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi) or other spotted fever group rickettsioses. The eschar represents the site of the arthropod (mite or tick) bite where local necrosis has occurred. The treatment of choice for most rickettsial diseases, including scrub typhus, is doxycycline. It is a bacteriostatic antibiotic that is highly effective and leads to rapid clinical improvement. Azithromycin is a suitable alternative, especially in pregnant women and children. Adding ceftriaxone is not indicated as beta-lactam antibiotics are ineffective against these obligate intracellular bacteria. Monotherapy with doxycycline is the standard and sufficient treatment for uncomplicated cases.

questions.stem: A patient on antitubercular therapy is reassessed 10 days after starting treatment. Their AST and ALT levels are normal, serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, but serum uric acid is elevated at 10 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate modification to their management plan?

options.text: Discontinue pyrazinamide while maintaining the rest of the antitubercular regimen.
Add uric acid reducing drugs and continue ATT as such with LFT/KFT monitoring.
Continue all drugs and monitor serum uric acid level and LFT and KFT.
Stop all ATT drugs till labs are normal

questions.explanation: Continue all drugs and monitor serum uric acid level and LFT and KFT. Hyperuricemia is a very common and expected side effect of pyrazinamide, one of the first-line anti-tubercular drugs. It occurs because pyrazinamide's metabolite, pyrazinoic acid, competes with uric acid for renal tubular secretion, leading to its retention. However, this asymptomatic hyperuricemia, in the absence of symptoms of gouty arthritis, is generally considered a benign and manageable side effect. Standard guidelines recommend to continue all anti-tubercular drugs and simply monitor the patient. Stopping a crucial first-line drug like pyrazinamide is not warranted for asymptomatic hyperuricemia. Adding uric acid-lowering agents is only considered if the patient develops symptomatic gout. Since the liver and renal functions are normal, continuing the current regimen with monitoring is the most appropriate course of action. 130.
