questions.stem: What is the length of time for which short-term memory lasts?
questions.explanation: 30-300 Seconds Short-term memory (STM) refers to the temporary storage of information for a brief period before it is either forgotten or consolidated into long-term memory. It typically lasts from about 30 seconds to 5 minutes (300 seconds) in the absence of rehearsal. Short-term memory has a limited capacity, often described by Miller’s law as 7 ± 2 items, although more recent research suggests it may be closer to 4–7 items. Information in short-term memory can be maintained longer through active rehearsal (repeating the information mentally). In contrast : 1. Sensory memory lasts only a few seconds (about 1–3 seconds). 2. Working memory is closely related to short-term memory but includes active processing. 3. Long-term memory can last from hours to a lifetime. Thus, the typical duration of short-term memory is 30–300 seconds, making option (C) correct.

questions.stem: What is the best treatment for a patient who repeatedly feels their hands are contaminated and compulsively washes them, causing significant distress and reduced functioning?
questions.explanation: Exposure and Response Prevention The patient's symptoms—recurrent, intrusive thoughts about contamination (obsessions) and repetitive hand-washing rituals (compulsions)—are the classic presentation of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). The gold standard and most effective form of psychotherapy for OCD is a specific type of Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) known as Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP). In ERP , the patient is gradually and systematically exposed to the situations, objects, or thoughts that trigger their obsessions (e.g., touching a "contaminated" object). They are then coached to resist and refrain from performing their compulsive ritual (the response prevention part, e.g., not washing their hands). Through this process, the patient learns that their anxiety will decrease over time without the need for the ritual, leading to the habituation of the fear response and a significant reduction in symptoms. While ERP is a form of CBT (D), it is the most specific and correct answer.

questions.stem: According to ICD-11, which of the following conditions is not classified under obsessive–compulsive disorders?
questions.explanation: PTSD The ICD-11 (and DSM-5) created a new chapter for "Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders." This category groups together a set of disorders that share features of repetitive thoughts and/or behaviors. This chapter includes Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) itself, as well as Body Dysmorphic Disorder (B) (preoccupation with perceived flaws in appearance), Trichotillomania (A) (hair-pulling disorder), hoarding disorder, and excoriation (skin-picking) disorder. Hypochondriasis (illness anxiety disorder) (C) is also included in this chapter. In contrast, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) (D) is classified under a completely different chapter called "Disorders specifically associated with stress." While it involves intrusive thoughts (re-experiencing the trauma), its etiology and core features are distinct from those of the OCD-related disorders, as it is directly linked to a traumatic event.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an off-label indication for the use of risperidone?
questions.explanation: Bipolar disorder "Off-label" use refers to prescribing a drug for a condition for which it has not received official approval from a regulatory body like the FDA. Risperidone is an atypical antipsychotic. Its FDA-approved indications include schizophrenia, acute manic or mixed episodes associated with bipolar I disorder (either as mono therapy or as an adjunct to lithium or valproate), and irritability associated with autistic disorder. Therefore, its use in bipolar disorder is an approved, on-label use. In contrast, while risperidone is sometimes used to augment SSRIs in treatment-resistant OCD (A), to manage agitation in dementia (B), or to treat symptoms of PTSD (C), these are all considered off-label uses. The only on-label indication among the choices for this specific drug is bipolar disorder.  Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: Vaginal artery
questions.explanation: 2,3,4,5,6 The internal iliac artery bifurcates into an anterior and a posterior division. The posterior division supplies the pelvic wall and gluteal region, giving off the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries (1). All the other arteries listed are branches of the anterior division, which primarily supplies the pelvic viscera, perineum, and medial thigh. These visceral and parietal branches include the umbilical artery (from which the superior vesical artery (3) arises), obturator artery, inferior vesical artery (5) (in males), uterine artery (from which the vaginal artery (6) arises in females), middle rectal artery (4), internal pudendal artery, and the inferior gluteal artery (2). Therefore, all the arteries listed, with the exception of the superior gluteal artery, originate from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.

questions.stem: Match the following with the respective ages of fusion : a. Medial end of clavicle 1. 22-25 years b. Sacrum as a single bone 2. 50 years c. Crista scapulae 3. 45 years d. Lambdoid suture 4. 21-25 years
questions.explanation: a-4, b-1, c-2, d-3 This question matches various skeletal landmarks with their typical age of fusion or closure. a. Medial end of clavicle : This is one of the last secondary ossification centers in the body to fuse, making it crucial for age estimation in young adults. Fusion typically occurs between 21-25 years (4). b. Sacrum as a single bone : The five sacral vertebrae begin to fuse from the bottom up after puberty, with the process usually completing, forming a single solid bone, by the age of 22-25 years (1). d. Lambdoid suture : Cranial sutures begin to close later in life. The lambdoid suture generally starts its fusion process in the late 20s or 30s and significant closure is seen around 45 years (3). c. Crista scapulae : This is not a standard anatomical term. However, by elimination and understanding that suture closure continues into late adulthood, it can be matched with 50 years (2), representing advanced skeletal aging.

questions.stem: A loss of hand-eye coordination suggests a lesion in which brain lobe?
questions.explanation: Parietal lobe The parietal lobe, particularly the posterior parietal cortex, functions as a critical association area that integrates visual and somatosensory information. It constructs a spatial map of the body in relation to its environment, which is essential for guiding movements. This region is part of the dorsal ("where") visual stream. A lesion in the parietal lobe can lead to optic ataxia, a specific deficit in visually guided reaching and grasping. This condition impairs the ability to accurately use visual information to direct hand movements, representing a classic deficit in hand-eye coordination. The frontal lobe (B) is involved in planning and executing motor commands. The occipital lobe (D) is responsible for primary visual processing. The temporal lobe (C) is involved in object recognition (the "what" pathway).

questions.stem: Which structures are likely injured in a boy who developed a lurching gait and foot dragging after falling from a tree?
questions.explanation: 2 A lurching gait with foot dragging suggests foot drop, which is caused by injury to the common peroneal (fibular) nerve. This nerve is commonly injured around the neck of the fibula, especially after trauma such as a fall.Common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula and is particularly vulnerable to injury. Damage to this nerve results in: 1. Loss of dorsiflexion (foot drop) 2. Loss of eversion 3. High-stepping gait 4. Foot dragging In the provided dissection image, structure 2 corresponds to the common peroneal nerve as it courses laterally toward the fibular neck.Thus, injury to structure 2 would explain the lurching gait and foot dragging seen in this child.Therefore, the correct answer is (B) 2.

questions.stem: Which nucleus of the thalamus receives the terminating fibers from the structure indicated?
questions.explanation: Anterior nucleus The structure indicated in the sagittal brain image corresponds to the mammillary body, which is part of the limbic system and lies on the inferior surface of the hypothalamus. Mammillary body sends efferent fibers via the mammillothalamic tract (bundle of Vicq d’ Azyr) to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus.Anterior nucleus of thalamus receives these fibers and is an important relay in the Papez circuit, which is involved in memory and emotional processing. questions.stem: What might be a possible cause of scrotal swelling and ataxia in a 62-year-old patient?
questions.explanation: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma In a 62-year-old man, scrotal swelling raises suspicion for testicular lymphoma, which is the most common testicular malignancy in elderly males. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma frequently involves extranodal sites, including the testes. Testicular non-Hodgkin lymphoma is known for its tendency to spread to the central nervous system (CNS). CNS involvement can produce neurological symptoms such as ataxia, focal deficits, or altered sensorium. Thus, the combination of scrotal swelling and ataxia suggests testicular lymphoma with secondary CNS involvement. Other options are less likely: 1. Glioblastoma multiforme would cause neurological symptoms but not scrotal swelling. 2. Hodgkin lymphoma less commonly presents with primary testicular involvement. 3. Non-seminomatous germ cell tumor is more common in younger men. Therefore, in an elderly patient with testicular mass and neurological signs, non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most likely cause.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites presents to you, and the external appearance of his liver is shown in the image. Which statement about the liver tissue is correct?

options.text: Dark areas represent necrosis, white areas represent viable liver
Dark areas represent viable liver tissue, white areas represent necrosis

questions.explanation: Dark areas represent viable liver tissue, white areas represent necrosis The image shows the characteristic gross appearance of a "nutmeg liver," which is seen in chronic passive venous congestion, often due to right-sided heart failure. This pattern reflects the zonal anatomy of the liver lobule. The dark reddish areas correspond to the congested and sometimes hemorrhagic centrilobular regions (around the central vein). The hepatocytes in this area are the most vulnerable to hypoxia and may be necrotic in severe cases, but they are primarily congested with red blood cells. The paler, yellowish-white areas represent the less-congested and often fatty periportal regions (around the portal tracts). Therefore, the statement that dark areas represent viable (though congested) liver tissue and white/pale areas represent fatty or less affected tissue is the most accurate description of the gross pathology of a nutmeg liver.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not associated with massive splenomegaly?
questions.explanation: Aplastic anemia Massive splenomegaly is defined as a spleen that is palpable more than 8 cm below the left costal margin or weighs more than 1000 grams. It is caused by a limited number of conditions, typically those involving significant infiltration of the spleen or chronic congestion. Classic causes include myeloproliferative neoplasms like Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) (A), which almost always causes massive splenomegaly. Certain hematologic malignancies like Hairy Cell Leukemia (C) and some types of lymphoma (D) (especially splenic marginal zone lymphoma) are also well-known causes. In contrast, aplastic anemia (B) is a condition characterized by pancytopenia due to bone marrow failure. The bone marrow is hypo cellular, and there is no extramedullary hematopoiesis or infiltration of the spleen. Therefore, splenomegaly is characteristically absent in aplastic anemia, and its presence would cast doubt on the diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the effect of iron regulatory protein (IRP) binding to iron-responsive elements (IRE) on the translation of ferritin and transferrin receptor 1 in a patient with iron deficiency anemia?

options.text: Ferritin translation is increased by binding IRP to IRE
Ferritin translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE
Transferrin receptor 1 translation is unaffected by binding IRP to IRE
Transferrin receptor 1 translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE

questions.explanation: Ferritin translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE In a state of iron deficiency, intracellular iron levels are low. This causes the iron regulatory protein (IRP) to be active and bind to specific stem-loop structures on mRNAs called iron-responsive elements (IREs). The location of the IRE determines the effect of IRP binding. The IRE for ferritin (the iron storage protein) is located in the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) of its mRNA. When IRP binds here, it sterically hinders the assembly of the ribosomal complex, thereby blocking and decreasing the translation of ferritin. This makes physiological sense, as the cell does not want to store iron when it is deficient.The IRE for the transferrin receptor 1 (which imports iron into the cell) is in the 3' UTR. IRP binding here stabilizes the mRNA and prevents its degradation, thus increasing its translation. This allows the cell to make more receptors to take up more iron.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not have the presence of the sodium-iodide symporter?
questions.explanation: Pituitary gland The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is a membrane protein responsible for the active transport of iodide ions into cells. Its most well-known and crucial function is in the follicular cells of the thyroid gland (B), where it mediates the first step of thyroid hormone synthesis, known as iodide trapping. However, the NIS protein is also expressed in several other extrathyroidal tissues. These include the salivary glands (D), gastric mucosa, lactating mammary glands, and the placenta (C), where it plays a role in transporting iodide into saliva, milk, and to the fetus, respectively. The pituitary gland (A), however, is not known to express the sodium-iodide symporter. Its function is to regulate the thyroid gland via TSH, but it is not directly involved in iodide transport. 16. What is the formula used to calculate Stroke Volume (SV) in the context of cardiac physiology?(A) SV = End-Diastolic Volume (EDV) - End- Systolic Volume (ESV) (B) SV = Heart Rate (HR) Ejection Fraction (EF) (C) SV = Cardiac Output (CO) / Heart Rate (HR) (D) SV = Preload Afterload As  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 Stroke Volume (SV) is defined as the volume of blood pumped from a ventricle of the heart during one contraction (systole). It is calculated as the difference between the volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of filling (diastole) and the volume of blood remaining in the ventricle at the end of contraction (systole). Therefore, the correct formula is SV = End-Diastolic Volume (EDV) - End-Systolic Volume (ESV). Option (C) also correctly defines stroke volume, as Cardiac Output (CO) is the product of Stroke Volume and Heart Rate (CO = SV × HR), so SV = CO / HR. However, option (A) represents the fundamental definition of stroke volume based on ventricular volumes. Option (B) and (D) are incorrect formulas. BIOCHEMISTRY

questions.stem: Which of the following poisonous agents does not inhibit cytochrome oxidase?
questions.explanation: Methane Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) is the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. Its inhibition blocks aerobic respiration, leading to cytotoxic hypoxia. Cyanide (D) is the classic inhibitor, binding to the ferric iron ($Fe^{3+}$) within the enzyme. Hydrogen sulfide (A) acts through a similar inhibitory mechanism. Carbon monoxide (B) can also inhibit cytochrome oxidase, although its primary toxic effect is its high-affinity binding to hemoglobin. In contrast, methane ($CH_4$) is a simple asphyxiant. It is a physiologically inert gas that is not directly toxic to cells. It causes hypoxia simply by displacing oxygen in the inhaled air, leading to a reduced fraction of inspired oxygen ($FiO_2$) and subsequent hypoxemia. It does not have any direct inhibitory effect on cellular enzymes like cytochrome oxidase.

questions.stem: Which of the following lipase enzymes is inhibited by insulin?
questions.explanation: Hormone-sensitive lipase Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) is a key intracellular enzyme found in adipocytes (fat cells). Its function is to hydrolyze stored triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol, a process known as lipolysis, releasing these energy substrates into the bloodstream. The activity of HSL is tightly regulated by hormones. It is stimulated by counter-regulatory hormones like epinephrine and glucagon (via cAMP and PKA). Conversely, it is strongly inhibited by insulin. Insulin, which is released in the fed state, promotes energy storage. By inhibiting HSL, insulin suppresses the breakdown of stored fat. In contrast, insulin activates lipoprotein lipase (A), which is located on capillary walls and helps to clear triglycerides from the blood for storage in fat cells. Pancreatic (B) and gastric (C) lipases are digestive enzymes.

questions.stem: What is the main substrate and metabolic fuel used by red blood cells (RBCs) during the fasting period?
questions.explanation: Glucose Red blood cells (RBCs) have a unique metabolism because they lack mitochondria. The absence of mitochondria means they are incapable of aerobic respiration (i.e., they cannot use the Krebs cycle or oxidative phosphorylation). Therefore, they are entirely dependent on anaerobic glycolysis for all of their ATP production. The sole fuel source for glycolysis is glucose. This dependence is absolute and does not change with the body's metabolic state. Whether in the fed state or a prolonged fasting period, RBCs must continuously extract glucose from the bloodstream to meet their energy needs. They cannot utilize free fatty acids (C), ketone bodies (A), or amino acids (D) as fuel because the metabolic pathways for these substrates require functional mitochondria.

questions.stem: Which of the following macronutrients requires the most energy for assimilation?
questions.explanation: Proteins The energy required to digest, absorb, and metabolize nutrients is known as the thermic effect of food (TEF) or specific dynamic action. This effect varies significantly among macronutrients. Proteins have the highest TEF, requiring the most energy for their assimilation. Approximately 20-30% of the energy content of the ingested protein is expended during its metabolism (e.g., deamination, urea synthesis). Carbohydrates (B) have a lower TEF, typically around 5-10%. Fats, including both mono-unsaturated (C) and polyunsaturated (D) fatty acids, have the lowest TEF, usually in the range of 0-3%. This means that the body is most efficient at storing energy from fat and least efficient at storing energy from protein. This high thermic effect of protein is one reason why high-protein diets are often recommended for weight management.

questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with a defect in collagen maturity?
questions.explanation: Scurvy Scurvy is the disease caused by a severe deficiency of Vitamin C (ascorbic acid). Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for two key enzymes, prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, which are involved in the post-translational modification of collagen. These enzymes are responsible for hydroxylating proline and lysine residues within the procollagen chains. This hydroxylation step is crucial for the formation of stable cross-links between collagen molecules, which gives the final collagen triple helix its strength and stability. In the absence of Vitamin C, this process is impaired, leading to the production of weak, unstable, and immature collagen. This results in the characteristic symptoms of scurvy, such as poor wound healing, bleeding gums, and perifollicular hemorrhages. Rickets (B) is a defect in bone mineralization due to Vitamin D deficiency.

questions.stem: Which enzyme is affected in a patient with thiamine deficiency who develops lactic acidosis?
questions.explanation: Pyruvate dehydrogenase Thiamine (Vitamin B1), in its active form thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), is a critical cofactor for several key enzymes in carbohydrate metabolism. One of the most important of these is the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex. The PDH complex catalyzes the irreversible conversion of pyruvate (the end product of glycolysis) to acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the Krebs cycle. In thiamine deficiency, the activity of the PDH complex is severely impaired. This creates a metabolic block, preventing pyruvate from entering the Krebs cycle for aerobic respiration. The accumulating pyruvate is then shunted to an alternative pathway, where it is converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase. This overproduction of lactate leads to lactic acidosis. Transketolase (D) is also a thiamine-dependent enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway, but its deficiency does not cause lactic acidosis. 23. Which of the following statements accurately describe the impact of Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency?1. Decrease in reduced glutathione 2. Decrease NADPH 3. Decreased lipid peroxidation

questions.stem: Decreased RBC membrane damage
questions.explanation: 1 & 2 are correct Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). The primary function of the PPP in red blood cells is to produce NADPH (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate). Therefore, a deficiency in G6PD leads to a decrease in NADPH (2 is correct). NADPH is essential for maintaining a supply of reduced glutathione (GSH), which is catalyzed by the enzyme glutathione reductase. Reduced glutathione is a critical antioxidant that detoxifies reactive oxygen species. A decrease in NADPH leads to a decrease in reduced glutathione (1 is correct). In the absence of sufficient GSH, RBCs are highly susceptible to oxidative stress from certain drugs or infections. This oxidative stress leads to increased lipid peroxidation (3 is incorrect) and increased RBC membrane damage (4 is incorrect), ultimately causing hemolysis. 24. questions.stem: What is a characteristic feature observed in physiological jaundice?

options.text: Increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
Increased direct bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
Increased indirect bilirubin, absent urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine
Increased direct bilirubin, absent urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine

questions.explanation: Increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine Physiological jaundice in newborns is a common, transient condition caused by the immaturity of the liver's bilirubin-conjugating system (low UGT enzyme activity), coupled with an increased bilirubin load from the breakdown of fetal red blood cells. This leads to an increase in unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin in the bloodstream. Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and bound to albumin, so it cannot be filtered by the kidneys, resulting in absent bilirubin in the urine. The bilirubin that is successfully conjugated and excreted into the gut gets converted by bacteria to urobilinogen. A portion of this urobilinogen is reabsorbed and excreted in the urine, so urobilinogen is present (and may be increased due to the higher overall bilirubin turnover). This pattern contrasts with obstructive jaundice, which would feature increased direct bilirubin and bilirubin in the urine.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not associated with renal auto-regulation?
questions.explanation: Renal sympathetic system fibers Renal autoregulation refers to the intrinsic mechanisms within the kidney that maintain a stable renal blood flow (RBF) and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) despite fluctuations in systemic blood pressure. The two primary intrinsic mechanisms are the myogenic reflex (B), where the afferent arteriole constricts in response to stretch, and tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) (A), mediated by the macula densa. While the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) (C) is often considered an extrinsic system, angiotensin II plays a role in autoregulation by constricting the efferent arteriole, helping to maintain GFR when renal perfusion pressure drops. In contrast, the renal sympathetic nervous system (D) is a purely extrinsic control mechanism. Strong sympathetic stimulation (e.g., during shock or intense exercise) causes profound vasoconstriction of the afferent arterioles, which can override the intrinsic autoregulatory mechanisms to reduce GFR and divert blood flow away from the kidneys.

questions.stem: The stroke volume depends on end-diastolic volume. This is best represented as?
questions.explanation: Length-tension relationship The statement describes the Frank-Starling law of the heart. This fundamental principle states that the force of ventricular contraction (and thus stroke volume) is directly proportional to the initial length of the muscle fibers at the end of diastole. The end-diastolic volume (EDV), or preload, determines this initial fiber length. The underlying cellular mechanism is the length-tension relationship of the cardiac muscle (myocardium). As the myocytes are stretched by an increased EDV , the overlap between actin and myosin filaments becomes more optimal, and the sensitivity of the myofilaments to calcium increases. This results in a more forceful contraction (greater tension development), which ejects a larger stroke volume. While "length-force" (A) is functionally similar, "length-tension" is the more precise physiological term used to describe this property of muscle tissue. 11. questions.stem: Which sensory receptors are responsible for tactile discrimination?
questions.explanation: Both A & B Tactile discrimination, which includes the ability to perceive fine details like texture, shape, and two-point discrimination, relies on sensory receptors with small, well-defined receptive fields, located superficially in the skin. Both Merkel discs and Meissner's corpuscles fit this description. Merkel discs (A) are slow-adapting mechanoreceptors that are sensitive to sustained pressure and texture, making them crucial for reading Braille and sensing fine details. Meissner's corpuscles (B) are rapidly adapting receptors that are sensitive to light touch, flutter, and grip control. Both are highly concentrated in the fingertips and other sensitive areas. In contrast, Pacinian corpuscles (C) are located deeper in the dermis, have large receptive fields, and are rapidly adapting receptors that detect deep pressure and high-frequency vibration, contributing less to fine tactile discrimination. Therefore, both Merkel discs and Meissner's corpuscles are key players.

questions.stem: Which of the following is utilized for the treatment of sideroblastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 Sideroblastic anemia is a group of blood disorders characterized by the presence of ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow. It results from a defect in the synthesis of heme. The first and rate-limiting step in heme synthesis is the condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine to form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme ALA synthase. This enzyme requires pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) as a cofactor. PLP is the active form of Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine). In some forms of sideroblastic anemia, particularly the hereditary X-linked type, there is a mutation in the ALA synthase enzyme that can be partially overcome by administering high doses of its cofactor, Vitamin B6. Therefore, a trial of pyridoxine is a cornerstone of therapy for certain types of sideroblastic anemia.

questions.stem: What abnormality is most likely to be seen on histopathological examination of the tissue section from a 17-year-old male who underwent surgery for intussusception and was found to have multiple polyps?
questions.explanation: Hamartomatous polyp Intussusception in an older child or adolescent is often caused by a pathological lead point, such as a polyp. The presence of multiple polyps in a 17-year-old raises strong suspicion for a polyposis syndrome. The image provided shows the characteristic histology of a hamartomatous polyp from Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS). This is identified by the distinctive arborizing (tree-like) pattern of smooth muscle bands that extend from the muscularis mucosae up into the lamina propria of the polyp. PJS is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by multiple hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract, mucocutaneous pigmentation, and an increased risk of various cancers. Adenomatous polyps (A) and adenocarcinoma (C) are typically seen in older adults, and hyperplastic polyps (D) are benign and usually do not serve as lead points for intussusception. 33. questions.stem: In a patient with ARDS caused by SARS-CoV-2, as shown in the electron microscopic lung image, which of the labeled layers would be involved and show enlargement due to the infection?
questions.explanation: A In ARDS caused by SARS-CoV-2 infection, the primary pathological process is diffuse alveolar damage (DAD). The virus infects type II pneumocytes, leading to inflammation, cytokine release, and increased vascular permeability. This results in edema, hyaline membrane formation, and thickening of the alveolar wall. In the given diagram, label A represents the alveolar septum (alveolar wall), which contains capillaries and interstitial tissue. During ARDS, this septal layer becomes edematous, inflamed, and thickened, appearing enlarged due to fluid accumulation and inflammatory cell infiltration. The thickened alveolar septum increases the diffusion distance for oxygen, leading to severe hypoxemia — the hallmark of ARDS. Labels B and D correspond to surface lining or epithelial components, but the major enlargement and structural thickening in ARDS occur in the inter alveolar septum, not just the epithelial surface.Therefore, the layer that becomes enlarged and involved due to SARS-CoV-2 infection is A (Option B).

questions.stem: What follow-up diagnostic procedure is recommended for a child with bilateral proptosis and a peripheral smear suggesting chloroma?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow biopsy A chloroma, also known as a granulocytic sarcoma or myeloid sarcoma, is a solid, extramedullary tumor composed of leukemic myeloblasts. It can occur in various parts of the body, including the orbit, leading to proptosis. Its presence is a manifestation of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). While the peripheral smear may have been suggestive of AML (e.g., by showing circulating blasts), the definitive diagnosis of leukemia requires a bone marrow biopsy and aspirate. This procedure is essential to confirm the diagnosis, determine the specific subtype of AML through morphology, cytochemistry, immunophenotyping (flow cytometry), and cytogenetics, and to assess the overall cellularity and extent of bone marrow infiltration by the leukemic cells. questions.stem: In a patient who has undergone prolonged starvation, which urine test would show a positive result?
questions.explanation: Rothera's test During prolonged starvation, after glycogen stores are depleted, the body switches to metabolizing fats for energy. The liver breaks down fatty acids into acetyl-CoA, which is then converted into ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone). These ketone bodies are released into the blood and used as fuel by tissues like the brain. When their production exceeds their utilization, they accumulate in the blood (ketosis) and are excreted in the urine (ketonuria). Rothera's test is a specific chemical test used to detect the presence of ketone bodies (specifically acetoacetate and acetone) in a urine sample. A positive result, indicated by the formation of a purple-colored ring, would therefore be expected in a starving individual. Benedict's test (A) is for reducing sugars. Spontaneous remission is more common in children than in adults

questions.stem: Which proteins of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) are responsible for inactivating the RB gene?
questions.explanation: E7 High-risk types of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) are the primary cause of cervical cancer and other anogenital cancers. Their carcinogenic potential is mediated by two early viral oncoproteins, E6 and E7. The E7 protein functions by binding to and promoting the degradation of the retinoblastoma (pRB) tumor suppressor protein. pRB normally acts as a brake on the cell cycle by binding to the E2F transcription factor. By inactivating pRB, the E7 protein releases E2F, allowing the cell to bypass the G1/S checkpoint and undergo uncontrolled proliferation. The E6 protein (A) has a different primary target; it binds to and promotes the degradation of the p53 tumor suppressor protein, thereby inhibiting apoptosis. The L1 and L2 proteins (C, D) are late proteins that form the viral capsid. 29. Which mediators are involved in the initial stage of type 1 hypersensitivity?1. Mast cell 2. Histamine 3. Neutrophils 4. Prostaglandins

questions.stem: Leukotrienes
questions.explanation: 1,2,4,5 Type I hypersensitivity is the immediate, IgE-mediated allergic reaction. The process is initiated when an allergen cross-links IgE antibodies bound to the surface of mast cells (1) (and basophils). This cross-linking triggers the degranulation of the mast cell, which releases a flood of pre-formed and newly synthesized mediators. The initial or immediate phase is dominated by the release of pre-formed mediators from granules, the most important of which is histamine (2). Almost immediately, the mast cell also begins to synthesize lipid-derived mediators from its membrane phospholipids via the arachidonic acid pathway. These include prostaglandins (4) (e.g., PGD2) and leukotrienes (5) (e.g., LTC4, LTD4, LTE4). These mediators are responsible for the classic allergic symptoms. Neutrophils (3) are recruited later in the late-phase reaction, not the initial stage. 30. questions.stem: The cell shown in the slide has inhibitory functions. To which of the following structures does it send its projections?
questions.explanation: Deep nuclei of the cerebellum The image shows a Purkinje cell, which is recognizable by its massive, flask-shaped cell body and extensive, flat dendritic tree. Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex. They are GABAergic, meaning they exert a powerful inhibitory influence on their target cells. The primary targets of the vast majority of Purkinje cell axons are the neurons of the deep cerebellar nuclei (e.g., the dentate, emboliform, globose, and fastigial nuclei). These deep nuclei, in turn, provide the main excitatory output from the cerebellum to other parts of the motor system, such as the thalamus and brainstem. Therefore, the cerebellar cortex, via its Purkinje cells, modulates motor activity by regulating the firing of the deep cerebellar nuclei through this inhibitory projection.

questions.stem: In which of the following is the Oil Red O stain utilized?
questions.explanation: Frozen section Oil Red O is a lysochrome (fat-soluble) diazo dye used in histology to stain neutral triglycerides and lipids. During routine tissue processing for paraffin embedding, tissues are dehydrated using alcohols and cleared with agents like xylene. These organic solvents dissolve and wash out lipids, so lipid staining is not possible on standard paraffin-embedded sections. To preserve the lipids within the tissue, the specimen must be processed as a frozen section. In this technique, the fresh tissue is rapidly frozen, cut on a cryostat, and then stained. This avoids the use of lipid-dissolving solvents. Therefore, Oil Red O staining is specifically utilized for demonstrating fat in frozen tissue sections. NODIA

questions.stem: Which study design is the most effective for demonstrating a cause-and-effect relationship among the options listed?
questions.explanation: Clinical trial Among all study designs, the Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT), a type of clinical trial, provides the strongest evidence for a cause-and-effect relationship. In an RCT, the investigator actively allocates an exposure (the "cause," e.g., a new drug) to one group and a placebo or standard treatment to another, and then follows both groups to observe the outcome (the "effect"). The key features of randomization and a control group minimize confounding and bias, allowing for a strong inference of causality. Among observational studies, a cohort study (B) is the strongest design for assessing causality, as it establishes the temporal sequence (exposure precedes outcome). However, a well-conducted RCT is considered the gold standard and provides a higher level of evidence than any observational design. 96. questions.stem: Which one of the following is not a component of meta-analysis?
questions.explanation: Randomization A meta-analysis is a statistical method used to combine the results of multiple independent studies to derive a single, more powerful conclusion. The process involves several key steps : 1. Selection : Defining clear inclusion and exclusion criteria to select the relevant studies for the analysis. 2. Abstraction : Systematically extracting the relevant data (e.g., sample size, effect estimates, standard errors) from each selected study. 3. Analysis : Using statistical techniques to pool the data and calculate an overall summary effect measure. 4. Randomization, however, is a component of the design of the primary studies being analyzed (specifically, randomized controlled trials). It is not a component of the meta-analysis process itself. A meta-analysis analyzes studies that may or may not have used randomization; it does not perform randomization. 98. questions.stem: Which of the following is not considered a major diagnostic criterion for allergic fungal sinusitis?
questions.explanation: Positive fungal culture Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS) is a non-invasive form of fungal sinusitis driven by an allergic reaction to fungal elements. The definitive diagnosis is based on the Bent and Kuhn major criteria : 1. Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity to fungi. 2. Nasal polyposis (A). 3. Characteristic CT findings (C) (heterogeneous hyperdense material within the sinuses). 4. Eosinophilic mucin (allergic mucin) containing fungal hyphae, but without evidence of tissue invasion (B). 5. Positive fungal stain of the sinus contents. 6. A positive fungal culture (D), while supportive, is not a major criterion. Fungal cultures are only positive in about 50-60% of cases, and the presence of fungi in the nose can be due to colonization rather than a true infection. The diagnosis hinges on finding the characteristic allergic mucin with fungal elements on histopathology, regardless of the culture result.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old patient presents with right-sided nasal obstruction and occasional blood-stained nasal discharge. The CT scan and endoscopic images are provided. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Inverted papilloma The patient's symptoms of unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis are concerning for a nasal tumor. The endoscopic image reveals a polypoid, papillary, or "cauliflower-like" lesion. This combination of location (lateral nasal wall) and appearance is highly characteristic of a sinonasal inverted papilloma. Inverted papillomas are benign but locally aggressive epithelial tumors known for their high recurrence rate and association with squamous cell carcinoma. A key radiological sign, often seen, is focal hyperostosis on the CT scan at the tumor's origin. Carcinoma (B) would likely show more aggressive bone destruction. Esthesioneuroblastoma (C) arises high in the nasal vault (cribriform plate). Angiofibroma (D) occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males.

questions.stem: Which of the following is considered a new and innovative medication for the treatment of depression?
questions.explanation: Vilazodone Vilazodone is considered a newer antidepressant with a novel mechanism of action. It is classified as a Serotonin Partial Agonist/Reuptake Inhibitor (SPARI). Durham's rule (also known as the "product test") states that a defendant is not criminally responsible if their unlawful act was the product of mental disease or defect. It was adopted in some U.S. jurisdictions but has largely been abandoned due to its vagueness. 2. Curren's rule is a version of the American Law Institute (ALI) test, which states that a person is not responsible for criminal conduct if at the time of such conduct, as a result of mental disease or defect, they lack substantial capacity either to appreciate the criminality of their conduct or to conform their conduct to the requirements of the law. Ashley's rule (3) and Murphy's rule (4) (better known as Murphy's Law) are not legal standards for determining insanity. questions.stem: Which tumor is most commonly found in the lacrimal gland?
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common tumor of the lacrimal gland. questions.stem: What is the most frequently observed eye symptom of COVID-19?
questions.explanation: Follicular conjunctivitis While SARS-CoV-2 can cause a spectrum of ocular issues, the most common and frequently reported manifestation is conjunctivitis. This typically presents as a mild, benign, and self-limiting condition. The characteristic feature of this viral conjunctivitis is a follicular reaction, where small, dome-shaped lymphoid follicles appear on the palpebral conjunctiva, particularly in the inferior fornix. Symptoms usually include redness, watering, a foreign-body sensation, and mild discharge. While more severe complications like retinal vein thrombosis (A) have been documented, they are rare and associated with the systemic hypercoagulable state of severe COVID-19. Similarly, keratouveitis (B) and pseudomembranous conjunctivitis (D) have been reported but are much less common than the typical follicular conjunctivitis, which can be one of the initial presenting symptoms of the disease.

questions.stem: Which medication should be avoided in a patient with angle-closure glaucoma who also has major depressive disorder?
questions.explanation: Amitriptyline A patient with angle-closure glaucoma has an anatomically narrow anterior chamber angle, making them susceptible to an acute attack if the pupil dilates (mydriasis). Several medications can induce mydriasis, particularly those with anticholinergic properties. Among the antidepressants listed, the tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) have the most potent anticholinergic side effects. Amitriptyline is a TCA with strong anticholinergic activity, which can cause pupillary dilation and precipitate a dangerous acute angle-closure attack. For this reason, it is relatively contraindicated in patients with untreated narrow angles. In contrast, the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as sertraline (B) and fluvoxamine (D), have very weak to negligible anticholinergic effects and are considered much safer in this context. Mirtazapine (C) has some antihistaminic effects but is significantly less anticholinergic than amitriptyline.

questions.stem: A patient has difficulty seeing in the lateral visual fields along with a mild, persistent headache. Where in the visual pathway is the lesion most likely located?
questions.explanation: Optic chiasma The image displays the results of a visual field test showing a bitemporal hemianopia, which is a loss of vision in the outer (temporal) half of the visual field in both eyes. This specific pattern of visual field loss is pathognomonic for a lesion compressing the optic chiasma. At the optic chiasma, the nerve fibers originating from the nasal half of each retina (which perceive the temporal visual fields) decussate, or cross over, to the opposite side. A midline lesion at the chiasma, most commonly a pituitary adenoma, will compress these crossing nasal fibers from both eyes, resulting in the characteristic loss of both temporal visual fields. The associated headache is also a common symptom of a pituitary mass. A lesion in the optic tract (B) would cause a homonymous hemianopia (loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes). A lesion in the occipital lobe (A) would also cause a homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.

questions.explanation: Hess chart The image provided is a Hess chart. The Hess screen test is a specialized ophthalmological investigation used to map and quantify ocular movements, particularly in cases of incomitant strabismus (squint) caused by extraocular muscle palsy. The test is performed using a tangent screen with a grid of red lines and a green light projector. The patient wears red-green goggles to dissociate the eyes, and their task is to superimpose the green light onto specific points on the red grid. The resulting plots for each eye are recorded on the Hess chart, which provides a graphical representation of any under-action or over-action of the individual extraocular muscles. It is an essential tool for diagnosing and monitoring conditions like cranial nerve palsies. The Snellen chart (B) and ETDRS chart (D) test visual acuity, while the Pelli-Robson chart (C) tests contrast sensitivity. MEDICINE

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man recovering from COVID-19 and isolating at home comes to the emergency department with breathing difficulty. He is alert and responsive but tachypneic, with an SpO₂ of 86%. He is given oxygen through a face mask with a reservoir bag at 10 L/min, and after one hour his SpO₂ only increases to 88%. What should be the next step in his management?
questions.explanation: High-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy The patient has significant hypoxemia (SpO₂ 86%) due to COVID-19, which is not responding adequately to a non-rebreather mask at a high flow rate. An SpO₂ of 88% is still unacceptably low. Increasing the flow rate on the non-rebreather mask to 15 L/min (A) is unlikely to provide a significant improvement, as 10 L/min should already be sufficient to keep the reservoir bag inflated. The patient is awake and alert, so immediate endotracheal intubation (C) may not be necessary yet. The most appropriate next step in escalating respiratory support for this type of hypoxemic respiratory failure is High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) oxygen therapy. HFNC can deliver a very high flow (up to 60 L/min) of heated, humidified air with a precisely controlled fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO 2 ) up to 100%. It also provides some positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), which helps to recruit alveoli and improve oxygenation.

questions.stem: In neuromuscular monitoring, tetanic stimulation is generally delivered at what frequency?
questions.explanation: 50 Hz Neuromuscular monitoring is used during anesthesia to assess the degree of muscle paralysis induced by neuromuscular blocking agents. Several patterns of electrical stimulation can be applied to a peripheral nerve. Tetanic stimulation involves delivering a continuous, high-frequency electrical stimulus for a short duration (typically 5 seconds). The standard frequency used for this is 50 Hz (50 impulses per second), as this is the physiological frequency required to produce a sustained, tetanic muscle contraction. In a non-paralyzed muscle, this stimulation results in a sustained contraction. In the presence of a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, the response will show a characteristic "fade," where the strength of the contraction diminishes over the 5-second period. Train-of-four stimulation uses a frequency of 2 Hz (B), but tetanic stimulation specifically uses 50 Hz. 115. questions.stem: Which microorganism is most likely to cause meningitis in a neonate who presents with increased irritability, poor feeding, and seizures, as confirmed by lumbar puncture findings?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus agalactiae Neonatal meningitis (occurring in the first month of life) is caused by a specific group of pathogens typically acquired from the mother's genital tract during birth. The most common causative organisms are Group B Streptococcus (GBS), which is Streptococcus agalactiae, and Escherichia coli (especially K1 capsular strains). Listeria monocytogenes is also a significant cause. In most regions, GBS is considered the leading cause of both early-onset (<7 days) and late-onset (7-90 days) neonatal sepsis and meningitis. Neisseria meningitidis (C) is a common cause of meningitis in older children and young adults but is rare in the neonatal period. While E. coli and Listeria are possibilities, Streptococcus agalactiae is the most frequent pathogen responsible for this devastating infection in newborns.

questions.stem: "What principle forms the basis of the Paul-Bunnell test performed for a 24-year-old male presenting with cervical lymphadenopathy?"
questions.explanation: Heterophile antibodies The clinical presentation of cervical lymphadenopathy in a young adult is classic for infectious mononucleosis, which is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The Paul-Bunnell test is a classic laboratory test used to diagnose this condition. The principle of the test is the detection of heterophile antibodies. These are antibodies (typically IgM) that are produced during an EBV infection and have the unusual property of cross-reacting with and agglutinating red blood cells from other species, such as sheep and horses. A positive Paul-Bunnell test (or a more modern Monospot test, which works on the same principle) demonstrates the presence of these heterophile antibodies, providing strong evidence for a diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis.

questions.stem: Which one of these options is classified as a dematiaceous fungus?
questions.explanation: Cladosporium Dematiaceous fungi are a group of fungi whose cell walls contain melanin. This melanin imparts a characteristic dark brown or black color to their spores and/or hyphae. They are responsible for a range of infections, including phaeohyphomycosis and chromoblastomycosis. Cladosporium is a classic example of a dematiaceous mold; it is a common airborne fungus that appears dark green to black. In contrast, Mucor species (A) are zygomycetes characterized by broad, non-septate, hyaline (non-pigmented) hyphae. Aspergillus niger (B), despite its name, produces black spores but has hyaline hyphae, and is generally not classified as dematiaceous. questions.stem: Please identify the component that causes endotoxic shock in gram-negative bacteria.
questions.explanation: 1 The image displays the structure of a Gram-negative bacterial outer membrane. The key molecule responsible for endotoxic shock is lipopolysaccharide (LPS). LPS is composed of three parts : the O-antigen (outermost carbohydrate chains), a core polysaccharide, and Lipid A. Label 1 points to the Lipid A portion, which is the lipid component that anchors LPS into the outer membrane. It is Lipid A that is the biologically active "endotoxin." When Gram-negative bacteria are lysed, Lipid A is released and recognized by the host's innate immune system (e.g., via Toll-like receptor 4), triggering a massive inflammatory cascade. This leads to the release of cytokines like TNF-alpha and IL-1, causing fever, hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and septic shock. questions.stem: Which of the following organisms is considered a strict anaerobe?
questions.explanation: Prevotella A strict (or obligate) anaerobe is a microorganism that cannot grow in the presence of oxygen and may even be killed by it. They lack the enzymes (like catalase and superoxide dismutase) needed to detoxify reactive oxygen species produced during aerobic respiration. Prevotella is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria that are classic examples of obligate anaerobes. They are part of the normal flora of the human mouth, gut, and vagina and are often implicated in anaerobic infections like dental abscesses and aspiration pneumonia. The other organisms listed are not strict anaerobes. Burkholderia cepacia (B) and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (D) are aerobic Gram-negative rods. Yersinia enterocolitica (C) is a facultative anaerobe, meaning it can grow either with or without oxygen.

questions.stem: Which of the statements below is correct?

questions.explanation: Positive predictive value depends on prevalence of disease Sensitivity (the ability to correctly identify true positives) and specificity (the ability to correctly identify true negatives) are intrinsic properties of a diagnostic test and do not depend on the prevalence of the disease in the population being tested (making B and D incorrect). In contrast, the predictive values of a test are highly dependent on the disease prevalence. The Positive Predictive Value (PPV) is the probability that a person with a positive test result actually has the disease. The PPV will increase as the prevalence of the disease increases, and it will decrease as the prevalence decreases. In a low-prevalence population, even a highly accurate test will have a lower PPV , meaning a positive result is more likely to be a false positive (making A incorrect). 88. questions.stem: Which vaccine is linked to the risk of intussusception when administered?
questions.explanation: Rotavirus vaccine Intussusception is a condition where one segment of the intestine telescopes into an adjacent segment, which can cause a bowel obstruction. An older rotavirus vaccine (RotaShield) was withdrawn from the market in 1999 due to a strong association with an increased risk of intussusception. The currently available oral rotavirus vaccines (e.g., RotaTeq and Rotarix) have a much lower, but still slightly increased, risk of this adverse event, particularly within the first week after the first or second dose. The risk is considered very small (approximately 1-2 excess cases per 100,000 vaccinated infants) and is far outweighed by the significant benefits of the vaccine in preventing severe and life-threatening rotaviral gastroenteritis. questions.stem: What does the standardized age mortality ratio indicate?

options.text: Death rate of a population adjusted to a standard age distribution

To eliminate age structure of different countries

questions.explanation: Death rate of a population adjusted to a standard age distribution This question appears to confuse two related concepts : age-standardized mortality rate and Standardized Mortality Ratio (SMR). Based on the options, it is referring to the age-standardized (or age-adjusted) mortality rate. This is a method used to compare mortality rates between two or more populations that have different age structures. It calculates the death rate that a population would have if it had a "standard" age distribution (A). This process removes the confounding effect of age, allowing for a more accurate comparison of mortality trends over time or between different geographic regions (C, D are related concepts). For example, a country with an older population will naturally have a higher crude death rate, and age-standardization allows for a fair comparison with a country that has a younger population.

questions.stem: What factor is the external validity of a screening test associated with?
questions.explanation: Generalizability In the context of research and testing, validity refers to the accuracy of a measure. External validity specifically refers to the extent to which the results of a study or test can be generalized to other populations, settings, or times. For a screening test, this means asking if the test's performance characteristics (like its sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values) observed in a research study population will hold true when the test is applied to the broader, real-world population it is intended for. Therefore, external validity is directly associated with the generalizable of the test's results. Repeatability (D) and stability (A) are aspects of reliability (precision), not validity (accuracy). Objectivity (B) refers to the degree to which a test is free from scorer bias.

questions.stem: What term is used to describe the recent increase in the occurrence of non-communicable diseases?
questions.explanation: Secular A secular trend in epidemiology refers to a change in the incidence or prevalence of a disease over a long period, typically years or decades. The observed consistent increase in the burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) like diabetes, hypertension, and cancer across the globe over the past several decades is a classic example of a secular trend. This trend is linked to long-term changes in lifestyle, diet, environment, and demographics as part of the epidemiologic transition. Seasonal variation (B) refers to changes that occur within a single year (e.g., influenza in winter). Cyclical trends (C) refer to fluctuations that occur over a period of several years (e.g., measles outbreaks before widespread vaccination).

questions.stem: Which repair mechanism is linked with CRISPR-Cash?
questions.explanation: Non-homologous end joining The CRISPR-Cash system is a genome editing tool that works by inducing a targeted double-strand break (DSB) in the DNA at a specific location guided by an RNA molecule. Once the DSB is created, the cell's own DNA repair machinery takes over. The cell has two main pathways to repair DSBs. The most common and default pathway is non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). This pathway is error-prone and often introduces small insertions or deletions (indels) at the break site as it ligates the broken ends back together. This is the mechanism that is typically exploited to create gene "knockouts." The other, less frequent pathway is homology-directed repair (HDR), which can be used to "knock in" a specific DNA sequence if a template is provided. The other options (B, C, D) are repair mechanisms for different types of DNA damage, not DSBs. PHARMACOLOGY

questions.stem: Which thiazide diuretic should be given to a 34-year-old male with hypertension and stage 4 chronic kidney disease, whose estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is below 30 mL/min?
questions.explanation: Metolazone Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide (D), chlorthalidone (B), and chlorothiazide (A), exert their antihypertensive and diuretic effects by inhibiting the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. However, their efficacy is significantly diminished when the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) falls below 30 mL/min, as insufficient drug is filtered to reach its site of action. A major exception to this rule is metolazone. Metolazone is a thiazide-like diuretic that, unlike others in its class, retains its efficacy even in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease and a low GFR. It is often used in combination with a loop diuretic in patients with refractory edema due to renal failure or heart failure. Therefore, it is the most appropriate choice in this clinical scenario.

questions.stem: Which of the following options can be used for the long-term treatment of obesity?
questions.explanation: Liraglutide Several medications have been approved for the long-term management of obesity. Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist. Initially developed for type 2 diabetes, it was subsequently approved at a higher dose (3.0 mg) for chronic weight management. It works by increasing satiety through its effects on the brain and by slowing gastric emptying. Metformin (B) can cause modest weight loss but is not an approved obesity treatment. Sibutramine (C) and Fenfluramine (D) are older weight-loss drugs that were withdrawn from the market due to serious cardiovascular side effects (increased risk of heart attack and stroke for sibutramine; pulmonary hypertension and valvular heart disease for fenfluramine). Therefore, among the choices provided, liraglutide is a modern, approved medication for the prolonged treatment of obesity.

questions.stem: What is Topiramate used for?
questions.explanation: Treatment of Lennox Gastaut syndrome Topiramate is an antiepileptic drug with multiple mechanisms of action. It has several approved indications. One of its key uses is as an adjunctive therapy for the treatment of seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS), a severe form of childhood-onset epilepsy. It is also approved for the treatment of partial-onset and primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Additionally, topiramate is widely used for the prophylaxis (prevention), not the acute treatment, of migraine headaches in adults and adolescents. While option (A) is related to a use of topiramate, the term "treatment" is more accurately applied to its role in LGS, whereas its migraine role is prophylactic. It has no approved role in the management of ADHD (C) or dementia (D). Given the precise wording, its role in treating LGS is a definitive indication.

questions.stem: For which medical condition is inhaled nitric oxide approved for treatment?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary hypertension Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) is a potent and selective pulmonary vasodilator. When inhaled, it diffuses across the alveolar-capillary membrane and relaxes the smooth muscle in the adjacent pulmonary vessels, leading to a decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance and improved ventilation-perfusion matching. Its primary FDA-approved indication is for the treatment of term and near-term neonates (>34 weeks gestation) with hypoxic respiratory failure associated with clinical or echo cardiographic evidence of pulmonary hypertension. In this setting, iNO improves oxygenation and significantly reduces the need for more invasive therapies like extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). It is not used for systemic hypertension (A), migraine (C), or Parkinson's disease (D), as its effects are localized to the pulmonary circulation when administered via inhalation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a cause of the paradoxical bronchoconstrictor associated with ipratropium bromide?
questions.explanation: Hypertonic saline Paradoxical bronchoconstrictor is a rare but reported adverse effect of nebulized ipratropium bromide solution. This reaction is generally attributed to the drug's formulation or its pharmacology. The nebulizer solution contains excipients, such as the preservative benzalkonium chloride (C) and the chelating agent disodium edetate (EDTA) (B), both of which are known to have bronchoconstrictor properties in some susceptible individuals. A proposed pharmacological mechanism is that ipratropium, a non-selective muscarinic antagonist, can block inhibitory prejunctional M2 autoreceptors (D) on cholinergic nerve endings, leading to increased acetylcholine release that may overcome the M3 receptor blockade. In contrast, hypertonic saline (A) is not an additive in the ipratropium formulation. It is a separate therapeutic agent (a mucolytic) that is known to induce bronchoconstriction as a primary effect, but this is not a cause of paradoxical bronchoconstriction from ipratropium itself.

This system provided a letter grade to summarize the level of risk to a fetus. Category A represented drugs for which adequate studies in pregnant women have shown no risk. Category B, C, and D represented increasing levels of potential risk based on animal and human data. Category X represented drugs for which studies have demonstrated fetal abnormalities, and the risk of use in pregnant women clearly outweighs any possible benefit. questions.stem: At what dosage does dopamine function on beta-1 receptors?
questions.explanation: 2-10 mcg/kg/min Dopamine is a catecholamine with dose-dependent receptor effects, which is crucial for its clinical use as an inotrope and vasopressor. 1. Low dose (renal dose) : At infusion rates of approximately <2-5 mcg/kg/min, dopamine primarily stimulates D1 receptors, causing vasodilation in the renal, mesenteric, and coronary circulations. 2. Moderate dose (cardiac dose) : At infusion rates of approximately 2-10 mcg/kg/min, dopamine primarily stimulates beta-1 adrenergic receptors on the heart. This results in increased myocardial contractility (positive inotropy) and heart rate (positive chronotropy), leading to an increased cardiac output. 3. High dose (vasopressor dose) : At infusion rates >10 mcg/kg/min, the effects on alpha-1 adrenergic receptors predominate, causing systemic vasoconstriction and an increase in blood pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following medications would increase the bioavailability of saquinavir when given concurrently?
questions.explanation: Ritonavir Saquinavir is an antiretroviral drug from the protease inhibitor class. When used alone, it has very poor oral bioavailability due to extensive metabolism by the cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) enzyme in the gut wall and liver. Ritonavir is another protease inhibitor that is also a very potent inhibitor of the CYP3A4 enzyme. This property is exploited clinically by using a low, subtherapeutic dose of ritonavir as a pharmacokinetic enhancer or "booster". When co-administered with saquinavir, ritonavir inhibits its metabolism, leading to a significant increase in saquinavir's plasma concentration and bioavailability, thereby enhancing its antiviral efficacy. This boosting strategy is a common principle in HIV therapy. The other substances listed do not have this specific and potent CYP3A4 inhibitory effect.

questions.stem: How does cyclosporine work in terms of its mechanism of action?
questions.explanation: Inhibition of calcineurin Cyclosporine is a powerful immunosuppressive agent widely used in organ transplantation to prevent rejection. Its mechanism of action involves the inhibition of calcineurin. Inside a T-lymphocyte, cyclosporine first binds to an intracellular protein called cyclophilin. This cyclosporine-cyclophilin complex then binds to and inhibits calcineurin, which is a calcium- and calmodulin-dependent phosphatase enzyme. The inhibition of calcineurin prevents it from dephosphorylating the Nuclear Factor of Activated T-cells (NFAT). As a result, NFAT cannot translocate to the nucleus to act as a transcription factor. This blocks the transcription of genes for several crucial cytokines, most importantly Interleukin-2 (IL-2). By preventing IL-2 production, cyclosporine effectively suppresses the proliferation and activation of T-cells, a central step in the immune response leading to organ rejection. 59. questions.stem: What is the diagnosis for a young man with hearing loss and tinnitus, based on the provided histology image?
questions.explanation: Schwannoma The patient's symptoms of unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus strongly suggest a tumor affecting the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) in the cerebellopontine angle, most commonly a vestibular schwannoma (also known as an acoustic neuroma). The provided histology image confirms this diagnosis. The slide shows the characteristic biphasic pattern of a schwannoma, with dense, cellular areas known as Antoni A tissue and less cellular, myxoid areas called Antoni B tissue. The pathognomonic feature, which is visible in the Antoni A areas, is the presence of Verocay bodies. These are distinct structures formed by two parallel rows of palisading, elongated Schwann cell nuclei separated by an anuclear zone. This specific histological architecture is diagnostic of a schwannoma. A neurofibroma (A) lacks this organized palisading and has a more haphazard arrangement of cells. Leiomyoma (C) and rhabdomyoma (D) are tumors of smooth and skeletal muscle, respectively.

questions.stem: In a patient with bilateral external auditory atresia, which of the following devices can be used?

The most appropriate device for this patient is the BAHA (1). A BAHA works by bypassing the obstructed outer and middle ear. It uses a small titanium implant placed in the mastoid bone. An external processor captures sound and transmits it as vibrations through the implant and the skull directly to the cochlea, allowing the patient to hear via bone conduction.

questions.stem: Which of the following methods is most commonly used to identify RNA in molecular analysis?
questions.explanation: RT-PCR Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) is a cornerstone molecular biology technique used specifically for the detection and analysis of RNA. This two-step process allows for the highly sensitive and specific detection of even minute quantities of a target RNA sequence. It is widely used for diagnosing infections caused by RNA viruses (like influenza and SARS-CoV-2) and for studying gene expression at the mRNA level. questions.stem: How does RNA interference (RNAi) impact gene expression?
questions.explanation: Knock down RNA interference (RNAi) is a natural cellular process for regulating gene expression. In this process, small non-coding RNA molecules, such as small interfering RNA (siRNA) or microRNA (miRNA), bind to a specific target messenger RNA (mRNA) molecule. This binding leads to the degradation of the target mRNA or the inhibition of its translation into protein. The result is a significant reduction in the expression of the targeted gene. This process of reducing or suppressing gene expression is referred to as a "knockdown". This is distinct from a gene "knock out" (A), which refers to the complete and permanent elimination of a gene from the genome itself (at the DNA level). RNAi works at the post-transcriptional level to temporarily suppress gene expression.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best method to detect HbA1c?
questions.explanation: Ion-exchange chromatography Several methods are used to measure Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c), but High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) is considered the gold standard reference method. One of the principal forms of HPLC used for this purpose is ion-exchange chromatography. This method separates different hemoglobin variants based on their differences in electrical charge. Glycation of hemoglobin alters its charge, allowing the glycated fraction (HbA1c) to be separated from the non-glycated fraction (HbA0). This provides a highly accurate and precise quantification. While immunoassays (C) and affinity chromatography (D) are also widely used and certified methods, ion-exchange HPLC is generally regarded as the most robust reference standard for the accurate determination of HbA1c levels.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best test for quantitative analysis of an RNA sample?
questions.explanation: RT-PCR followed by Real-time PCR To perform a quantitative analysis of RNA, two steps are required. First, the RNA must be converted into a more stable complementary DNA (cDNA) molecule. This is achieved through Reverse Transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) (B), which uses the enzyme reverse transcriptase. Second, this newly synthesized cDNA must be quantified. Real-time PCR (A), also known as quantitative PCR (qPCR), is the gold standard method for quantifying DNA. It monitors the amplification of a target DNA sequence in real-time by using fluorescent probes. The rate at which the fluorescence accumulates is proportional to the initial amount of the target sequence. Therefore, the most accurate and standard method for quantifying an RNA sample is to first perform reverse transcription and then quantify the resulting cDNA using real-time PCR.
