questions.stem: Mansonia spp
questions.explanation: A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2 This question requires matching parasites with their respective vectors or hosts. A. Brugia malayi : This is a nematode that causes lymphatic filariasis. It is transmitted by the bite of infected mosquitoes, primarily from the genus Mansonia (4). B. Diphyllobothrium latum : This is the fish tapeworm. Its life cycle involves two intermediate hosts. The first is a freshwater crustacean, a copepod (3), which is ingested by the second intermediate host, a freshwater fish. C. Fasciola hepatica : This is the sheep liver fluke. The main definitive hosts for this parasite are herbivores, particularly sheep (1) and cattle, where the adult flukes reside in the bile ducts. D. Paragonimus westermani : This is the oriental lung fluke. Humans become infected by eating raw or undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish (2) that contain the metacercariae, the infective stage of the parasite. 69. Match the following Column A Column B A. Balamuthia man-drillaris 1. Flagella B. Balantidium coli 2. Cilia C. Trichomonas vagi-nalis

questions.stem: pseudopod D. Toxoplasma gondii 4. No particular lo - comotive organ
questions.explanation: A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4 This question matches various protozoan parasites with their characteristic organ of locomotion. A. Balamuthia mandrillaris : This is a free-living amoeba that can cause rare but fatal granulomatous amoebic encephalitis. As an amoeba, its primary mode of movement is through the extension of pseudopods (3). B. Balantidium coli : This is a large intestinal protozoan and is the only member of the ciliate group that is pathogenic to humans. Its entire surface is covered with rows of cilia (2), which it uses for motility and feeding. C. Trichomonas vaginalis : This is a sexually transmitted parasite that causes vaginitis. It is characterized by its tumbling motility, which is achieved through the action of several anterior flagella (1) and an undulating membrane. D. Toxoplasma gondii : This is an apicomplexan parasite. The motile stages, such as tachyzoites and sporozoites, do not possess cilia, flagella, or pseudopods. They move via a unique mechanism called gliding motility, so "no particular locomotive organ" (4) is the most appropriate description.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man presents with painful lesions on the glans penis. What is the likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus) The image displays multiple small blisters (vesicles) clustered together on a reddened base located on the glans penis. This clinical appearance of "grouped vesicles on an erythematous base" is the pathognomonic sign of a genital herpes infection, caused by the Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-2. The patient's symptom of pain is also a classic feature of a herpetic outbreak, which can be accompanied by burning and itching. The vesicles eventually rupture to form painful, shallow ulcers that then crust over and heal. Haemophilus ducreyi (B) causes chancroid, which presents as a painful ulcer from the start, not vesicles. Chlamydia (C) typically causes urethritis, not external lesions. Primary syphilis (D) classically presents as a single, painless ulcer (chancre). The vesicular nature of the lesions is the key diagnostic clue pointing directly to HSV .

questions.stem: A 22-year-old sexually active male presents with painful ulcers (as shown in the image). What is the likely finding?
questions.explanation: Tzanck smear The presence of painful genital ulcers in a sexually active male has a differential diagnosis that primarily includes genital herpes (caused by Herpes Simplex Virus, HSV) and chancroid (caused by Haemophilus ducreyi). The lesions of HSV classically begin as painful vesicles that then rupture to form ulcers. A useful and rapid bedside diagnostic test for a suspected herpetic lesion is a Tzanck smear. This test involves scraping the base of a fresh ulcer or vesicle, smearing the cells onto a glass slide, and staining them with Giemsa or Wright stain. A positive finding is the presence of multinucleated giant cells with molded nuclei and intranuclear inclusions, known as Tzanck cells. This finding is highly suggestive of a herpesvirus infection. HP bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies) (A) are found in molluscum contagiosum, which causes papules, not ulcers. The other options are not relevant to this clinical presentation.

questions.stem: Which disease has an almost 100% fatality rate once symptoms develop?
questions.explanation: Rabies Rabies is an acute progressive viral encephalitis transmitted to humans through the saliva of infected animals, typically via a bite. While the disease is preventable with timely post-exposure prophylaxis, once clinical signs and symptoms develop, the disease is almost invariably fatal. The case fatality rate for symptomatic rabies approaches 100%. There are only a very small number of documented survivors of clinical rabies in the entire history of modern medicine, most of whom were treated with an experimental and not reliably successful protocol. This makes rabies one of the most lethal infectious diseases known. In contrast, while Nipah virus infection (B) and Ebola virus disease (C) are also extremely dangerous and have very high case fatality rates (which can range from 40% to over 90% depending on the strain and outbreak), survival is possible with intensive supportive care. Measles (D) has a much lower mortality rate. NODIA

questions.stem: A 50-year-old alcoholic is brought to the hospital with bleeding esophageal varices and dies. At autopsy, his distended abdomen contains a large amount of serous fluid. What is the correct term for this fluid?
questions.explanation: Ascites The clinical history describes a patient with decompensated liver cirrhosis, evidenced by bleeding esophageal varices. A major complication of cirrhosis is the development of portal hypertension. The high pressure in the portal venous system, combined with low serum albumin levels (due to impaired liver synthesis), causes fluid to shift from the vascular space into the peritoneal cavity. The accumulation of this serous fluid within the peritoneal cavity is specifically termed ascites. This fluid is typically a transudate, characterized by a low protein content, as opposed to an exudate (A), which is protein-rich and associated with inflammation. Hemorrhage (C) refers to bleeding, and lymphedema (D) is the accumulation of lymphatic fluid in the interstitial tissues, usually in the limbs. The correct term for the intra-abdominal fluid in this context is ascites.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old patient is rapidly gaining weight and has elevated TSH levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism The patient's symptoms of weight gain, combined with an elevated Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) level, point directly to a diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism. In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland itself is failing and cannot produce enough thyroid hormone (T4 and T3). The low levels of circulating thyroid hormone lead to a loss of negative feedback on the pituitary gland. In response, the pituitary secretes an increased amount of TSH in an attempt to stimulate the failing thyroid. The clinical symptoms of hypothyroidism, such as weight gain, fatigue, and cold intolerance, are due to the deficiency of thyroid hormone. Hashimoto's thyroiditis (A) is the most common cause of primary hypothyroidism, but "hypothyroidism" (D) is the overall diagnosis. Graves' disease (B) is a cause of hyperthyroidism with a suppressed TSH. A TSH-secreting pituitary tumor (C) would cause hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A woman presents with dark knuckles and anemia. What type of anemia is most likely?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic anemia The combination of anemia and hyperpigmentation, particularly over the knuckles and other sun-exposed areas or in skin creases, is a classic, though not universally present, clinical sign of megaloblastic anemia caused by Vitamin B12 deficiency. This hyperpigmentation is thought to be due to increased melanin synthesis, although the exact mechanism is not fully understood. Vitamin B12 deficiency leads to impaired DNA synthesis, affecting rapidly dividing cells in the bone marrow and resulting in the production of large, immature red blood cells (megaloblasts) and anemia. While iron deficiency anemia (B) and anemia of chronic disease (C) are common, they are not typically associated with knuckle hyperpigmentation. This specific skin finding, when present with anemia, should strongly raise the suspicion of Vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient has a gangrenous ulcer on the left toe and experiences early fatigue in the right lower limb while walking. What is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.explanation: Digital subtraction angiography The patient's symptoms are highly indicative of severe, multilevel peripheral arterial disease (PAD). The gangrenous ulcer on the left toe represents critical limb ischemia, while the fatigue (claudication) in the right lower limb indicates significant arterial stenosis on that side as well. While a duplex scan (C) is an excellent initial non-invasive test, and CT or MR angiography (A, B) provide detailed anatomical maps, the gold standard for both diagnosis and guiding intervention is Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA). DSA is an invasive procedure where a catheter is inserted into the arterial system and contrast dye is injected. It provides the highest-resolution images of the vascular lumen, allowing for precise localization of stenoses and occlusions, and detailed assessment of collateral circulation. Crucially, it also allows for percutaneous intervention (like angioplasty or stenting) to be performed during the same procedure.

questions.stem: A patient has had fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and an erythematous chest rash for 4 days, with no recent travel or tick bite history. Which cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings would most likely be seen in this case?
questions.explanation: All of the above The patient's clinical presentation of fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia is a classic meningeal syndrome. The presence of a rash and the likely subacute onset point towards a viral or aseptic cause rather than a typical bacterial cause. The characteristic cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profile for aseptic (viral) meningitis includes several key findings. There is typically a pleocytosis (increased white blood cell count), which is predominantly lymphocytic (C). The protein level is usually mildly to moderately elevated (A) due to inflammation and disruption of the blood-brain barrier. Crucially, the glucose level is typically normal (B), as viruses do not consume glucose in the CSF. This is a key feature that distinguishes viral from bacterial meningitis, where the glucose is usually low. Since all three of these CSF findings are characteristic of viral meningitis, the correct answer is all of the above.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a recent syncopal episode, congestive heart failure, and a grade III/IV harsh systolic murmur is found on echocardiography to have marked ventricular septal thickening and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. Which of the following findings is most likely to be present in this patient?

options.text: Radiation of the murmur to the neck
Decrease of the murmur with handgrip

questions.explanation: Decrease of the murmur with handgrip The patient's presentation and echocardiographic findings are diagnostic of Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM). The harsh systolic murmur in HOCM is caused by the dynamic outflow tract obstruction created by the thickened septum and the systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve. The intensity of this murmur is unique in that it changes with maneuvers that alter preload and afterload. Maneuvers that decrease preload or afterload (like standing or Valsalva) make the obstruction worse and increase the murmur's intensity. Conversely, maneuvers that increase preload (squatting) or increase afterload (like a sustained handgrip) will decrease the outflow gradient and therefore decrease the intensity of the murmur. Delayed carotid upstroke (C) and radiation to the neck (A) are characteristic of aortic stenosis. The ejection fraction in HOCM is typically preserved or hyperdynamic, not reduced (D).

questions.stem: What are the admission criteria for COVID-19?
questions.explanation: All the above The decision to admit a patient with COVID-19 to the hospital is based on an assessment of the severity of their illness and their risk for deterioration. While mild cases can be managed at home, certain signs and symptoms warrant hospital admission for monitoring and treatment. The most important indication is evidence of respiratory compromise, such as dyspnea (shortness of breath) (C) or a low oxygen saturation. The presence of chest discomfort or pain (B) is also a significant symptom that requires evaluation and admission. Additionally, patients with multiple comorbidities (A) (such as diabetes, heart disease, chronic lung disease, or immunosuppression) are at a much higher risk for developing severe disease, and a lower threshold for admission is often applied to this group, even with seemingly mild symptoms. Therefore, all of the factors listed are valid criteria that would contribute to the decision to admit a patient with COVID-19.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a part of high-quality CPR?
questions.explanation: Respiratory rate of 20-25/min High-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is critical for improving outcomes in cardiac arrest. The key components, as defined by international guidelines (e.g., American Heart Association), include : Pushing hard and fast : Compressing the chest at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute (A) to an adequate depth of at least 2 inches (5-6 cm) in adults (C).Allowing for full chest recoil between compressions (B) to permit the heart to fill with blood. Minimizing interruptions in chest compressions. When providing rescue breaths with an unprotected airway, the correct compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30 :2. If an advanced airway is in place, breaths are given at a rate of 1 breath every 6 seconds, which equates to a respiratory rate of 10 breaths per minute. A respiratory rate of 20-25/min (D) is too high and would constitute hyperventilation, which is detrimental as it increases intrathoracic pressure and decreases venous return.

questions.stem: A female develops pallor and cyanosis when exposed to cold water. All of the following conditions can cause this except which one?
questions.explanation: Hyperthyroidism The patient's symptoms of episodic, cold-induced digital color changes (pallor followed by cyanosis) describe Raynaud's phenomenon. This is a condition of exaggerated vasospasm of the digital arteries. It can be primary (Raynaud's disease) or secondary to various conditions. Many factors are known to precipitate or are associated with Raynaud's. Smoking (D) is a major vasoconstrictor and a well-known exacerbating factor. Certain medications, such as sumatriptan (C), which is a serotonin agonist used for migraines, can cause vasospasm and are associated with Raynaud's. There is also a known association between migraine headaches (B) and Raynaud's phenomenon, likely due to a shared underlying predisposition to vasospasm. In contrast, hyperthyroidism (A) is a state of hypermetabolism characterized by heat intolerance and peripheral vasodilation, not vasospasm. Hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism, can sometimes be associated with secondary Raynaud's phenomenon. 114. questions.stem: A patient develops fever, prostration, malaise, dysentery, and dehydration. The illness is likely due to a diarrheagenic strain of Escherichia coli (E. coli), and no antibiotics were given. Which type of virulent E. coli best fits this presentation?
questions.explanation: Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) Escherichia coli has several diarrheagenic strains, each producing distinct clinical syndromes.Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) invades and destroys colonic epithelial cells, producing an illness similar to shigellosis. It causes fever, malaise, prostration, abdominal cramps, and dysentery (blood and mucus in stool). Because it invades the intestinal mucosa, it produces inflammatory diarrhea with systemic symptoms and dehydration — matching this clinical presentation.In contrast: 1. EAEC causes persistent watery diarrhea, mainly in children and travelers, without prominent dysentery. 2. EHEC (e.g., O157:H7) causes bloody diarrhea but typically has little or no fever and may lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). Antibiotics are avoided due to HUS risk. 3. EPEC causes watery diarrhea, mainly in infants, without invasive dysentery. Since this patient has fever, systemic toxicity, dysentery, and dehydration, the presentation is most consistent with Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC).

questions.stem: A patient presents with pneumonia, and culture shows Gram-positive branching rods with molar-tooth colonies on chocolate agar under strict anaerobic conditions. The organism is also catalase- and oxidase-positive. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Actinomyces This question describes the key laboratory features of the genus Actinomyces. Actinomyces species are Gram-positive, filamentous, branching rods that are part of the normal oral flora. They are fastidious and grow best under strict anaerobic conditions. When cultured, they characteristically form colonies that are rough, white, and raised, resembling the surface of a molar tooth. The patient's presentation with pneumonia suggests an aspiration event, which is the typical route for pulmonary actinomycosis. While the question states the organism is catalase and oxidase positive, this is variable among species and may be an error in the question stem, as A. israelii is typically catalase-negative. However, the combination of Gram-positive branching rods, anaerobic growth, and molar tooth colonies is highly specific for Actinomyces. H. influenzae (B), Pseudomonas (C), and E. coli (D) are all Gram-negative organisms.

questions.stem: A chest X-ray shows cavitary lesions. The organism grows slowly on buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar and produces aerial hyphae. A Gram-stained image of the cultured organism is provided. What is the causative agent of this disease?
questions.explanation: Nocardia asteroides This question provides a classic constellation of findings for pulmonary nocardiosis. The chest radiograph showing cavitary lesions indicates a necrotizing pneumonia. The key microbiological clues are the growth on Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract (BCYE) agar, which is a special medium used for isolating fastidious organisms like Legionella and Nocardia. The Gram stain image shows Gram-positive, fine, branching, filamentous rods, which is the characteristic morphology of Nocardia. These filaments often fragment into rod-like or coccoid forms. Furthermore, Nocardia species are weakly acid-fast (using a modified stain) and form chalky, white-to-orange aerial hyphae on culture media, consistent with the description. Legionella (C) is a Gram-negative rod. Histoplasma (B) is a fungus. Mycobacterium (D) is strongly acid-fast and has a different appearance. Therefore, the etiology is Nocardia asteroides.

questions.stem: The Gram-stained smear of urethral exudate from a male (shown in the photo) is diagnostic for which disease?
questions.explanation: Gonorrhea The image provided is a Gram stain of a urethral smear. It shows multiple polymorphonuclear leukocytes (neutrophils), and critically, within the cytoplasm of these neutrophils, there are numerous small, kidney-bean-shaped, Gram-negative (pink) cocci arranged in pairs (diplococci). The presence of these intracellular Gram-negative diplococci is the pathognomonic and diagnostic microscopic finding for gonorrhea, an infection caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae. This finding has very high specificity (>99%) for diagnosing gonococcal urethritis in a symptomatic male. Chancroid (A) is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi (Gram-negative coccobacilli). Lymphogranuloma venereum (C) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, an obligate intracellular bacterium that cannot be seen on a Gram stain. Nongonococcal urethritis (D) is a diagnosis of exclusion when gonorrhea is ruled out. 84. What are the features of chancroid?1. School of fish on Gram staining 2. Painful ulcer 3. Bleeds on touch 4. Groove sign (A) C & D (B) A,B & D (C) A B & C (D) A,C & D As  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020 (C) A, B & C. Chancroid, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi, has several distinct features : 1. School of fish on Gram staining (A) : This is the classic microscopic finding. When a sample from the ulcer is Gram-stained, the gram-negative coccobacilli arrange themselves in parallel chains, which is described as a "school of fish" or "railroad track" appearance. 2. Painful ulcer (B) : Unlike the painless chancre of primary syphilis, the genital ulcer of chancroid is typically soft, tender, and very painful. 3. Bleeds on touch (C) : The base of the chancroid ulcer is friable, meaning it is delicate and bleeds easily upon contact or scraping. The Groove sign (D) is not a feature of chancroid. It is characteristic of lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), where enlarged inguinal and femoral lymph nodes are separated by the inguinal ligament, creating a visible groove. PSM

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate method for reviewing previous research studies?
questions.explanation: Meta analysis To synthesize and study the findings from a collection of previously conducted research studies on a specific topic, the most rigorous and powerful method is a meta-analysis. A meta-analysis is a quantitative, formal, epidemiological study design used to systematically assess the results of previous research to derive conclusions about that body of research. It goes beyond a simple literature review by using statistical methods to combine the effect estimates from individual studies, resulting in a single, more precise, and powerful summary estimate. This allows for a comprehensive and objective evaluation of the existing evidence. A chi-square test (B) is a statistical test used within a single study. Cross-sectional (C) and case-control (D) studies are designs for conducting primary research, not for synthesizing the results of previous studies.

questions.stem: What is the most suitable option for mass chemoprophylaxis against anemia in a population?

options.text: Ferrous Fumarate + B12 + Folic Acid + Vitamin C

questions.explanation: Ferrous Sulphate For mass chemoprophylaxis of anemia in a population, the ideal preparation should be effective, safe, inexpensive, widely available, and suitable for large-scale public health distribution. Ferrous sulphate fulfills these criteria and is the most commonly recommended iron preparation in national anemia control programs. Ferrous sulphate contains a high proportion of elemental iron, is cost-effective, and has well-established efficacy in preventing and treating iron deficiency anemia. It is included in government initiatives such as the Anemia Mukt Bharat strategy under the National Health Mission in India. The tablet form allows easy distribution in schools, antenatal clinics, and community health programs.Combination preparations containing vitamin B12, folic acid, and vitamin C are more expensive and unnecessary for routine mass prophylaxis unless specific deficiencies are documented. Intravenous iron is reserved for severe anemia or malabsorption and is not practical for community-level prophylaxis.Therefore, for large-scale public health prevention of anemia, ferrous sulphate is the most suitable option.

questions.stem: Persistent dribbling of urine in a child who otherwise urinates normally is most likely due to which condition?
questions.explanation: Ectopic ureter since birth The clinical history of continuous, day-and-night urinary dribbling in a female child who also has a normal pattern of voiding (i.e., she can hold urine and void voluntarily) is the classic and pathognomonic presentation of an ectopic ureter. In this congenital anomaly, the ureter from the upper pole of a duplicated renal system or a single system does not insert correctly into the bladder trigone. Instead, it inserts distally to the urethral sphincter mechanism, typically into the urethra, vagina, or vestibule. Because the opening is outside the control of the sphincter, urine from the kidney it drains will leak continuously, causing constant wetness, while the normally draining kidney and bladder function correctly, allowing for normal voiding patterns. A ureterocele (B) may cause obstruction or reflux but not this specific pattern of incontinence.

questions.stem: A patient with nephrotic syndrome is currently taking steroids. Which statement regarding the vaccines that can be administered is true?

options.text: Pneumococcal vaccine has to be given prior to treatment
Only killed vaccines can be given
OPV should not be given to siblings

questions.explanation: Only killed vaccines can be given A patient with nephrotic syndrome who is receiving high-dose steroids is considered immunocompromised. Corticosteroids suppress cell-mediated immunity, increasing the risk of infection and reducing the body’s ability to handle live attenuated vaccines safely. In such patients, live vaccines are contraindicated during immunosuppressive therapy because they may cause vaccine-derived infection. Live vaccines include OPV , MMR, varicella, and BCG. These should be deferred until steroid therapy is stopped and immune function has recovered (usually after at least 1 month of stopping high-dose steroids).However, inactivated (killed) vaccines are safe and can be administered, although their immune response may be slightly reduced. Vaccines such as inactivated influenza vaccine and pneumococcal vaccine are recommended because nephrotic patients are at increased risk of infections.Vaccination strictly “as per schedule” is not correct during active immunosuppression. Pneumococcal vaccine ideally should be given before steroid therapy but can still be given later if missed. Thus, during steroid therapy in nephrotic syndrome, only killed vaccines should be given.

questions.stem: Identify the equipment shown in the image.
questions.explanation: Neonatal Resuscitation Tray The image shows a radiant warmer, also known as an infant warmer. This is a key piece of equipment found in delivery rooms and neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). Its primary function is to provide overhead infrared heat to maintain the body temperature of a newborn infant and prevent hypothermia, to which newborns are extremely vulnerable. The open design of the warmer allows for complete access to the infant for assessment, procedures, and resuscitation. It is the central component of a neonatal resuscitation station or tray. A fully equipped resuscitation station would include the warmer, along with all the necessary equipment for airway management (suction, bag-mask), oxygen delivery, and emergency medications. Therefore, it is most accurately identified as part of the neonatal resuscitation setup.

questions.stem: Congenital pyloric stenosis presents with which of the following?
questions.explanation: A & B Both Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a condition seen typically in infants between 2–8 weeks of age. It occurs due to hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle, leading to gastric outlet obstruction. Projectile, non-bilious vomiting is the hallmark feature because the obstruction is proximal to the duodenum; therefore, bile does not mix with gastric contents. Hence, option (C) bilious vomiting is incorrect.Due to repeated vomiting of gastric contents (which contain hydrochloric acid), there is loss of hydrogen and chloride ions. This results in hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, making option (A) correct. Persistent vomiting also leads to dehydration.On abdominal examination, a firm, olive-shaped mass may be palpated in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. This palpable “pyloric olive” represents the hypertrophied pylorus, making option (B) correct.Thus, congenital pyloric stenosis presents with metabolic alkalosis and an abdominal mass, so the correct answer is A and B (Option D).

questions.stem: A child has a bed-wetting habit, and organic causes have been excluded. What is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Bed alarm The condition described is primary nocturnal enuresis, which is bed-wetting in a child older than 5 years who has never achieved a consistent period of nighttime dryness, and in whom organic causes have been excluded. The first-line management involves conservative measures and behavioral therapy. The most effective and recommended behavioral therapy with the highest long-term success rate is the enuresis alarm, or bed alarm. This device consists of a moisture sensor placed in the child's underwear that is connected to an alarm. When the child begins to urinate, the sensor triggers the alarm, which wakes the child. Over time, this conditions the child to recognize the sensation of a full bladder and to wake up to void before the alarm goes off. Pharmacotherapy (A), such as with desmopressin or imipramine, is considered a second-line option for short-term control but has a high relapse rate when stopped. ORTHOPEDIC

questions.stem: If a doctor is inserting screws into the vertebrae, where will these screws be placed?
questions.explanation: Pedicle In modern spinal fusion and instrumentation surgery, the most common and biomechanically robust method for achieving fixation to the vertebrae is through the use of pedicle screws. The pedicle is a strong, cylindrical pillar of bone that connects the posterior elements (lamina, facets) of a vertebra to the vertebral body. Placing a screw down the central axis of the pedicle and into the vertebral body allows for a rigid, three-column purchase on the vertebra. This provides a very strong anchor point to which rods can be attached to stabilize the spine, correct deformities, or facilitate fusion. While other fixation methods exist (e.g., laminar hooks or screws, facet screws), pedicle screw instrumentation is the workhorse of contemporary spinal surgery due to its superior strength and versatility. questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding patients with primary open-angle glaucoma?

options.text: Relatives have 1% chance of developing the same condition
Relatives are more likely to develop steroid- induced glaucoma
When a pupil is dilated, IOP increases
Visual loss can be seen in the peripheral field with normal vision in the central field

questions.explanation: Visual loss can be seen in the peripheral field with normal vision in the central field Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic, progressive optic neuropathy characterized by a specific pattern of optic nerve head damage and corresponding visual field loss. A hallmark feature of glaucoma is that it typically affects the peripheral visual field first, while central visual acuity remains preserved until the late stages of the disease. The characteristic visual field defects include nasal steps, arcuate scotomas, and eventually tunnel vision. This insidious loss of peripheral vision is why glaucoma is often called the "silent thief of sight." Statement (A) is incorrect; first-degree relatives have a significantly higher risk (up to 10-fold) than 1%. A family history of POAG is a risk factor for steroid-induced glaucoma (B), but this is a more complex association. An increase in IOP upon pupillary dilation (C) is the mechanism for angle-closure glaucoma, not open-angle glaucoma.

questions.stem: All the following are true about subconjunctival hemorrhage except :

options.text: It can occur spontaneously in elder people with systolic hypertension
The blood gets absorbed gradually in 6-8 weeks time without treatment.
Use of NSAIDs and aspirin to treat the condition should be avoided.

questions.explanation: The blood gets absorbed gradually in 6-8 weeks time without treatment. This statement is the exception because the time frame is incorrect. A subconjunctival hemorrhage is a common and usually benign condition where a small blood vessel breaks underneath the conjunctiva, causing a bright red patch on the white of the eye. (A) is true : In the vast majority of cases, it is a trivial condition that is painless and does not affect vision. (B) is true : It can occur spontaneously, especially in the elderly with risk factors like hypertension or those on anticoagulants, or it can be precipitated by minor trauma, coughing, or straining. (D) is true : No treatment is needed, but patients should be advised to avoid NSAIDs or aspirin if possible, as these can promote further bleeding. (C) is false : The blood is reabsorbed by the body over time, similar to a bruise. However, the typical resolution time is much shorter than 6-8 weeks. A small hemorrhage usually clears within 1 to 2 weeks.

questions.stem: In which of the following conditions is iritis commonly observed?
questions.explanation: Behçet's disease. Iritis, which is inflammation of the iris (the colored part of the eye), is a form of anterior uveitis. While it can be associated with several systemic inflammatory conditions, it is a hallmark feature of Behçet's disease. 1. Behçet's Disease : This is a rare autoimmune disorder that causes inflammation in blood vessels throughout the body. Ocular involvement is very common, affecting up to 70% of patients. Iritis (anterior uveitis) is one of the most frequent eye problems seen in this condition, often being recurrent and severe. 2. SLE (Systemic Lupus Erythematosus) : While SLE can affect almost any part of the body, including the eyes, severe iritis is not a common manifestation. More frequent ocular problems in SLE include dry eye syndrome (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and retinal disease. 3. Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) : In adults with RA, the most common inflammatory eye condition is scleritis (inflammation of the white part of the eye), not iritis. Dry eye syndrome is also very common. Iritis is more typically associated with the juvenile form of arthritis (JIA). 4. Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) : Iritis does occur in patients with psoriatic arthritis, with a prevalence of about 7-25%. However, the association and frequency are considered strongest and most characteristic in Behçet's disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs are used to distinguish a fixed, dilated pupil?
questions.explanation: Pilocarpine A fixed dilated pupil can be caused by several conditions, including a third nerve palsy, pharmacological blockade (mydriasis), or Adie's tonic pupil. A pharmacological test using dilute pilocarpine is used to help differentiate the cause. Pilocarpine is a direct-acting cholinergic agonist that constricts the pupil. 1. Adie's tonic pupil : This is caused by denervation of the postganglionic parasympathetic supply to the iris sphincter. The denervated muscle becomes supersensitive to acetylcholine. A very dilute (e.g., 0.125%) pilocarpine solution, which would have no effect on a normal pupil, will cause marked constriction in an Adie's pupil, confirming the diagnosis. 2. Pharmacological blockade : If the pupil is dilated by an anticholinergic drug (like atropine), it will not constrict even to a standard strength (1%) pilocarpine solution. 3. Third nerve palsy : A pupil dilated due to a third nerve palsy will constrict in response to a standard strength (1%) pilocarpine solution.

questions.stem: Regarding the Kayser-Fleischer ring, which of the following is true?

options.text: Starts first in superior and inferior cornea
Seen in all cases of hepatic involvement
Seen in all cases of brain involvement of Wilson's disease

questions.explanation: Starts first in superior and inferior cornea The Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring is the pathognomonic clinical sign of Wilson's disease, a disorder of copper metabolism. It consists of a golden-brown to greenish deposit of copper in Descemet's membrane at the periphery of the cornea (the limbus). 1. (B) is true : The deposition of copper typically starts in the superior and inferior aspects of the cornea first and then progresses to become circumferential. This is best visualized using a slit lamp. 2. (A) is false : The KF ring fades and can eventually disappear with effective copper chelation therapy, but the agent used is D-penicillamine or trientine, not desferrioxamine, which is an iron chelator. 3. (C) is false : The KF ring is not present in all patients with Wilson's disease, particularly in those who present with purely hepatic symptoms. 4. (D) is false : While the KF ring is present in over 95% of patients who have neurological or psychiatric symptoms of Wilson's disease, it is not seen in absolutely all cases.

questions.stem: Identify the nerve from the list provided that does not play a role in moving the eyeball.
questions.explanation: Optic Nerve The movements of the eyeball are controlled by the six extraocular muscles, which are innervated by three specific cranial nerves, known as the oculomotor nerves. 1. The oculomotor nerve (CN III) (B) innervates the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. 2. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) (C) innervates the superior oblique muscle. 3. The abducens nerve (CN VI) (D) innervates the lateral rectus muscle. These three nerves are purely motor (or mixed motor/parasympathetic in the case of CN III) and are responsible for all voluntary and reflex eye movements. In contrast, the optic nerve (CN II) (A) is a purely sensory nerve. It is responsible for transmitting visual information from the retina to the brain. It has no motor function and therefore does not cause any movement of the eyeball. MEDICINE 102. From the options listed below, which one is not considered a standard treatment for COVID-19?1. Remdesivir 2. Dexamethasone 3. Fluids 4. Antibiotics (A) 1 & 2 (B) 1, 2 & 3 (C) 1 & 3 (D) None As  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2020 (D) None This question asks which of the listed interventions are not included in the treatment of COVID-19. 1. Remdesivir : An antiviral medication that has been authorized and used for the treatment of hospitalized patients with COVID-19 to shorten recovery time. 2. Dexamethasone : A corticosteroid that has been proven to reduce mortality in hospitalized patients with COVID-19 who require supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation. 3. Fluids : Intravenous or oral fluids are a cornerstone of supportive care for any critically ill patient, including those with COVID-19, to maintain hydration and organ perfusion. 4. Antibiotics : While antibiotics have no effect on the SARS-CoV-2 virus itself, they are frequently used in hospitalized COVID-19 patients to treat or prevent secondary bacterial pneumonia, which is a common complication. Since all four interventions have a role in the comprehensive management of patients with moderate to severe COVID-19, the correct answer is that none of them are excluded from the potential treatment plan.

questions.stem: All of the following are true about Gout, except :

options.text: Occurs due to accumulation of urate crystals in joint
Birefringent crystals are present in joint

questions.explanation: Occurs more in females This statement is the exception because it is false. Gout has a strong predilection for males, who are affected much more commonly than females, especially before the age of menopause. The incidence in women increases after menopause as the uricosuric effect of estrogen is lost. The other statements are all true. Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in and around the joints (A), which occurs in the setting of hyperuricemia. Examination of synovial fluid from an affected joint under polarized light reveals needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals (C), which is the gold standard for diagnosis. Gouty attacks can be precipitated by certain medications that increase uric acid levels by decreasing its renal excretion, a classic example of which is the anti-tuberculosis drug pyrazinamide (B). 104. questions.stem: What does the difference between the maximum and minimum values in a dataset represent?
questions.explanation: Range In descriptive statistics, several measures are used to summarize a dataset. The range is the simplest measure of dispersion or variability. It is defined as the difference between the maximum (highest) and minimum (lowest) observed values in a dataset. It provides a quick and easy-to-calculate indication of the spread of the data. For example, if the test scores in a class are from 65 to 95, the range is 95 - 65 = 30. While it is simple, it is highly sensitive to outliers and does not provide information about the distribution of values between the two extremes. The mean (A) is the average, the median (B) is the middle value, and the mode (D) is the most frequent value; these are all measures of central tendency, not dispersion.

questions.stem: All of the following clinical features are seen in Zika fever except :
questions.explanation: Petechial rash Zika virus infection is typically a mild febrile illness. The most common clinical features are a low-grade fever with arthralgia (joint pain) (C), a diffuse maculopapular rash, and non-purulent conjunctivitis (D). While the acute illness is usually mild, Zika is known for its severe neurological complications. It is a recognized trigger for the development of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) (A), an acute autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy, in adults. The most devastating complication is congenital Zika syndrome in infants born to mothers infected during pregnancy. The rash associated with Zika is typically maculopapular (composed of flat red spots and small raised bumps). A petechial rash (B), which consists of small, non-blanching spots caused by intradermal hemorrhage, is not a characteristic feature of Zika fever. Petechiae are more commonly associated with other viral infections like dengue fever or with meningococcemia.

questions.stem: When to use hand sanitizer?A. Before touching the patient B. After touching the patient C. When hands are soiled. D. After touching patient's surrounding.
questions.explanation: A, B & D The World Health Organization's "5 Moments for Hand Hygiene" outline the critical points during patient care when hand hygiene is required to prevent the transmission of healthcare-associated infections. Alcohol-based hand sanitizer is the preferred method for hand hygiene when hands are not visibly soiled. These moments include : 1. Moment : Before touching a patient (A), to protect the patient from harmful germs carried on your hands. 2. Moment : Before a clean or aseptic procedure. 3. Moment : After a body fluid exposure risk. 4. Moment : After touching a patient (B), to protect yourself and the healthcare environment from the patient's germs. 5. Moment : After touching the patient's surroundings (D), even if you haven't touched the patient directly. Crucially, hand sanitizer is not effective when hands are visibly dirty or soiled (C). In that situation, hands must be washed with soap and water.

questions.stem: Which discrete probability distribution describes the likelihood of a certain number of events occurring within a fixed interval of time or space?
questions.explanation: Poisson The Poisson distribution is a discrete probability distribution that is used to model the number of events occurring within a specified, fixed interval of time or space. It is applicable when these events occur with a known constant mean rate and independently of the time since the last event. Classic examples include the number of phone calls received by a call center in one hour, the number of mutations in a given stretch of DNA, or the number of radioactive decay events in a second. The Binomial distribution (B) describes the number of successes in a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials. The Gaussian (Normal) distribution (A) is a continuous probability distribution, not a discrete one. The Erlang distribution (D) is a continuous distribution related to waiting times.

questions.stem: Which device is used to indicate heat exposure in vaccines?
questions.explanation: VVM A Vaccine Vial Monitor (VVM) is a small, heat-sensitive label that is placed on a vaccine vial to provide a visual indication of its cumulative heat exposure over time. The VVM consists of a dark outer circle and a lighter inner square. The inner square is made of a heat-sensitive material that darkens gradually and irreversibly when exposed to heat. The rule for interpreting a VVM is : "If the inner square is the same color as or darker than the outer circle, do not use the vaccine." This simple tool allows healthcare workers to determine if a vaccine has been exposed to potentially damaging temperatures and should be discarded, ensuring that only potent vaccines are administered. It is a critical component of the cold chain management system for many vaccines. ENT

questions.stem: All of the following are complications of Otitis Media, except :
questions.explanation: Battle Sign Otitis media can lead to several serious intracranial and extracranial complications. Griesinger's sign (B) is edema and tenderness over the mastoid process due to thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein, a sign of sigmoid sinus thrombosis. Bezold's abscess (D) is a deep neck abscess that forms when pus from mastoiditis erodes through the mastoid tip and tracks down the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The "empty delta sign" (A) is a radiological sign seen on contrast-enhanced CT or MRI, representing dural sinus thrombosis (often the sigmoid or superior sagittal sinus). In contrast, Battle's sign (C) is a clinical sign of a basal skull fracture. It consists of ecchymosis (bruising) over the mastoid process that appears 24-48 hours after head trauma. It is related to trauma, not a complication of otitis media.

questions.stem: Name the structure marked as MT in the provided image.
questions.explanation: Middle turbinate The image is an endoscopic view of the inside of the nasal cavity. Several key landmarks are labeled. NS indicates the nasal septum, the midline wall separating the two nasal passages. IT indicates the inferior turbinate, which is the largest of the three turbinates and is located along the floor of the nasal cavity. The structure labeled MT is located superior to the inferior turbinate. This is the middle turbinate. The space underneath the middle turbinate is the middle meatus, which is a critically important area as it is the drainage site for the maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoid sinuses. The superior turbinate (C) is located higher and more posteriorly and is not typically visible on a routine anterior nasal endoscopy without special angulation. The structure labeled MT is clearly identifiable as the middle turbinate. 94. Sequence of Auditory Pathway?1. Cochlear nucleus 2. Spiral ganglion 3. Auditary cortex 4. Inferior colliculus 5. Superior olivary nucleus 6. Lateral lemniscus

questions.stem: Medial geniculate body
questions.explanation: 2156473 The central auditory pathway follows a specific sequence from the ear to the brain. 1. The first-order neurons are in the spiral ganglion (2) in the cochlea. Their axons form the auditory nerve. 2. The auditory nerve synapses on the cochlear nucleus (1) in the brainstem. 3. From the cochlear nucleus, fibers ascend bilaterally, with many crossing over and synapsing in the superior olivary nucleus (5), which is crucial for sound localization. 4. Axons from these nuclei then ascend in a tract called the lateral lemniscus (6). 5. The fibers of the lateral lemniscus synapse in the inferior colliculus (4) of the midbrain. 6. From the inferior colliculus, neurons project to the medial geniculate body (7) of the thalamus, the main auditory relay station. 7. Finally, fibers from the medial geniculate body project to the primary auditory cortex (3) in the temporal lobe. The correct sequence is 2 → 1 → 5 → 6 → 4 → 7 → 3.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an objective test?
questions.explanation: Pure Tone Audiometry Audiological tests can be classified as objective or subjective (behavioral). Objective tests do not require a behavioral response from the patient; they measure a physiological response. Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA) or ABR (A), Impedance Audiometry (including tympanometry and acoustic reflex testing) (C), and otoacoustic emissions are all objective tests. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) (B) is an objective imaging test used in ophthalmology, not audiology. In contrast, Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA) is a subjective or behavioral test. It requires the patient to listen to tones of specific frequencies and intensities and provide a conscious response (e.g., by raising a hand or pressing a button) when they hear the tone. The results depend entirely on the patient's perception and cooperation, making it a subjective measure of hearing thresholds. NODIA

questions.stem: What is the size of a pink IV cannula?
questions.explanation: 20 G Intravenous (IV) cannulas are universally color-coded to allow for rapid identification of their gauge size. The gauge number indicates the internal diameter of the cannula, with a smaller number corresponding to a larger diameter and a higher potential flow rate. The standard color code for a 20-gauge IV cannula is pink. This is a very common, general-purpose size used in adults for routine IV fluid administration, giving IV medications, and for blood transfusions when a larger gauge is not necessary. For reference, an 18-gauge cannula is green (B), a 22-gauge cannula is blue (C), and a 16-gauge cannula is gray (D). Remembering these color codes is an essential practical skill in clinical settings.

questions.stem: A farmer develops a painless foot lesion with multiple discharging sinuses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mycetoma The clinical triad of a painless, tumefied (swollen) subcutaneous lesion, the formation of multiple draining sinuses, and the discharge of grains (macroscopic colonies of the causative agent) is pathognomonic for mycetoma, also known as Madura foot. This is a chronic, progressive, granulomatous infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissues that can extend to involve the underlying fascia and bone. It is typically caused by the traumatic inoculation of soil-dwelling organisms into the foot, making farmers a high-risk group. The infection can be caused by either fungi (eumycetoma) or filamentous bacteria (actinomycetoma). Sporotrichosis (C) classically presents with lymphocutaneous spread. Squamous cell carcinoma (B) would present as a non-healing ulcer or fungating mass, but not typically with multiple sinuses discharging grains.

questions.stem: What is the first and specific marker for myocardial infarction (MI)?
questions.explanation: Troponin Cardiac troponins (specifically troponin T and troponin I) are regulatory proteins that are components of the contractile apparatus of cardiac muscle. They are highly specific to the myocardium. When myocardial cells are damaged and undergo necrosis during a myocardial infarction (MI), these proteins are released into the bloodstream. The measurement of serum cardiac troponin levels is the current gold standard and the most sensitive and specific biochemical marker for the diagnosis of MI. Troponins begin to rise in the blood within 2-4 hours of the onset of injury, peak at 12-24 hours, and can remain elevated for 7-14 days. While Creatine Kinase (CK), especially the CK-MB isoenzyme, was previously used, it is less specific than troponin as it is also found in skeletal muscle. questions.stem: A road-traffic-accident (RTA) patient with polytrauma has unstable vitals, is intubated due to a low Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), shows no eye opening, no verbal response, no motor response to pain, and CT scan reveals brain edema. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: CO2 retention due to respiratory depression by morphine

questions.explanation: Diffuse axonal injury This is a duplicate of a previous question. The patient has suffered a severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) from an RTA, resulting in a deep coma with a GCS score of 3 (E1, V1, M1). The CT scan finding of brain edema without a focal mass lesion like a hematoma, in the context of a high-impact trauma and severe neurological deficit, is highly suggestive of diffuse axonal injury (DAI). DAI is caused by shearing forces from acceleration-deceleration, which lead to widespread microscopic damage to axons throughout the brain. This widespread disruption of neuronal pathways results in immediate and profound coma. The subsequent development of cytotoxic and vasogenic brain edema is a common consequence of this severe primary injury. Post-concussion syndrome (C) follows a mild TBI. PRES (A) has a different etiology and imaging appearance.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female reports breast pain, edema, redness, warmth, and rapid enlargement over 15 days. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: IBC (Inflammatory Breast Cancer) The patient's presentation with a rapidly progressive, painful, red, warm, and swollen breast is a classic and highly concerning picture for Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC). IBC is a rare but extremely aggressive form of breast cancer. It is characterized by the diffuse infiltration and blockage of the dermal lymphatics by cancer cells. This lymphatic obstruction is what causes the characteristic signs of inflammation : erythema (redness), edema (swelling), and a "peau d'orange" (orange peel) appearance of the skin. A key feature is the rapid onset and progression of these symptoms, often over a period of days to weeks, frequently without a distinct palpable lump. This clinical diagnosis must be considered an emergency, and an urgent skin punch biopsy is required for confirmation. While mastitis is a differential, in a non-lactating woman, IBC must be ruled out first.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about a pilonidal sinus is incorrect?

options.text: It is more common in men.
Hair follicles are seen in the wall of sinus.
Treatment of choice is surgical excision of sinus tract.

questions.explanation: Mostly congenital. This statement is incorrect. For many years, pilonidal sinus disease was thought to be a congenital condition arising from a remnant of the neural tube. However, the modern and widely accepted understanding is that it is an acquired condition. The process is believed to begin with the stretching and blockage of hair follicles in the natal cleft. Loose hairs are then driven into these dilated follicles by friction and pressure, creating a foreign body reaction that leads to the formation of a sinus tract and recurrent inflammation or abscess. The other statements are correct. Pilonidal sinus is significantly more common in men (A), particularly in hirsute individuals. The sinus tracts characteristically contain nests of hair, but hair follicles are not seen in the wall of the sinus (B), which supports the acquired theory (hair is driven in from the outside). The definitive treatment is surgical excision of the sinus tract (D). 122. According to the European Hernia Society (EHS) classification, what defines an M3 hernia?

questions.stem: What is the most common retroperitoneal tumor?
questions.explanation: Liposarcoma Primary retroperitoneal tumors are rare, and the vast majority are malignant soft tissue sarcomas. The single most common histological type of primary retroperitoneal sarcoma in adults is liposarcoma. These tumors arise from adipose tissue within the retroperitoneum and can grow to an enormous size before they cause symptoms. They account for approximately one-third of all retroperitoneal sarcomas. The second most common type is leiomyosarcoma, which arises from smooth muscle. While other sarcomas like rhabdomyosarcoma (B), synovial sarcoma (C), and neurofibrosarcoma (D) (now more commonly called malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor) can occur in the retroperitoneum, they are all significantly less common than liposarcoma.

questions.explanation: a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i Identification: 1. (A) shows a large calibrated collection bag with a long catheter and measurement markings → Urobag (iii). 2. questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis for the ulcer shown in the image?
questions.explanation: Neuropathic ulcer The image shows a deep, "punched-out" ulcer located on a pressure-bearing point on the sole of the foot, specifically over a metatarsal head. The surrounding skin is often callused. This appearance and location are classic for a neuropathic ulcer, also known as a mal perforans ulcer. These ulcers are the result of peripheral neuropathy, most commonly caused by diabetes mellitus. The loss of protective sensation due to the neuropathy means that the patient is unaware of repetitive minor trauma and pressure on the foot. This, combined with motor neuropathy causing foot deformities (like claw toes) and autonomic neuropathy causing dry, cracked skin, leads to tissue breakdown and the formation of these characteristic painless ulcers. A trophic ulcer (B) is a similar term. A venous ulcer (C) typically occurs on the medial malleolus ("gaiter area") and is associated with signs of chronic venous insufficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following instruments can be used to stop esophageal variceal bleeding?
questions.explanation: a, b, c, d. All four instruments shown are used in the management of bleeding esophageal varices. Here is a breakdown of each :a & b. Balloon Tamponade Tubes : These are Sengstaken-Blakemore tubes (or similar variants like the Minnesota tube). They are inserted into the esophagus and stomach. The device has two balloons : a gastric balloon that is inflated and pulled taut to anchor it, and a long esophageal balloon that is then inflated to apply direct pressure (tamponade) on the bleeding varices. This is a temporary, life-saving measure used to control severe, uncontrolled hemorrhage. c & d. Flexible Endoscopes : These are standard upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopes. Endoscopy is the primary and definitive method for both diagnosing and treating esophageal variceal bleeding. Through the endoscope, a gastroenterologist can perform procedures like :Endoscopic Variceal Ligation (EVL or Banding) : The preferred treatment, where small rubber bands are placed around the varices to cut off their blood supply.Sclerotherapy : Injecting a solution into the varices to make them clot and shrink. Since both balloon tamponade devices (a, b) and endoscopes (c, d) are crucial tools for stopping esophageal variceal bleeding, the correct option includes all four. 127. questions.stem: A 40-year-old male with varicose veins presents with eczema and lipodermatosclerosis. According to the CEAP classification, this falls under which category?
questions.explanation: C4 The CEAP (Clinical, Etiological, Anatomical, Pathophysiological) classification is the standard system for describing chronic venous disorders. The "C" component describes the clinical signs on a scale from 0 to 6. 1. C0 : No visible or palpable signs of venous disease. 2. C1 : Telangiectasias or reticular veins. 3. C2 : Varicose veins. 4. C3 : Edema. 5. C4 : Changes in the skin and subcutaneous tissue secondary to chronic venous disease. This class is further subdivided :iii. C4a : Pigmentation or eczema. iv. C4b : Lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie blanche. v. C4c : Corona phlebectatica. 6. C5 : Healed venous ulcer. 7. C6 : Active venous ulcer. Since the patient has both eczema and lipodermatosclerosis, he falls under the C4 clinical category.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a component of the qSOFA score?
questions.explanation: Heart rate The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score is a simple bedside tool used to identify patients with suspected infection who are at a high risk of poor outcomes (i.e., sepsis). It consists of three clinical criteria, with one point awarded for each : 1. Respiratory Rate (RR) : A high respiratory rate of ≥ 22 breaths per minute. 2. Mental Status : An altered mental status, typically assessed with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of < 15. 3. Blood Pressure (BP) : A low systolic blood pressure of ≥ 100 mmHg. A score of 2 or more suggests a high risk of sepsis and warrants further investigation and management. Heart rate is not a component of the qSOFA score, although tachycardia is a common sign of sepsis and is included in the more comprehensive SIRS criteria and the full SOFA score.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl presents with a left-sided neck swelling that has grown slowly since childhood and feels hard on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Neural tumor In a young patient presenting with a slow-growing, hard, deep-seated neck mass, a benign neural tumor should be a primary consideration. Specifically, a schwannoma or a neurofibroma, which are tumors arising from the nerve sheaths of peripheral nerves, fit this description well. These tumors can originate from various nerves in the neck, such as the vagus nerve or branches of the cervical plexus. They are typically firm, mobile, and grow very slowly over many years. A cystic hygroma (D), a lymphatic malformation, is typically soft, cystic, and present in infancy. A lipoma (C) is a benign tumor of fat cells and is characteristically soft and doughy, not hard. A chemodectoma (B), or carotid body tumor, is a paraganglioma that is typically found in middle-aged adults, is pulsatile, and is classically mobile side-to-side but not vertically (Fontaine's sign). Therefore, a neural tumor is the most likely diagnosis for a hard, slow-growing mass in this age group.

questions.stem: Regarding the boundaries of the laparoscopic anatomy of an inguinal hernia, which of the following statements is false?

options.text: Medial boundary of triangle of Doom is vas deferens
Lateral boundary of triangle of pain is Iliopubic tract
Myopectineal orifice is bounded by internal oblique & transverse abdominis superiorly
Myopectineal orifice is bounded by Iliopubic tract inferiorly

questions.explanation: Myopectineal orifice is bounded by Iliopubic tract inferiorly In laparoscopic inguinal anatomy, understanding the Myopectineal Orifice of Fruchaud is vital for successful hernia repair. The statement in (D) is false because the inferior boundary of this orifice is the pectineal ligament (Cooper’s ligament) and the superior pubic ramus, not the iliopubic tract.The iliopubic tract actually serves as a key landmark for the Triangle of Pain, forming its lateral and superior border. This triangle is clinically significant because it contains the lateral femoral cutaneous and genitofemoral nerves; placing surgical tacks here can lead to chronic nerve entrapment. Conversely, the Triangle of Doom is defined medially by the vas deferens and laterally by the spermatic vessels. Surgeons must avoid this zone to prevent life-threatening injury to the external iliac artery and vein. Finally, the superior boundary of the Myopectineal Orifice consists of the arching fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. Mastering these boundaries allows surgeons to safely navigate the "Circle of Death" and ensure mesh coverage over all potential hernia sites.

questions.stem: A patient has had severe abdominal pain for 2 hours, blood pressure 90/60, pulse 112/min with an irregular rhythm, repeated vomiting, a soft abdomen, and absent bowel sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute mesenteric ischemia This clinical presentation is a classic picture of acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI). The most pathognomonic feature described is the significant disparity between the patient's severe, excruciating abdominal pain and the relatively benign findings on physical examination (a soft, often non-tender abdomen). This "pain out of proportion to physical findings" is the hallmark of AMI. The patient is also in shock (hypotension and tachycardia) due to bowel ischemia and third-spacing of fluid. The presence of an irregular pulse strongly suggests atrial fibrillation, which is the most common cause of superior mesenteric artery embolism, the leading cause of AMI. The absent bowel sounds indicate an adynamic ileus secondary to the bowel infarction. A peptic perforation (A) would cause peritonitis and a rigid abdomen. Severe pancreatitis (D) and a ruptured aneurysm (B) would typically be associated with significant abdominal tenderness and guarding on examination.

questions.stem: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with hyper-resonance, hypotension, and absent breath sounds on the right side. What is the next step in the investigation?

options.text: Wide bore needle followed by intercostal tube drainage in 5th ICS

questions.explanation: Wide bore needle followed by intercostal tube drainage in 5th ICS The clinical triad of unilateral absent breath sounds, hyper-resonance to percussion, and hypotension in a trauma patient is diagnostic of a tension pneumothorax. This is a life-threatening emergency that causes obstructive shock and requires immediate intervention without waiting for radiological confirmation. The first and most critical step is to decompress the chest by inserting a wide-bore needle into the pleural space to release the trapped air, converting the tension pneumothorax into a simple one. The current ATLS guidelines recommend the 5th intercostal space (ICS) at the anterior axillary line as the preferred site. This emergency needle decompression is a temporizing measure and must be immediately followed by the definitive treatment, which is the insertion of an intercostal drain (chest tube), also typically in the 5th ICS. Option (B) correctly includes both the immediate life-saving decompression and the necessary subsequent definitive management.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female has a 4.5 × 3 cm irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, not fixed to the pectoralis major, with no skin changes, and a 2 × 1.5 cm palpable lymph node in the right axilla. The opposite breast is normal. What is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation to confirm the diagnosis?a. Mammography b. PET scan c. Biopsy of breast mass d. Ultrasound-guided biopsy of the enlarged axillary lymph node
questions.explanation: a, c & d The patient has a clinically suspicious breast mass and a palpable axillary lymph node, which is highly concerning for locally advanced breast cancer. The "triple test" or "triple assessment" is the standard of care to confirm the diagnosis. This includes clinical examination, imaging, and tissue sampling. Mammography (a) (and often an ultrasound) is the essential initial imaging modality to characterize the mass and look for other lesions. A core needle biopsy of the breast mass (c) is absolutely mandatory to obtain a definitive histological diagnosis, which will also provide information on the tumor type, grade, and receptor status (ER, PR, HER2). Additionally, because there is a clinically suspicious axillary lymph node, an ultrasound-guided biopsy (d) (either FNA or core biopsy) of that node is crucial to confirm the presence of metastasis. This accurately stages the axilla (N-stage) and is critical for planning treatment. A PET scan (b) is a staging tool used to look for distant metastases after the primary diagnosis is confirmed; it is not part of the initial diagnostic confirmation process.

questions.stem: In the Strasberg classification of biliary injury, a posterior sectoral duct injury falls under which class?
questions.explanation: Type C The Strasberg classification is a widely used system to categorize iatrogenic bile duct injuries that occur during cholecystectomy. 1. Type A : Leak from the cystic duct stump or a small duct in the gallbladder fossa. 2. Type B : Occlusion of a part of the biliary tree, most commonly an aberrant right hepatic duct. 3. Type C : A transected (but not ligated) duct that is leaking bile. This most commonly involves a transected aberrant right hepatic duct or a posterior sectoral duct. 4. Type D : A lateral or partial injury to a major bile duct, such as the common bile duct, with bile leakage. 5. Type E : A circumferential injury or transection of the main bile duct, further subdivided based on the level of the injury. Therefore, an injury involving the transection and subsequent leak from a posterior sectoral duct is classified as a Strasberg Type C injury.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old female undergoes cholecystectomy and later develops postoperative abdominal pain. Which test is used to detect a bile leak?
questions.explanation: HIDA When a post-cholecystectomy bile leak is suspected, the most sensitive and specific functional imaging study to identify the leak is a HIDA scan (Hepatobiliary Iminodiacetic Acid scan), also known as cholescintigraphy. This is a nuclear medicine test where a radioactive tracer (e.g., technetium-99m labeled mebrofenin) is injected intravenously. The tracer is taken up by the hepatocytes and excreted into the biliary system, mimicking the flow of bile. The flow of the tracer is imaged over time with a gamma camera. In a patient with a bile leak, the scan will show the tracer flowing normally through the bile ducts but will also demonstrate the abnormal extravasation of the tracer from the biliary tree into the peritoneal cavity, confirming the presence, and often the location, of the leak. While MRCP (B) shows anatomy and ERCP (A) is therapeutic, HIDA is the best test to functionally demonstrate an active leak. 137. What is the Tillaux sign in mesenteric cysts?
