questions.explanation: A-Auriculotemporal, B - Greater auricular, C-Vagus, D-Lesser occipital The auricle (external ear) receives sensory innervation from several nerves derived from the trigeminal nerve, cervical plexus, and vagus nerve. Each region of the auricle has a specific nerve supply. A Auriculotemporal nerve : The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), supplies the anterior and superior part of the auricle and the external acoustic meatus. B Greater auricular nerve : The greater auricular nerve, arising from the cervical plexus (C2–C3), supplies the lower part of the auricle and the skin over the parotid region. It is one of the main sensory nerves of the external ear. C Vagus nerve : The auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold’s nerve) supplies the concha and part of the external auditory canal. Stimulation of this nerve may sometimes produce a cough reflex. NODIA

questions.stem: In a patient with sciatica who has tenderness of the hamstring muscles, which nerve supplies a hybrid muscle that is partially spared in this condition?
questions.explanation: Common peroneal nerve Sciatica occurs due to irritation or compression of the sciatic nerve, which commonly causes pain along the posterior thigh and may affect the hamstring muscles. Most hamstring muscles— semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris—are supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. However, the biceps femoris is considered a hybrid muscle because its two heads receive different nerve supplies. The long head of the biceps femoris is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, while the short head of the biceps femoris is supplied by the common peroneal (fibular) division of the sciatic nerve. In cases of sciatica affecting the tibial component, the muscles innervated by the tibial part may become painful or weak. However, the short head of the biceps femoris, supplied by the common peroneal nerve, may remain partially functional. Because of this dual innervation, the muscle is described as hybrid and can be partially spared in certain sciatic nerve injuries. Therefore, the nerve responsible for supplying the spared portion of this hybrid muscle is the common peroneal nerve.

questions.stem: After lifting heavy weights, a patient develops pain radiating along the back of the thigh and leg. Involvement of which spinal nerve segment is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: S1 Pain that radiates down the posterior aspect of the thigh and leg follows the dermatome of the S1 nerve root. This pattern is classic for sciatica caused by S1 radiculopathy. The most common cause is a herniated disc at the L5-S1 intervertebral level, which compresses the traversing S1 nerve root. Besides pain, S1 compression can cause sensory loss on the posterior leg and lateral aspect of the foot, weakness of plantar flexion (difficulty standing on tiptoes), and a diminished or absent ankle jerk reflex. Pain from L5 radiculopathy (Option B) typically radiates to the posterolateral thigh and leg down to the top of the foot and great toe. L4 radiculopathy (Option A) pain involves the anterior thigh and medial leg. The acute onset after lifting heavy weights is a typical history for disc herniation.

questions.stem: Which anatomical location is the most frequent site for a congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
questions.explanation: Posterolateral Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a birth defect where there is an opening in the diaphragm, allowing abdominal organs to move into the chest cavity. The vast majority of CDH cases occur in the posterolateral region of the diaphragm. This type is known as a Bochdalek hernia, and it results from the failure of the pleuroperitoneal fold to close during fetal development. Bochdalek hernias account for about 85-90% of all CDH cases and are most common on the left side. Anterolateral defects (Option D), known as Morgagni hernias, are much less frequent. Hernias through the central tendon (Option A) or esophageal hiatus (part of the crura, Option C) are also rare compared to the posterolateral location. The herniation can impede lung development, leading to life- threatening pulmonary hypoplasia.

questions.stem: Loss of sensation over the lateral three and a half fingers along with thenar muscle wasting suggests injury to which nerve?
questions.explanation: Median This combination of symptoms is classic for a lesion of the median nerve, typically at the level of the wrist (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome). The median nerve provides sensory innervation to the palmar aspect of the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and the lateral half of the ring finger (lateral 3 1/2 fingers). It also supplies motor function to the three thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis) via its recurrent motor branch. Chronic compression or injury to this nerve results in numbness and tingling in its sensory distribution and weakness, which over time leads to wasting or atrophy of the thenar eminence. The ulnar nerve (Option B) supplies the medial 1 1/2 fingers. The radial nerve (Option C) supplies sensation to the dorsum of the hand. The anterior interosseous nerve (Option D) is a pure motor branch and does not supply skin sensation.

questions.stem: A patient with a nerve injury is unable to form an O shape using the thumb and index finger. Damage to which muscle most likely explains this finding?
questions.explanation: Opponens pollicis The ability to form a perfect O by touching the tips of the thumb and index finger requires fine motor control and intact flexion at the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger. This is the classic test for the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN), a branch of the median nerve, which supplies flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger. However, none of the AIN-supplied muscles are listed. Interpreting the question as a general inability to bring the thumb and finger together in that shape, the action of opposition is critical. Opposition, which allows the thumb to touch the other fingertips, is primarily carried out by the opponens pollicis muscle, innervated by the median nerve. Weakness here would severely impair the ability to form a round O. The other thenar muscles assist but are not the prime movers of opposition.

questions.stem: This particular type of epithelium is most frequently found lining which organ?
questions.explanation: Ureter The photomicrograph shows transitional epithelium, also known as urothelium. This is a specialized stratified epithelium characterized by a surface layer of large, dome-shaped (umbrella) cells that can flatten and stretch. This unique property allows the organ to distend significantly to accommodate varying volumes of fluid. This type of epithelium is found exclusively lining the urinary tract, including the renal calyces, renal pelvis, ureters, urinary bladder, and the proximal urethra. Its function is to provide an impermeable barrier to the toxic components of NODIA

questions.stem: A patient presents with progressively increasing pain associated with a swelling located below the ear lobule. Involvement of which of the following anatomical structures is responsible for this pain?
questions.explanation: Great auricular nerve The swelling described is located in the parotid gland region. The gland is enclosed by a tough, inelastic capsule formed by the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia. When the gland swells, this capsule stretches, causing intense pain. The sensory innervation for the parotid capsule and the overlying skin is provided by the great auricular nerve, a branch of the cervical plexus (C2, C3). Therefore, it is the nerve responsible for transmitting the pain sensation. The auriculotemporal nerve (B) carries secretomotor fibers to the gland. The facial nerve (A) provides motor supply to the muscles of facial expression and passes through the gland but does not convey pain sensation from it. While the deep cervical fascia (D) is the structure being stretched, the question implicitly asks for the neurological structure responsible for perceiving the pain, making the great auricular nerve the most accurate answer.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with features of acute tonsillitis complains of ear pain. Which nerve is responsible for this referred ear pain?
questions.explanation: Tympanic branch of glossopharyngeal nerve This clinical scenario is a classic example of referred pain. The palatine tonsils are primarily innervated by the tonsillar branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). This same cranial nerve also provides sensory innervation to the middle ear cavity and the inner surface of the tympanic membrane via its tympanic branch (Jacobsons nerve). Because both the inflamed tonsil and the middle ear share a common sensory pathway through the glossopharyngeal nerve, the brain misinterprets the origin of the pain signals from the tonsils, perceiving them as coming from the ear. This phenomenon is known as referred otalgia. The other nerves listed innervate the external ear and surrounding skin but do not share a common sensory pathway with the palatine tonsils, making them incorrect choices for this specific clinical presentation.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures originates from the part indicated by the arrow?
questions.explanation: Falciform ligament The figure represents a transverse section of the embryonic foregut region showing ventral and dorsal mesenteries. The arrow in the diagram indicates the ventral mesogastrium, which lies between the developing stomach and the anterior abdominal wall. During embryological development, the primitive gut tube is suspended by two mesenteries: the dorsal mesentery (present throughout the gut) and the ventral mesentery (present only in the foregut region). The ventral mesogastrium develops due to the growth of the liver within this mesentery. As development progresses, the ventral mesogastrium differentiates into two important peritoneal ligaments. The part between the liver and the lesser curvature of the stomach becomes the lesser omentum, while the part between the liver and the anterior abdominal wall forms the falciform ligament. The falciform ligament attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and the diaphragm and contains the ligamentum teres hepatis (remnant of the umbilical vein). In contrast, the gastrosplenic ligament and lienorenal ligament are derivatives of the dorsal mesogastrium, and the phrenicocolic ligament is unrelated to the ventral mesogastrium. Therefore, the structure indicated by the arrow gives rise to the falciform ligament.

questions.stem: Which ligament develops from the indicated structure?
questions.explanation: Falciform ligament The image shows a transverse section of the developing abdomen with an arrow pointing to the ventral mesentery. The ventral mesentery is a fold of peritoneum that attaches the stomach and liver to the anterior (ventral) body wall. The falciform ligament is the primary derivative of this structure in the adult. It connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and the diaphragm. The free, inferior edge of the falciform ligament contains the ligamentum teres hepatis (or round ligament of the liver), which is the obliterated remnant of the fetal umbilical vein. The hepatogastric ligament (D) is also a derivative of the ventral mesentery, forming part of the lesser omentum that connects the liver to the stomach. Given the options, the falciform ligament is a direct and major derivative of the structure attaching the gut tube to the ventral wall.

questions.stem: Pen Test is for which nerve
questions.explanation: PIN The Pen Test is used to assess the function of the Posterior Interosseous Nerve (PIN), which is a deep motor branch of the radial nerve. This nerve primarily supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm, especially those responsible for extension of the fingers and thumb. In the pen test, a pen is placed on the palm, and the patient is asked to extend the fingers to flick or lift the pen off the palm. Successful performance of this movement requires proper functioning of the finger extensor muscles, which are innervated by the posterior interosseous nerve. If the PIN is injured or compressed, the patient cannot extend the fingers properly, resulting in finger drop, while wrist extension may still be partially preserved due to other radial nerve branches. questions.stem: In a patient of liver cirrhosis anastomotic blood flow increase in

options.text: Middle colic vein & left colic vein

questions.explanation: Left gastric vein & esophageal veins Liver cirrhosis leads to portal hypertension, which forces blood from the high-pressure portal system into the low-pressure systemic venous system through sit es of portosystemic anastomosis. One of the most critical of these sites is at the gastroesophageal junction. Here, blood from the left gastric vein (a tributary of the portal vein) is shunted into the esophageal veins (which drain into the systemic azygos vein). The resulting massive increase in blood flow through this connection causes the veins to dilate, forming esophageal varices. These varices are prone to rupture and can cause life- threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding, a major complication of cirrhosis. The other options do not represent major portosystemic anastomoses; they are either connections within the portal system or entirely within the systemic circulation.

questions.stem: A young boy presents with multiple fractures of the humerus and subsequently develops sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the forearm, along with weakness in elbow flexion and forearm supination. Which nerve injury is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: Musculocutaneous nerve This combination of symptoms points directly to an injury of the musculocutaneous nerve. This nerve supplies the major flexors of the elbow, including the biceps brachii and brachialis, and a key supinator of the forearm (biceps brachii). Therefore, injury to this nerve would cause difficulty with elbow flexion and forearm supination. Furthermore, after passing through the arm muscles, the musculocutaneous nerve continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, providing sensation to the lateral aspect of the forearm. The history of humerus fractures provides a plausible mechanism for injury to this nerve as it courses through the anterior compartment of the arm. The median nerve (B) primarily controls wrist/finger flexion, while the radial nerve (D) governs extension.

questions.stem: Which blood vessel is responsible for carrying deoxygenated blood from the fetus back to the placenta?
questions.explanation: Umbilical artery In fetal circulation, the roles of the umbilical arteries and vein are reversed compared to systemic circulation in an adult. The umbilical artery, of which there are two, carries deoxygenated blood and waste products from the fetus to the placenta for oxygenation and removal. Conversely, the single umbilical vein (B) carries highly oxygenated and nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus. The ductus venosus (C) is a shunt that allows a portion of this oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein to bypass the fetal liver and go directly to the inferior vena cava (D). Therefore, it is the umbilical arteries that are responsible for returning deoxygenated blood to the maternal circulation via the placenta.

questions.stem: Which nerve is responsible for mediating the gag reflex?
questions.explanation: 9th Cranial Nerve The gag reflex (or pharyngeal reflex) involves two key cranial nerves. The afferent (sensory) limb of the reflex is mediated by the 9th cranial nerve (glossopharyngeal nerve). When the posterior pharynx, tonsils, or base of the tongue is touched, sensory signals are transmitted via the glossopharyngeal nerve to the brainstem. The efferent (motor) limb, which causes the contraction of the pharyngeal muscles, is primarily mediated by the 10th cranial nerve (vagus nerve). Since the question asks which nerve is responsible for the reflex, and the 9th nerve is the primary sensory trigger, it is the correct answer among the choices. The 6th (abducens) and 11th (accessory) nerves are purely motor, and the 7th (facial) nerve has different sensory and motor functions.

questions.stem: A patient undergoes coronary artery bypass grafting using the great saphenous vein and later develops neuralgia along the medial aspect of the leg and foot. Which nerve is most likely to have been injured during the procedure?
questions.explanation: Saphenous nerve The great saphenous vein is commonly harvested for use as a conduit in CABG surgery. The saphenous nerve runs in close proximity to this vein along the medial aspect of the leg and foot. During the surgical harvesting of the vein, the saphenous nerve is highly susceptible to stretching, transection, or entrapment. Injury to this nerve results in sensory disturbances, such as pain (neuralgia), numbness, or tingling, in its distribution area, which is the medial aspect of the leg and foot. This is a well- recognized complication of great saphenous vein harvesting. The sural nerve (A) supplies the lateral aspect of the foot, while the tibial (B) and common peroneal (D) nerves have different and more extensive sensory and motor distributions.

questions.stem: Upward movement of the thyroid gland is prevented by which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: Sternothyroid muscle The thyroid gland is intimately connected to the larynx by the suspensory ligament of Berry and is enclosed within the pretracheal fascia, which also attaches to the larynx. These connections cause the thyroid to move superiorly and inferiorly during swallowing. However, excessive upward movement is restrained by the infrahyoid muscles, commonly known as the strap muscles. The sternothyroid muscle, in particular, plays a crucial role in this restraint. Originating from the posterior surface of the manubrium sterni and inserting onto the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage, this muscle lies directly anterior to the thyroid gland. Its primary action is to depress the larynx after it has been elevated during swallowing or phonation. questions.stem: The elongated path of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is a result of the persistence of which embryonic aortic arch?
questions.explanation: 6th Arch The asymmetrical course of the right and left recurrent laryngeal nerves is a direct consequence of the embryological development of the aortic arches. Both nerves initially hook around the 6th aortic arch on their respective sides. On the right side, the distal portion of the 6th arch and the entire 5th arch artery degenerate. This allows the right recurrent laryngeal nerve to ascend and hook underneath the next persistent structure, which is the 4th aortic arch artery (forming the right subclavian artery). On the left side, however, the distal part of the 6th aortic arch persists to form the ductus arteriosus (which later becomes the ligamentum arteriosum). Because this structure remains, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is trapped and cannot ascend. It is held down in the thorax, where it loops under the arch of the aorta (formed by the left 4th arch) adjacent to the ligamentum arteriosum. This explains its longer, recurrent course from the chest back up to the larynx.

questions.stem: Ligation of the hepatic artery will compromise blood flow to which of the following arteries?

options.text: Right gastric and Right gastroepiploic artery
Right gastric and Left gastric artery
Right gastroepiploic and Short gastric vessels
Right gastric and Short gastric vessels

questions.explanation: Right gastric and Right gastroepiploic artery The common hepatic artery is a branch of the celiac trunk. It gives rise to the gastroduodenal artery before continuing as the hepatic artery proper. Ligation of the common hepatic artery proximal to this branch would compromise all of its downstream vessels. The gastroduodenal artery gives rise to the right gastroepiploic artery, which supplies the greater curvature of the stomach. The hepatic artery proper gives rise to the right gastric artery, which supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach. Therefore, ligating the common hepatic artery would directly impair blood flow to both the right gastric and right gastroepiploic arteries. The left gastric artery (B) is a direct branch of the celiac trunk and would not be affected. The short gastric vessels (C, D) are branches of the splenic artery, which is another direct branch of the celiac trunk, so their supply would also be preserved. The dual supply to the stomach from other celiac branches often provides sufficient collateral circulation.

questions.stem: Which of the following nerves does not contribute to the innervation of the extraocular muscles?
questions.explanation: Ophthalmic nerve The motor innervation to the six extraocular muscles is provided by three specific cranial nerves. This is commonly remembered by the mnemonic (LR 6SO4)3. The oculomotor nerve (CN III) supplies the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) supplies only the superior oblique muscle. The abducent nerve (CN VI) supplies only the lateral rectus muscle. The ophthalmic nerve, which is the first division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V 1), is a purely sensory nerve. It is not involved in motor supply to the extraocular muscles. Instead, it provides sensation to the eyeball, cornea, conjunctiva, upper eyelid, forehead, and scalp. Therefore, the ophthalmic nerve is not part of the motor nerve supply to the muscles that move the eye. 55. Which of the following structures in females is a remnant of the Wolffian duct? questions.stem: Claudication resulting from popliteal-femoral incompetence primarily affects which area?
questions.explanation: Calf Claudication refers to muscle pain or cramping that is induced by exercise and relieved by rest. It is a hallmark symptom of peripheral artery disease (PAD), caused by insufficient blood flow to meet the metabolic demands of the exercising muscle. The location of the claudication pain directly corresponds to the muscle group distal to the arterial stenosis or occlusion. The femoropopliteal arterial segment, comprising the superficial femoral artery and the popliteal artery, is the most common site of atherosclerotic disease in the lower limbs. When this segment is incompetent (stenosed), blood flow is restricted to the muscles of the lower leg. The calf muscles (gastrocnemius and soleus) have a very high oxygen demand during walking. Therefore, stenosis in the femoral or popliteal arteries most classically and primarily causes claudication pain in the calf. Buttock and thigh claudication (A, C) suggest more proximal disease in the aortoiliac segment.

questions.stem: A patient shows hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and flexion at the interphalangeal (IP) joints. Which muscle is most likely paralyzed?
questions.explanation: Interossei and lumbricals The posture described is a classic claw hand deformity. This deformity arises from an imbalance between the extrinsic and intrinsic muscles of the hand. The intrinsic hand muscles, specifically the lumbricals and interossei, are responsible for flexing the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extending the interphalangeal (IP) joints. When these intrinsic muscles are paralyzed (typically due to a combined ulnar and median nerve injury), their actions are lost. This allows the unopposed action of the extrinsic muscles to dominate. The long extensor, extensor digitorum, pulls the MCP joints into hyperextension. Simultaneously, the long flexors, flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, pull the IP joints into flexion. This combination of MCP hyperextension and IP flexion creates the characteristic claw- like appearance. Therefore, paralysis of the interossei and lumbricals is the direct cause of this deformity.

questions.stem: Identify the cell type marked in the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells While no image is provided, questions asking to identify the key cell type in the cerebellum almost invariably point to the Purkinje cell. The cerebellar cortex has a distinct three-layered structure. The central layer is the Purkinje cell layer, which consists of a single, uniform row of the very large, flask-shaped bodies of Purkinje cells. These are some of the largest neurons in the human brain. Their most striking feature is an incredibly elaborate and extensively branched dendritic tree that extends up into the molecular layer, oriented in a single plane like a fan. Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, and they exert an inhibitory (GABAergic) influence on the deep cerebellar nuclei. Their unique size, shape, and position make them the most recognizable cell type in the cerebellum.

questions.stem: A tumor located in the uncinate process of the pancreas is most likely to compress which artery?
questions.explanation: Superior Mesenteric Artery The uncinate process is a hook-like projection of pancreatic tissue that extends from the lower part of the head of the pancreas. It has a crucial anatomical relationship with the major mesenteric vessels. The uncinate process curves posteriorly behind the superior mesenteric vein and is situated just to the left of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). The SMA and superior mesenteric vein emerge from behind the neck of the pancreas and pass anterior to the uncinate process. Because of this intimate anatomical relationship, a tumor or mass arising from the uncinate process can directly invade or compress these vessels. Specifically, it is positioned to compress the superior mesenteric artery and vein. The other vessels listed are not in direct contact with the uncinate process and would not be compressed by a tumor in this specific location.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with a vascular injury involving the inferior frontal gyrus. Which functional area is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation: Motor speech The posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere (typically the left) is the location of Broca's area. This area is the primary center for the motor programming of speech. It is responsible for planning the coordinated muscle movements of the larynx, tongue, and lips that are necessary for articulate speech production. A vascular injury, such as a stroke, affecting this region leads to Broca's aphasia, also known as expressive or non-fluent aphasia. Patients with this condition have difficulty producing fluent, grammatical speech. Their speech is often slow, labored, and consists of short, telegraphic phrases, although their comprehension of language generally remains intact. The primary visual cortex (A) is in the occipital lobe, the primary auditory cortex (B) is in the superior temporal gyrus, and Wernicke's area (C) for language comprehension is in the posterior superior temporal gyrus.

questions.stem: Thrombosis of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) is associated with which syndrome?
questions.explanation: Wallenberg syndrome Wallenberg syndrome, also known as the lateral medullary syndrome, is a neurological condition caused by an ischemic stroke in the lateral part of the medulla oblongata in the brainstem. The most common vascular cause for this infarct is an occlusion of the intracranial portion of the vertebral artery, followed by its largest branch, the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). This stroke leads to a characteristic pattern of neurological deficits due to damage to specific tracts and nuclei. Key features include vertigo, nystagmus, and ataxia (damage to the inferior cerebellar peduncle and vestibular nuclei); dysphagia and hoarseness (damage to the nucleus ambiguus); and a distinctive crossed sensory loss. The patient experiences loss of pain and temperature sensation on the ipsilateral (same) side of the face (spinal trigeminal nucleus) and the contralateral (opposite) side of the body (spinothalamic tract). Medial medullary syndrome (B, D) is caused by occlusion of the anterior spinal artery.

questions.stem: In which organ is the Space of Disse located?
questions.explanation: Liver The Space of Disse, or the perisinusoidal space, is a unique anatomical location found within the liver. It is the microscopic space situated between the basolateral surface of the hepatocytes (liver cells) and the fenestrated endothelial lining of the liver sinusoids (specialized capillaries). This space is filled with blood plasma that filters through the fenestrations of the sinusoidal endothelium. The Space of Disse is a critical site for the metabolic exchange between the blood and the hepatocytes; plasma solutes can directly contact the microvilli of the hepatocytes, allowing for efficient uptake of nutrients and secretion of proteins like albumin. It also contains the hepatic stellate cells (also known as Ito cells), which are responsible for storing Vitamin A and are involved in the pathogenesis of liver fibrosis. This perisinusoidal space is a feature unique to the liver's microarchitecture. 69. Which nerve innervates the region labeled as Area B in the image? questions.stem: What are Gitter cells?
questions.explanation: Modified macrophages in CNS Gitter cells are a specific type of cell found in the central nervous system (CNS) at sites of injury, necrosis, or inflammation. They are essentially modified, activated macrophages that are filled with phagocytosed lipid debris. Their origin is twofold : they are derived from the brain's resident immune cells, the microglia, as well as from blood-borne monocytes that migrate into the CNS in response to the injury. When a CNS injury occurs (e.g., an ischemic stroke or trauma), these cells become activated and adopt a phagocytic role. They engulf the lipid- rich debris from degenerating myelin sheaths and necrotic neurons. The accumulation of this lipid material within their cytoplasm gives them a characteristic enlarged, foamy, or granular appearance, leading to the name Gitter cells (from the German word for lattice). Their presence is a key histological marker of tissue breakdown and scavenging in the CNS.

questions.stem: The cholecystocaval line separates which anatomical structures?

options.text: Right lobe of liver with Gall Bladder
Left lobe of liver with Gall Bladder

questions.explanation: Right lobe of liver with Gall Bladder The cholecystocaval line, also known as Cantlie’s line, is an imaginary anatomical line used to divide the liver into functional right and left lobes. It extends from the gallbladder fossa on the inferior surface of the liver anteriorly to the inferior vena cava posteriorly. This line represents the plane along which the middle hepatic vein runs, and it separates the liver based on its vascular supply and biliary drainage rather than on external anatomical appearance. Although the liver appears to be divided into right and left lobes by the falciform ligament, this division is only superficial. The true functional division is represented by the cholecystocaval line. Structures located to the right of this line belong to the functional right lobe, while those to the left belong to the functional left lobe. The gallbladder lies to the right side of Cantlie’s line, in the gallbladder fossa on the visceral surface of the liver. Therefore, the cholecystocaval line effectively separates the right lobe of the liver from the region containing the gallbladder, making option (C) Right lobe of liver with Gall Bladder the correct answer.

questions.stem: The marked area in the image corresponds to which dermatome?
questions.explanation: T10 The image points to the skin at the level of the umbilicus. The sensory innervation of the skin of the trunk is supplied by spinal nerves in a segmental pattern, with each segment known as a dermatome. There are several key dermatomal landmarks on the torso that are used for clinical localization of spinal cord injuries. The dermatome that corresponds to the skin at the level of the umbilicus is the T10 dermatome. Other useful landmarks include the T4 dermatome at the level of the nipples and the T12/L1 dermatome at the inguinal region. Therefore, a loss of sensation at or below the level of the umbilicus would suggest a spinal cord lesion at or above the T10 spinal level. This anatomical relationship is a fundamental concept in clinical neurology and physical diagnosis.

questions.stem: What type of fiber is indicated in the image of the internal capsule?
questions.explanation: Projection fibres The image shows a coronal section of the brain with the internal capsule highlighted. The internal capsule is a massive, compact bundle of white matter fibers. These fibers are classified as projection fibers. Projection fibers are axons that connect the cerebral cortex with subcortical structures, the brainstem, and the spinal cord. They project information to and from the cortex. The internal capsule contains both ascending (thalamocortical) and descending (corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine) tracts. In contrast, commissural fibers (D) are fibers that connect corresponding areas of the two cerebral hemispheres (e.g., the corpus callosum). Association fibers (B, C) connect different areas within the same cerebral hemisphere. Because the internal capsule is NODIA

questions.stem: Which anatomical structure is indicated by the arrow in the image?
questions.explanation: Fornix The CT scan of the brain shown in the image indicates a midline structure located near the lateral ventricles, highlighted by the red arrow. This structure corresponds to the fornix, an important component of the limbic system. The fornix is a C-shaped bundle of white matter fibers that serves as a major output tract of the hippocampus. Anatomically, the fornix lies just beneath the corpus callosum and above the thalamus, forming part of the roof of the third ventricle and the medial walls of the lateral ventricles. It connects the hippocampus to other limbic structures such as the mammillary bodies and septal nuclei, playing a key role in memory processing and emotional regulation. The other options represent different structures. The great vein of Galen is a deep cerebral vein located more posteriorly. The pineal gland lies posterior to the third ventricle in the midline. The falx cerebri is a dural fold separating the two cerebral hemispheres and appears along the midline of the skull. Thus, the structure indicated by the arrow is the fornix.

questions.stem: Which nerve innervates the structure indicated in the image?
questions.explanation: Median nerve The image displays the intrinsic muscles of the hand, with an arrow pointing to the lumbrical muscles. The lumbricals are four small muscles that originate from the tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus and insert into the extensor expansions of the digits. Their action is to flex the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints while extending the interphalangeal (IP) joints. The innervation of the lumbricals is unique and is divided between the median and ulnar nerves. The first and second lumbricals (the radial two, for the index and middle fingers) are innervated by the median nerve. The third and fourth lumbricals (the ulnar two, for the ring and little fingers) are innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Since the arrow appears to point towards the more radial lumbricals, the median nerve is the correct answer. NODIA

questions.stem: The nerve injured in Frey's syndrome is :
questions.explanation: Auriculotemporal Nerve Frey's syndrome, also known as gustatory sweating, is a condition characterized by sweating and flushing of the skin in the preauricular and temporal region (the area supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve) that is triggered by eating or thinking about food. It is a common complication of surgery involving the parotid gland, such as a parotidectomy. The syndrome is caused by an injury to the auriculotemporal nerve during the surgery. This nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland to stimulate salivation. After being injured, these parasympathetic fibers undergo aberrant regeneration. Instead of reinnervating the parotid gland, they mistakenly reinnervate the sympathetic sweat glands and blood vessels in the overlying skin. As a result, when the patient eats, the gustatory stimulus intended to produce saliva instead activates these misdirected fibers, causing localized sweating and flushing.

questions.stem: Which nerve traverses the foramen marked in the image?
questions.explanation: Inferior alveolar nerve The image shows a medial view of the mandible. The arrow is pointing to the mandibular foramen, a prominent opening on the internal surface of the ramus of the mandible. This foramen is the entrance to the mandibular canal, a bony channel that runs through the body of the mandible. The primary structure that passes through the mandibular foramen and into this canal is the inferior alveolar nerve, along with the inferior alveolar artery and vein. The inferior alveolar nerve is a major sensory branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V 3). It provides sensory innervation to all the teeth in the lower jaw on that side. It also gives off the mental nerve, which exits through the mental foramen to supply sensation to the lower lip and chin. This foramen is a critical landmark for administering an inferior alveolar nerve block in dentistry.

questions.stem: In Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), the characteristic boot-shaped heart appearance is due to which factor?
questions.explanation: Right ventricular hypertrophy The boot-shaped heart, or cœur en sabot, is the classic radiographic sign seen on a chest X-ray

questions.stem: Identify the marked muscle 'A' in the diagram.
questions.explanation: Extensor carpi radialis longus The muscle labeled “A” in the diagram is the Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus (ECRL). This muscle belongs to the superficial group of extensor muscles in the posterior compartment of the forearm. It originates from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and runs along the lateral side of the forearm. The tendon then passes down the dorsum of the wrist to insert at the base of the second metacarpal bone. The primary function of the extensor carpi radialis longus is to extend and abduct the wrist (radial deviation). It also assists in stabilizing the wrist during activities such as gripping or making a fist. The muscle is innervated by the radial nerve, which supplies most of the extensor muscles of the forearm. It differs from the brachioradialis, which mainly flexes the elbow and does not extend the wrist. Flexor carpi radialis is located in the anterior forearm and acts as a wrist flexor. Extensor carpi ulnaris lies on the medial side of the posterior forearm and produces wrist extension with ulnar deviation. Thus, the marked muscle corresponds to Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus.

questions.stem: Identify the marked structure in the image.
questions.explanation: Cerebellum The image provided is a sagittal view of the human brain, showing its major components. The arrow is pointing to the large structure located in the posterior cranial fossa, inferior to the cerebrum and posterior to the pons and medulla of the brainstem. This is the cerebellum. The cerebellum is a highly convoluted structure with a characteristic, finely foliated appearance, which is evident in the image. It is a crucial part of the motor system and plays a vital role in coordinating voluntary movements, posture, NODIA

questions.stem: Damage to which structure results in contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation?
questions.explanation: Lateral spinothalamic tract The sensations of pain and temperature are transmitted from the periphery to the brain via the spinothalamic tract, which is a key component of the anterolateral system. The first-order neurons have their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion and enter the spinal cord. They synapse in the dorsal horn with second- order neurons. The axons of these second- order neurons immediately decussate (cross over) to the opposite side of the spinal cord within one or two spinal segments. They then ascend in the contralateral white matter as the lateral spinothalamic tract. Because these fibers cross at the level of the spinal cord, an injury to the lateral spinothalamic tract on one side will result in a loss of pain and temperature sensation on the contralateral (opposite) side of the body, beginning a few segments below the level of the lesion. The fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus (dorsal columns) carry ipsilateral proprioception and fine touch.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures is not derived from the external oblique muscle?
questions.explanation: Cooper ligament The aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle forms several important structures in the inguinal region. The thickened, inferior free edge of the aponeurosis rolls back on itself to form the inguinal ligament (Poupart's ligament). Medially, some fibers of the inguinal ligament extend backward to attach to the pectineal line of the pubis, forming the crescent-shaped lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's ligament). The linea semilunaris represents the lateral border of the rectus sheath, where the aponeuroses of the three flat abdominal muscles (including the external oblique) fuse. In contrast, the pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament) is a strong, fibrous band that extends along the pectineal line of the pubic bone. It is formed by the periosteum of the pubic bone and is reinforced by fibers from the lacunar ligament and the pectineus fascia. It is not a direct derivative of the external oblique muscle itself.

questions.stem: The ducts of Bellini are found in which organ?
questions.explanation: Kidney The ducts of Bellini, also known as the papillary ducts, are anatomical structures found within the kidney. They represent the most distal part of the collecting duct system. The collecting ducts from multiple nephrons progressively merge in the renal medulla to form larger and larger ducts. The final, large-caliber ducts that are formed just before the collecting system opens into the minor calyx at the tip of the renal papilla are called the ducts of Bellini. These ducts are lined by tall columnar epithelium and are responsible for channeling the final, concentrated urine from the renal medulla into the renal pelvis. They are the terminal conduits of the nephron and play a final role in concentrating the urine under the influence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). 85. questions.stem: Which joint is responsible for allowing the head to move from side to side (left to right)?
questions.explanation: Atlanto-axial joint The rotational movement of the head, such as shaking the head no from left to right, occurs primarily at the atlanto-axial joint. This is a complex of three synovial joints between the first cervical vertebra (the atlas, C1) and the second cervical vertebra (the axis, C2). The main component responsible for rotation is the pivot joint between the dens (odontoid process) of the axis and the anterior arch of the atlas. This arrangement allows the atlas, which carries the skull, to pivot or rotate around the dens of the axis. Approximately 50% of all cervical spine rotation occurs at this specific joint. In contrast, the atlanto-occipital joint (B), between the atlas and the occipital condyles of the skull, is primarily responsible for flexion and extension of the head (the yes motion).

questions.stem: Which nerve supplies the submandibular gland?
questions.explanation: Lingual nerve The secretomotor innervation of the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands follows a complex parasympathetic pathway. The preganglionic parasympathetic fibers originate from the superior salivatory nucleus in the brainstem and travel with the facial nerve (CN VII). These fibers then branch off as the chorda tympani nerve, which joins the lingual nerve (a branch of the mandibular nerve, CN V 3) in the infratemporal fossa. The preganglionic fibers travel along the lingual nerve until they synapse in the submandibular ganglion, which is suspended from the lingual nerve itself. Postganglionic fibers then arise from this ganglion and directly supply the submandibular and sublingual glands, stimulating saliva secretion. Therefore, while the original fibers are from the facial nerve, the lingual nerve is the final carrier of these secretomotor fibers to the gland and its ganglion.

questions.stem: During autotransplantation, the parathyroid gland is usually implanted into which muscle?
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis During a total thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy, the parathyroid glands are at risk of being inadvertently removed or devascularized, which would lead to permanent hypoparathyroidism. To prevent this, if the glands cannot be preserved in situ, they are removed, minced into small pieces, and immediately autotransplanted into a well- vascularized muscle bed. The most common and preferred site for this implantation is the brachioradialis muscle in the non-dominant forearm. This location is chosen because it is easily accessible under local anesthesia and is distant from the primary surgical field in the neck. Implanting the tissue into a muscle provides an excellent blood supply for the graft NODIA

questions.stem: The right coronary artery originates from which structure?
questions.explanation: Right Aortic Sinus The coronary arteries, which supply blood to the heart muscle itself, are the first branches of the aorta. They originate from the aortic sinuses (also known as the sinuses of Valsalva), which are three small dilations at the root of the ascending aorta, located just superior to the cusps of the aortic valve. There are three aortic sinuses : the right, the left, and the posterior (non-coronary) sinus. The right coronary artery (RCA) arises from the right aortic sinus (also called the anterior aortic sinus). The left coronary artery (LCA) arises from the left aortic sinus (also called the left posterior aortic sinus). The posterior aortic sinus is typically non- coronary, meaning no coronary artery arises from it.

questions.stem: From where are the nerves associated with the branchial (pharyngeal) arches derived?
questions.explanation: Neural crest The pharyngeal (branchial) arches are crucial embryonic structures that give rise to most of the structures of the head and neck. Each arch consists of a core of mesenchyme covered externally by ectoderm and internally by endoderm. The mesenchyme itself is derived from two sources : the mesoderm, which forms the muscular components of each arch, and the neural crest cells. Neural crest cells are a specialized population of migratory cells that originate from the dorsal neural tube (neuroectoderm). These cells migrate into the pharyngeal arches and differentiate into a wide variety of tissues, including the bones, cartilage, and connective tissues of the face and skull (the pharyngeal arch skeleton). Schwann cells, and the neurons of the specific cranial nerves that supply each arch (e.g., CN V for the 1st arch, CN VII for the 2nd arch). Therefore, the nerves associated with the branchial arches are directly derived from these ectoderm-origin neural crest cells, making this the correct answer. The neuroectoderm (D) is the broader tissue from which the neural crest originates, but neural crest is the more specific answer.

questions.stem: The hard palate contains:

options.text: Keratinized epithelium, submucosa, minor salivary gland
Keratinized epithelium, absent submucosal layer, minor salivary gland
Non-keratinized epithelium, submucosal layer, minor salivary gland
Non-keratinized epithelium, absent submucosa, minor salivary gland

questions.explanation: Keratinized epithelium, submucosa, minor salivary gland The hard palate forms the roof of the oral cavity and is subject to significant friction during mastication. For this reason, its surface is covered by a protective layer of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. The underlying structure of the hard palate varies by region. In the anterolateral regions, which contain the palatine rugae, the mucous membrane is tightly bound directly to the periosteum of the underlying bone, and a distinct submucosal layer is absent. However, in the posterolateral region, a well- defined submucosa is present. This submucosa is rich in adipose tissue anteriorly and contains numerous minor mucous salivary glands posteriorly, which secrete mucus to lubricate the oral cavity. Since the question refers to the hard palate in general, and the posterolateral part contains both a submucosa and salivary glands, option A is the most comprehensive and correct description. Option B is incorrect because a submucosa is present in parts of the hard palate. Options C and D are incorrect as the epithelium

questions.stem: Which muscle functions to tense the vocal folds?
questions.explanation: Cricothyroid The pitch of the voice is primarily controlled by altering the tension and length of the vocal cords. The muscle solely responsible for tensing and elongating the vocal cords is the cricothyroid muscle. It is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle located on the external surface of the larynx and is uniquely innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. When the cricothyroid muscle contracts, it pulls the thyroid cartilage anteriorly and inferiorly, tilting it forward on the cricoid cartilage. This action increases the distance between the thyroid and arytenoid cartilages, thereby stretching and tensing the vocal ligaments. Tenser vocal cords vibrate at a higher frequency, resulting in the production of a higher-pitched sound. The thyroarytenoid muscles (C), particularly the vocalis part, have the opposite effect; they shorten and relax the vocal cords, lowering the pitch. The lateral cricoarytenoid (B) adducts the cords, and the posterior cricoarytenoid (D) abducts them. Hence, for vocal cord tension and high pitch, the cricothyroid is the key muscle.

questions.stem: The ureteric bud develops from:
questions.explanation: Mesonephros During the embryonic development of the urinary system, three successive kidney systems form : the pronephros, mesonephros, and metanephros. The definitive, permanent kidney develops from the metanephros. The development of the metanephros itself involves a reciprocal induction between two structures derived from the intermediate mesoderm. The ureteric bud, which gives rise to the entire collecting system of the kidney (the ureter, renal pelvis, major and minor calyces, and collecting ducts), arises as an outgrowth from the caudal portion of the mesonephric duct (Wolffian duct), which is the excretory duct of the transient mesonephros (A). This ureteric bud then grows into and induces the differentiation of a separate mass of mesoderm called the metanephric blastema (related to B), which in turn forms the nephrons (the excretory units of the kidney). The pronephros (C) is the earliest, most rudimentary kidney and degenerates completely. The genital sinus (D) is related to the development of the lower urogenital tract, not the ureteric bud.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Weber’s syndrome is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Contralateral Parkinsonism Weber's syndrome is a midbrain stroke syndrome caused by an infarction in the territory of the posterior cerebral artery, specifically affecting the anterior cerebral peduncle (D). This area contains two crucial structures : the descending corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, and the exiting fascicles of the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Therefore, a lesion here produces a characteristic pattern of deficits. It causes an ipsilateral oculomotor nerve palsy (B), leading to a down and out eye position, ptosis, and a dilated pupil on the same side as the lesion. It also affects the corticospinal tract before it decussates, resulting in contralateral hemiplegia or hemiparesis (A), affecting the opposite side of the body. Contralateral Parkinsonism (C) — characterized by tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia — is caused by damage to the substantia nigra, which is located more dorsally in the midbrain tegmentum. A lesion affecting the substantia nigra along with the red nucleus and CN III causes Benedikt's syndrome, not Weber's. Therefore, contralateral Parkinsonism is not a feature of classic Weber's syndrome. NODIA

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding Sibson’s fascia is not correct?

options.text: Attached to the inner border of the 2nd rib

questions.explanation: Vessels pass above the fascia Sibson's fascia, also called the suprapleural membrane, is a thickening of the endothoracic fascia that covers the apex of the lung. It reinforces the cervical pleura and prevents bulging of the lung apex into the neck during respiration. Statement-wise analysis: A Attached to the inner border of the 2nd rib – Incorrect attachment detail in strict anatomy (it is attached to the inner border of the 1st rib, not the 2nd), but this is often tested carefully. B Covers apical part of lung – Correct. It covers and protects the lung apex. C Part of scalenus anterior muscle – Incorrect wording; it is not a part of the muscle but is derived from the deep cervical fascia and attached to the transverse process of C7. D Vessels pass above the fascia – Incorrect. Major vessels such as the subclavian artery and vein pass anterior to or through the region, not above the fascia.

questions.stem: Occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) results in which of the following effects?
questions.explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome Thrombosis or occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), or the vertebral artery from which it often arises, is the classic cause of the lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg's syndrome. This artery supplies the dorsolateral portion of the medulla oblongata. An infarct in this area damages several key structures, leading to a characteristic constellation of signs. These include vertigo, nausea, and nystagmus (from involvement of the vestibular nuclei); dysphagia and hoarseness (from the nucleus ambiguus, affecting CN IX and X); ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature on the face (from the spinal trigeminal nucleus); contralateral loss of pain and temperature on the body (from the spinothalamic tract); and an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (from descending sympathetic fibers). Weber syndrome (B) is a midbrain syndrome, and medial medullary syndrome (C) is caused by occlusion of the anterior spinal artery, affecting the medial structures of the medulla.

questions.stem: What is the structure seen in the given X-ray?
questions.explanation: Stent The X-ray image clearly shows a medical device placed within the urinary tract. This device is a ureteral stent, also commonly known as a JJ stent or double-J stent. It is a thin, flexible tube that is placed inside the ureter to keep it open and allow urine to drain from the kidney to the bladder. The characteristic J shape or pigtail curl at both ends of the stent is designed to hold it in place, with one curl sitting in the renal pelvis of the kidney and the other curl sitting inside the urinary bladder. These stents are used to relieve or prevent ureteral obstruction caused by kidney stones, tumors, strictures, or swelling after surgery. They are radiopaque, making them clearly visible on an X-ray, as seen in the image. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: Which of the following structures does not pass through the aortic hiatus?
questions.explanation: Vagus nerve The aortic hiatus is an opening in the diaphragm at the level of T12 vertebra. It allows important structures to pass between the thorax and abdomen. The main structures that pass through the aortic hiatus are the Aorta, the Thoracic duct, and the Azygos vein. The vagus nerve does not pass through the aortic hiatus. Instead, it passes through the esophageal hiatus (at T10 level) along with the esophagus. Therefore, the Vagus nerve is not a structure that traverses the aortic opening. Hence, the correct answer is (D) Vagus nerve.

questions.stem: The costal cartilages of the 8th and 9th ribs form which type of joint?
questions.explanation: Inter chondral joint The costal cartilages of the 8th and 9th ribs articulate with each other to form interchondral joints. These joints are plane synovial joints formed between the adjacent costal cartilages of the lower ribs (usually 7th–10th ribs). They allow slight gliding movements, which help in the expansion and contraction of the thoracic cavity during respiration. The 8th and 9th ribs are false ribs, and their costal cartilages do not attach directly to the sternum. Instead, they connect to the cartilage of the rib above, forming interchondral joints. Other options are incorrect because: 1. Costochondral joints are between the rib and its own costal cartilage. 2. Synchondrosis is a primary cartilaginous joint, such as the first sternocostal joint. 3. Costovertebral joints are between the ribs and thoracic vertebrae. Therefore, the correct answer is (B) Interchondral joint.

questions.stem: Chordoma originates from which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: Notochord Chordoma is a rare, slow-growing malignant tumor that arises from remnants of the Notochord. The notochord is an embryological midline structure that plays a crucial role in the development of the vertebral column. Although it largely disappears during development, small remnants may persist in the axial skeleton. Chordomas most commonly occur along the midline, particularly in the sacrococcygeal region and the clivus at the base of the skull, reflecting the original course of the notochord. These tumors are locally aggressive and may cause symptoms due to compression of nearby structures. The other options are unrelated to chordoma formation: 1. Pharyngeal bursa is a mucosal recess in the nasopharynx. 2. Rathke’s pouch gives rise to the anterior pituitary gland. 3. Luschka’s bursa is associated with the nasopharynx. Therefore, chordoma originates from the notochord, making option (B) correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures is derived from the dorsal mesentery?
questions.explanation: Greater omentum The Greater omentum is derived from the dorsal mesentery of the stomach. During embryological development, the primitive gut tube is suspended by two mesenteries: the dorsal mesentery and the ventral mesentery. The dorsal mesentery persists throughout the length

questions.stem: Which of the following structures does not belong to the special visceral efferent (SVE) column?
questions.explanation: Oculomotor Nerve The special visceral efferent (SVE) column, also known as branchial motor column, supplies muscles derived from the pharyngeal (branchial) arches. Cranial nerves that contain SVE fibers include the Trigeminal nerve, Glossopharyngeal nerve, and Vagus nerve. These nerves innervate muscles of mastication, stylopharyngeus, and muscles of the pharynx and larynx respectively. The Oculomotor nerve does not belong to the SVE column. Instead, it carries general somatic efferent (GSE) fibers that supply extraocular muscles derived from somites, not from branchial arches. Therefore, since the oculomotor nerve is not associated with branchial arch derivatives, it does not form part of the special visceral efferent column. Hence, the correct answer is (B) Oculomotor Nerve.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the iliolumbar ligament?

options.text: Upper fibres attached to iliac crest
Lower fibres attached to base of sacrum
Help in maintaining lumbosacral ioint stability
Upper attachment to tranwerse process ofT12

questions.explanation: Upper attachment to tranwerse process ofT12 The Iliolumbar ligament is a strong fibrous band that connects the transverse process of the L5 vertebra to the iliac crest. It plays an important role in stabilizing the lumbosacral junction and limiting excessive movement between the lumbar spine and sacrum. The upper fibers of the iliolumbar ligament are attached to the iliac crest, while the lower fibers extend to the base of the sacrum. Its primary function is to help maintain lumbosacral joint stability and prevent anterior displacement of L5 over S1. The statement that its upper attachment is to the transverse process of T12 is incorrect. The ligament is attached to the transverse process of L5, not T12. Therefore, option (D) is the incorrect statement and the correct answer. ************** NODIA

questions.stem: Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) is most commonly seen in :
questions.explanation: Primary biliary cholangitis Anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMAs) are the serological hallmark of Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC), an autoimmune liver disease characterized by the chronic, progressive destruction of the small intrahepatic bile ducts. AMAs are present in approximately 90- 95% of patients with PBC and have a very high specificity for the disease. The primary target of these autoantibodies is the E2 component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC-E2), located on the inner mitochondrial membrane. The presence of AMA, particularly at a high titer, in a patient with a cholestatic pattern of liver enzyme elevation (predominantly elevated alkaline phosphatase) is virtually diagnostic of PBC. In contrast, autoimmune hepatitis (A) is associated with anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) and anti-smooth muscle antibodies (ASMA). Primary sclerosing cholangitis (C) is often associated with perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA).

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions most commonly follows this pattern of inheritance?
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome The provided pedigree chart demonstrates a classic autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. The key features are : 1. The trait appears in every generation (vertical transmission). 2. Affected individuals transmit the trait to about half of their children. 3. Males and females are affected in roughly equal numbers. 4. Father-to-son transmission is observed. 5. We need to identify the condition from the list that follows this inheritance pattern. 6. Marfan syndrome (B) is a connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. 7. Prader-Willi syndrome (A) is a genetic disorder caused by genomic imprinting or deletions on chromosome 15 and is typically sporadic. 8. Kearns-Sayre syndrome (C) is a mitochondrial myopathy, which follows a mitochondrial (maternal) inheritance pattern. 9. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (D) is an X-linked recessive disorder.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with persistent fatigue and generalized lymphadenopathy. His complete blood count shows leukocytosis with an absolute lymphocyte count of 35,000/ µL. Which investigation is the test of choice to confirm the diagnosis and assess CD markers in suspected chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
questions.explanation: Flow cytometry of peripheral blood The patient's presentation with a persistent, marked lymphocytosis (lymphocyte count >5,000/µL) and lymphadenopathy in an older adult is highly suspicious for Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL). In most cases, the diagnosis of CLL can be definitively made without the need for a bone marrow or lymph node biopsy. The investigation of choice for confirming the diagnosis and establishing the characteristic immunophenotype is flow cytometry performed on a peripheral blood sample. This technique uses fluorescently labeled antibodies to identify a specific profile of cell surface antigens (CD markers) on the monoclonal population of B-lymphocytes. The classic diagnostic immunophenotype for CLL is the co-expression of the B-cell markers CD19, CD20 (dim), and CD23, along with the aberrant expression of the T-cell marker CD5. This specific clonal population confirmed by flow cytometry is the gold standard for diagnosing CLL.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman undergoes abdominal imaging for vague right upper quadrant pain, which reveals a liver mass that is subsequently excised. Based on the gross appearance of the specimen shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Focal nodular hyperplasia The image shows a well-circumscribed, non- encapsulated liver lesion. The most striking and pathognomonic feature is the presence of a central stellate scar from which fibrous septa radiate outwards, dividing the lesion into nodules. This gross appearance is the classic feature of Focal Nodular Hyperplasia (FNH). FNH is a benign, regenerative lesion of the liver, not a true neoplasm. It is the second most common benign liver tumor after hemangioma. It is thought to be a hyperplastic response of hepatocytes to a congenital vascular anomaly. The central scar contains a large, dysplastic artery. FNH is typically asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on imaging. On contrast- NODIA

questions.stem: A patient presents with cough, chest pain, and dyspnea. Imaging and pathology show granuloma formation with giant cells containing stellate inclusions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis The key to this diagnosis is the specific histopathological findings described. Sarcoidosis is a multisystem inflammatory disease of unknown etiology characterized by the formation of non-caseating epithelioid granulomas in various organs, most commonly the lungs and lymph nodes. While granuloma formation can be seen in other conditions like tuberculosis, the granulomas in sarcoidosis have specific microscopic features. Within the giant cells of these granulomas, two types of cytoplasmic inclusions can be found : Schaumann bodies, which are laminated concretions of calcium and protein, and asteroid bodies, which are star- shaped or stellate eosinophilic inclusions. The presence of these specific inclusions within a non-caseating granuloma is highly characteristic of, though not entirely specific for, sarcoidosis. In tuberculosis (A), the granulomas are typically caseating.

questions.stem: A very tall man presents with visual disturbances, and ophthalmologic examination reveals ectopia lentis. Which gene defect is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: FBN1 (chromosome 15) The combination of a tall stature (marfanoid habitus) and ectopia lentis (dislocation of the ocular lens) is a classic presentation of Marfan syndrome. Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder that affects multiple systems, including the skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular systems. The underlying cause of Marfan syndrome is a mutation in the FBN1 gene, which is located on chromosome 15. This gene encodes the protein fibrillin-1, a major component of extracellular microfibrils that provide structural support to connective tissues throughout the body. The defective fibrillin-1 leads to the characteristic features of the syndrome. Mutations in COL1A1 (B) cause osteogenesis imperfecta. Mutations in FGFR3 (C) cause achondroplasia. Mutations in PAX6 (D) cause aniridia.

questions.stem: A patient presents with hearing impairment and balance disturbances. Histopathological examination of the lesion reveals Antoni A and Antoni B areas along with Verocay bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Schwannoma The patient's symptoms of unilateral hearing loss and balance problems point to a tumor in the cerebellopontine angle, most likely affecting the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). The histopathological description is pathognomonic for a schwannoma. Schwannomas are benign tumors arising from Schwann cells, which myelinate peripheral nerves. The classic histology is a biphasic pattern with two distinct components : 1. Antoni A areas : These are dense, hypercellular regions composed of spindle- shaped Schwann cells arranged in fascicles and palisades. 2. Antoni B areas : These are loose, hypocellular, myxoid regions. The most specific diagnostic feature, found within the Antoni A areas, is the presence of Verocay bodies. These are structures formed by two parallel rows of palisading nuclei

questions.stem: A child presents with visual disturbances and delayed growth. Imaging shows a suprasellar mass, and histopathology reveals wet keratin with compact, eosinophilic anucleate keratin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Craniopharyngioma The patient's symptoms of visual disturbances (due to compression of the optic chiasm) and growth failure (due to compression of the pituitary stalk/gland) are characteristic of a suprasellar mass in a child. The histopathological findings are definitive. Craniopharyngiomas are benign, slow-growing tumors that arise from remnants of Rathke's pouch. The most common type in children is the adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma. A pathognomonic histological feature of this tumor is the presence of nodules of "wet keratin." This is composed of nests of squamous epithelium undergoing abrupt keratinization, forming pale, anucleated, eosinophilic masses that are soft and tend to flake away during processing. This finding, often accompanied by calcification and a "machine oil-like" cystic fluid, is diagnostic of craniopharyngioma. A Rathke's cleft cyst (B) has a different lining, and pituitary adenomas (C) are rare in this age group and have a different histology.

questions.stem: Which laboratory technique is most commonly used to compare and quantify CD (cluster of differentiation) markers on cells?
questions.explanation: Flow cytometry Flow cytometry is the gold-standard laboratory technique for the analysis of cell surface and intracellular antigens, known as Cluster of Differentiation (CD) markers. This powerful technology allows for the rapid, multiparametric analysis of single cells in a suspension. Cells are labeled with fluorescently-tagged monoclonal antibodies that are specific for different CD markers. As the cells flow one-by-one through a laser beam, the fluorochromes are excited and emit light, which is detected and quantified. This allows for the precise quantification of cell populations based on their unique CD marker expression profiles (immunophenotyping). It is an indispensable tool in hematology and immunology for diagnosing and classifying leukemias and lymphomas, monitoring HIV infection (by counting CD4 T-cells), and assessing immune status. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) (D) also detects these markers but is qualitative and performed on tissue sections, not for quantification in a cell suspension.

questions.explanation: Interstitial lung disease Anti-Scl-70 antibodies, also known as anti- topoisomerase I antibodies, are a highly specific serological marker for systemic sclerosis (scleroderma). The presence of these antibodies is particularly and strongly associated with the diffuse cutaneous subtype of the disease. Furthermore, within this subtype, anti-Scl-70 positivity is a significant predictor of a more severe disease course and specific organ involvement. The strongest of these associations is with the development of interstitial lung disease (ILD), which is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with systemic sclerosis. Patients who are positive for anti-Scl-70 antibodies have a much higher risk of developing progressive pulmonary fibrosis compared to those who are negative or have other autoantibodies (like anti-centromere antibodies). questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with a painless testicular mass. Ultrasound reveals a well- circumscribed, homogeneous, non-hemorrhagic tumor, and histopathological features are shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Seminoma The patient's age and presentation with a painless testicular mass are classic for a testicular germ cell tumor. The ultrasound findings of a well- circumscribed, homogeneous mass are highly suggestive of a seminoma, which is the most common type of testicular germ cell tumor. The provided histology image confirms this diagnosis. The image shows the characteristic features of a classic seminoma : large, uniform tumor cells with distinct cell borders, clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm (rich in glycogen), and a large central nucleus with a prominent nucleolus. These tumor cells are arranged in sheets or lobules that are separated by delicate fibrous septa. A key feature is that these septa are typically infiltrated by lymphocytes, a finding that is highly characteristic of seminoma. This uniform "fried egg" appearance and the lymphocytic infiltrate are diagnostic.

questions.stem: A lymphoma composed of centrocytes and centroblasts that shows BCL2 positivity and CD10 expression is most commonly associated with which chromosomal translocation?
questions.explanation: t(14;18) The description provided is the classic profile of Follicular Lymphoma. This is a common type of indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Histologically, it is characterized by a nodular (follicular) growth pattern composed of a mixture of small, cleaved cells (centrocytes) and larger, non-cleaved cells (centroblasts), which recapitulate a normal germinal center. The immuno phenotype is that of a germinal center B-cell, with positivity for CD20, CD10, and BCL6. The defining molecular hallmark of over 85% of follicular lymphomas is the specific chromosomal translocation t(14;18)(q32;q21). This translocation juxtaposes the BCL2 gene on chromosome 18 with the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene locus on chromosome 14. This leads to the massive overexpression of the BCL2 protein, which is an anti-apoptotic protein. This overexpression prevents the normal process of apoptosis, leading to the accumulation of the neoplastic B-cells.

questions.stem: A middle-aged woman presents with dry eyes and dry mouth, and laboratory evaluation shows positive anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies. What is the most likely underlying pathological mechanism responsible for her condition?

Lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of salivary and lacrimal glands
Deposition of amyloid in salivary glands

questions.explanation: Lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of salivary and lacrimal glands The patient's symptoms of sicca (dry eyes or keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and dry mouth or xerostomia), combined with the presence of positive anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) autoantibodies, are diagnostic of Sjögren's syndrome. This is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease. The underlying pathological mechanism is an autoimmune attack on the exocrine glands, primarily the lacrimal and salivary glands. A biopsy of a minor salivary gland from the lip is a key diagnostic test. The characteristic histopathological finding is a dense, focal lymphocytic infiltration of the glandular tissue, primarily composed of CD4+ T-cells and B-cells, which often form germinal center-like structures. questions.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with bleeding, and peripheral blood smear reveals the presence of a faggot cell. Which chromosomal translocation is most commonly associated with this finding?
questions.explanation: t(15;17) The patient's presentation with bleeding suggests a coagulopathy, a common feature of a specific type of acute leukemia. The key diagnostic finding is the presence of a "faggot cell" on the peripheral blood smear. A faggot cell is a pathognomonic finding in Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL), also known as AML M3. It is a malignant promyelocyte whose cytoplasm is packed with numerous Auer rods, which are abnormal, needle-like azurophilic granules, often arranged in bundles or "faggots." APL is a medical emergency due to its strong association with life-threatening disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The defining genetic abnormality in virtually all cases of APL is the specific chromosomal translocation t(15;17)(q24;q21). This translocation creates a fusion gene between the PML gene on chromosome 15 and the retinoic acid receptor- alpha (RARA) gene on chromosome 17, which is the underlying driver of the disease.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a neck mass associated with painful swallowing and difficulty breathing. Histopathological examination reveals amyloid deposition. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma A neck mass presenting with compressive symptoms like odynophagia (painful swallowing) and dyspnea is concerning for a thyroid malignancy. The key to the diagnosis is the histopathological finding of amyloid deposition within the tumor stroma. The presence of extracellular amyloid deposits in a thyroid tumor is the pathognomonic feature of Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC). MTC is a neuroendocrine neoplasm that arises from the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid gland. These tumor cells produce and secrete large amounts of the hormone calcitonin. A pro-hormone of calcitonin, procalcitonin, can be processed into an insoluble amyloid protein that gets deposited in the stroma surrounding the tumor cells. This amyloid can be identified with a Congo red stain, which shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. This finding is unique to MTC among all thyroid cancers.

questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed with acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) M3. Which characteristic chromosomal translocation is associated with this subtype?
questions.explanation: t(15;17) This is a duplicate of a previous question. AML M3 is the designation in the older French- American-British (FAB) classification for Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL). APL is a distinct subtype of Acute Myeloid Leukemia that is characterized by the proliferation of malignant promyelocytes. It is a medical emergency because of its strong association with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The defining and pathognomonic genetic lesion in over 95% of cases of APL is the specific balanced reciprocal translocation t(15;17)(q24;q21). This translocation creates a fusion gene between the PML (promyelocytic leukemia) gene on chromosome 15 and the RARA (retinoic acid receptor-alpha) gene on chromosome 17. The resulting PML-RARA fusion protein is the oncogenic driver of the disease and is the target for the differentiating agent, all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA). 18.
