questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient with chronic hepatitis B is HBeAg positive, has a viral load of 10⁵ copies/ mL, and shows a doubling of SGPT levels. Which treatment should be initiated for this patient?

options.text: Pegylated interferon with Tenofovir for 6 months
Pegylated interferon with Lamivudine for 48 weeks

questions.explanation: Tenofovir >48 weeks This patient has HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B in the immune-active phase, which is an indication for treatment. The criteria for treatment are met: elevated HBV DNA (viral load > 20,000 IU/mL; 10^5 copies/mL is roughly equivalent) and elevated ALT (SGPT). According to current international guidelines, the preferred first-line treatments are potent nucleos(t)ide analogs with a high barrier to resistance, such as tenofovir or entecavir, or a finite course of pegylated interferon. A long-term course (>48 weeks) of tenofovir monotherapy is a standard and highly effective first-line option. Combination therapy with two nucleos(t)ide analogs (B) is not recommended for initial treatment. Combination of interferon and a nucleoside analog (C, D) is not standard practice. Lamivudine alone is no longer preferred due to high rates of resistance.

Neuroimaging, such as CT or MRI, classically shows inflammation, edema, and often hemorrhage and necrosis, asymmetrically affecting the medial temporal lobes and inferior frontal lobes. The involvement is often bilateral, though typically one side is more severely affected than the other. This specific anatomical localization is a key diagnostic clue for HSV encephalitis. Silicosis (B) is a lung disease. questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with neck swelling, tremors, and palpitations. She is a known case of asthma and was found to have a blood pressure of 180/110 mm Hg. Electrocardiography revealed atrial fibrillation. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation: Diltiazem This patient is presenting with a thyroid storm, a life-threatening thyrotoxic state characterized by high fever, tachycardia (atrial fibrillation), hypertension, and CNS effects. A key part of management is controlling the heart rate and blood pressure. Beta-blockers are typically used for this purpose. However, this patient has a history of asthma, which is a relative contraindication to non-selective beta-blockers like propranolol (C), as they can cause bronchospasm. While a cardioselective beta-blocker like esmolol (B) might be used cautiously, the safest choice among the options to control the heart rate in a patient with thyrotoxicosis and reactive airway disease is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, such as diltiazem. It will effectively control the ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation without the risk of precipitating an asthma attack. Propylthiouracil (A) is also essential to block thyroid hormone synthesis, but rate control is the most immediate priority.

questions.stem: A patient presented with fatigue and was found to have a mid-diastolic murmur along with a prominent A wave in the jugular venous pulse. In which condition is this finding seen?
questions.explanation: TS The combination of a mid-diastolic murmur and a prominent a wave in the jugular venous pulse (JVP) is the classic presentation of Tricuspid Stenosis (TS). The mid-diastolic murmur is caused by turbulent blood flow across the narrowed tricuspid valve as the right ventricle fills. The prominent a wave in the JVP reflects the forceful contraction of the right atrium against the stenotic, resistant tricuspid valve, leading to increased pressure being transmitted back into the jugular veins. Mitral stenosis (MS) also causes a mid-diastolic murmur, but it does not cause a prominent a wave in the JVP. Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) causes a prominent v wave, and aortic regurgitation (AR) causes a decrescendo diastolic murmur.

questions.stem: Test for diagnosis of HSV Encephalitis
questions.explanation: CSF PCR Viral load Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) encephalitis is the most common cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt diagnosis and treatment with acyclovir. The diagnostic test of choice and the gold standard is the detection of HSV DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) using Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). CSF PCR for HSV is highly sensitive (>95%) and specific (>99%). It allows for a rapid and accurate diagnosis, which is crucial for initiating antiviral therapy early. Viral culture of the CSF (D) is very rarely positive and is too slow to be clinically useful. Tzanck smear (C) is used for skin lesions, not CSF. Chick embryo culture (B) is an outdated method. 78. questions.stem: A 74-year-old patient with coronary artery disease presents with palpitations. The ECG shown below demonstrates characteristic findings, and the blood pressure is 120/84 mmHg. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: IV amiodarone The ECG shows a regular, monomorphic, wide-complex tachycardia (WCT). In a 74-year- old patient with a history of coronary artery disease (CAD), any WCT should be presumed to be ventricular tachycardia (VT) until proven otherwise. The patient is currently hemodynamically stable (BP 120/84 mmHg). According to ACLS guidelines for stable VT, the first-line treatment is an intravenous antiarrhythmic agent. Intravenous amiodarone is a preferred and widely recommended agent for this purpose. It is a class III antiarrhythmic that blocks potassium channels, prolonging the action potential duration and refractory period, which can terminate the reentrant circuit of the VT. IV procainamide is another option. IV metoprolol (B), a beta-blocker, is generally avoided in undifferentiated WCT as it can cause hemodynamic collapse if the underlying rhythm is pre-excited AF. Oral medications (A, C) are not appropriate for the acute termination of VT.

questions.stem: An adult patient presents with palpitations and an irregularly irregular pulse. Examination reveals a pulse deficit of 20, a heart rate of 120/ min, and blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg. Which of the following findings is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation: Absent a wave The presence of an irregularly irregular pulse is the clinical hallmark of atrial fibrillation (AF). The pulse deficit (the difference between the apical heart rate and the palpated peripheral pulse rate) occurs because many of the rapid, chaotic ventricular contractions are too weak to generate a palpable pulse wave. The jugular venous pressure (JVP) waveform reflects pressure changes in the right atrium. The 'a' wave of the JVP is caused by atrial contraction. In atrial fibrillation, the atria do not contract in a coordinated fashion; they merely fibrillate. As a result, there is no atrial systole, and consequently, the 'a' wave is absent from the JVP tracing. Instead, the baseline may show fine, chaotic fibrillatory ('f') waves. Cannon 'a' waves (B) are seen in AV dissociation when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old patient with dental caries is scheduled for dental extraction. Which of the following conditions does not require prophylaxis for infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation: ASD Antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis (IE) is recommended for certain dental procedures only in patients with the highest risk of adverse outcomes from IE. According to current guidelines (AHA/ACC), the highest-risk cardiac conditions include : 1. Prosthetic (artificial) cardiac valve or prosthetic material used for valve repair. 2. A previous history of infective endocarditis. 3. Certain types of congenital heart disease (CHD), including unrepaired cyanotic CHD, a completely repaired defect with prosthetic material for the first 6 months, or a repaired defect with residual defects. 4. Cardiac transplantation recipients who develop valvulopathy. An isolated, uncomplicated, and unrepaired secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) is not considered a high-risk lesion and therefore does not require antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures.

questions.stem: A woman with known diabetes mellitus who is non-compliant with treatment presents to the emergency room with abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, and recent-onset confusion. On examination, she is dehydrated with a systolic blood pressure of 90 mmHg. Investigations reveal positive urine ketones and a random blood sugar of 598 mg/dL. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Normal Saline with regular insulin The patient is in Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), a life-threatening medical emergency. This is evidenced by hyperglycemia (RBS-598), ketonuria, and clinical signs of dehydration, hypotension, and altered mental status. The cornerstone of DKA management involves three main components : fluid resuscitation, insulin therapy, and electrolyte correction. The immediate and most critical first step is aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic Normal Saline to correct the profound dehydration and hypovolemia. Simultaneously or shortly after starting fluids, an intravenous infusion of regular insulin (a short-acting insulin) should be initiated. Regular insulin is used because its IV infusion allows for precise, titratable control to gradually lower blood glucose and switch off ketone production. Long- acting insulins (A, D) have no role in the acute management of DKA. Oral fluids (B) are not appropriate for a confused, vomiting patient.

questions.stem: A female patient presents with loosening of a tooth and hemifacial pain. She has a history of COVID-19 infection treated about four months ago. Which of the following investigations should be performed on a priority basis?
questions.explanation: Ferritin A patient presenting with loosening of a tooth and hemifacial pain after a history of COVID-19 infection raises suspicion for post-COVID mucormycosis, also known as black fungus infection. This infection commonly affects the nose, sinuses, maxilla, orbit, and brain, producing symptoms such as facial pain, tooth mobility, sinus involvement, and facial swelling. During and after COVID-19, many patients develop elevated serum ferritin levels due to severe inflammation and cytokine release. Ferritin is an iron-storage protein, and high ferritin levels indicate increased iron availability in tissues. Mucor species require free iron for growth, and elevated iron levels create a favorable environment for the fungus to proliferate. Therefore, serum ferritin measurement becomes an important priority investigation in suspected post-COVID mucormycosis to assess iron overload and the inflammatory state that predisposes to fungal infection. Other investigations may also be performed later, such as nasal swab or biopsy for fungal identification and imaging of sinuses or brain, but the immediate priority among the given options is assessing serum ferritin levels. Hence, the correct answer is (B) Ferritin.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient presents with recurrent pituitary tumor secreting excess growth hormone. Which medication is most appropriate for treatment?
questions.explanation: Octreotide The patient has recurrent acromegaly due to a GH-secreting pituitary tumor. The first-line medical treatment for acromegaly is a somatostatin analogue. Octreotide and lanreotide are synthetic analogues of somatostatin, the natural hormone that inhibits GH release from the pituitary gland. These drugs bind to somatostatin receptors (predominantly SSTR2) on the pituitary adenoma cells, leading to a potent suppression of GH secretion. This, in turn, lowers the levels of IGF-1 and helps to control the clinical symptoms of the disease. In many patients, these drugs can also cause a modest reduction in tumor size. Pegvisomant (C) is a GH receptor antagonist and is typically considered a second-line medical therapy if somatostatin analogues are not effective or tolerated. Bromocriptine (A) is a dopamine agonist and is less effective. Goserelin (D) is a GnRH analogue.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man weighing 70 kg is found to have a serum sodium level of 120 mEq/L. Calculate the total sodium deficit in this patient.
questions.explanation: 840 mEq The sodium deficit can be calculated using a standard formula that considers the total body water (TBW) and the desired change in serum sodium concentration. The formula is : Sodium Deficit = Total Body Water (TBW) × (Desired Na + - Measured Na+) First, we calculate the TBW, which is approximately 60% of the body weight in an adult male. TBW = 70 kg × 0.60 = 42 L. Next, we determine the desired change in sodium. The desired sodium level is typically 140 mEq/L. Desired change = 140 mEq/L - 120 mEq/L = 20 mEq/L. Finally, we calculate the deficit : Sodium Deficit = 42 L × 20 mEq/L = 840 mEq. This represents the total amount of sodium required to correct the serum sodium level from 120 to 140 mEq/L. It is important to note that this deficit should be corrected slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient with hypertension, peripheral edema, and chronic kidney disease presents for treatment. Which medication would be the most appropriate choice for managing this condition?
questions.explanation: Chlorthalidone This patient has hypertension and peripheral edema, indicating volume overload, which is common in chronic kidney disease (CKD). Diuretics are a cornerstone of management in this setting to control both blood pressure and volume status. While loop diuretics are often required in advanced CKD (GFR < 30 ml/ min), thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics such as chlorthalidone are highly effective in earlier stages of CKD. Recent major clinical trials (like the CLICK trial) have demonstrated that chlorthalidone is effective at lowering blood pressure even in patients with advanced CKD. It helps reduce extracellular fluid volume, thereby treating both the hypertension and the edema. While RAAS inhibitors are also crucial in CKD for their anti-proteinuric effects, diuretics are essential for volume control, making chlorthalidone an excellent choice.

options.text: There is extremely forceful peristaltic activity leading to episodes of chest pain and dysphagia.
There is no medical treatment available.
It is a type of esophageal malignancy.

questions.explanation: There is extremely forceful peristaltic activity leading to episodes of chest pain and dysphagia. Nutcracker esophagus, also known as hypertensive peristalsis, is a motility disorder of the esophagus. It is defined by manometric findings of normal, coordinated peristalsis in the esophageal body, but with extremely high- amplitude or long-duration contractions. The peristaltic waves are normally sequenced but are simply too powerful. This hyper contractility is thought to be the cause of the primary symptoms, which are non-cardiac chest pain and dysphagia (difficulty swallowing). The diagnosis is made exclusively by high-resolution esophageal manometry, which will show distal contractile integral (DCI) values greater than 8,000 mmHg·s·cm. questions.stem: Which of the following electrolyte imbalances is associated with ECG findings of ST-segment depression and prominent U waves?
questions.explanation: Hypokalemia Low serum potassium levels, or hypokalemia, produce a characteristic sequence of changes on the electrocardiogram (ECG). As the potassium level falls, the primary findings are : 1. Flattening or inversion of the T wave. 2. ST-segment depression. 3. The appearance of a prominent U wave, which is a small deflection that follows the T wave and is best seen in the mid-precordial leads (V2-V4). The prominent U wave can sometimes merge with the flattened T wave, giving the appearance of a prolonged QT interval (although the actual QT interval is normal, the Q-U interval is prolonged). This combination of ST depression, flat T waves, and prominent U waves is the classic ECG manifestation of hypokalemia. Hyperkalemia (A) causes peaked T waves and QRS widening. Calcium abnormalities (C, D) primarily affect the QT interval.

questions.stem: A patient receiving antidepressant therapy presents with hyperthermia, dilated pupils, palpitations, and hypotension. ECG reveals broad QRS complex tachycardia with right axis deviation. Which of the following interventions should be performed immediately?
questions.explanation: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate This clinical presentation is classic for a severe Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) overdose. TCAs have three major toxic effects : anticholinergic effects (hyperthermia, dilated pupils), cardiovascular toxicity, and CNS toxicity. The cardiovascular toxicity is the most life- threatening and is caused by the blockade of fast sodium channels in the cardiac myocytes. This effect slows conduction, leading to a prolonged QRS interval (\>100 ms), a right axis deviation of the terminal QRS (a prominent R wave in aVR), and ventricular arrhythmias like the wide complex tachycardia seen here. The immediate and life-saving intervention for TCA cardiotoxicity is the administration of intravenous sodium bicarbonate. Sodium bicarbonate works by increasing the extracellular sodium concentration, which helps to overcome the sodium channel blockade, and by increasing the serum pH, which decreases the binding of the TCA to the sodium channels.

The CURB-65 criteria are : Confusion (not present), Urea >42 mg/dl (present, 44 mg/dl), Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min (not present, 20/min), Blood pressure (systolic <90 or diastolic ≤ 60 mmHg) (not present, 110/70), and age ≥ 65 years (present, 68 years). This patient scores 2 points (one for Urea and one for Age). A CURB-65 score of 2 indicates moderate severity pneumonia and warrants hospital admission for treatment with intravenous antibiotics and monitoring. However, the patient is not in respiratory failure (RR is normal) and is hemodynamically stable, so ICU admission is not required. Therefore, the appropriate next step is admission to a general medical ward (room admission). Home treatment is for low-risk patients (score 0-1).

questions.stem: A patient presents with numbness of the fingertips and tight, thickened facial skin. Antinuclear antibody testing is positive with a nucleolar immunofluorescence pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Systemic sclerosis The clinical presentation of numb fingertips (suggesting Raynauds phenomenon) and tight facial skin (sclerodactyly and masked facies) is highly characteristic of Systemic Sclerosis (scleroderma). This is an autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by vasculopathy and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs. The immunological findings further support this diagnosis. While Antinuclear Antibodies (ANA) are positive in many autoimmune diseases, certain immunofluorescence patterns are more specific. A nucleolar pattern on ANA testing is strongly associated with systemic sclerosis. It is often seen in patients who have specific autoantibodies like anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) or anti- fibrillarin, which are markers for the diffuse cutaneous form of the disease. This combination of clinical and serological findings is classic for systemic sclerosis.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old patient presents with fever, severe calf pain, and fatigue. On examination, conjunctival suffusion is noted along with petechial eruptions and thrombocytopenia. Abdominal examination reveals tender hepatomegaly and icterus. Renal function tests are within normal limits, but urinalysis shows hematuria. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leptospirosis This clinical picture is highly suggestive of leptospirosis. The key features pointing to this diagnosis are the acute febrile illness with severe myalgia, particularly in the calves, and the pathognomonic sign of conjunctival suffusion (redness of the conjunctiva without discharge). The presence of icterus (jaundice), tender hepatomegaly, petechiae, and thrombocytopenia indicates a more severe form of the disease, often called Weil's disease, which involves hepatic and sometimes renal dysfunction (though KFTs are normal here, hematuria is present). While Dengue fever (B) can cause fever, petechiae, and thrombocytopenia, the severe calf pain and conjunctival suffusion are much more characteristic of leptospirosis. Chikungunya (C) causes severe arthralgia but not typically jaundice or conjunctival suffusion.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old male infant presents with pain in the extremities and is admitted to the hospital. There is a history of a previous chest infection occurring two years ago. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis reveals increased levels of hemoglobin F (HbF) and hemoglobin S (HbS). Based on these clinical and laboratory findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sickle cell anemia The definitive diagnostic test result is the High- Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC), which analyzes the types of hemoglobin present. The results show the presence of Hemoglobin S (HbS), which is the abnormal hemoglobin that causes sickle cell anemia. In sickle cell disease (HbSS genotype), normal adult hemoglobin (HbA) is absent, and the primary hemoglobins are HbS and fetal hemoglobin (HbF). HbF levels are high at birth and gradually decline, but they often remain elevated in patients with sickle cell disease, which is somewhat protective. The clinical presentation of a 6-month-old with pain in the extremities (dactylitis or hand-foot syndrome) and a history of chest infection (acute chest syndrome) is also classic for the initial manifestations of sickle cell anemia, as this is the age when HbF levels have dropped sufficiently for sickling to become clinically significant. 103. questions.stem: An 11-year-old child with rheumatic fever is started on secondary prophylaxis with intramuscular benzathine penicillin (0.6 million units). Which of the following statements regarding secondary prevention is correct?

options.text: Till 10 years 3 weekly or till 25 years of age

questions.explanation: Till 10 years 3 weekly or till 25 years of age After an episode of Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF), secondary prophylaxis with penicillin is crucial to prevent recurrent Group A streptococcal infections, which could trigger further episodes of ARF and worsen cardiac damage (rheumatic heart disease). The duration of prophylaxis depends on the severity of the initial disease. For a patient with rheumatic fever with carditis but no residual heart disease, the standard recommendation (e.g., from the American Heart Association) is to continue prophylaxis for 10 years after the last episode or until age 21 (whichever is longer). Some guidelines, particularly in high-prevalence areas, may recommend continuing until age 25. Therefore, continuing prophylaxis for 10 years or until age 25 is the most appropriate option. Lifelong prophylaxis (A) is reserved for patients with severe residual heart disease.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old female presents to the clinic with a severe, throbbing headache localized to the left side of her head. She describes the pain as pulsating and reports that these headache episodes have been occurring intermittently over the past few months. Each episode is accompanied by significant nausea and occasional vomiting. Prior to the onset of the headache, she frequently experiences visual disturbances such as flashing lights and zigzag patterns, suggestive of an aura. She also notes increased sensitivity to light (photophobia) and sound (phonophobia) during these episodes, which interferes with her ability to perform daily activities. Given her symptoms and overall clinical presentation, what is the most appropriate treatment option for immediate relief of her migraine?
questions.explanation: Sumatriptan The patient's presentation of a unilateral, throbbing headache accompanied by nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, and preceded by a visual aura is a classic description of migraine with aura. The question asks for treatment for immediate relief, which refers to abortive therapy. The first-line and most specific abortive medications for moderate to severe migraine attacks are the triptans. Sumatriptan is the prototypical drug in this class. Triptans are serotonin 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists. They work by causing vasoconstriction of painfully dilated cranial blood vessels and by inhibiting the release of pro-inflammatory neuropeptides in the trigeminal nervous system, thereby aborting the headache attack. Propranolol (B), topiramate (C), and flunarizine (D) are all medications used for prophylaxis (prevention) of migraines and are not effective for treating an acute attack. questions.stem: A software engineer presents to the outpatient department with easy fatigability and reports prolonged computer use for 12–14 hours daily, frequent consumption of junk food, and minimal intake of fruits and vegetables. His complete blood count shows a hemoglobin level of 7 g/dL and an MCV of 120 fL. What is the most likely cause of his anemia?
questions.explanation: Cyanocobalamin deficiency The patient has severe anemia (hemoglobin 7 g/dL) with a high mean corpuscular volume (MCV = 120 fL), which indicates macrocytic anemia. Macrocytic anemia is commonly caused by vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) deficiency or folate deficiency, both of which impair DNA synthesis in developing red blood cells and lead to megaloblastic anemia. In this case, the key clues are the very high MCV and the patient’s poor dietary habits, including frequent junk food intake and minimal consumption of nutritious foods. Vitamin B12 deficiency is particularly associated with diets lacking animal products such as meat, eggs, and dairy, or with malabsorption conditions. When B12 levels are low, DNA synthesis in bone marrow cells becomes defective, resulting in the production of large, immature red blood cells (macrocytes). Unlike folate deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency may also lead to neurological symptoms, although these may not appear early. Other options are less likely: 1. Sideroblastic anemia usually produces microcytic anemia. 2. Acute blood loss causes normocytic anemia. Thus, the most likely cause is cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about pheochromocytoma?

options.text: Propranolol is the preferred drug for hypertension control
Surgery is the treatment of choice

questions.explanation: Propranolol is the preferred drug for hypertension control The statement that propranolol is the preferred drug for hypertension control is false and represents a dangerous misunderstanding of pheochromocytoma management. Pheochromocytomas are tumors that secrete excessive catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine), which act on both alpha and beta-adrenergic receptors, causing severe hypertension and tachycardia. If a beta-blocker like propranolol is given alone before alpha- blockade, it will block the beta-2 mediated vasodilation. This leaves the alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which can lead to a paradoxical and life-threatening hypertensive crisis. The correct pharmacological management requires initiating an alpha-blocker (like phenoxybenzamine or prazosin) first to control blood pressure, followed by a beta-blocker if tachycardia persists. The definitive treatment is surgical resection of the tumor (B), and diagnosis is confirmed by measuring plasma or urinary catecholamines and their metabolites like VMA (C, D).

The electrolyte concentrations are : Sodium () 130 mEq/L, Potassium () 4 mEq/L, Calcium () 2.7 mEq/L (sometimes written as 3), Chloride () 109 mEq/L, and Lactate 28 mEq/L. This specific formulation is that of Lactated Ringer's (LR) solution, also known as Hartmann's solution. It is an isotonic crystalloid fluid that is one of the most commonly used resuscitation fluids in medicine. Its electrolyte composition is designed to be similar to that of plasma. The lactate in the solution is metabolized by the liver into bicarbonate, which can help to buffer metabolic acidosis. Haemaccel (B) is a colloid. Isolyte-P and Isolyte-M (C, D) are other crystalloid solutions but have different electrolyte compositions, typically with more potassium and less sodium, and are used for pediatric maintenance.

Its components are : 1. Aggressive medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). 2. Pheochromocytoma. 3. A unique phenotype that includes multiple mucosal neuromas (A) on the lips and tongue, a tall, slender Marfanoid habitus (C), and diffuse intestinal ganglioneuromatosis, which can lead to motility issues and complications like megacolon (B). The feature that is notably absent in MEN 2B is parathyroid hyperplasia or adenoma, which causes primary hyperparathyroidism. Hyperparathyroidism is a key component of the closely related MEN 2A syndrome but not MEN 2B. This is a crucial distinction between the two subtypes.

questions.stem: A patient presents with breathlessness and wheezing, has an absolute eosinophil count of 500 cells/µL, and a chest X-ray showing a miliary pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia (TPE) is a specific clinical manifestation of an occult filarial infection (usually Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi). It is a hypersensitivity reaction to the microfilariae that become trapped in the lungs. The classic clinical presentation includes paroxysmal coughing and wheezing, often worse at night, breathlessness, and a very high peripheral eosinophil count (typically >3000 cells/µL, though the value given is low). Chest X-rays can show a variety of findings, including diffuse miliary mottling or reticulonodular infiltrates. While the eosinophil count in the question is lower than typical, the combination of respiratory symptoms (wheezing), a miliary pattern on X-ray, and eosinophilia in a patient from a tropical region strongly points towards TPE over the other diagnoses. Miliary TB does not typically cause wheezing or significant eosinophilia.

questions.stem: A patient presents with shortness of breath and generalized weakness. Cardiac auscultation reveals a mid-diastolic murmur, and jugular venous pulse examination shows a prominent a wave. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tricuspid Stenosis (TS) The combination of a mid-diastolic murmur and a prominent a wave in the jugular venous pulse (JVP) is the pathognomonic finding for Tricuspid Stenosis (TS). The murmur is generated by turbulent blood flow across the narrowed tricuspid valve during ventricular filling. The a wave in the JVP corresponds to right atrial contraction. In TS, the right atrium must contract with much greater force to push blood through the stenotic valve, leading to a markedly elevated right atrial pressure and a visible, giant a wave in the neck veins. The resulting backup of pressure and reduced cardiac output cause the symptoms of generalized weakness and breathing difficulty (due to systemic venous congestion and low output). Mitral stenosis (B) also causes a mid-diastolic murmur but affects the JVP differently, if at all.

questions.stem: A patient with known HIV infection presents with fever, productive cough, and sputum. Clinical examination shows consolidation in the right infra scapular region, and chest X-ray reveals right lower lobe consolidation. The CD4 count is 55 cells/µL. What is the most common cause of this presentation?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae While patients with severe immunosuppression (CD4 count < 200) are at high risk for opportunistic infections, the most common overall cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in HIV-positive individuals remains Streptococcus pneumoniae. The clinical presentation of an acute onset of fever, productive cough, and radiological evidence of a focal lobar consolidation is the classic picture of typical bacterial pneumonia, for which S. pneumoniae is the leading pathogen. The risk of invasive pneumococcal disease is significantly higher in HIV-positive individuals compared to the general population, even at higher CD4 counts. In contrast, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP), though common in this population, typically presents with a non- productive cough, dyspnea, and diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest X-ray, not a focal consolidation. Staphylococcus aureus is a less common cause of CAP but can occur post- influenza.

questions.stem: A patient is found to have a mediastinal mass and is diagnosed with pure red cell aplasia. What is the most likely underlying cause of this association?
questions.explanation: Thymic neoplasia Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a rare disorder characterized by a severe normocytic, normochromic anemia with marked reticulocytopenia and a near-complete absence of red blood cell precursors (erythroblasts) in the bone marrow. While it can be idiopathic or associated with various conditions, there is a well-established paraneoplastic association between PRCA and thymic neoplasia, specifically thymoma. Approximately 5-10% of patients with thymoma develop PRCA, and conversely, about 30-50% of adult patients with PRCA are found to have an underlying thymoma. The thymus is located in the anterior mediastinum, which would appear as a mediastinal mass on imaging. The exact mechanism is thought to be autoimmune, with T-cells generated in NODIA

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with recurrent infections and a characteristic skin rash, as shown in the image. Laboratory investigations reveal thrombocytopenia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome The clinical triad of recurrent infections, eczema (the rash shown), and thrombocytopenia in a male child is the classic presentation of Wiskott- Aldrich Syndrome (WAS). WAS is a rare, X-linked recessive primary immunodeficiency disorder caused by a mutation in the WAS gene. The defective WAS protein leads to impaired function and survival of T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes, and platelets. The immunodeficiency results in susceptibility to recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections. The thrombocytopenia is characterized by the presence of abnormally small platelets (micro thrombocytopenia) and leads to an increased risk of bleeding, which can manifest as petechiae, purpura, or severe hemorrhage. The eczematous rash is often severe and difficult to control. This unique combination of eczema, immunodeficiency, and micro thrombocytopenia is pathognomonic for Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

questions.stem: Which prognostic scoring system for liver disease is depicted in the image?
questions.explanation: Child-Pugh score While no picture is provided, the question asks for a prognostic scoring system for liver conditions. The Child-Pugh score (also known as the Child-Turcotte-Pugh score) is a widely used system to assess the severity and prognosis of chronic liver disease, particularly cirrhosis. It was originally designed to predict mortality during surgery but is now used to predict overall prognosis and the need for liver transplantation. The score is calculated based on five clinical and laboratory parameters : serum bilirubin, serum albumin, prothrombin time (or INR), and the degree of ascites and hepatic encephalopathy. Patients are classified into three classes (A, B, or C) based on their total score, with Class A having the best prognosis and Class C having the worst. The MELD score is also used, especially for transplant allocation, but Child-Pugh is a classic prognostic tool.

questions.stem: A patient’s arterial blood gas analysis shows a pH of 7.2, bicarbonate level of 10–12 mmol/L, and a pCO₂ of 35 mmHg. What is the most likely cause of this metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation: HCO3⁻ loss by the kidney The patient has a metabolic acidosis, indicated by a low pH (7.2) and a low serum bicarbonate (HCO 3⁻) level (10-12 mmol/L). The pCO 2 is at the lower end of normal, suggesting some respiratory compensation has begun. Metabolic acidosis can be broadly divided into two types based on the anion gap (AG = Na + - (Cl ⁻ + HCO3⁻)). Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) is caused by the loss of bicarbonate, which is replaced by chloride, keeping the gap normal. The two main causes of NAGMA are diarrhea (loss of bicarbonate from the gut) and renal tubular acidosis (RTA). In RTA, the kidneys fail to either reabsorb filtered bicarbonate (proximal RTA) or excrete hydrogen ions (distal RTA), leading to a net loss of bicarbonate from the body via the kidney. This would be a primary renal cause of the metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: Impaired aquaporin function leads to which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus (DI) Aquaporins are a family of water channel proteins that are crucial for regulating water transport across cell membranes. In the kidney, Aquaporin-2 (AQP2) channels play a vital role in the collecting ducts. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) binds to V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of principal cells, which triggers a signaling cascade that causes AQP2-containing vesicles to fuse with the apical membrane. This inserts the AQP2 channels into the membrane, making it permeable to water and allowing for water reabsorption. Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus (NDI) is a condition where the renal tubules are unable to respond to ADH. While the most common cause is a mutation in the V2 receptor, a significant number of hereditary NDI cases are caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AQP2 gene. This impaired function of the aquaporin channels prevents water reabsorption, leading to the excretion of large volumes of dilute urine (polyuria).

questions.stem: What is the most serious complication of measles?
questions.explanation: Meningo-encephalitis While pneumonia is the most common cause of death from measles and otitis media is the most frequent complication overall, the most serious and devastating complication is acute meningoencephalitis. This neurological complication occurs in approximately 1 in 1,000 cases of measles, typically appearing a few days after the onset of the rash. It can manifest with seizures, altered consciousness, and focal neurological deficits. The mortality rate from measles encephalitis is high (around 15%), and a significant proportion of survivors (25-40%) are left with permanent neurological sequelae, including intellectual disability, seizure disorders, deafness, and motor impairments. Another even more devastating, though much rarer, neurological complication is Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE), a progressive and universally fatal disease that develops years after the initial infection. questions.stem: Water hammer pulse is classically observed in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Aortic regurgitation A water hammer pulse, also known as a collapsing pulse or Corrigan's pulse, is a classic physical sign of severe, chronic aortic regurgitation (AR). In AR, the incompetent aortic valve allows a significant volume of blood to leak back from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole. This regurgitant fraction leads to a very large stroke volume being ejected during systole. The result is a wide pulse pressure (a large difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressure). This creates a characteristic pulse that has a very rapid, forceful upstroke followed by a sudden, precipitous collapse as blood runs off both peripherally and back into the ventricle. The sensation, best felt by palpating the radial artery with the patient's arm elevated, is likened to the historical water hammer toy, which had a similar sudden, forceful impact.

For a child with a cough or difficulty breathing, the presence of any general danger sign or specific signs of severe respiratory distress mandates an immediate and urgent referral to a higher-level facility. Chest indrawing (visible retraction of the lower chest wall during inspiration) is a key sign of increased work of breathing and is classified as a sign of Severe Pneumonia or Very Severe Disease. According to the IMNCI algorithm, any child with chest indrawing must be classified as having a severe condition. The correct management is to give the first dose of an appropriate antibiotic and then refer urgently to a hospital or tertiary care center for inpatient management, including potential oxygen therapy and parenteral antibiotics.

questions.stem: At what temperature should rewarming be performed in cases of frostbite?
questions.explanation: 42°C. Standard medical protocol for frostbite is rapid rewarming of the affected area in a controlled water bath. The goal is to thaw the frozen tissue quickly without causing additional thermal injury. The recommended water temperature is between 37°C and 42°C (98.6°F to 107.6°F). This range is optimal because it's warm enough to restore circulation and thaw tissue efficiently, yet safely below the temperature that would burn the skin. Because the frostbitten area is numb, the individual cannot feel pain, making them highly susceptible to burns from water that is too hot. Temperatures like 44°C or 46°C are dangerously high and can cause severe burns, worsening the injury. Rewarming is typically continued for 15–30 minutes until the skin becomes red and soft. This process is often extremely painful as sensation returns, requiring medical supervision and pain management.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is not associated with pituitary apoplexy?
questions.explanation: Hyperthyroidism Pituitary apoplexy is a rare but life-threatening medical emergency caused by either hemorrhage or infarction within a pituitary adenoma. This leads to a rapid enlargement of the tumor, causing a sudden onset of severe headache, visual disturbances (due to compression of the optic chiasm), cranial nerve palsies, and altered mental status. Several predisposing factors have been identified that can precipitate this event in a patient with a pre-existing pituitary adenoma. These include diabetes mellitus, hypertension, major surgeries, and coagulation disorders. Conditions that affect blood viscosity and flow, like sickle cell anemia, can also be a risk factor. Hyperthyroidism, however, is not a recognized or common predisposing condition for pituitary apoplexy. The association is primarily with vascular and hematological conditions that can compromise the fragile blood supply of a pituitary tumor.

questions.stem: Loss of pain and temperature sensation on the same side of the face and the opposite side of the body occurs due to thrombosis of which artery?
questions.explanation: Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) This pattern of crossed sensory loss is the hallmark of Wallenberg syndrome, also known as the lateral medullary syndrome. This syndrome is caused by an infarct in the dorsolateral medulla of the brainstem. The artery most commonly occluded to cause this syndrome is the vertebral artery, followed by its branch, the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA). The infarct damages several key structures in this region. Specifically, it affects the spinal trigeminal nucleus, which receives pain and temperature sensation from the ipsilateral face, causing loss of sensation there. It also damages the spinothalamic tract, which carries pain and temperature sensation from the contralateral side of the body, causing a loss of sensation on the opposite side. questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents for a routine health check-up. He is tall in stature and, on examination, an early diastolic murmur is detected. His family pedigree is shown below. What is the most likely mode of inheritance of this condition?
questions.explanation: AD The provided pedigree chart is the key to determining the mode of inheritance. Analysis of the chart reveals several key features : 1. Vertical Transmission : The trait appears in every generation (Generation I, II, and III all have affected individuals), which is a hallmark of dominant inheritance. 2. Affected individuals have at least one affected parent : For example, individuals II-1, II-5, and II-8 all have an affected father (I-1). This further supports a dominant pattern. 3. Male-to-male transmission is present : The affected father in generation I (I-1) passes the trait to his son (II-1). This observation definitively rules out X-linked inheritance. 4. Both males and females are affected : This makes autosomal inheritance more likely than sex-linked. This combination of vertical transmission and male-to-male transmission is pathognomonic for an Autosomal Dominant (AD) inheritance pattern. The clinical findings of tall stature and an early diastolic murmur (suggestive of aortic root dilation leading to aortic regurgitation) are consistent with conditions like Marfan syndrome, which is a well-known autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder.

questions.stem: What is the leading cause of mortality in children diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)?
questions.explanation: Lupus nephritis Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem autoimmune disease that can have severe manifestations in children. While modern treatments have significantly improved survival, mortality is still a concern. The most common cause of death in children with SLE has historically been related to end-organ damage from the disease itself, and the most frequently and severely affected organ is the kidney. Lupus nephritis, which is the inflammation of the kidneys caused by the deposition of immune complexes, is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. It can progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), requiring dialysis or transplantation. While infections (D), often related to the immunosuppressive therapies used to treat SLE, have emerged as a leading cause of death in recent years, renal failure from uncontrolled lupus nephritis remains a primary and classic cause of mortality in this population. Lupus cerebritis (B) and cardiac complications (C) are also serious but are less common causes of death than renal disease.

questions.stem: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) is used to treat a tumor associated with which specific genetic mutation?
questions.explanation: PML-RARA All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) is a highly specific and effective differentiation agent used as the cornerstone of treatment for Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL), a subtype of AML. The pathognomonic genetic hallmark of APL is the chromosomal translocation t(15;17) (q22;q21). This translocation results in the fusion of the Promyelocytic Leukemia (PML) gene on chromosome 15 with the Retinoic Acid Receptor Alpha (RARA) gene on chromosome 17, creating the oncogenic fusion gene PML- RARA. The abnormal PML-RARA protein acts as a transcriptional repressor, blocking the normal differentiation of myeloid cells at the promyelocyte stage. ATRA works by binding to the RARA portion of this fusion protein, which overcomes the transcriptional block and induces the malignant promyelocytes to differentiate into mature neutrophils. This targeted therapy has revolutionized the treatment of APL, transforming it into a highly curable disease.

questions.stem: A patient presents with the following arterial blood gas (ABG) and electrolyte values : pH=7.24 pO 2=80 mmHg, PaCO 2=36 mmHg, HCO3⁻=14 mmol/L, Na+=131 mmol/L, Cl⁻=90 mmol/L, Base excess (BE)=-13, Glucose =135 mg/dL. What is the most likely acid-base disturbance?

This indicates an acidosis. 2. Check the PaCO 2 : The PaCO2 is 36 mmHg, which is within the normal range (35-45 mmHg). This suggests the primary problem is not respiratory. Check the HCO 3⁻ : The bicarbonate level is 14 mmol/L, which is significantly lower than the normal range (22-28 mmol/L). A low bicarbonate level is the defining feature of a metabolic acidosis. This is a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A woman with bipolar disorder has been taking lithium for six months. After several days of fasting for religious reasons, she develops seizures, tremors, confusion, and weakness. Which investigations should be performed to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Serum lithium The patient's symptoms of seizures, coarse tremors, and confusion are classic signs of lithium toxicity. Lithium has a very narrow therapeutic index, and its levels can be easily pushed into the toxic range. The history of prolonged fasting is a critical clue. Fasting leads to dehydration and sodium depletion. The kidneys handle lithium and sodium in a similar way; in a state of sodium depletion, the proximal tubules increase the reabsorption of sodium in an attempt to conserve it. This process also leads to a concomitant increase in the reabsorption of lithium, causing its serum levels to rise dangerously. Therefore, the single most important and immediate investigation to confirm the diagnosis is to measure the serum lithium level. While serum electrolytes are also important to assess for dehydration and other imbalances, the lithium level will be the definitive diagnostic test.

questions.stem: Which electrolyte imbalance is commonly associated with lithium therapy?
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia Long-term therapy with lithium is associated with several endocrine and electrolyte abnormalities. One well-recognized complication is its effect on calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH) metabolism. Lithium can cause hyperparathyroidism, leading to hypercalcemia. It is thought to do this by altering the set point of the calcium-sensing receptors on the parathyroid glands, making them less sensitive to suppression by serum calcium. This leads to an inappropriate secretion of PTH, which in turn increases serum calcium levels through its actions on bone and the kidneys. The hypercalcemia is usually mild and asymptomatic, but it can be more significant and requires monitoring of serum calcium and PTH levels in patients on chronic lithium therapy. Lithium's primary effect on renal tubules can also cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, leading to hypermetropia, but hypercalcemia is the most specific electrolyte disturbance listed.

questions.stem: Pulmonary plethora is seen in all of the following conditions except :
questions.explanation: Ebstein anomaly Pulmonary plethora refers to increased pulmonary blood flow, which appears on a chest X-ray as engorged pulmonary arteries and increased vascular markings. It is a feature of congenital heart defects that cause a left-to- right shunt or mixing of circulations that results in excess blood flowing to the lungs. Conditions like Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA), Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome (HLHS), and Double Outlet Right Ventricle (DORV) all involve complex mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous returns, typically resulting in increased pulmonary blood flow and plethora. In contrast, Ebstein's anomaly is a malformation of the tricuspid valve where it is displaced downwards into the right ventricle. This leads to severe tricuspid regurgitation and a poorly functioning right ventricle. The result is a significant decrease in effective forward blood flow from the right heart into the pulmonary circulation. Therefore, the characteristic finding in Ebstein's anomaly is pulmonary oligemia (decreased blood flow), not plethora.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man has had a wrist swelling for two years. Histopathology shows spindle- shaped cells with Verocay bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Schwannoma The key to this diagnosis is the histopathological findings. A Schwannoma (also known as a neurilemmoma) is a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor composed of Schwann cells. The microscopic appearance is classic and often biphasic. It consists of compact, cellular areas of spindle-shaped cells with palisading nuclei, which are organized into structures known as Verocay bodies. These are pathognomonic for schwannomas. A Verocay body consists of two parallel rows of palisading nuclei separated by an acellular, eosinophilic zone. The tumor also has less cellular, myxoid areas (Antoni B pattern). The patient's presentation of a slow- growing mass on the wrist is consistent with a peripheral nerve tumor. A neurofibroma (C) is also a nerve sheath tumor but is composed of a mixed population of cells (Schwann cells, fibroblasts, perineurial cells) and does not typically form Verocay bodies.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old patient presents with features of obstructive jaundice, and laboratory tests reveal raised alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, and haptoglobin levels. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Alcohol The patient presents with a cholestatic pattern of liver injury, indicated by the elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). A disproportionately high GGT compared to ALP is particularly suggestive of alcohol-related liver disease. Heavy alcohol consumption induces the GGT enzyme, often leading to marked elevations even in the early stages of alcoholic liver injury. Furthermore, alcohol can cause a spectrum of liver damage, from fatty liver to alcoholic hepatitis and cirrhosis, all of which can present with cholestasis and jaundice. The mention of elevated haptoglobin is unusual in this context as haptoglobin is typically decreased in hemolysis. However, GGT is an acute-phase reactant and can be elevated in many liver conditions, but its significant elevation along with ALP strongly points towards alcohol as a primary cause. questions.stem: What feature best distinguishes irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) from organic gastrointestinal disease?
questions.explanation: Stool calprotectin Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder, meaning it is characterized by symptoms without any visible or structural organic disease. Its symptoms, such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and mucus in the stools, can significantly overlap with those of organic diseases like Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD - Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis). A key challenge is to differentiate between these conditions. Fecal calprotectin is an excellent non-invasive biomarker for this purpose. Calprotectin is a protein released by neutrophils. Its presence in the stool indicates neutrophilic inflammation in the intestinal mucosa. In organic inflammatory diseases like IBD, there is significant inflammation, leading to a high fecal calprotectin level. In contrast, IBS is a non-inflammatory condition, so the fecal calprotectin level will be normal. This makes it a highly useful test to differentiate the functional symptoms of IBS from the inflammatory symptoms of organic GI disease.

questions.stem: Which condition is most commonly associated with the sudden onset of severe headache along with neck stiffness?
questions.explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) The combination of a sudden, explosive onset of a severe headache (often described as the worst headache of my life or a thunderclap headache) and signs of meningeal irritation, such as neck rigidity (nuchal rigidity), is the classic presentation of a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). An SAH is most commonly caused by the rupture of an intracranial saccular (berry) aneurysm, which releases arterial blood directly into the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain. This blood irritates the meninges, leading to the nuchal rigidity, photophobia, and vomiting. While bacterial meningitis (C) also causes headache and neck rigidity, the onset is typically more subacute (over hours to days) and is accompanied by high fever. The sudden, cataclysmic nature of the headache is the key feature pointing towards SAH.

questions.stem: Vegetations involving the mitral valve are most commonly seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Infective Endocarditis Vegetations on heart valves are the pathognomonic lesion of infective endocarditis (IE). A vegetation is an infected mass composed of a mixture of platelets, fibrin, microorganisms (bacteria or fungi), and inflammatory cells. In native valve endocarditis, the mitral valve is the most commonly affected valve, followed closely by the aortic valve. These vegetations are often friable and can break off, leading to septic emboli that can cause infarcts or abscesses in distant organs like the brain, spleen, or kidneys. While other conditions can cause valvular vegetations—such as the sterile vegetations of Libman-Sacks endocarditis (A) in SLE or nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (C) in malignancy—infective endocarditis is by far the most common cause of large, destructive valvular vegetations. 123. questions.stem: All of the following conditions are associated with low glucose levels in pleural fluid, except which one?
questions.explanation: Dressler's syndrome A low glucose level in pleural fluid (pleural fluid glucose < 60 mg/dL or a fluid-to-serum ratio < 0.5) indicates increased metabolic activity within the pleural space. This is typically caused by the utilization of glucose by a high number of cells, such as bacteria, inflammatory cells, or malignant cells. The classic causes of a low glucose pleural effusion include : 1. Empyema or complicated para pneumonic effusion, where bacteria and neutrophils consume glucose. 2. Malignant pleural effusion, where the tumor cells have high metabolic rates. 3. Pleural effusion associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis, due to impaired glucose transport into the pleural space and high inflammatory activity. 4. Tuberculous pleurisy. Dressler's syndrome is a form of post-myocardial infarction pericarditis (and sometimes pleuritis). The associated pleural effusion is typically a sterile, inflammatory exudate, but it is not characteristically associated with a low glucose level.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with a one-month history of fever presents with headache and ataxia. Brain imaging reveals ventricular dilatation with prominent basal exudates. Which cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) finding is most likely in this condition?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytosis, Low Glucose, High Protein The clinical presentation of a subacute or chronic meningitis (fever, headache, ataxia for one month) combined with imaging findings of communicating hydrocephalus (dilated ventricles) and basal exudates (inflammation and enhancement at the base of the brain) is classic for Tuberculous (TB) Meningitis. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profile in TB meningitis is highly characteristic. The inflammatory process disrupts the blood-brain barrier, leading to a very high protein level. The mycobacteria metabolize glucose, and inflammation impairs glucose transport into the CSF, resulting in a low glucose level (hypoglycorrhachia). The inflammatory cell response is typically a pleocytosis that is predominantly lymphocytic. This classic triad of lymphocytosis, low glucose, and high protein is the hallmark CSF finding for TB meningitis, distinguishing it from acute bacterial meningitis (which is neutrophilic) and viral meningitis (which typically has normal glucose). 151. questions.stem: What condition is indicated by the ECG shown in the image?
questions.explanation: Atrial flutter The ECG strip displays the classic features of atrial flutter. The most prominent and diagnostic finding is the presence of characteristic flutter waves that create a saw-tooth pattern for the baseline. These waves are most clearly visible in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). They represent rapid, regular, and organized atrial depolarization, typically at a rate of around 300 beats per minute, originating from a re-entrant circuit in the right atrium. The QRS complexes are narrow, indicating a supraventricular origin. The ventricular response is regular, suggesting a fixed atrioventricular (AV) block (e.g., a 2 :1 or 4 :1 block). In this strip, the atrial rate is approximately 300 bpm, and the ventricular rate is about 75 bpm, indicating a 4 :1 block. This saw-tooth baseline is the pathognomonic feature that distinguishes atrial flutter from atrial fibrillation, which has a chaotic, irregular baseline.

questions.stem: Identify the image with the diagnosis :
questions.explanation: PSVT (Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia) The ECG strip shows a regular, rapid tachycardia with narrow QRS complexes and a fairly uniform rhythm. P waves are either absent or not clearly visible, which is typical of PSVT, as atrial depolarization often occurs simultaneously with or just after ventricular depolarization. The heart rate usually ranges between 150–250 beats per minute, consistent with the tracing shown. Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is characterized by wide QRS complexes, which are not seen here. Atrial tachycardia (AT) usually shows identifiable abnormal P waves preceding each QRS complex. Ventricular fibrillation produces a completely chaotic, irregular waveform with no discernible QRS complexes, unlike this organized rhythm. Therefore, based on the regular rhythm, narrow QRS complexes, and absent visible P waves, the ECG is most consistent with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT).

questions.stem: Which metal results in “Saturnine gout” formation?
questions.explanation: Lead “Saturnine gout” refers to gout that occurs as a result of chronic lead poisoning. Lead interferes with renal tubular function, reducing the kidneys’ ability to excrete uric acid. This leads to hyperuricemia (elevated uric acid levels in the blood), which promotes the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints, producing painful gouty arthritis. Historically, the term “Saturnine” comes from “Saturn,” an old alchemical name for lead. Individuals with long- term occupational or environmental exposure— such as workers in battery manufacturing, smelting, or those exposed to contaminated water or paint—are at higher risk. questions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly describes the Bundle of Kent?

options.text: It is a muscular or nodal pathway between the atria and ventricle in WPW syndrome
It is slower than the AV nodal pathway

questions.explanation: It is a muscular or nodal pathway between the atria and ventricle in WPW syndrome The Bundle of Kent is the eponym for the accessory atrioventricular (AV) pathway that is the anatomical substrate for Wolff-Parkinson- White (WPW) syndrome. In a normal heart, the only electrical connection between the atria and the ventricles is through the AV node, which imposes a physiological delay. In WPW syndrome, this abnormal muscular bundle forms an additional electrical bridge that directly connects the atrial and ventricular myocardium, bypassing the AV node. This accessory pathway conducts impulses much faster than the AV node (C is incorrect). This pre-excitation of the ventricles via the Bundle of Kent is what produces the characteristic ECG findings of WPW : a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex, known as a delta wave. The presence of this bypass tract creates a potential circuit for re-entrant tachycardias, such as atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT).

questions.stem: A punched-out ulcer in the esophagus is seen in :
questions.explanation: Herpes The endoscopic appearance of esophageal ulcers can provide important clues to the underlying etiology, especially in immuno compromised patients. Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) esophagitis is characteristically associated with the formation of multiple, small, well- demarcated, punched-out ulcers. These ulcers are typically less than 2 cm in diameter and have a volcano-like appearance, with raised edges and a depressed, often white or yellow base. They are most commonly found in the mid-to-distal esophagus. In contrast, CMV esophagitis (B) typically causes large, linear, and deep ulcers. Candida esophagitis (D) presents with diffuse, white, plaque-like lesions that can be wiped off, revealing an erythematous, friable mucosa. The specific finding of small, discrete, punched- out ulcers is the classic endoscopic feature that strongly suggests HSV as the causative agent.

questions.explanation: ARDS (Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome) Acute pancreatitis is a major risk factor for the development of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS). ARDS is a form of acute, diffuse, inflammatory lung injury characterized by a severe impairment of oxygenation and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. questions.stem: Infarction of which region of the myocardium is most commonly associated with the development of a post-MI aneurysm?
questions.explanation: Anterior transmural A left ventricular aneurysm is a late complication of a myocardial infarction (MI), where a thinned, scarred, and dyskinetic segment of the ventricular wall bulges outward during systole. This complication is most likely to occur after a large, transmural (full-thickness) MI. The anatomical location most frequently associated with aneurysm formation is the anterior wall and apex of the left ventricle. This region is supplied by the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. A large, transmural anterior wall MI, typically resulting from a proximal LAD occlusion, leads to extensive necrosis of the myocardium in this area. During the healing process, this necrotic muscle is replaced by a thin, non-contractile fibrous scar. The constant intraventricular pressure then causes this weak, scarred area to progressively stretch and bulge outwards, forming a true ventricular aneurysm over weeks to months.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors increases the risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease?
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is a major and well-established genetic risk factor for the development of early-onset Alzheimer's disease. The gene for the amyloid precursor protein (APP) is located on chromosome 21. Individuals with Down syndrome have three copies of this chromosome and therefore three copies of the APP gene. This gene dosage effect leads to a lifelong overexpression and overproduction of APP. The subsequent processing of this excess APP results in an overproduction of the amyloid- beta peptide, which is the primary component of the amyloid plaques that are the pathological hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. As a result, almost all individuals with Down syndrome will develop the neuropathological changes of Alzheimer's by the age of 40, and a significant proportion will develop the clinical symptoms of dementia in their 50s and 60s.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has oral ulcers, photosensitivity, and a malar rash that spares the nasolabial folds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus This is a classic presentation of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), a multisystem autoimmune disease that predominantly affects young women. The patient exhibits several of the key diagnostic criteria for SLE : 1. Malar Rash : This is the characteristic butterfly rash, an erythematous rash over the cheeks and bridge of the nose that characteristically spares the nasolabial folds. 2. Photosensitivity : The development or worsening of a rash after exposure to sunlight. 3. Oral Ulcers : These are typically painless ulcers on the hard palate or in the nasopharynx. The presence of these features together is highly suggestive of SLE. Further workup would include serological tests for autoantibodies, particularly antinuclear antibodies (ANA), which are positive in nearly all patients with SLE, and more specific antibodies like anti- dsDNA and anti-Sm. Sturge-Weber syndrome involves a facial port-wine stain, not a malar rash. NODIA

questions.stem: In Brown-skinned syndrome, which type of sensation is lost on the ipsilateral side of the lesion?
questions.explanation: Proprioception Brown-skinned syndrome results from the hemisection (damage to one half) of the spinal cord. This injury leads to a distinct pattern of neurological deficits below the level of the lesion, based on the specific tracts that are damaged. 1. Ipsilateral (same side) deficits : The injury damages the dorsal columns and the corticospinal tract. The dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) carry sensory information for fine touch, vibration, and proprioception (joint position sense) without crossing in the spinal cord. Therefore, there is a loss of these sensations on the same side as the lesion. Damage to the corticospinal tract, which has already crossed in the medulla, causes ipsilateral spastic paralysis. 2. Contralateral (opposite side) deficits : The injury damages the spinothalamic tract. Since the fibers of this tract (carrying pain and temperature sensation) cross to the opposite side shortly after entering the cord, there is a loss of pain and temperature sensation on the side opposite the lesion.

questions.stem: Achondroplasia shows which type of inheritance?
questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant Achondroplasia is the most common form of skeletal dysplasia and disproportionate short stature (dwarfism). It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. The condition is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene. This mutation leads to a constitutive activation of the receptor, which severely inhibits the proliferation and differentiation of chondrocytes in the growth plates of long bones. This impairs endochondral ossification, resulting in the characteristic features of short limbs, macrocephaly, and frontal bossing. Although it is an autosomal dominant disorder, over 80% of cases of achondroplasia are the result of a de novo (new) mutation occurring in a child of unaffected, average-stature parents. When an individual with achondroplasia has children, they have a 50% chance of passing the condition on to each child.

questions.stem: Chronic alcohol consumption is most commonly associated with which type of cardiomyopathy?
questions.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy Chronic, heavy alcohol consumption is a major cause of secondary, non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). This condition is known as alcoholic cardiomyopathy. Alcohol and its metabolites, such as acetaldehyde, have a direct toxic effect on cardiomyocytes (heart muscle cells). This toxicity leads to impaired contractile function, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptosis of cardiac muscle cells. Over time, this results in the characteristic features of DCM : dilation of the ventricular chambers (especially the left ventricle), thinning of the ventricular walls, and severely impaired systolic function (reduced ejection fraction). This progressive myocardial dysfunction eventually leads to the clinical syndrome of congestive heart failure. Alcoholic cardiomyopathy is one of the leading causes of reversible DCM, as abstinence from alcohol can lead to a significant improvement in cardiac function in some patients.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not related to HIV?
questions.explanation: Tertiary syphilis HIV is associated with a wide range of opportunistic infections and malignancies due to progressive immunosuppression. 1. Primary CNS lymphoma is strongly associated with advanced HIV infection, particularly in patients with very low CD4 counts. It is considered an AIDS-defining illness. 2. Oesophageal candidiasis is also a classic opportunistic infection seen in HIV patients and is an AIDS-defining condition when it occurs. However, tertiary syphilis is not specifically related to HIV. While syphilis (caused by Treponema pallidum) may coexist with HIV because both are sexually transmitted infections, tertiary syphilis is a late complication of untreated syphilis and is not caused by HIV infection itself. It can occur in HIV-negative individuals as well. Thus, among the given options, the condition not specifically related to HIV infection is : (B) Tertiary syphilis

questions.stem: What are the key major blood-culture criteria used to diagnose infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation: Both a & b Infective endocarditis is diagnosed using the Modified Duke Criteria, which include major and minor criteria. Major blood-culture criteria are crucial for diagnosis. One major criterion is positive blood cultures for typical organisms known to cause infective endocarditis. These include the HACEK group organisms (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella). Although diagnosis usually requires two separate positive cultures, HACEK organisms are considered typical pathogens and form part of the major microbiological criteria. Another major criterion is a single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetii or a high phase I IgG antibody titer. Coxiella is highly specific for infective endocarditis, so even a single positive culture qualifies as a major criterion. Corynebacterium species are not typically included among the classic major organisms unless repeatedly isolated. Thus, both HACEK organisms and Coxiella burnetii are included under major blood-culture criteria in diagnostic guidelines. Therefore, the correct answer is : (D) Both a & b 171. Respiratory centers are stimulated by : NODIA

questions.stem: A patient presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, a pulse of 112/ min, systolic BP of 80 mmHg, and the chest X-ray shown. What is the next appropriate management step?
questions.explanation: Exploratory laprotomy The chest X-ray shows a large amount of free air under both hemidiaphragms (pneumoperitoneum), a definitive sign of a perforated hollow viscus. The patient is also in shock, as evidenced by the hypotension (SBP 80 mmHg) and tachycardia (pulse 112/min), and has severe abdominal pain, suggesting peritonitis. This combination of a perforated viscus with hemodynamic instability is a surgical emergency that requires immediate intervention to control the source of contamination and treat the sepsis. The next and most appropriate step in management is an emergency exploratory laparotomy. This surgical procedure allows for direct exploration of the abdominal cavity to identify and repair the perforation (most commonly a perforated peptic ulcer), followed by a thorough washout (lavage) of the peritoneal cavity to remove the contamination. Delaying surgery for further investigations would be life- threatening.

questions.stem: Which cardiovascular abnormality is most typically associated with congenital rubella syndrome?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary artery stenosis Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) is known for its classic triad of defects : sensorineural deafness, cataracts, and congenital heart disease. While Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) is the most common cardiac lesion, peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis is also a very characteristic and frequent finding, often occurring in combination with PDA. The rubella virus has a direct teratogenic effect on the developing cardiovascular system, leading to hypoplasia and stenosis of the main pulmonary artery and its branches. This combination of PDA and pulmonary artery stenosis is highly suggestive of CRS. Coarctation of the aorta (B) is more commonly associated with Turner syndrome. Ankylosing spondylitis (C) and Rheumatic fever (D) are acquired conditions, not congenital defects. Note : While PDA is the single most common defect, pulmonary artery stenosis is also highly characteristic and is a correct answer among the choices.

questions.stem: Osborn J waves are seen in :
questions.explanation: Hypothermia The Osborn wave, also known as the J wave, is a distinctive electrocardiogram (ECG) finding that is considered pathognomonic for hypothermia. It appears as a slow, positive deflection at the J-point, which is the junction between the end of the QRS complex and the beginning of the ST segment. This gives the J-point a humped or dome-like appearance. The amplitude of the Osborn wave is generally proportional to the degree of hypothermia, becoming more prominent as the core body temperature falls below 32°C (90°F). While J waves can occasionally be seen in other conditions such as hypercalcemia or early repolarization, their classic and most significant association is with hypothermia. questions.stem: Identify the condition shown in the CT scan image.
questions.explanation: Lacunar infarct The axial CT scan of the brain shows a small, well-defined, round, low-density (dark) lesion located deep within the brain parenchyma, specifically in the thalamus or basal ganglia region. This is the characteristic appearance of a lacunar infarct. Lacunar infarcts are small ischemic strokes (typically <15 mm in diameter) that occur in the deep, subcortical areas of the brain. They are caused by the occlusion of a single, small, penetrating artery (a lenticulostriate or thalamoperforating artery). The most common underlying pathology is lipohyalinosis or microatheroma of these small vessels, which is strongly associated with chronic hypertension and diabetes mellitus. The tissue necrosis from the infarct is eventually replaced by a small fluid-filled cavity or lacune. These small, deep infarcts produce classic clinical syndromes depending on their location.

questions.stem: The causative organism for the condition depicted in the image is?
questions.explanation: Staphylococci The image shows multiple inflamed nodular lesions on the palate and oral mucosa, giving a swollen and congested appearance. Such lesions may occur in bacterial infections of the oral cavity, particularly those caused by Staphylococcus species, most commonly Staphylococcus aureus. These bacteria are gram- positive cocci that frequently infect the skin and mucous membranes and can produce localized inflammatory lesions. Staphylococcal infections in the oral cavity may present with erythema, swelling, pustular or nodular lesions, and mucosal inflammation. They may develop due to poor oral hygiene, trauma to the mucosa, immunocompromised states, or secondary bacterial infection of existing oral lesions. The infection leads to acute inflammatory reactions, resulting in redness and raised lesions similar to those visible in the image. Other options are less consistent with the appearance.
