questions.stem: A patient develops swelling of the upper limb following a modified radical mastectomy. What is the most likely cause of this complication?
questions.explanation: Upper limb Lymphedema A modified radical mastectomy (MRM) is a surgical procedure for breast cancer that involves the removal of the entire breast tissue, nipple- areolar complex, and the axillary lymph nodes. The removal of the axillary lymph nodes disrupts the primary lymphatic drainage pathway from the ipsilateral arm. This disruption can lead to impaired drainage of lymphatic fluid, causing it to accumulate in the interstitial tissues of the arm. The resulting chronic, progressive swelling is known as secondary lymphedema. It is one of the most common and troublesome long- term complications following axillary lymph node dissection. While recurrence or metastasis could cause swelling, diffuse limb lymphedema is the most frequent cause in this post-operative setting. Angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome) is a very rare, late complication of chronic lymphedema.

questions.stem: Which surgical repair technique is most commonly used for the treatment of a direct inguinal hernia?
questions.explanation: Lichtenstein repair The Lichtenstein repair is currently the most widely performed open surgical technique for inguinal hernias worldwide and is considered the gold standard for tension-free repair. The procedure involves reinforcing the weak posterior wall of the inguinal canal (Hesselbachs triangle) with a synthetic, non-absorbable mesh. The mesh is sutured to the inguinal ligament, conjoint tendon, and other surrounding structures, creating a durable, tension-free barrier that prevents hernial recurrence. Its popularity stems from its technical simplicity, low recurrence rates, and the fact that it can be performed under local anesthesia. Bassinis repair is a historical tension repair that has higher recurrence rates. Herniotomy alone (excision of the sac) is typically only sufficient for pediatric inguinal hernias.

questions.stem: A patient develops breathlessness, hypotension, and reduced air entry on the right side of the chest following a road traffic accident. What should be the next immediate step in management?

options.text: Needle insertion at 2nd ICS in midclavicular line (MCL)
Needle insertion at 5th ICS in mid-axillary line
Fluid resuscitation using wide bore cannula

questions.explanation: Needle insertion at 2nd ICS in midclavicular line (MCL) This patients presentation following chest trauma—unilateral decreased air entry, breathlessness, and hypotension—is the classic triad for a tension pneumothorax. This is a life- threatening emergency where air enters the NODIA

questions.stem: Following a total thyroidectomy, the surgeon is unable to extubate the patient, who develops cyanosis and signs of respiratory distress. What is the most likely reason for the failure to extubate in this situation?
questions.explanation: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy The recurrent laryngeal nerves (RLN) innervate all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. They are responsible for abduction (opening) and adduction (closing) of the vocal cords. During a total thyroidectomy, these nerves are at risk of injury. While a unilateral RLN injury causes hoarseness, an acute bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy is a surgical emergency. The paralysis of both vocal cords in the paramedian position results in severe glottic obstruction, making it impossible for the patient to breathe adequately once the endotracheal tube is removed. This leads to immediate stridor, respiratory distress, and cyanosis, making extubation impossible. This situation requires an immediate surgical airway (tracheostomy). A hemorrhage would cause a visible neck hematoma and tracheal compression, which is another possibility, but bilateral RLN palsy is the classic cause of post-extubation stridor.

questions.stem: Asymptomatic varicose veins are classified under which category of the CEAP classification system?
questions.explanation: C2a The CEAP (Clinical, Etiological, Anatomical, Pathophysiological) classification is used to standardize the description of chronic venous disorders. The C or Clinical component describes the signs of the disease. C 2 is the classification for the presence of varicose veins. This category is further modified by a subscript a for asymptomatic or s for symptomatic. The question specifies asymptomatic varicose veins. While the options use a and b, a is the standard descriptor for asymptomatic. Therefore, the correct classification is C 2a. C 3 indicates the presence of edema. The subscripts a and b are not standardly used with C 3 in the way they are with C 2. The patient has visible varicose veins (C2) but no symptoms like pain, aching, or swelling, hence the a modifier.

questions.stem: A 0-year-old man is diagnosed with antral gastric carcinoma that has extended to the head of the pancreas and shows multiple small metastases in the right lobe of the liver. What is the most appropriate treatment strategy for this patient?
questions.explanation: Palliative care This patient has Stage IV, metastatic gastric cancer. The cancer has spread locally to involve the head of the pancreas and, more importantly, has spread distantly to the liver (liver metastases). The presence of distant metastases makes the cancer incurable by surgery. Major surgical resections like a Whipples procedure or a gastrectomy with lobectomy are curative- intent surgeries and are contraindicated in the setting of metastatic disease, as they would

questions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly describes the condition depicted in the image?

options.text: Associated with mixed aerobic and anaerobic infection
Anti- gas gangrene serum should always be used

questions.explanation: Associated with mixed aerobic and anaerobic infection The image depicts Fourniers gangrene, a rapidly progressing necrotizing fasciitis of the perineal and genital regions. This is a severe soft tissue infection that is a true surgical emergency. The most accurate statement regarding its etiology is that it is typically a polymicrobial infection, involving a synergistic combination of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. Common isolates include E. coli, Klebsiella, Streptococci, Staphylococci, Bacteroides, and Clostridium. This mixed infection leads to rapid tissue necrosis, gas formation, and systemic toxicity. The mainstay of treatment is urgent surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Orchidectomy (B) is rarely necessary as the testes have a separate blood supply and are usually spared. Anti-gas gangrene serum (C) is not routine. A urinary catheter is placed, but a formal diversion (D) is not always done.

questions.stem: Which nerve is most frequently at risk of injury during surgery of the submandibular gland?
questions.explanation: Lingual nerve During submandibular gland surgery (submandibular gland excision), the lingual nerve is the nerve most frequently at risk of injury. The Lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3) and carries general sensory fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. It also carries taste fibers from the chorda tympani (branch of facial nerve) and parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands. Anatomically, the lingual nerve lies close to the submandibular gland and the submandibular (Wharton’s) duct. During gland excision, particularly when the surgeon dissects around the duct and deep part of the gland, the lingual nerve may be stretched, compressed, or accidentally injured. Damage to the lingual nerve can result in loss of sensation in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, loss of taste, and reduced salivary secretion from the submandibular and sublingual glands. Other nerves like the hypoglossal nerve are also nearby but are less commonly injured compared with the lingual nerve. Therefore, the nerve most frequently at risk is the lingual nerve.

questions.explanation: Keep on active surveillance NODIA

questions.stem: A patient presents to the emergency department after a road traffic accident with hypotension, respiratory distress, subcutaneous emphysema, and absent air entry on one side. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Needle decompression in the 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line
Secure IV line and start fluid resuscitation after insertion of the wide-bore IV line

questions.explanation: Needle decompression in the 5th intercostal space in the mid axillary line The patient's clinical signs—respiratory distress, hypotension, unilateral absent breath sounds, and subcutaneous emphysema following trauma—are classic for a tension pneumothorax. This is a life-threatening emergency that causes obstructive shock and requires immediate intervention to relieve the pressure in the chest. The definitive immediate management is needle decompression (thoracostomy). The most recent Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) guidelines recommend inserting a large-bore needle into the 5th intercostal space in the anterior or mid-axillary line. This site is preferred over the traditional 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line because the chest wall is thinner here, reducing the risk of the needle not reaching the pleural space. This procedure converts the tension pneumothorax into a simple pneumothorax, which should then be followed by the insertion of a formal chest tube. Fluid resuscitation is also important, but relieving the tension physiology is the first priority.

questions.stem: Identify the condition shown in the CT scan image.
questions.explanation: Peutz-Jeghers This CT scan shows two critical findings : multiple polyps within the small bowel and a classic target sign (indicated by the arrow). This sign is a hallmark of intussusception, a condition where one segment of the intestine telescopes into an adjacent segment. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is a genetic disorder characterized by the growth of numerous benign hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract, particularly in the small intestine. A major complication of this syndrome is that these polyps often act as a lead point, dragging the bowel wall with them and causing recurrent episodes of intussusception and potential obstruction. The combination of multiple small bowel polyps and evidence of an active intussusception makes Peutz-Jeghers the most likely diagnosis. The other conditions listed are far less likely to cause this specific radiological picture. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: Examine the abdominal X-ray shown. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the findings?
questions.explanation: Intestinal obstruction The supine abdominal X-ray shows multiple dilated loops of small bowel located centrally in the abdomen. A key feature is the presence of fine, linear markings that traverse the entire diameter of the bowel lumen. These are the valvulae conniventes (or plicae circulares), which are the mucosal folds of the small intestine. The presence of these prominent folds in dilated loops confirms that the obstruction is in the small bowel. The image also demonstrates multiple air-fluid levels, which would be seen on an upright film and are another sign of intestinal obstruction. Haustra are the sacculations of the large bowel and do not cross the entire lumen. Therefore, the overall diagnosis based on these classic radiological signs is small bowel obstruction.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old man sustains a straddle injury in a road traffic accident and presents to the emergency department with blood visible at the urethral meatus. What is the next appropriate step in his management?

options.text: Perform suprapubic catheterization (SPC) and drain the urine
Obtain a contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) of the pelvis

questions.explanation: Perform retrograde urethrogram (RUG) The triad of a pelvic fracture mechanism (straddle injury), blood at the urethral meatus, and inability to void is highly suspicious for a urethral injury. In this situation, attempting to blindly insert a Foley catheter is absolutely contraindicated as it can convert a partial urethral tear into a complete one and introduce infection. The correct and mandatory next diagnostic step is to perform a retrograde urethrogram (RUG). This procedure involves injecting contrast dye into the urethra under fluoroscopy to visualize its integrity. Extravasation of contrast from the urethra will confirm the presence and location of the injury. Based on the findings of the RUG, a decision can then be made regarding bladder drainage (e.g., carefully placed Foley or a suprapubic catheter).

questions.stem: What is the typical metabolic abnormality seen in an infant diagnosed with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS)?
questions.explanation: Hypochloremic hyponatremic metabolic alkalosis Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS) causes gastric outlet obstruction, leading to persistent, non-bilious, projectile vomiting. The vomitus contains gastric juice, which is rich in hydrochloric acid (HCl) and potassium chloride (KCl). The persistent loss of these substances leads to a very characteristic electrolyte and acid-base disturbance. The loss of hydrogen ions (H +) results in metabolic alkalosis. questions.stem: Identify the condition shown in the image.
questions.explanation: MCU with Bulbar urethral stricture This X-ray is a contrast study of the male urethra that clearly shows a significant narrowing, which is a urethral stricture. The key to answering this question is to identify the location of this stricture and the type of imaging study. The stricture is located in the bulbar urethra, which is the segment of the anterior urethra found at the base of the penis. This is a very common site for strictures, often caused by straddle injuries or instrumentation. The imaging procedure could be either a Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU) or a Retrograde Urethrogram (RGU). While an RGU is typically better for viewing the anterior urethra, the options provided link the correct anatomical location (bulbar urethra) with the MCU procedure. Since the other options incorrectly identify the location of the stricture (penile, membranous, or prostatic), option (A) is the best and most accurate choice, as it correctly identifies the primary pathology and its location.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not seen in the ASEPSIS score?
questions.explanation: Induration The ASEPSIS score is a validated wound scoring system used to assess and quantify the severity of a surgical site infection (SSI). It assigns points based on both clinical findings observed during the postoperative period and the need for additional treatment. The clinical criteria scored as part of the ASEPSIS system include : 1. The presence of serous discharge. 2. The presence of erythema (redness). 3. The presence of purulent exudate (pus). 4. The separation of the deep tissues. Additional points are given if the patient requires antibiotic treatment for the wound infection or requires drainage of pus under local or general anesthesia. The system also considers the results of microbiological culture from the wound. Induration (hardening of the tissue) is a common sign of inflammation and infection but is not a specific, scored component of the ASEPSIS scoring system itself.

questions.stem: What is the clinical use or purpose of the instrument shown in the image?
questions.explanation: Laparoscopic sterilization The instrument shown in the image is a laparoscopic tubal ring applicator, commonly known as the Falope ring applicator. It is a long, slender laparoscopic instrument with a handle, locking mechanism, and applicator tip designed to place a silastic ring (Falope ring) around the fallopian tube. This instrument is primarily used during laparoscopic sterilization procedures for female contraception. During the procedure, the NODIA

questions.stem: The barium swallow study shown in the image reveals abnormal findings. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Esophageal Cancer The image shows a barium swallow study of the esophagus. The contrast column demonstrates an irregular, narrowed segment with shouldering and mucosal irregularity, producing an “apple-core” or irregular stricture appearance. This pattern is highly suggestive of esophageal carcinoma. In esophageal cancer, the tumor grows within the wall of the esophagus and progressively narrows the lumen, causing an irregular filling defect on contrast imaging. The edges appear asymmetric and irregular, unlike the smooth tapering seen in benign conditions. Clinically, patients with esophageal cancer commonly present with progressive dysphagia, initially to solid foods and later to liquids, along with weight loss, regurgitation, and chest discomfort. The most common types are squamous cell carcinoma (usually in the upper or middle esophagus) and adenocarcinoma (commonly in the distal esophagus). Why other options are incorrect: 1. Esophageal ring (Schatzki ring): shows a smooth, thin concentric narrowing. 2. Esophageal tear: usually shows contrast leakage. 3. Achalasia cardia: shows a smooth “bird- beak” tapering at the lower esophagus. Thus, the radiological findings most strongly indicate esophageal cancer.

questions.stem: Identify the condition shown in the image below.
questions.explanation: Chronic lymphedema The image displays the foot and ankle of a patient with severe, non-pitting edema. A key diagnostic feature visible is the inability to pinch or lift the skin at the base of the second toe. This is known as a positive Stemmer's sign. A positive Stemmer's sign is considered pathognomonic for lymphedema. The swelling in lymphedema is caused by the accumulation of protein-rich lymphatic fluid in the interstitial space, which leads to subcutaneous tissue thickening and fibrosis over time. This fibrosis is what makes the skin difficult to pinch. Other visible features consistent with chronic lymphedema include the squared-off appearance of the toes and the deep skin creases over the ankle and dorsum of the foot. This condition is distinct from other causes of edema, such as venous insufficiency or heart failure, where the edema is typically pitting and Stemmer's sign is negative. questions.stem: A patient with an abdominal stab injury is brought to the emergency department, as shown in the image below. Examination reveals penetration of the fascia, but the patient’s vital signs are stable. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Further investigation In cases of penetrating abdominal stab injury, management depends largely on the hemodynamic status of the patient and the extent of injury. In this scenario, examination reveals penetration of the fascia, which indicates that the wound has crossed the abdominal wall and may involve intra-abdominal organs. However, the patient’s vital signs are stable, meaning there is no immediate evidence of life- threatening hemorrhage or shock. For hemodynamically stable patients with penetrating abdominal trauma, the next best step is further evaluation with imaging and diagnostic tests rather than immediate surgery. Investigations may include contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen, Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST), or local wound exploration to determine whether the peritoneum has been breached and whether internal organs are injured. Immediate exploratory laparotomy is reserved for patients who are hemodynamically unstable, have signs of peritonitis, evisceration, or obvious internal injury. Simply waiting after dressing the wound could miss serious intra- abdominal injury, and IV fluids alone do not address the need for diagnosis. Therefore, in a stable patient with fascial penetration, the most appropriate next step is further investigation to assess intra-abdominal damage.

questions.stem: What surgery is shown here in the image.
questions.explanation: Thiersch wiring The image illustrates the Thiersch wiring procedure, a surgical technique used in the management of rectal prolapse, especially in children and elderly patients who are not suitable for major abdominal surgery. NODIA

questions.stem: What is the recommended treatment for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) measuring less than cm?
questions.explanation: Partial nephrectomy For small, localized renal masses, the goal of treatment is to achieve a complete oncological cure while preserving as much healthy kidney function as possible. For a Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) that is less than 4 cm in size and confined to the kidney (Stage T1a), the standard of care is a nephron-sparing approach, specifically a partial nephrectomy. This procedure involves the surgical excision of the tumor along with a small margin of normal kidney tissue, leaving the rest of the healthy kidney intact. This approach has been shown to have equivalent long-term cancer control and survival outcomes compared to a radical nephrectomy (complete removal of the kidney) for these small tumors, but with the significant advantage of better long-term preservation of renal function and a lower risk of developing chronic kidney disease.

questions.stem: Esophageal manometry shows panesophageal pressurization with preserved distal contractile integrity (>50 mmHg) in the esophageal body. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Type 3 achalasia Esophageal manometry is the gold standard test used to evaluate esophageal motility disorders. According to the Chicago Classification, achalasia is divided into three types based on manometric findings. Type 3 achalasia (spastic achalasia) is characterized by premature or spastic contractions in the distal esophagus along with impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). On manometry, it shows very high distal contractile integral (DCI) values, often greater than 450 mmHg·s·cm, indicating strong spastic contractions. Although panesophageal pressurization can be seen, the distinguishing feature of Type 3 achalasia is the presence of abnormal spastic contractions with preserved or excessive contractile activity in the esophageal body. Other options are less consistent with the findings: 1. Type 1 achalasia : Minimal contractility and no significant pressurization (classic achalasia). 2. Type 2 achalasia : Panesophageal pressurization but without strong distal contractions. 3. Jackhammer esophagus: Shows extremely strong contractions but normal LES relaxation, unlike achalasia. Therefore, the findings of high contractile integrity with panesophageal pressurization are most consistent with Type 3 achalasia (spastic achalasia). 113. questions.stem: Which of the following is not a component of the Thoracoscore?
questions.explanation: Genetics The Thoracoscore is a multivariate logistic regression model designed to predict the risk of in-hospital mortality after general thoracic surgery. It incorporates several pre-operative and intra-operative variables to provide a patient- specific risk assessment. The key components of the Thoracoscore include patient-related factors such as age, sex, ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) physical status classification, and performance status (e.g., dyspnea score). It also includes procedure-related factors, such as the diagnosis (malignant vs. benign), the type of surgery performed, and the priority of the surgery (elective vs. emergency). The model uses these variables to calculate a predicted mortality risk. Genetic factors or specific gene mutations are not components of the Thoracoscore model.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly describes a retrosternal goiter?

options.text: All patients should undergo CT chest
All patients require a median sternotomy
It receives blood supply from thoracic vessels
Majority of retrosternal goiters should be operated on immediately

questions.explanation: All patients should undergo CT chest A retrosternal (or substernal) goiter is defined as a thyroid gland that has a significant portion (>50%) of its mass located below the thoracic inlet. The most accurate statement regarding its management is that all patients should undergo a CT scan of the neck and chest. A CT scan is the imaging modality of choice to precisely define the extent of the goiter's descent into the mediastinum, delineate its relationship to adjacent vital structures (trachea, esophagus, great vessels), and assess the degree of tracheal compression or deviation, which is crucial for operative planning. Statement B is false; over 90% of retrocessional goiters can be safely removed through a standard cervical (neck) incision without requiring a sternotomy. Statement C is false; the vast majority of retrocessional goiters maintain their blood supply from the cervical vessels (superior and inferior thyroid arteries). Statement D is also generally false; surgery is usually performed electively.

questions.stem: Which of the following components is not part of the primary survey?
questions.explanation: CECT to look for bleeding The primary survey in trauma management, as outlined by the Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) protocol, is a rapid, systematic assessment designed to identify and immediately treat life- threatening injuries. It follows the mnemonic ABCDE : A : Airway maintenance with cervical spine protection. B : Breathing and ventilation. C : Circulation with hemorrhage control (this includes assessing pulse and recording BP). D : Disability (neurological status, e.g., GCS). E : Exposure and Environmental control (undressing the patient completely to allow for a thorough examination). These steps are performed rapidly at the bedside. A Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography (CECT) scan is a time-consuming diagnostic imaging study. It is part of the secondary survey, which is a more detailed, head-to-toe examination performed only after the primary survey is complete and the patient has been resuscitated and is hemodynamically stable.

questions.stem: What is the most frequent site of gastrinoma occurrence in patients with MEN- syndrome?
questions.explanation: Duodenum Gastrinomas are neuroendocrine tumors that secrete excess gastrin, leading to Zollinger- Ellison syndrome. They can occur sporadically or as part of the Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN-1) syndrome. While it was once thought that most gastrinomas were pancreatic in origin, it is now established that the vast majority, both sporadic and MEN-1 associated, arise in the duodenum, particularly in the first and second portions. It is estimated that 70- 90% of all gastrinomas are located within the gastrinoma triangle, an area defined by the junction of the cystic and common bile ducts, the second and third portions of the duodenum, and the junction of the neck and body of the pancreas. Within this triangle, the duodenal wall is the single most common site of origin. MEN- 1 associated gastrinomas are often multiple and are almost always found within the duodenum.

questions.stem: A patient presents with precancerous lesions, abdominal distension, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. On examination, enlarged lymph nodes are noted. Which carcinoma is most likely associated with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Carcinoma of the Penis The clinical picture described points towards carcinoma of the penis. Precancerous lesions on the penis, such as erythroplasia of Queyrat or Bowen's disease (carcinoma in situ), are known precursors to invasive squamous cell carcinoma, the most common type of penile cancer. The primary tumor on the penis can then metastasize via the lymphatic system. The first site of lymphatic drainage from the skin and glans of the penis is to the superficial and deep inguinal lymph nodes. Therefore, the presence of inguinal lymphadenopathy in a patient with a penile lesion is highly suggestive of metastatic spread. The abdominal swelling could be related to more advanced disease with involvement of pelvic or retroperitoneal lymph nodes. In contrast, testicular cancer metastasizes primarily to the retroperitoneal lymph nodes, and prostate cancer spreads to the pelvic nodes initially, not typically causing inguinal adenopathy. questions.stem: What is the T stage of a lung carcinoma measuring . cm that does not involve the pleura?
questions.explanation: T1c The T stage in lung cancer is determined by the size of the primary tumor and whether it has invaded nearby structures. According to the 8th edition of the AJCC (American Joint Committee on Cancer) staging manual, the T1 category is for tumors that are 3 cm or less in their greatest dimension and do not have other invasive features (like invading the main bronchus or visceral pleura). The T1 category is further subdivided by size : T1a : Tumor is 1 cm or less. T1b : Tumor is greater than 1 cm but 2 cm or less. T1c : Tumor is greater than 2 cm but 3 cm or less. Since the carcinoma in question is 2.5 cm and is not involving the pleura, it falls squarely into the T1c category.

questions.stem: A middle-aged man presents with a neck swelling that has been present since childhood. The overlying skin is disrupted, and the lesion has a bag- or worm-like appearance with a central black spot. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lymphangioma The patient presents with a long-standing neck swelling since childhood, which is an important clue for a congenital lesion. Lymphangiomas are benign malformations of lymphatic vessels that commonly appear in infancy or childhood, particularly in the neck region. A common type occurring in the neck is cystic hygroma. The description of the swelling as “bag- like” or “worm-like” with a central black spot and disrupted skin suggests multiple dilated lymphatic channels near the skin surface, which may appear as vesicle-like or cystic structures. These lesions are typically soft, compressible, and may transilluminate due to their lymphatic fluid content. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Cirsoid aneurysm: A vascular malformation involving arteries, usually seen on the scalp with pulsations and bruit. 2. Varicocele: Dilated veins of the pampiniform plexus in the scrotum, not the neck. questions.stem: A young man suffers a motorbike accident resulting in injury to the ileum and jejunum, requiring resection of the entire ileum and part of the jejunum. Which condition is he most likely to develop as a consequence?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency The small intestine is responsible for the absorption of most nutrients, but specific sites are responsible for absorbing specific substances. The terminal ileum is the sole site for the absorption of two crucial substances : Vitamin B12 (bound to intrinsic factor) and bile acids. In this patient, the entire ileum has been resected. This surgical removal eliminates the body's ability to absorb dietary Vitamin B12. The body has significant hepatic stores of Vitamin B12, so a clinical deficiency may not become apparent for several years. However, the patient will inevitably develop a Vitamin B12 deficiency over time, leading to megaloblastic anemia and potentially irreversible neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration of the cord) if not recognized and treated with parenteral B12 injections. The patient is also at risk for fat malabsorption and diarrhea due to the loss of bile acid reabsorption.

questions.stem: A patient develops epigastric pain after a heavy meal, with tenderness and rigidity in the upper abdomen. An X-ray reveals pneumomediastinum. What is the most likely underlying cause?

questions.explanation: Spontaneous esophageal rupture The clinical scenario described is classic for Boerhaave syndrome, which is a spontaneous, full-thickness rupture of the esophagus. This typically occurs after an episode of forceful vomiting or retching (often after a heavy meal or alcohol binge), which causes a sudden, massive increase in intra esophageal pressure. The rupture most commonly occurs in the posterolateral aspect of the distal esophagus. The rupture allows air, gastric contents, and oral flora to escape into the mediastinum, leading to chemical mediastinitis. The key radiological finding is pneumomediastinum (air in the mediastinum), which may be seen on a chest X-ray. The clinical presentation includes severe retrosternal or epigastric pain, tenderness, and sometimes subcutaneous emphysema. This is a surgical emergency with a high mortality rate. questions.stem: A man intoxicated with alcohol falls into a manhole and sustains a perineal injury, followed by swelling of the scrotum and upper thigh, blood at the urethral meatus, and difficulty in passing urine. What is the most likely associated injury in this case?
questions.explanation: Bulbar urethra injury This is a classic presentation of an anterior urethral injury, specifically a rupture of the bulbar urethra. The mechanism described, a straddle injury where the perineum is forcefully struck, is the most common cause of this injury. The bulbar urethra is fixed to the perineal membrane and is crushed against the inferior pubic arch. The clinical signs are pathognomonic : blood at the urethral meatus, a perineal hematoma, and an inability or difficulty in passing urine. The swelling of the scrotum and upper thigh is due to the extravasation of urine and blood into the superficial perineal space, which is limited by Colles' fascia. This extravasated fluid can track up onto the anterior abdominal wall but is confined to the penis and scrotum inferiorly. Membranous urethral injuries are associated with pelvic fractures.

questions.stem: A patient with carcinoma of the bladder presents with breathlessness, clinical features of deep vein thrombosis, and tachycardia. According to the Wells score, what is the patient’s risk category for developing pulmonary embolism?
questions.explanation: High The Wells score is a clinical prediction rule used to estimate the pre-test probability of pulmonary embolism (PE). Points are assigned for various clinical findings : Clinical signs and symptoms of DVT : +3 points (present in this patient) PE is the #1 diagnosis OR equally likely : +3 points Heart rate > 100 bpm : +1.5 points (Tachycardia is present) Immobilization or surgery in the previous 4 weeks : +1.5 points Previous DVT/PE : +1.5 points Hemoptysis : +1 point Malignancy (on treatment, treated in last 6 months, or palliative) : +1 point (Carcinoma of the bladder is present) This patient has at least 3 points for DVT signs, 1.5 for tachycardia, and 1 for malignancy, for a total of at least 5.5 points. According to the standard interpretation of the Wells score, a score greater than 6 indicates a high clinical probability of PE. Even with a score of 5.5, the probability is at least moderate to high, and further investigation is mandatory.

questions.stem: Four months after undergoing a renal transplant, which infection is the patient most likely to develop?
questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) The risk of specific opportunistic infections after solid organ transplantation follows a typical timeline based on the patient's net state of immunosuppression. The period from 1 to 6 months post-transplant is the time of maximal immunosuppression and is when opportunistic viral infections are most common. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the single most important and frequent pathogen during this window. CMV infection can arise from reactivation of latent virus in the recipient, or more commonly, as a primary infection from a CMV-positive donor organ transplanted into a CMV-negative recipient. It can cause a wide spectrum of disease, from a mononucleosis-like syndrome to invasive tissue disease affecting the lungs, GI tract, and the allograft itself. Fungal infections like Candida and Aspergillus typically occur in the first month, while late infections (>6 months) are more often community-acquired pathogens or related to PTLD (driven by EBV). 122. questions.stem: A patient planned for elective inguinal hernia repair has a past history of myocardial infarction and has undergone coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). What is the most appropriate preoperative evaluation for this patient?

options.text: History + c/e + routine labs + angiography to look for stent patency
History + c/e + routine labs + stress test

questions.explanation: History + c/e + routine labs The key to this question is that the patient has a history of coronary artery disease but has already undergone definitive re vascularization with CABG. For a patient undergoing a low- to-intermediate risk elective surgery (like an inguinal hernia repair), if they have no current cardiac symptoms (e.g., no angina, no dyspnea) and have good functional capacity, the previous re vascularization is considered protective. According to major preoperative cardiac assessment guidelines (e.g., from the ACC/AHA), in such a patient who is asymptomatic with good functional status, no further cardiac testing is required before the elective non-cardiac surgery. Therefore, a thorough history and clinical examination (c/e) to confirm the absence of symptoms, along with routine preoperative labs (including an ECG), is sufficient. Invasive tests like angiography or non-invasive stress tests are not indicated unless the patient has developed new symptoms suggesting ischemia.

questions.stem: A patient arrives with a stab wound to the right lower chest and is found to have hypotension and bradycardia, both of which respond to intravenous fluid resuscitation. After stabilization, the blood pressure returns to normal, and a chest X-ray reveals no abnormalities in the lung fields. What should be the next appropriate management step?
questions.explanation: eFAST The patient has a penetrating injury (stab wound) to the right lower chest with initial hypotension and bradycardia, which improved after intravenous fluid resuscitation, indicating that the patient is now hemodynamically stabilized. In trauma evaluation, the next immediate step after initial stabilization is to rapidly assess for internal bleeding or organ injury. The eFAST (Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) is a bedside ultrasound examination used in trauma patients to quickly detect: 1. Hemoperitoneum (blood in the abdominal cavity) 2. Hemothorax 3. Pneumothorax 4. Pericardial tamponade Since the chest X-ray shows normal lung fields, obvious pneumothorax or hemothorax is unlikely. However, a right lower chest stab wound can injure the liver, diaphragm, or cause intra-abdominal bleeding, which may not be visible on X-ray. NODIA

questions.stem: In a patient who has undergone surgery for a parathyroid adenoma, what postoperative finding or test is used to confirm that the diseased parathyroid gland has been successfully and correctly removed?
questions.explanation: 50% reduction in PTH after 10 minutes During a minimally invasive parathyroidectomy for a single adenoma, it is crucial to confirm that the hypersecreting gland has been successfully removed before concluding the operation. This is done using an intraoperative parathyroid hormone (IOPTH) assay. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) has a very short half-life of only 3 to 5 minutes. This property allows for a rapid assessment of surgical success. A baseline PTH level is drawn before the adenoma is excised. After the suspected adenoma is removed, another blood sample is drawn, typically at 5 minutes and 10 minutes post-excision. The most widely accepted criterion for a successful parathyroidectomy (known as the Miami criterion) is a greater than 50% reduction in the PTH level from the highest pre-excision baseline level at the 10-minute post-excision sample. A successful drop confirms that the source of the excess PTH has been removed.

questions.stem: What type of flap is most commonly utilized for breast reconstruction procedures?

options.text: DIEP based on deep inferior epigastric vessels
TRAM based on superior gluteal vessels
Gluteal flap based on thoracodorsal artery
Latissimus dorsi flap based on the inferior epigastric artery

questions.explanation: DIEP based on deep inferior epigastric vessels Autologous breast reconstruction uses the patient's own tissue to create a new breast mound. One of the most advanced and commonly used techniques is the Deep Inferior Epigastric Perforator (DIEP) flap. This is a free flap procedure where a segment of skin and subcutaneous fat from the lower abdomen is harvested to create the breast. The key to this flap is its blood supply, which is based on one or more perforating arteries that arise from the deep inferior epigastric artery and vein. The vessels are carefully dissected and then microsurgically anastomosed to recipient vessels in the chest (e.g., the internal mammary artery). The DIEP flap is considered a muscle-sparing flap because it does not sacrifice the rectus abdominis muscle, unlike the older TRAM flap, leading to less abdominal wall morbidity. The other options incorrectly match the flap with its blood supply.

questions.stem: What is the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasm?
questions.explanation: Insulinoma Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs) are rare tumors that can be functional (hormone- secreting) or non-functional. Among the functional PNETs, the most common type is the insulinoma. Insulinomas are tumors of the pancreatic beta cells that autonomously secrete excessive amounts of insulin. This leads to inappropriate hyperinsulinemia, which causes recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia, particularly during fasting or after exercise. The clinical presentation is characterized by Whipple's triad : symptoms of hypoglycemia (e.g., confusion, sweating, palpitations), a documented low plasma glucose level during the episode, and relief of symptoms upon administration of glucose. The vast majority (>90%) of insulinomas are benign and solitary. Gastrinomas are the second most common functional PNET, but they are more often located in the duodenum than the pancreas itself.

questions.stem: An elderly man presents with a long-standing facial mole that has recently enlarged and developed irregular margins. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lentigo maligna The clinical description of a long-standing pigmented lesion on the chronically sun- exposed skin of an elderly individual (the face) that is now showing changes (increasing size, irregular borders) is the classic presentation of lentigo maligna melanoma. This type of melanoma begins as an in-situ lesion known as lentigo maligna, which is a slow-growing, flat, irregularly pigmented macule. It can remain in this horizontal growth phase for many years. When it progresses and invades the dermis, it becomes a lentigo maligna melanoma. The key features are its location on sun-damaged skin, its occurrence in the elderly, and its long history of slow evolution. Superficial spreading melanoma is the most common type overall but is less specifically tied to chronic sun exposure on the face. Nodular melanoma has a rapid vertical growth phase from the outset.

questions.stem: The CEAP score is used to indicate which of the following?
questions.explanation: Venous disorders The CEAP classification is used to evaluate and categorize chronic venous disorders. CEAP stands for: C – Clinical classification E – Etiology A – Anatomy P – Pathophysiology It is primarily applied in patients with chronic venous insufficiency, varicose veins, venous ulcers, and other venous abnormalities. Clinical classification ranges from: C0 – No visible signs C1 – Telangiectasia or reticular veins C2 – Varicose veins C3 – Edema C4 – Skin changes (pigmentation, eczema) C5 – Healed venous ulcer C6 – Active venous ulcer The CEAP system helps guide diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognosis in venous disease. It is not used for arterial, neurological, or trauma-related conditions. Therefore, the correct answer is : (B) Venous disorders 137. Post-mastectomy radiation therapy (PMRT) is recommended when four or more axillary lymph nodes are positive, as this significantly reduces the risk of local recurrence and improves overall survival. It may also be considered in selected patients with 1–3 positive nodes depending on other risk factors. 1. Option (C) is incorrect because tamoxifen is beneficial in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women with hormone receptor–positive breast cancer. 3. The triangle outlined in the image is the gastrinoma triangle, also known as Passaro's triangle. This is an anatomical region in the abdomen where the vast majority (>80%) of gastrinomas (tumors that cause Zollinger- Ellison syndrome) are located. The boundaries of this triangle are classically defined as : Superiorly : The junction of the cystic duct and the common bile duct. Inferiorly : The junction of the second and third portions of the duodenum.

questions.stem: Identify the blade shown in the image.
questions.explanation: Blade no. 11 The image displays a standard surgical scalpel blade. This particular blade is characterized by its triangular shape and a long, sharply pointed tip with a cutting edge along one side. This is the characteristic design of a No. 11 surgical blade. The sharp, pointed tip makes it ideal for making precise stab incisions and for incising and draining abscesses. It is also used for delicate procedures that require a sharp, pointed entry, such as inserting chest drains or performing arthroscopy. The other common blades have different shapes for different purposes : the No. 10 blade has a large curved cutting edge for making large skin incisions, the No. 15 blade is a smaller version of the No. 10 for more delicate incisions, and the No. 12 blade is a small, crescent-shaped blade used in specific situations like tonsillectomy.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not form a boundary of the area depicted in the image?
questions.explanation: Gall bladder The image depicts the cystohepatic triangle, more commonly known as Calot's triangle. This is a crucial anatomical space in the porta hepatis that surgeons must carefully identify during a cholecystectomy to avoid iatrogenic injury to vital structures. The boundaries of this triangle are classically defined as : Medially : The common hepatic duct. Laterally : The cystic duct. Superiorly : The inferior surface (or edge) of the liver. The cystic artery, a branch of the right hepatic artery, is a key content that traverses this triangle and must be identified and ligated. The gallbladder itself lies within the fossa on the inferior surface of the liver, adjacent to the triangle, but it is not a boundary of the triangle. Therefore, the gallbladder is the structure listed that is not a formal boundary of Calot's triangle.

questions.stem: The most common type of gallstone is :
questions.explanation: Pure cholesterol stones Gallstones are classified into three main types: cholesterol stones, pigment stones, and mixed stones. The most common type worldwide is cholesterol stones, particularly in Western populations. These stones are primarily composed of cholesterol monohydrate crystals and form when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol. Factors that predispose to cholesterol stone formation include obesity, female sex, multiparity, advancing age, rapid weight loss, and estrogen exposure. Pure cholesterol stones are typically yellowish and radiolucent on X-ray. Although mixed stones (containing cholesterol along with calcium salts and bile pigments) are also common, they are generally considered variants of cholesterol stones. Pigment stones (including calcium bilirubinate stones) are more common in patients with chronic hemolysis, biliary infection, or cirrhosis and are less common overall compared to cholesterol stones.

questions.stem: What is the most frequent reason for performing liver transplantation in pediatric patients?
questions.explanation: Biliary atresia The indications for liver transplantation in children differ from those in adults. In the pediatric population, the single most common indication for liver transplantation worldwide is biliary atresia. Biliary atresia is a rare neonatal liver disease characterized by the progressive, idiopathic fibrotic obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts. This leads to a complete obstruction of bile flow, resulting in cholestatic jaundice, cirrhosis, and ultimately end-stage liver failure. While the initial surgical management is a Kasai portoenterostomy to attempt to restore bile flow, this procedure is not curative for many patients. The progressive liver damage and development of portal hypertension often continue, and liver transplantation is ultimately required for long-term survival. Biliary atresia accounts for approximately half of all pediatric liver transplants.

questions.stem: Omphalocele is caused by :

options.text: Abnormal rotation of the intestinal loop
Failure of gut to return to the body cavity from its physiological herniation
Reversed rotation of the intestinal loop

questions.explanation: Failure of gut to return to the body cavity from its physiological herniation An omphalocele is a congenital ventral abdominal wall defect characterized by the herniation of abdominal viscera through the umbilical ring. The herniated organs are covered by a protective sac composed of the amnion, Wharton's jelly, and the peritoneum. The underlying embryological cause of an omphalocele is the failure of the midgut to return to the abdominal cavity after its normal physiological herniation. During early fetal development (around the 6th week of gestation), the midgut grows rapidly and herniates out into the umbilical cord. This is a normal process. The gut then rotates and should return completely to the abdominal cavity by the 10th-12th week. An omphalocele occurs when this return fails to happen, leaving some of the abdominal organs (most commonly the liver and intestines) outside the abdominal cavity, contained within the umbilical cord sac.

questions.stem: What is the most frequent cause of chronic pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Chronic alcohol Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disease of the pancreas characterized by irreversible destruction of the pancreatic parenchyma, fibrosis, and loss of both exocrine and endocrine function. While there are numerous causes, the most common etiology by a significant margin in the Western world and many other parts of the globe is chronic and heavy alcohol consumption. Alcohol abuse is responsible for approximately 70-80% of all cases of chronic pancreatitis. Alcohol is believed to be directly toxic to pancreatic acinar cells and to alter the composition of pancreatic secretions, leading to the formation of protein plugs that obstruct small pancreatic ducts. This obstruction and direct toxicity initiate a cycle of inflammation and fibrosis that eventually destroys the gland. Gallstones are the most common cause of acute pancreatitis, but not chronic. Pancreatic calculi are a consequence, not a primary cause. Pancreas divisum is a congenital anomaly that is a less common cause.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about keloid is true?

options.text: Extended excision is the treatment of choice
It does not extend beyond the wound

questions.explanation: It contains growth factor A keloid is a type of abnormal scar that results from an overgrowth of dense fibrous tissue, developing after a skin injury heals. Unlike a hypertrophic scar, a keloid characteristically extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound. This uncontrolled proliferation is driven by a dysregulation in the wound healing process, involving an overproduction of extracellular matrix components, particularly collagen. A key factor in this pathogenesis is the excessive production of various growth factors, most notably Transforming Growth Factor- beta (TGF- β) and Platelet-Derived Growth Factor (PDGF). These growth factors stimulate fibroblasts to proliferate and synthesize collagen at an abnormally high rate, leading to the formation of the large, raised scar tissue. Statement (C) is incorrect, as extending beyond the wound margin is the defining feature of a keloid. Simple wide excision (B) is not the treatment of choice as it is associated with an extremely high recurrence rate, often resulting in an even larger keloid. Treatment is challenging and usually involves a combination of therapies like intralesional steroid injections, cryotherapy, or excision with adjuvant radiation.

questions.stem: Which nerve is thickened in the image shown?
questions.explanation: Greater auricular nerve The image shows marked thickening of a nerve in the head and neck region, a classic sign of leprosy (Hansen's disease). The nerve shown is the greater auricular nerve. This is a sensory nerve that arises from the cervical plexus (C2, C3) and ascends vertically over the sternocleidomastoid muscle towards the ear. It supplies sensation to the skin over the angle of the jaw, the parotid gland, and a large part of the auricle (ear). NODIA

questions.stem: Bell’s palsy is caused by a lesion involving which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: 7th cranial nerve Bell's palsy is the most common cause of acute, unilateral facial paralysis. It is an idiopathic, lower motor neuron paralysis of the seventh cranial nerve (the facial nerve). The facial nerve controls the muscles of facial expression on one side of the face. In Bell's palsy, inflammation and swelling of the nerve as it passes through its narrow bony canal in the temporal bone (the facial canal) leads to nerve compression and dysfunction. This results in the sudden onset of unilateral weakness or paralysis of all the muscles of facial expression. Clinical features include an inability to raise the eyebrow, inability to close the eye completely (lagophthalmos), drooping of the corner of the mouth, and disappearance of the nasolabial fold on the affected side. The cause is thought to be a reactivation of a latent viral infection, most commonly Herpes Simplex Virus.

questions.stem: Cushing's ulcer is seen in cases of :
questions.explanation: Head injury A Cushing's ulcer is a specific type of acute stress ulcer that occurs in the stomach or duodenum of patients who have sustained a severe intracranial injury, such as a traumatic head injury, brain tumor, or intracranial hemorrhage. The pathophysiology is thought to be related to direct stimulation of the vagal nuclei in the brainstem due to increased intracranial pressure. This vagal stimulation leads to hypersecretion of gastric acid (hyperchlorhydria), which then overwhelms the protective mucosal defenses and causes deep, often perforating ulcers. These ulcers are typically single and are most common in the stomach, duodenum, or esophagus. This is in contrast to a Curling's ulcer, which is another type of stress ulcer that is seen in patients with severe burns (A) and is caused by hypovolemia and mucosal ischemia.

questions.stem: What is the first-line treatment of mastitis in a lactating mother?
questions.explanation: Cloxacillin Lactational mastitis is an infection of the breast tissue that commonly occurs in breastfeeding women, usually within the first few weeks postpartum. The most frequent causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus, which enters through cracks or fissures in the nipple. Cloxacillin is a penicillinase-resistant penicillin and is considered the first-line treatment for uncomplicated lactational mastitis. It is effective against penicillinase- producing Staphylococcus aureus, the most common pathogen involved. The typical course is 10–14 days, along with continued breastfeeding or milk expression to prevent milk stasis. Supportive measures such as warm compresses, adequate hydration, and analgesics are also recommended. Cefazolin is usually reserved for intravenous use in severe cases. Ceftriaxone is a broad- spectrum antibiotic and not routinely required. Ampicillin is not reliable against penicillinase- producing staphylococci. Thus, for a lactating mother with mastitis, the first-line treatment is cloxacillin.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a bourdary of the calot's triangle ?
questions.explanation: Gall bladder Calot’s triangle (also called the cystohepatic triangle) is an important anatomical landmark in hepatobiliary surgery, especially during cholecystectomy. The classical boundaries of Calot’s triangle are: 1. Medial – Common hepatic duct 2. Inferior (lateral) – Cystic duct 3. Superior – Inferior surface of the liver The cystic artery usually passes through this triangle, making it a key structure to identify during surgery to avoid bile duct injury. The gallbladder itself is not a boundary of Calot’s triangle. Although it is anatomically related to the region, it does not form one of the defined borders of the triangle. Therefore, among the given options, the structure that is not a boundary of Calot’s triangle is : (D) Gall bladder

questions.stem: Estimate the amount of Ringer’s lactate required during the first hours for a 0-kg male patient with 0% second-degree burns.
questions.explanation: 4 liters Fluid resuscitation in burn patients is calculated using the Parkland formula, which is: 4 mL × body weight (kg) × % Total Body Surface Area (TBSA) burned For this patient: 4 mL × 50 kg × 40 = 8000 mL (8 litres) in the first 24 hours. According to the Parkland protocol: Half of the total fluid is given in the first 8 hours (from the time of burn injury). The remaining half is administered over the next 16 hours. So, half of 8 litres = 4 litres in the first 8 hours. Therefore, the correct answer is (B) 4 litres. Urine output (target: 0.5–1 mL/kg/hour in adults) is closely monitored to adjust fluid therapy. Adequate resuscitation is essential to prevent burn shock and maintain organ perfusion. 159. In which condition is the Ankle–Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) falsely elevated? NODIA

questions.stem: Which factor is not included in the Van Nuys Prognostic Index (VNPI)?
questions.explanation: Estrogen receptor (ER) status The Van Nuys Prognostic Index (VNPI) is a scoring system used to assess the risk of local recurrence in patients with ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and to guide treatment decisions (e.g., excision alone, excision with radiotherapy, or mastectomy). The VNPI includes the following factors: 1. Tumor size 2. Margin width (surgical margin status) 3. Pathological classification — specifically nuclear grade and presence of comedo necrosis 4. (In the modified VNPI) Age Each factor is scored, and the total score determines the recommended management strategy. Estrogen receptor (ER) status is important for deciding hormonal therapy (such as tamoxifen) but is not part of the VNPI scoring system. Therefore, the factor not included in the Van Nuys Prognostic Index is (C) Estrogen receptor (ER) status.

questions.stem: Identify the condition shown in the image.
questions.explanation: Lobar Pneumonia The image displays the gross pathological appearance of a lung affected by lobar pneumonia. This pattern of pneumonia is characterized by the inflammation and consolidation of a large, continuous area involving a significant portion or an entire lobe of a lung. The image shows the stage of red hepatization, which typically occurs in the first few days of the infection. In this stage, the affected lobe is heavy, airless, and has a consistency resembling that of a liver (hence hepatization). The reddish-brown color is due to massive congestion of the capillaries and the exudation of red blood cells, neutrophils, and fibrin into the alveolar spaces. The most common cause of classic lobar pneumonia is Streptococcus pneumoniae. In contrast, bronchopneumonia is characterized by

questions.stem: When a mother donates a kidney to her son, this type of transplant is referred to as what?
questions.explanation: Allograft Transplants are classified based on the genetic relationship between the donor and the recipient. An allograft, or allogeneic transplant, is the transplantation of cells, tissues, or organs between two genetically non-identical individuals of the same species. A kidney transplant from a mother to her son falls into this category. Since the mother and son are not genetically identical (the son inherits half of his genes from his mother and half from his father), their human leukocyte antigens (HLA) will be different. This genetic disparity means the son's immune system will recognize the mother's kidney as foreign and will mount an immune response to reject it. Therefore, allograft transplantation requires lifelong immunosuppressive medication to prevent rejection. An isograft (A) is between identical twins. An autograft (C) is tissue from the same individual. A xenograft (D) is a transplant between different species.

questions.stem: The uvula vesicae is formed by enlargement of which lobe of the prostate?
questions.explanation: Median lobe The uvula vesicae is a small, rounded eminence located on the floor of the urinary bladder, situated just behind the internal urethral orifice. This structure is formed by the underlying median lobe of the prostate gland. The prostate is classically described as having five lobes : anterior, posterior, median, and two lateral lobes. The median lobe is located between the two ejaculatory ducts and the urethra. In benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), the median lobe is often one of the first and most significantly affected lobes. Its enlargement causes it to project upward into the floor of the bladder, creating the prominent uvula vesicae. This can act like a ball valve, contributing significantly to the symptoms of bladder outlet obstruction by blocking the internal urethral orifice.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Barrett’s esophagus is not correct?
questions.explanation: Paraesophageal hernia Barrett's esophagus is a condition where the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus is replaced by a specialized columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. This is an example of metaplasia (D), which occurs as a protective adaptation to chronic injury from gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). This metaplastic tissue is prone to developing complications. It can become eroded by acid, leading to the formation of a Barrett's ulcer, a type of peptic ulcer (B). Most importantly, Barrett's esophagus is the single most important risk factor for the development of esophageal adenocarcinoma (A); the metaplastic tissue can progress through stages of dysplasia to invasive cancer. In contrast, a paraesophageal hernia is a type of hiatal hernia where a portion of the gastric fundus herniates into the chest alongside the esophagus. While sliding hiatal hernias are strongly associated with GERD and therefore Barrett's, a paraesophageal hernia is a different anatomical entity and is not a direct feature or consequence of Barrett's esophagus itself. 152. Parathyroid autoimplantation is performed into which muscle? (A) Biceps (B) Triceps NODIA

questions.stem: Which tissue layers are incised during a fasciotomy?

options.text: Skin + subcutaneous tissue + superficial fascia + deep fascia

questions.explanation: Skin + subcutaneous tissue + superficial fascia + deep fascia A fasciotomy is an emergency surgical procedure performed to treat acute compartment syndrome. Compartment syndrome occurs when increased pressure within a confined fascial compartment compromises the circulation and function of the tissues within that space, potentially leading to muscle and nerve necrosis. The goal of the procedure is to relieve this pressure by decompressing the affected compartment(s). To achieve this, the surgeon must make an incision through all the layers that are confining the swollen muscle. This involves making a long incision through the skin, followed by the underlying subcutaneous tissue and the superficial fascia. The most critical step is then to incise the tough, inelastic deep fascia that encases the muscle compartment. This final incision allows the swollen muscle to bulge out, immediately relieving the intra compartmental pressure and restoring blood flow. Merely incising the skin and subcutaneous layers would be insufficient to decompress the muscle compartment, which is the primary goal of the procedure.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Crohn’s disease is not true?
questions.explanation: Continuous lesion visualized in endoscopy Crohn's disease is a type of inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus. One of its hallmark features is the discontinuous nature of the inflammation, which is described as skip lesions. This means there are areas of active inflammation separated by segments of normal-appearing mucosa. Therefore, the statement that a continuous lesion is visualized on endoscopy is not true and is, in fact, the characteristic pattern of ulcerative colitis, where inflammation typically starts in the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous and circumferential manner. In Crohn's disease, the rectum is often spared (A). Histological examination frequently reveals non-caseating granulomas (C), another hallmark of the disease. The combination of deep linear ulcers and transmural inflammation with submucosal edema creates a nodular appearance of the mucosa on endoscopy or barium studies, which is described as a cobblestone appearance (D).

EUS involves passing an endoscope with a high- frequency ultrasound transducer at its tip into the stomach and duodenum. This allows for high-resolution imaging of the pancreas from a very close proximity, without interference from bowel gas. questions.stem: In congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which method best demonstrates the abdominal mass?
questions.explanation: In palpation over the epigastrium In congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS), the classical clinical finding is a palpable “olive-shaped” mass. This mass represents the hypertrophied pylorus. The mass is best felt in the epigastric region, slightly to the right of the midline. It is typically palpated by gently examining the upper abdomen when the infant is calm and relaxed. Sometimes, it is easier to feel after the baby has vomited, when the stomach is empty. Although the pyloric mass lies anatomically toward the right side, it is most accurately described as being palpable in the epigastrium, not the left hypochondrium or right iliac fossa. Feeding may make the pyloric peristaltic waves more visible, but palpation over the epigastrium remains the best method to demonstrate the mass. Therefore, the correct answer is (A) In palpation over the epigastrium.

questions.stem: Determine the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score for a 5-year-old head-injury patient who is confused, opens eyes to pain, and localizes pain.
questions.explanation: 11 The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a neurological scale used to assess a person's level of consciousness after a brain injury. It is scored out of 15 and has three components : Eye Opening, Verbal Response, and Motor Response. 1. Eye Opening (E) : The patient opens their eyes in response to pain. This corresponds to a score of 2. (Spontaneous=4, To speech=3, To pain=2, None=1). 2. Verbal Response (V) : The patient is confused. This means they are able to speak in sentences but are disoriented. This corresponds to a score of 4. (Oriented=5, Confused=4, Inappropriate words=3, Incomprehensible sounds=2, None=1). 3. Motor Response (M) : The patient localizes pain. This means they make a purposeful movement towards a painful stimulus. This corresponds to a score of 5. (Obeys commands=6, Localizes pain=5, Withdraws from pain=4, Flexion to pain=3, Extension to pain=2, None=1). The total GCS score is the sum of the scores from the three components : Total GCS = E + V + M = 2 + 4 + 5 = 11.

questions.stem: The RET proto-oncogene is linked to the development of which condition?
questions.explanation: Medullary carcinoma thyroid The RET proto-oncogene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase that is crucial for the normal development of several cell types, including neuroendocrine cells. Germline activating mutations in the RET proto-oncogene are the underlying genetic cause of the Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2) syndromes, which include MEN 2A, MEN 2B, and Familial Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (FMTC). The hallmark and most common feature of all these syndromes is the development of Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC), a cancer of the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid. Nearly 100% of individuals with a germline RET mutation will develop MTC. Somatic (non-inherited) NODIA

questions.stem: Identify the organism related to the blood smear image.
questions.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum The image shows a peripheral blood smear with red blood cells infected by a malaria parasite. The specific features are diagnostic for Plasmodium falciparum. The key identifying characteristics of P. falciparum on a thin smear are : Multiple infections of a single red blood cell : It is common to see two or more small ring- form trophozoites within one RBC. Delicate, fine rings : The rings have a very thin cytoplasm. Appliqué or accole forms : The rings appear plastered against the edge of the red blood cell membrane. Double chromatin dots : Some rings may have two chromatin dots, giving them a headphones appearance. Absence of older stages : In falciparum malaria, typically only the early ring forms and gametocytes are seen in the peripheral blood, as the older trophozoites and schizonts are sequestered in the deep microvasculature. These features are all characteristic of P. falciparum, the most virulent species of human malaria parasite.

questions.stem: What is the minimum aneurysm size in an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) that warrants surgical intervention?
questions.explanation: 5.5 cm An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a localized dilation of the abdominal aorta. The primary risk associated with an AAA is rupture, which is a catastrophic event with a very high mortality rate. The risk of rupture is directly proportional to the maximum diameter of the aneurysm. For smaller aneurysms, the risk of rupture is low, and the risks of surgical repair outweigh the benefits. These patients are managed with surveillance (e.g., regular ultrasound monitoring). However, as the aneurysm grows, the rupture risk increases exponentially. Based on large clinical trials, the threshold at which the risk of rupture begins to exceed the risk of elective repair is an aneurysm diameter of 5.5 cm for men. Therefore, elective surgical repair (either open surgery or endovascular aneurysm repair - EVAR) is generally recommended for asymptomatic patients once the AAA reaches a diameter of 5.5 cm. The threshold may be slightly lower (e.g., 5.0 cm) for women.

questions.stem: A -week-old infant is brought by the mother with a history of vomiting. An abdominal X-ray reveals a single bubble appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) The single bubble sign on an abdominal X-ray in a vomiting infant represents a distended stomach with a relative paucity of gas in the intestines distal to it. This indicates an obstruction at the level of the gastric outlet. The classic cause for a gastric outlet obstruction in an infant of this age (3-6 weeks) with non-bilious projectile vomiting is Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS). The thickened pyloric muscle prevents gastric emptying, causing the stomach to become massively distended with air and fluid, creating the single bubble. In contrast, duodenal atresia (Option A) or an annular pancreas (Option B) would cause a more proximal duodenal obstruction, leading to the classic double bubble sign (one bubble in the stomach, one in the proximal duodenum). Jejunal atresia (D) would cause a more distal obstruction with multiple dilated loops of bowel.

questions.stem: A child presents with anemia, intellectual disability, bone pain, and hepatosplenomegaly. Bone marrow biopsy reveals cells with a characteristic crumpled tissue paper appearance. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: Glucocerebrosidase The clinical findings of hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and bone pain, combined with the pathognomonic finding of a cell with a crumpled tissue paper or wrinkled silk appearance in the bone marrow, are definitive for Gaucher disease. This characteristic cell is the Gaucher cell, a macrophage laden with undigested lipid. Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (also known as acid

questions.stem: A family pedigree shows several affected members with progressive limitation of eye movements, retinal pigmentary changes, and abnormalities of cardiac conduction. Considering these features and the pattern of inheritance, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kearns-Sayre Syndrome The pedigree chart displays a classic pattern of mitochondrial inheritance. The key feature is that the disease is transmitted exclusively from an affected mother to all of her offspring, while an affected father does not transmit the disease to any of his children. This is because mitochondria, and their unique DNA, are inherited almost exclusively from the mother's egg cell. The clinical triad of symptoms described— progressive external ophthalmoplegia (eye movement limitation), pigmentary retinopathy, and cardiac conduction defects (like heart block)—is the defining triad of Kearns-Sayre Syndrome (KSS). KSS is a mitochondrial myopathy caused by large-scale deletions in the mitochondrial DNA. Therefore, both the specific clinical features and the pattern of inheritance shown in the pedigree are diagnostic of Kearns- Sayre Syndrome. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (A) is X-linked recessive, Friedreich ataxia (C) is autosomal recessive, and myotonic dystrophy (D) is autosomal dominant.

questions.stem: A -year-old child presents to the emergency department with generalized convulsions following a high-grade fever. Which medication is most appropriate as the first-line treatment to control seizures in this acute febrile episode?
questions.explanation: Diazepam The patient is presenting with a febrile seizure. The immediate priority in managing any ongoing seizure (convulsion) is to terminate the seizure activity to prevent neurological injury and other complications. The first-line medications for the acute termination of a seizure, including a febrile seizure, are benzodiazepines. These drugs are fast-acting and highly effective. Diazepam is a classic choice and can be administered intravenously or, very commonly in the pediatric setting, rectally as a gel for rapid absorption. Other benzodiazepines like lorazepam (IV) or midazolam (intranasal, buccal, or IV) are also first-line options. Fosphenytoin (C) or phenytoin is a second-line agent used if the seizure does not respond to benzodiazepines. Valproate (B) is a maintenance antiepileptic drug and is not used for acute seizure termination. Antibiotics (D) would be used if a bacterial infection is the cause of the fever, but not for the seizure itself. NODIA

questions.stem: A mother brings her 4-year-old son with intellectual disability to the outpatient department. He has joint pain and exhibits compulsive self-mutilation by biting his fingers and lips, and his serum uric acid level is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome The combination of neurological dysfunction (intellectual disability, dystonia), compulsive self-injurious behavior (biting lips and fingers), and profound hyperuricemia (elevated uric acid) is the pathognomonic triad for Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. This is a rare, X-linked recessive disorder of purine metabolism caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT). This enzyme is part of the purine salvage pathway. Its absence leads to a massive overproduction of uric acid, causing gouty arthritis (joint pain), tophi, and kidney stones. The severe neurological and behavioral manifestations are a hallmark of the disease. Xanthine oxidase deficiency (B) causes hypouricemia. The other options are related to different metabolic pathways and do not fit this unique clinical picture.
