questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a long history of chronic alcohol consumption is admitted to the hospital after developing anxiety, tremors, and agitation approximately 24 hours after his last intake of alcohol. Which medication is most appropriate for managing and controlling his alcohol withdrawal symptoms?
questions.explanation: Lorazepam The patient is experiencing acute alcohol withdrawal syndrome. Chronic alcohol use enhances the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA and inhibits the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate. Sudden cessation leads to a state of CNS hyperexcitability, causing symptoms like anxiety, tremors, agitation, and potentially seizures or delirium tremens. The mainstay of treatment is to substitute a long-acting GABA-agonist to manage this hyperexcitability. Benzodiazepines, such as lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide, or diazepam, are the drugs of choice. They are cross-tolerant with alcohol and effectively suppress the symptoms of withdrawal. Lorazepam is often preferred in patients with liver disease as it is metabolized through glucuronidation, which is less affected by hepatic impairment. Fomepizole (Option B) is for toxic alcohol poisoning. Disulfiram (Option C) is for relapse prevention. Buspirone (Option D) is an anxiolytic not used for acute alcohol withdrawal.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding ciclesonide is not correct?

options.text: Oral candidiasis is common with its use.
It has fewer side effects than other inhalational corticosteroids.
It is a prodrug activated by bronchial esterase.
It has comparable efficacy to other inhalational corticosteroids.

questions.explanation: Oral candidiasis is common with its use. Ciclesonide is a unique inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) used for asthma management. It is administered as a prodrug that is largely inactive until it reaches the lower airways. There, it is converted by intracellular bronchial esterases into its active metabolite, des-ciclesonide (Statement C is correct). This site-specific activation is a key feature that leads to a very favorable safety profile, with fewer local and systemic side effects compared to conventional ICS (Statement B is correct). Because very little active drug is deposited in the oropharynx, the risk of local side effects like oral candidiasis (thrush) and dysphonia (hoarseness) is significantly lower, making Statement A incorrect. Clinical trials have shown that, when used at appropriate doses, ciclesonide has comparable efficacy to other ICS like fluticasone or budesonide in controlling asthma (Statement D is correct).

questions.stem: For what purpose is atropine added to diphenoxylate in fixed-dose combination preparations?

options.text: Atropine decreases the adverse effects of diphenoxylate

questions.explanation: To prevent abuse of diphenoxylate Diphenoxylate is an opioid agonist that acts on µ-receptors in the gastrointestinal tract to decrease motility, making it an effective antidiarrheal agent. However, because it is an opioid, at high doses, it can cross the blood-brain barrier and produce central effects, including euphoria, creating a potential for abuse and dependence. To mitigate this risk, diphenoxylate is formulated in combination with a subtherapeutic dose of atropine (e.g., in the product Lomotil). The small amount of atropine has negligible effects at the recommended therapeutic dose for diarrhea. However, if a person takes large quantities of the tablets in an attempt to achieve an opioid high, they will also ingest a significant dose of atropine, which will produce unpleasant anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention). This serves as a deterrent to prevent the abuse of diphenoxylate.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of burning sensation during urination along with purulent penile discharge. He gives a history of unprotected sexual intercourse with a new partner about two weeks prior to the onset of symptoms. On physical examination, the urethral meatus appears erythematous, and a thick purulent discharge is noted. Gram staining of the urethral discharge demonstrates intracellular Gram-negative diplococci. The patient is otherwise healthy and has no known drug allergies. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

options.text: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly

questions.explanation: Cefixime 400 mg orally The most appropriate treatment is (B) Cefixime 400 mg orally. The patient’s symptoms and, most importantly, the Gram stain showing intracellular gram-negative diplococci, are diagnostic for uncomplicated gonococcal urethritis (gonorrhea). The primary goal is to treat the confirmed Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Cefixime, a third-generation cephalosporin, is an effective oral therapy for gonorrhea. While the preferred first-line treatment is an intramuscular injection of Ceftriaxone (not an option here), Cefixime is a suitable alternative, making it the best choice from the list. The other medications are incorrect : Benzathine penicillin G is for syphilis, Metronidazole targets trichomoniasis, and Doxycycline is the primary treatment for chlamydia. It is important to note that because co-infection with chlamydia is very common, standard guidelines recommend adding a course of doxycycline to the cephalosporin to treat both potential infections simultaneously. However, Cefixime is the only option listed that effectively treats the confirmed diagnosis of gonorrhea.

questions.stem: A patient with HIV infection who is receiving antiretroviral therapy with zidovudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine is newly diagnosed with tuberculosis. In view of potential drug– drug interactions, which antitubercular drug should be modified or replaced in this patient?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin This question addresses a critical drug-drug interaction between anti-tuberculosis therapy (ATT) and antiretroviral therapy (ART). The patient is on an ART regimen containing nevirapine, which is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI). The key issue is with rifampicin, a cornerstone of standard TB treatment. Rifampicin is a potent inducer of the cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzyme system, particularly CYP3A4. Nevirapine is extensively metabolized by these same enzymes. When rifampicin and nevirapine are co-administered, rifampicin significantly accelerates the metabolism of nevirapine, leading to a drastic reduction in its plasma concentration. This can result in subtherapeutic levels of nevirapine, leading to virological failure and the development of HIV drug resistance. Therefore, in a patient on a nevirapine-based regimen, rifampicin must be avoided. It is typically replaced with a less potent enzyme inducer, such as rifabutin, or the ART regimen is switched to one that is not affected by rifampicin (e.g., an efavirenz or dolutegravir-based regimen).

questions.stem: Which medication is most commonly used for maintenance therapy in the management of opioid dependence or abuse?
questions.explanation: Buprenorphine Opioid maintenance therapy (OMT) is a long-term treatment strategy for opioid use disorder. It involves replacing the illicit opioid with a prescribed, long-acting opioid agonist or partial agonist to reduce cravings, prevent withdrawal symptoms, and block the euphoric effects of other opioids. The two most common medications used for OMT are methadone and buprenorphine. Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the mu-opioid receptor and an antagonist at the kappa-opioid receptor. Its partial agonist activity provides enough opioid effect to prevent withdrawal and cravings but has a ceiling effect that lowers the risk of respiratory depression and overdose compared to full agonists like methadone. It is often co-formulated with naloxone (e.g., Suboxone) to deter intravenous abuse. Clonidine (Option A) is used for managing acute withdrawal symptoms but not for long-term maintenance. Naloxone (Option D) is a pure antagonist used to reverse overdose.

questions.stem: Caffeine is a commonly consumed stimulant that increases alertness and promotes wakefulness. Which underlying mechanism is responsible for this effect?

options.text: Increased discharge of norepinephrine from the locus ceruleus

questions.explanation: Adenosine antagonism The primary mechanism by which caffeine exerts its stimulant and wakefulness-promoting effects is through competitive antagonism of adenosine receptors in the brain. Adenosine is an inhibitory neuromodulator that builds up during waking hours, and its action on adenosine receptors (particularly A1 and A2A) promotes sleepiness. Caffeine's molecular structure is similar to adenosine, allowing it to bind to these receptors without activating them. By blocking adenosine from binding, caffeine prevents its sleep-inducing effects, leading to increased neuronal firing and enhanced alertness. While caffeine can also inhibit phosphodiesterase (Option D), leading to increased cAMP, this effect typically requires much higher concentrations than are achieved with normal consumption. The increased release of norepinephrine (Option B) is a downstream consequence of adenosine antagonism, not the primary mechanism itself.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with a sudden onset of palpitations, shortness of breath, and dizziness. There is no significant past medical history. On examination, the child has a heart rate of 220 beats per minute, a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, and appears anxious but remains hemodynamically stable. An electrocardiogram confirms the diagnosis of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT). What is the recommended initial dose of adenosine for treating this child?
questions.explanation: 0.1 mg/kg For a hemodynamically stable child with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT), the first-line pharmacological treatment is adenosine, following the failure of vagal maneuvers. According to pediatric advanced life support (PALS) guidelines, the recommended initial dose of adenosine is 0.1 mg/kg, administered as a rapid intravenous (IV) push, with a maximum initial dose of 6 mg. Adenosine works by slowing conduction through the AV node, which can interrupt the re-entrant circuit that is responsible for most cases of PSVT. Due to its extremely short half-life (less than 10 seconds), it must be given very rapidly, followed immediately by a saline flush. If the initial dose is ineffective, a second, larger dose of 0.2 mg/kg (with a maximum of 12 mg ) may be administered. Therefore, the correct initial dose is 0.1 mg/kg.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old patient presents with bone pain, anemia, hypercalcemia, and renal dysfunction. Bone marrow biopsy confirms a diagnosis of multiple myeloma, and appropriate treatment is initiated. Among the treatment options used for multiple myeloma, which one is most commonly associated with reactivation of herpes zoster infection?
questions.explanation: Bortezomib The treatment of multiple myeloma has evolved significantly with the introduction of novel agents. Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor and is a cornerstone of therapy for newly diagnosed and relapsed multiple myeloma. A well-documented and significant side effect associated with bortezomib treatment is an increased risk of herpes zoster (shingles) reactivation. This is believed to be due to the drug's impact on T-cell function and overall cell-mediated immunity, which is crucial for controlling the latent varicella-zoster virus. The incidence of zoster reactivation can be as high as 10-20% in patients treated with bortezomib without prophylaxis. For this reason, it is standard practice to administer antiviral prophylaxis, typically with acyclovir or valacyclovir, for the duration of bortezomib-based therapy to prevent this complication. While other agents can be immunosuppressive, the link is strongest and most established with proteasome inhibitors like bortezomib.

questions.stem: Which medication acts as a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) and is used in the treatment of attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)?
questions.explanation: Reboxetine Reboxetine is a Selective Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitor (NRI). Its mechanism involves blocking the norepinephrine transporter, which increases the levels of norepinephrine in the brain's synapses. This action helps to improve focus, attention, and impulse control, making it a viable, though often off-label, treatment for ADHD. A more widely recognized NRI specifically approved for ADHD is Atomoxetine, which belongs to the same pharmacological class. The other options are incorrect because they have different mechanisms of action. 1. Methylphenidate is a stimulant and a Norepinephrine-Dopamine Reuptake Inhibitor (NDRI). 2. Guanfacine is a non-stimulant alpha-2A adrenergic agonist, which works on nerve receptors. 3. Modafinil is a wakefulness-promoting agent with a complex mechanism that is distinct from an NRI.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old boy from Rajasthan, weighing 50 kg, is diagnosed with mixed malaria due to Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum. What is the appropriate treatment regimen to be given on day 2?

options.text: Artesunate 50 mg (4 tablets) + Primaquine 2.5 mg (6 tablets)
Artesunate 50 mg (4 tablets) + Primaquine 7.5 mg (6 tablets)
Artesunate 50 mg (4 tablets) + Sulfadoxine/ pyrimethamine (750/37.5 mg) (2 tablets) + Primaquine 2.5 mg (6 tablets)
Artesunate 50 mg (4 tablets) + Sulfadoxine/ pyrimethamine (750/37.5 mg) (2 tablets) + Primaquine 7.5 mg (6 tablets)

questions.explanation: Artesunate 50 mg (4 tablets) + Sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine (750/37.5 mg) (2 tablets) + Primaquine 2.5 mg (6 tablets) 1. In mixed malaria infection with Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum, treatment should cover both species. According to malaria treatment guidelines used in many parts of India, including Rajasthan, the recommended therapy is Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) along with primaquine. 2. Artesunate is an artemisinin derivative that rapidly reduces parasitemia by killing the blood stages of the parasite. For a patient weighing 50 kg, the recommended dose is 200 mg, which corresponds to four tablets of 50 mg. Artesunate is given for three days. 3. Sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (SP) is administered as a single dose on day 1 or day 2 along with artesunate as part of ACT. It works by inhibiting folate synthesis in the parasite, enhancing the effectiveness of artesunate. 4. Primaquine is added to eliminate gametocytes of P. falciparum and prevent transmission. A low single dose of primaquine (0.25 mg/kg) is recommended in falciparum or mixed infections. Therefore, the appropriate day-2 regimen includes artesunate, sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine, and low-dose primaquine, corresponding to Option (C).

questions.stem: Which of the following growth hormone analogues is not used for the treatment of GH deficiency but is used in the treatment of HIV- associated lipodystrophy?
questions.explanation: Tesamorelin Tesamorelin is a synthetic analogue of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). It works by stimulating the pituitary gland to produce and release endogenous growth hormone. Its specific indication is for the reduction of excess visceral abdominal fat in patients with HIV-associated lipodystrophy, a condition characterized by abnormal fat redistribution. It is not used for treating growth hormone (GH) deficiency itself. In contrast, Somatropin (Option C) is a recombinant form of human growth hormone and is the standard treatment for GH deficiency. Sermorelin (Option B) is another GHRH analogue that has been used to diagnose and sometimes treat GH deficiency, but it is less common now. Pegvisomant (Option D) is a GH receptor antagonist and is used to treat acromegaly (GH excess), not deficiency. Therefore, Tesamorelin is the correct answer as its primary use is for HIV lipodystrophy. 110. A 45-year-old man with a known history of depression was initially treated with sertraline, but his symptoms did not improve adequately. His treatment was subsequently modified to NODIA

questions.stem: In a patient with eclampsia receiving magnesium sulfate therapy, which clinical finding or parameter indicates that the drug should be discontinued?

options.text: Respiratory rate more than 18 per minute
Urine output less than 60 ml in 4 hours

questions.explanation: Urine output less than 60 ml in 4 hours Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for seizure prophylaxis and treatment in pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. However, it has a narrow therapeutic index, and toxicity can occur. Magnesium is cleared exclusively by the kidneys, so adequate renal function is essential. A urine output of less than 100 ml over 4 hours (or <30 ml/hour) indicates oliguria and impaired renal function. This is a critical warning sign because it means magnesium will not be cleared effectively, leading to its accumulation and potentially life-threatening toxicity (respiratory depression, cardiac arrest). Therefore, oliguria is a clear indication to withhold or stop the magnesium sulfate infusion. Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the first sign of toxicity, so exaggerated reflexes (Option B) are not an indication to stop. A normal respiratory rate (Option A) is reassuring. Visual disturbances (Option D) are a symptom of pre-eclampsia itself, not magnesium toxicity.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman in late pregnancy presents with seizures and severe hypertension and is diagnosed with eclampsia. She is started on magnesium sulfate therapy. During treatment, several clinical and laboratory parameters must be carefully monitored to avoid magnesium toxicity. Which of the following parameters does not require routine monitoring during magnesium sulfate therapy in this patient?
questions.explanation: Serum magnesium levels When administering magnesium sulfate for eclampsia, close clinical monitoring is essential to prevent toxicity. The standard parameters to check regularly (often hourly) are : urine output (to ensure adequate renal clearance, must be >30 ml/hr), deep tendon reflexes (specifically the patellar reflex, as its disappearance is the first clinical sign of toxicity), and respiratory rate (as respiratory depression is a life-threatening sign of severe toxicity, rate should be >12 breaths/min). These clinical assessments are reliable, readily available, and sufficient for safe management in most cases. While serum magnesium levels can be measured, they are not routinely checked as part of standard monitoring protocols. This is because the test results are often not available quickly enough to guide immediate clinical decisions, and clinical signs are highly reliable indicators of impending or present toxicity. Serum levels are typically reserved for cases where clinical signs are unclear or if renal failure is present.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old individual with a history of drug abuse presents to the emergency department with features suggestive of acute poisoning from an unknown substance. The patient has dilated pupils, excessive sweating, tachycardia, and tremors. On examination, blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg and heart rate is 120 beats per minute. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cocaine intoxication The patient's clinical presentation is a classic sympathomimetic toxidrome. This is characterized by widespread stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system, leading to tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis (dilated pupils), diaphoresis (sweating), tremors, and agitation. Cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic agent that works by blocking the reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin, leading to this state of hyperexcitability. Dhatura poisoning (Option B) would cause an anticholinergic toxidrome, characterized by mydriasis, tachycardia, and hypertension, but with dry skin and mucous membranes (mad as a hatter, blind as a bat, red as a beet, hot as a hare, dry as a bone). Cannabis (Option C) typically causes tachycardia and conjunctival injection but not usually severe hypertension or tremors. Alcohol intoxication (Option D) is a CNS depressant. The presence of diaphoresis is a key feature that points towards a sympathomimetic rather than an anticholinergic syndrome.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman at 37 weeks of gestation has a history of prosthetic heart valve replacement and is currently on warfarin therapy. She presents for a routine antenatal check-up. What is the most appropriate management or advice in this situation?

options.text: Switch to low molecular weight heparin

questions.explanation: Switch to low molecular weight heparin Warfarin is an oral anticoagulant that crosses the placenta and can cause fetal bleeding, especially during labor and delivery. Its anticoagulant effect is also long-lasting and difficult to reverse quickly. For these reasons, it is standard practice to discontinue warfarin in pregnant women with prosthetic heart valves as they approach term. The patient should be admitted to the hospital and switched from warfarin to an anticoagulant that does not cross the placenta and has a shorter half-life, such as unfractionated heparin (UFH) or low molecular weight heparin (LMWH). This is typically done around 36 weeks of gestation. The heparin can then be stopped shortly before a planned induction of labor or cesarean section to minimize the risk of maternal hemorrhage. Continuing warfarin (Option C) up to delivery is dangerous for both mother and fetus. The decision to induce labor (Option A) or perform an LSCS (Option B) will be made after the anticoagulation has been safely managed.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with head injury following a road traffic accident. During hospitalization, he develops seizures, and an urgent CT scan shows diffuse cerebral edema. Which diuretic is the drug of choice for the management of cerebral edema in this patient?
questions.explanation: Mannitol In the setting of acute traumatic brain injury with cerebral edema and signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), the diuretic of choice is an osmotic diuretic, with mannitol being the gold standard. Mannitol is a large sugar molecule that is administered intravenously. It remains in the intravascular space, increasing the osmotic pressure of the blood. This creates an osmotic gradient that draws excess water out of the brain tissue (the edematous parenchyma) and into the bloodstream, thereby reducing cerebral edema and lowering ICP. The excess fluid is then excreted by the kidneys. Hypertonic saline is another osmotic agent used for this purpose. Loop diuretics like furosemide (Option C) are less effective for cerebral edema and are sometimes used as adjuncts. Spironolactone (Option B) and hydrochlorothiazide (Option D) have no role in the acute management of cerebral edema. FORENSIC MEDICINE

questions.stem: A child is born eight months after the death of the father. The grandparents dispute the child’s paternity, but DNA testing confirms that the deceased man is the biological father. What is the legal term used to describe such a child?
questions.explanation: Posthumous child The term posthumous literally means after death (from Latin post 'after' and humus 'ground', referring to burial). A posthumous child is a child who is born after the death of their biological father. In legal contexts, such a child is generally considered the legitimate heir of the deceased father, provided they were conceived before the father's death. The scenario describes exactly this situation : the child was born 8 months after the father passed away, which is well within the normal gestation period, making conception before his death possible. The DNA test confirming paternity solidifies the child's status as the deceased's offspring. A suppositious child (Option A) is one who is fraudulently substituted for another. An illegitimate child (Option D) is one born to unmarried parents, which is a separate legal concept.

questions.stem: On examination of a suspicious stain, the finding shown is observed. Which forensic test is being demonstrated by this finding?
questions.explanation: Teichman test The image shows the characteristic dark brown, rhombic-shaped crystals that are formed in the Teichmann test, also known as the hemin crystal test. This is a classic forensic confirmatory test for the presence of blood. The test involves heating a suspected bloodstain on a microscope slide with a reagent containing a halide (like sodium chloride) in glacial acetic acid. If hemoglobin is present, the heme portion is cleaved and reacts with the halide and acetic acid to form crystals of hemin chloride (or hematin chloride). The formation of these specific crystals under microscopic examination confirms that the stain is blood. The Florence test (Option B) and Barberio's test (Option A) are used for the detection of semen by identifying choline and spermine crystals, respectively. The Takayama test (Option D) is another confirmatory test for blood that forms pink hemochromogen crystals.

questions.stem: The dead body exhibits the finding shown in the image. Based on this observation, what is the most likely cause of death?
questions.explanation: Smothering Smothering is a form of asphyxial death that occurs when the external air passages (nose and mouth) are forcibly obstructed, preventing air from entering the respiratory tract. This obstruction may be caused by a hand, pillow, cloth, or other soft object placed over the nose and mouth. In such cases, characteristic forensic findings may include: 1. Abrasions or bruises around the mouth and nose due to pressure applied during obstruction. 2. Petechial hemorrhages on the face, conjunctiva, or eyelids caused by increased venous pressure during asphyxia. 3. Cyanosis and congestion of the face. 4. Sometimes fibers, saliva stains, or signs of struggle around the mouth or nostrils. These findings strongly suggest that air entry was blocked externally, which is the defining feature of smothering. The other options show different signs: 5. Hanging produces a ligature mark on the neck. 6. Throttling (manual strangulation) shows finger marks or bruising on the neck. 7. Choking involves obstruction of the airway by a foreign body inside the throat. Since the observed signs indicate external obstruction of the nose and mouth, the most likely cause of death is smothering.

questions.stem: During a medicolegal examination, an 18-year- old male claims that he is only 16 years old. Which joint X-ray should be performed to accurately estimate his age?
questions.explanation: Knee and wrist For medicolegal age estimation in adolescents and young adults, radiographic examination of ossification centers is a standard method. The age of 18 is a crucial legal threshold, and the fusion of various epiphyses occurs around this time. The most commonly used and reliable joints for assessing the 16-18 year age range are the wrist and the knee. In the wrist, the fusion of the distal radial and ulnar epiphyses is a key indicator. At the knee, the fusion of the distal femoral and proximal tibial epiphyses is assessed. The fusion of these centers is generally complete or nearing completion around 18 years of age in males, providing strong evidence to differentiate a 16-year-old from an 18-year-old. The elbow joint (Option D) fuses earlier, typically around 14-16 years, making it less useful for distinguishing 16 from 18. The hip also fuses in the mid-to-late teens.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl who is a victim of sexual assault presents with a pregnancy of 22 weeks and is brought for medical termination of pregnancy (MTP). Which of the following statements is correct in this situation?

options.text: MTP done in 2nd trimester only when mother's life is in danger
MTP can be carried out up to 24 weeks
MTP cannot be more than 20 weeks

questions.explanation: MTP can be carried out up to 24 weeks According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021, of India, the gestational age limit for MTP has been extended. For special categories of women, including minors and survivors of sexual assault, the upper gestational limit for termination is 24 weeks. This case, involving a 14-year-old (minor) victim of sexual assault at 22 weeks gestation, falls squarely within this special category. Therefore, MTP can be legally carried out up to 24 weeks. For a pregnancy between 20 and 24 weeks, the opinion of two registered medical practitioners is required, so Option A is incorrect. The older law had a 20-week limit (making Option D incorrect) and stricter rules for second-trimester terminations (making Option B outdated). The amended act specifically allows for termination up to 24 weeks in such cases to protect the physical and mental health of the survivor.

questions.stem: A 27-week pregnant woman with a fetus diagnosed with congenital anomalies is considering a Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP). Whose presence is not required for the authorization of MTP in this case?
questions.explanation: Lawyer Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021, of India, there is no upper gestational limit for termination in cases of substantial fetal abnormalities diagnosed by a Medical Board. For a pregnancy that has advanced beyond 24 weeks (the patient is at 27 weeks), the decision to permit an MTP must be made by this board. The board is constituted by the government and typically includes a Gynaecologist/Obstetrician, a Pediatrician, a Radiologist/Sonologist, and other members as the state government deems necessary. These medical professionals are required to assess the medical condition of the fetus and the risks to the pregnant woman. There is no requirement for a lawyer to be a member of this Medical Board or to be present for the authorization process. The decision is a medical one, based on the diagnosis and prognosis of the congenital anomaly.

questions.stem: Which chelating agent is specifically indicated for the management of iron overdose?
questions.explanation: Desferrioxamine The specific chelating agent used for the treatment of acute iron poisoning is desferrioxamine (also spelled deferoxamine). It is a hexadentate iron chelator, meaning one molecule of desferrioxamine can bind tightly to one atom of ferric iron (), forming a stable, water-soluble complex called ferrioxamine. This complex is non-toxic and is readily excreted by the kidneys, giving the urine a characteristic reddish-brown or vin rosé color. This process effectively removes excess free iron from the plasma and tissues, preventing it from causing severe cellular damage, metabolic acidosis, and shock. British Anti-Lewisite (BAL, dimercaprol) (Option B) is used for arsenic, mercury, and lead poisoning. Calcium disodium edetate (EDTA) (Option C) is used for lead poisoning. Diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid (DTPA) (Option D) is used for internal contamination with transuranic radioactive elements.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct concerning the formation of adipocere?
questions.explanation: Preservation by saponification Adipocere, also known as grave wax, is a waxy, soap-like substance formed on a dead body in certain conditions. Its formation is a modification of the normal decomposition process and results in the preservation of the body's soft tissues. This process occurs through the saponification of body fats. In a moist, anaerobic (oxygen-poor) environment, bacterial enzymes, particularly clostridial lecithinase, hydrolyze body fats into fatty acids. These fatty acids then react with alkali ions (like calcium and magnesium) present in the surrounding environment to form insoluble, waxy soaps. This process requires a damp or wet environment and is inhibited by high temperatures (Option B) or cool, dry climates (Option C). It is a slow process, typically taking several weeks or months to develop, not minutes or hours (Option D).

questions.stem: In cases of death due to a road traffic accident (RTA), who is legally authorized to order the autopsy?
questions.explanation: Police In deaths that are unnatural, sudden, suspicious, or where the cause is unknown, a medicolegal investigation is required. A death resulting from a Road Traffic Accident (RTA) falls into this category. The legal authority responsible for investigating such deaths and requesting a medicolegal autopsy is the police or a magistrate. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) in India, an Investigating Officer (police) conducts an inquest (panchnama) at the scene. If they suspect foul play or if the cause of death is not apparent, they have the authority to send the body to a government-authorized medical officer for a post-mortem examination (autopsy) to determine the cause and manner of death. The forensic doctor (Option D) performs the autopsy but does not order it. A forensic expert (Option A) or lawyer (Option C) does not have the legal authority to order an autopsy in this context. NODIA

questions.stem: Aldrich–Mees lines along with raindrop pigmentation on the hands are characteristic findings seen in poisoning due to which substance?
questions.explanation: Arsenic The combination of Aldrich-Mees lines and raindrop pigmentation is highly characteristic of chronic arsenic poisoning. Aldrich-Mees lines are transverse white bands (leukonychia) that appear across the fingernails and toenails. They are caused by the deposition of arsenic in the keratin of the growing nail plate, which disrupts normal nail formation. These lines appear weeks to months after exposure and grow out with the nail. Raindrop pigmentation refers to a pattern of hyperpigmentation interspersed with small, hypopigmented macules, giving a speckled appearance, typically on the trunk and extremities. These signs, along with other features like hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles, neuropathy, and an increased risk of skin cancer, are classic indicators of long-term arsenic exposure. Thallium poisoning (Option B) is known for causing severe alopecia (hair loss).

questions.stem: Based on the image provided, identify the bullet range.
questions.explanation: Close range The image displays the key features of a close-range (or near-contact) gunshot wound. In addition to the central entry wound, there is a prominent surrounding pattern of stippling or tattooing. This is caused by unburnt and partially burnt grains of gunpowder being forcefully embedded into the skin, creating small punctate abrasions. The presence of dense stippling indicates that the muzzle of the firearm was close enough for these particles to strike the skin with sufficient force but not in direct contact with it. A contact wound (Option B) would show a muzzle imprint, searing of the skin, and soot deposited within the wound track. A distant range wound (Option A) would only have a clean entry hole with an abrasion collar, as the gunpowder would have dispersed and lacked the velocity to mark the skin. The clear presence of stippling is the defining feature of a close-range shot.

questions.stem: An ultrasound examination reveals two fetuses, with one appearing to be approximately one month more developed than the other. What is the term used to describe this condition?
questions.explanation: Superfetation Superfetation is an extremely rare phenomenon where a second, new conception occurs during an already established pregnancy. It involves the fertilization and implantation of a second oocyte in a uterus that is already gravid. This results in two fetuses of different gestational ages and developmental stages coexisting in the uterus. The scenario of one baby appearing a month older than the other on ultrasound is the classic description of superfetation. Superfecundation (Option B) is the fertilization of two or more ova from the same ovulatory cycle by sperm from separate acts of intercourse, often leading to twins with different fathers, but the fetuses are of the same gestational age. Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (Option C) is a complication of monochorionic twin pregnancies characterized by unequal blood flow, leading to size discrepancy, but not a difference in gestational age.

questions.stem: What does the image depict?
questions.explanation: Wall contains silica and chlorophyll The image shows diatoms. These are a major group of unicellular algae found in oceans, freshwater, and soils. A defining characteristic of diatoms is their unique cell wall, called a frustule, which is made of silica (hydrated silicon dioxide). This silica shell is often intricately patterned with pores and ribs. As photosynthetic organisms, diatoms also contain chlorophyll and other pigments within their chloroplasts, giving them a golden-brown color. In forensic medicine, the presence of diatoms in the bone marrow or deep organs of a body recovered from water is strong evidence of antemortem drowning, as they must be inhaled with water and circulated by a functioning heart to reach these sites. Diatoms are not bacteria (Option C), and their silica walls make them highly resistant to acid digestion (Option D), a property used to isolate them from tissue samples. PATHOLOGY

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with anemia, a platelet count of 25,000/mm³, and prolonged PT and APTT. A peripheral blood smear image is provided. Based on these findings, which fusion gene is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: PML-RARA The clinical presentation of pancytopenia, coagulopathy (raised PT/APTT, suggesting DIC), and the key morphological finding of a promyelocyte with multiple Auer rods (a faggot cell) on the peripheral smear are pathognomonic for Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL), a subtype of AML. APL is cytogenetically characterized by a specific translocation between chromosome 15 and 17, denoted as t(15;17)(q24;q21). This translocation creates a fusion gene between the Promyelocytic Leukemia (PML) gene on chromosome 15 and the Retinoic Acid Receptor Alpha (RARA) gene on chromosome 17. The resulting PML-RARA fusion protein acts as a transcriptional repressor, blocking the differentiation of myeloid cells at the promyelocyte stage. This is the molecular hallmark of APL. The other fusion genes are associated with different subtypes of AML : RUNX1-RUNX1T1 with t(8;21) and INV 16 with inv(16).

questions.stem: The immunohistochemical marker TTF- 1 (thyroid transcription factor-1) is most commonly expressed in which of the following tumors or tissues?
questions.explanation: Lung adenocarcinoma Thyroid Transcription Factor-1 (TTF-1), also known as NKX2-1, is a nuclear transcription factor that plays a crucial role in the development of the thyroid, lung, and forebrain. In pathology, TTF-1 is used as an immunohistochemical (IHC) marker to determine the origin of tumors. It shows strong nuclear staining in the vast majority of lung adenocarcinomas (around 75-85%) and small cell lung carcinomas. It is also positive in all types of well-differentiated thyroid carcinomas, including papillary (Option C) and follicular types. However, when differentiating metastatic tumors of unknown primary, a positive TTF-1 stain is most commonly indicative of a lung or thyroid origin. Between the options of lung adenocarcinoma and papillary thyroid carcinoma, it is a key marker for both. In the context of lung cancer differentiation, it is the primary marker for adenocarcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung (Option A) is typically TTF-1 negative.

questions.stem: A patient is found to have a cerebellar mass along with a renal tumor and reports a family history of similar illnesses. Which genetic mutation is most likely present in this family?
questions.explanation: VHL The triad of a cerebellar mass (specifically a hemangioblastoma), a renal tumor (specifically clear cell renal cell carcinoma), and a positive family history is the classic presentation of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease. VHL is an autosomal dominant hereditary cancer syndrome caused by a germline mutation in the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3. This mutation predisposes individuals to the development of various benign and malignant tumors. In addition to cerebellar hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinomas, patients with VHL disease are also at risk for retinal angiomas, pheochromocytomas, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. The other options are different hereditary cancer syndromes : Neurofibromatosis (NF) involves neurofibromas and optic gliomas, Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) involves hamartomas in multiple organs, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome (p53 mutation) is associated with sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenal cortical carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old football player is brought to the emergency department after a sudden collapse due to cardiac arrest. A histological image is provided. Based on the microscopic findings shown, what is the most likely cause of death?
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM) Sudden cardiac death in a young athlete is most commonly caused by an underlying, often undiagnosed, cardiac condition. The histological image shows the pathognomonic features of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM), which include cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, extensive myofiber disarray (where the muscle cells are arranged in a chaotic, whorled pattern instead of being parallel), and interstitial fibrosis. HCM is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins, leading to unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy. This hypertrophy and disarray create a substrate for fatal ventricular arrhythmias (like ventricular fibrillation), which are the usual cause of sudden death, especially during or after intense physical exertion. The other cardiomyopathies have different histological features : DCM (Option B) shows thinned walls and attenuated fibers, RCM (Option C) often shows infiltration (e.g., amyloid), and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (Option D) is characterized by fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium.

questions.stem: The skin biopsy image shown is most characteristic of which of the following clinical conditions?
questions.explanation: Morphea The image displays histological features characteristic of morphea, also known as localized scleroderma. The key finding is in the dermis, which appears markedly thickened and sclerotic, with dense, eosinophilic collagen bundles that have replaced the normal dermal architecture and subcutaneous fat. There is also a notable loss of skin adnexal structures, such as hair follicles and sweat glands, which become entrapped and atrophied within the fibrotic tissue. The overlying epidermis is often thinned and flattened. This picture reflects the clinical process of excessive collagen deposition leading to hardened, indurated skin plaques. Lichen planus (Option A) is an interface dermatitis with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate. Lichen nitidus (Option B) shows a claw-and-ball granulomatous infiltrate. Viral myocarditis (Option D) is an inflammation of the heart muscle, not a skin condition.

questions.stem: A child presents with pruritic skin lesions along with diarrhea and has been advised to follow a gluten-free diet. What is the most likely underlying etiology of this condition?
questions.explanation: Celiac disease Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder triggered by ingestion of gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. It leads to immune-mediated damage of the small intestinal mucosa, particularly the villi, resulting in malabsorption. In children, common symptoms include chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies. A distinctive extraintestinal manifestation is pruritic skin lesions, known as dermatitis herpetiformis, which occur due to IgA deposition in the dermal papillae. This skin condition is strongly associated with celiac disease and improves with a gluten-free diet. Because gluten triggers the immune response that damages the intestinal lining, the primary treatment is lifelong avoidance of gluten-containing foods. Following a gluten-free diet helps restore the intestinal villi and reduces both gastrointestinal and skin symptoms. The other options are less consistent with the scenario. Whipple's disease is a rare bacterial infection, Crohn’s disease is an inflammatory bowel disease not specifically related to gluten, and dermatitis herpetiformis is actually a cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease rather than the underlying cause. Therefore, the most likely underlying etiology is celiac disease. 140. Which specific antibody is most commonly associated with celiac disease? (A) Anti-TTG (Tissue Transglutaminase) (B) ANCA (Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies) NODIA

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman with a height of 4 feet is evaluated, and her karyotype is shown in the image below. Which of the following options best explains the underlying etiology of her condition?
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome The provided karyotype is 45,X, which is the classic genetic signature for Turner syndrome. This condition is a chromosomal disorder in females characterized by the complete or partial absence of one of the two X chromosomes. The clinical features described, particularly short stature (height of 4 feet), are cardinal signs of Turner syndrome. Other common features include gonadal dysgenesis (streak ovaries) leading to primary amenorrhea and infertility, a webbed neck, a low posterior hairline, and a broad chest with widely spaced nipples. Cardiac and renal anomalies are also common. Klinefelter's syndrome (Option B) is 47,XXY and affects males. Down syndrome (Option C) is Trisomy 21. Edward's syndrome (Option D) is Trisomy 18. The karyotype is definitive for Turner syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient presents with hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal pain, and a markedly elevated white blood cell count exceeding 50,000/mm³. Which underlying gene abnormality is most likely responsible for these findings, and what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: t(9 :22) The clinical presentation of marked splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, and a very high white blood cell count (leukocytosis) with a spectrum of myeloid precursors is classic for Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML). The molecular hallmark and diagnostic criterion for CML is the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, which results from a reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosome 9 and 22, denoted as t(9;22)(q34;q11). This translocation creates a fusion gene called BCR-ABL1 on the shortened chromosome 22 (the Philadelphia chromosome). The protein product of this fusion gene is a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives the massive proliferation of granulocytic cells, leading to the clinical and laboratory features of CML. The translocation t(15;17) (Option C) is characteristic of Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL).

questions.stem: A male patient diagnosed with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is not responding to oxygen therapy. What role does interleukin-8 (IL-8) play in the pathogenesis of ARDS?
questions.explanation: Recruitment of neutrophils Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is a form of acute, diffuse, inflammatory lung injury characterized by severe hypoxemia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. The pathophysiology involves an uncontrolled inflammatory response within the lungs. A key event is the massive infiltration of neutrophils into the interstitium and alveolar spaces. Interleukin-8 (IL-8), also known as CXCL8, is a potent neutrophil chemoattractant and activator. It is released by activated alveolar macrophages and epithelial cells early in the inflammatory cascade. The high levels of IL-8 in the alveolar fluid of ARDS patients create a strong chemotactic gradient that is primarily responsible for the recruitment of neutrophils from the circulation into the lung tissue. These recruited neutrophils then release proteases, reactive oxygen species, and other inflammatory mediators that damage the alveolar-capillary barrier, leading to protein-rich edema and impaired gas exchange.

questions.stem: An adult male presents with a protuberant abdomen, chronic diarrhea, visual disturbances, and neurological symptoms. Laboratory investigations reveal low LDL cholesterol levels, and a peripheral blood smear image is provided. Based on the clinical features and the smear findings shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Abetalipoproteinemia The key finding in the peripheral smear is the presence of acanthocytes, which are red blood cells with irregular, spiky projections of varying length and width. This finding, combined with the clinical picture of fat malabsorption (diarrhea, protruding abdomen), neurological problems (ataxia, peripheral neuropathy), and visual symptoms (retinitis pigmentosa), along with very low or absent LDL, is diagnostic of Abetalipoproteinemia (also known as Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome). This is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the MTTP gene, which is essential for assembling and secreting apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins (chylomicrons, VLDL, and LDL) from enterocytes and hepatocytes. The inability to absorb and transport fats leads to steatorrhea and severe deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), which causes the neurological and visual symptoms. The acanthocytosis results from abnormal lipid composition of the red cell membrane.

questions.stem: A patient presents with respiratory distress and is diagnosed with panacinar emphysema. Deficiency of which substance is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 antitrypsin Emphysema is characterized by the permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by the destruction of their walls. Panacinar (or panlobular) emphysema, which affects the entire acinus uniformly and is most severe in the lower lobes of the lungs, is the classic form associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency. AAT is a protease inhibitor produced by the liver that circulates in the blood. Its primary function in the lung is to protect the elastic tissue of the alveolar walls from destruction by proteases, particularly neutrophil elastase, which is released by neutrophils during inflammation. In AAT deficiency, this protective shield is absent, leading to unchecked elastase activity and progressive destruction of the lung parenchyma. Centriacinar emphysema, in contrast, is typically associated with smoking. Surfactant (Option B) deficiency causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is most commonly seen on laboratory investigations in a patient with iron deficiency anemia (IDA)?
questions.explanation: Decreased transferrin saturation Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is characterized by the depletion of the body's iron stores. This leads to a distinct pattern on iron studies. Serum ferritin is a measure of stored iron, so in IDA, it is the first marker to fall and will be decreased, not increased (Option A is incorrect). Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) is an indirect measure of transferrin, the protein that transports iron. The liver increases transferrin production in an attempt to capture more iron, so TIBC is increased, not normal (Option D is incorrect). Serum iron measures the amount of iron circulating in the blood, which will be low in IDA (Option C is incorrect). Transferrin saturation is the ratio of serum iron to TIBC (Serum Iron / TIBC × 100%). Since serum iron is low and TIBC is high, the resulting saturation percentage is significantly decreased, typically to less than 15%. This is a hallmark of IDA.

questions.stem: An adult woman presents with pallor and fatigue, and laboratory investigations reveal low hemoglobin, reduced serum iron, low ferritin levels, decreased transferrin saturation, and increased total iron-binding capacity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA) The pattern of laboratory results provided is the classic and definitive profile for Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). The low hemoglobin confirms anemia. The low serum ferritin indicates that the body's iron stores are depleted. The low serum iron shows there is insufficient iron in circulation. The increased Total Iron-Binding Capacity (TIBC) reflects the liver's compensatory response of producing more transferrin protein to try and bind more iron from the diet. Finally, the low transferrin saturation (the percentage of transferrin that is actually carrying iron) is a direct consequence of low iron and high TIBC. In contrast, Anemia of Chronic Disease (Option B) typically presents with low serum iron but normal or increased ferritin (as it's an acute phase reactant) and a low TIBC. Hemolytic anemia (Option C) involves red cell destruction, and thalassemia (Option D) is a disorder of globin chain synthesis; neither shows this iron study pattern.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings or complications is not typically associated with resection of the ileum?
questions.explanation: Microcytic hypochromic anemia The terminal ileum is the primary site for absorption of vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) and bile salts. When the ileum is resected, absorption of vitamin B₁₂ is impaired, which can lead to vitamin B₁₂ deficiency. Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency results in megaloblastic anemia, characterized by macrocytic red blood cells and impaired DNA synthesis. One important microscopic feature of this condition is nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony, where the nucleus matures more slowly than the cytoplasm in developing blood cells. Therefore, nuclear cytological asynchrony is associated with ileal resection. Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency can also cause neurological manifestations, such as peripheral neuropathy, paresthesia, ataxia, and degeneration of the spinal cord (subacute combined degeneration). In severe cases, it may lead to cognitive impairment or reversible dementia, which can improve after vitamin B₁₂ supplementation. In contrast, microcytic hypochromic anemia is usually caused by iron deficiency. Iron is primarily absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, not the ileum. Therefore, ileal resection does not typically lead to iron deficiency anemia. Hence, the finding not associated with ileal resection is microcytic hypochromic anemia, making Option (A) correct.

questions.stem: A child presents with recurrent infections, and imaging of the mediastinum shows absence of the thymus. Further laboratory evaluation reveals low levels of adenosine deaminase (ADA). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)The combination of an absent thymus (or thymic shadow on X-ray) and recurrent severe infections points towards a profound T-cell immunodeficiency. While an absent thymus is the hallmark of DiGeorge syndrome (Option B), the laboratory finding of low adenosine deaminase (ADA) levels is specific for a particular autosomal recessive form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID). ADA deficiency accounts for about 15% of SCID cases. The ADA enzyme is crucial for purine metabolism. Its absence leads to the accumulation of toxic metabolites (deoxyadenosine and dATP), which are particularly toxic to developing lymphocytes. This results in a severe impairment of both T-cell and B-cell function, leading to the combined immunodeficiency. Although both conditions can have an absent thymus on imaging, the specific enzyme deficiency (low ADA) definitively points to SCID as the diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following pathological markers or abnormal protein deposits is characteristically found in Alzheimer’s disease?
questions.explanation: Aβ 40/42 (Amyloid-beta 40/42) Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by two key pathological hallmarks : 1. Extracellular amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques → Deposits of Aβ 40/42 peptides, derived from amyloid precursor protein (APP). 2. Intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) → Composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein. 3. Among the given options : Tau protein (A) : Involved in neurofibrillary tangles, but Aβ 40/42 deposition is more specific as a marker of AD. Aβ 40/42 (B) : The main marker/deposition in AD → forms amyloid plaques. Alpha-synuclein (C) : Found in Lewy body dementia and Parkinson’s disease, not AD. TDP-43 (D) : Seen in frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) and ALS, not primarily AD. Therefore, the most important marker/deposition in Alzheimer’s disease is Amyloid-beta 40/42 (B).

questions.stem: A patient presents with episodic headaches, palpitations, and hypertension, and urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) testing is positive. A biopsy image is provided. Based on the clinical features and histopathological findings, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.explanation: Associated with MEN 2A The clinical triad of episodic headaches, palpitations, and sweating, along with hypertension and elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), is classic for a pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla. The histology shows the characteristic Zellballen pattern (nests of chief cells). While most pheochromocytomas are sporadic, a significant portion (around 25-30%) are hereditary. They are a key feature of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2A (MEN 2A) and 2B. MEN 2A is an autosomal dominant syndrome (caused by RET proto-oncogene mutations) characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism. Regarding the other options : approximately 10% are malignant (A is incorrect), they can occur in children but are more common in adults (B is incorrect), and about 10% are bilateral (more common in hereditary cases) (C is incorrect). The association with MEN 2A is a well-established and important clinical fact.

questions.stem: An adult tall male presents with an increased arm span, pectus excavatum, and associated cardiac abnormalities. Deficiency or defect of which protein is most likely responsible for these features?
questions.explanation: Fibrillin This clinical presentation is classic for Marfan syndrome. It is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder characterized by skeletal abnormalities (tall stature, long limbs and fingers - arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum or carinatum, scoliosis), ocular problems (ectopia lentis - lens dislocation), and cardiovascular manifestations (aortic root aneurysm and dissection, mitral valve prolapse). Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the FBN1 gene, which codes for the protein fibrillin-1. Fibrillin-1 is a major component of extracellular microfibrils, which provide structural support to connective tissues throughout the body, particularly in the aorta, ligaments, and the ciliary zonules of the eye. Defective fibrillin-1 leads to weakened connective tissue, explaining the multisystemic features of the disease. Elastin (Option B) mutations cause other conditions like cutis laxa. 161. A 32-year-old woman presents with a gradually progressive, painless swelling on the left side of her neck that has been present for the past two months. She also complains of low- grade fever, night sweats, and unintentional NODIA

questions.stem: A nasal surgical procedure was performed using the incision shown in the image. Based on the location and type of incision, which surgical procedure was most likely carried out?
questions.explanation: Open rhinoplasty The image displays a small incision across the columella, the strip of tissue that separates the nostrils. This is known as a trans-columellar incision and is the hallmark of the open or external approach to rhinoplasty. This incision connects with marginal incisions made just inside each nostril, allowing the surgeon to lift the entire skin-soft tissue envelope off the underlying nasal cartilages and bones. This provides wide, direct visualization of the nasal framework, which is ideal for complex reshaping of the nasal tip, placing grafts, or performing difficult septal work. In contrast, Submucosal resection (SMR) (Option A) and FESS (Option B) are performed endonasally without external incisions. A Caldwell-Luc procedure (Option D) involves an incision in the gingivobuccal sulcus (inside the upper lip) to access the maxillary sinus.

questions.stem: A female patient presents with mild conductive hearing loss and tinnitus. A pure tone audiometry (PTA) graph is shown. Based on the audiometric findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Otosclerosis The audiogram shows a conductive hearing loss, indicated by the gap between the air conduction (AC) and bone conduction (BC) thresholds. The most specific finding on this audiogram is the dip or notch in the bone conduction threshold centered at 2000 Hz (2K). This finding is known as Carhart's notch and is pathognomonic for otosclerosis. Otosclerosis is a disease of the otic capsule causing abnormal bone remodeling, which leads to fixation of the stapes footplate in the oval window. This fixation impairs the transmission of sound to the inner ear, causing conductive hearing loss. The Carhart's notch is an artifact of stapes fixation that mechanically affects the cochlea's resonant frequency. Ménière's disease (Option A) causes low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Ototoxicity (Option C) and NIHL (Option D) cause high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.stem: In a patient diagnosed with right-sided vestibular neuronitis, what finding would be expected on performing the head impulse (head thrust) test?

options.text: Head turned to right, eyeball moves to left with nystagmus
Head turned to left, eyeball moves to right with nystagmus
Head turned to right, eyeball moves to right with nystagmus
Head turned to left, eyeball moves to left with nystagmus

questions.explanation: Head turned to right, eyeball moves to left with nystagmus The head impulse (head thrust) test is used to assess the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR). In a normal VOR, when the head is rapidly rotated, the eyes move in the opposite direction to keep gaze fixed on the target. In right vestibular neuronitis, the right horizontal semicircular canal and nerve are impaired. When the examiner quickly turns the head to the right (affected side), the vestibular system cannot generate the compensatory eye movement. As a result, the eyes briefly move with the head (to the right) and then make a corrective saccade to the left to refocus on the target. This appears as the eyeball moving to the left with a corrective saccade/nystagmus after a head thrust to the right. Thus, the abnormal finding is : Head turned to right fv eyeball moves to left with corrective nystagmus. 165.
