questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman, G2L2, with cervical elongation presents for surgical management. What is the surgery of choice?
questions.explanation: Fothergill The Fothergill operation, also known as the Manchester repair, is a surgical procedure specifically designed to correct uterovaginal prolapse, particularly when it is associated with elongation of the cervix. The procedure involves a combination of an anterior colporrhaphy (repair of the anterior vaginal wall), amputation of the elongated supravaginal portion of the cervix, and plication of the uterosacral ligaments in front of the remaining cervical stump to provide support and antevert the uterus. This procedure is uterine-sparing, making it an option for women who wish to preserve their uterus, although future fertility is often compromised. A hysterectomy (D) is an option but is not uterus-sparing. A McCall culdoplasty (B) supports the vaginal vault, and a Le Fort colpocleisis (C) is an obliterative procedure for elderly, non-sexually active women.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with cervical erosion and a two-month history of spotting. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: LBC+HPV The patient is presenting with symptoms (postcoital or intermenstrual spotting) and a physical finding (cervical erosion or ectropion) that require evaluation to rule out cervical dysplasia or cancer. Current cervical cancer screening guidelines for women over 30 often recommend co-testing. This involves collecting a single cervical sample to perform both a cytology test and a Human Papillomavirus (HPV) DNA test. Liquid-Based Cytology (LBC) is a newer method of Pap testing that is often preferred over the conventional Pap smear for its improved sample quality and ability to perform reflex HPV testing from the same vial. The HPV test detects the presence of high-risk HPV types, which are the causative agents of most cervical cancers. This combination of LBC and HPV testing is the most sensitive and effective screening strategy in this age group to assess the risk of cervical neoplasia.

questions.stem: A G5P4 woman presents for her first routine ultrasound. She has four daughters and requests fetal sex determination, expressing a desire for a male child. In accordance with ethical and legal guidelines, what should be your appropriate response?

options.text: Check routine ANC and sex for developmental abnormalities and do not reveal gender to the patient
Check routine ANC and sex for developmental abnormalities and do reveal gender to the patient
Do reveal gender if a girl
Check only routine ANC, do not check sex

questions.explanation: Check routine ANC and sex for developmental abnormalities and do not reveal gender to the patient In India, prenatal sex determination is illegal under the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, 1994. This law was enacted to combat female foeticide and address the declining child sex ratio. It is illegal for any person to conduct or assist in conducting prenatal diagnostic techniques to determine the sex of the fetus, and it is illegal to communicate the sex of the fetus to the pregnant woman or her relatives. Therefore, the ethically and legally correct course of action for the sonographer is to perform the routine antenatal ultrasound to assess fetal well-being, growth, and to screen for developmental abnormalities (which may include examining the genitalia as part of a complete anomaly scan), but to strictly not reveal the gender to the patient or her family under any circumstances.

questions.stem: A young woman presents with pelvic organ prolapse and is planned for mesh repair. To which anatomical structure is the mesh typically fixed?
questions.explanation: Ischial spine In mesh repair for pelvic organ prolapse, especially transvaginal mesh procedures or sacrospinous fixation, the mesh or sutures are anchored to the Ischial spine. The ischial spine serves as a key surgical landmark because the sacrospinous ligament attaches to it, and the mesh is fixed to this ligament to support the vaginal apex or uterus. This procedure helps restore pelvic floor support while maintaining normal pelvic anatomy. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Ischial tuberosity – mainly serves for muscle attachment and is not used for prolapse mesh fixation. 2. Sacral promontory – used in Sacrocolpopexy, typically via abdominal or laparoscopic approach rather than standard transvaginal mesh repair. 3. Pubic symphysis – not used as an anchoring site for prolapse mesh. Therefore, the correct answer is (A) Ischial spine.

questions.stem: Which tumor marker is associated with solid- cystic masses of the ovary?
questions.explanation: AFP When evaluating a solid-cystic (complex) adnexal mass, particularly in a younger woman, it is important to consider the possibility of a germ cell tumor. Certain germ cell tumors produce specific tumor markers. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a key marker produced by yolk sac tumors (endodermal sinus tumors), which are a type of malignant ovarian germ cell tumor. These tumors often present as complex, solid-cystic masses. Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) (Option B) is another germ cell tumor marker, produced by choriocarcinomas and some embryonal carcinomas. Often, both AFP and hCG are measured as part of the workup. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) (Option A) is a non-specific marker, often elevated in mucinous tumors. HER2/neu (Option C) is a marker used primarily in breast and gastric cancers.

questions.stem: On which part of the fallopian tube is tubectomy usually performed, and what is the reason for choosing this site?
questions.explanation: Isthmus narrowest Tubectomy is most commonly performed on the Isthmus of fallopian tube. The isthmus is chosen primarily because it is the narrowest part of the fallopian tube and has a thick muscular wall. Because of its narrow lumen, when the tube is ligated and cut, the chances of recanalization (rejoining of the tube) are much lower. This makes sterilization more effective and reliable. In addition, the isthmus is relatively less vascular and easier to access during procedures such as Pomeroy’s tubal ligation, reducing the risk of bleeding and surgical complications. The ampulla, although wider and the usual site of fertilization, is not preferred because its lumen is broader and the walls are thinner, which increases the possibility of failure of sterilization. Therefore, tubectomy is typically performed at the isthmus because it is the narrowest part of the fallopian tube. NODIA

questions.stem: Identify the degree of the perineal tear shown in the image below :
questions.explanation: 3rd degree Perineal tears that occur during childbirth are classified by their depth : 1. 1st degree : Injury to the perineal skin and/or vaginal mucosa only. 2. 2nd degree : Injury extends to the fascia and muscles of the perineum (perineal body), but the anal sphincter complex is intact. 3. 3rd degree : Injury extends through the perineal muscles and involves disruption of the anal sphincter complex (either the external anal sphincter, internal anal sphincter, or both). 4. 4th degree : Injury extends through the anal sphincter complex and also involves the anal or rectal mucosa. The image shows a tear that involves the anal sphincter, but the rectal mucosa appears intact. This correctly classifies it as a 3rd-degree tear.

questions.stem: A teenage girl presents with primary amenorrhea, and the local genital examination findings are shown in the image. Which karyotype analysis would be most appropriate for further evaluation?
questions.explanation: 46 XX A teenage girl presenting with primary amenorrhea and the genital finding shown in the image is most consistent with an Imperforate hymen. In this condition, menstrual blood cannot exit the vagina, leading to hematocolpos or hematometra, which may present as primary amenorrhea with cyclic abdominal pain. Importantly, imperforate hymen is an outflow tract obstruction, not a chromosomal abnormality. The ovaries, uterus, and hormonal function are usually normal, and secondary sexual characteristics develop normally. Therefore, the patient typically has a normal female karyotype, which is 46 XX.Other options are associated with different conditions: 1. 46 XY – seen in androgen insensitivity syndrome or gonadal dysgenesis. 2. 45 XO – seen in Turner syndrome, associated with streak ovaries and delayed puberty. 3. 47 XXY – seen in Klinefelter syndrome. Thus, the most appropriate karyotype is 46 XX. 366. A woman presents with bleeding after sexual intercourse. What is the most appropriate investigation to evaluate this symptom?(A) Pap smear, HCV DNA, electrophoresis(B) Liquid-based cytology, cervical biopsy(C) Cervical biopsy, HBV DNA(D) Pap smear, HPV DNA testing Ans : (D) Pap smear, HPV DNA testing Postcoital bleeding (bleeding after intercourse) is a potential symptom of cervical pathology, including cervical cancer, and it always warrants a thorough investigation. The initial workup should include a speculum examination to visualize the cervix and screening for cervical cancer. Current screening guidelines emphasize co-testing, which combines a Pap smear (or its modern equivalent, Liquid-Based Cytology) with HPV DNA testing. The Pap smear looks for abnormal cells (dysplasia) on the cervix, while the HPV test detects the presence of high-risk strains of the Human Papillomavirus, which is the causative agent of nearly all cervical cancers. If the speculum exam reveals a visible lesion, a direct cervical biopsy (Option B) would be performed immediately. However, in the absence of a gross lesion, co-testing is the standard initial investigatory step.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with a newly developed 2 cm black nodular lesion near her episiotomy scar. The lesion is painful and enlarges during menstruation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Endometriosis The key feature in this clinical history is the cyclical nature of the symptoms—the mass becomes painful and larger during mens truation. This strongly suggests that the tissue is hormonally responsive, specifically to estrogen and progesterone. This is the hallmark of endometriosis, which is the presence of ectopic endometrial tissue. Scar endometriosis can occur when endometrial cells are inadvertently seeded into a surgical incision, such as an episiotomy scar or a C-section scar, during delivery. This ectopic tissue then responds to hormonal cycles, proliferating and bleeding monthly, which causes the cyclical pain and swelling. The black or bluish appearance is due to trapped, hemolyzed blood. While melanoma (B) can be a black nodule, it would not have cyclical changes. A foreign body granuloma (C) or inclusion cyst (D) would also not be expected to fluctuate with the menstrual cycle. ORTHOPEDICS

questions.stem: Which classification system is used to describe the fracture shown in the image, and what is the corresponding stage or type?
questions.explanation: Gartland 3 The X-ray images show a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, which commonly occurs in children following a fall on an outstretched hand. These fractures are classified using the Gartland classification. The Gartland classification includes three main types: 1. Type I : Undisplaced fracture. The bone alignment is maintained with minimal or no displacement. 2. Type II : Partially displaced fracture with an intact posterior cortex. 3. Type III : Completely displaced fracture with no cortical contact, often showing significant displacement and possible rotation. In the given X-ray, the distal fragment of the humerus is completely displaced from the proximal fragment, indicating complete loss of cortical contact. This appearance is characteristic of Gartland Type III supracondylar fracture. These fractures are clinically important because they carry a higher risk of neurovascular injury, particularly involving the brachial artery or median nerve, and usually require urgent orthopedic management such as closed reduction and percutaneous pin fixation. Therefore, the fracture is classified as Gartland Type III. 369. Identify the implant shown in the image : Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: A patient presents with a fracture of the fifth metatarsal. For how many days should immobilization with a cast be maintained?
questions.explanation: 6-8 weeks The treatment and healing time for a 5th metatarsal fracture depend on its exact location. There are three main types : 1. Avulsion fracture of the tuberosity (most common) : Usually treated non-operatively in a walking boot or cast for 4-6 weeks. 2. Jones fracture : A transverse fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction. This area has a tenuous blood supply, leading to a higher risk of non-union. Treatment often involves non-weight-bearing in a cast for 6-8 weeks, and sometimes longer. 3. Diaphyseal stress fracture : Also requires prolonged immobilization, often 6-8 weeks or more. Given the options, 6-8 weeks is the most appropriate and common duration of immobilization for the more significant types of 5th metatarsal fractures (like a Jones fracture) to ensure adequate healing. Shorter periods might be insufficient and risk non-union.

questions.stem: A man presents with back pain after a road traffic accident, with no associated neurological deficits. An X-ray of the spine is performed. Based on the imaging findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Spinous process fracture The X-ray of the cervical spine shows an avulsion fracture of the spinous process, most likely involving the lower cervical vertebra, which is classically called a Clay-shoveler’s fracture. This injury usually occurs due to sudden forceful flexion or muscle pull, and it is typically a stable fracture. The clue in the question is that the patient has back/neck pain after trauma but no neurological deficit. Spinous process fractures usually do not involve the spinal canal or spinal cord, so neurological findings are generally absent. Why the other options are less likely: 1. Chance fracture is a flexion-distraction injury usually seen in the thoracolumbar spine, often from seat-belt injuries. 2. Fracture of base of vertebrae would suggest a more serious vertebral body injury. 3. Compressed fracture involves collapse of the vertebral body, not an isolated posterior element injury. Thus, the imaging and clinical picture are most consistent with an isolated spinous process fracture (Clay-shoveler’s fracture).

questions.stem: A football player sustains a twisting injury to the ankle and knee, with no clinical evidence of a fracture. The examiner is shown performing a specific maneuver in the image. Which clinical test is being performed?
questions.explanation: Lachman The image demonstrates the Lachman test, which is considered the most sensitive and specific clinical test for diagnosing a tear of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL). Here's how the maneuver shown in the image matches the test : 1. Patient Position : The patient is lying supine (on their back). 2. Knee Flexion : The examiner has positioned the knee in 20-30 degrees of flexion. This angle is the key feature that distinguishes the Lachman test from the anterior drawer test. 3. Hand Placement : One hand stabilizes the distal femur (thigh), while the other hand grips the proximal tibia (shin). 4. Action : The examiner applies a sharp, anteriorly directed force, pulling the tibia forward to assess the amount of translation and the quality of the endpoint. A soft or mushy endpoint with increased translation is a positive sign for an ACL tear. Why Other Options Are Incorrect : (A) Posterior drawer for PCL and (D) Anterior drawer for ACL : Both of these tests are performed with the patient's knee bent to 90 degrees, not 20-30 degrees. (B) McMurray : This test is for a meniscus tear and involves a different, dynamic motion of rotating and extending the knee, looking for a painful click. 373. Based on the X-ray image shown, what is the most likely diagnosis? NODIA

questions.stem: Fracture of which part of a bone leads to disturbance of its linear growth?
questions.explanation: Epiphyseal plate The epiphyseal plate, also known as the physis or growth plate, is the area of growing cartilage located between the epiphysis and metaphysis of long bones in children and adolescents. Linear (longitudinal) growth of the bone occurs at this plate through a process of endochondral ossification, where cartilage cells proliferate and are progressively replaced by bone. A fracture that extends into or across the epiphyseal plate (classified by the Salter-Harris system) can damage the delicate columns of proliferating chondrocytes. This damage can disrupt the normal growth process, potentially leading to premature fusion of the plate and subsequent growth arrest. This can result in a limb length discrepancy or an angular deformity as the bone grows asymmetrically. Fractures confined to the diaphysis, metaphysis, or epiphysis that do not involve the growth plate do not affect linear growth.

questions.stem: The patient is unable to form the O sign by opposing the thumb and index finger. Injury to which muscle is most likely responsible for this deficit?
questions.explanation: Opponens pollicis The “O sign” refers to the ability to bring the thumb and index finger together to form a circle, which requires opposition of the thumb. The muscle primarily responsible for this movement is the Opponens pollicis. Opponens pollicis acts to rotate and flex the first metacarpal, allowing the thumb to oppose the fingers. This muscle is supplied by the Median nerve (specifically the recurrent branch). If this muscle is paralyzed due to median nerve injury, the patient cannot properly oppose the thumb to the index finger, making it difficult or impossible to form the “O sign.” Why other options are incorrect: 1. Flexor pollicis brevis – mainly flexes the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joint. 2. Abductor pollicis brevis – abducts the thumb away from the palm. 3. Flexor digitorum – flexes the fingers but does not produce thumb opposition. Thus, inability to form the O sign due to impaired thumb opposition most strongly indicates dysfunction of the opponens pollicis muscle.

questions.stem: An X-ray shows a fracture that has been treated with plating. By which mechanism does this fracture primarily heal?
questions.explanation: Primary healing The image shows a fracture that has been treated with rigid internal fixation using a compression plate and screws. When a fracture is anatomically reduced (the ends are perfectly aligned) and rigidly compressed, such that there is no motion at the fracture site (absolute stability), it can heal by primary bone healing, also known as direct or Haversian healing. In this process, there is no formation of a significant external callus. Instead, osteoclasts from cutting cones tunnel across the fracture line, followed by osteoblasts that lay down new lamellar bone, directly remodeling and uniting the fracture fragments. This is in contrast to secondary bone healing (B), which occurs in fractures treated with less rigid methods (like casts or intramedullary nails). Secondary healing involves the formation of a large external callus that progressively ossifies.

questions.stem: Identify the condition shown in the image :
questions.explanation: Spondylolisthesis The X-ray of the lumbar spine shows forward displacement of one vertebral body over the vertebra below it, indicated by the arrow. This finding is characteristic of Spondylolisthesis, most commonly occurring at the L4–L5 or L5–S1 level. Spondylolisthesis often results from defects in the pars interarticular is, degenerative changes, trauma, or congenital abnormalities. The condition can lead to lower back pain, spinal instability, and sometimes nerve compression, which may cause radiating pain or neurological symptoms. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Renal osteodystrophy – causes generalized bone changes due to chronic kidney disease, not vertebral slippage. 2. Tuberculosis (Pott’s spine) – typically shows vertebral body destruction, disc space narrowing, and kyphotic deformity. 3. Spondylolysis – may lead to spondylolisthesis but does not itself show the vertebral displacement seen in this image. Thus, the imaging demonstrates forward vertebral slippage consistent with spondylolisthesis. 378. A patient presents with sensory loss over the thenar eminence and the lateral three and a half fingers. At what anatomical site is the injury most likely located? (A) Carpal Tunnel syndrome (B) Median nerve at a higher level (C) Ulnar nerve (D) Radial nerve

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with inward angulation of the elbows, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cubitus varus deformity The image displays a cubitus varus deformity, also commonly known as a gun stock deformity. This is a mal alignment of the elbow where the extended forearm is deviated inwards, towards the midline of the body, resulting in a decreased carrying angle. The most common cause of this deformity is a malunited supracondylar fracture of the humerus in childhood. If the fracture heals with the distal fragment tilted into varus, this deformity results. While it is often more of a cosmetic issue, it can sometimes lead to elbow instability or delayed ulnar nerve palsy. Made lung deformity (B) is a wrist deformity. Nursemaid's elbow (C) is a subluxation of the radial head. Klippel-Feil syndrome (D) is a congenital fusion of cervical vertebrae. The inward angulation at the elbow is specific for cubitus varus. ************** NODIA

questions.stem: A patient presents with progressively increasing pain associated with a swelling located below the ear lobule. Involvement of which of the following anatomical structures is responsible for this pain?
questions.explanation: Great auricular nerve The swelling described is located in the parotid gland region. The gland is enclosed by a tough, inelastic capsule formed by the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia. When the gland swells, this capsule stretches, causing intense pain. The sensory innervation for the parotid capsule and the overlying skin is provided by the great auricular nerve, a branch of the cervical plexus (C2, C3). Therefore, it is the nerve responsible for transmitting the pain sensation. The auriculotemporal nerve (B) carries secretomotor fibers to the gland. The facial nerve (A) provides motor supply to the muscles of facial expression and passes through the gland but does not convey pain sensation from it. While the deep cervical fascia (D) is the structure being stretched, the question implicitly asks for the neurological structure responsible for perceiving the pain, making the great auricular nerve the most accurate answer.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child with features of acute tonsillitis complains of ear pain. Which nerve is responsible for this referred ear pain?
questions.explanation: Tympanic branch of glossopharyngeal nerve This clinical scenario is a classic example of referred pain. The palatine tonsils are primarily innervated by the tonsillar branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). This same cranial nerve also provides sensory innervation to the middle ear cavity and the inner surface of the tympanic membrane via its tympanic branch (Jacobsons nerve). Because both the inflamed tonsil and the middle ear share a common sensory pathway through the glossopharyngeal nerve, the brain misinterprets the origin of the pain signals from the tonsils, perceiving them as coming from the ear. This phenomenon is known as referred otalgia. The other nerves listed innervate the external ear and surrounding skin but do not share a common sensory pathway with the palatine tonsils, making them incorrect choices for this specific clinical presentation.

questions.stem: In a patient of liver cirrhosis anastomotic blood flow increase in

options.text: Middle colic vein & left colic vein

questions.explanation: Left gastric vein & esophageal veins Liver cirrhosis leads to portal hypertension, which forces blood from the high-pressure portal system into the low-pressure systemic venous system through sites of portosystemic anastomosis. One of the most critical of these sites is at the gastroesophageal junction. Here, blood from the left gastric vein (a tributary of the portal vein) is shunted into the esophageal veins (which drain into the systemic azygos vein). The resulting massive increase in blood flow through this connection causes the veins to dilate, forming esophageal varices. These varices are prone to rupture and can cause life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding, a major complication of cirrhosis. The other options do not represent major portosystemic anastomoses; they are either connections within the portal system or entirely within the systemic circulation. PHYSIOLOGY

questions.stem: A transport mechanism across the cell membrane is shown below. This process represents which of the following?
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion The image displays molecules moving across a cell membrane from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration. This movement is mediated by transmembrane proteins (a channel and a carrier protein). This process is the definition of facilitated diffusion. It is a form of passive transport, as it does not require metabolic energy (ATP) and relies on the concentration gradient. The proteins simply facilitate the passage of substances that cannot easily cross the lipid bilayer on their own, such as ions, glucose, and amino acids. Simple diffusion (A) does not involve proteins. Primary active transport (D) directly uses energy to move substances against their concentration gradient.

questions.stem: A family that predominantly consumes polished rice presents with signs of a vitamin deficiency. Which vitamin deficiency is likely, and which investigation is used to detect it?
questions.explanation: Thiamine with Transketolase Polished rice is rice that has had its outer bran and germ layers removed. These layers are the primary dietary source of Thiamine (Vitamin B1). A diet heavily reliant on polished rice is a classic cause of thiamine deficiency, which leads to the condition known as beriberi. The functional status of thiamine in the body is biochemically assessed by measuring the activity of the enzyme transketolase in red blood cells. Transketolase, an enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway, requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) as a cofactor. In a thiamine-deficient state, the enzymes baseline activity is low, but it increases significantly when TPP is added to the test tube, confirming the deficiency. 14. When the insulin-to-glucagon ratio is low, which of the following enzymes is stimulated? (A) Lipoprotein lipase NODIA

questions.stem: An infant presented with difficulty opening the eyes, a cloudy cornea, and excessive watering from the eyes since birth. Based on the clinical picture shown, what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Congenital glaucoma The image and clinical description point strongly to congenital glaucoma. This condition results from abnormal development of the eyes aqueous humor drainage system, leading to elevated intraocular pressure (IOP). In an infant, whose sclera is still elastic, this high pressure causes the eyeball to stretch and enlarge, a condition called buphthalmos (ox eye), as seen in the picture. The elevated IOP also causes edema in the cornea, leading to the cloudy cornea. The classic triad of symptoms for congenital glaucoma is epiphora (excessive watering), photophobia (light sensitivity, leading to difficulty opening the eye), and blepharospasm. Congenital cataract involves opacification of the lens, not the cornea. Ophthalmia neonatorum is conjunctivitis with discharge.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presented with colored halos and a gradual decrease in vision. He has a long- standing history of diabetes mellitus. Based on the slit-lamp examination findings shown, what is the diagnosis and the appropriate management for this patient?

options.text: Sunflower cataract/ snow flake cataract- control sugar levels

questions.explanation: Immature senile cataract- Phacoemulsification & IMSC The slit lamp image shows a uniformly opacified lens, consistent with a cataract. The patient is 65 years old, making an age-related senile cataract the most common type. The symptoms of gradual vision decrease and colored halos (due to diffraction of light by water clefts in the lens) are classic for cataracts. While diabetes can cause specific types of cataracts (like snowflake cataracts), senile cataracts are still the most prevalent in this age group, even with diabetes. The image shows a significant but not completely opaque (mature) cataract, so it could be classified as an immature senile cataract. The definitive and standard modern management for a visually significant cataract is surgical removal. Phacoemulsification with implantation of an intraocular lens (IOL) is the current gold standard procedure. IMSC is incorrect as it is an outdated method.

questions.stem: Which is the best diagnostic modality for this corneal condition

options.text: Fluorescein dye with cobalt blue light

questions.explanation: Fluorescein dye with cobalt blue light The image shows a classic dendritic ulcer of the cornea, which is pathognomonic for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) keratitis. This ulcer has a characteristic branching, tree-like pattern. The best way to visualize and diagnose such corneal epithelial defects is by using fluorescein dye staining followed by examination with a cobalt blue light. Fluorescein is a yellow dye that stains areas where the corneal epithelium is absent (the stroma), but it does not stain intact epithelial cells. When viewed under the cobalt blue filter of a slit lamp, the stained ulcerated area fluoresces a brilliant green, making the dendritic pattern clearly visible. While Rose Bengal and Lissamine Green dyes can also be used to stain devitalized cells, fluorescein with a cobalt blue light is the standard and most effective method for identifying epithelial defects like this one.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old patient presented with binasal visual field loss. Imaging revealed a space- occupying lesion in the brain, for which the patient is receiving treatment. What is the most probable location of this lesion?
questions.explanation: Chiasma The visual pathway has a precise organization. The optic chiasm is where the nerve fibers from the nasal (medial) half of each retina cross to the opposite side, while the temporal (lateral) fibers remain uncrossed. The nasal retinal fibers are responsible for vision in the temporal visual fields. A lesion that compresses the optic chiasm from the center (like a pituitary adenoma) will damage these crossing nasal fibers from both eyes. This results in the loss of vision in both temporal fields, a defect known as bitemporal hemianopia. The question describes binasal vision loss, which is the loss of vision in the fields closest to the nose. This rare defect is caused by bilateral lesions compressing the lateral, uncrossed fibers of the optic chiasm, for example, from bilateral internal carotid artery aneurysms. However, chiasmal lesions are the only single location that can produce bilateral field defects like this. The options likely contain an error, intending to say bitemporal, which points directly to the chiasm. 88. A child presented with a dark-colored, progressively enlarging lesion on one side of the

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with a history of fever and is diagnosed with ventricular tachycardia and cardiac dysfunction. Histopathology of the heart is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytic myocarditis The histopathology image (HPE) of the heart muscle reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate composed mainly of lymphocytes, with associated damage and necrosis of adjacent cardiac muscle cells (myocytes). This finding, combined with the clinical presentation in a child—acute onset of fever, cardiac arrhythmia (ventricular tachycardia), and myocardial dysfunction—is the classic pi cture of acute lymphocytic myocarditis. This condition is an inflammation of the heart muscle, most commonly triggered by a viral infection (e.g., Coxsackievirus B). The immune response to the virus leads to the infiltration of lymphocytes and subsequent cardiac damage. Rheumatic heart disease (B) is characterized by Aschoff bodies. Chagas disease (A) would show a parasitic infiltrate. Pericarditis (D) is inflammation of the pericardial sac, not the muscle itself.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man employed in the cement industry presented with a history of breathing difficulty. On examination, a chest X-ray revealed an opacity, and histological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of mesothelioma. Which of the following is the most likely causative factor?
questions.explanation: Asbestosis Malignant mesothelioma, a cancer arising from the mesothelial cells lining the pleura, has an exceptionally strong and well-established causal link to asbestos exposure. Although the patient works in the cement industry, this is a known risk factor, as asbestos was frequently incorporated into cement products for many years to provide reinforcement and fire resistance. The diagnosis of mesothelioma is considered a sentinel event for prior asbestos exposure, which often occurred decades before the cancer develops. The other listed dusts are associated with different pneumoconioses: silica causes silicosis (A), coal dust causes coal workers pneumoconiosis (C), and iron oxide causes siderosis (D). None of these are known to cause mesothelioma.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old patient presented with a history of pedal edema and was found to have proteinuria on investigation. Kidney biopsy revealed a characteristic spike-and-dome appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Membranous glomerulonephritis The clinical presentation of pedal edema and proteinuria suggests a nephrotic syndrome. The key to the diagnosis is the kidney biopsy finding. A spike and dome appearance is pathognomonic for Membranous Glomerulonephritis (MGN). This appearance is seen on silver staining, where the domes are subepithelial immune complex deposits on the outer side of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), and the spikes are new GBM material laid down by podocytes between these deposits. This process thickens the GBM and damages the filtration barrier, causing the massive proteinuria characteristic of nephrotic syndrome. Minimal change disease (A) shows normal light microscopy. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (C) shows segmental scarring. Neither has a spike and dome pattern.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child with a history of pyoderma two weeks earlier was evaluated and found to have hematuria with a serum creatinine level of 2 mg%. On follow-up three weeks later, the creatinine level increased to 4.5 mg%. Which of the following electron microscopy findings is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation: Subepithelial deposit This clinical scenario describes an acute nephritic syndrome (hematuria, rising creatinine) following a skin infection (pyoderma), which is a classic presentation of Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN). The question asks for the finding on electron microscopy (EM). The pathognomonic ultrastructural feature of PSGN is the presence of large, discrete, hump-shaped, electron-dense immune complex deposits on the epithelial side of the glomerular basement membrane. These are referred to as subepithelial deposits or humps. While the rapidly worsening renal function suggests the development of a crescentic glomerulonephritis, crescents (C) are a finding on light microscopy, not EM. Subendothelial deposits (B) and intramembranous deposits (D) are characteristic of other types of glomerulonephritis. PHARMACOLOGY

questions.stem: A patient with elevated uric acid levels is receiving treatment for gout. Which of the following drugs acts by inhibiting the synthesis of uric acid?
questions.explanation: Allopurinol Uric acid is the final product of purine metabolism. The enzyme xanthine oxidase catalyzes the last two steps of this pathway. Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor. By blocking this enzyme, allopurinol decreases the production of uric acid, thereby lowering serum uric acid levels and preventing gout attacks. It is a first-line medication for the chronic management of gout. In contrast, probenecid (A) is a uricosuric agent that works by increasing the excretion of uric acid by the kidneys. Colchicine (C) and diclofenac (D) are anti-inflammatory drugs used to treat the pain and inflammation of an acute gout flare, but they do not alter uric acid levels.

questions.stem: A patient receiving digoxin developed toxicity, with a serum digoxin level of 4 ng/mL. Given that digoxin has a half-life of 40 hours, how long will it take for the drug concentration to decrease to the therapeutic level of 1 ng/mL?
questions.explanation: 80 hours A drugs half-life is the time it takes for its plasma concentration to decrease by 50%. The initial toxic concentration is 4 ng/ml, and the target is 1 ng/ml. After the first half-life (40 hours), the concentration will fall from 4 ng/ml to 2 ng/ml. After the second half-life (another 40 hours), the concentration will fall again by half, from 2 ng/ml to 1 ng/ml. To get from 4 ng/ml to 1 ng/ml requires two half-lives. Total time = 2 half-lives × 40 hours/half-life = 80 hours.

questions.stem: A patient undergoing cancer chemotherapy developed thrombocytopenia. Which of the following drugs is used to promote recovery from chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation: Oprelvekin Chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia (a low platelet count) can be treated with thrombopoietic growth factors that stimulate platelet production in the bone marrow. Oprelvekin is a recombinant form of interleukin-11 (IL-11), a cytokine that stimulates the proliferation of hematopoietic progenitor cells and the maturation of megakaryocytes, the cells that produce platelets. This leads to an increase in the peripheral platelet count. Epoetin (A) is erythropoietin, which stimulates red blood cell production. Filgrastim (C) is a granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) that stimulates neutrophil production. Amifostine (D) is a cytoprotective agent used to reduce certain toxicities of chemotherapy but does not stimulate hematopoiesis.

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs acts as both an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor and a neprilysin inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Omapatrilat Omapatrilat is a vasopeptidase inhibitor, a class of drugs designed to inhibit both angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and neprilysin simultaneously. By inhibiting ACE, it reduces the production of the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II. By inhibiting neprilysin, it increases the levels of vasodilating natriuretic peptides. This dual action provides potent blood pressure reduction. Sacubitril (B) is a neprilysin inhibitor, but it is combined with an angiotensin receptor blocker (valsartan), not an ACE inhibitor, to avoid the high incidence of angioedema associated with omapatrilat. Enalapril (C) is solely an ACE inhibitor, and candesartan (D) is an angiotensin receptor blocker. 29. Which drug is the treatment of choice for dialysis disequilibrium syndrome? NODIA

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with easy fatigability. The mother reports that the child becomes very hungry between meals but recovers after eating. Liver examination shows no glycogen storage. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glycogen synthase The clinical presentation of fasting hypoglycemia (fatigue and hunger between meals) that is relieved by feeding, combined with the definitive finding of an absence of glycogen in the liver, points to a defect in glycogen synthesis. The key enzyme responsible for creating glycogen from glucose is glycogen synthase. A deficiency in this enzyme (Glycogen Storage Disease Type 0) means the liver cannot store glucose as glycogen after a meal. As a result, during a fast, the liver has no glycogen stores to break down (glycogenolysis) to maintain blood glucose levels, leading to hypoglycemia. Deficiencies in branching (A) or debranching (B) enzymes lead to abnormal glycogen structures, not absence. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (C) leads to a massive accumulation of normal glycogen. PATHOLOGY

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with fatigue and weakness. Peripheral blood smear shows the findings illustrated below. What is the most likely genetic change associated with this patient?
questions.explanation: T(15,17) The peripheral blood smear in the image shows numerous abnormal promyelocytes containing heavy cytoplasmic granules and likely Auer rods. This appearance is characteristic of Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL), a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia. Patients with APL commonly present with symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, anemia, and bleeding tendencies due to bone marrow failure and coagulopathy. The most common genetic abnormality associated with APL is the translocation t(15;17). This translocation occurs between chromosome 15 and chromosome 17 and results in the fusion of the PML gene on chromosome 15 with the RARA (retinoic acid receptor alpha) gene on chromosome 17. The resulting PML-RARA fusion protein blocks the normal differentiation of myeloid precursor cells at the promyelocyte stage, leading to accumulation of abnormal promyelocytes in the bone marrow and peripheral blood. This genetic defect is clinically important because APL is highly responsive to targeted therapy. Treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) or arsenic trioxide helps overcome the differentiation block, allowing the leukemic promyelocytes to mature into normal cells. Therefore, the correct answer is (B) t(15;17), which is the hallmark cytogenetic abnormality of Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old patient presents with lymphadenopathy. On examination, generalized lymphadenopathy is noted without organomegaly. Peripheral blood smear shows lymphocytosis with smudge cells. What is the next appropriate step in the diagnostic workup?
questions.explanation: Flow cytometry This clinical presentation is highly characteristic of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL), a malignancy of mature B-lymphocytes. Key features include an older patient, generalized lymphadenopathy, significant lymphocytosis, and the presence of smudge cells (fragile neoplastic lymphocytes) on the peripheral smear. The gold standard and essential next step to confirm the diagnosis is immunophenotyping by flow cytometry on the peripheral blood. This test identifies a monoclonal population of B-cells expressing a unique pattern of surface markers (typically CD19, CD20-dim, CD5, and CD23). This confirms the clonality and specific cell type, establishing the diagnosis of CLL without initially needing more invasive procedures like a bone marrow (BM) examination or lymph node biopsy, which are reserved for atypical cases or staging.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents to the outpatient department with swelling of the jaw. On examination, cytopenias are noted, and bone marrow aspiration shows the cells depicted below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Burkitts lymphoma This combination of features—a jaw mass in a child (a classic location for endemic Burkitts), cytopenias indicating bone marrow infiltration, and the characteristic cell morphology—is pathognomonic for Burkitts lymphoma/leukemia. The bone marrow aspirate shows uniform, medium-sized lymphoblasts with round nuclei, stippled chromatin, and, most distinctively, intensely basophilic cytoplasm filled with prominent lipid vacuoles. This morphology is classified as L3 in the FAB system. Burkitts lymphoma is an extremely aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Follicular lymphoma (A) is a low-grade lymphoma typically found in adults. Adult T-cell leukemia (B) is also rare in children. Infectious mononucleosis (D) features reactive atypical lymphocytes, not a uniform population of malignant blasts.

questions.stem: Identify the structure in the below histology slide?
questions.explanation: Glomerulus The histology slide clearly shows the microscopic architecture of the kidney cortex. The prominent, ball-like structures are glomeruli, which are tufts of capillaries responsible for the initial filtration of blood. Each glomerulus is surrounded by Bowmans capsule and is interspersed among numerous cross-sections of renal tubules. This appearance is uniquely characteristic of the kidney. Islets of Langerhans (A) are endocrine cell clusters found in the pancreas. A lymph node (C) has a distinct architecture with follicles and sinuses. Hassalls corpuscles (D) are structures found only in the medulla of the thymus. The image is unequivocally a view of the renal cortex, and the identified structures are glomeruli.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements are true regarding the relative risk associated with Mendelian patterns of inheritance?
questions.explanation: 1/4 autosomal recessive This question asks for the correct recurrence risk for an affected child in a typical Mendelian inheritance scenario. For an autosomal recessive disorder, an affected child (genotype aa) is most commonly born to two heterozygous carrier parents (genotype Aa). In such a cross (Aa x Aa), the probability for each pregnancy is as follows: a 1 in 4 chance of having an affected child (aa), a 2 in 4 (or 1/2) chance of having an unaffected carrier child (Aa), and a 1 in 4 chance of having an unaffected, non-carrier child (AA). Therefore, the risk of having another child affected with the same autosomal recessive condition is 1/4 or 25%. The other options are incorrect for standard Mendelian patterns.
