questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman diagnosed with stage IIB carcinoma of the cervix is planned for treatment with radiotherapy. Which of the following statements regarding ionizing radiation is correct?

options.text: The normal cell & cancer cell will be equally sensitive
Gl mucosa is more resistant part
The radiation at a point is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source
Small blood vessels are resistant to the effect of radiation

questions.explanation: The radiation at a point is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source This question tests a fundamental principle of physics as it applies to radiation therapy. The Inverse Square Law states that the intensity of radiation from a point source decreases with the square of the distance from that source. This means that if you double the distance from the radiation source, the dose received at that point will be reduced to one-quarter. This principle is critically important in radiotherapy for treatment planning and for radiation safety, as it explains why small changes in distance can have a large effect on the radiation dose delivered to the tumor and surrounding healthy tissues. The other statements are false: cancer cells are generally more sensitive than normal cells (A), GI mucosa is highly sensitive (B), and small blood vessels are also sensitive to radiation (D).

questions.stem: A CT scan of a 50-year-old patient who presented with abdominal pain is shown below. Which of the following statements regarding this CT finding is correct?
questions.explanation: Etiology is echinococcus spp. The axial CT scan shows a very large, well-encapsulated, multiseptated cystic lesion in the liver. A key feature is the presence of multiple smaller daughter cysts within the larger mother cyst. This appearance is pathognomonic for a hydatid cyst, which is caused by infection with the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. The statement that the etiology is Echinococcus species is therefore correct. Surgery is one treatment option but is not always mandatory; medical therapy or percutaneous techniques (PAIR) can also be used. Fine-needle aspiration or cytology (FNAC) is generally contraindicated due to the high risk of anaphylactic shock and peritoneal dissemination of protoscolices if the cyst ruptures.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presented with non-axial proptosis of the left eye for the past three years. She had a history of ocular trauma 10 years earlier. Imaging showed a homogeneous lesion in the left frontal sinus, as seen in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Frontal mucocele The CT scan shows a well-defined, homogenous, non-enhancing, expansile lesion completely filling and expanding the left frontal sinus. This lesion is eroding the bony walls of the sinus and extending inferiorly into the orbit, causing proptosis (protrusion of the eyeball). This is the classic radiological appearance of a frontal sinus mucocele. A mucocele is an accumulation of mucoid secretions and desquamated epithelium within a para nasal sinus, caused by obstruction of the sinus ostium. This obstruction can be a result of chronic inflammation, polyps, or, as in this patients history, previous trauma. The slow, expansile growth leads to bone remodeling and displacement of adjacent structures like the orbit.

questions.stem: A radiograph of a 10-year-old boy with knee pain for the past three months is shown below. There is no definite history of trauma. Which of the following statements regarding the diagnosis and management is correct?

options.text: Avulsion fracture of patella- tension band wiring
Bipartite patella- Do radiograph of the other knee
Avulsion fracture of patella- Inter fragmentary screw fixation

questions.explanation: Bipartite patella- Do radiograph of the other knee The radiograph shows what appears to be a fracture line at the superolateral pole of the patella. However, the fragment has smooth, well-corticated (rounded) edges, which is not typical for an acute fracture. This appearance is characteristic of a bipartite patella, which is a normal congenital variant where a secondary ossification center of the patella fails to fuse with the main body. It is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally. A key step to confirm that this is a developmental variant and not a fracture is to obtain a radiograph of the contralateral (other) knee, as a bipartite patella is bilateral in about 40-50% of cases. Finding a similar appearance in the other knee would confirm the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks of gestation presented with complaints of difficulty in breathing and walking. Fetal movements were normal. On examination, the abdomen was tense but non-tender, and the symphysis–fundal height measured 41 cm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Polyhydramnios The clinical findings are highly suggestive of polyhydramnios, which is an excessive amount of amniotic fluid. The key finding is the significant discrepancy between the gestational age (32 weeks) and the symphysial-fundal height (41 cm), indicating a uterus that is much larger than expected. The tense abdomen and the patients symptoms of dyspnea (difficulty breathing, due to the enlarged uterus pushing up on the diaphragm) and difficulty walking are also classic consequences of the increased intra-abdominal pressure from the excess fluid. Fetal parts are often difficult to palpate in cases of polyhydramnios, and the fetal heart sound may be muffled. Oligohydramnios (B) is a deficiency of amniotic fluid and would present with a uterus that is small for dates.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea has normal breast development but absent pubic and axillary hair. Bilateral inguinal masses are palpable. Ultrasonography shows absence of the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. Which of the following best explains this clinical scenario?
questions.explanation: Complete AIS This constellation of findings is classic for Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS). These individuals are genetically male (46,XY). They have testes (the bilateral inguinal masses) which produce normal male levels of testosterone. However, due to a defect in the androgen receptor, their bodies are completely unable to respond to testosterone. The testosterone is peripherally converted to estrogen, which results in the development of normal female breasts. Since there is no response to androgens, Wolffian ducts regress, and male external genitalia do not form. The testes still produce anti-Müllerian hormone, which causes the regression of Müllerian structures, hence the absence of the uterus and fallopian tubes. The lack of androgen effect also explains the scant or absent pubic and axillary hair.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman scheduled for a total laparoscopic hysterectomy expressed concern and asked her gynecologist about the procedure. What is the main disadvantage of a total laparoscopic hysterectomy?
questions.explanation: Increased chances of Bladder injury Compared to traditional abdominal hysterectomy, total laparoscopic hysterectomy (TLH) offers numerous advantages, including less blood loss, shorter hospital stays, and less postoperative pain. However, the laparoscopic approach is associated with a unique set of potential complications. Due to the need to dissect the cervix away from the bladder using electrosurgical instruments in a space with limited tactile feedback, there is a slightly increased risk of thermal or direct injury to the urinary tract, particularly the bladder. While the overall complication rate is low in experienced hands, bladder injury is a recognized disadvantage when compared to the abdominal approach, where the anatomy can be more directly visualized and palpated.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old woman was diagnosed with carcinoma of the cervix. On clinical examination, a necrotic cervical lesion was found extending into the parametrium. What is the appropriate management for this stage of cervical cancer?
questions.explanation: Chemoradiation The patient has been diagnosed with cervical cancer that has extended into the parametrium (the connective tissue adjacent to the uterus). According to the FIGO staging system for cervical cancer, parametrial involvement signifies at least Stage IIB disease. For locally advanced cervical cancer (Stage IIB through IVA), the standard of care and the treatment that offers the best survival outcomes is definitive chemoradiation. This involves a course of external beam radiation therapy to the pelvis, often combined with brachytherapy (internal radiation), given concurrently with a platinum-based chemotherapy agent (typically cisplatin). The chemotherapy acts as a radiosensitizer, making the cancer cells more susceptible to the effects of radiation. Surgery is not the primary treatment for this stage of disease.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old female who was sexually active with multiple sexual partners presents with swelling in the wall of labia majora. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bartholin abscess The Bartholins glands are located in the posterolateral aspect of the vaginal vestibule, at the base of the labia majora. Their function is to secrete mucus for lubrication. If the duct of one of these glands becomes blocked, fluid can accumulate, forming a cyst. If this cyst becomes infected, it develops into a Bartholin abscess. This presents as a tender, fluctuant, erythematous swelling in the labia majora. The infection is often polymicrobial and can be associated with sexually transmitted pathogens, making a history of multiple sexual partners a risk factor. Gartners cysts are located on the anterolateral wall of the vagina. Trichomoniasis causes a vaginal discharge, and cystic fibrosis is a systemic disease. DERMATOLOGY

questions.stem: An obese woman presented with facial acne that did not improve despite appropriate medical treatment. What is the most likely underlying cause of her persistent acne?
questions.explanation: PCOS The combination of obesity and persistent, treatment-resistant acne in a female should raise suspicion for an underlying endocrine disorder, specifically Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is a common hormonal disorder characterized by hyperandrogenism (excess male hormones), ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology. The excess androgens are responsible for the clinical signs of hirsutism (excess hair growth) and persistent acne. The acne is often inflammatory and located on the lower face and jawline. Obesity is also a very common feature of PCOS and contributes to insulin resistance, which can exacerbate the hypermodernism. While diet and cosmetics can influence acne, a persistent case unresponsive to standard treatment warrants investigation for PCOS.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with a known history of HIV infection presented with a painful lesion on the palate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kaposi sarcoma Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an AIDS-defining illness. It is a vascular tumor caused by Human Herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8). While it most commonly presents as purplish, non-blanching macules, papules, or nodules on the skin, it can also affect mucosal surfaces. The hard palate is the most common intraoral site for KS. Oral lesions can be painful, especially if they become ulcerated, and can interfere with eating. In an HIV-positive patient, the appearance of a pigmented, painful lesion on the palate is highly suggestive of Kaposi sarcoma. Squamous cell carcinoma is also possible but KS is more specific to this clinical context.

questions.stem: Which chemical causes following allergic reaction
questions.explanation: PPD The image shows a delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction on the skin, which is the basis of patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis and tests like the Mantoux test. PPD (Purified Protein Derivative) is the substance used in the Mantoux test to screen for tuberculosis. When injected intradermally into an individual who has been previously sensitized to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, it elicits a classic Type IV hypersensitivity reaction, which manifests as an indurated, erythematous papule after 48-72 hours, similar to a positive patch test reaction. Balsam of Peru (C) is a common contact allergen, but PPD is the classic example of a substance that induces this type of immunologic reaction for diagnostic purposes. Pollen (A) typically causes Type I hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., hay fever). NODIA

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman has difficulty performing daily activities and presents with resting tremors, rigidity, visual hallucinations, and episodes of staring into space. Lewy bodies are identified on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dementia with Lewy bodies The patient presents with resting tremors, rigidity, visual hallucinations, and cognitive impairment affecting daily activities, which are key features of Dementia with Lewy bodies. This condition is characterized by the presence of Lewy bodies in neurons of the brain. Lewy bodies are abnormal protein aggregates mainly composed of Alpha-synuclein. Their accumulation leads to neuronal degeneration, especially in the cerebral cortex and brainstem. Clinically, dementia with Lewy bodies presents with a combination of cognitive decline, fluctuating attention, recurrent visual hallucinations, and parkinsonian motor features such as tremor and rigidity. A distinguishing feature of this disease is early visual hallucinations and fluctuating cognition, which helps differentiate it from Alzheimer disease, where memory loss is usually the earliest symptom. Although Parkinson disease also has Lewy bodies, dementia typically develops later in its course. Thus, the combination of parkinsonian symptoms, dementia, hallucinations, and Lewy bodies strongly indicates Dementia with Lewy bodies. ************** Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: A patient presented with bone deformities along with associated skin lesions, as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fibrous Dysplasia The radiograph shows a shepherds crook deformity of the proximal femur, with an expansile, ground-glass appearance of the bone. This is a classic finding in fibrous dysplasia, a benign bone disorder where normal bone is replaced by fibrous tissue. The combination of bone deformities and skin lesions is highly suggestive of McCune-Albright syndrome, a specific form of polyostotic (multiple bone) fibrous dysplasia. This syndrome is defined by the triad of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, endocrine abnormalities (like precocious puberty), and characteristic café-au-lait skin macules. These skin lesions are typically large, unilateral, and have irregular coast of Maine borders.

questions.stem: Identify the fracture seen in the given radiograph that results in inability to dorsiflex the foot.
questions.explanation: Fibula fracture The inability to dorsiflex the foot (foot drop) is caused by an injury to the common peroneal (fibular) nerve. This nerve is anatomically vulnerable as it winds around the neck of the fibula. The radiograph shows an ankle fracture, but the question implies a fracture at a location that would cause foot drop. A fracture of the proximal fibula, specifically at the fibular neck, is a common cause of common peroneal nerve palsy. Therefore, among the choices, a fibula fracture (specifically, a proximal one) is the injury that would lead to an inability to dorsiflex the foot. The image itself shows a distal tibiofibular fracture, which doesnt typically cause foot drop unless there is a compartment syndrome, but based on the text of the question, fibular neck fracture is the intended answer.

questions.stem: A pediatric patient presented with a swelling over the head that has been present since birth (for the past two months). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cephalhematoma This question describes a head swelling in a newborn. Caput succedaneum is edema of the scalp that is present at birth, pits on pressure, and importantly, crosses suture lines. It resolves within a few days. A cephalhematoma, on the other hand, is a subperiosteal collection of blood. It appears a few hours after birth, is firm, and is strictly limited by the suture lines of the skull bone it overlies. Critically, a cephalhematoma can take several weeks to months to resolve. The history of a swelling that has been present for 2 months since birth makes caput succedaneum impossible. This prolonged duration is highly characteristic of a cephalhematoma, which may even calcify over time.

questions.stem: A construction worker developed a persistent cough and shortness of breath and was later diagnosed with mesothelioma. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis or cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: Asbestosis The development of mesothelioma, a rare and aggressive cancer of the pleura, is almost exclusively linked to prior exposure to asbestos. Construction work is a high-risk occupation for asbestos exposure. The patients respiratory symptoms (cough and shortness of breath) are likely due to the underlying interstitial lung disease caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibers, which is known as asbestosis. Asbestosis is a form of pulmonary fibrosis. Therefore, the overall diagnosis, encompassing both the benign fibrotic lung disease and the resulting malignancy, is asbestosis. While the patient also has cancer, the term asbestosis refers to the underlying pneumoconiosis that led to the development of mesothelioma. PSYCHIATRY

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with recurrent episodes of anxiety, palpitations, sweating, breathlessness, chest pain, and a feeling of impending doom, as if she were having a heart attack. These episodes occur 5–6 times per month, last about 30 minutes each, and have been ongoing for six months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Panic disorder The patient is describing discrete, recurrent episodes of intense fear or discomfort that have an abrupt onset and peak within minutes. The symptoms she experiences during these episodes—palpitations, sweating, breathlessness, chest pain, and a fear of d ying (feeling of impending doom)—are classic symptoms of a panic attack. The diagnosis of Panic Disorder is made when an indivi dual experiences recurrent, unexpected panic attacks, followed by at least one month of persistent concern about having additional attacks or their consequences. Her history of 5-6 episodes per month for the past 6 months fits this diagnosis perfectly. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) involves chronic, pervasive worry, not discrete attacks.

questions.stem: A male patient with a history of marital conflicts presented with complaints of premature ejaculation. Which of the following non- pharmacological methods can be useful in managing this condition?
questions.explanation: Squeeze technique Premature (early) ejaculation is a common male sexual dysfunction. A cornerstone of non-pharmacological, behavioral therapy for this condition is the squeeze technique, developed by Masters and Johnson. This technique involves the man or his partner stimulating the penis until he feels the urge to ejaculate. At that point, the partner firmly squeezes the head of the penis for several seconds, which diminishes the ejaculatory urge. This process is repeated multiple times before allowing ejaculation to occur. The goal is to help the man gain better awareness of his pre-ejaculatory sensations and develop voluntary control over the ejaculatory reflex. Sensate focus (D) is a technique used more for arousal disorders and erectile dysfunction. 196. A patient diagnosed with schizophrenia did not respond to treatment with haloperidol and thioridazine. He was started on another NODIA

questions.stem: A patient with tuberculosis on isoniazid therapy for six months presents with tingling and paresthesia. Deficiency of which vitamin is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 A well-known side effect of the anti-tuberculosis drug isoniazid (INH) is a dose-dependent peripheral neuropathy, which presents with symptoms like tingling, numbness, and paresthesias in a glove and stocking distribution. This neurotoxicity occurs because isoniazid structurally resembles vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) and interferes with its metabolism. INH increases the excretion of vitamin B6 and inhibits the enzyme pyridoxine phosphokinase, which is necessary to convert pyridoxine into its active form, pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (PLP). PLP is an essential cofactor for numerous enzymatic reactions, including the synthesis of neurotransmitters. The resulting deficiency of active vitamin B6 leads to the development of peripheral neuropathy. To prevent this complication, it is standard practice to co-administer prophylactic pyridoxine supplementation to all patients receiving isoniazid therapy.

questions.stem: Which vitamin deficiency is responsible for the condition shown in the image?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A The image shows a foamy, whitish patch on the conjunctiva of the eye, which is characteristic of Bitot’s spots. Bitot’s spots are a classical ocular manifestation of Vitamin A deficiency. Vitamin A plays an essential role in maintaining normal vision, epithelial integrity, and immune function. In the eye, it is required for the formation of rhodopsin, a pigment present in the rod cells of the retina that helps in vision under dim light. When there is a deficiency of Vitamin A, several eye changes collectively known as xerophthalmia develop. One of the earliest symptoms is night blindness (nyctalopia), where the person has difficulty seeing in low light. As the deficiency progresses, the conjunctiva becomes dry (conjunctival xerosis) and Bitot’s spots appear as triangular, foamy, keratinized patches on the bulbar conjunctiva, as seen in the image. If untreated, the condition can progress to corneal xerosis, keratomalacia, and eventually blindness. Other options are incorrect because Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets/osteomalacia, Vitamin E deficiency causes neurological problems, and Vitamin K deficiency leads to bleeding disorders. Therefore, the condition shown is due to Vitamin A deficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following enzyme activities measured in red blood cells can be used to diagnose vitamin B₂ deficiency?
questions.explanation: Glutathione reductase The functional status of several vitamins can be assessed by measuring the activity of a vitamin-dependent enzyme in red blood cells (RBCs), both with and without the addition of the vitamin's active coenzyme form. For Vitamin B2 (riboflavin), the key enzyme is erythrocyte glutathione reductase (EGR). This enzyme is crucial for reducing oxidized glutathione (GSSG) to its reduced form (GSH), which is essential for protecting the cell against oxidative damage. EGR requires flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), the active coenzyme form of riboflavin, to function. In a riboflavin-deficient individual, the EGR enzyme will be undersaturated with FAD, and its basal activity will be low. When FAD is added to the assay in vitro, the enzyme activity increases significantly. The extent of this stimulation (the EGR activity coefficient or EGRAC) is a sensitive and specific functional marker of riboflavin status. Transketolase (B) is used to assess thiamine (B1) status.

questions.stem: A woman on antidepressant therapy presents with bleeding and reports bulky, greasy stools that stick to the toilet pan. Deficiency of which vitamin is most likely responsible for the bleeding in this condition?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K The patient's history of bulky, fatty stools that stick to the pan is descriptive of steatorrhea, which is the malabsorption of fat. Several of the older antidepressants, particularly tricyclics, can have anticholinergic effects that reduce gut motility, potentially contributing to malabsorption. Steatorrhea impairs the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, which include A, D, E, and K. Vitamin K is an essential cofactor for the enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which is required for the synthesis of several crucial blood coagulation factors (Factors II, VII, IX, and X) in the liver. A deficiency of vitamin K leads to the production of inactive clotting factors and a resultant coagulopathy, manifesting as an elevated prothrombin time (PT) and an increased tendency for bleeding. Therefore, in a patient with fat malabsorption, a bleeding diathesis is most likely caused by Vitamin K deficiency.

questions.stem: A paint shopkeeper presents with anemia. Inhibition of which enzyme is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: ALA Dehydratase Inhibition of both enzymes impairs heme synthesis, which is a necessary component of hemoglobin, resulting in a microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Between the choices given, ALA dehydratase is a primary target of lead toxicity.

questions.stem: Primaquine can precipitate hemolytic anemia in individuals with a specific enzyme deficiency. This enzyme is associated with which metabolic pathway?
questions.explanation: HMP shunt The antimalarial drug primaquine is an oxidizing agent. In individuals with a deficiency of the enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), administration of primaquine can trigger an acute hemolytic crisis. G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme of the Hexose Monophosphate (HMP) shunt, also known as the pentose phosphate pathway. The primary function of the HMP shunt in red blood cells is to produce NADPH. NADPH is essential for maintaining a supply of reduced glutathione (GSH) via the enzyme glutathione reductase. Reduced glutathione is a critical antioxidant that protects the red blood cell from oxidative damage. In G6PD-deficient individuals, NADPH production is impaired. When exposed to an oxidizing drug like primaquine, the red cells cannot cope with the oxidative stress, leading to hemoglobin denaturation (Heinz bodies) and subsequent hemolysis.

questions.stem: Which of the following proteins is involved in DNA packaging?
questions.explanation: Histones In eukaryotic cells, the vast amount of DNA must be tightly and efficiently packaged to fit within the nucleus. This packaging is accomplished by a group of small, basic proteins known as histones. The fundamental unit of this packaging is the nucleosome, which consists of a segment of DNA wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins (an octamer containing two copies each of histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4). Another histone, H1, acts as a linker, helping to coil the nucleosomes into a more compact structure called a chromatin fiber. This hierarchical coiling and folding allows for the extreme condensation of DNA into visible chromosomes during mitosis. Chaperones (B) assist in protein folding. Cyclins (C) are proteins that regulate the cell cycle. Albumin (D) is a major plasma protein.

questions.stem: Identify the acid base disorder in a patient with the following values : pH - 7.2, pO 2 - 90 mm of Hg, pCO 2 - 80 mm of Hg, Bicarbonate - 35 meq/L.
questions.explanation: Respiratory acidosis To interpret these arterial blood gas (ABG) values, we follow a systematic approach : 1. Look at the pH : The pH is 7.2, which is lower than the normal range of 7.35-7.45. This indicates an acidosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following facilitates the transport of fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane for their utilization within mitochondria?
questions.explanation: Carnitine Beta-oxidation, the process of breaking down fatty acids to produce energy, occurs within the mitochondrial matrix. However, long-chain fatty acids cannot freely cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. They require a specific transport system known as the carnitine shuttle. First, the fatty acid is activated in the cytoplasm to form a fatty acyl-CoA. Then, the enzyme carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT1), located on the outer mitochondrial membrane, transfers the acyl group from CoA to carnitine, forming acylcarnitine. The acylcarnitine is then transported across the inner mitochondrial membrane by a translocase. Once inside the matrix, the enzyme carnitine palmitoyltransferase II (CPT2) transfers the acyl group back to CoA, regenerating fatty acyl-CoA for beta-oxidation and freeing carnitine to be shuttled back out. Malate (A) is part of another shuttle. Acyl carrier protein (D) is involved in fatty acid synthesis. 23. Which of the following acts as an inhibitor of Complex IV ?

questions.stem: Identify the cartilage.
questions.explanation: Fibrous The image provided is a micrograph of fibrous cartilage, also known as fibrocartilage. Here's how we can identify it : 1. Prominent Collagen Fibers : The most distinct feature is the presence of thick, parallel bundles of collagen fibers running through the matrix. These are the wavy, light-pink bands visible in the image. 2. Arrangement of Chondrocytes : The cartilage cells, called chondrocytes, are typically arranged in rows, nestled in lacunae between the dense collagen bundles. You can see the small, dark dots (the cell nuclei) aligned in rows following the direction of the fibers. 3. This structure provides immense tensile strength and the ability to absorb compressive shock. You can find fibrous cartilage in places like the intervertebral discs, the pubic symphysis, and the menisci of the knee. Why Not the Other Options? A. Hyaline Cartilage : Has a smooth, glassy-looking matrix because its fine collagen fibers are not visible under a standard light microscope. C. Articular Cartilage : This is a specific type of hyaline cartilage that covers the surfaces of bones in joints. Its appearance is hyaline, not fibrous. D. Elastic Cartilage : Contains a dense network of branching elastic fibers, which give it a more web-like appearance and require special stains to be seen clearly. Its structure provides flexibility and is found in the external ear and epiglottis.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding a cystometrogram?

options.text: Dotted line represents pressure with no micturition
Segment Ia denotes pressure due to residual urine
Vertical line indicates pressure at constant volume

questions.explanation: Segment Ib represents Laplace law The cystometrogram plots intravesical pressure against the volume of fluid in the bladder. 1. Segment Ia shows a brief initial rise in pressure as the bladder begins to fill. 2. Segment Ib is a long, flat phase where the bladder accommodates a large increase in volume with very little change in pressure. This ability to maintain low pressure despite increasing volume is a property of the bladder's viscoelastic wall and is explained by the Law of Laplace (Pressure = 2 × Tension / Radius). As the bladder fills and its radius increases, the wall tension also increases, keeping the pressure relatively constant. 3. Segment II (the vertical line) shows a sharp, significant rise in pressure as the micturition reflex is triggered and the detrusor muscle contracts powerfully. This is a change in pressure at a nearly constant volume. 4. Therefore, statement (A) is correct. The vertical line (D) is a pressure rise, not pressure at a constant volume.

questions.stem: Hemiballismus is associated with a lesion of which nucleus?
questions.explanation: Subthalamic Hemiballismus is a rare hyperkinetic movement disorder characterized by involuntary, violent, flinging movements of the limbs on one side of the body (contralateral to the lesion). The classic cause of hemiballismus is a lesion, most commonly a lacunar stroke or hemorrhage, affecting the subthalamic nucleus (STN). The STN is a key component of the basal ganglia's indirect pathway, which normally functions to inhibit unwanted movements. A lesion in the STN disrupts this pathway, leading to reduced inhibitory output from the basal ganglia to the thalamus. This disinhibition of the thalamocortical pathway results in the release of the uncontrolled, large-amplitude, ballistic movements that are characteristic of the disorder. While other basal ganglia nuclei are involved in motor control, the subthalamic nucleus is the specific anatomical structure most directly linked to hemiballismus. BIOCHEMISTRY

questions.stem: A young boy experiences difficulty breathing while running, is unable to rise from a squatting position, and has splenomegaly. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Gaucher's disease The combination of splenomegaly, difficulty rising from a squatting position (suggesting muscle weakness or bone involvement), and difficulty breathing on exertion (which can be due to anemia or pulmonary infiltration) points towards a systemic storage disorder. Gaucher's disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and fits this clinical picture. It is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase, leading to the accumulation of glucocerebroside in macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system. This results in massive hepatosplenomegaly, bone marrow infiltration causing anemia, thrombocytopenia, and bone pain/fractures (explaining the weakness), and sometimes pulmonary involvement. Tay-Sachs disease (A) is primarily a neurodegenerative disorder. Fabry's disease (C) involves pain crises, angiokeratomas, and renal failure. Krabbe's disease (D) is a rapidly progressive infantile neurodegenerative disorder. 13. A child presents with anemia and thrombocytopenia, with hepatosplenomegaly on examination and complaints of bone pain. Light microscopy shows a crumpled tissue

questions.stem: A patient undergoes cystoscopy revealing multiple yellow-white plaques in the bladder, with a history of fever and recurrent cystitis. Biopsy shows infiltration of the lamina propria as depicted below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Malakoplakia The combination of cystoscopic findings (yellowish plaques) and the specific histopathological features is pathognomonic for malakoplakia. Malakoplakia is a rare, chronic granulomatous inflammatory condition that most commonly affects the urinary bladder, often in the setting of recurrent E. coli infections. The histological hallmark is the presence of a dense infiltrate of large macrophages with abundant granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm, known as von Hansemann cells. Crucially, within the cytoplasm of these macrophages are characteristic laminated, calcified, targetoid inclusions called Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. These bodies represent calcified, undigested bacterial fragments within phagolysosomes, reflecting a defect in macrophage function. Interstitial cystitis (A) shows mast cell infiltrates, while acute (C) and chronic (D) cystitis show neutrophilic and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, respectively, without these specific cells or bodies.

questions.stem: Identify the marked structure in the image below.
questions.explanation: Islet of Langerhans The marked structure in the image represents an Islet of Langerhans, which is found in the pancreas. In histological sections of the pancreas, two main components are visible: the exocrine part (pancreatic acini) and the endocrine part (Islets of Langerhans). The Islets of Langerhans appear as lighter-stained, rounded clusters of cells scattered within the darker-staining pancreatic acinar tissue. The surrounding darker cells are the exocrine acinar cells, which produce digestive enzymes such as amylase, lipase, and proteases. These endocrine islets contain different types of hormone-secreting cells. Beta (β) cells secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose levels. Alpha (α) cells produce glucagon, which increases blood glucose. Delta (δ) cells secrete somatostatin, while PP cells produce pancreatic polypeptide. The pale circular area indicated by the arrow lacks the typical acinar arrangement and shows endocrine cell clusters with rich capillary networks, which is characteristic of an Islet of Langerhans. The other options are incorrect because salivary glands show serous or mucous acini, lymph nodes have lymphoid follicles, and the spleen shows red pulp and white pulp structures.

questions.stem: Which of the following features is not observed in MEN type 2B?
questions.explanation: Parathyroid Adenoma Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B) is a rare, autosomal dominant syndrome caused by a specific mutation in the RET proto-oncogene. It has a characteristic constellation of features. The three core components are : 1. Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC) : Occurs in nearly 100% of cases and is more aggressive than in MEN 2A. 2. Pheochromocytoma : Occurs in about 50% of cases. 3. Distinctive physical features : These include multiple mucosal neuromas (C) on the lips, tongue, and eyelids; a tall, slender Marfanoid habitus (D); and intestinal ganglioneuromatosis, which can lead to complications like constipation or toxic megacolon (B). Parathyroid adenoma/hyperplasia (A), which causes primary hyperparathyroidism, is a hallmark feature of MEN 2A, but it is characteristically absent in MEN 2B. This is a key feature used to differentiate the two syndromes.

questions.stem: A woodcutter sustains an injury while cutting wood in the forest. The sample shows sclerotic bodies with a copper-penny appearance on staining. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chromoblastomycosis The history describes a traumatic inoculation injury in a person with occupational exposure to soil and plant material. The key diagnostic finding is the microscopic appearance of sclerotic bodies, also known as Medlar bodies or copper pennies. These are thick-walled, round, brownish, multicellular structures that divide by internal septation (sclerosis) rather than budding. The presence of sclerotic bodies in tissue is the pathognomonic hallmark of chromoblastomycosis. This is a chronic, localized fungal infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue caused by several different pigmented (dematiaceous) fungi. Clinically, it presents as slow-growing, verrucous (wart-like), crusted nodules or plaques. Phaeohyphomycosis (A) is another infection by pigmented fungi, but it is characterized by the presence of yeast-like cells or hyphae in tissue, not sclerotic bodies. Sporotrichosis (C) forms asteroid bodies, and mycetoma (D) forms granules.

questions.stem: A 28 year old lady with HBsAg positive, IgM HBc positive, IgG HBs and IgG HBe negative, Anti HCV negative. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute HBV infection Let's interpret the hepatitis B serology panel : 1. HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) positive : This indicates that the person is currently infected with the hepatitis B virus (HBV). 2. IgM HBc (IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen) positive : This is the key marker for an acute infection. The IgM antibody is the first antibody to appear after infection and typically persists for about 6 months. Its presence signifies a recent or new infection. 3. IgG HBs (Antibody to HBsAg) negative : This means the patient has not recovered from the infection and has not developed protective immunity. 4. IgG HBe (Antibody to HBeAg) negative : This indicates the infection is likely in the active replicative phase. 5. The combination of a positive HBsAg and a positive IgM anti-HBc is diagnostic of acute HBV infection. In chronic HBV infection (B), IgM anti-HBc would be negative, and IgG anti-HBc would be positive.

questions.stem: A patient admitted for sepsis receives prolonged antibiotic therapy and subsequently develops diarrhea and dehydration. Which investigation is preferred in this case?
questions.explanation: GDH Ag and Exotoxins The patient's history of hospital admission, long-term antibiotic use, and subsequent development of diarrhea is a classic scenario for Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI). Antibiotic therapy disrupts the normal gut flora, allowing C. difficile to overgrow and produce toxins. The diagnosis of CDI requires demonstrating the presence of the organism and/or its toxins in the stool. Current guidelines recommend a multi-step algorithm for diagnosis. The best initial approach is to simultaneously test for both the glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) antigen and the C. difficile toxins (Toxin A and Toxin B). GDH is an enzyme produced by all C. difficile strains (both toxigenic and non-toxigenic), making it a very sensitive screening test. Toxin detection (usually by an enzyme immunoassay or a nucleic acid amplification test like PCR for the toxin genes) is highly specific for clinically significant disease. Combining these two tests provides the best diagnostic accuracy.

questions.stem: A woman presents with curdy white vaginal discharge. Microscopy of the sample shows budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae. Which medium is used to differentiate the species of the causative organism?
questions.explanation: Chromagar The clinical presentation of a curdy white vaginal discharge and the microscopic finding of budding yeasts and pseudohyphae are classic for vulvovaginal candidiasis, most commonly caused by Candida albicans. While C. albicans is the most frequent species, other species like C. glabrata or C. tropicalis can also cause infection and may be resistant to standard antifungal agents. CHROMagar Candida is a selective and differential culture medium specifically designed for the rapid identification of different Candida species. It contains chromogenic substrates that are metabolized by species-specific enzymes, resulting in the colonies of different species growing in distinct, characteristic colors. For example, C. albicans typically grows as green colonies, C. tropicalis as blue colonies, and C. krusei as pink, fuzzy colonies. Sabouraud Dextrose Agar (SDA) (A) is a general-purpose medium for fungal growth but does not differentiate species.

questions.stem: A patient is receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Which of the following is the most appropriate method to monitor the effectiveness of this treatment?
questions.explanation: Monitoring viral load The primary goal of Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) is to suppress the replication of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) as much as possible. Therefore, the most important and direct measure of the effectiveness of HAART is the HIV viral load, which is the quantity of HIV RNA in the blood. A successful ART regimen should lead to a rapid and sustained decrease in the viral load to an undetectable level (typically \<20-50 copies/mL) within a few months of starting treatment. Monitoring the viral load is crucial for assessing treatment adherence, detecting the development of drug resistance, and confirming virological failure, which would prompt a change in the drug regimen. While the CD4 count (B) is also monitored as a measure of immune system recovery, the viral load is the most direct indicator of the antiretroviral effect of the therapy.

questions.stem: A patient on Directly Observed Treatment Short-course (DOTS) for tuberculosis completes both the intensive and continuation phases of therapy, and the sputum test is negative for acid- fast bacilli at the end of treatment. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Treatment completed According to the definitions used in national tuberculosis control programs, the treatment outcome is categorized based on specific criteria. A patient who has completed the prescribed course of treatment as per the protocol but does not have a sputum smear microscopy result at the end of treatment (or for whom bacteriological results are unavailable) is classified as Treatment Completed. To be classified as Cured (A), a patient must have a negative sputum smear result at the end of treatment and on at least one previous occasion during the continuation phase. Since the question only states that the sputum was negative at the end of treatment without mentioning a previous negative result, the most precise programmatic outcome is Treatment Completed. Default (C) or Loss to follow up (D) would apply if the patient interrupted treatment for a specified period. PSM

questions.stem: A woman residing in an urban area of Madhya Pradesh delivers her baby in a healthcare institution after counseling by an ASHA worker in 2018. What monetary benefits are the woman and the ASHA worker entitled to under the Janani Suraksha Yojana scheme?
questions.explanation: 600 to mother, 1400 to ASHA Under the Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), financial incentives are provided to promote institutional deliveries, especially in states with low institutional delivery rates. Madhya Pradesh is classified as a Low Performing State (LPS) under this scheme. NODIA

questions.stem: A patient presents to the outpatient department with fatigue. Routine complete blood count shows hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, MCV of 60 fL, and an RBC count of 3.2 million/mm³. Peripheral smear reveals microcytic red blood cells. Which of the following should be the next investigation?
questions.explanation: Ferritin The patient has a microcytic anemia, as indicated by the low Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) of 60 fL (normal is 80-100 fL). The two most common causes of microcytic anemia are iron deficiency anemia (IDA) and thalassemia trait. The next step in the investigation is to differentiate between these two possibilities. The most specific and sensitive test to assess the body's iron stores is the serum ferritin level. A low serum ferritin is diagnostic of iron deficiency. If the ferritin level is normal or elevated in a patient with microcytic anemia, then the suspicion shifts towards thalassemia. In that case, the next investigation would be hemoglobin electrophoresis to measure HbA2 levels (B), which are typically elevated in beta-thalassemia trait. RDW (D) is part of the CBC and is usually high in IDA. Serum folate (C) is for macrocytic anemia.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man presents with dragging abdominal pain and is found to have a palpable spleen on examination. Peripheral smear reveals leukocytosis with increased basophils, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes. Which of the following findings is most likely to be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation: T (9,22) The clinical presentation of massive splenomegaly (dragging abdominal pain) and the peripheral smear findings of marked leukocytosis with a left shift (presence of immature granulocytes like myelocytes and metamyelocytes) and an increase in basophils are classic features of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML). The pathognomonic genetic hallmark of CML is the Philadelphia chromosome, which results from a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, denoted as t(9;22) (q34;q11). This translocation creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene, which codes for a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives the hyper proliferation of the myeloid cell line. Detection of this translocation or its gene product is essential for the diagnosis of CML. The translocation t(15;17) (D) is characteristic of Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old individual presents with an ulcerated nodule measuring 0.3 mm on the tip of the nose. Biopsy reveals the findings shown in the image below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Basal Cell carcinoma The clinical history of a nodulo-ulcerative lesion on a sun-exposed area like the nose in a middle-aged person is highly suggestive of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), the most common type of skin cancer. The histological image confirms this diagnosis. The key features of BCC on biopsy are nests of basaloid tumor cells (cells that resemble the basal layer of the epidermis) with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei. A pathognomonic feature is peripheral palisading, where the nuclei of the cells at the edge of the tumor nests are aligned in a row, like a picket fence. The tumor nests are also often seen retracting from the surrounding stroma, creating an artifactual cleft. Squamous cell carcinoma (A) would show keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. Melanoma (B) would consist of atypical melanocytes.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with arthralgia, oral ulcers, arthritis, oliguria, hematuria, and skin rashes. Routine urine examination reveals red blood cells in the urine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lupus Nephritis The patient presents with a multi-systemic disease involving the joints (arthralgia, arthritis), mucous membranes (oral ulcers), skin (rashes), and kidneys (oliguria, hematuria). This constellation of symptoms is highly characteristic of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). Renal involvement is a common and serious complication of SLE and is known as Lupus Nephritis. It can present with a wide spectrum of findings, from asymptomatic proteinuria and hematuria to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and renal failure. The presence of red blood cells in the urine indicates glomerular inflammation (glomerulonephritis), which is a hallmark of active lupus nephritis. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) (A) would typically follow a throat infection and not have the other systemic features. Acute interstitial nephritis (B) is often drug-induced. Cystitis (D) is a bladder infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following drug resistance leads to MDR TB?
questions.explanation: Isoniazid & Rifampicin Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is defined as infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis that shows resistance to both isoniazid and rifampicin, which are the two most potent first-line anti-tubercular drugs. Isoniazid acts by inhibiting mycolic acid synthesis, which is essential for the bacterial cell wall, while rifampicin works by inhibiting DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, preventing bacterial RNA synthesis. When Mycobacterium tuberculosis becomes resistant to both of these key drugs, the infection becomes significantly more difficult to treat and requires second-line anti-tubercular medications and longer treatment duration. Other options are incorrect because: 1. Resistance to isoniazid and fluoroquinolones is not the definition of MDR-TB. 2. Resistance to isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide indicates broader resistance but MDR-TB is specifically defined by the first two drugs. 3. Resistance to isoniazid, rifampicin, and kanamycin suggests extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) patterns. Therefore, MDR-TB is defined by resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin.

questions.stem: A patient on antidepressant therapy presents with bleeding and passes fatty stools that stick to the toilet pan. Deficiency of which vitamin can cause this condition?
questions.explanation: K The patient's history describes steatorrhea (fatty stools), which indicates fat malabsorption. This can be a side effect of certain medications or an independent issue. Steatorrhea compromises the absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins : A, D, E, and K. The clinical sign of bleeding points specifically to a deficiency of Vitamin K. Vitamin K is a crucial cofactor for the post-translational gamma-carboxylation of several clotting factors synthesized in the liver (Factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S). Without adequate Vitamin K, these factors are non-functional, leading to a coagulopathy (prolonged PT/INR) and an increased risk of bleeding. Therefore, the combination of fat malabsorption and bleeding is a classic presentation of Vitamin K deficiency.

questions.stem: Primaquine, an antimalarial drug, precipitates hemolysis in individuals with a specific enzyme deficiency. This enzyme is associated with which metabolic cycle?
questions.explanation: HMP Shunt The enzyme deficiency in question is Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme of the Hexose Monophosphate (HMP) Shunt, also known as the pentose phosphate pathway. The primary role of the HMP shunt in red blood cells (RBCs) is to produce NADPH. NADPH is essential for regenerating reduced glutathione (GSH) from its oxidized state. GSH is a vital antioxidant that protects RBCs from damage by reactive oxygen species. Oxidizing drugs, like the antimalarial agent primaquine, increase oxidative stress on RBCs. In G6PD-deficient individuals, the lack of NADPH and GSH leaves the cells vulnerable to this oxidative damage, leading to hemoglobin denaturation, Heinz body formation, and acute intravascular hemolysis. Glycolysis (C) is the main energy pathway in RBCs. The Luebering-Rapoport shunt (B) is involved in 2,3-DPG synthesis.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with rigidity, tremor, bradykinesia, and masked facies. Which of the following agents is most appropriate for treatment?
questions.explanation: Selegiline The patient's clinical presentation with the cardinal motor symptoms of resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia (slowness of movement), and a masked facial expression is classic for Parkinson's disease. This neurodegenerative disorder is caused by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. Treatment is aimed at restoring dopaminergic activity. Selegiline is a selective, irreversible inhibitor of the enzyme monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B). MAO-B is responsible for the breakdown of dopamine in the brain. By inhibiting this enzyme, selegiline reduces the degradation of dopamine, thereby increasing its availability in the synapse and providing mild symptomatic relief, especially in the early stages of the disease. Donepezil (A) is for Alzheimer's disease. Thioridazine (C) and Haloperidol (D) are antipsychotics that block dopamine receptors and would worsen Parkinson's symptoms.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with a fungal infection. The isolated organism shows dimorphism, appearing as yeast at 37°C and as mold at 27°C, and produces red pigmentation around its growth in culture. What is the most likely causative organism, and which drug is recommended for its treatment?
questions.explanation: Talaromyces & Amphotericin B This question describes the classic microbiological features of Talaromyces marneffei (formerly Penicillium marneffei). This fungus is a significant opportunistic pathogen in immuno compromised individuals, particularly HIV-positive patients in Southeast Asia. It is thermally dimorphic, growing as a mold at room temperature (25-27°C) and converting to a yeast-like form at body temperature (37°C). The most distinctive feature is that the mold form produces a characteristic, water-soluble red pigment that diffuses into the culture medium. The standard treatment for severe, disseminated talaromycosis, especially in an HIV-positive patient, is initial therapy with intravenous Amphotericin B, often followed by a long course of oral itraconazole for maintenance. Blastomyces (A) is dimorphic but doesn't produce a red pigment. Aspergillus (C) is a mold, not dimorphic. P. jirovecii (D) is a fungus that cannot be cultured.

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs has the least adverse effects on the pleura?
questions.explanation: Metformin Several drugs are known to cause pleural disease, including pleural effusions and pleuropulmonary fibrosis. Ergot derivatives, such as bromocriptine (A) and methysergide (D), are well-known for causing pleuropulmonary and retroperitoneal fibrosis with long-term use. Methotrexate (C), a commonly used immunosuppressant, can cause an acute pneumonitis which may be associated with a pleural effusion. In contrast, metformin (B), a biguanide and the first-line oral medication for type 2 diabetes, is not associated with adverse effects on the pleura. Its most common side effects are gastrointestinal (diarrhea, nausea), and the most serious (but rare) adverse effect is lactic acidosis, particularly in patients with renal impairment. It does not have a known propensity to cause pleural effusions or fibrosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following hypolipidemic drugs works by inhibiting PCSK-9?
questions.explanation: Evolocumab Evolocumab is a monoclonal antibody and a member of the drug class known as PCSK9 inhibitors. PCSK9 (Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) is a protein that binds to LDL receptors on the surface of liver cells. This binding promotes the degradation of the LDL receptors inside the cell, which reduces the number of receptors available to clear LDL cholesterol from the blood. By binding to and inhibiting PCSK9, evolocumab prevents it from destroying LDL receptors. This leads to a significant increase in the number of LDL receptors on the hepatocyte surface, which in turn enhances the clearance of LDL cholesterol from the circulation, dramatically lowering LDL-C levels. Atorvastatin (A) is a statin that inhibits HMG-CoA reductase. Ezetimibe (C) inhibits cholesterol absorption at the brush border of the small intestine. Fenofibrate (D) is a fibrate that primarily works by activating PPAR-alpha.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient with asthma on theophylline therapy presents with frequent and increased urination. What is the most likely mechanism by which theophylline causes diuresis?
questions.explanation: Adenosine A1 antagonism Theophylline is a methylxanthine used as a bronchodilator in asthma and COPD. Besides its effects on the airways, it also has a mild diuretic effect. The primary mechanism for this diuresis is its action as a non-selective antagonist of adenosine receptors. Specifically, antagonism of the A1 adenosine receptor in the kidney has two main effects that promote diuresis. First, it causes afferent arteriolar vasodilation, which increases the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Second, it inhibits sodium reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule. The combination of an increased GFR and reduced proximal sodium reabsorption leads to an increased delivery of fluid and solute to the distal parts of the nephron, resulting in diuresis. The Na+K+2Cl- blocker (C) is the mechanism of loop diuretics, and the Na+Cl- blocker (D) is the mechanism of thiazide diuretics. 53. MRI of the brain shows a NODIA

questions.stem: Which of the following agents acts as a growth hormone receptor antagonist?
questions.explanation: Pegvisomant Pegvisomant is a unique medication used in the treatment of acromegaly, a condition of excess growth hormone (GH). Its mechanism of action is as a growth hormone receptor antagonist. It is a pegylated, genetically engineered variant of human GH that binds to the GH receptor on cell surfaces but does not activate it. By competitively blocking the binding of endogenous GH to its receptors, pegvisomant prevents the synthesis and secretion of Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1), which is the primary mediator of GH's growth-promoting and metabolic effects. This leads to a reduction in IGF-1 levels and an improvement in the clinical signs and symptoms of acromegaly. Mecasermin (B) is recombinant IGF-1. Tesamorelin (C) is a GHRH analogue. Bromocriptine (D) is a dopamine agonist that can sometimes lower GH levels but is not a receptor antagonist.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman with a urinary tract infection was treated with antimicrobial drugs. Her baby later developed tendon rupture and arthropathy. What is the likely mechanism of action of the antimicrobial agent taken during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: DNA gyrase inhibitor The adverse effects of tendon damage (including tendon rupture) and arthropathy (cartilage damage) in a neonate or child are specifically associated with the use of fluoroquinolone antibiotics by the mother during pregnancy or by the child directly. Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) are a class of antibiotics that exert their bactericidal effect by inhibiting two key bacterial enzymes involved in DNA replication : DNA gyrase (also known as topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV. Due to the concerns about potential damage to developing cartilage and tendons, fluoroquinolones are generally contraindicated during pregnancy and in children, except in specific situations where the benefits outweigh the risks. Folic acid synthesis inhibitors (A) include sulfonamides and trimethoprim. Mycolic acid synthesis inhibitors (B) are for tuberculosis (e.g., isoniazid). Protein synthesis inhibitors (D) include macrolides, tetracyclines, and aminoglycosides. FORENSIC MEDICINE

questions.stem: A woman consults a gynecologist for hysterectomy and discusses with the doctor the advantages and disadvantages of the available procedures. What type of consent is this?
questions.explanation: Informed The scenario describes the process of obtaining informed consent. Informed consent is not just a signature on a form; it is a fundamental ethical and legal principle based on a comprehensive communication process between a healthcare provider and a patient. The core elements involve the doctor providing the patient with all relevant information about their diagnosis, the nature of the proposed procedure (hysterectomy), the potential risks and benefits, the available alternative treatments with their own risks and benefits, and the prognosis with and without treatment. The patient must have the capacity to understand this information and must then voluntarily make a decision. The discussion of advantages and disadvantages is a key part of this process, ensuring the patient's consent is truly informed. Implied consent (C) is for emergencies, and blanket consent (B) is an overly broad, legally questionable form of consent.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with acute hair loss involving the scalp, lateral eyebrows, and eyelashes. His wife reports recent behavioral changes, and examination reveals white lines on the nails. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Thallium This combination of signs is highly characteristic of thallium poisoning. Thallium is a heavy metal that is highly toxic. A hallmark and often delayed sign of significant thallium exposure is severe, diffuse, and rapid alopecia (hair loss), which typically begins about 2-3 weeks after ingestion. The hair loss is extensive, often affecting the scalp, the lateral third of the eyebrows, eyelashes, and other body hair. Thallium also causes severe peripheral neuropathy and gastrointestinal symptoms. While white lines on the nails (Mees' lines) can be seen in both thallium and arsenic poisoning, the profound and rapid hair loss is the most distinguishing feature pointing towards thallium. Arsenic (A) causes Mees' lines but not typically such dramatic alopecia. Lead (B) and mercury (D) poisoning have different clinical presentations.

questions.stem: Identify the type of Injury.
questions.explanation: Defense Wounds The image shows multiple incised wounds on the palmar and ulnar aspect of the hand and fingers. These types of injuries are highly characteristic of defense wounds. Defense wounds are sustained by a victim while actively trying to ward off an attack, typically from a sharp-edged weapon like a knife. When a person raises their hands and arms to protect their face, head, or torso, the extensor surfaces of the forearms and the backs of the hands are often injured. If they try to grab the weapon, the palms of the hands and flexor surfaces of the fingers will be cut, as seen here. These injuries are considered antemortem (B) and are crucial evidence indicating a struggle and refuting claims of suicide or accident. Self-inflicted injuries (C) for suicide are often on the flexor wrists and may have hesitation marks.

questions.stem: During a court trial, the defense lawyer asks a leading question, prompting the opposing lawyer to object. The judge sustains the objection and instructs the defense lawyer to avoid leading questions, as they are not permitted in any of the following situations except which one?
questions.explanation: Cross examination In legal proceedings, a leading question is one that suggests the answer or contains the information the examiner is looking to have confirmed (e.g., You were at the scene of the crime, weren't you?). According to the rules of evidence, leading questions are generally not permitted during the examination-in-chief (also called direct examination) (A, B), which is when a lawyer questions their own witness. This is to ensure that the witness provides testimony in their own words. However, leading questions are explicitly allowed during cross-examination (C). Cross-examination is when a lawyer questions a witness called by the opposing party. The purpose is to test the veracity of the witness's testimony, and leading questions are a primary tool for achieving this.

questions.stem: A child is brought to the emergency department after ingesting a large quantity of iron tablets. The child presents with severe abdominal pain, profuse gastrointestinal bleeding, lethargy, and coma. What is the preferred treatment in this situation?
questions.explanation: Deferoxamine mesylate The patient is presenting with severe, systemic iron toxicity. The specific antidote and preferred treatment for significant iron poisoning is the chelating agent deferoxamine mesylate (also spelled desferrioxamine). Deferoxamine has a high affinity for ferric iron (), binding with it to form a stable, non-toxic, water-soluble complex called ferrioxamine. This complex is then excreted by the kidneys, giving the urine a characteristic reddish-brown vin rosé color. Intravenous deferoxamine is indicated in patients with signs of systemic toxicity, such as shock, coma, severe acidosis, or very high serum iron levels. It is crucial for removing the toxic free iron from the circulation and preventing further cellular damage. Activated charcoal (D) is not effective as it does not bind well to iron. Penicillamine (B) and BAL (C) are chelators used for other heavy metals. 62. Identify the finding shown in image. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: A 15-year-old patient presents with nasal obstruction and recurrent episodes of epistaxis. The nasal endoscopy image is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma The clinical triad of recurrent, severe, unilateral epistaxis (nosebleeds), nasal obstruction, and a nasopharyngeal mass in an adolescent male is the classic presentation of a Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA). The endoscopic image of a firm, lobulated, reddish, and highly vascular mass arising from the region of the sphenopalatine foramen further supports this diagnosis. JNAs are benign but locally aggressive vascular tumors that almost exclusively affect adolescent males. Due to their extreme vascularity, biopsy in an outpatient setting is contraindicated as it can cause torrential hemorrhage. The diagnosis is typically made on the basis of the characteristic clinical presentation and imaging findings (CT/MRI/Angiography). A simple nasal polyp (A) is pale and edematous. Rhinosporidiosis (B) appears as a pinkish, friable mass with spores.

questions.stem: A patient has damage to the basilar membrane leading to loss of high-frequency hearing. At which location are the hair cells most likely damaged?
questions.explanation: Oval window The cochlea is tonotopically organized, meaning that different frequencies of sound are processed at different locations along the basilar membrane. The physical properties of the basilar membrane vary from its base to its apex. The base of the basilar membrane, located near the oval window, is narrow and stiff. This region is tuned to vibrate maximally in response to high-frequency sounds. The apex of the basilar membrane, near the helicotrema (C), is wide and floppy and is tuned for low-frequency sounds. Therefore, if a patient has a hearing loss specifically for high-frequency sounds, the damage to the hair cells (the sensory receptors) must have occurred at the basal turn of the cochlea, the region closest to the oval window. The modiolus (A) is the bony core of the cochlea, and the stria vascularis (B) produces endolymph.

questions.stem: A patient with nasal polyps and a history of generalized allergy presents to the ENT outpatient department and is diagnosed with Samter’s triad. Which drug should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation: Aspirin Samter's triad, also known as Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD), is a clinical syndrome defined by the presence of three conditions : 1. Asthma 2. Nasal polyposis 3. Respiratory reactions upon ingestion of aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The underlying pathophysiology involves an abnormality in the arachidonic acid metabolism pathway, leading to an overproduction of pro-inflammatory leukotrienes upon inhibition of the COX enzyme by aspirin/NSAIDs. In these patients, ingestion of aspirin can precipitate a severe reaction, including acute bronchospasm (asthma attack), profuse rhinorrhea, and nasal congestion. Therefore, aspirin and all other NSAIDs must be strictly avoided. Gentamicin (A) is an antibiotic, and cetirizine (C) is an antihistamine; neither is contraindicated in this syndrome.

questions.stem: A young man suddenly develops acute shortness of breath while eating at a restaurant, as shown in the image below. What should be the immediate next step in management for this patient?

options.text: Blindly sweep through the mouth to look for foreign body

questions.explanation: Heimlich maneuver The image shows an individual exhibiting the universal sign for choking, which is a severe foreign body airway obstruction. The patient is conscious. According to basic life support (BLS) and first aid guidelines, the appropriate first response for a conscious adult or child with a severe airway obstruction is to perform abdominal thrusts, also known as the Heimlich maneuver. This involves standing behind the person, wrapping your arms around their waist, making a fist with one hand, placing the thumb side of the fist against the person's abdomen (midway between the navel and the xiphoid process), and delivering a series of quick, forceful, upward thrusts. This action is designed to rapidly increase intrathoracic pressure, creating an artificial cough to expel the foreign body. Blind finger sweeps (D) are contraindicated as they may push the object further down. Back slaps are also part of the sequence, often preceding abdominal thrusts.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presents to the emergency department with respiratory distress. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation of the right lung with a normal left lung. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Decreased air entry on particular part of auscultation is suggestive of foreign body
Removal by flexible bronchoscopy is the TOC

questions.explanation: Decreased air entry on particular part of auscultation is suggestive of foreign body The clinical history of sudden onset respiratory distress in a toddler, combined with the X-ray finding of unilateral hyperinflation, is highly suggestive of an inhaled foreign body in the bronchus. The foreign body can act as a ball-valve, allowing air to enter the lung during inspiration but trapping it during expiration, leading to air trapping and hyperinflation on the affected side. A key physical finding on auscultation would be focal wheezing or decreased air entry over the affected lung area (A). A complete airway obstruction (C) would lead to atelectasis (collapse), not hyperinflation. The treatment of choice (TOC) for removing a foreign body from the airway in a child is rigid bronchoscopy, not flexible bronchoscopy (B), as the rigid scope provides a better airway, superior optics, and larger channels for the retrieval instruments.
