questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient presents with discharging sinuses on the foot containing granules. The granules are crushed and examined histopathologically, showing the features seen in the image. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?

options.text: Caused by both bacteria and fungi

questions.explanation: Caused by both bacteria and fungi The clinical presentation of a chronic, suppurative infection with draining sinus tracts that discharge granules is known as mycetoma. The image shows a sulfur granule, which is a macroscopic colony of the causative organism. The key fact about mycetoma is that it can be caused by two distinct groups of organisms : 1. Actinomycetoma : Caused by filamentous bacteria (aerobic and anaerobic actinomycetes) like Nocardia, Actinomadura, and Actinomyces. 2. Eumycetoma : Caused by true fungi like Madurella mycetomatis. Therefore, the statement that the condition is caused by both bacteria and fungi is true. The infection is a chronic, localized subcutaneous infection that spreads by direct extension to contiguous deep tissues like fascia and bone (so C is false); it does not typically spread hematogenously (so B is false).

questions.stem: Enzyme affected in case of lead poisoning is
questions.explanation: ALA Dehydratase Lead poisoning (plumbism) disrupts the heme synthesis pathway by inhibiting several key enzymes, leading to anemia and the accumulation of precursors. Two of the most clinically significant enzymes inhibited by lead are : 1. Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) dehydratase : This enzyme catalyzes an early step in the pathway. Its inhibition leads to an accumulation of ALA in the blood and urine, which is a sensitive marker of lead exposure. 2. Ferrochelatase : This is the final enzyme in the pathway, responsible for inserting iron into the protoporphyrin IX ring to form heme. Its inhibition leads to an accumulation of protoporphyrin in red blood cells (erythrocyte protoporphyrin or zinc protoporphyrin). Both enzymes are critically affected. Given that ALA dehydratase is an option and its inhibition is a hallmark of lead toxicity, it is a correct answer. Ferrochelatase is also correct.

questions.stem: A woman presents to the emergency department with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain after ingesting 20 paracetamol (acetaminophen) tablets. Which medication should be initiated for her treatment?
questions.explanation: N-acetylcysteine The patient has taken a toxic dose of paracetamol (acetaminophen). Paracetamol overdose is a major cause of acute liver failure. In the liver, a small fraction of paracetamol is metabolized by the cytochrome P450 system into a highly toxic intermediate called N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI). Normally, NAPQI is detoxified by conjugation with glutathione. In an overdose, the glutathione stores are depleted, and the excess NAPQI accumulates, causing severe hepatocellular necrosis. The specific antidote for paracetamol poisoning is N-acetylcysteine (NAC). NAC acts as a precursor for glutathione, thereby replenishing the liver's stores and enhancing the detoxification of NAPQI. It may also bind directly to NAPQI. It is most effective when administered within 8 hours of ingestion but can provide benefit even later. Naloxone (B) and naltrexone (C) are opioid antagonists.

questions.stem: Identify the ligature mark.
questions.explanation: Ligature Strangulation The image displays a ligature mark with features that are characteristic of ligature strangulation. The key features are : 1. Horizontal position : The mark runs transversely around the neck, perpendicular to the long axis of the body. 2. Low position : It is typically located lower on the neck, at or below the level of the thyroid cartilage. 3. Complete circumference : It often completely encircles the neck. This is in contrast to the mark seen in hanging (D), which is typically oblique (angled upwards towards the point of suspension), incomplete (with a gap at the knot), and high up on the neck. The force in strangulation is applied by an assailant, constricting the neck horizontally, whereas in hanging, the force is the gravitational pull of the body's weight. Garroting (C) is a specific method of strangulation, and mugging (B) is a type of assault that may involve strangulation. DENTAL MATERIALS

questions.stem: Calculate the burn% area in this flame burn case of a 10 year old child.
questions.explanation: 15-20 The burn area in the image involves approximately one side of the body (anterior half of one side) in a 10-year-old child. To estimate burn surface area in children, clinicians commonly use the Rule of Nines (with slight pediatric modifications) or the Lund and Browder chart, which provides a more accurate assessment for children. According to the Rule of Nines, the body surface is divided into sections representing percentages of the Total Body Surface Area (TBSA). In children, the approximate values are similar but slightly adjusted because the head accounts for a larger percentage and the lower limbs slightly less compared to adults. In the image, the burn shading covers half of the anterior trunk and half of the anterior limbs on one side of the body. The an terior trunk contributes about 18% TBSA, so half of it equals about 9%. The involvement of parts of the upper limb and lower limb on the same side adds additional percentage, bringing the total to roughly 15–20% TBSA. Thus, the estimated burn surface area is approximately 15–20%.

questions.stem: A surgeon consumes alcohol (four pegs) before coming on duty and performs surgery with an unsteady hand, drops instruments, and injures major blood vessels. What is this considered to be ?
questions.explanation: Criminal negligence This scenario describes a severe breach of the duty of care that goes far beyond simple error or incompetence. Negligence becomes criminal when the act is so reckless and shows such a wanton disregard for the life and safety of others that it amounts to a crime against the state. A surgeon knowingly choosing to operate while intoxicated demonstrates a level of recklessness that is grossly negligent. The act is performed with the knowledge that it could lead to grave injury or death, showing a culpable indifference to the patient's life. This elevates the case from civil negligence (B), which would involve a lawsuit for damages due to a breach of duty, to a criminal matter, where the state can prosecute the surgeon for offenses like culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Medical misadventure (D) implies an unexpected outcome from a competently performed procedure. MICROBIOLOGY 68. An HIV-positive patient presents with fever, cough, and breathlessness. The isolated fungal organism shows a yeast form at 37 °C and a mold form at 25 °C, as seen in the image. What is the causative agent?

questions.stem: Which of the following agencies is responsible for providing seeds and manure under the Applied Nutrition Programme?
questions.explanation: CARE The Applied Nutrition Programme (ANP) was launched in India in 1963 with the objective of improving the nutritional status of vulnerable groups, particularly children, pregnant women, and lactating mothers. The programme aimed to increase the availability and consumption of protective foods such as vegetables, fruits, milk, eggs, and fish through community participation. Under this programme, kitchen gardens, school gardens, poultry farming, and fish farming were encouraged so that communities could produce nutritious foods locally. To support these activities, different agencies were assigned specific responsibilities. The international voluntary organization CARE (Cooperative for Assistance and Relief Everywhere) played an important role in the programme. CARE provided assistance in the form of seeds, fertilizers/manure, and other agricultural inputs to help communities develop gardens and food production units. Other organizations had different roles. UNICEF mainly supported nutrition and child welfare programs, WHO focused on health-related technical guidance, and UNDP supported broader development initiatives. However, the responsibility for providing seeds and manure under the Applied Nutrition Programme was mainly undertaken by CARE. Therefore, the correct answer is (A) CARE.

questions.stem: Broken vaccine vial you will be throw in?
questions.explanation: Blue According to the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules in India, different types of waste must be segregated into color-coded bags or containers at the point of generation. Broken or discarded glassware, which includes broken vaccine vials, ampoules, and other glass items, should be disposed of in a blue color-coded, puncture-proof container or cardboard box. This ensures that the sharp glass items are handled safely and do not pose an injury risk to healthcare workers and waste handlers. The yellow bag (A) is for human anatomical waste, soiled waste, and expired medicines. The red bag (C) is for contaminated recyclable waste like plastic tubing and gloves. The white translucent, puncture-proof container (D) is specifically for sharps, which are defined as items that can cause a puncture or cut, such as needles, scalpels, and blades.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding the norm requirements for an Urban Community Health Centre (CHC)?

options.text: No district/subdistrict hospital should be located in that area

questions.explanation: Minimum 100 beds in metropolitan areas Under the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM), Community Health Centers (CHCs) are established to provide secondary care services. The norms for Urban-CHCs are different from those in rural areas. An Urban-CHC is established in cities with a population of more than 5 lakhs. A key norm is the bed strength. In non-metropolitan cities, an Urban-CHC should have a minimum of 30-50 beds. However, in large metropolitan cities, the bed strength is higher, with a requirement for a minimum of 100 beds. The U-CHC serves as a referral facility for Urban Primary Health Centers (U-PHCs), but the number is not fixed at 2-3 (B is a rural norm). The population norm is for every 2.5 lakh population in non-metro cities and up to 5 lakh in metro cities (D is incorrect).

questions.stem: An ANM is scheduled to conduct a vaccination camp in a village and has received two opened vials of pentavalent vaccine and MR vaccine. What should be done next?
questions.explanation: Use penta discard MR This question relates to the Open Vial Policy of the Universal Immunization Programme. This policy states that certain multi-dose vaccine vials, once opened, can be used for up to 28 days, provided that specific conditions are met (the expiry date has not passed, the vials have been stored correctly, the vaccine vial monitor (VVM) is intact, and aseptic technique was used). This policy applies to vaccines like Pentavalent, DPT, Td, and IPV. However, the policy does not apply to freeze-dried, reconstituted vaccines. Vaccines like BCG, Measles-Rubella (MR), and Japanese Encephalitis must be discarded at the end of the immunization session or within 6 hours of reconstitution, whichever is earlier. Therefore, the ANM can use the opened Pentavalent vial (if the conditions are met), but she must discard the opened MR vial from the previous session.

questions.stem: You are a PHC Officer posted at a Primary Health Centre in an earthquake-prone area. What are your responsibilities as an MO in disaster management?

options.text: Giving instructions over phone or radio
Preparedness at phc level by utilising resources

questions.explanation: Simulation of disaster & assessing response In disaster-prone areas such as regions vulnerable to earthquakes, the Medical Officer (MO) at a Primary Health Centre (PHC) plays a key role in disaster preparedness and response planning. One of the most important responsibilities is conducting simulation exercises (mock drills) to test how effectively the health system responds during emergencies. Simulation of disaster and assessing response involves organizing mock disaster drills, where healthcare staff practice emergency protocols such as triage, casualty management, referral, communication, and coordination with emergency services. These exercises help identify gaps in preparedness, staff training needs, resource shortages, and weaknesses in communication systems. After the simulation, the response is evaluated so that improvements can be made in disaster management plans. Although the other options are related to health administration, they are not the primary responsibility highlighted in disaster preparedness. Giving instructions over phone or radio is part of communication, public health education is a general health promotion activity, and resource utilization at PHC level is routine management. Therefore, the most appropriate responsibility of the MO in disaster management among the given options is (B) Simulation of disaster & assessing response.

questions.stem: A study was conducted to assess the relationship between green tea consumption and diabetes. The calculated risk ratio was 0.8. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Green tea reduces the risk of DM
Green tea increases the risk of DM

questions.explanation: Green tea reduces the risk of DM The Risk Ratio (RR), also known as the Relative Risk, compares the risk of an outcome (in this case, diabetes) in an exposed group (green tea drinkers) to the risk in an unexposed group. 1. An RR of 1.0 means there is no difference in risk between the groups (No Effect). 2. An RR greater than 1.0 means the exposure increases the risk (risk factor). 3. An RR less than 1.0 means the exposure decreases the risk (protective factor). 4. In this study, the RR is 0.8, which is less than 1.0. This indicates that the risk of developing diabetes in the group that drinks green tea is 0.8 times the risk in the group that does not. This can also be interpreted as a 20% reduction in risk (1.0 - 0.8 = 0.2). Therefore, the correct conclusion is that green tea reduces the risk of DM, or is a protective factor. The question of statistical significance (D) cannot be determined without a p-value or confidence interval.

questions.stem: Most logical & effective approach of controlling rabies in urban population.

options.text: Testing all the dogs for rabies
Removing stray dogs & vaccinating dog population

questions.explanation: Removing stray dogs & vaccinating dog population Rabies is a zoonotic disease, and in urban India, over 95% of human cases are caused by bites from infected dogs. Therefore, the most logical and effective approach to control and eventually eliminate human rabies is to control the disease in the reservoir host population, which is the dog population. The World Health Organization (WHO) and other global health bodies recommend a two-pronged strategy : 1. Mass vaccination of dogs : Vaccinating at least 70% of the dog population (both owned and stray) can create herd immunity and effectively break the transmission cycle. 2. Stray dog population management : This involves humane methods like Animal Birth Control (ABC) programs (sterilization) to control the number of stray dogs. Simply removing stray dogs is often not feasible or humane, but combining population management with mass vaccination is the cornerstone of rabies control. Testing all dogs (A) is impractical. ENT

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with difficulty blowing his cheek and dribbling of saliva on the right side of the face, along with recent-onset facial weakness. Examination reveals facial asymmetry, inability to fully close the right eye, and an uneven smile. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: 7th cranial nerve The patient's symptoms are all related to the paralysis of the muscles of facial expression on the right side. This includes the inability to puff out the cheek (buccinator muscle), dribbling saliva (orbicularis oris muscle weakness), inability to close the eye (orbicularis oculi muscle), and an asymmetric smile (zygomaticus and other muscles). All of these muscles are innervated by the 7th cranial nerve, the facial nerve. A lesion of the facial nerve or its nucleus causes a lower motor neuron type of facial palsy, affecting all the muscles on one side of the face. This can be idiopathic (Bell's palsy) or due to other causes like trauma, infection, or tumors. The trigeminal nerve (5th CN, A) is for facial sensation and mastication. The 8th CN (B) is for hearing and balance. The 12th CN (D) is for tongue movement. 93. A young child presents with ear pain and hearing loss. The otoscopic image shown below reveals characteristic findings. What is the diagnosis? (A) Myringitis bullosa (B) Otitis media with effusion (C) Pneumo-tympanum (D) Bulging TM NODIA

questions.stem: Warburg effect is used by cancer cells because-

options.text: Provides more energy available to cancer cells (ATP)
Prevents apoptosis and makes them immortal
Provides elements required for cellular metabolism

questions.explanation: Provides elements required for cellular metabolism The Warburg effect, or aerobic glycolysis, describes the phenomenon where cancer cells preferentially metabolize glucose through glycolysis, converting it to lactate, even in the presence of ample oxygen. This is metabolically inefficient for ATP production; oxidative phosphorylation yields far more ATP per molecule of glucose (so A is incorrect). However, this metabolic shift is advantageous for rapidly proliferating cells. The high rate of glycolysis, while yielding less ATP, shunts glucose-derived carbon intermediates into various anabolic pathways. These intermediates serve as essential building blocks (elements) for the synthesis of nucleotides (for DNA/RNA), lipids (for membranes), and amino acids, which are all required to build new cells. This redirection of metabolism from energy production to biosynthesis is crucial for supporting the high proliferative demands of cancer cells.

questions.stem: All of the following statements regarding neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are true except which one?
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial DNA is involved Neutrophil Extracellular Traps (NETs) are web-like structures released by neutrophils as a defense mechanism against pathogens. These NETs are composed of a backbone of decondensed nuclear DNA, which is studded with various antimicrobial proteins from the neutrophil's granules, such as histones, elastase, and myeloperoxidase (so D is true). The primary function of NETs is to trap and kill extracellular pathogens like bacteria (B) and fungi, preventing their dissemination. This process, called NETosis, is a distinct form of cell death. NETs are prominently observed in various inflammatory and infectious conditions, including sepsis (A). The DNA that forms the scaffold of NETs is derived from the nucleus, not from the mitochondria (so C is the incorrect statement). Mitochondrial DNA may be released during other forms of cell death but is not the primary component of the NET scaffold.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true for telomerase?

options.text: It reduces the length of telomere
It maintains the length of Chromosome

questions.explanation: It maintains the length of Chromosome Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase enzyme that is responsible for maintaining the length of telomeres. Telomeres are repetitive nucleotide sequences at the ends of linear chromosomes that protect them from degradation and from being recognized as DNA breaks. During each round of DNA replication, the telomeres shorten slightly (the end-replication problem). Telome rase counteracts this by adding telomeric repeat sequences back onto the ends of the chromosomes. This action effectively maintains the length of the chromosome ends (C). Its activity is high in embryonic stem cells and germ cells. Most mature somatic cells (D) have very low or undetectable telome rase activity, which leads to progressive telomere shortening with each cell division. This shortening acts as a mitotic clock and is linked to cellular senescence and aging (so A is incorrect). Therefore, telome rase does not reduce the length of telomeres (B), but rather maintains it.

questions.stem: Which is AR inheritance?
questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis Autosomal recessive (AR) inheritance means that a person must inherit two copies of the mutated gene (one from each parent) to be affected by the disorder. Parents are typically asymptomatic carriers. Cystic fibrosis is a classic example of an autosomal recessive disease, caused by mutations in the CFTR gene. In contrast, the other options are autosomal dominant (AD) disorders. In AD inheritance, inheriting just one copy of the mutated gene from one parent is sufficient to cause the disease. Huntington disease (B), achondroplasia (C), and Treacher Collins syndrome (D) are all well-known examples of autosomal dominant conditions. They typically show vertical transmission in a pedigree (appearing in every generation), whereas AR disorders like cystic fibrosis often appear in siblings with unaffected parents (horizontal transmission).

questions.stem: A middle-aged man presents with a painless, slowly enlarging neck swelling. On examination, lymph nodes are positive. Surgery is performed, and biopsy findings are shown in the image below. Which of the following statements regarding the histopathological findings is false?

options.text: Nuclear features are the characteristic of this tumor

questions.explanation: FNAC is not diagnostic The image displays the classic histopathological features of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC). The key to the diagnosis lies in the characteristic nuclear features (B), which include enlarged, overlapping nuclei with finely dispersed, clear chromatin (Orphan Annie eye nuclei), nuclear grooves, and intranuclear pseudo inclusions. Because these nuclear features are so distinct, they can be reliably identified on Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC). In fact, FNAC is the gold standard and most important initial diagnostic test for thyroid nodules, and it is highly accurate for diagnosing PTC. Therefore, the statement that FNAC is not diagnostic is false. The other statements are true : PTC characteristically spreads to regional lymph nodes via lymphatics (C), and despite this, it typically has a very slow-growing, indolent course and an excellent prognosis (D), with over 95% 10-year survival for most cases. 36. questions.stem: Identify the surgery is done for :
questions.explanation: Keratoconus The image depicts a corneal condition characterized by thinning and a cone-shaped protrusion of the cornea, which is typical of Keratoconus. Keratoconus is a progressive, non-inflammatory ectatic disorder of the cornea where the normal dome-shaped cornea becomes irregularly conical, resulting in distorted vision due to irregular astigmatism and myopia. In early stages, spectacles or rigid gas-permeable contact lenses can improve vision. However, as the disease progresses and corneal thinning and scarring worsen, conservative management becomes inadequate. In such advanced cases, surgical intervention like corneal transplantation (penetrating keratoplasty or deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty) is required to restore corneal clarity and regular curvature. Other options include collagen cross-linking and intrastromal corneal ring segments in less advanced cases. The other options—keratoglobus, Vogt limbal girdle, and corneal dystrophies—have different clinical features and are not typically treated by t his surgical approach. Thus, the surgery shown in the image is done for Keratoconus.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient presents with preretinal hemorrhage and neovascularization at the optic disc. What is the appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) The patient's findings of neovascularization at the optic disc (NVD) and pre-retinal hemorrhages are the hallmarks of proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR). This is an advanced stage of the disease where widespread retinal ischemia leads to the production of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which stimulates the growth of new, abnormal blood vessels on the surface of the retina and optic disc. These vessels are fragile and prone to bleeding, leading to vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment. The gold standard treatment to cause regression of this neovascularization and prevent severe vision loss is panretinal photocoagulation (PRP). This procedure involves applying thousands of scattered laser burns to the peripheral retina, which destroys the ischemic retinal tissue, reduces VEGF production, and causes the new vessels to regress. Focal (C) and grid (B) laser are used for diabetic macular edema.

questions.stem: A patient presents with photophobia, excessive tearing, drooling of saliva, and periorbital pain accompanied by headache. Which nerve supply is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Trigeminal Nerve The patient's symptoms of periorbital pain, headache, and photophobia are all sensory modalities mediated by the trigeminal nerve (CN V), specifically its first (ophthalmic) division, which provides sensory innervation to the eye, orbit, and forehead. The trigeminal nerve is the principal sensory nerve for the face and head. The tearing and drooling are likely reflex actions secondary to the severe pain and irritation. For example, corneal irritation, sensed by the ophthalmic division of CN V, can trigger a reflex arc leading to increased lacrimation (tearing) via parasympathetic fibers that travel with the facial nerve (CN VII). However, the primary afferent limb for the pain and light sensitivity is the trigeminal nerve. The optic nerve (A) is for vision. The oculomotor nerve (B) controls eye movements. The facial nerve (D) controls muscles of facial expression and mediates taste and salivation/lacrimation. MEDICINE 106. A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample from a patient shows mononuclear cell predominance, moderately reduced glucose levels, and elevated protein concentration. Which of the following is the most likely etiology? NODIA

questions.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida who is two weeks overdue presents to the outpatient department with complaints of vaginal bleeding and right- sided abdominal pain. On examination, her vital signs are stable, and abdominal examination reveals no significant findings. Bimanual pelvic examination shows a bulky, soft, non-tender uterus with no adnexal mass, and mild vaginal bleeding is present. Her serum beta-hCG level is 1400 IU/L. Ultrasound examination demonstrates a trilaminar endometrium with normal-appearing adnexa. Based on these findings, what is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: Repeat serum beta hCG after 48 hours This patient presents with symptoms concerning for an ectopic pregnancy (pain and bleeding in early pregnancy). The transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is inconclusive; it doesn't show an intrauterine pregnancy (IUP), but it also doesn't show a clear ectopic mass. The β-hCG level of 1400 IU/L is in the discriminatory zone, a level above which an IUP should typically be visible on TVS. Since no IUP is seen, the suspicion for an ectopic pregnancy is high. The next and most crucial step is to repeat the serum β-hCG level in 48 hours. In a normal, viable IUP, the β-hCG level should rise by at least 53-66% (approximately double) in 48 hours. In an ectopic or nonviable IUP, the rise is typically much slower, or the levels may plateau or decline. This trend is critical for differentiating between a very early IUP, a nonviable pregnancy, and an ectopic pregnancy, and will guide further management.

questions.stem: A 22-week pregnant woman presents with profuse vaginal bleeding. On examination, her vital signs are stable, with normal blood pressure and blood sugar levels. She has no abdominal pain, and the fetal heart rate is within normal limits. Ultrasonography reveals a normally developing fetus with no evidence of placental abruption. Based on these clinical findings, what is the most likely site of placental implantation?
questions.explanation: Internal Os The clinical presentation of painless, profuse vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester is the classic sign of placenta previa. Placenta previa is a condition where the placenta implants in the lower segment of the uterus, either partially or completely covering the internal cervical os. As the lower uterine segment begins to form and the cervix starts to efface or dilate later in pregnancy, the placental attachment is disrupted, leading to bleeding from the exposed maternal vessels. The absence of abdominal pain helps to distinguish it from placental abruption, which typically causes painful bleeding. An ovarian (A), tubal (B), or abdominal (D) pregnancy are types of ectopic pregnancies and would not typically present for the first time with bleeding at 22 weeks in this manner.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old G2P1 woman presents at 18 weeks and 5 days of gestation for a routine targeted fetal anomaly scan. Fetal anatomy is normal, but transvaginal ultrasound shows a cervical length of 15 mm. Although she is counseled that there is no clear proven benefit in her case, the patient insists on undergoing cervical cerclage. Which of the following conditions is an absolute (complete) contraindication to cervical cerclage?
questions.explanation: Ruptured membranesA cervical cerclage is a stitch placed around the cervix to provide mechanical support and prevent preterm birth in women with cervical insufficiency. A short cervical length of 15 mm (\<25 mm) is an indication for considering a cerclage. However, there are several absolute contraindications to the procedure. Preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), or ruptured membranes, is an absolute contraindication. Placing a cerclage in the presence of ruptured membranes would seal the uterine cavity, trapping any potential ascending bacteria and dramatically increasing the risk of chorioamnionitis, a severe intra-amniotic infection that is dangerous for both the mother and fetus. Other contraindications include active preterm labor, vaginal bleeding, and evidence of chorioamnionitis. Bulging membranes (B) make the procedure technically difficult and risky, but it is not an absolute contraindication in all cases, unlike confirmed rupture.

questions.stem: A 34 weeks primigravida presents with jaundice & BP of 140/96 mmHg. Her investigations revealed a serum bilirubin of 1.5 mg/dl, SGOT- 150, SGPT-200. Her LDH is 700 & platelet count is 75000. Her KFT & coagulation profile were normal. What is her diagnosis?
questions.explanation: HELLP Syndrome The patient's presentation with hypertension (BP \>140/90 mmHg) after 20 weeks of gestation indicates a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, such as pre-eclampsia. The laboratory findings are the key to the specific diagnosis. The triad of Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets defines HELLP syndrome, which is a severe variant of pre-eclampsia. This patient meets the criteria : 1. Hemolysis : Indicated by the significantly elevated Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) of 700 U/L (a marker of red cell breakdown). 2. Elevated Liver enzymes : SGOT (AST) of 150 U/L and SGPT (ALT) of 200 U/L are both markedly elevated. 3. Low Platelets : The platelet count of 75,000/mm³ is well below the threshold of 100,000/mm³. 4. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (A) typically presents with more severe liver failure and hypoglycemia. ICP (C) presents with pruritus and elevated bile acids.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with type I diabetes mellitus is in the postoperative ward after undergoing a cesarean section for failed induction in the setting of pre-eclampsia with severe features. She now complains of drowsiness and altered sensorium. She is receiving a maintenance infusion of magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) along with intravenous insulin. On examination, her pulse rate is 70/min, blood pressure is 140/98 mmHg, and respiratory rate is 10/min. Chest auscultation reveals normal bilateral air entry. Abdominal examination shows a firm uterus with normal postoperative tenderness, and the Pfannenstiel incision site is clean with no significant vaginal bleeding. Bilateral patellar reflexes are absent. Urine dipstick testing is negative for protein and sugar, and capillary blood glucose is 270 mg/dL. Based on this clinical scenario, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Magnesium toxicity The patient is displaying the classic signs and symptoms of magnesium sulfate toxicity. Magnesium sulfate is used to prevent seizures in severe pre-eclampsia. It has a narrow therapeutic window, and overdose can be life-threatening. The clinical signs of toxicity appear in a predictable, dose-dependent manner. The earliest sign is the loss of deep tendon reflexes, such as the patellar reflexes, which are noted to be absent in this patient. As the magnesium level continues to rise, it leads to respiratory depression, evidenced by the low respiratory rate of 10 breaths/min. Further increases can cause altered sensorium, muscle paralysis, and ultimately, cardiac arrest. The immediate management would be to stop the magnesium infusion and administer the antidote, calcium gluconate. DKA (B) is less likely with a glucose of 270 and no ketones mentioned in the urine. Eclampsia (C) would involve seizures. 164. A 34-year-old G2P1 woman presents at 35 weeks of gestation with no complaints and reports regular fetal movements. Her obstetric history is significant for a previous classical cesarean section performed at 25 weeks due to eclampsia and severe fetal growth restriction. questions.stem: An 11-year-old child with rheumatic fever is started on secondary prophylaxis with intramuscular benzathine penicillin (0.6 million units). Which of the following statements regarding secondary prevention is correct?

options.text: Till 10 years 3 weekly or till 25 years of age

questions.explanation: Till 10 years 3 weekly or till 25 years of age After an episode of Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF), secondary prophylaxis with penicillin is crucial to prevent recurrent Group A streptococcal infections, which could trigger further episodes of ARF and worsen cardiac damage (rheumatic heart disease). The duration of prophylaxis depends on the severity of the initial disease. For a patient with rheumatic fever with carditis but no residual heart disease, the standard recommendation (e.g., from the American Heart Association) is to continue prophylaxis for 10 years after the last episode or until age 21 (whichever is longer). Some guidelines, particularly in high-prevalence areas, may recommend continuing until age 25. Therefore, continuing prophylaxis for 10 years or until age 25 is the most appropriate option. Lifelong prophylaxis (A) is reserved for patients with severe residual heart disease.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old female presents to the clinic with a severe, throbbing headache localized to the left side of her head. She describes the pain as pulsating and reports that these headache episodes have been occurring intermittently over the past few months. Each episode is accompanied by significant nausea and occasional vomiting. Prior to the onset of the headache, she frequently experiences visual disturbances such as flashing lights and zigzag patterns, suggestive of an aura. She also notes increased sensitivity to light (photophobia) and sound (phonophobia) during these episodes, which interferes with her ability to perform daily activities. Given her symptoms and overall clinical presentation, what is the most appropriate treatment option for immediate relief of her migraine?
questions.explanation: Sumatriptan The patient's presentation of a unilateral, throbbing headache accompanied by nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, and preceded by a visual aura is a classic description of migraine with aura. The question asks for treatment for immediate relief, which refers to abortive therapy. The first-line and most specific abortive medications for moderate to severe migraine attacks are the triptans. Sumatriptan is the prototypical drug in this class. Triptans are serotonin 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists. They work by causing vasoconstriction of painfully dilated cranial blood vessels and by inhibiting the release of pro-inflammatory neuropeptides in the trigeminal nervous system, thereby aborting the headache attack. Propranolol (B), topiramate (C), and flunarizine (D) are all medications used for prophylaxis (prevention) of migraines and are not effective for treating an acute attack. 120. questions.stem: Identify the image in a new born child.
questions.explanation: Bladder exstrophy The image shows a newborn with a reddish mucosal mass in the lower abdominal wall just above the genital area, which is characteristic of bladder exstrophy. In this congenital anomaly, the anterior wall of the bladder and the lower abdominal wall fail to develop properly, resulting in the posterior wall of the bladder being exposed externally. Bladder exstrophy is part of the exstrophy–epispadias complex and occurs due to failure of the infra umbilical abdominal wall and bladder to close during embryonic development. The exposed bladder mucosa appears as a moist, red mass on the lower abdomen, and urine continuously leaks from the ureteric openings. It is often associated with epispadias, widening of the pubic symphysis, and abnormal external genitalia. The other options are different congenital abdominal wall defects: 1. Gastroschisis: bowel loops protrude through a defect near the umbilicus without a covering membrane. 2. Omphalocele: abdominal organs protrude through the umbilical ring and are covered by a membrane. 3. Evisceration of bowel: usually occurs after trauma or surgery. Since the image shows exposed bladder mucosa in the suprapubic region, the diagnosis is bladder exstrophy.

questions.stem: A mother of a newborn is concerned because her baby has not passed urine on the first postnatal day. What advice should be given to her?
questions.explanation: Continue breast feeding and observe It is quite common for a healthy, full-term newborn not to pass urine for the first 12 to 24 hours of life. Approximately 99% of newborns will void within the first 48 hours. During the first few days, the mother produces colostrum, which is low in volume but rich in nutrients and antibodies. The infant's fluid intake is minimal until the mother's milk comes in around day 3-5. As long as the baby is otherwise well, feeding effectively, and has no other signs of illness or congenital anomalies (like posterior urethral valves), the failure to pass urine on Day 1 is not typically a cause for alarm. The appropriate advice is to reassure the mother, encourage her to continue breastfeeding on demand to ensure adequate hydration, and observe the infant. Intervention with formula (A), IV fluids (C), or NICU admission (D) is not indicated unless there are other concerning signs or the anuria persists beyond 48 hours.

questions.stem: An 11-month-old infant presents with currant jelly stools, a palpable right lumbar mass, and recurrent episodes of abdominal pain. The X-ray shown below reveals characteristic findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Intussusception The clinical triad of paroxysmal, colicky abdominal pain, a palpable, sausage-shaped mass (often in the right upper quadrant), and the passage of currant jelly stools (a mixture of blood and mucus) in an infant or toddler is pathognomonic for intussusception. Intussusception is a condition where one segment of the intestine telescopes into the adjacent distal segment, leading to bowel obstruction and potential ischemia. The X-ray described would likely be from a contrast (barium or air) enema, which is both a diagnostic and therapeutic procedure. The image would show a characteristic claw sign or a concave filling defect where the contrast outlines the head of the intussusceptum. This finding confirms the diagnosis. Volvulus (A) and malrotation (B) have different presentations and radiological signs (e.g., corkscrew sign).

questions.stem: A child presents with exercise-induced fatigue and clinical features suggestive of McArdle disease. Deficiency of which enzyme is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: Phosphorylase McArdle disease is Glycogen Storage Disease Type V. It is a metabolic myopathy caused by a deficiency of the enzyme myophosphorylase, which is the muscle isoform of glycogen phosphorylase. This enzyme is responsible for the first step of glycogenolysis (the breakdown of glycogen) in skeletal muscle. In McArdle disease, the muscles are unable to break down their glycogen stores to produce glucose for energy. This leads to the classic symptoms of exercise intolerance, severe muscle fatigue, cramping, and pain that occur shortly after starting strenuous activity. Patients often experience a second wind phenomenon if they rest and allow blood-borne fuels like glucose and free fatty acids to reach the muscles. A failure of serum lactate to rise after ischemic forearm exercise is a characteristic diagnostic finding. Glucose-6-phosphatase (A) is deficient in Von Gierke disease. Lysosomal glucosidase (C) is deficient in Pompe disease. ORTHOPEDICS

questions.stem: Identify the procedure shown below. In which clinical condition is this procedure indicated?

options.text: Periarticular fracture of knee, spanning fixator

questions.explanation: Periarticular fracture of knee, spanning fixator The image shows a spanning external fixator applied across the knee. This device consists of pins or wires inserted into the femur (above the knee) and the tibia (below the knee), which are then connected by external rods. The fixator spans or bridges the knee joint, providing rigid stability to the limb while avoiding the placement of hardware directly at the site of the fracture. This technique is indicated for complex, high-energy periarticular fractures of the knee, such as tibial plateau fractures or distal femur fractures, especially when there is severe soft tissue injury, open fractures, or contamination. The external fixator acts as a temporary damage control measure to stabilize the fracture, protect the soft tissues, and allow for their recovery before definitive internal fixation is performed at a later stage. An Ilizarov fixator (A) is a circular frame used for limb lengthening or complex reconstructions.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old child presents after a fall on the elbow, and a radiograph is provided below. Which bone is fractured?
questions.explanation: Humerus The radiograph clearly shows a fracture in the distal part of the humerus, just above the condyles. This specific type of fracture, common in children after a fall on an outstretched hand, is known as a supracondylar humerus fracture. The image likely depicts a displaced fracture, which is a common and serious injury in this age group due to the risk of neurovascular compromise, particularly to the brachial artery and median nerve. The other bones listed are not part of the elbow joint. The clavicle (B) is the collarbone, the scapula (C) is the shoulder blade, and the ribs (D) form the chest wall. The injury is localized to the elbow, and the fracture line is visible in the distal humerus, making it the correct answer. Proper diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent long-term complications like malunion, which can lead to a gunstock deformity (cubitus varus). 152. questions.stem: A 6-month-old male infant presents with pain in the extremities and is admitted to the hospital. There is a history of a previous chest infection occurring two years ago. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis reveals increased levels of hemoglobin F (HbF) and hemoglobin S (HbS). Based on these clinical and laboratory findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sickle cell anemia The definitive diagnostic test result is the High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC), which analyzes the types of hemoglobin present. The results show the presence of Hemoglobin S (HbS), which is the abnormal hemoglobin that causes sickle cell anemia. In sickle cell disease (HbSS genotype), normal adult hemoglobin (HbA) is absent, and the primary hemoglobins are HbS and fetal hemoglobin (HbF). HbF levels are high at birth and gradually decline, but they often remain elevated in patients with sickle cell disease, which is somewhat protective. The clinical presentation of a 6-month-old with pain in the extremities (dactylitis or hand-foot syndrome) and a history of chest infection (acute chest syndrome) is also classic for the initial manifestations of sickle cell anemia, as this is the age when HbF levels have dropped sufficiently for sickling to become clinically significant. questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the outpatient department. The physical examination findings are shown in the image below. Which anatomical structure is affected in this condition?
questions.explanation: Involvement of subdermal lymphatics The image displays peau d'orange (French for orange peel skin), a clinical sign that is highly suggestive of an underlying inflammatory breast cancer or a locally advanced breast carcinoma. This characteristic appearance of thickened, pitted skin is caused by tumor invasion and obstruction of the dermal lymphatic vessels. The blockage of these lymphatics leads to lymphedema of the skin. The edema causes the skin to swell, but it is tethered down by the hair follicles and sweat ducts, which results in the characteristic dimpling or pitting that resembles the skin of an orange. Involvement of Cooper's ligaments (C) causes skin retraction or dimpling, but not the specific edematous, pitted appearance of peau d'orange. Involvement of the chest wall (A) is a sign of more advanced disease (T4).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman undergoes thyroidectomy and, on the third postoperative day, develops perioral numbness. Which further investigation should be performed in this case?
questions.explanation: Calcium, phosphate and PTH levels The patient's symptom of perioral numbness and tingling, occurring a few days after a total thyroidectomy, is the classic presentation of acute hypocalcemia. This is a common complication of thyroid surgery, caused by the inadvertent damage to, devascularization, or removal of the parathyroid glands, which are located on the posterior surface of the thyroid. The parathyroid glands produce parathyroid hormone (PTH), which is the primary regulator of serum calcium levels. A lack of PTH (hypoparathyroidism) leads to a rapid drop in serum calcium. The appropriate next step is to confirm the diagnosis by urgently checking the serum calcium (total and ionized), phosphate (which would be elevated), and PTH levels (which would be low or inappropriately normal). Thyroid function tests (A, D) are not relevant to this acute complication.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing hemorrhoids presents for a routine check-up. Blood investigations reveal a hemoglobin level of 7 g/ dL. Peripheral blood smear shows the findings depicted below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Iron Deficiency Anemia The patient has a history of long-standing hemorrhoids, which is a source of chronic blood loss. The hemoglobin level of 7 g/dL confirms severe anemia. The peripheral blood smear findings of microcytic (small) and hypochromic (pale) red blood cells are the classic morphological features of Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). Chronic, slow blood loss is the most common cause of IDA in adults. The body's iron stores are gradually depleted as iron is lost in the blood faster than it can be absorbed from the diet. This leads to impaired hemoglobin synthesis, resulting in the production of smaller red cells that contain less hemoglobin. Megaloblastic anemia (C) is macrocytic. Hemolytic anemia (D) would show signs of hemolysis like spherocytes or schistocytes. Sideroblastic anemia (B) can be microcytic but would show ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with recurrent, painful perianal nodules over the buttocks associated with serous discharge. The image shown below demonstrates characteristic findings. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pilonidal sinus The clinical presentation of recurrent painful nodules in the perianal or natal cleft region with serous discharge is highly suggestive of a pilonidal sinus. This condition commonly occurs in young adult males, particularly those who are hairy, obese, or sit for long periods. A pilonidal sinus is a chronic inflammatory condition that occurs in the natal cleft (intergluteal region). It develops due to ingrowth of loose hair into the skin, which causes a foreign body reaction and chronic infection. Over time, this leads to the formation of sinus tracts that may discharge serous or purulent material. The image shows multiple openings and inflamed sinus tracts in the midline of the gluteal cleft, which is a classic appearance of pilonidal disease. Patients often present with pain, swelling, and recurrent discharge in this area. Other options are less likely: 1. Perianal boils are usually single, acute infections of hair follicles. 2. Carbuncle involves multiple interconnected boils but typically occurs on the neck or back. 3. Fistula-in-ano is associated with the anal canal and usually follows a perianal abscess. Thus, the most probable diagnosis is pilonidal sinus.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old patient with a history of hypertension presents with acute onset of breathlessness. The chest X-ray shown below reveals characteristic findings. What should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation: IV Nitroglycerine The patient, an elderly individual with hypertension, presents with acute breathlessness, and the chest X-ray shows classic features of acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. This is a medical emergency caused by acute left ventricular failure, leading to a rapid buildup of fluid in the lung interstitium and alveoli. The immediate management goals are to improve oxygenation, reduce preload, and reduce afterload. Intravenous nitroglycerine is a cornerstone of therapy. As a potent venodilator, it rapidly reduces preload by increasing venous capacitance, which decreases pulmonary venous pressure and helps to clear fluid from the lungs. At higher doses, it also acts as an arterial vasodilator, reducing afterload and improving cardiac output. This, along with oxygen, diuretics (like furosemide), and sitting the patient upright, is the standard initial treatment. Salbutamol (B, D) is for bronchospasm, not pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: A known case of chronic liver disease with ascites presents with abdominal pain and tenderness. Ascitic fluid analysis reveals 600 polymorphonuclear (PMN) cells per cubic millimeter. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis The patient, a known case of chronic liver disease (CLD) with ascites, is presenting with symptoms of peritonitis (abdominal pain and tenderness). The ascitic fluid analysis is the key to diagnosis. The presence of an elevated ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) leukocyte count of 250 cells/mm³ is the diagnostic criterion for Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP). The patient's count of 600 PMN cells/mm³ is well above this threshold. SBP is a common and life-threatening infection of the ascitic fluid that occurs in patients with advanced cirrhosis, typically without an evident intra-abdominal source of infection. The most common causative organisms are gram-negative bacteria like E. coli translocating from the gut. Tubercular ascites (A) would show a lymphocytic predominance. Malignant ascites (B) is diagnosed by cytology. Chylous ascites (D) is milky with high triglycerides.

questions.stem: An adult patient presents with palpitations and an irregularly irregular pulse. Examination reveals a pulse deficit of 20, a heart rate of 120/ min, and blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg. Which of the following findings is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation: Absent a wave The presence of an irregularly irregular pulse is the clinical hallmark of atrial fibrillation (AF). The pulse deficit (the difference between the apical heart rate and the palpated peripheral pulse rate) occurs because many of the rapid, chaotic ventricular contractions are too weak to generate a palpable pulse wave. The jugular venous pressure (JVP) waveform reflects pressure changes in the right atrium. The 'a' wave of the JVP is caused by atrial contraction. In atrial fibrillation, the atria do not contract in a coordinated fashion; they merely fibrillate. As a result, there is no atrial systole, and consequently, the 'a' wave is absent from the JVP tracing. Instead, the baseline may show fine, chaotic fibrillatory ('f') waves. Cannon 'a' waves (B) are seen in AV dissociation when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old patient with coronary artery disease presents with palpitations. The ECG shown below demonstrates characteristic findings, and the blood pressure is 120/84 mmHg. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: IV amiodarone The ECG shows a regular, monomorphic, wide-complex tachycardia (WCT). In a 74-year-old patient with a history of coronary artery disease (CAD), any WCT should be presumed to be ventricular tachycardia (VT) until proven otherwise. The patient is currently hemodynamically stable (BP 120/84 mmHg). According to ACLS guidelines for stable VT, the first-line treatment is an intravenous antiarrhythmic agent. Intravenous amiodarone is a preferred and widely recommended agent for this purpose. It is a class III antiarrhythmic that blocks potassium channels, prolonging the action potential duration and refractory period, which can terminate the reentrant circuit of the VT. IV procainamide is another option. IV metoprolol (B), a beta-blocker, is generally avoided in undifferentiated WCT as it can cause hemodynamic collapse if the underlying rhythm is pre-excited AF. Oral medications (A, C) are not appropriate for the acute termination of VT.

questions.stem: A patient presents with digoxin toxicity, with a pulse rate of 54/min and ECG evidence of third- degree heart block. What is the best treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: Digoxin Immune Fab The patient is exhibiting signs of life-threatening digoxin toxicity, specifically severe bradycardia (54/min) and a high-degree atrioventricular block (3rd degree heart block). Digoxin toxicity can cause a wide range of arrhythmias, but severe bradyarrhythmias and conduction blocks are particularly dangerous. The specific and definitive treatment for severe or life-threatening digoxin toxicity is the administration of digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Digoxin Immune Fab), also known as Digibind or DigiFab. These antibody fragments bind with high affinity to free digoxin molecules in the blood, forming a complex that is then renally excreted. This rapidly removes digoxin from its binding sites on the Na+/K+-ATPase pump, reversing the toxic effects on the heart's conduction system. Lidocaine (B) and phenytoin (D) are used for digoxin-induced tachyarrhythmias, not bradyarrhythmias. 112. A 25-year-old patient with dental caries is scheduled for dental extraction. Which of NODIA

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with galactorrhea and has a negative urine pregnancy test. MRI of the brain reveals a large pituitary tumor, and the patient refuses surgical intervention. Which drug is the treatment of choice for this patient?
questions.explanation: Bromocriptine The clinical syndrome of galactorrhea and amenorrhea, in the presence of a pituitary tumor, is diagnostic of a prolactinoma. This is a benign adenoma of the pituitary gland that secretes excess prolactin. For patients with prolactinomas who decline surgery or for whom surgery is not indicated, medical therapy is the first-line treatment. The drugs of choice are dopamine agonists, such as bromocriptine or the newer, more potent cabergoline. These drugs act on D2 dopamine receptors on the tumor cells, which powerfully inhibits prolactin secretion. This leads to a rapid normalization of prolactin levels, cessation of galactorrhea, and resumption of normal menstrual cycles. A major additional benefit is that these drugs also cause significant shrinkage of the tumor itself in the majority of patients. The other drugs listed are GnRH modulators and are not used for this purpose.

questions.stem: A patient with an abdominal stab injury is brought to the emergency department, as shown in the image below. Examination reveals penetration of the fascia, but the patient’s vital signs are stable. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Further investigation In cases of penetrating abdominal stab injury, management depends largely on the hemodynamic status of the patient and the extent of injury. In this scenario, examination reveals penetration of the fascia, which indicates that the wound has crossed the abdominal wall and may involve intra-abdominal organs. However, the patient’s vital signs are stable, meaning there is no immediate evidence of life-threatening hemorrhage or shock. For hemodynamically stable patients with penetrating abdominal trauma, the next best step is further evaluation with imaging and diagnostic tests rather than immediate surgery. Investigations may include contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen, Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST), or local wound exploration to determine whether the peritoneum has been breached and whether internal organs are injured. Immediate exploratory laparotomy is reserved for patients who are hemodynamically unstable, have signs of peritonitis, evisceration, or obvious internal injury. Simply waiting after dressing the wound could miss serious intra-abdominal injury, and IV fluids alone do not address the need for diagnosis. Therefore, in a stable patient with fascial penetration, the most appropriate next step is further investigation to assess intra-abdominal damage. PEDIATRICS

questions.stem: An 11-month-old infant presents with recurrent jerky movements of the limbs along with regression of developmental milestones. Electroencephalography reveals a hypsarrhythmia pattern. What is the antiepileptic drug of choice for this patient?
questions.explanation: ACTH The clinical triad of infantile spasms (the recurrent jerky movements), developmental regression, and an EEG pattern of hypsarrhythmia (a chaotic, high-voltage, disorganized pattern of spikes and slow waves) is diagnostic of West syndrome. This is a severe, age-specific epileptic encephalopathy of infancy. The first-line treatment and drug of choice for West syndrome is hormonal therapy with either adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) or high-dose oral corticosteroids (prednisolone). Another first-line option, particularly in cases caused by tuberous sclerosis, is vigabatrin. Standard antiepileptic drugs like phenobarbital (C) and phenytoin (D) are generally ineffective for treating the spasms and do not alter the poor neurodevelopmental outcome associated with an untreated hypsarrhythmic pattern.

questions.stem: A young child is brought by his mother with complaints of multiple episodes of loose stools along with drowsiness and lethargy. On examination, the skin pinch returns very slowly, and the child is unable to accept breast feeds. Based on these clinical features, what is the class of dehydration?
questions.explanation: Severe Dehydration According to the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) guidelines from the WHO, the classification of dehydration is based on key clinical signs. This child exhibits multiple signs of severe dehydration : 1. Lethargy/drowsiness : A change in mental status is a cardinal sign of severe dehydration. 2. Inability to drink or breast feed : The child did not accept breast feeds, which is another danger sign. 3. Skin pinch goes back very slowly (\>2 seconds) : This indicates a significant loss of skin turgor and severe fluid deficit. Any two of these signs are sufficient to classify the child as having severe dehydration, which is a life-threatening condition requiring immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation (Plan C). Some dehydration (D) is characterized by restlessness, sunken eyes, and a skin pinch that goes back slowly. No dehydration (A) would have none of these signs. 145.
