questions.stem: Route of metastasis of prostate cancer to lumbar vertebrae.
questions.explanation: Prostatic venous plexus Prostate cancer has a strong predilection for metastasizing to the bones of the axial skeleton, particularly the lumbar vertebrae. The primary route for this metastasis is believed to be hematogenous (via the bloodstream). The prostatic venous plexus (plexus of Santorini) surrounds the prostate gland. This plexus communicates with the vertebral venous plexus (also known as Batson's plexus). Batson's plexus is a network of valveless veins that runs along the length of the vertebral column. This valveless system allows for the retrograde (backward) flow of blood. During moments of increased intra-abdominal pressure (like coughing or straining), cancerous cells from the prostate can be forced from the prostatic venous plexus into the vertebral venous plexus, allowing them to seed directly into the lumbar vertebrae, bypassing the systemic circulation and the lungs.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with scrotal swelling, ecchymosis, fever, and serous discharge. The image shown below reveals characteristic findings. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fournier's gangrene The clinical presentation of acute, painful scrotal swelling with rapid progression to erythema, ecchymosis, necrosis (gangrene), and systemic signs of sepsis (fever) is the classic picture of Fournier's gangrene. This is a life-threatening, fulminant necrotizing fasciitis of the perineal, genital, or perianal regions. It is a polymicrobial infection, often involving both aerobes and anaerobes, that spreads rapidly along the fascial planes, leading to thrombosis of the subcutaneous vessels and necrosis of the overlying skin and soft tissue. It is a true surgical emergency that requires immediate and aggressive surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and intensive supportive care. Epididymo-orchitis (B) and torsion (C) present with scrotal pain but not typically with the rapid skin necrosis seen here.

questions.stem: A patient presents to the emergency department with calf muscle claudication, numbness in the thigh, and impotence. An image showing gangrene of the foot is provided below. Which artery is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: Aortic iliac bifurcation The patient presents with a classic triad of symptoms : 1) bilateral claudication of the buttocks, hips, and thighs; 2) erectile dysfunction (impotence); and 3) diminished or absent femoral pulses. This triad is known as Leriche syndrome. It is caused by chronic, severe atherosclerotic occlusive disease at the level of the infrarenal aorta and the aortic bifurcation into the common iliac arteries. The blockage at this high level severely restricts blood flow to the pelvis (causing impotence via internal iliac artery compromise) and to both lower extremities (causing claudication and, in severe cases, rest pain and gangrene as shown in the image). Occlusion of the internal iliac artery alone (B) would cause impotence but not claudication. Femoral or popliteal artery disease (C, D) would cause more distal claudication (in the calf) but not impotence or buttock claudication.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man has been bedridden for 15 years, as shown in the image below, and has developed a bedsore. What is the grade of the bedsore?
questions.explanation: Grade IV The image displays a severe pressure ulcer (bedsore) in a chronically immobile patient. The staging of pressure ulcers is based on the depth of tissue destruction. 1. Stage I : Non-blanchable erythema. 2. Stage II : Partial-thickness skin loss. 3. Stage III : Full-thickness skin loss with visible subcutaneous fat. 4. Stage IV : Full-thickness tissue loss with exposed bone, tendon, or muscle. The image shows a deep crater-like wound where underlying structures such as bone or tendon are visible at the base of the ulcer. This extent of tissue destruction, extending through all layers of skin and subcutaneous tissue to expose deeper support structures, defines a Stage IV pressure ulcer. These are the most severe type of pressure ulcers and are often associated with undermining, tunneling, and a high risk of osteomyelitis.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of chronic alcoholism presents to the outpatient department with a whitish patch as shown in the image below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leukoplakia The image shows a white patch on the oral mucosa. The clinical term for a white patch or plaque that cannot be scraped off and cannot be characterized as any other specific disease is leukoplakia. It is a diagnosis of exclusion. Leukoplakia is considered a premalignant lesion, meaning there is an increased risk that it may transform into squamous cell carcinoma over time. The primary risk factors for developing oral leukoplakia are tobacco use (in any form) and chronic alcohol consumption. The appearance of a new, persistent white patch in a chronic alcoholic should therefore be taken very seriously. A biopsy is mandatory to rule out dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. Erythroplakia (B) is a red patch with a higher malignant potential. OSMF (C) is oral submucous fibrosis, characterized by blanching and stiffness of the mucosa.

questions.stem: Following surgery for varicose veins, a patient develops numbness along the medial aspect of the leg. Which nerve is most commonly affected?
questions.explanation: Saphenous nerve Surgery for varicose veins often involves stripping or ablation of the great saphenous vein (GSV). The saphenous nerve is a pure sensory nerve that is the terminal branch of the femoral nerve. It runs in close proximity to the GSV along the medial aspect of the knee and leg. During vein stripping or other procedures on the GSV, the saphenous nerve is highly vulnerable to injury, either through direct trauma, stretching, or entrapment. Injury to the saphenous nerve results in numbness, tingling, or pain along its distribution, which is the medial aspect of the lower leg and foot. This is the most common neurological complication of varicose vein surgery. The sural nerve (D) runs with the small saphenous vein on the posterior aspect of the leg. The peroneal nerves (A, B) are on the lateral side. NODIA

questions.stem: What is the ideal treatment for a fracture of the fibula?
questions.explanation: Neurological assessment-Analgesics-Cast The fibula is the thinner and non–weight-bearing bone of the leg. Most isolated fibular fractures are usually stable injuries and often do not require surgical fixation unless associated with ankle instability or other fractures. The ideal management begins with a neurological assessment. This is important because the common peroneal nerve runs close to the fibular neck and can be injured in fibular fractures. Therefore, checking motor function (dorsiflexion of the foot) and sensory function over the dorsum of the foot is essential. After confirming there is no neurovascular compromise, the next step is to provide analgesics to control pain and make the patient comfortable. Finally, the fracture is immobilized using a cast or supportive splint, which allows proper healing while preventing movement at the fracture site. Since the fibula bears minimal weight, conservative treatment with casting is usually sufficient. Surgical procedures like CRIF (Closed Reduction and Internal Fixation) are generally reserved for unstable fractures or those associated with tibial or ankle injuries. Therefore, the correct sequence of management is Neurological assessment → Analgesics → Cast.

questions.stem: Identify the types of hymen?
questions.explanation: Septate The image shows a type of hymenal anomaly. A normal hymen is typically annular (ring-shaped) or crescentic. In this image, a band of tissue runs vertically or horizontally across the vaginal opening, creating two separate orifices instead of one. This is known as a septate hymen. This condition can sometimes cause discomfort or difficulty with tampon insertion or sexual intercourse. It can be easily corrected with a minor surgical procedure to resect the dividing septum. An annular hymen (C) is a ring-like hymen that surrounds the vaginal opening. A cribriform hymen (D) has multiple small perforations, like a sieve. A semilunar hymen is crescent-shaped. The presence of a dividing band is the defining feature of a septate hymen. 158. What is the complication of this? (A) Oligomenorrhea (B) Ectopic Pregnancy

questions.stem: A patient receiving antidepressant therapy presents with hyperthermia, dilated pupils, palpitations, and hypotension. ECG reveals broad QRS complex tachycardia with right axis deviation. Which of the following interventions should be performed immediately?
questions.explanation: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate This clinical presentation is classic for a severe Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) overdose. TCAs have three major toxic effects : anticholinergic effects (hyperthermia, dilated pupils), cardiovascular toxicity, and CNS toxicity. The cardiovascular toxicity is the most life-threatening and is caused by the blockade of fast sodium channels in the cardiac myocytes. This effect slows conduction, leading to a prolonged QRS interval (\>100 ms), a right axis deviation of the terminal QRS (a prominent R wave in aVR), and ventricular arrhythmias like the wide complex tachycardia seen here. The immediate and life-saving intervention for TCA cardiotoxicity is the administration of intravenous sodium bicarbonate. Sodium bicarbonate works by increasing the extracellular sodium concentration, which helps to overcome the sodium channel blockade, and by increasing the serum pH, which decreases the binding of the TCA to the sodium channels.

questions.stem: A patient on antidepressant medication presents with increased body temperature, dilated pupils, palpitations, and hypotension. Electrocardiography shows a broad QRS complex tachycardia with right axis deviation. Which of the following interventions should be initiated immediately?
questions.explanation: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate This clinical presentation is classic for a severe Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) overdose. TCAs have three major toxic effects : anticholinergic effects (hyperthermia, dilated pupils), cardiovascular toxicity, and CNS toxicity. The cardiovascular toxicity is the most life-threatening and is caused by the blockade of fast sodium channels in the cardiac myocytes. This effect slows conduction, leading to a prolonged QRS interval (\>100 ms), a right axis deviation of the terminal QRS (a prominent R wave in aVR), and ventricular arrhythmias like the wide complex tachycardia seen here. The immediate and life-saving intervention for TCA cardiotoxicity is the administration of intravenous sodium bicarbonate. Sodium bicarbonate works by increasing the extracellular sodium concentration, which helps to overcome the sodium channel blockade, and by increasing the serum pH, which decreases the binding of the TCA to the sodium channels.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child presents with abdominal pain and melena. On physical examination, palpable purpura is noted over the calves and buttocks. The child also has joint pain and swelling involving the knees and ankles, and the parents report recurrent episodes of crampy abdominal pain lasting for several days. Based on this clinical presentation, which medication should be used to manage the severe abdominal pain and gastrointestinal manifestations?
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids The clinical tetrad of palpable purpura (typically on the lower extremities and buttocks), arthralgia/arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal disease is the classic presentation of Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP), now also called IgA vasculitis. HSP is the most common systemic vasculitis in children and is often preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection. The disease is generally self-limiting, and treatment is primarily supportive. However, for patients who develop severe abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding (like the melena described), or significant nephritis, a course of systemic corticosteroids (e.g., oral prednisone or prednisolone) is the treatment of choice. Steroids can rapidly reduce the inflammation and edema in the bowel wall, providing significant relief from the severe, colicky abdominal pain and reducing the risk of complications like intussusception. More potent immunosuppressants like azathioprine (A) or methotrexate (B) are reserved for severe, refractory nephritis.

questions.stem: Which fluid is shown below?
questions.explanation: Ringer's lactate The label provides the precise composition of the intravenous fluid. The electrolyte concentrations are : Sodium () 130 mEq/L, Potassium () 4 mEq/L, Calcium () 2.7 mEq/L (sometimes written as 3), Chloride () 109 mEq/L, and Lactate 28 mEq/L. This specific formulation is that of Lactated Ringer's (LR) solution, also known as Hartmann's solution. It is an isotonic crystalloid fluid that is one of the most commonly used resuscitation fluids in medicine. Its electrolyte composition is designed to be similar to that of plasma. The lactate in the solution is metabolized by the liver into bicarbonate, which can help to buffer metabolic acidosis. Haemaccel (B) is a colloid. Isolyte-P and Isolyte-M (C, D) are other crystalloid solutions but have different electrolyte compositions, typically with more potassium and less sodium, and are used for pediatric maintenance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not Found in MEN2B Syndrome?
questions.explanation: Parathyroid adenoma Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B) is an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by a specific triad of tumors and distinct physical features. Its components are : 1. Aggressive medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). 2. Pheochromocytoma. 3. A unique phenotype that includes multiple mucosal neuromas (A) on the lips and tongue, a tall, slender Marfanoid habitus (C), and diffuse intestinal ganglioneuromatosis, which can lead to motility issues and complications like megacolon (B). The feature that is notably absent in MEN 2B is parathyroid hyperplasia or adenoma, which causes primary hyperparathyroidism. Hyperparathyroidism is a key component of the closely related MEN 2A syndrome but not MEN 2B. This is a crucial distinction between the two subtypes.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old patient presents with fever, severe calf pain, and fatigue. On examination, conjunctival suffusion is noted along with petechial eruptions and thrombocytopenia. Abdominal examination reveals tender hepatomegaly and icterus. Renal function tests are within normal limits, but urinalysis shows hematuria. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leptospirosis This clinical picture is highly suggestive of leptospirosis. The key features pointing to this diagnosis are the acute febrile illness with severe myalgia, particularly in the calves, and the pathognomonic sign of conjunctival suffusion (redness of the conjunctiva without discharge). The presence of icterus (jaundice), tender hepatomegaly, petechiae, and thrombocytopenia indicates a more severe form of the disease, often called Weil's disease, which involves hepatic and sometimes renal dysfunction (though KFTs are normal here, hematuria is present). While Dengue fever (B) can cause fever, petechiae, and thrombocytopenia, the severe calf pain and conjunctival suffusion are much more characteristic of leptospirosis. Chikungunya (C) causes severe arthralgia but not typically jaundice or conjunctival suffusion. NODIA

questions.stem: A primigravida presents to the labor room at 40 weeks of gestation and has been in labor for 3 hours. Which of the following findings would determine that she is in active labor?

options.text: 2 contractions each lasting 30 sec in 10 mins

questions.explanation: Cervical dilation \>5cm Labor is divided into a latent phase and an active phase. The latent phase is characterized by regular uterine contractions and slow, gradual cervical change (effacement and early dilation). The active phase of the first stage of labor is defined by an accelerated rate of cervical dilation. Historically, the threshold for the active phase was considered to be 4 cm. However, contemporary obstetric guidelines have been updated based on modern labor curves. The current definition for the start of the active phase of labor is a cervical dilation of 5-6 cm in the presence of regular uterine contractions. Therefore, a cervical dilation of greater than 5 cm is the most definitive indicator that the patient has transitioned from the latent to the active phase of labor. The frequency of contractions (A) is variable, and rupture of membranes (D) can occur at any time. OBS & GYNE

questions.stem: A multigravida woman has been in the second stage of labor for 2 hours with strong uterine contractions. On abdominal examination, the fetal head is 1/5th palpable, and the fetal heart rate is 140 beats per minute. Vaginal examination shows a fully dilated cervix with the fetal head at the level of the ischial spines in the right occipito-transverse (ROT) position, along with moderate caput and molding. What is the most appropriate management approach for delivery in this case?
questions.explanation: Emergency LSCS The patient is a multigravida who has been in the second stage of labor for 2 hours with strong contractions, which is considered a prolonged second stage. The critical finding is that the fetal head is at the level of the ischial spines (station 0) in a transverse position (ROT). This indicates a deep transverse arrest. The fetal head has descended into the mid-pelvis but has failed to rotate to the required occiput-anterior position to negotiate the pelvic curve. Attempts at an operative vaginal delivery (forceps or vacuum) from this high station with an unrotated head are considered mid-cavity deliveries. These are technically difficult and carry a high risk of significant maternal and fetal trauma. In modern obstetrics, a mid-cavity rotational forceps delivery (B) is rarely performed. The safest and most appropriate management for deep transverse arrest is an emergency Lower Segment Cesarean Section (LSCS).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old previously healthy woman is in active labor at term when she suddenly collapses during delivery, developing severe hypotension and acute respiratory distress. Soon afterward, she experiences profuse vaginal bleeding and features suggestive of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), including extensive bruising and bleeding from intravenous sites. There is no prior history of preeclampsia, placental abruption, or any other underlying condition that could account for this presentation. What is the most likely cause of her sudden collapse and the subsequent complications?
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid embolism This clinical scenario describes the catastrophic and classic presentation of an amniotic fluid embolism (AFE), also known as anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy. AFE is a rare but often fatal complication of labor and delivery. It is characterized by the sudden onset of cardiopulmonary collapse (hypotension, respiratory distress, hypoxia) followed rapidly by the development of a severe coagulopathy (disseminated intravascular coagulation - DIC), which leads to profuse hemorrhage. It is thought to be caused by the entry of amniotic fluid and fetal debris into the maternal circulation, triggering a massive, anaphylactoid-like inflammatory response that leads to cardiovascular collapse and activation of the clotting cascade. While postpartum hemorrhage (B) is a consequence, the initial event of sudden collapse is the key. Eclampsia (C) would present with seizures and hypertension.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman presents at 28 weeks of gestation for a routine antenatal checkup. On clinical examination, the uterine size is smaller than expected, corresponding to 24 weeks of gestation. Ultrasonography demonstrates absence of amniotic fluid (anhydramnios). Based on these findings, what is the most likely cause of the absence of amniotic fluid in this patient?
questions.explanation: Fetal Renal anomalies In the second half of pregnancy, the primary source of amniotic fluid is fetal urine production. The fetus continuously swallows amniotic fluid, which is absorbed, processed by the fetal kidneys, and then excreted back into the amniotic sac as urine. Therefore, any condition that severely impairs or prevents fetal urine production will lead to a profound reduction in amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios) or its complete absence (anhydramnios). The most common causes of this are fetal renal anomalies, such as bilateral renal agenesis (absence of both kidneys), multicystic dysplastic kidneys, or a severe obstructive uropathy like posterior urethral valves. Tracheoesophageal fistula (C) is associated with polyhydramnios (excess fluid) because the fetus cannot swallow the fluid effectively.

questions.stem: A delayed intravenous urogram of a patient is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis based on this imaging finding?
questions.explanation: Pelviureteric junction obstruction The image shows a delayed intravenous urogram (IVU) demonstrating marked dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces with narrowing at the junction where the renal pelvis meets the ureter. This appearance is typical of pelviureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction. Pelviureteric junction obstruction occurs when there is a blockage at the junction between the renal pelvis and the proximal ureter, preventing normal drainage of urine from the kidney into the ureter. As a result, urine accumulates in the renal pelvis, leading to hydronephrosis, which appears on imaging as ballooning or dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces with a normal or narrow ureter. In the IVU image, the contrast outlines a dilated renal pelvis while the ureter distal to the obstruction is poorly visualized, which strongly suggests obstruction at the pelviureteric junction. Other options are less likely: 1. Staghorn calculus would show a large branching stone occupying the renal pelvis and calyces. 2. Putty kidney is associated with renal tuberculosis and shows a calcified, shrunken kidney. 3. Renal cyst appears as a smooth round filling defect rather than dilated calyces. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is pelviureteric junction obstruction.

questions.stem: A middle-aged man presents with acute-onset pain in the right lower limb, and an investigation is performed as shown below. What is the name of this investigation?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound Doppler A middle-aged man with acute onset pain in the lower limb raises suspicion of vascular compromise, such as arterial occlusion or deep vein thrombosis (DVT). The investigation commonly performed first in such situations is Ultrasound Doppler. Ultrasound Doppler (Doppler ultrasonography) is a non-invasive imaging technique that uses high-frequency sound waves to evaluate blood flow in arteries and veins. It works based on the Doppler effect, where the frequency of ultrasound waves changes when reflected from moving blood cells. This allows clinicians to assess blood flow velocity, direction, and any obstruction in the vessel. In cases of acute limb pain, Doppler ultrasound helps detect: 1. Arterial blockage or reduced blood flow 2. Deep vein thrombosis 3. Peripheral arterial disease It is usually the initial investigation of choice because it is quick, safe, cost-effective, and does not require contrast injection. Other options are less appropriate as first-line tests: 4. Digital subtraction angiography is invasive and used mainly for detailed vascular imaging or intervention. 5. Plethysmography measures volume changes in limbs but is less commonly used for acute diagnosis. 6. MR angiography is more advanced imaging but not typically the first investigation. Therefore, the investigation shown is Ultrasound Doppler.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man involved in a road traffic accident is brought to the emergency department. Although his vital signs are stable, he is unable to pass urine, and blood is noted at the urethral meatus. A retrograde urethrogram (RGU) is performed and shows the findings illustrated below. Based on the clinical presentation and imaging, what is the most likely site of urethral injury?
questions.explanation: Membranous urethra The patient has a history of road traffic accident with inability to pass urine and blood at the urethral meatus, which are classic signs of urethral injury. In trauma cases, the most common mechanism is pelvic fracture, which is strongly associated with injury to the posterior urethra, particularly the membranous urethra. The retrograde urethrogram (RGU) is the investigation of choice to identify the site of urethral injury. In the image, contrast is seen filling the anterior urethra but not passing normally into the proximal urethra, indicating a disruption at the level of the membranous urethra. This pattern is typical for posterior urethral injury associated with pelvic fractures. Anatomically, the membranous urethra lies between the prostatic urethra and the bulb of the penis and passes through the urogenital diaphragm. It is relatively fixed in position, making it more susceptible to shearing forces during pelvic trauma. Other options are less likely: 1. Penile and spongy urethral injuries usually occur from straddle injuries. 2. Bulbar urethral injury is also commonly due to perineal trauma rather than pelvic fractures. Therefore, based on the clinical features and RGU findings, the most likely site of injury is the membranous urethra.

questions.stem: Name the investigation shown?
questions.explanation: PET-CT The image displayed is a Positron Emission Tomography-Computed Tomography (PET-CT) scan. This is a hybrid imaging modality that combines two different types of scans performed in a single session. The PET scan provides functional information by detecting the metabolic activity of tissues. The patient is injected with a radiotracer, most commonly 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a glucose analog. Tissues with high metabolic activity, such as cancer cells, take up more FDG and appear as hot spots (bright areas) on the PET image. The CT scan provides detailed anatomical information. The two sets of images are then fused together, allowing for the precise anatomical localization of areas of abnormal metabolic activity. This is invaluable in oncology for cancer staging, assessing treatment response, and detecting recurrence. 190. A 35-year-old woman presents with fever, expectoration, and difficulty in breathing. A high-resolution CT (HRCT) scan of the chest is performed and shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? NODIA

questions.stem: What is the causative agent of anogenital wart?
questions.explanation: HPV 11 Anogenital warts, also known as condylomata acuminata, are benign epithelial growths caused by infection with the Human Papillomavirus (HPV). HPVs are classified into high-risk (oncogenic) types and low-risk types. The vast majority (over 90%) of anogenital warts are caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11. Of these two, HPV 11 (B) is a very common cause. High-risk HPV types, such as HPV 16 and 18 (D), are the primary cause of cervical, anal, and other anogenital cancers, but they do not typically cause visible warts. HPV 2 (A) is a common cause of cutaneous warts on the hands and feet (verruca vulgaris). HPV 5 (C) is a type associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis.

questions.stem: A patient receiving treatment for borderline tuberculoid leprosy presents with lesions involving the forehead, nose, and extending to both cheeks. Which nerve is most commonly affected in this condition?
questions.explanation: Trigeminal nerve Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae infection) has a predilection for cooler areas of the body, including the skin and peripheral nerves. The patient's facial lesions suggest involvement of the nerves supplying the face. While the facial nerve (CN VII) is commonly affected, leading to motor weakness (lagophthalmos), sensory loss on the face is due to the involvement of the trigeminal nerve (CN V). The trigeminal nerve is a commonly affected cranial nerve in leprosy, leading to patches of anesthesia or hypoesthesia on the face. This sensory loss is particularly dangerous as it can lead to an insensitive cornea (neurotrophic keratitis) and unnoticed facial injuries. The ulnar nerve (C) is the most commonly affected peripheral nerve in the body overall, but for facial sensory lesions, the trigeminal nerve is the primary nerve involved. The trochlear (A) and abducens (B) nerves are pure motor nerves to the extraocular muscles and are not typically affected. ANAESTHESIA

questions.stem: Identify the following equipment which is often used for Covid 19 patients.
questions.explanation: Non re breathing face mask The device shown is a non-re breathing face mask (NRM). Its key features are a face mask connected to an oxygen reservoir bag and a one-way valve system. A valve between the mask and the bag prevents the patient's exhaled air from entering the reservoir, while valves on the side ports of the mask allow exhaled gas to escape but prevent room air from being entrained during inhalation. This design allows the NRM to deliver a high concentration of oxygen (FiO2 of 60% to over 90%) to a spontaneously breathing patient. It was frequently used in the management of hypoxemic respiratory failure in COVID-19 patients who required more oxygen than could be delivered by a simple mask or nasal cannula, but before escalation to high-flow nasal cannula or mechanical ventilation. A Venturi mask (A) delivers a precise FiO2, and a simple/Hudson mask (B, D) delivers a lower, more variable FiO2.

questions.stem: Identify the nerve that is being assessed using the following neuromuscular blockade monitoring procedure.
questions.explanation: Ulnar During general anesthesia, neuromuscular blockade is monitored using a peripheral nerve stimulator to assess the degree of muscle relaxation. The most common site for this monitoring is the ulnar nerve at the wrist. Electrodes are placed over the path of the ulnar nerve, and the response of the adductor pollicis muscle is observed or measured. The adductor pollicis, which adducts the thumb, is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Its contraction causes thumb adduction towards the palm. This muscle is chosen because its response is a reliable indicator of the level of blockade at the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles, which are more resistant to neuromuscular blocking agents. The pattern of muscle twitches in response to a train-of-four (TOF) stimulation is used to quantify the depth of the block. RADIOLOGY

questions.stem: A 25-year-old patient presents with fever, dry cough, breathlessness, and night sweats. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis The combination of constitutional symptoms (fever, night sweats), respiratory symptoms (cough, breathlessness), and the classic chest X-ray finding of bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in a young adult is highly suggestive of Stage I sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis is a multisystem inflammatory disorder of unknown cause, characterized by the formation of non-caseating granulomas in various organs, with the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes being the most commonly affected sites. The symmetrical enlargement of the hilar lymph nodes is a hallmark finding. While lymphoma (C) and tuberculosis (D) are also important causes of hilar lymphadenopathy, the bilateral and symmetrical nature strongly favors sarcoidosis. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (A) typically presents with interstitial lung patterns, not isolated hilar adenopathy. 185. A 6-year-old child presents with recurrent urinary tract infections. A delayed intravenous urogram of the patient is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? (A) Vesicoureteric reflux (B) Vesico-colic fistula (C) Urinary bladder hernia (D) Urinary bladder diverticula NODIA

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient presents with recurrent swelling on one side of the neck. She reports fear of eating because the swelling worsens during meals. Imaging findings are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Isolated osteoma of the floor of mouth

questions.explanation: Sialolithiasis The patient's history is classic for sialolithiasis, which is the formation of a stone (sialolith) within a salivary gland or its duct. The symptom of swelling that worsens with eating (mealtime syndrome) is pathognomonic. When a person eats or even thinks about food, salivary flow is stimulated. If the duct is obstructed by a stone, the saliva cannot drain, causing the gland to become painfully swollen. The imaging confirms the diagnosis by showing a distinct, radio-opaque calcification located in the path of the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct), which is the most common site for salivary stones. The submandibular gland produces thick, mucinous saliva, which predisposes it to stone formation. An osteoma (C) would be part of the bone, and lymphadenitis (D) would not be related to meals in this manner.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-impact road traffic accident. On examination, he has visible chest bruising, a pulse rate of 120 beats per minute, blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, and a respiratory rate of 40 breaths per minute. He is in severe respiratory distress. Breath sounds are diminished on the left side and absent on the right side. A chest X-ray is obtained as shown below. What should be the immediate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: Chest tube placement & drainage The patient's presentation following a high-impact motor vehicle accident—respiratory distress with absent breath sounds on one side—is a classic sign of a life-threatening chest injury, most likely a tension pneumothorax (air in the chest cavity) or a m assive hemothorax (blood in the chest cavity). Both conditions cause the lung on the affected (right) side to collapse. The buildup of pressure inside the chest not only prevents breathing but can also push the heart and major blood vessels to the opposite side, leading to cardiovascular collapse. The immediate, life-saving intervention is to decompress the chest cavity. Chest tube placement (also known as tube thoracostomy) is the definitive procedure for this. A tube is inserted through the chest wall into the pleural space to drain the trapped air or blood. This allows the collapsed lung to re-expand and relieves the pressure on the heart, stabilizing the patient's breathing and circulation. Why Other Options Are Incorrect (A) Immediate thoracotomy : This is a major open-chest surgery. It may be required later to repair severe internal injuries but is not the first step for stabilization. (B) Pleurodesis : This is a non-emergency procedure used to prevent recurrent collapsed lungs, not for treating an acute traumatic injury. (C) Pericardiocentesis : This procedure drains fluid from the sac around the heart and is used to treat cardiac tamponade, which presents with different clinical signs (e.g., muffled heart sounds). 193. A 35-year-old patient presents with severe abdominal pain accompanied by vomiting. His vital signs are stable. What is the most effective approach to manage this patient? (A) Gastric lavage with cold saline (B) Tracheostomy (C) Resuscitation & exploratory laparotomy NODIA

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presents with sudden-onset breathing difficulty while playing, with no prior history of respiratory disease. Chest X-ray shows unilateral hyperinflation with a normal left lung. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?

options.text: Focal area of decrease air entry confirms the diagnosis
Reactive Pulmonary secretions leads to complete obstruction
Prefer way of removing is flexible bronchoscopy

questions.explanation: Prefer way of removing is flexible bronchoscopy A 2-year-old child with sudden-onset breathing difficulty while playing strongly suggests foreign body aspiration, which is common in young children. The chest X-ray showing unilateral hyperinflation indicates air trapping caused by a partial obstruction of a bronchus, producing a ball-valve effect where air enters during inspiration but cannot escape easily during expiration. Clinically, children may present with sudden cough, wheezing, respiratory distress, and decreased breath sounds on the affected side. Imaging often shows unilateral hyperinflation, mediastinal shift, or localized atelectasis, depending on the degree of obstruction. The definitive management is bronchoscopy to remove the foreign body. In this context, flexible bronchoscopy can be used for visualization and removal of the aspirated object, especially in diagnostic evaluation and selected therapeutic situations. It allows direct visualization of the airway and identification of the obstructing material. Other options are incorrect because: 1. Acute laryngotracheitis causes stridor and barking cough. 2. Decreased air entry is a clinical sign but not the key statement regarding management. 3. Reactive pulmonary secretions are not the primary mechanism. Thus, the correct statement regarding this condition is (D) Prefer way of removing is flexible bronchoscopy.

questions.stem: Which of the following clinical findings is most likely to occur following rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm in the brain?
questions.explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage Saccular (or berry) aneurysms are abnormal outpouchings that typically occur at the bifurcation points of the major arteries at the base of the brain, within the Circle of Willis. These arteries are located in the subarachnoid space, the space between the arachnoid and pia mater that contains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). When one of these aneurysms ruptures, blood is released under high arterial pressure directly into the subarachnoid space. This results in a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Clinically, this presents with the sudden onset of a severe thunderclap headache. A CT scan will show blood layering in the basal cisterns, sulci, and fissures. While the bleeding can sometimes extend into the brain parenchyma (D) or cause hydrocephalus (C) as a complication, the primary and defining event is the hemorrhage into the subarachnoid space. PSYCHIATRY

questions.stem: A 35-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after being found unresponsive at home. He has a known history of opioid use and, on arrival, shows signs of respiratory depression with a respiratory rate of 6 breaths per minute, pinpoint pupils, and a decreased level of consciousness. His vital signs reveal a heart rate of 50 bpm, blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, and an oxygen saturation of 85% on room air. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the next most appropriate step in the management of a suspected opioid overdose?
questions.explanation: Naloxone The patient is presenting with the classic clinical triad of an opioid overdose : 1. Central nervous system depression (decreased level of consciousness). 2. Respiratory depression (bradypnea, RR of 6). 3. Miosis (constricted or pinpoint pupils). This is a life-threatening emergency, and the immediate priority is to reverse the respiratory depression. The specific antidote for opioid overdose is naloxone. Naloxone is a pure, competitive antagonist at the mu, kappa, and delta opioid receptors. When administered (typically intravenously, intramuscularly, or intranasally), it rapidly displaces the opioid from its receptors, reversing all of its effects, including the life-threatening respiratory depression. Naltrexone (B) is a long-acting oral antagonist used for relapse prevention. Flumazenil (C) is a benzodiazepine antagonist. Buprenorphine (D) is a partial agonist used for opioid maintenance therapy.

questions.stem: A patient with depression ingests a large quantity of tricyclic antidepressants (TCA). What is the drug of choice for the management of TCA poisoning?
questions.explanation: NaHCO3 Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose is a medical emergency, with cardiotoxicity being the most life-threatening complication. TCAs block fast sodium channels in the cardiac conduction system, which slows depolarization and leads to QRS widening on the ECG. This predisposes the patient to fatal ventricular arrhythmias like ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation. The cornerstone and drug of choice for treating TCA cardiotoxicity is intravenous sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3). It works through two primary mechanisms : 1. It increases the serum pH (alkalinization), which decreases the binding affinity of the TCA for the sodium channel. 2. It provides a large sodium load, which increases the electrochemical gradient across the cardiac myocyte membrane, helping to overcome the sodium channel blockade. Administration of sodium bicarbonate can narrow the QRS complex, reverse hypotension, and terminate arrhythmias. Other antiarrhythmics are generally avoided.

questions.stem: A woman presents on the third postpartum day with tearfulness, mood swings, and occasional insomnia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Postpartum blue The patient is describing mild, transient mood disturbances occurring in the immediate postpartum period. This is characteristic of postpartum blues, also known as baby blues. The key features are its timing (typically peaking around day 3-5 postpartum), its mildness (tearfulness, irritability, anxiety, mood lability), and its transient nature (symptoms usually resolve on their own within two weeks). Postpartum blues are extremely common, affecting up to 80% of new mothers, and are thought to be related to the rapid hormonal shifts, sleep deprivation, and emotional adjustment after childbirth. It does not significantly impair the mother's ability to function and care for her baby. Postpartum depression (B) is more severe, persistent (lasting \>2 weeks), and involves anhedonia and functional impairment. Postpartum psychosis (C) is a rare psychiatric emergency involving delusions and hallucinations.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl has intense food cravings, eats large quantities of food, and then induces recurrent vomiting. She also has a history of using appetite-suppressing drugs. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bulimia nervosa This clinical vignette describes the core features of Bulimia Nervosa. The diagnostic criteria include : 1. Recurrent episodes of binge eating, which is defined as eating an unusually large amount of food in a discrete period of time w hile feeling a lack of control. 2. Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain. The description of recurrent vomiting is a classic example of this purging behavior. Other behaviors can include misuse of laxatives, diuretics, or, as mentioned, anti-appetite drugs. 3. The binge eating and compensatory behaviors occur, on average, at least once a week for 3 months. 4. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight. This is distinct from Anorexia Nervosa (A), where the central feature is a significantly low body weight due to restricted intake. Binge eating disorder (C) involves binging but without the subsequent compensatory behaviors. ************** Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is advised to undergo an ultrasound Doppler study along with a double marker test between 11 and 14 weeks of gestation. Doppler assessment of the umbilical artery helps in predicting which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Early onset Pre-eclampsia During the first-trimester screening (11-14 weeks), the Doppler ultrasound assesses the uterine arteries (blood flow from mother to placenta), not the umbilical artery. The question likely refers to this standard practice. This uterine artery Doppler measures the pressure and resistance in the vessels supplying the placenta. High resistance at this early stage indicates that the placenta is not embedding properly into the uterine wall. This process, known as poor placentation, is the fundamental cause of early-onset pre-eclampsia—the more severe form of the condition that manifests before 34 weeks of gestation. While fetal growth restriction (C) is also linked to placental issues, it is typically evaluated later in pregnancy with an umbilical artery Doppler (flow from placenta to fetus). Late-onset pre-eclampsia (A) is thought to have a different underlying cause and is not predicted as effectively by this early screening. Placenta accreta (D) is a condition of abnormal placental attachment, identified differently.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops preeclampsia at 28 weeks of gestation and is anxious to know the cause of her condition. You explain that preeclampsia is related to a problem in the development of maternal–fetal circulation during early pregnancy. What is the underlying pathophysiological cause of this complication?

options.text: Poor invasion by villous trophoblast of the spiral arterioles
Poor invasion by villous trophoblast of the radial arterioles
Poor invasion by extra villous trophoblast of the arcuate arteries
Poor invasion by extra villous trophoblast of the spiral arterioles

questions.explanation: Poor invasion by extra villous trophoblast of the spiral arterioles The underlying pathophysiology of pre-eclampsia is rooted in abnormal placentation during the first half of pregnancy. In a normal pregnancy, specialized placental cells called extravillous trophoblasts invade the maternal spiral arterioles in the decidua and myometrium. This invasion remodels the vessels, destroying their muscular and elastic layers and transforming them from narrow, high-resistance vessels into wide, low-resistance, high-capacitance channels. This ensures a massive increase in blood flow to the placenta to meet the demands of the growing fetus. In pre-eclampsia, this process is incomplete. There is a failure of the extravillous trophoblasts to properly invade and remodel the spiral arterioles. The vessels remain narrow and spastic, leading to placental hypoperfusion, ischemia, and hypoxia. The stressed placenta then releases anti-angiogenic factors into the maternal circulation, causing the systemic endothelial dysfunction that manifests as hypertension and proteinuria.

questions.stem: On the 2nd post natal day, where will the fundus of the uterus be?
questions.explanation: 2F below the umbilicus After delivery, the uterus begins a rapid process of involution, returning to its non-pregnant size. Immediately after delivery, the uterine fundus is typically palpable at or just below the level of the umbilicus. In the subsequent days, the fundus descends into the pelvis at a predictable rate of approximately one fingerbreadth (about 1 cm) per day. Therefore, on the first postnatal day (24 hours after delivery), the fundus is expected to be about 1 fingerbreadth below the umbilicus. On the second postnatal day, it would have descended further and should be palpable approximately 2 fingerbreadths (2 cm) below the umbilicus. By about 10-14 days postpartum, the uterus has typically descended completely into the pelvis and is no longer palpable abdominally.

questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates the male fetus to produce testosterone?
questions.explanation: hCG from placenta During the first trimester of pregnancy, the development of the male internal and external genitalia is dependent on the production of testosterone by the fetal testes (Leydig cells). The fetal pituitary-gonadal axis is not yet mature. The primary stimulus for this early fetal testosterone production is human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which is produced in large quantities by the syncytiotrophoblast of the placenta. The hCG molecule has a structure similar to Luteinizing Hormone (LH) and can bind to and activate the LH receptors on the fetal Leydig cells. This stimulation is crucial for initiating testosterone synthesis, which is essential for the virilization of the male fetus. Later in gestation, the fetal pituitary begins to produce its own LH, which then takes over this role. Maternal LH (C) does not cross the placenta in significant amounts.

questions.stem: You are preparing the discharge summary for a patient who has undergone surgical repair of a vesicovaginal fistula (VVF). For how long should she be advised to abstain from sexual intercourse and delay conception after the procedure?

options.text: 6 weeks abstinence & delay conception by 6 months
6 months abstinence & delay conception by 6 years
3 weeks abstinence & delay conception by 2 years
3 months abstinence & delay conception by 1 year

questions.explanation: 6 weeks abstinence & delay conception by 6 months After surgical repair of a vesicovaginal fistula (VVF), proper postoperative care is essential to allow adequate healing of the repaired tissues and to prevent recurrence of the fistula. Patients are usually advised to abstain from sexual intercourse for about 6 weeks after surgery. This period allows the vaginal tissues and the surgical repair site to heal completely, reducing the risk of wound disruption or infection. In addition, women are advised to delay conception for at least 6 months after VVF repair. This waiting period ensures complete healing and strengthening of the repaired bladder and vaginal tissues before the stress of pregnancy and childbirth. Early pregnancy could place excess pressure on the pelvic organs, increasing the risk of fistula recurrence. Furthermore, when the patient eventually becomes pregnant, delivery is usually recommended by elective cesarean section to avoid prolonged obstructed labor, which is a common cause of fistula formation. Therefore, the recommended advice after VVF repair is 6 weeks of sexual abstinence and delaying conception for about 6 months, making option (A) the correct answer.

questions.stem: What is the position of the uterus on the 5th day of postpartum?
questions.explanation: 4 fingers below the umbilicus. The position of the uterus after childbirth is tracked by a process called uterine involution, where the organ gradually shrinks and returns to its pre-pregnancy size and location in the pelvis. This process is measured by the height of the uterine fundus (the top of the uterus) in relation to the umbilicus (belly button). Here's the typical time line : Immediately after delivery : The fundus is located at or just below the umbilicus. Rate of descent : The uterus then descends at a rate of approximately 1 centimeter (or one finger breadth) per day. Therefore, on the 5th day postpartum, the fundus would be expected to be about 4 to 5 finger breadths below the umbilicus, making option (B) the most accurate description of its involutional state. Why Other Options Are Incorrect (A) Between bladder and rectum : This describes the uterus's general anatomical location within the pelvis at all times, not its specific size and position during postpartum recovery. (C) Anteverted & (D) Retroflexed : These terms describe the tilt or orientation of the uterus. While the uterus will eventually return to its pre-pregnancy orientation (most commonly anteverted), the most significant and measurable change in the immediate postpartum period is the descent of the fundus, not its tilt. DERMATOLOGY

questions.stem: A woman presents with hair loss for the past one month and gives a history of COVID-19 infection eight weeks earlier. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Telogen Effluvium The patient is experiencing diffuse hair shedding approximately 2-3 months after a significant physiological stressor (a COVID-19 infection). This is the classic history and timeline for telogen effluvium. A major stressor—such as a severe illness, high fever, surgery, or major emotional distress—can cause a large number of hair follicles in the growing phase (anagen) to prematu rely shift into the resting phase (telogen). About 2-4 months later, these telogen hairs are shed as new anagen hairs begin to grow beneath them, resulting in a noticeable and often alarming increase in hair fall. The condition is self-limiting, and hair growth typically returns to normal within 6-9 months once the trigger has resolved. Anagen effluvium (C) is a much more abrupt and severe hair loss that occurs within days to weeks of an insult that damages growing hair follicles, such as chemotherapy. 179. questions.stem: A man is found sitting naked on a balcony overlooking a public park for the purpose of sexual gratification. What is this behavior known as?
questions.explanation: Exhibitionism Exhibitionism is a paraphilic disorder characterized by recurrent, intense sexual arousal from the exposure of ones genitals to an unsuspecting stranger. The act of exposing oneself is done for the purpose of achieving sexual gratification. The scenario described—a man exposing himself in a public-facing location to be seen by others—is the defining behavior of exhibitionism. Vo yeurism (A) is the act of secretly watching others in sexual or private situations. Masochism (B) involves deriving sexual gratification from being humiliated, beaten, or made to suffer. Fetishism (D) involves sexual arousal from non-living objects or non-genital body parts.

questions.stem: A daily wage laborer working outdoors on a hot summer day suddenly collapses and is brought to the hospital, where his body temperature is recorded as 106°F. Which of the following clinical features is least likely to be observed in this condition?
questions.explanation: Sweating This patient has heat stroke, a medical emergency defined by a core body temperature above 40°C (104°F) and central nervous system dysfunction (collapse, disorientation). There are two types : classic and exertional. In classic heat stroke, the bodys thermoregulatory center fails, and sweating ceases (anhidrosis), leaving the skin hot and dry. In exertional heat stroke, which is more likely in a laborer, the patient may still be sweating profusely. However, anhidrosis is the classic textbook sign that differentiates heat stroke from heat exhaustion. Therefore, of the options listed, the absence of sweating is the most likely intended least likely symptom, particularly for classic heat stroke. Hot skin, hypotension, and disorientation are all defining features of the condition. MICROBIOLOGY

questions.stem: A child presents with fever, a rash that starts behind the ears, conjunctivitis, coryza, cough, and Koplik spots. Based on these clinical features, which description best characterizes the causative pathogen?
questions.explanation: Single-stranded enveloped RNA virus The clinical presentation—the triad of cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, along with fever and pathognomonic Koplik spots—is di agnostic of measles. Measles is caused by the measles virus (also known as rubeola virus). Virologically, the measles virus is a member of the Morbillivirus genus within the Paramyxoviridae family. Its genome consists of a single-stranded, negative-sense RNA. The virus particle is surrounded by a lipid bilayer, making it an enveloped virus. Therefore, the correct description of the pathogen is a single-stranded enveloped RNA virus. This structural information is important as enveloped viruses are generally more susceptible to disinfectants than non-enveloped (naked) viruses.

questions.stem: Which parasite produces microfilariae that are sheathed and lack nuclei at the tail end?
questions.explanation: Wuchereria Bancrofti The microscopic differentiation of various microfilariae species is based on key features, including the presence or absence of a sheath and the arrangement of nuclei in the tail. The microfilaria of Wuchereria bancrofti is characterized by being sheathed and having a tail tip that is devoid of nuclei. In contrast, Brugia malayi (B) is also sheathed but has two distinct, terminal nuclei at the tip of its tail. Loa loa (C) is sheathed, and its nuclei extend continuously to the tip of the tail. Onchocerca volvulus (D) is unsheathed and has no nuclei in its tail tip. The combination of a sheath and an anucleated tail tip is the specific identifying feature for W. bancrofti.

questions.stem: A patient develops food poisoning after consuming pastries. Which organism is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus Food poisoning characterized by a rapid onset of nausea and vomiting (typically within 1-6 hours) after consuming contaminated food is classic for Staphylococcus aureus intoxication. This bacterium produces a heat-stable enterotoxin. Foods that are rich in protein and are handled and then left at room temperature, such as cream-filled pastries, custards, potato salad, and processed meats, are common vehicles for transmission. The toxin is pre-formed in the food, which is why the symptoms appear so quickly after ingestion. The emetic (vomiting) form of Bacillus cereus food poisoning (B) has a similar presentation and is associated with reheated rice, but S. aureus is classically linked to foods like pastries.

questions.stem: A patient with 70% burns has a sample taken from the burn wound. Microscopy reveals Gram- negative rods, and the suspected organism is an obligate aerobe. What is the most likely causative microorganism?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a notorious opportunistic pathogen that frequently colonizes and infects the wounds of patients with extensive burns. It is a Gram-negative rod and a strict obligate aerobe, meaning it requires oxygen for growth. It is known for its intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics and its ability to form biofilms, making infections difficult to treat. Burn wounds provide a moist, protein-rich environment ideal for its growth. Infections are often characterized by a blue-green exudate and a grape-like odor. The streptococci listed (C, D) are Gram-positive cocci, and Neisseria (B) is a Gram-negative diplococcus not typically associated with burn wounds.

questions.stem: A truck driver presents with a painless, well- defined ulcer on the penis along with inguinal lymphadenopathy. What is the best technique to demonstrate the motility of the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Dark field microscopy The clinical presentation of a painless ulcer (chancre) on the genitals accompanied by regional lymphadenopathy is classic for primary syphilis, caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. This organism is a thin, spiral-shaped bacterium that is too narrow to be seen with a standard light microscope. The definitive method for visualizing the live spirochete directly from an ulcer exudate is dark-field microscopy. This technique uses a special condenser to illuminate the specimen from the side, so that only light scattered by the organism enters the objective lens. This makes the spirochetes appear as bright, motile spirals against a dark background, allowing for identification based on their characteristic corkscrew motility.

questions.stem: Swab is discarded in which color bin
questions.explanation: Yellow bag According to biomedical waste management guidelines, waste is segregated into different colored bins based on its nature and disposal method. Any item contaminated with human blood or body fluids, such as used cotton swabs, dressings, and plaster casts, is considered infectious or soiled waste. This category of waste must be discarded in the yellow bag. Waste collected in yellow bags is destined for incineration or deep burial to ensure the complete destruction of potentially infectious pathogens. Red bags are for recyclable contaminated waste like plastics (syringes, catheters), white bags are for sharps (needles), and blue bags are for glass waste.

questions.stem: Pen Test is for which nerve
questions.explanation: PIN The Pen Test is used to assess the function of the Posterior Interosseous Nerve (PIN), which is a deep motor branch of the radial nerve. This nerve primarily supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm, especially those responsible for extension of the fingers and thumb. In the pen test, a pen is placed on the palm, and the patient is asked to extend the fingers to flick or lift the pen off the palm. Successful performance of this movement requires proper functioning of the finger extensor muscles, which are innervated by the posterior interosseous nerve. If the PIN is injured or compressed, the patient cannot extend the fingers properly, resulting in finger drop, while wrist extension may still be partially preserved due to other radial nerve branches. Sensory loss is usually absent because the posterior interosseous nerve is mainly a motor nerve. Therefore, inability to perform the pen test suggests posterior interosseous nerve palsy, making this test useful in identifying PIN lesions caused by trauma, fractures, or compression in the forearm.

questions.stem: Through which secondary messenger system do β₂-adrenergic receptors exert their effects?
questions.explanation: Adenylate Cyclase Beta-2 adrenergic receptors are a type of G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR). Specifically, they are coupled to a stimulatory G-protein (Gs). When a ligand like epinephrine binds to the beta-2 receptor, it activates the Gs protein. This activated protein, in turn, stimulates the membrane-bound enzyme adenylate cyclase. Adenylate cyclase then catalyzes the conversion of ATP into the second messenger, cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). The increased intracellular levels of cAMP activate Protein Kinase A (PKA), which then phosphorylates various downstream targets to produce the final physiological effect, such as bronchodilation or vasodilation. Tyrosine kinase receptors (B) are a different class of receptors used by insulin and growth factors.

questions.stem: A child with dehydration is treated with oral rehydration solution (ORS). Which receptor or transporter in the gastrointestinal tract facilitates glucose absorption in this process?
questions.explanation: SGLT 1 The effectiveness of Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) is based on the coupled transport of sodium and glucose in the small intestine. The absorption of glucose from the intestinal lumen into the enterocytes is primarily mediated by the Sodium-Glucose Linked Transporter 1 (SGLT1). This transporter is located on the apical membrane of intestinal epithelial cells. It functions by using the electrochemical gradient of sodium to co-transport one molecule of sodium along with one molecule of glucose into the cell. This process is a form of secondary active transport. The absorption of sodium and glucose creates an osmotic gradient that drives the passive absorption of water, effectively rehydrating the patient. SGLT2 (B) is found in the kidneys, while GLUT transporters (C, D) are involved in facilitated diffusion of glucose. 9. A patient presents with cold skin, fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and hepatomegaly. NODIA

questions.stem: A patients body fluid compartment analysis shows the following ion concentrations : sodium 10 mEq/L, potassium 140 mEq/L, and chloride 15 mEq/L. Based on these electrolyte values, which fluid compartment is being represented?
questions.explanation: ICF The bodys fluid compartments have distinct ionic compositions. The intracellular fluid (ICF), which is the fluid inside the cells, is characterized by a high concentration of potassium (K+) and a low concentration of sodium (Na+) and chloride (Cl-). The values provided (K+ 140 mEq/L, Na+ 10 mEq/L) are classic for the intracellular environment. In contrast, the extracellular fluid (ECF), which includes plasma and interstitial fluid, is characterized by a high concentration of sodium (around 140 mEq/L) and chloride, and a very low concentration of potassium (around 4 mEq/L). The given ion profile is the inverse of the ECF and is definitively representative of the intracellular fluid compartment.

questions.stem: An elderly woman presents with involuntary dribbling of urine that occurs only during coughing or straining. What type of urinary incontinence is she most likely experiencing?
questions.explanation: Stress incontinence Stress incontinence is defined as the involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure. The patients symptom of urine dribbling specifically on coughing and straining is the classic presentation of this condition. It is typically caused by weakness of the pelvic floor muscles and/or the urethral sphincter, which are unable to counteract the sudden increase in pressure on the bladder. This is common in elderly women, especially those who have had multiple pregnancies. Urge incontinence (B) is leakage preceded by a sudden, intense urge to urinate. Overflow incontinence (C) is due to an overfull bladder that cannot empty properly.

questions.stem: A young patient presents with muscle spasms, tingling in the hands and feet, seizures, and episodes of breathing difficulty due to laryngospasm, and laboratory investigations show an electrolyte abnormality. What is the most likely underlying cause of these symptoms?
questions.explanation: Respiratory Alkalosis The patients symptoms of muscle spasms (tetany), perioral and extremity numbness (paresthesias), seizures, and laryngospasm are all signs of acute hypocalcemia. Specifically, they are caused by a decrease in the level of ionized calcium in the blood. Acute respiratory alkalosis, often caused by hyperventilation, is a common cause of these symptoms. The increase in blood pH (alkalosis) causes more calcium to bind to albumin, which decreases the physiologically active ionized calcium fraction. This reduction in ionized calcium increases neuromuscular excitability, leading to tetany and the other neurological symptoms described. While other electrolyte imbalances can cause some of these symptoms, the full constellation in an acute setting is highly suggestive of symptomatic hypocalcemia secondary to respiratory alkalosis. BIOCHEMISTRY

questions.stem: A patient consuming a predominantly maize- based diet presents with diarrhea, dementia, and dysentery. Deficiency of which vitamin is responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: NiacinThe classic triad of diarrhea, dementia, and dermatitis (the 3 Ds) is pathognomonic for pellagra, the disease caused by a severe deficiency of niacin (Vitamin B3). A diet consisting predominantly of maize (corn) is a major risk factor for pellagra. This is because the niacin present in maize is in a bound, non-bioavailable form. Additionally, maize is low in the amino acid tryptophan, which the body can use to synthesize niacin. Therefore, individuals on a maize-based diet are at high risk for developing this deficiency. The symptoms described, including diarrhea and dementia, are classic components of the pellagra syndrome. The question likely uses dysentery interchangeably with severe diarrhea.

questions.stem: A patient presents with dry eyes, a gritty or foreign-body sensation, and evidence of corneal softening. What is the most probable underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency The ocular manifestations described are classic signs of severe Vitamin A deficiency, collectively known as xerophthalmia. The initial symptom is often night blindness, followed by xerosis, which is an abnormal dryness of the conjunctiva and cornea, leading to a gritty sensation. As the deficiency worsens, it can lead to keratomalacia, which is a softening, melting, and liquefaction of the cornea. This is a medical emergency that can rapidly progress to corneal ulceration, perforation, and permanent blindness. The combination of dry eyes and corneal softening is highly specific for advanced Vitamin A deficiency. Riboflavin deficiency can cause ocular symptoms, but not corneal softening.

questions.stem: In a patient with cystathionine β-synthase deficiency, which amino acid must be supplemented through the diet?
questions.explanation: Cysteine Cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) is a key enzyme in the transforation pathway, which converts homocysteine to cystathionine. This pathway is the primary route for the synthesis of the amino acid cysteine from the essential amino acid methionine. In a patient with a deficiency of CBS (the cause of classic homo cystinuria), this conversion is blocked. As a result, cysteine cannot be synthesized endogenously from methionine. This makes cysteine a conditionally essential amino acid for these patients, meaning it must be supplied directly through the diet. Conversely, methionine and homocysteine accumulate, so the dietary intake of methionine (B) must be restricted, not supplemented.

questions.stem: Corneal transparency is primarily maintained by which glycosaminoglycan (GAG)?
questions.explanation: Keratan Sulphate The transparency of the cornea is a remarkable feature that depends on the highly organized and uniform arrangement of its collagen fibrils within the stroma. The specific glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) present in the corneal stroma play a crucial role in maintaining this precise architecture and hydration level. The predominant GAGs in the cornea are keratan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate. Keratan sulfate, in particular, is essential for regulating the spacing between collagen fibrils and controlling stromal hydration. This precise organization minimizes light scattering and allows light to pass through unimpeded, thus maintaining corneal transparency. Defects in keratan sulfate metabolism, as seen in macular corneal dystrophy, lead to corneal clouding.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is associated with a defect in the DNA mismatch repair system?
questions.explanation: Hereditary NPCC Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC), also known as Lynch syndrome, is an autosomal dominant genetic condition that confers a high risk of colorectal cancer and other cancers (e.g., endometrial, ovarian, gastric). The underlying genetic cause of HNPCC is a germline mutation in one of the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, most commonly MSH2 or MLH1. These genes are responsible for correcting errors that occur during DNA replication. A defect in this system leads to the accumulation of mutations throughout the genome, a state known as microsatellite instability (MSI), which drives carcinogenesis. The other conditions are caused by different genetic defects : Bloom disorder involves a DNA helicase, and MUTYH-associated polyposis involves a base excision repair gene.

questions.stem: A patient eats dinner at 8 PM and undergoes a blood glucose test at 7 AM the next morning. What is the primary source of glucose in the blood at this time?
questions.explanation: Liver Glycogen The blood test is performed after an 11-hour overnight fast. During the post-absorptive or early fasting state (from about 4 to 12-16 hours after a meal), the primary mechanism for maintaining blood glucose homeostasis is the breakdown of stored glycogen in the liver, a process called hepatic glycogenolysis. The liver stores enough glycogen to supply the bodys glucose needs for this period. As the fast progresses beyond 12 hours, liver glycogen stores become depleted, and gluconeogenesis (C), the synthesis of new glucose primarily in the liver, becomes the predominant source. Muscle glycogen (A) cannot be released into the bloodstream to maintain blood glucose because muscle lacks the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase.
