questions.stem: In which condition is the Ankle–Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) falsely elevated?
questions.explanation: Arteriosclerosis calcified arteries The Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI or ABI) is a simple, non-invasive test used to assess for peripheral artery disease (PAD). It is calculated by dividing the systolic blood pressure at the ankle by the systolic blood pressure in the arm. A normal ABI is between 1.0 and 1.4. An ABI < 0.9 is diagnostic of PAD, with the value correlating to disease severity (intermittent claudication, ischemic ulcers). However, in some patients, particularly those with long-standing diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or advanced age, the arteries of the lower leg (tibial arteries) can become heavily calcified and hardened due to medial arterial calcification (Mönckeberg's sclerosis). These calcified arteries are non-compressible. When a blood pressure cuff is inflated around the ankle, it cannot fully compress the rigid artery, leading to a falsely and artificially elevated ankle pressure reading. This can result in a misleadingly normal or even abnormally high ABI (e.g., > 1.4), masking the presence of severe underlying PAD.

questions.stem: What is the most frequent cause of chronic pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Chronic alcohol Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disease of the pancreas characterized by irreversible destruction of the pancreatic parenchyma, fibrosis, and loss of both exocrine and endocrine function. While there are numerous causes, the most common etiology by a significant margin in the Western world and many other parts of the globe is chronic and heavy alcohol consumption. Alcohol abuse is responsible for approximately 70-80% of all cases of chronic pancreatitis. Alcohol is believed to be directly toxic to pancreatic acinar cells and to alter the composition of pancreatic secretions, leading to the formation of protein plugs that obstruct small pancreatic ducts. This obstruction and direct toxicity initiate a cycle of inflammation and fibrosis that eventually destroys the gland. Gallstones are the most common cause of acute pancreatitis, but not chronic. Pancreatic calculi are a consequence, not a primary cause. Pancreas divisum is a congenital anomaly that is a less common cause.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about keloid is true?

options.text: Extended excision is the treatment of choice
It does not extend beyond the wound

questions.explanation: It contains growth factor A keloid is a type of abnormal scar that results from an overgrowth of dense fibrous tissue, developing after a skin injury heals. Unlike a hypertrophic scar, a keloid characteristically extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound. This uncontrolled proliferation is driven by a dysregulation in the wound healing process, involving an overproduction of extracellular matrix components, particularly collagen. A key factor in this pathogenesis is the excessive production of various growth factors, most notably Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-β) and Platelet-Derived Growth Factor (PDGF). These growth factors stimulate fibroblasts to proliferate and synthesize collagen at an abnormally high rate, leading to the formation of the large, raised scar tissue. Statement (C) is incorrect, as extending beyond the wound margin is the defining feature of a keloid. Simple wide excision (B) is not the treatment of choice as it is associated with an extremely high recurrence rate, often resulting in an even larger keloid. Treatment is challenging and usually involves a combination of therapies like intralesional steroid injections, cryotherapy, or excision with adjuvant radiation.

questions.stem: Which nerve is thickened in the image shown?
questions.explanation: Greater auricular nerve The image shows marked thickening of a nerve in the head and neck region, a classic sign of leprosy (Hansen's disease). The nerve shown is the greater auricular nerve. This is a sensory nerve that arises from the cervical plexus (C2, C3) and ascends vertically over the sternocleidomastoid muscle towards the ear. It supplies sensation to the skin over the angle of the jaw, the parotid gland, and a large part of the auricle (ear). The greater auricular nerve is one of the most commonly affected peripheral nerves in leprosy, along with the ulnar and common peroneal nerves. Its superficial course makes it easily visible and palpable when it becomes thickened due to the inflammatory and granulomatous infiltration caused by Mycobacterium leprae. Thickening of this nerve, often associated with loss of sensation in its distribution, is a cardinal sign of leprosy.

questions.stem: Which tissue layers are incised during a fasciotomy?

options.text: Skin + subcutaneous tissue + superficial fascia + deep fascia

questions.explanation: Skin + subcutaneous tissue + superficial fascia + deep fascia A fasciotomy is an emergency surgical procedure performed to treat acute compartment syndrome. Compartment syndrome occurs when increased pressure within a confined fascial compartment compromises the circulation and function of the tissues within that space, potentially leading to muscle and nerve necrosis. The goal of the procedure is to relieve this pressure by decompressing the affected compartment(s). To achieve this, the surgeon must make an incision through all the layers that are confining the swollen muscle. This involves making a long incision through the skin, followed by the underlying subcutaneous tissue and the superficial fascia. The most critical step is then to incise the tough, inelastic deep fascia that encases the muscle compartment. This final incision allows the swollen muscle to bulge out, immediately relieving the intra compartmental pressure and restoring blood flow. Merely incising the skin and subcutaneous layers would be insufficient to decompress the muscle compartment, which is the primary goal of the procedure.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Crohn’s disease is not true?
questions.explanation: Continuous lesion visualized in endoscopy Crohn's disease is a type of inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus. One of its hallmark features is the discontinuous nature of the inflammation, which is described as skip lesions. This means there are areas of active inflammation separated by segments of normal-appearing mucosa. Therefore, the statement that a continuous lesion is visualized on endoscopy is not true and is, in fact, the characteristic pattern of ulcerative colitis, where inflammation typically starts in the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous and circumferential manner. In Crohn's disease, the rectum is often spared (A). Histological examination frequently reveals non-caseating granulomas (C), another hallmark of the disease. The combination of deep linear ulcers and transmural inflammation with submucosal edema creates a nodular appearance of the mucosa on endoscopy or barium studies, which is described as a cobblestone appearance (D).

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate investigation for diagnosing carcinoma of the pancreatic head?
questions.explanation: EUS (Endoscopic Ultrasound) For the diagnosis and staging of pancreatic cancer, particularly tumors in the head of the pancreas, Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS) is considered the most sensitive and accurate imaging modality. EUS involves passing an endoscope with a high-frequency ultrasound transducer at its tip into the stomach and duodenum. This allows for high-resolution imaging of the pancreas from a very close proximity, without interference from bowel gas. EUS is superior to CT and MRI for detecting small tumors (<2 cm), assessing the depth of tumor invasion, and evaluating local lymph node involvement and vascular invasion (T and N staging). A crucial advantage of EUS is that it also allows for EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA), which can be performed during the same procedure to obtain a tissue diagnosis. This combination of superior imaging and the ability to obtain a cytological sample makes EUS the best single investigation for both diagnosing and staging pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. ERCP is more therapeutic for relieving biliary obstruction. NODIA

questions.stem: The skull X-ray is demonstrating which type of brain lesion?
questions.explanation: Paget's disease The skull X-ray demonstrates the classic features of Paget's disease of bone (osteitis deformans). Paget's disease is a chronic metabolic bone disorder characterized by excessive and disorganized bone remodeling. The disease progresses through stages of increased osteoclastic activity (lytic phase), followed by a compensatory increase in disorganized osteoblastic activity (mixed and sclerotic phases). In the skull, this process leads to significant thickening of the calvarium. The characteristic radiological appearance in the mixed or sclerotic phase is often described as a cotton wool appearance. This is due to the presence of large, patchy, ill-defined areas of sclerosis (the cotton wool spots) interspersed with areas of lucency, representing the chaotic bone turnover. Multiple myeloma causes punched-out lytic lesions. Osteosarcoma would show a sunburst pattern.

questions.stem: What is meant by Perilunate dislocation?

options.text: Lower radius, scaphoid, and lunate and capitate all in the same plane
Lower radius, scaphoid, and capitate in alignment, lunate alone out of the plane
Lower radius, scaphoid, and lunate in alignment, capitate alone is out of the plane
Both lunate and capitate are out of the plane

questions.explanation: Lower radius, scaphoid, and lunate in alignment, capitate alone is out of the plane Perilunate dislocation is a severe and unstable wrist injury that results from high-energy trauma, typically a fall onto an outstretched, hyperextended hand. The injury involves the disruption of the ligaments that connect the carpal bones. The key to understanding this injury is the relationship between the radius, lunate, and capitate on a lateral wrist radiograph. Normally, these three bones are co-linear, forming a straight line. In a perilunate dislocation, the ligaments holding the capitate to the lunate are torn, and the capitate (along with the rest of the carpus) dislocates dorsally relative to the lunate. The lunate, however, maintains its normal alignment with the distal radius. Therefore, the lower radius and lunate remain in alignment, while the capitate alone is out of the plane (dislocated dorsally). If the injury progresses, the lunate can also dislocate, rotating volarly into the carpal tunnel, which is then called a lunate dislocation.

questions.stem: Fallen fragment sign is seen in:
questions.explanation: Simple bone cyst The fallen fragment sign is a pathognomonic radiological sign that is highly specific for a Simple Bone Cyst, also known as a Unicameral Bone Cyst (UBC). A UBC is a benign, fluid-filled lesion that typically occurs in the metaphysis of long bones in children and adolescents. The cyst can thin and expand the overlying bone cortex, making it susceptible to a pathological fracture. When a fracture occurs, a fragment of the weakened cortical bone can break off and fall into the fluid-filled cavity of the cyst. On a radiograph, this piece of bone is seen lying in the dependent portion of the cystic lesion. The presence of this fallen fragment is diagnostic of a UBC because it confirms that the lesion is cystic (fluid-filled) rather than solid, and it has fractured. This sign is not seen in solid tumors like osteosarcoma or in the blood-filled, septated aneurysmal bone cyst.

questions.stem: As an intern in the casualty, which of the following fracture patients should you prioritize for immediate notification of the orthopedic postgraduate?

options.text: Intra-articular fracture of the elbow joint

questions.explanation: Patient's finger is blackening In an emergency setting, the principle of triage dictates that patients with life- or limb-threatening conditions must be prioritized. A patient with a fracture whose finger is blackening is showing a sign of severe vascular compromise or impending gangrene. This is an orthopedic emergency. The blackening indicates a lack of blood supply (ischemia) to the digit, which could be due to an arterial injury, thrombosis, or severe swelling causing compartment syndrome associated with the fracture. If blood flow is not restored urgently, the tissue will die, leading to the need for amputation. This is a limb-threatening situation that requires immediate assessment and intervention by the orthopedic team. Inability to extend the arm (B) suggests a nerve or tendon injury, a 10 cm abrasion (C) is a soft tissue injury, and an intra-articular fracture (D) requires attention, but none of these are as immediately limb-threatening as acute vascular compromise.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly describes the suture material shown in the image?
questions.explanation: Degraded by enzymatic degradation The image shows a package of Catgut Plain suture material. Catgut is a natural, absorbable suture. Despite its name, it is not made from the intestines of cats. It is manufactured from the purified submucosal layer of the small intestine of healthy ruminants, typically sheep or goats. Therefore, options A and B are incorrect. Catgut is an absorbable suture, meaning it is broken down and absorbed by the body over time, so statement C is incorrect. The mechanism by which catgut is absorbed is unique among sutures. It is a natural collagen material, and it is degraded by the body's own proteolytic enzymes, which recognize it as a foreign protein. This enzymatic degradation process provokes a significant inflammatory response. In contrast, modern synthetic absorbable sutures (like Vicryl or PDS) are broken down by a more predictable and less inflammatory process called hydrolysis.

questions.stem: Which immune cells are predominantly found in the synovial fluid of patients with rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation: T cells Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease characterized by inflammation of the synovial joints. The synovial fluid in an actively inflamed RA joint is typically inflammatory, with a high white blood cell count (usually 5,000 to 50,000 cells/μL). The predominant cell type in this inflammatory infiltrate is the neutrophil, which can make up >75% of the cells. However, among the mononuclear cells that drive the chronic autoimmune process, T-lymphocytes are the most abundant. Specifically, activated CD4+ T-helper cells are considered to play a central role in orchestrating the autoimmune response in RA. They recognize an unknown antigen presented by antigen-presenting cells like macrophages and dendritic cells, and in turn, they activate these cells and B-cells. This leads to the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (like TNF-α and IL-6) and autoantibodies (like rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP), which perpetuate the synovial inflammation and joint destruction.

questions.stem: Tom Smith’s septic arthritis refers to which condition?
questions.explanation: Septic arthritis of infancy Tom Smith's arthritis is an eponym for a particularly destructive form of septic arthritis of the hip joint that occurs in infancy. It was described by the surgeon Thomas Smith in 1874. The condition is characterized by a rapid and often complete destruction of the femoral head. In infants, the blood supply to the femoral head epiphysis passes through the joint capsule. An infection in the hip joint can cause a septic effusion that rapidly increases the intra-articular pressure. This pressure can compress the blood vessels, leading to avascular necrosis (death) of the femoral head. The infection can also directly destroy the cartilage. Because the femoral head in infants is largely cartilaginous, it can be completely destroyed by this process, leading to a pathological dislocation of the hip and severe long-term disability. This condition is an absolute surgical emergency requiring immediate drainage of the joint. 237. What condition is demonstrated in the Hysterosalpingography (HSG) image shown?

questions.stem: Which vaccine is not included under Mission Indradhanush?
questions.explanation: Japanese Encephalitis Mission Indradhanush is a flagship immunization program of the Government of India, launched in 2014. Its goal is to rapidly increase full immunization coverage for children up to two years of age and pregnant women. The program initially focused on strengthening the delivery of the vaccines included in the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP). The original seven vaccines targeted by Mission Indradhanush (representing the seven colors of the rainbow, Indradhanush) were for tuberculosis (BCG), poliomyelitis (OPV), hepatitis B, diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus (Pentavalent vaccine), and measles (MR vaccine). Subsequently, the program has been expanded to include other vaccines like the rotavirus vaccine, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV), and others. However, the Japanese Encephalitis (JE) vaccine is not part of the core nationwide UIP package. It is sub-national and is administered only in specific districts that are identified as endemic for the disease. Therefore, it was not one of the original universal vaccines targeted by the mission.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of neonatal blindness?
questions.explanation: Neisseria gonorrhoeae Neonatal blindness most commonly results from ophthalmia neonatorum, a severe conjunctival infection occurring within the first month of life. Among infectious causes, Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the most dangerous and classically associated with rapid progression to corneal ulceration, perforation, and permanent blindness if not treated promptly. Gonococcal conjunctivitis typically presents within 2–5 days after birth with profuse purulent discharge, eyelid edema, and conjunctival redness. The organism can invade an intact corneal epithelium, making it particularly aggressive. Without immediate systemic antibiotic therapy (usually intravenous or intramuscular ceftriaxone), serious ocular damage may occur. Chlamydia trachomatis is also a common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis, but it is generally less destructive to the cornea and less likely to cause blindness compared to gonococcal infection. Klebsiella and Enterobacter are uncommon causes of neonatal conjunctivitis and are not typical causes of neonatal blindness. Therefore, the most common and most serious cause leading to neonatal blindness is (A) Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questions.stem: A 1-year-old child weighing 6 kg presents with acute gastroenteritis, along with sunken, dry eyes and a skin pinch that returns very slowly (more than 2 seconds). What is the appropriate management?

options.text: RL infusion 120 ml in the first hour followed by 360 ml in the next 5 hours
RL infusion 180 ml in the first hour followed by 420 ml in the next 5 hours
RL infusion 180 ml in the first hour followed by 480 ml in the next 5 hours
RL infusion 240 ml in the first hour followed by 360 ml in the next 5 hours

questions.explanation: RL infusion 180 ml in the first hour followed by 420 ml in the next 5 hours The child shows signs of severe dehydration (sunken eyes and skin pinch returning very slowly >2 seconds). According to WHO guidelines, severe dehydration in children requires Plan C management with intravenous fluids, preferably Ringer’s lactate (RL). For children below 12 months, the recommended regimen is: 100 mL/kg total IV fluid 30 mL/kg in the first 1 hour 70 mL/kg over the next 5 hours For this 6 kg child: Total fluid = 100 × 6 = 600 mL First hour = 30 × 6 = 180 mL Next 5 hours = 70 × 6 = 420 mL This matches option (B). After initial resuscitation, reassessment is essential. Once the child can drink, oral rehydration solution (ORS) should be started. Monitoring urine output, pulse, and hydration status is critical to ensure adequate correction of dehydration. Therefore, the correct management is (B) RL infusion 180 ml in the first hour followed by 420 ml in the next 5 hours.

questions.stem: A newborn with a heart rate below 60 beats per minute can be resuscitated using all of the following methods except which one?
questions.explanation: Slapping the back In neonatal resuscitation, management follows the Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines. If a newborn has a heart rate below 60 beats per minute despite adequate ventilation, positive pressure ventilation (PPV) is initiated first. If the heart rate remains below 60 bpm after effective ventilation, chest compressions are started along with oxygen support. 1. Chest compressions (A) are indicated when HR < 60 bpm despite adequate ventilation. 2. Oxygen therapy (B) is part of resuscitation to improve oxygenation. 3. Tactile stimulation (C) such as gentle rubbing of the back or flicking the soles is appropriate in the initial steps if the baby is not breathing adequately. However, slapping the back (D) is not recommended. It is potentially harmful and not part of standard neonatal resuscitation protocols. Only gentle stimulation is advised. Therefore, the method not used in neonatal resuscitation is (D) Slapping the back.

questions.stem: When can acute respiratory distress be diagnosed in a child?

options.text: Within 7 days of a known clinical event

questions.explanation: Within 7 days of a known clinical event Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) in children is diagnosed based on established criteria (such as the Berlin definition and pediatric ARDS guidelines). One of the key diagnostic criteria is that respiratory symptoms must develop within 7 days of a known clinical insult (such as sepsis, pneumonia, trauma, aspiration, or pancreatitis) or worsening respiratory symptoms. Other essential features include: 1. Acute onset 2. Bilateral opacities on chest imaging 3. Respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload 4. Impaired oxygenation based on oxygenation indices Option (B) is incorrect because ARDS requires an identifiable clinical insult; it is not classified simply as respiratory failure of unknown cause. Option (C) is incorrect because respiratory distress due to left ventricular dysfunction is cardiogenic pulmonary edema, which is excluded from ARDS diagnosis. Therefore, the correct answer is (A) Within 7 days of a known clinical event. ORTHOPEDIC

questions.stem: Which muscles are involved in De Quervain’s tenosynovitis?

options.text: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Adductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Abductor pollicis longus and Flexor pollicis brevis
Adductor pollicis longus and Flexor pollicis brevis

questions.explanation: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis De Quervain's tenosynovitis is a common and painful condition affecting the wrist and thumb. It is a stenosing tenosynovitis, meaning it involves inflammation and thickening of the synovial sheath that surrounds the tendons at the base of the thumb. Specifically, it affects the two tendons that run through the first dorsal (extensor) compartment of the wrist. These two tendons are the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and the extensor pollicis brevis (EPB). The inflammation of the tendon sheath (tenosynovium) and the thickening of the overlying extensor retinaculum constrict the movement of these tendons, causing pain, tenderness, and swelling on the radial (thumb) side of the wrist. The pain is typically exacerbated by movements involving thumb abduction and wrist ulnar deviation. The diagnosis is often confirmed clinically with the Finkelstein test. 229. What is the diagnosis based on the given image? NODIA

questions.stem: After performing the McRoberts maneuver in shoulder dystocia, what is the next step in management?

options.text: Sharp flexion of hip joints towards the abdomen

questions.explanation: Suprapubic pressure Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency where the anterior shoulder of the fetus becomes impacted behind the mother's pubic symphysis after the delivery of the head. A sequence of maneuvers is used to resolve it. The first maneuver is the McRoberts maneuver (A), which involves hyperflexion of the mother's hips onto her abdomen. This flattens the sacral promontory and rotates the pubic symphysis, often creating enough space for the shoulder to deliver. If this maneuver alone is unsuccessful, the next step is to apply suprapubic pressure. An assistant applies firm, downward pressure on the maternal abdomen just above the pubic bone, in an attempt to adduct the fetal shoulder and push it under the symphysis. The McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure are often performed simultaneously. Internal rotational maneuvers, such as the Rubin or Wood's screw maneuver (C), are performed next if the initial steps fail. An emergency C-section (D) is not possible at this stage as the head is already delivered.

questions.stem: Peripartum cardiomyopathy usually develops within what time period?
questions.explanation: Within 5 months Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a rare but potentially life-threatening form of idiopathic cardiomyopathy defined as the development of heart failure in women towards the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, without any other identifiable cause. The standard diagnostic criteria for PPCM require the onset of symptoms of heart failure to occur in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum. The patient must have evidence of left ventricular systolic dysfunction (typically an ejection fraction of less than 45%) and no other known cause of heart failure. While many cases present within the first week or month postpartum, the diagnostic window extends up to 5 months. The clinical presentation is that of acute heart failure, with symptoms like dyspnea, orthopnea, and peripheral edema. The condition is a diagnosis of exclusion.

questions.stem: Which nerve is most frequently compressed during pregnancy and the puerperium?
questions.explanation: Median nerve During pregnancy, hormonal changes and significant fluid retention are common. This generalized edema can lead to compression of peripheral nerves as they pass through anatomical tunnels or canals. The most common peripheral nerve entrapment syndrome in pregnancy is carpal tunnel syndrome, which is caused by the compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist. The increased fluid volume during pregnancy increases the pressure within this confined space, leading to symptoms of pain, numbness, and tingling in the distribution of the median nerve (the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger). Symptoms are often worse at night and can be bilateral. While other nerve palsies can occur (e.g., from positioning during labor), carpal tunnel syndrome due to median nerve compression is by far the most frequent peripheral neuropathy associated with pregnancy.

questions.stem: Which bone labeled in the X-ray is most frequently fractured during a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH)?
questions.explanation: 1 The question describes a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH), which is a very common mechanism of wrist injury. The bone that is most frequently fractured in this type of fall is the scaphoid bone, which is indicated by the number 1 in the provided X-ray. The scaphoid is the largest bone in the proximal row of carpal bones, and its position bridging the proximal and distal carpal rows makes it particularly vulnerable to fracture during hyperextension of the wrist. The force of the impact is transmitted up the hand through the capitate bone, which then impacts and fractures the narrow waist of the scaphoid. A scaphoid fracture is a clinically important injury because the bone has a tenuous, retrograde blood supply, which puts it at high risk for non-union or avascular necrosis if the fracture is missed or not properly treated.

questions.stem: During pregnancy, which of the following laboratory values undergoes the greatest change?
questions.explanation: Total T3 Pregnancy induces profound physiological changes in the thyroid gland and thyroid hormone levels. The high levels of estrogen during pregnancy stimulate the liver to produce more thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), the main protein that carries thyroid hormones in the blood. This significant increase in TBG leads to a higher binding capacity for thyroid hormones. As a result, the levels of total thyroxine (Total T4) and total triiodothyronine (Total T3), which measure both the bound and free hormone, are markedly elevated. They are typically about 1.5 times the non-pregnant levels. However, the physiologically active hormones are the free hormones. The levels of free T4 and free T3 generally remain within the normal range for non-pregnant women, although they may fluctuate slightly. TSH levels are often transiently suppressed in the first trimester due to the weak TSH-like activity of hCG, but they also typically normalize later in pregnancy. The most dramatic and sustained change is the elevation in total hormone levels.

questions.stem: What is the definition of superfecundation?

options.text: Fertilization of two or more ova in one intercourse
Fertilization of two or more ova in different intercourses in the same menstrual cycle
Fertilization of ova and then its division
Fertilization of second ovum, first being implanted

questions.explanation: Fertilization of two or more ova in different intercourses in the same menstrual cycle Superfecundation is the fertilization of two or more ova released during the same ovulatory cycle by sperm from separate acts of sexual intercourse. This can result in dizygotic (fraternal) twins who have different biological fathers, a phenomenon known as heteropaternal superfecundation. This occurs if a woman has intercourse with two different men within a short time frame around her ovulation. It is a rare event in humans but is well-documented. This is different from the fertilization of two ova from a single act of intercourse (A), which is the standard way dizygotic twins are conceived from one father. It is also distinct from superfetation, which is the fertilization and subsequent implantation of a second ovum when a pregnancy is already established, an extremely rare occurrence in humans.

questions.stem: At what stage of development does the fetal heart begin to contract?
questions.explanation: 3-5 weeks The development of the cardiovascular system is one of the earliest and most critical events in embryogenesis. The primitive heart begins to form as a simple tube from the fusion of cardiogenic cords in the mesoderm during the third week of gestation. This heart tube begins to beat and pump blood in a coordinated, peristaltic fashion at approximately 21 to 22 days post-conception. This corresponds to the beginning of the fourth week of gestation, or the 5th week of pregnancy as dated from the last menstrual period. Therefore, the fetal heart starts its rhythmic contractions very early, within the 3-5 week gestational window. By the end of the fourth week, a rudimentary but functional circulation is established. The heartbeat can typically be detected by transvaginal ultrasound around 5.5 to 6 weeks of gestation.

questions.stem: What is the preferred anesthetic technique for performing a cesarean section in a patient with severe pre-eclampsia?
questions.explanation: Spinal Spinal anesthesia is the preferred anesthetic technique for performing a cesarean section in a patient with severe pre-eclampsia because it provides rapid, reliable, and dense anesthesia while avoiding the risks associated with general anesthesia. In severe pre-eclampsia, patients often have hypertension, airway edema, and an increased risk of difficult intubation. General anesthesia can cause a marked rise in blood pressure during laryngoscopy and intubation, which may precipitate complications such as intracranial hemorrhage or cardiac failure. Therefore, avoiding airway manipulation is beneficial. Spinal anesthesia produces sympathetic blockade, which can help reduce elevated blood pressure in pre-eclamptic patients. Contrary to earlier concerns, studies have shown that hypotension following spinal anesthesia is generally less severe in pre-eclamptic patients compared to healthy pregnant women because of their already vasoconstricted state. It also allows the mother to remain conscious and reduces fetal exposure to anesthetic drugs. Epidural anesthesia may be used, but it has a slower onset. Combined spinal-epidural is an option, but spinal alone is commonly preferred for its simplicity and rapid effect in emergency or urgent cesarean deliveries.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations is not classified as a high-risk pregnancy?

options.text: Previous history of manual removal of placenta

questions.explanation: Previous history of manual removal of placenta A high-risk pregnancy is one in which the mother or the fetus has an increased risk of morbidity or mortality before, during, or after delivery. Conditions like pre-existing or gestational diabetes (C), severe anemia (B), and significant maternal obesity (D) are all well-established risk factors that classify a pregnancy as high-risk. These conditions can lead to numerous complications, including pre-eclampsia, fetal growth abnormalities, preterm birth, and delivery complications. In contrast, a previous history of manual removal of the placenta is a risk factor for a retained placenta in a subsequent pregnancy, but it is not typically considered a factor that categorizes the entire pregnancy as high-risk from the outset, in the same way that a major medical condition like diabetes does. While it requires vigilance during the third stage of labor, it does not have the same level of systemic impact on the antepartum course as the other conditions listed. 255. Which of the following is not used in the management of preeclampsia? (A) Methyldopa (B) Atenolol (C) Labetalol (D) Hydralazine Ans : (B) Atenolol

questions.stem: The surgical procedure known as fimbrectomy corresponds to which sterilization technique?
questions.explanation: Kroener method Fimbrectomy refers to a method of female sterilization in which the fimbrial end of the fallopian tube is surgically removed. This procedure is specifically known as the Kroener method. In this technique, the distal (fimbrial) portion of the fallopian tube is excised, thereby preventing the ovum from entering the tube and eliminating the possibility of fertilization. Since the fimbriae play a crucial role in capturing the ovulated egg from the ovary and guiding it into the fallopian tube, their removal effectively results in permanent contraception. The Kroener method is considered a definitive sterilization procedure and is generally performed when permanent contraception is desired. Unlike other techniques such as the Irving method, Uchida method, or Madlener technique—which involve ligation, rese ction, or burying segments of the fallopian tube—the Kroener method specifically targets and removes the fimbrial end. Because of this distinctive feature, fimbrectomy is synonymous with the Kroener method in gynecological surgical practice. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the placenta is correct?

options.text: Placental artery provides nutrients through the umbilical cord to the baby
The placenta is attached to the umbilical cord that has Wharton's jelly
Estrogen is secreted by the placenta

questions.explanation: The placenta is attached to the umbilical cord that has Wharton's jelly The placenta is a temporary organ that develops in the uterus during pregnancy and serves as the connection between the mother and the developing fetus. It is firmly attached to the uterine wall and connected to the fetus through the umbilical cord. The umbilical cord contains two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein. These blood vessels are surrounded and protected by a soft, gelatinous connective tissue called Wharton’s jelly, which prevents compression of the vessels and ensures continuous blood flow between the mother and fetus. Option (A) is incorrect because the umbilical vein carries oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus, not the artery. Option (C) is incorrect because the umbilical cord contains two arteries and one vein, not two veins and one artery. Option (D) is incorrect because although the placenta secretes hormones including estrogen and progesterone, the statement given in the options is incomplete and less specific compared to option (B), which is clearly accurate.

questions.stem: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy most commonly occurs during which stage of pregnancy?
questions.explanation: 3rd trimester Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy (AFLP) is a rare but life-threatening obstetric emergency characterized by microvesicular fatty infiltration of hepatocytes, leading to acute liver failure. The onset of the disease is almost exclusively in the third trimester of pregnancy, with the majority of cases presenting between 30 and 38 weeks of gestation. It can also occur in the immediate postpartum period, but the classic presentation is late in pregnancy. The symptoms are often non-specific initially, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and malaise, but can rapidly progress to jaundice, hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and multi-organ failure. The exact cause is unknown but is linked to a genetic defect in fetal fatty acid oxidation. Prompt recognition and immediate delivery of the fetus, along with intensive supportive care for the mother, are crucial for survival.

questions.stem: At which stage is fetoplacental circulation established?
questions.explanation: 20 to 22 days The development of the circulatory system between the fetus and the placenta is a critical early event in embryogenesis. The process begins with the formation of blood islands in the mesoderm of the yolk sac, connecting stalk, and chorion around day 17. These blood islands coalesce to form primitive blood vessels. By the end of the third week of gestation, these fetal vessels have developed and connected with the vessels forming in the chorionic villi of the placenta. At the same time, the primitive heart tube has formed and begins to beat and pump blood around day 21 or 22. This establishes a rudimentary but functional fetoplacental circulation, allowing for the exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products between the maternal and fetal bloodstreams within the placenta. Therefore, the period of 20 to 22 days post-conception is the correct timeframe for the initial establishment of this vital circulatory loop.

questions.stem: A patient sustained a road traffic accident 2 years ago and now presents with pain and swelling at the same site. An X-ray reveals the findings shown. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic osteomyelitis The patient's history of a previous trauma (RTA), which likely caused an open fracture, combined with the current presentation of pain and swelling and the classic X-ray findings, is diagnostic of chronic osteomyelitis. Chronic osteomyelitis is a long-standing infection of the bone. The radiological features are pathognomonic. The X-ray shows a sequestrum, which is a piece of dead, necrotic bone that has become separated from the living bone during the inflammatory process. This sequestrum acts as a nidus for persistent infection. The body attempts to wall off the infection by forming new bone around it; this shell of new bone is called the involucrum. The lucent area surrounding the sequestrum represents the abscess cavity. This triad of sequestrum, involucrum, and bone destruction is the hallmark of chronic osteomyelitis. Malignant tumors like osteosarcoma or Ewing's sarcoma would typically show more aggressive bone destruction and a soft tissue mass.

questions.stem: What is the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) of iodine during lactation, in micrograms?
questions.explanation: 250 µg Iodine is an essential micronutrient required for the synthesis of thyroid hormones, which are critical for regulating metabolism and for the normal growth and development of the brain and nervous system. The requirement for iodine increases significantly during pregnancy and lactation to meet the needs of both the mother and the developing fetus or newborn. The Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for iodine in non-pregnant adult women is 150 µg/day. During pregnancy, this increases to 220 µg/day to support fetal neurodevelopment. The requirement is highest during lactation, as a significant amount of iodine is secreted into breast milk to provide for the infant's needs. The World Health Organization (WHO) and other health bodies recommend an iodine intake of 250 µg/day for lactating women. This ensures that the mother remains euthyroid while also providing sufficient iodine to the breastfed infant for their own thyroid hormone production and brain development.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a cause of secondary postpartum hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: Placenta previa Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is classified as primary or secondary. Primary PPH occurs within the first 24 hours after delivery. Secondary PPH is defined as excessive vaginal bleeding that occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks postpartum. The most common cause of secondary PPH is subinvolution of the placental site, which is often associated with retained placental fragments or membranes. The second most common cause is uterine infection, such as endometritis. Other less common causes include the breakdown of uterine incision scars, placental site polyps, or underlying congenital bleeding disorders. Placenta previa, a condition where the placenta implants over or near the cervical os, is a major cause of antepartum hemorrhage (bleeding before delivery) and is a significant risk factor for primary PPH due to poor uterine contractility at the lower segment after placental separation. It is not a direct cause of secondary PPH.

questions.stem: During which gestational period is the quadruple test optimally performed?
questions.explanation: 15-20 weeks The quadruple screen, or quad test, is a maternal blood screening test performed during the second trimester of pregnancy to assess the risk of certain chromosomal abnormalities and neural tube defects in the fetus. The test measures the levels of four specific substances in the mother's blood : alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), unconjugated estriol (uE3), and inhibin A. The results of these four markers, combined with the mother's age and other factors, are used to calculate a risk score for Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18), and open neural tube defects (like spina bifida). The optimal time window for performing the quadruple test to ensure the most accurate results is between 15 and 20 weeks of gestation. The ideal time within this window is often cited as 16 to 18 weeks. Performing the test outside this timeframe can lead to less reliable results.

questions.stem: In congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which method best demonstrates the abdominal mass?
questions.explanation: In palpation over the epigastrium In congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS), the classical clinical finding is a palpable “olive-shaped” mass. This mass represents the hypertrophied pylorus. The mass is best felt in the epigastric region, slightly to the right of the midline. It is typically palpated by gently examining the upper abdomen when the infant is calm and relaxed. Sometimes, it is easier to feel after the baby has vomited, when the stomach is empty. Although the pyloric mass lies anatomically toward the right side, it is most accurately described as being palpable in the epigastrium, not the left hypochondrium or right iliac fossa. Feeding may make the pyloric peristaltic waves more visible, but palpation over the epigastrium remains the best method to demonstrate the mass. Therefore, the correct answer is (A) In palpation over the epigastrium.

questions.stem: Determine the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score for a 25-year-old head-injury patient who is confused, opens eyes to pain, and localizes pain.
questions.explanation: 11 The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a neurological scale used to assess a person's level of consciousness after a brain injury. It is scored out of 15 and has three components : Eye Opening, Verbal Response, and Motor Response. 1. Eye Opening (E) : The patient opens their eyes in response to pain. This corresponds to a score of 2. (Spontaneous=4, To speech=3, To pain=2, None=1). 2. Verbal Response (V) : The patient is confused. This means they are able to speak in sentences but are disoriented. This corresponds to a score of 4. (Oriented=5, Confused=4, Inappropriate words=3, Incomprehensible sounds=2, None=1). 3. Motor Response (M) : The patient localizes pain. This means they make a purposeful movement towards a painful stimulus. This corresponds to a score of 5. (Obeys commands=6, Localizes pain=5, Withdraws from pain=4, Flexion to pain=3, Extension to pain=2, None=1). The total GCS score is the sum of the scores from the three components : Total GCS = E + V + M = 2 + 4 + 5 = 11.

questions.stem: The RET proto-oncogene is linked to the development of which condition?
questions.explanation: Medullary carcinoma thyroid The RET proto-oncogene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase that is crucial for the normal development of several cell types, including neuroendocrine cells. Germline activating mutations in the RET proto-oncogene are the underlying genetic cause of the Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2) syndromes, which include MEN 2A, MEN 2B, and Familial Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (FMTC). The hallmark and most common feature of all these syndromes is the development of Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC), a cancer of the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid. Nearly 100% of individuals with a germline RET mutation will develop MTC. Somatic (non-inherited) RET mutations are also found in a significant proportion of sporadic MTC cases. Therefore, the association between RET mutations and medullary thyroid cancer is one of the strongest and most well-established in oncology. The other tumors listed are not primarily associated with RET mutations.

questions.stem: Identify the organism related to the blood smear image.
questions.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum The image shows a peripheral blood smear with red blood cells infected by a malaria parasite. The specific features are diagnostic for Plasmodium falciparum. The key identifying characteristics of P. falciparum on a thin smear are : Multiple infections of a single red blood cell : It is common to see two or more small ring-form trophozoites within one RBC. Delicate, fine rings : The rings have a very thin cytoplasm. Appliqué or accole forms : The rings appear plastered against the edge of the red blood cell membrane. Double chromatin dots : Some rings may have two chromatin dots, giving them a headphones appearance. Absence of older stages : In falciparum malaria, typically only the early ring forms and gametocytes are seen in the peripheral blood, as the older trophozoites and schizonts are sequestered in the deep microvasculature. These features are all characteristic of P. falciparum, the most virulent species of human malaria parasite.

questions.stem: What is the minimum aneurysm size in an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) that warrants surgical intervention?
questions.explanation: 5.5 cm An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a localized dilation of the abdominal aorta. The primary risk associated with an AAA is rupture, which is a catastrophic event with a very high mortality rate. The risk of rupture is directly proportional to the maximum diameter of the aneurysm. For smaller aneurysms, the risk of rupture is low, and the risks of surgical repair outweigh the benefits. These patients are managed with surveillance (e.g., regular ultrasound monitoring). However, as the aneurysm grows, the rupture risk increases exponentially. Based on large clinical trials, the threshold at which the risk of rupture begins to exceed the risk of elective repair is an aneurysm diameter of 5.5 cm for men. Therefore, elective surgical repair (either open surgery or endovascular aneurysm repair - EVAR) is generally recommended for asymptomatic patients once the AAA reaches a diameter of 5.5 cm. The threshold may be slightly lower (e.g., 5.0 cm) for women.

questions.stem: In the Maastricht classification system for donation after cardiac death (DCD), which condition corresponds to Category III?
questions.explanation: Awaiting cardiac arrest The Maastricht classification categorizes donors after circulatory (cardiac) death (DCD) based on the circumstances of death. The categories are: 1. Category I – Brought in dead 2. Category II – Unsuccessful resuscitation 3. Category III – Awaiting cardiac arrest (controlled DCD) 4. Category IV – Cardiac arrest in a brain-dead donor 5. Later, Category V was added in some updates. Category III refers to patients in whom life-sustaining treatment is withdrawn in a controlled hospital setting due to poor prognosis, and cardiac arrest is anticipated. Organ retrieval occurs after circulatory death is confirmed. This is known as controlled DCD. Therefore, the correct answer is (A) Awaiting cardiac arrest.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with shock, and imaging reveals ascites, bowel wall thickening, and poor enhancement of a strangulated bowel segment confirmed as gangrenous during surgery. Which statement regarding intestinal anastomosis is correct?

options.text: It should be performed in continuous layers to save time
It should be performed using catgut
It should be done using single-layer seromuscular Lembert sutures
It should be done in a single layer including the submucosa

questions.explanation: It should be done using single-layer seromuscular Lembert sutures In cases of gangrenous bowel following strangulation, especially in a child who has presented with shock, the bowel is edematous and inflamed. In such situations, a single-layer seromuscular (extramucosal) Lembert anastomosis is preferred in many surgical teachings. This technique: 1. Avoids penetrating the mucosa 2. Reduces the risk of contamination 3. Preserves blood supply 4. Causes less tissue trauma 5. Is quicker and technically safer in compromised bowel The Lembert sutures invert the bowel edges and approximate the serosa, promoting good healing due to the strong serosal adhesion response. Although the submucosa provides tensile strength, in edematous or inflamed bowel, extramucosal single-layer anastomosis is commonly recommended in pediatric and emergency surgery settings. Therefore, as per exam-based surgical principles, the correct answer is : (C) It should be done using single-layer seromuscular Lembert sutures.

questions.stem: Which of the following graft materials is considered the most suitable choice for a femoropopliteal bypass procedure?
questions.explanation: Reversed saphenous vein For a femoropopliteal bypass procedure, the reversed great saphenous vein is considered the best and most suitable graft material, especially for below-knee bypass. Autologous vein grafts have several advantages: 1. Superior long-term patency rates 2. Better resistance to infection 3. Improved limb salvage outcomes 4. Better compliance matching with native arteries In the reversed saphenous vein technique, the vein is harvested and reversed so that the venous valves do not obstruct arterial flow. Synthetic grafts such as Dacron and PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene) are alternatives when the saphenous vein is unavailable. However, they have lower long-term patency rates, particularly in below-knee bypasses, and carry a higher risk of infection compared to autologous vein grafts. Therefore, whenever available and suitable, the reversed saphenous vein is the graft of choice for femoropopliteal bypass. Hence, the correct answer is (B) Reversed saphenous vein. PEDIATRICS

questions.stem: Which fontanelle is the last to close?
questions.explanation: Anterior (frontal) Fontanelles are the soft, membranous gaps between the cranial bones in an infant's skull, which allow for the growth of the brain and the molding of the head during birth. There are six fontanelles at birth. The posterior fontanelle is triangular and typically closes early, by about 2 to 3 months of age. The anterolateral (sphenoidal) fontanelles on the sides of the skull usually close by about 6 months of age. The posterolateral (mastoid) fontanelles close later, between 6 and 18 months. The anterior fontanelle is the largest, diamond-shaped fontanelle, commonly known as the soft spot. It is the last one to close, with the process of ossification typically being completed between 18 and 24 months of age. Its persistence beyond this age may indicate an underlying medical condition. Because it remains open for the longest period, the anterior fontanelle is a crucial landmark for clinical assessment in infants. 221. Which type of retractor is shown in the image? NODIA

questions.stem: Which chromosomal pattern is most commonly associated with true hermaphroditism?
questions.explanation: 46 XX Ovotestis True hermaphroditism, now more appropriately termed ovotesticular disorder of sex development (DSD), is a rare condition in which an individual has both ovarian and testicular tissue. This may be present as an ovotestis (a single gonad containing both ovarian and testicular tissue) or as one ovary and one testis. The most common karyotype seen in individuals with ovotesticular DSD is 46,XX. Despite having a typical female chromosomal pattern, these individuals develop both types of gonadal tissue. The presence of testicular tissue may be due to translocation of the SRY gene or other genetic variations influencing sex differentiation. Option (A), 45,XO, is associated with Turner syndrome and streak gonads. Option (C), 47,XXY, is associated with Klinefelter syndrome. Option (D), 47,XX, is not a recognized standard karyotype. Therefore, the karyotype most commonly linked with true hermaphroditism is 46,XX with ovotestis formation.

questions.stem: Identify the condition shown in the MRI scan image below.
questions.explanation: Dandy-Walker malformation The MRI image displays the classic neuroimaging triad of a Dandy-Walker malformation, a congenital brain malformation involving the cerebellum and the fourth ventricle. The characteristic features are : Cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle : The fourth ventricle is markedly enlarged and extends posteriorly. Agenesis or hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis : The vermis, which is the central part of the cerebellum, is either completely absent or significantly underdeveloped. The enlarged fourth ventricle can be seen communicating with the cisterna magna through the defect in the vermis. Enlargement of the posterior fossa with upward displacement of the tentorium cerebelli and transverse sinuses.This combination of findings is pathognomonic for Dandy-Walker malformation. A mega cisterna magna is an enlargement of the cisterna magna but with an intact cerebellar vermis and fourth ventricle. Isolated cerebellar vermis hypoplasia can occur without the cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle.

questions.stem: Paget's disease is associated with which other cancer?
questions.explanation: Vulva Paget’s disease in gynecology usually refers to extramammary Paget’s disease, a rare intraepithelial adenocarcinoma that most commonly affects the vulvar region. It is strongly associated with malignancy of the vulva and may either arise primarily in the vulvar skin or be associated with an underlying adenocarcinoma of apocrine gland origin. Clinically, vulvar Paget’s disease presents with chronic itching, redness, eczematous changes, or ulcerated lesions of the vulva. Because its appearance can mimic dermatitis or eczema, diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy showing characteristic Paget cells within the epidermis. Although Paget’s disease is classically associated with breast carcinoma in the mammary form, in the genital tract it is most commonly linked with vulvar malignancy. It is not typically associated with cancers of the vagina, cervix, or uterus. Therefore, Paget’s disease in gynecology is most commonly associated with carcinoma of the vulva.

questions.stem: What are the contraceptive effects of progesterone-only pills?

options.text: Thin the lining of the uterus

questions.explanation: All of the above Progesterone-only pills (also known as mini-pills) prevent pregnancy through multiple mechanisms. First, they can suppress ovulation. Although ovulation suppression is not as consistent as with combined oral contraceptive pills, many users experience inhibition of follicular development and ovulation, especially with continuous and timely use. Second, progesterone causes thinning of the endometrial lining. A thinner endometrium becomes less suitable for implantation of a fertilized ovum, thereby reducing the likelihood of pregnancy. Third, progesterone significantly thickens cervical mucus. This thickened mucus forms a barrier that impedes sperm penetration into the uterine cavity, making fertilization less likely. This effect occurs consistently and is one of the primary mechanisms of action. Because progesterone-only pills suppress ovulation (to varying degrees), thin the uterine lining, and thicken cervical mucus, all listed options are correct. Therefore, the best answer is (D) All of the above.

questions.stem: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is most commonly associated with which type of pseudohermaphroditism?
questions.explanation: Female pseudohermaphroditism Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a group of inherited disorders caused by enzyme deficiencies in cortisol synthesis, most commonly 21-hydroxylase deficiency. This enzyme defect leads to decreased cortisol production and a compensatory increase in adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), resulting in adrenal hyperplasia and excess androgen production. In genetic females (46,XX), the excess androgens cause varying degrees of virilization of the external genitalia, such as clitoromegaly and labioscrotal fusion, while the internal reproductive organs (uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries) remain female. This condition is therefore termed female pseudohermaphroditism, meaning the chromosomal and gonadal sex is female, but the external genitalia are masculinized. Male pseudohermaphroditism involves undervirilization in 46,XY individuals and is not typically caused by CAH. The other options are not standard classifications. Thus, CAH is classically associated with female pseudohermaphroditism.

questions.stem: Which ligament is primarily responsible for maintaining the anteverted position of the uterus?
questions.explanation: Round ligament The uterus normally lies in an anteverted and anteflexed position, meaning it tilts forward over the urinary bladder. The maintenance of this forward tilt (anteversion) is mainly supported by the round ligaments of the uterus. The round ligaments arise from the uterine horns, pass laterally within the broad ligament, traverse the inguinal canal, and insert into the labia majora. Their forward pull helps keep the uterus tilted anteriorly. The cardinal (transverse cervical) ligaments provide lateral support to the cervix and help prevent uterine prolapse. The uterosacral ligaments support the uterus posteriorly and maintain its position within the pelvis. The pubocervical ligaments provide anterior support to the cervix and bladder. Although these ligaments contribute to overall uterine support, the round ligaments specifically help maintain anteversion. Therefore, the ligament responsible for maintaining the anteverted position of the uterus is the round ligament.

questions.stem: Chronic or long-standing pelvic inflammatory disease can result in which of the following complications?
questions.explanation: Pyometra Long-standing pelvic inflammation, particularly chronic pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), can cause persistent infection and damage to the upper genital tract. Over time, chronic inflammation may lead to scarring, obstruction of the cervical canal, and impaired drainage of uterine secretions. When the outflow of uterine contents is blocked, pus may accumulate within the uterine cavity, resulting in a condition known as pyometra. Pyometra is characterized by the collection of purulent material inside the uterus. It may present with lower abdominal pain, foul-smelling discharge, fever, or may sometimes be asymptomatic in elderly women. It is more commonly seen in postmenopausal women or in cases where cervical stenosis is present. Uterine polyps and cystic endometrial hyperplasia are usually related to hormonal imbalance rather than infection. Pseudopregnancy is a psychological condition and is not caused by pelvic inflammation. Therefore, chronic pelvic inflammation may lead to pyometra. DERMATOLOGY 267.
