questions.stem: A child presents with the rash shown in the image and has a family history of asthma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Atopic dermatitis Although no image of the rash is provided, the clinical information strongly points to a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis, also commonly known as eczema. The key clue is the patient's family history of asthma. Atopic dermatitis is part of the atopic triad, which also includes allergic rhinitis (hay fever) and asthma. These conditions are linked by a shared genetic predisposition to developing hypersensitivity reactions (atopy). It is very common for a child with atopic dermatitis to have a personal or family history of one of the other atopic conditions. Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, pruritic (itchy) inflammatory skin disease. The rash typically presents as erythematous papules and plaques, which may have scaling, excoriations, and lichenification from scratching. The distribution of the rash varies with age (face and extensors in infants, flexural areas in children). Seborrheic dermatitis has a different distribution (scalp, face). Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed-type hypersensitivity to a specific allergen.

questions.stem: What constitutes the Malpigiian layer?
questions.explanation: Stratum Spinosum and Stratum Basde The Malpighian layer, also known as the germinative layer of the epidermis, refers to the actively dividing portion of the epidermis responsible for regeneration of the skin. It is composed of two layers: the stratum basale (basal layer) and the stratum spinosum (prickle cell layer). The stratum basale is the deepest layer of the epidermis. It consists of a single row of cuboidal or columnar cells that continuously undergo mitosis to produce new keratinocytes. These newly formed cells gradually move upward into the stratum spinosum. The stratum spinosum lies just above the basal layer and contains several layers of polygonal cells connected by desmosomes, giving them a spiny appearance under the microscope. These cells provide strength and flexibility to the skin. The stratum granulosum and stratum lucidum are more superficial layers and are not part of the Malpighian layer. Thus, the Malpighian layer consists of the stratum basale and stratum spinosum.

questions.stem: The spot radiograph from a double-contrast esophagram shown below represents which condition?
questions.explanation: Feline esophagus The image from the barium esophagram shows multiple, thin, symmetric, transverse folds that are closely spaced, creating a ringed or corrugated appearance in the distal esophagus. This radiological finding is known as feline esophagus because of its resemblance to the appearance of a cat's esophagus, which has prominent circumferential muscle folds. In humans, this finding is most commonly associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). It is thought to represent the transient contraction of the muscularis mucosae in response to refluxed gastric acid. While it is a non-specific finding, its presence is a strong indicator of underlying esophagitis or esophageal dysmotility related to GERD. It can also be seen, though less commonly, in eosinophilic esophagitis, which also presents with esophageal rings. Esophageal stenosis would show a fixed narrowing, and atresia is a congenital discontinuation of the esophagus. ANAESTHESIA

questions.stem: Murphy's eye is seen in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Endotracheal tube The Murphy's eye is a specific design feature of most modern endotracheal tubes (ETTs). It is a small, oval-shaped hole located on the side of the ETT, opposite the beveled tip. The primary purpose of the Murphy's eye is to serve as a safety feature that ensures ventilation can continue even if the main opening at the beveled tip of the tube becomes occluded. For example, if the tip of the ETT rests against the tracheal wall or becomes blocked by mucus, respiratory gases can still flow into and out of the lungs through the Murphy's eye. This provides an alternative pathway for air movement and reduces the risk of complete airway obstruction. Laryngoscopes are used for intubation, and an LMA is a supraglottic airway device; neither has a Murphy's eye.

questions.stem: Modified Mallampati grading is used in the assessment of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Difficult intubation The Modified Mallampati classification is a simple, non-invasive bedside test used by anesthesiologists and other healthcare providers as part of the preoperative airway assessment. Its purpose is to predict the ease of direct laryngoscopy and tracheal intubation. The test involves assessing the visibility of specific anatomical structures in the pharynx. The patient is asked to sit upright, open their mouth as wide as possible, and protrude their tongue without phonating. The view is then graded from Class I (full visibility of the soft palate, fauces, uvula, and pillars) to Class IV (only the hard palate is visible). A higher Mallampati score (Class III or IV) correlates with a more restricted view of the glottis during laryngoscopy and a higher likelihood of encountering a difficult intubation. It is one of several tools used to anticipate and prepare for potential airway management challenges.

questions.stem: Which nerve is assessed to determine the adequacy of anaesthesia?
questions.explanation: Ulnar Nerve This question refers to the monitoring of neuromuscular blockade during general anesthesia. When neuromuscular blocking agents (muscle relaxants) are used, a peripheral nerve stimulator is employed to assess the depth of the block. The stimulator delivers a small electrical current to a peripheral nerve, and the resulting muscle contraction (twitch) is observed or measured. The most common site for this monitoring is the ulnar nerve at the wrist or elbow. Stimulation of the ulnar nerve causes contraction of the adductor pollicis muscle, which results in adduction (movement towards the palm) of the thumb. The response of the adductor pollicis to different patterns of stimulation (e.g., train-of-four) allows the anesthesiologist to precisely titrate the dose of muscle relaxant and to determine when the block has sufficiently worn off for the patient to breathe safely on their own.

questions.stem: Most effective circuit in spontaneous anaesthesia is-
questions.explanation: Mapleson A The Mapleson breathing circuits are a series of breathing systems used in anesthesia. Their efficiency at preventing rebreathing of exhaled carbon dioxide depends on the fresh gas flow (FGF) rate and whether the patient is breathing spontaneously or being ventilated. For a patient who is breathing spontaneously, the Mapleson A circuit (also known as the Magill circuit) is by far the most efficient. In this circuit, during the expiratory pause, fresh gas fills the breathing tube, pushing the alveolar gas (which is high in CO2) out through the expiratory valve. On the next inspiration, the patient breathes in the fresh gas. This design allows for the prevention of re breathing with a fresh gas flow rate that is equal to the patient's alveolar ventilation (approximately 70 mL/kg/min), making it highly efficient. In contrast, the Mapleson A circuit is the least efficient for controlled ventilation, where the Mapleson D circuit is preferred.

questions.stem: How do curare-like (Curanium) muscle relaxant drugs exert their effect?

options.text: Act competitively on Ach receptors blocking post-synaptically
Repetitive stimulation of Ach receptors on the muscle endplate
Inhibiting the calcium channel on presynaptic membrane

questions.explanation: Act competitively on Ach receptors blocking post-synaptically The -curonium and -curium drugs (e.g., rocuronium, vecuronium, atracurium) are non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents. They are derivatives or analogues of d-tubocurarine, the active component of curare. Their mechanism of action is to act as competitive antagonists at the nicotinic acetylcholine (ACh) receptors on the motor endplate of the neuromuscular junction. By binding to these postsynaptic ACh receptors, they physically block acetylcholine from binding. This prevents the endplate from depolarizing, which in turn prevents the initiation of an action potential in the muscle fiber and results in flaccid muscle paralysis. This blockade can be overcome by increasing the concentration of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, which is the principle behind using acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (like neostigmine) for reversal. In contrast, depolarizing agents like succinylcholine (A) act as agonists, causing persistent depolarization. NODIA

questions.stem: During strabismus (squint) surgery, the anesthesiologist notices a sudden fall in the patient’s blood pressure to 40 mmHg. What should be the immediate management?

options.text: Ask the surgeon to stop the surgery

questions.explanation: Ask the surgeon to stop the surgery Strabismus surgery can trigger the oculocardiac reflex, a trigemino-vagal reflex that occurs due to traction on the extraocular muscles. This reflex may cause sudden bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmias, or even cardiac arrest. A sudden fall in blood pressure to 40 mmHg is a serious event and requires immediate intervention. The first and most important step is to stop the surgical stimulus. Asking the surgeon to immediately release traction on the eye muscles often results in rapid resolution of the reflex and stabilization of vital signs. After stopping the stimulus, the anesthesiologist can assess and manage the patient further. If bradycardia persists, atropine may be administered. However, the priority is removal of the triggering factor. Therefore, the best immediate management is to ask the surgeon to stop the surgery. RADIOLOGY

questions.stem: Which contrast dye is preferred for diagnosing esophageal perforation?
questions.explanation: lohexol In suspected esophageal perforation, a water-soluble contrast agent is used initially to confirm the diagnosis. Iohexol is a non-ionic, water-soluble iodinated contrast medium commonly used for this purpose. It is preferred because if leakage occurs into the mediastinum or pleural cavity, it causes much less inflammatory reaction compared to barium. Barium sulphate, although excellent for outlining mucosal detail, is contraindicated in suspected perforation because extravasated barium can cause severe mediastinitis and fibrosis if it leaks outside the esophagus. Gadolinium is used primarily as a contrast agent in MRI studies and is not used for evaluating esophageal perforation. Lipiodol is an oil-based contrast medium and is not routinely used for this indication. Therefore, in cases of suspected esophageal perforation, a water-soluble contrast such as iohexol is the dye of choice.

questions.stem: In which type of radiation is the Bragg peak effect most prominent?
questions.explanation: Proton The Bragg peak is a characteristic physical phenomenon describing the energy loss of heavy charged particles as they travel through matter. Unlike photons (X-rays) or electrons, which deposit their energy gradually from the surface inwards, a heavy charged particle like a proton travels through tissue and deposits a relatively small amount of energy along its initial path. As the particle slows down, its rate of energy loss increases dramatically, reaching a sharp maximum at a specific depth. This sharp peak in energy deposition is the Bragg peak. Beyond this peak, the energy deposition falls off to almost zero very rapidly. This physical property is exploited in proton beam therapy for cancer. It allows for the delivery of a very high, conformal dose of radiation precisely to the tumor volume, while sparing the healthy tissues located both in front of and, most importantly, behind the tumor.

questions.stem: The salt and pepper appearance of the skull is characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation: Hyperparathyroidism The salt-and-pepper appearance of the skull on a lateral radiograph is a classic sign of bone disease caused by hyperparathyroidism, particularly primary hyperparathyroidism. Excess parathyroid hormone (PTH) leads to increased osteoclastic activity and bone resorption. In the skull, this process results in the loss of trabeculae in the diploic space (the spongy bone between the inner and outer tables of the calvarium). This resorption creates numerous tiny, punctate lucencies (the pepper) interspersed with areas of more normal or slightly sclerotic bone (the salt). This fine, granular pattern of demineralization is highly characteristic. In severe, long-standing cases, it can be associated with other skeletal findings of hyperparathyroidism, such as subperiosteal bone resorption in the hands and the presence of brown tumors. Multiple myeloma typically causes larger, well-defined, punched-out lytic lesions, not a fine granular pattern.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not used as an imaging technique for diagnosing uterine anomalies?
questions.explanation: CT-guided HSG The evaluation of congenital uterine anomalies requires imaging techniques that can clearly delineate both the internal (endometrial cavity) and external (serosal) contour of the uterus. Ultrasound (USG), particularly 3D ultrasound, is an excellent, non-invasive initial tool. Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is a fluoroscopic procedure that uses contrast dye to outline the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes, effectively showing the internal contour but not the external fundal shape. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is considered the gold standard as it provides superior soft tissue contrast and multiplanar imaging, allowing for a detailed and accurate classification of the anomaly by showing both internal and external uterine morphology without radiation exposure. MRI can be used alongside HSG concepts. However, Computed Tomography (CT) provides poor soft tissue resolution of the uterine zonal anatomy and involves significant ionizing radiation exposure, making it unsuitable and not a standard modality for the primary diagnosis of congenital uterine anomalies. A CT-guided HSG is not a recognized or utilized procedure for this purpose.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not correct?

options.text: Some hematomas can be managed conservatively

questions.explanation: MRI needed to assess hemorrhage. In acute head injury, the investigation of choice to assess intracranial hemorrhage is a non-contrast CT scan, not MRI. CT scan is rapid, widely available, and highly sensitive for detecting acute bleeding, skull fractures, and mass effect. MRI is more useful for detecting subtle brain injuries such as diffuse axonal injury, small contusions, or subacute and chronic lesions, but it is not the first-line imaging modality in emergency settings. 1. Option (B) is correct because the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is an important clinical tool used to assess the severity of head injury and helps predict prognosis. 2. Option (C) is also correct, as some small hematomas without significant mass effect or neurological deterioration can be managed conservatively with close monitoring. Therefore, the incorrect statement is that MRI is needed to assess hemorrhage.

questions.stem: Which of the following tumors is not typically found in the anterior mediastinum?
questions.explanation: Neurogenic tumor The mediastinum is anatomically divided into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments. The anterior mediastinum commonly contains structures such as the thymus, lymph nodes, fat, and ectopic thyroid tissue. Therefore, tumors typically seen in the anterior mediastinum include: 1. Thymoma (arising from the thymus) 2. Lymphoma 3. Thyroid tumors (especially substernal or retrosternal goiter) These are often remembered as part of the classic “4 Ts” of anterior mediastinal masses: Thymoma, Thyroid tumor, Teratoma, and “Terrible” lymphoma. In contrast, neurogenic tumors—such as schwannomas and neurofibromas—arise from nerve sheaths and are most commonly located in the posterior mediastinum, where the sympathetic chain and intercostal nerves are situated. Therefore, neurogenic tumors are not typically found in the anterior mediastinum, making option (D) the correct answer.

questions.stem: What is the treatment of choice for radiation in Chordoma?
questions.explanation: Protons Chordoma is a rare, slow-growing malignant tumor that arises from remnants of the notochord. It most commonly occurs in the sacrum, clivus, or along the spine. Because chordomas are located near critical structures such as the brainstem, spinal cord, and major nerves, precise radiation delivery is essential. Proton beam therapy is considered the treatment of choice for radiation in chordoma. Proton therapy has a unique physical property known as the Bragg peak, which allows it to deposit the majority of its energy directly within the tumor while minimizing radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissues. This is especially important for chordomas, which often require high radiation doses for effective control. Electrons and gamma radiation do not provide the same level of dose precision. Although 3D-CRT improves targeting compared to conventional techniques, proton therapy offers superior dose distribution and reduced collateral damage. Therefore, proton beam therapy is the preferred radiation modality for chordoma. PSYCHIATRY

questions.stem: Minimal brain dysfunction (MBD) syndrome is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: ADHD [Attention Deficit H]ryeractivity Disorder) Minimal brain dysfunction (MBD) is an older term that was historically used to describe children who exhibited hyperactivity, impulsivity, poor attention span, and learning difficulties without obvious structural brain abnormalities. Over time, the term fell out of use and was replaced by more specific diagnostic categories. The condition most closely associated with what was previously called minimal brain dysfunction is Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). ADHD is characterized by persistent patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that interfere with functioning or development. It is a neurodevelopmental disorder typically diagnosed in childhood and may continue into adolescence and adulthood. Dyslexia is a specific learning disorder affecting reading skills, not equivalent to MBD. Mental subnormality (intellectual disability) involves significantly impaired intellectual functioning. Down syndrome is a chromosomal disorder (Trisomy 21) and is unrelated to MBD. Thus, minimal brain dysfunction is most closely associated with ADHD.

questions.stem: The semen squeeze technique is used to treat which condition?
questions.explanation: Premature ejaculation The squeeze technique, developed by Masters and Johnson, is a behavioral therapy method specifically designed for the treatment of premature ejaculation. The technique involves the man or his partner stimulating the penis until he feels he is about to ejaculate. At that point, the partner firmly squeezes the head of the penis (the glans), where the coronal ridge meets the shaft, for several seconds. This squeeze diminishes the ejaculatory urge. After a brief pause, stimulation is resumed, and the process is repeated several times before ejaculation is finally allowed to occur. The goal of this technique is to help the man gain better awareness of the sensations leading up to orgasm and to develop voluntary control over the ejaculatory reflex. It teaches the man to recognize and tolerate higher levels of sexual arousal without ejaculating immediately. This method is a cornerstone of sex therapy for premature ejaculation but is not used for erectile dysfunction or retrograde ejaculation.

questions.stem: A man two months post–road traffic accident reports vivid dreams about the event, experiences flashbacks when visiting the crash site, and avoids the location out of fear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) The patient's symptoms are the classic triad for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), occurring after a significant traumatic event (the RTA). The core symptom clusters of PTSD are all present : Re-experiencing : The patient has recurrent, intrusive memories of the trauma in the form of vivid dreams (nightmares) and dissociative reactions (flashbacks) when triggered by reminders of the event (visiting the site). Avoidance : He actively avoids external reminders (the accident site) that arouse distressing memories of the trauma. Negative alterations in cognition and mood : Although not fully detailed, the fear suggests this component. Marked alterations in arousal and reactivity : While not explicitly mentioned, this is the fourth criterion. The symptoms have persisted for two months, which is longer than the one-month duration required for a PTSD diagnosis. Adjustment disorder involves distress in response to a stressor but does not typically include re-experiencing and flashbacks. Anxiety disorder is a broader category, but the specific symptom pattern here points directly to PTSD. 287. questions.stem: All of the following are components of Freud’s theory of dreams except:
questions.explanation: Correlation In his seminal work The Interpretation of Dreams, Sigmund Freud proposed that dreams are a form of wish-fulfillment, representing the disguised expression of repressed unconscious thoughts and desires. He described the process by which the hidden, true meaning of a dream (the latent content) is transformed into the story the dreamer remembers (the manifest content). This transformation process is called dream work and involves several mechanisms. These mechanisms include : 1. Condensation : Multiple dream thoughts or elements are combined and represented by a single image or idea in the manifest dream. 2. Displacement : The emotional significance of a dream object or person is separated from its real object and attached to an entirely different one that is less threatening. 3. Symbolization (or Representation) : Abstract thoughts and feelings are converted into concrete visual images or symbols. Correlation is a statistical term describing a relationship between variables and is not a concept used by Freud to describe the mechanisms of dream work.

questions.stem: What is the term for the expression and release of previously repressed emotions?
questions.explanation: Abreaction Abreaction, also known as catharsis, is a psychoanalytic term used to describe the process of reliving a past, traumatic emotional experience and expressing the intense, repressed emotions associated with it. Freud and Breuer initially developed this concept, believing that neurotic symptoms were caused by strangulated affect—emotions that were not adequately expressed at the ti me of a traumatic event. The therapeutic process involved bringing the memory of the trauma back to conscious awareness, allowing the patient to experience and discharge these pent-up emotions (the abreaction), which was believed to lead to the alleviation of the symptoms. This emotional release and expression is the core of abreaction. Regression is a defense mechanism involving a return to an earlier stage of development. Dissociation is a defense mechanism involving a disconnection between thoughts, feelings, memories, and sense of identity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not classified as a habit disorder?
questions.explanation: Temper tantrum Habit disorders are characterized by repetitive, stereotyped behaviors that an individual has difficulty controlling. These are often body-focused repetitive behaviors. Nail-biting (onychophagia), thumb sucking, and hair-pulling (trichotillomania) are classic examples of habit disorders. Tics, which are sudden, rapid, recurrent, nonrhythmic motor movements or vocalizations (as seen in Tourette's syndrome), are also classified under a related category of motor disorders. In contrast, a temper tantrum is not a habit disorder but rather an intense, uncontrolled emotional outburst of anger and frustration. It is a behavioral issue, common in young children as a normal part of development, and is related to an inability to express needs or regulate strong emotions. It is a complex behavioral response to a specific trigger, not a repetitive, automatic habit in the same way as nail-biting or a tic.

questions.stem: What is the new term replacing mental retardation as per the American Association of Mental Retardation?
questions.explanation: Intellectual disability Over the past few decades, there has been a significant shift in the terminology used to describe conditions involving cognitive impairments, moving away from terms that are considered pejorative and stigmatizing. The term mental retardation was widely used for many years but has now been largely replaced. In 2007, the American Association on Mental Retardation (AAMR) officially changed its name to the American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (AAIDD). In line with this, and as reflected in major diagnostic manuals like the DSM-5 and ICD-11, the preferred and current term for this condition is Intellectual Disability. This term is considered more accurate and respectful. It is defined by significant limitations in both intellectual functioning (reasoning, learning, problem-solving) and adaptive behavior (everyday social and practical skills), with an onset during the developmental period. Feeble-mindedness and madness are archaic and offensive terms.

questions.stem: Identify the lesion shown in the image.
questions.explanation: Becker nevus The image displays the classic clinical features of a Becker nevus, also known as Becker's melanosis. This is a benign, acquired cutaneous hamartoma that typically appears during puberty, most commonly in males. It is characterized by the development of a large, unilateral, well-demarcated patch of hyperpigmentation with an irregular border. The most common locations are the shoulder, upper trunk, or scapular region. A key and highly characteristic feature that develops within the pigmented patch a few years after its appearance is hypertrichosis, which is the growth of coarse, dark hair. The combination of a large, unilateral, hyperpigmented macule with overlying hypertrichosis, developing around puberty in a male, is pathognomonic for a Becker nevus. A Spitz nevus is a benign melanocytic nevus. An epidermal nevus is a hamartoma of the epidermis, often appearing linear.

questions.stem: What is the modern medical term used to describe Down syndrome?
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 Down syndrome is currently described in medical terminology as Trisomy 21. This term reflects the underlying genetic cause of the condition—an extra copy of chromosome 21. Instead of the usual two copies, individuals with this condition have three copies of chromosome 21, leading to a total of 47 chromosomes. The term “Trisomy 21” is preferred in scientific and clinical settings because it accurately describes the chromosomal abnormality responsible for the condition. It avoids outdated and potentially stigmatizing language. Option (A), intellectual developmental disorder, refers to a broader category of cognitive impairment and is not specific to Down syndrome. Option (B), chromosomal mental retardation, uses outdated terminology and is not medically appropriate. Option (D), congenital psychiatric syndrome, is incorrect because Down syndrome is a genetic chromosomal condition, not a primary psychiatric disorder. Therefore, the current and correct medical term for Down syndrome is Trisomy 21.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with irrelevant speech, tremors, and sweating, having taken his last drink 3 days earlier. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Delirium tremens The patient's clinical presentation is the classic picture of Delirium Tremens (DTs), the most severe manifestation of alcohol withdrawal syndrome. DTs typically occur in individuals with a long history of heavy alcohol use after a period of cessation or significant reduction in intake. The onset is usually 48 to 96 hours (2 to 4 days) after the last drink, which fits the patient's time line of 3 days. The hallmark features of DTs are all present : Delirium : Characterized by confusion, disorientation, and altered consciousness, leading to irrelevant speech. Autonomic Hyperactivity : Manifesting as sweating (diaphoresis), tachycardia, hypertension, and fever. Agitation and Tremors : A severe, coarse tremor is characteristic. Visual or tactile hallucinations are also common. Korsakoff psychosis is a chronic memory disorder associated with thiamine deficiency. Post-acute withdrawal syndrome involves more subtle, prolonged symptoms. Delirium tremens is a medical emergency with significant mortality if untreated.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes delirium from dementia?
questions.explanation: sudden change The key difference between delirium and dementia lies in the onset and course of symptoms. Delirium is characterized by an acute and sudden onset of confusion, typically developing over hours to days. It often fluctuates throughout the day and is usually caused by an underlying medical condition such as infection, metabolic imbalance, drug toxicity, or withdrawal. In contrast, dementia is a chronic, progressive decline in cognitive function that develops gradually over months to years. It primarily affects memory, thinking, reasoning, and behavior. The progression is slow and usually irreversible. Although both conditions may present with confusion, difficulty in communication, and even hallucinations, these features can occur in either disorder. Therefore, they do not reliably distinguish one from the other. The most important differentiating feature is the sudden onset and fluctuating course seen in delirium, compared to the gradual progression seen in dementia. Hence, sudden change is the correct answer.

questions.stem: Broca's area is located in which of the following regions?
questions.explanation: Inferior frontal gyrus Broca’s area is located in the posterior part of the Inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant cerebral hemisphere, usually the left hemisphere. It corresponds mainly to Brodmann areas 44 and 45 and plays a crucial role in speech production and motor aspects of language. Damage to Broca’s area results in expressive (motor) aphasia, also known as Broca’s aphasia, where the patient has difficulty in producing speech but comprehension is relatively preserved. The speech is typically non-fluent, slow, and effortful. The superior temporal gyrus contains Wernicke’s area, which is responsible for language comprehension, while the angular gyrus is involved in reading and writing functions.
